Exam A1: Circuits

A1 Practice Paper 1

Problem 1 [A1-001] Equivalent circuits, series-parallel reduction and source transformations

A bench supply is modelled as an ideal 48 V source whose positive terminal is node a and whose negative terminal is the reference node g. A 12 Ω resistor R1 connects node a to node b. A 24 Ω resistor R2 connects node b to g. A 8 Ω resistor R3 connects node b to node c. Two 16 Ω resistors, R4 and R5, are each connected directly between node c and g, so they are in parallel with each other. No other elements are present and all values are constant. Treat the circuit as linear and in steady state. The source and R1 together form the branch that feeds node b.

  1. (a) Find the current delivered by the 48 V source. [6]
  2. (b) Replace the source and R1 by a Norton equivalent connected at node b. Using that equivalent, find the voltage at node b with respect to g. [7]
  3. (c) Find the power dissipated in R3. [7]
(a)

Reduce the network from the far end. R4 and R5 are both connected between c and g, so R4||R5 = (16×16)/(16+16) = 8 Ω. This 8 Ω is in series with R3 = 8 Ω between b and g, giving 16 Ω. That 16 Ω branch is in parallel with R2 = 24 Ω, so the resistance from b to g is (24×16)/(24+16) = 9.6 Ω. The source sees R1 in series with this, so Rtotal = 12 + 9.6 = 21.6 Ω. By Ohm's law, I = 48/21.6 = 2.222 A. The source current is the same as the current in R1 because there is only one path out of the source. Answer: 2.22 A.

Answer: 2.22 A

(b)

A series voltage source and resistor transform to a current source in parallel with the same resistor. The Norton current is In = 48/12 = 4 A, directed toward node b, in parallel with 12 Ω. Node b now has three conductances to g: the Norton resistor (1/12 S), R2 (1/24 S) and the 16 Ω series branch through R3 (1/16 S). Total conductance G = 0.08333 + 0.04167 + 0.06250 = 0.1875 S. The node voltage is Vb = In/G = 4/0.1875 = 21.33 V. Check by the first method: Vb = 48 − 12×2.222 = 21.33 V, which agrees. Answer: 21.3 V.

Answer: 21.3 V

(c)

The 16 Ω series branch (R3 plus the 8 Ω parallel pair) carries the current I3 = Vb/16 = 21.333/16 = 1.3333 A, since Vb is applied across it. This is the same current that flows in R3 because R3 is in series with the pair R4||R5. The power in R3 is P = I3² R3 = (1.3333)² × 8 = 1.7778 × 8 = 14.22 W. As a cross-check, the pair R4||R5 dissipates 1.7778 × 8 = 14.22 W as well, and the total in the 16 Ω branch is 28.4 W, which equals Vb²/16 = 455.1/16 = 28.4 W. Answer: 14.2 W.

Answer: 14.2 W

Problem 2 [A1-002] Nodal analysis of resistive circuits with dependent sources

A small-signal bias network has two non-reference nodes, 1 and 2, and a reference node g. An independent 2 A current source drives current from g into node 1. A 5 Ω resistor connects node 1 to g. A 10 Ω resistor connects node 1 to node 2. A 20 Ω resistor connects node 2 to g. A voltage-controlled current source drives a current of 0.2·V1 amperes from g into node 2, where V1 is the voltage of node 1 with respect to g (V1 in volts). There are no other connections. All quantities are DC and the circuit is linear. Use node g as the 0 V reference.

  1. (a) Write the two nodal equations and find the voltage V1. [8]
  2. (b) Find the voltage V2. [4]
  3. (c) Find the power delivered to the circuit by the dependent source, using the passive sign convention to decide whether it delivers or absorbs. [8]
(a)

Apply KCL at each node, summing currents leaving the node through resistors and equating to the current injected. At node 1: V1/5 + (V1 − V2)/10 = 2, which simplifies to 0.3 V1 − 0.1 V2 = 2. At node 2: (V2 − V1)/10 + V2/20 = 0.2 V1, which becomes −0.1 V1 + 0.15 V2 = 0.2 V1, so 0.15 V2 = 0.3 V1 and V2 = 2 V1. Substitute into the first equation: 0.3 V1 − 0.2 V1 = 2, so 0.1 V1 = 2 and V1 = 20 V. The dependent source only adds a term proportional to V1 to node 2 and must be moved to the left-hand side as a conductance-like term, as done here. Answer: V1 = 20 V.

Answer: 20 V

(b)

From the second nodal equation, the relation V2 = 2 V1 holds exactly. With V1 = 20 V from part (a), V2 = 2 × 20 = 40 V. Verify using the first equation: 0.3×20 − 0.1×40 = 6 − 4 = 2 A, which equals the injected source current, so the solution is consistent. Verify using the second node: (40 − 20)/10 + 40/20 = 2 + 2 = 4 A, and the dependent source supplies 0.2 × 20 = 4 A. Both nodes balance, so no sign slip has occurred. Answer: V2 = 40 V.

Answer: 40 V

(c)

The dependent source pushes 4 A from g into node 2, so current leaves the source at its terminal that is connected to node 2. The terminal voltage there is V2 = 40 V above g, so the current leaves the positive terminal and the source delivers power. Delivered power P = V2 × (0.2 V1) = 40 × 4 = 160 W. As a check on energy conservation: the independent source delivers 2 × 20 = 40 W, so total delivered is 200 W. The resistors absorb 20²/5 = 80 W, (20)²/10 = 40 W, and 40²/20 = 80 W, totalling 200 W, which equals the sum delivered. Answer: 160 W delivered.

Answer: 160 W

Problem 3 [A1-003] Mesh analysis and supermesh

A planar circuit has a top node T and a bottom node B joined by three parallel vertical branches. The left branch contains a 30 V source, positive terminal toward T, in series with a 4 Ω resistor. The middle branch contains only an ideal 3 A current source, directed upward from B to T. The right branch contains a 10 Ω resistor from T in series with a 12 V source whose positive terminal is on the B side. Define mesh current I1 clockwise in the left mesh (up the left branch, down the middle branch) and I2 clockwise in the right mesh (up the middle branch, down the right branch). Both currents are in amperes.

  1. (a) State the constraint from the current source and find I1. [7]
  2. (b) Find I2. [5]
  3. (c) Find the power delivered by the 3 A current source. [8]
(a)

The middle branch carries an upward current of 3 A. I2 flows up through it and I1 flows down through it, so I2 − I1 = 3. Because the current source is shared by two meshes, a KVL equation cannot be written for either mesh alone; form a supermesh around the outer loop (left branch up, across the top, right branch down, back along the bottom). KVL: 30 − 4 I1 − 10 I2 − 12 = 0, which gives 4 I1 + 10 I2 = 18. Substitute I2 = I1 + 3: 4 I1 + 10 I1 + 30 = 18, so the sign of the 12 V term must be checked carefully. The right branch is traversed downward: after the 10 Ω the path enters the source at its negative terminal and leaves at its positive terminal, which is a rise of 12 V. The supermesh KVL is therefore 30 − 4 I1 − 10 I2 + 12 = 0, giving 4 I1 + 10 I2 = 42. Substituting I2 = I1 + 3 gives 14 I1 + 30 = 42, so 14 I1 = 12 and I1 = 0.857 A.

Answer: 0.857 A

(b)

The current-source constraint gives I2 = I1 + 3. With I1 = 0.857 A, I2 = 0.857 + 3 = 3.857 A. Check this against the supermesh equation: 4 × 0.857 + 10 × 3.857 = 3.429 + 38.571 = 42.0, which matches. The positive sign means that the current flows down the right branch through the 10 Ω resistor from T to B. The 3 A source current splits at node T between the left branch, where 0.857 A flows into T, and the right branch where 3.857 A leaves T, so KCL at T balances: 0.857 + 3 = 3.857. Answer: I2 = 3.86 A.

Answer: 3.857 A

(c)

The voltage across the current source is the voltage between T and B. Take the right branch: moving from T to B, the 10 Ω drops 10 × 3.857 = 38.57 V and the 12 V source contributes a rise of 12 V, so V_TB = 38.57 − 12 = 26.57 V, with T positive. Check on the left branch: V_TB = 30 − 4 × 0.857 = 26.57 V, which agrees. Current flows upward through the source from B to T, i.e. out of the positive terminal at T, so the source delivers power P = 26.57 × 3 = 79.7 W. A current source has no fixed voltage, so this value depends on the rest of the circuit, which is why it was found last. Answer: 79.7 W delivered.

Answer: 79.7 W

Problem 4 [A1-004] Thevenin and Norton equivalents and maximum power transfer

A sensor interface has terminals A and B, with B at the reference. Internally, a 36 V source has its positive terminal at node 1 and its negative terminal at B. A 6 Ω resistor connects node 1 to terminal A. A 12 Ω resistor connects terminal A to B. A 2 A ideal current source pushes current from B into terminal A. An adjustable load resistor RL will be connected between A and B. The circuit contains only these elements and is linear. All values are DC. Treat the network seen by RL as a two-terminal source.

  1. (a) Find the open-circuit voltage between A and B. [6]
  2. (b) Find the Thevenin resistance seen by RL. [4]
  3. (c) Find the value of RL that receives maximum power and that maximum power. [5]
  4. (d) The load is fixed at RL = 10 Ω. Find the power it receives. [5]
(a)

With RL disconnected, apply KCL at terminal A, taking Va as the voltage of A relative to B. Currents leaving A through resistors: (Va − 36)/6 toward node 1 and Va/12 to B, while 2 A is injected. So (Va − 36)/6 + Va/12 = 2. Multiplying by 12: 2(Va − 36) + Va = 24, so 3 Va = 96 and Va = 32 V. Thus Voc = 32 V. This is the Thevenin voltage. As a check, superposition gives 36 × 12/18 = 24 V from the voltage source plus 2 A × (6||12) = 2 × 4 = 8 V from the current source, a total of 32 V.

Answer: 32 V

(b)

To find Rth, deactivate the independent sources: the voltage source becomes a short circuit and the current source becomes an open circuit. With the 36 V source shorted, the 6 Ω resistor runs from A to B (through the short at node 1), and it is in parallel with the 12 Ω resistor. Rth = (6 × 12)/(6 + 12) = 72/18 = 4 Ω. The open-circuited current source contributes nothing. The Norton current would then be In = Voc/Rth = 32/4 = 8 A, which can be confirmed as the short-circuit current found by shorting A to B directly. Answer: Rth = 4 Ω.

Answer: 4 Ω

(c)

Maximum power transfer to a resistive load from a linear source occurs when RL = Rth = 4 Ω. At that point the load voltage is half of Voc, so V_L = 16 V and I = 32/(4 + 4) = 4 A. Maximum power P = Voc²/(4 Rth) = 32²/(4 × 4) = 1024/16 = 64 W. The Thevenin source itself dissipates an equal 64 W in Rth, so the efficiency is 50 percent, which is acceptable in signal circuits but poor in power supplies. Answer: RL = 4 Ω, Pmax = 64 W.

Answer: 64 W

(d)

Connect RL = 10 Ω to the Thevenin equivalent of 32 V in series with 4 Ω. The load current is I = 32/(4 + 10) = 2.2857 A. The load power is P = I² RL = (2.2857)² × 10 = 5.2245 × 10 = 52.2 W. This is below the 64 W maximum, as expected for any load different from 4 Ω. The load voltage is 22.86 V, and the power can be cross-checked as V²/RL = 522.4/10 = 52.2 W. Without the Thevenin equivalent, the same result would require re-solving the whole network with RL in place. Answer: 52.2 W.

Answer: 52.2 W

Problem 5 [A1-005] Superposition and linearity in circuits with several sources

A node N is connected to the reference node g through a 15 Ω resistor. A 20 V source, positive terminal on the P side, is connected from reference g to node P, and a 10 Ω resistor joins P to N. A 12 V source, positive terminal on the Q side, is connected from g to node Q, and a 30 Ω resistor joins Q to N. A 2 A current source injects current from g into N. There are no other elements, and all quantities are DC. The circuit is linear, so the principle of superposition applies. Let VN be the voltage at node N relative to g.

  1. (a) Find the contribution to VN from the 20 V source alone, with the other sources deactivated. [5]
  2. (b) Find the contribution to VN from the 2 A current source alone. [5]
  3. (c) Find the total VN with all three sources active. [4]
  4. (d) With the other sources unchanged, find the value of the 12 V source (call it Vq) needed to make VN = 25 V. [6]
(a)

Deactivate the 12 V source (short) and the 2 A source (open). Then node N is fed from P through 10 Ω and has 15 Ω and 30 Ω to g (the shorted Q source), so the two shunt resistors are in parallel. The conductances at N are 1/10 + 1/15 + 1/30 = 0.2 S. By the nodal equation, VN' = (20/10)/0.2 = 2/0.2 = 10 V. Equivalently a voltage divider: 10 Ω in series with 15||30 = 10 Ω gives half of 20 V. Answer: 10 V.

Answer: 10 V

(b)

Short both voltage sources. The current source now drives node N, which sees the three resistors to g in parallel: 10 Ω (to P, shorted source), 15 Ω and 30 Ω. The total conductance is 0.2 S, so the equivalent resistance is 5 Ω. By Ohm's law the contribution is VN'' = 2 A × 5 Ω = 10 V. The current source is deactivated by an open circuit only when it is not the source under study, so here it must remain active. Answer: 10 V.

Answer: 10 V

(c)

The 12 V source acts through the 30 Ω branch and contributes (12/30)/0.2 = 2 V by the same method. Superposition requires summing all three contributions: 10 V from the 20 V source, 10 V from the 2 A source and 2 V from the 12 V source, giving VN = 22 V. Direct nodal check: (22 − 20)/10 + 22/15 + (22 − 12)/30 = 0.2 + 1.4667 + 0.3333 = 2.0 A, which equals the injected current, so the result is correct. Answer: 22 V.

Answer: 22 V

(d)

Linearity says each source contribution scales with its own value. The 12 V source contributes (Vq/30)/0.2 = Vq/6 volts at N. The other two sources still contribute 10 + 10 = 20 V. We need 20 + Vq/6 = 25, so Vq/6 = 5 and Vq = 30 V. Check with the original: at 12 V the contribution is 2 V, which equals 12/6, consistent. This avoids re-solving the full node equation, which is the practical advantage of superposition when only one source is adjusted. Answer: Vq = 30 V.

Answer: 30 V

A1 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A1-006] Ideal inductors and capacitors, energy storage and lumped models

A 2 mH ideal inductor carries a current that is zero at t = 0, rises linearly to 8 A at t = 4 ms, stays at 8 A until t = 6 ms, then falls linearly to zero at t = 10 ms. Separately, a 100 μF capacitor is charged to 50 V and then connected through a switch and wiring of total resistance 0.5 Ω to an uncharged 25 μF capacitor, the two being connected in parallel after switch closure. Both capacitors are ideal apart from the wiring resistance. Assume the inductor current and voltage use the passive sign convention, and ignore any radiation.

  1. (a) Find the inductor voltage during 0 < t < 4 ms. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum energy stored in the inductor. [4]
  3. (c) Find the final common voltage across the two capacitors after the transient. [6]
  4. (d) Find the energy dissipated in the wiring resistance during the charge sharing. [6]
(a)

For an ideal inductor v = L di/dt. During the first interval the current rises linearly from 0 to 8 A in 4 ms, so di/dt = 8/0.004 = 2000 A/s. Then v = 2×10⁻³ × 2000 = 4 V, constant over the interval. The voltage is positive because the current is increasing, i.e. the source is pushing energy into the magnetic field. During 4 to 6 ms the current is constant so v = 0, and during 6 to 10 ms the slope is −8/0.004 = −2000 A/s so the voltage is −4 V. Answer: 4 V.

Answer: 4 V

(b)

The stored energy in an ideal inductor is W = ½ L i². The energy is greatest when the current is greatest, which occurs from 4 to 6 ms at 8 A. W = 0.5 × 2×10⁻³ × 8² = 0.5 × 2×10⁻³ × 64 = 0.064 J = 64 mJ. This energy is stored in the magnetic field and is returned to the source as the current falls to zero between 6 and 10 ms, so the net energy absorbed over the full cycle is zero. Answer: 64 mJ.

Answer: 64 mJ

(c)

Charge is conserved when the capacitors are joined, because the wiring resistance only dissipates energy and does not remove charge. Initial charge Q = 100 μF × 50 V = 5000 μC. After the connection the parallel capacitance is 100 + 25 = 125 μF, so the final voltage is V = Q/C = 5000/125 = 40 V. At t = 0+ the voltage difference between the capacitors is 50 V, so the initial current would be 50/0.5 = 100 A, which decays with time constant τ = R × (series capacitance) = 0.5 × 20 μF = 10 μs. Answer: 40 V.

Answer: 40 V

(d)

Energy balance gives the loss. Initial energy W1 = ½ × 100×10⁻⁶ × 50² = 0.125 J. Final energy W2 = ½ × 125×10⁻⁶ × 40² = 0.100 J. The difference, 0.125 − 0.100 = 0.025 J = 25 mJ, was dissipated in the resistance. The loss is independent of the value of the wiring resistance, which only sets how fast it is dissipated, because the integral of i²R over the exponential decay depends on R only through the product that cancels. A check by formula: ½ × (C1C2/(C1+C2)) × V0² = 0.5 × 20×10⁻⁶ × 2500 = 25 mJ. Answer: 25 mJ.

Answer: 25 mJ

Problem 2 [A1-007] First-order RC and RL transients with switching

In a data-logger power stage a 10 μF capacitor C is connected from node x to the reference node g. A 30 V source, positive terminal at node s, feeds node x through a 2 kΩ resistor R1 from s to x, and a 3 kΩ resistor R2 connects x to g. For t < 0 the switch in series with R1 was open for a long time and the capacitor had been charged to 4 V (positive at x) from a separate supply, which is then removed. At t = 0 the switch closes, connecting R1 between s and x. Let v(t) be the capacitor voltage for t ≥ 0.

  1. (a) Find the time constant of the circuit for t ≥ 0. [4]
  2. (b) Find the capacitor voltage at t = 10 ms. [6]
  3. (c) Find the time at which the capacitor voltage reaches 15 V. [5]
  4. (d) Find the current drawn from the 30 V source at t = 0+. [5]
(a)

After the switch closes, the capacitor sees the Thevenin resistance of the network connected to node x, with the source deactivated (short). R1 and R2 are then both connected from x to g, so Rth = (2000 × 3000)/(2000 + 3000) = 1200 Ω. The time constant is τ = Rth C = 1200 × 10×10⁻⁶ = 0.012 s = 12 ms. This is the time for the transient term to fall to 36.8 percent of its starting value. Answer: τ = 12 ms.

Answer: 12 ms

(b)

The final voltage is the Thevenin voltage, found as a divider: Vth = 30 × 3000/(2000 + 3000) = 18 V. The initial voltage is v(0) = 4 V because a capacitor voltage cannot change instantaneously. The first-order solution is v(t) = Vf + (v(0) − Vf) e−t/τ = 18 + (4 − 18) e−t/τ = 18 − 14 e−t/τ. At t = 10 ms, t/τ = 10/12 = 0.8333 and e−0.8333 = 0.4346. So v = 18 − 14 × 0.4346 = 18 − 6.085 = 11.92 V. Answer: 11.9 V.

Answer: 11.9 V

(c)

Set v(t) = 15 in the same expression: 18 − 14 e−t/τ = 15, so e−t/τ = 3/14 = 0.2143. Taking natural logarithms, t/τ = ln(14/3) = ln 4.667 = 1.5404. Therefore t = 12 ms × 1.5404 = 18.48 ms. The voltage passes 15 V after roughly one and a half time constants, which is consistent with the curve having covered 11/14 = 79 percent of its total swing from 4 V toward 18 V. This logarithmic form is the standard way to find a switching or settling time for a first-order circuit. Answer: 18.5 ms.

Answer: 18.5 ms

(d)

At t = 0+ the capacitor voltage is still 4 V, so node x sits at 4 V. The current from the source flows through R1 only, so i = (30 − 4)/2000 = 26/2000 = 0.013 A = 13 mA. This is larger than the final steady-state source current of 30/(2000 + 3000) = 6 mA because the capacitor initially draws charging current: at t = 0+ R2 carries 4/3000 = 1.33 mA and the capacitor takes 13 − 1.33 = 11.67 mA. Answer: 13 mA.

Answer: 13 mA

Problem 3 [A1-008] Second-order RLC natural and step response

A series RLC circuit is formed from a 40 Ω resistor, a 0.1 H inductor and a 100 μF capacitor connected in series. A 12 V DC source, with positive terminal to the resistor, is switched in at t = 0. The capacitor is initially uncharged and the inductor current is initially zero. Let vC(t) be the capacitor voltage, taken across the capacitor, which is the output of interest. The series current is i(t) in amperes. Assume ideal components. The step response has the form vC(t) = 12[1 − e−αt(cos ωd t + (α/ωd) sin ωd t)] for the underdamped case.

  1. (a) Find the damping coefficient α. [3]
  2. (b) Find the damped natural frequency ωd. [4]
  3. (c) Find the time of the first peak of vC(t). [5]
  4. (d) Find the peak value of vC(t) and the percentage overshoot. [5]
  5. (e) Find the value of R that would make the circuit critically damped, with L and C unchanged. [3]
(a)

For a series RLC circuit the damping coefficient is α = R/(2L). Here α = 40/(2 × 0.1) = 40/0.2 = 200 rad/s (nepers per second). The undamped natural frequency is ω0 = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(0.1 × 100×10⁻⁶) = 1/√(1×10⁻⁵) = 316.2 rad/s. Because α is less than ω0 (200 < 316.2), the response is underdamped, so the oscillatory form stated in the problem applies. The ratio ζ = α/ω0 = 0.632 confirms moderate damping. Answer: α = 200 rad/s.

Answer: 200 rad/s

(b)

The damped frequency is ωd = √(ω0² − α²). Using ω0² = 1/(LC) = 1×10⁵ and α² = 4×10⁴, ωd = √(1×10⁵ − 4×10⁴) = √(6×10⁴) = 244.9 rad/s. This is the frequency of the ringing observed in vC(t), corresponding to a period of 2π/244.9 = 25.65 ms. The decay envelope has time constant 1/α = 5 ms, so the ringing dies out in about 25 ms, roughly five time constants. The resistor value therefore sets both the decay rate and, through α, the damped frequency. Answer: ωd = 245 rad/s.

Answer: 245 rad/s

(c)

The peak occurs where the derivative of the response is zero. Differentiating gives dvC/dt = 12 (ω0²/ωd) e−αt sin ωd t, which is zero first at ωd t = π. Hence tp = π/ωd = 3.1416/244.95 = 0.012825 s = 12.83 ms. The first overshoot therefore occurs just over half a period of the damped oscillation after the step is applied. The formula holds for the step response of vC and for current zero crossing, which coincide at this instant because i = C dvC/dt. Answer: tp = 12.8 ms.

Answer: 12.8 ms

(d)

At t = tp, the cosine term equals −1 and the sine term is zero, so vC(tp) = 12[1 + e−α tp]. With α tp = 200 × 0.012825 = 2.565, e−2.565 = 0.0769. Thus vC(peak) = 12 × 1.0769 = 12.92 V. The overshoot is exp(−πα/ωd) = 0.0769, i.e. 7.69 percent of the final 12 V value. Equivalent expression: percent overshoot = 100 exp(−π ζ/√(1 − ζ²)) with ζ = α/ω0 = 0.632, giving the same 7.7 percent. Answer: 12.92 V, 7.7 percent.

Answer: 12.92 V

(e)

Critical damping occurs when α = ω0, that is R/(2L) = 1/√(LC). Solving for R gives R = 2√(L/C) = 2 √(0.1/100×10⁻⁶) = 2 √1000 = 2 × 31.62 = 63.25 Ω. A larger resistance would give an overdamped response with no overshoot but a slower rise, while a smaller resistance such as the original 40 Ω gives the 7.7 percent overshoot found above. The inductance and capacitance fix the characteristic impedance √(L/C) = 31.6 Ω, and critical damping needs twice that. Answer: R = 63.2 Ω.

Answer: 63.2 Ω

Problem 4 [A1-009] Sinusoidal steady state with phasors

A series circuit consists of a 30 Ω resistor, an 80 mH inductor and a 60 μF capacitor connected to a sinusoidal source of 120 V rms at 60 Hz. Use the source voltage as the phase reference (angle 0°) and take the current positive in the direction of source-driven flow. The circuit is in sinusoidal steady state and all transients have died out. Treat all components as ideal and give the angle of the current as positive if it leads the source voltage. Use ω = 2π × 60 rad/s. Report magnitudes as rms values.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the total impedance. [5]
  2. (b) Find the rms current. [4]
  3. (c) Find the phase angle of the current relative to the source voltage, in degrees, positive if it leads. [5]
  4. (d) Find the rms voltage across the capacitor. [6]
(a)

At 60 Hz, ω = 2π × 60 = 376.99 rad/s. The inductive reactance is XL = ωL = 376.99 × 0.080 = 30.16 Ω. The capacitive reactance is XC = 1/(ωC) = 1/(376.99 × 60×10⁻⁶) = 1/0.022619 = 44.21 Ω. The series impedance is Z = R + j(XL − XC) = 30 + j(30.16 − 44.21) = 30 − j14.05 Ω. Its magnitude is |Z| = √(30² + 14.05²) = √(900 + 197.4) = √1097.4 = 33.13 Ω. The negative reactance means the circuit is net capacitive. Answer: |Z| = 33.1 Ω.

Answer: 33.1 Ω

(b)

With the source as reference, V = 120∠0° V. The current magnitude follows Ohm's law for phasors: I = V/|Z| = 120/33.13 = 3.622 A rms. Because it is a series circuit the same current flows through the resistor, inductor and capacitor. A quick check on the voltages: the resistor drops 3.622 × 30 = 108.7 V, the inductor 3.622 × 30.16 = 109.2 V and the capacitor 3.622 × 44.21 = 160.1 V, and the vector sum of 108.7 and j(109.2 − 160.1) has magnitude √(108.7² + 50.9²) = 120 V. Answer: 3.62 A.

Answer: 3.62 A

(c)

The current phasor is I = V/Z, so its angle is the negative of the impedance angle. The impedance angle is θZ = arctan((XL − XC)/R) = arctan(−14.05/30) = −25.08°. Therefore the current angle is +25.08°, i.e. the current leads the voltage by about 25.1°. This agrees with the net capacitive character found in part (a): in a capacitive circuit the current leads. The power factor is cos 25.08° = 0.906 leading, so the source supplies real power 120 × 3.622 × 0.906 = 394 W, all of which is dissipated in the resistor, since 3.622² × 30 = 394 W. Answer: +25.1°.

Answer: +25.1°

(d)

The capacitor voltage magnitude is VC = I XC = 3.622 × 44.21 = 160.1 V rms. It exceeds the 120 V source voltage because the series circuit is partly resonant: the inductive and capacitive voltages are 109.2 V and 160.1 V and are in opposite phase, so their difference of 50.9 V is combined in quadrature with the resistor drop of 108.7 V to give 120 V. Capacitor voltage ratings must therefore be chosen with respect to the voltage across it, not the supply. Answer: 160 V.

Answer: 160 V

Problem 5 [A1-010] AC power, complex power and power factor correction

A single-phase industrial feeder in Ontario supplies a motor load of 40 kW at a power factor of 0.75 lagging. The supply is 600 V rms at 60 Hz and the voltage stays constant. A plant engineer proposes to connect a capacitor bank in parallel with the load, at the load terminals, to raise the power factor to 0.95 lagging without changing the real power drawn. Take the supply voltage as the reference and neglect the feeder impedance and any harmonic distortion. Use ω = 2π × 60 rad/s and give the capacitor in microfarads.

  1. (a) Find the reactive power drawn by the load. [4]
  2. (b) Find the reactive power the capacitor bank must supply. [5]
  3. (c) Find the capacitance required. [5]
  4. (d) Find the reduction in the line current produced by the correction. [6]
(a)

The real power is P = 40 kW and cos φ = 0.75 gives φ = 41.41°. The reactive power is Q = P tan φ = 40 × tan(41.41°) = 40 × 0.8819 = 35.28 kvar, lagging (inductive). The apparent power is S = P/cos φ = 40/0.75 = 53.33 kVA. As a check, √(S² − P²) = √(2844.4 − 1600) = √1244.4 = 35.27 kvar, which agrees. The load is inductive because a motor needs magnetizing current, so Q is taken as positive lagging. Answer: Q = 35.3 kvar.

Answer: 35.3 kvar

(b)

After correction the real power is still 40 kW. At cos φ2 = 0.95, φ2 = 18.19° and tan φ2 = 0.3287. The remaining reactive power is Q2 = 40 × 0.3287 = 13.15 kvar, so the new apparent power is 40/0.95 = 42.1 kVA. The capacitor must supply the difference Qc = Q − Q2 = 35.28 − 13.15 = 22.13 kvar. Capacitors produce reactive power so their reactive power is leading, and it subtracts from the load's lagging reactive power. Answer: Qc = 22.1 kvar.

Answer: 22.1 kvar

(c)

For a capacitor across a voltage V, Qc = V² ω C. Solving, C = Qc/(ω V²) = 22.13×10³/(376.99 × 600²) = 22130/(376.99 × 360000) = 22130/1.3572×10⁸ = 1.631×10⁻⁴ F = 163.1 μF. This assumes the voltage at the load stays at 600 V rms and that the bank is connected at the load terminals. A real bank would be built from several standard 600 V capacitor units in parallel to approximate this value, and the bank should not be sized so large that the power factor goes leading at light load. Answer: C = 163 μF.

Answer: 163 μF

(d)

Before correction the current is I1 = S1/V = 53 333/600 = 88.89 A. After correction the apparent power is S2 = P/0.95 = 40 000/0.95 = 42 105 VA and I2 = S2/V = 42 105/600 = 70.18 A. The reduction is 88.89 − 70.18 = 18.71 A, about 21 percent. The lower current reduces I²R losses in the feeder and transformer by about 1 − (70.18/88.89)² = 38 percent, and frees capacity for additional load. Answer: 18.7 A reduction.

Answer: 18.7 A

A1 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A1-011] Frequency response, resonance and quality factor

A metal detector search coil is modelled as a series RLC branch driven by an ideal sinusoidal voltage source of 10 V rms. The loop contains, in order, a resistance R = 3.0 Ω (coil winding plus drive losses), an inductance L = 2.5 mH and a capacitance C = 10 μF, all in a single series loop with no other elements. The source frequency can be varied, and the quantity of interest is the current in the loop and the voltage across the capacitor alone, measured between its two terminals. Treat all elements as ideal apart from the stated resistance. Analyse the circuit at and near resonance using standard series resonance relations.

  1. (a) Find the resonant frequency in hertz. [4]
  2. (b) Find the quality factor Q of the circuit at resonance. [4]
  3. (c) Find the half-power bandwidth in hertz. [6]
  4. (d) Find the rms voltage across the capacitor at resonance, in volts. [6]
(a)

In a series RLC loop the reactances cancel when ωL = 1/(ωC), so ω0 = 1/√(LC). Substituting L = 2.5×10⁻³ H and C = 10×10⁻⁶ F gives LC = 2.5×10⁻⁸ s², hence √(LC) = 1.581×10⁻⁴ s and ω0 = 6324.6 rad/s. Dividing by 2π gives f0 = 6324.6 / 6.2832 = 1006.6 Hz. At this frequency the impedance is purely resistive and equal to R, so the current is at its maximum. I assume the ideal source has zero internal impedance, so the full source voltage appears across the loop.

Answer: f0 = 1006.6 Hz

(b)

For a series circuit Q = ω0L/R, the ratio of the reactive energy stored to the energy dissipated per radian. First ω0L = 6324.6 × 2.5×10⁻³ = 15.81 Ω, which equals 1/(ω0C) as a check: 1/(6324.6 × 10×10⁻⁶) = 15.81 Ω. Then Q = 15.81 / 3.0 = 5.27. A Q above about 5 means the response is reasonably sharp and the half-power bandwidth is much smaller than the resonant frequency, so the approximations used in the next part are well justified.

Answer: Q = 5.27

(c)

The half-power bandwidth of a series RLC circuit is exactly BW = R/(2πL) in hertz, which also equals f0/Q. Using the first form, BW = 3.0 / (2π × 2.5×10⁻³) = 3.0 / 0.015708 = 191.0 Hz. Check with the second form: 1006.6 / 5.27 = 191.0 Hz, which agrees. The two half-power frequencies sit about 95.5 Hz either side of f0, slightly asymmetrically in practice since they are geometrically centred on f0. At those frequencies the current falls to 1/√2 of its peak, so the power delivered to R falls to one half.

Answer: BW = 191 Hz

(d)

At resonance the loop current is I = V/R = 10/3.0 = 3.333 A rms, limited only by the resistance. The capacitor voltage magnitude is I × Xc, where Xc = 1/(ω0C) = 15.81 Ω. So Vc = 3.333 × 15.81 = 52.7 V rms. This is the same as Q × V = 5.27 × 10 = 52.7 V, showing the voltage magnification of a series resonant circuit. The inductor voltage has the same magnitude but opposite phase, so the two cancel in the loop sum while each individually exceeds the 10 V source.

Answer: Vc = 52.7 V rms

Problem 2 [A1-012] Transfer functions and Bode magnitude of passive circuits

A sensor interface uses a passive attenuator and filter with no active parts. The input voltage vin is applied between node 1 and ground. A resistor R1 = 47 kΩ connects node 1 to node 2. Between node 2 and ground are two elements in parallel: a resistor R2 = 4.7 kΩ and a capacitor C = 22 nF. The output voltage vo is taken at node 2 with respect to ground, and nothing else is connected to node 2, so the output is unloaded. Treat the circuit as linear with zero initial charge. Derive the transfer function H(s) = Vo(s)/Vin(s) and use it to examine the magnitude response in decibels, 20 log10 |H|.

  1. (a) Find the dc gain in decibels. [4]
  2. (b) Find the corner (pole) frequency in hertz. [5]
  3. (c) Find the exact gain in decibels at 5 kHz. [5]
  4. (d) Find the frequency in hertz at which the gain falls to −40 dB. [6]
(a)

Write the divider in the s domain. The parallel branch has impedance Z2 = R2/(1 + sR2C), so H(s) = Z2/(R1 + Z2) = R2 / (R1 + R2 + sR1R2C). Dividing through by R1 + R2 gives H(s) = [R2/(R1+R2)] / [1 + s C (R1‖R2)]. At dc the capacitor is open, so H(0) = 4.7/(47+4.7) = 0.09091. In decibels, 20 log10(0.09091) = −20.83 dB. This is the flat low-frequency attenuation set by the resistive divider alone, because at dc the capacitor carries no current and the output is not loaded.

Answer: dc gain = −20.83 dB

(b)

The single pole occurs at s = −1/(C·R1‖R2). The parallel resistance is R1‖R2 = (47k × 4.7k)/(51.7k) = 4.2727 kΩ. The time constant is τ = 4272.7 × 22×10⁻⁹ = 9.400×10⁻⁵ s, so ωp = 1/τ = 10 638 rad/s. Dividing by 2π, fp = 10 638 / 6.2832 = 1693 Hz. Below this frequency the magnitude is flat at the dc value, so the circuit passes slow sensor signals with fixed attenuation, and above it the asymptote falls at −20 dB per decade, as for any first-order lag.

Answer: fp = 1693 Hz

(c)

Evaluate |H(jω)| = 0.09091 / √(1 + (ω/ωp)²) with ω = 2π × 5000 = 31 416 rad/s. The ratio ω/ωp = 31 416/10 638 = 2.953, so the square-root term is √(1 + 8.721) = 3.118. Then |H| = 0.09091/3.118 = 0.02916. In decibels this is −20.83 − 20 log10(3.118) = −20.83 − 9.88 = −30.70 dB. The asymptotic estimate would give −20.83 − 20 log10(2.953) = −30.2 dB, so the straight-line approximation is about 0.5 dB optimistic here, a typical error just beyond the corner.

Answer: gain at 5 kHz = −30.70 dB

(d)

Require |H| = 10−40/20 = 0.01. Then 0.09091/√(1 + x²) = 0.01 with x = f/fp, giving √(1 + x²) = 9.091 and 1 + x² = 82.64, so x = 9.0 (exactly √81.64 = 9.0355). The frequency is f = x·fp = 9.0355 × 1693.1 = 15 299 Hz, about 15.3 kHz. This is close to the asymptote prediction: from −20.83 dB, a further 19.17 dB drop needs a factor 9.04 above the corner, which agrees because the response is already well in the −20 dB per decade region.

Answer: f = 15.3 kHz

Problem 3 [A1-013] Impulse response and convolution in circuits

A level-sensing circuit consists of an ideal voltage source vin(t) in series with a resistor R = 4.7 kΩ, which connects to a capacitor C = 100 μF, the other capacitor terminal returning to the source ground. The output y(t) is the voltage across the capacitor, and the circuit is initially relaxed (capacitor uncharged). Nothing loads the capacitor. The input is a rectangular pulse: vin(t) = 5 V for 0 ≤ t ≤ 0.6 s and zero otherwise. Find the unit impulse response h(t) of the system relating vin to y, then use convolution to find the response to the pulse at selected times, treating the circuit as linear and time invariant.

  1. (a) Find the time constant τ of the circuit in seconds. [3]
  2. (b) Evaluate the unit impulse response you derived at t = 0.2 s, in s⁻¹. [4]
  3. (c) Use convolution to find y(0.6 s) in volts. [6]
  4. (d) Find y(1.0 s) in volts, after the pulse has ended. [7]
(a)

For a series RC circuit with the output across the capacitor, the governing equation is RC dy/dt + y = vin, so the time constant is τ = RC. Substituting R = 4700 Ω and C = 100×10⁻⁶ F gives τ = 0.47 s. This is the time scale over which the capacitor charges to 63.2 percent of a step input, and it sets the width of the impulse response, so all later parts are expressed in multiples of 0.47 s.

Answer: τ = 0.47 s

(b)

The impulse response is found by applying a unit impulse, which instantly sets y(0⁺) = 1/τ because the impulse delivers unit area of vin/τ to dy/dt, after which the output decays freely. Hence h(t) = (1/τ) e−t/τ = 2.1277 e−t/0.47. At t = 0.2 s, the exponent is −0.2/0.47 = −0.4255, and e−0.4255 = 0.6533. So h(0.2) = 2.1277 × 0.6533 = 1.390 s⁻¹. As a check, the area under h from 0 to infinity is exactly 1, which means unit dc gain.

Answer: h(0.2 s) = 1.390 s⁻¹

(c)

The convolution is y(t) = ∫ h(λ) vin(t − λ) dλ over the overlap. For t = 0.6 s the input is 5 V throughout 0 to 0.6 s, so y = 5 ∫₀0.6 (1/τ) e−λ/τ dλ = 5 [1 − e−0.6/τ]. Here 0.6/0.47 = 1.2766 and e−1.2766 = 0.2790, so y(0.6) = 5 × (1 − 0.2790) = 3.605 V. This is identical to the step response of an RC circuit evaluated at the end of the pulse, since the pulse is still on at that moment.

Answer: y(0.6 s) = 3.605 V

(d)

For t > 0.6 s the overlap is limited to the pulse, so y(t) = 5 ∫ from (t−0.6) to t of (1/τ) e−λ/τ dλ = 5 e−(t−0.6)/τ [1 − e−0.6/τ]. This equals the voltage at the end of the pulse, 3.605 V, multiplied by the free decay factor. At t = 1.0 s the elapsed time is 0.4 s, so the factor is e−0.4/0.47 = e−0.8511 = 0.4270. Then y(1.0) = 3.605 × 0.4270 = 1.539 V. Physically the capacitor discharges through R into the ideal source, which is a short circuit once vin returns to zero.

Answer: y(1.0 s) = 1.539 V

Problem 4 [A1-014] Differential equation formulation and solution for circuits

A series circuit is built from a switch, a resistor R = 500 Ω, an inductor L = 0.5 H and a capacitor C = 2 μF, connected in a single loop in that order with the capacitor last. At t = 0 the switch closes and connects an ideal 24 V dc source across the whole series combination. Before closing, the inductor current is zero and the capacitor voltage is zero. Take vC(t), the voltage across the capacitor, as the unknown. Formulate the second-order differential equation for vC, classify its response from the roots of the characteristic equation, and obtain the solution and its key time-domain features. Assume ideal components throughout.

  1. (a) Find the damping coefficient α = R/(2L) in s⁻¹. [3]
  2. (b) Find the damped natural frequency ωd in rad/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find vC at t = 2 ms in volts. [6]
  4. (d) Find the percentage overshoot of vC above its final value. [7]
(a)

Apply Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop: L di/dt + Ri + vC = 24 with i = C dvC/dt. This gives LC d²vC/dt² + RC dvC/dt + vC = 24, or d²vC/dt² + (R/L) dvC/dt + (1/LC) vC = 24/(LC). Comparing with s² + 2αs + ω0² the damping coefficient is α = R/(2L) = 500/(2 × 0.5) = 500 s⁻¹. The natural frequency is ω0 = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(10⁻⁶) = 1000 rad/s, which is needed in the next part.

Answer: α = 500 s⁻¹

(b)

The characteristic equation s² + 1000 s + 10⁶ = 0 has roots s = −α ± √(α² − ω0²) = −500 ± √(250 000 − 1 000 000) = −500 ± j866. Since α < ω0, the roots are complex and the circuit is underdamped. The damped natural frequency is ωd = √(ω0² − α²) = √750 000 = 866.0 rad/s. The damping ratio is ζ = α/ω0 = 0.5, which predicts a noticeable oscillation before the response settles to its final value.

Answer: ωd = 866 rad/s

(c)

The particular solution is the dc final value 24 V. The homogeneous part is e−αt(A cos ωd t + B sin ωd t). With vC(0) = 0, A = −24. With i(0) = 0, dvC/dt(0) = 0, so −αA + ωd B = 0, giving B = αA/ωd = −24 × 500/866.0 = −13.856. Hence vC = 24 − e−500t(24 cos 866t + 13.856 sin 866t). At t = 2 ms, 866t = 1.7321 rad, cos = −0.1604, sin = 0.9871, e−1 = 0.3679. The bracket is −3.850 + 13.677 = 9.827, so vC = 24 − 0.3679 × 9.827 = 20.39 V.

Answer: vC(2 ms) = 20.39 V

(d)

The first peak occurs when dvC/dt = 0, which for zero initial current is at ωd t = π, so tp = π/866.0 = 3.628 ms. At that instant cos = −1 and sin = 0, so vC = 24 + 24 e−απ/ωd = 24 (1 + e−500 × 0.003628) = 24 (1 + 0.1630) = 27.91 V. The overshoot is e−απ/ωd = e−1.8138 = 0.1630, that is 16.3 percent, equal to the standard second-order formula exp(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)) for ζ = 0.5. The peak exceeds the final value by about 3.9 V.

Answer: Overshoot = 16.3 percent

Problem 5 [A1-015] Laplace transform analysis of circuits with initial conditions

A series RLC loop contains a resistor R = 60 Ω, an inductor L = 0.1 H and a capacitor C = 100 μF. For t < 0 the loop is open and stores energy: the inductor current is i(0) = 0.2 A in the direction of the assumed loop current i(t), and the capacitor voltage is vC(0) = 5 V with the reference polarity such that i(t) flowing through it increases vC. At t = 0 an ideal 30 V dc source is inserted in the loop in a polarity that drives positive i(t). Use the Laplace transform with the initial conditions to find i(t), solving for t ≥ 0, and then evaluate the response.

  1. (a) Find the real part of the complex roots of the characteristic equation, as the decay rate α in s⁻¹. [4]
  2. (b) Find the damped frequency ωd in rad/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find i(t) at t = 1 ms in amperes. [6]
  4. (d) Find i(t) at t = 5 ms in amperes. [6]
(a)

Transform the loop equation L di/dt + Ri + vC = 30/s with initial energy included: L[sI − i(0)] + R I + [I/(Cs) + vC(0)/s] = 30/s. Collect terms: I(s)[Ls + R + 1/(Cs)] = 30/s − 5/s + L i(0) = 25/s + 0.02. Multiplying numerator and denominator by s gives I(s) = (25 + 0.02 s)/(0.1 s² + 60 s + 10 000) = (0.2 s + 250)/(s² + 600 s + 10⁵). The denominator roots are s = −300 ± √(90 000 − 100 000) = −300 ± j100, so α = 300 s⁻¹.

Answer: α = 300 s⁻¹

(b)

From the quadratic s² + 600 s + 100 000, completing the square gives (s + 300)² + 10 000, so the imaginary part of the roots is √10 000 = 100 rad/s. This is ωd. It is the radian frequency of the oscillation inside the decaying envelope e−300t. Because α = 300 s⁻¹ and ω0 = 1/√(LC) = √10⁵ = 316.2 rad/s, ω0 slightly exceeds α, confirming an underdamped but heavily damped response with ζ = α/ω0 = 0.949, so only a fraction of one cycle of oscillation is visible before the envelope dies away.

Answer: ωd = 100 rad/s

(c)

Write I(s) = (0.2 s + 250)/[(s + 300)² + 100²]. Express the numerator as 0.2(s + 300) + 190. Then the inverse transform is i(t) = e−300t [0.2 cos 100t + (190/100) sin 100t] = e−300t(0.2 cos 100t + 1.9 sin 100t) A. As a check, i(0) = 0.2 A, matching the stated initial current. At t = 1 ms, 100t = 0.1 rad, cos = 0.9950, sin = 0.09983, e−0.3 = 0.7408. The bracket is 0.1990 + 0.1897 = 0.3887, so i = 0.7408 × 0.3887 = 0.2879 A.

Answer: i(1 ms) = 0.2879 A

(d)

Using the same expression at t = 5 ms: 100t = 0.5 rad, cos 0.5 = 0.8776, sin 0.5 = 0.4794, and e−1.5 = 0.2231. The bracket is 0.2 × 0.8776 + 1.9 × 0.4794 = 0.1755 + 0.9109 = 1.0864. Then i(5 ms) = 0.2231 × 1.0864 = 0.2424 A. The current has risen above its initial value early in the transient, because the 25 V net drive acts on the inductor, then decays to zero in the long run since the capacitor charges to 30 V and blocks dc.

Answer: i(5 ms) = 0.2424 A

A1 Practice Paper 4

Problem 1 [A1-016] Transient response by Laplace with switching and sources

A 60 Hz instrument supply is modelled as a sinusoidal voltage source v(t) = 170 sin(377t) V in series with a switch, a resistor R = 8 Ω and an inductor L = 40 mH, forming a single loop. The inductor has zero current before the switch closes. The switch closes at t = 0, which is the instant the source voltage passes through zero while increasing. Use the Laplace transform to find the current i(t) for t ≥ 0, separate it into the forced (steady state) component and the transient component, and use the result to assess the worst-case starting surge. Take ω = 377 rad/s exactly and ignore source impedance.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the loop impedance at 377 rad/s, in ohms. [4]
  2. (b) Find the amplitude of the steady-state current in amperes. [4]
  3. (c) Find the initial amplitude of the decaying transient term in amperes. [6]
  4. (d) Find the total current i(3 ms) in amperes. [6]
(a)

The inductive reactance is X = ωL = 377 × 0.040 = 15.08 Ω. The impedance magnitude is |Z| = √(R² + X²) = √(64 + 227.41) = √291.41 = 17.071 Ω. The impedance angle is θ = arctan(15.08/8) = 62.05°. These values are used in the forced current. I assume the inductor is ideal, with the stated resistance as the only loss, so the Laplace denominator is simply Ls + R and the time constant is L/R = 5 ms.

Answer: |Z| = 17.07 Ω

(b)

The Laplace equation is (Ls + R) I(s) = 170 × 377/(s² + 377²). The forced component follows from the phasor result, so the steady-state amplitude is Im = Vm/|Z| = 170/17.071 = 9.959 A. It lags the voltage by 62.05°, so the forced current is 9.959 sin(377t − 62.05°) A. The partial fraction expansion of I(s) gives sine and cosine terms of this exact form, plus one term in 1/(s + R/L) that is the transient. Therefore the peak steady current is 9.96 A.

Answer: Im = 9.959 A

(c)

The total current is the sum of forced and natural parts, and i(0) = 0 because inductor current cannot jump. The forced part at t = 0 is 9.959 sin(−62.05°) = −8.797 A, so the transient must cancel it: its initial value is +8.797 A, giving i = 9.959 sin(377t − 62.05°) + 8.797 e−200t. Equivalently the amplitude is Im sin θ = 9.959 × 0.8833 = 8.797 A. Closing at a voltage zero is nearly the worst case for dc offset in an inductive circuit, since θ is near 90°.

Answer: Transient amplitude = 8.797 A

(d)

At t = 3 ms the forced term has argument 377 × 0.003 − 1.0830 = 1.131 − 1.083 = 0.0480 rad (using θ = 62.05° = 1.0830 rad), so 9.959 × sin 0.0480 = 0.4774 A. The transient is 8.797 e−0.003/0.005 = 8.797 × 0.5488 = 4.828 A. The total is 0.477 + 4.828 = 5.305 A. The transient is why the current at this moment is far above what the steady-state expression alone predicts, and the offset decays with the 5 ms time constant.

Answer: i(3 ms) = 5.305 A

Problem 2 [A1-017] Two-port parameters (z, y, h, ABCD)

A resistive T-network is used as a test attenuator. It has port 1 on the left and port 2 on the right, with all voltages and currents defined by the standard convention: V1 and I1 at port 1, V2 and I2 at port 2, both currents positive into the network. The network has a series resistor Ra = 10 Ω from the upper port 1 terminal to a centre node, a series resistor Rc = 15 Ω from that centre node to the upper port 2 terminal, and a shunt resistor Rb = 20 Ω from the centre node to the common lower rail shared by both ports. Contains no sources and is reciprocal. Determine its two-port parameters.

  1. (a) Find the open-circuit impedance parameter z11 in ohms. [3]
  2. (b) Find the short-circuit admittance parameter y11 in millisiemens. [5]
  3. (c) Find the hybrid parameter h21, the short-circuit current gain (dimensionless). [5]
  4. (d) Find the transmission parameter B (ABCD form, V1 = A V2 − B I2) in ohms. [7]
(a)

Open-circuit port 2 (I2 = 0). Then I1 flows through Ra and Rb, and Rc carries no current, so V1 = (Ra + Rb) I1. Hence z11 = V1/I1 = 10 + 20 = 30 Ω. In the same condition V2 equals the voltage across Rb, so z21 = V2/I1 = 20 Ω. By symmetry of the argument at port 2, z22 = Rb + Rc = 35 Ω and z12 = 20 Ω. These form the z matrix [30 20; 20 35] Ω, with determinant Δz = 30 × 35 − 20 × 20 = 650 Ω².

Answer: z11 = 30 Ω

(b)

The y matrix is the inverse of the z matrix. With Δz = 650, y11 = z22/Δz = 35/650 = 0.053846 S, which is 53.85 mS. For the other entries, y12 = y21 = −z12/Δz = −20/650 = −30.77 mS and y22 = z11/Δz = 30/650 = 46.15 mS. As a direct check, short port 2 and apply V1: the load on port 1 is Ra in series with Rb‖Rc = 20‖15 = 8.571 Ω, total 18.571 Ω, and 1/18.571 = 53.85 mS, which matches.

Answer: y11 = 53.85 mS

(c)

The h parameter h21 = I2/I1 with V2 = 0. Using z equations with V2 = 0: 0 = z21 I1 + z22 I2, so I2/I1 = −z21/z22 = −20/35 = −0.5714. The negative sign arises from both currents being defined into the network, so the physical current out of port 2 is 57.1 percent of the input current, from the current divider between Rb (20 Ω) and Rc (15 Ω): 20/35 = 0.5714. Also h11 = Δz/z22 = 650/35 = 18.57 Ω.

Answer: h21 = −0.5714

(d)

The ABCD relations are V1 = A V2 − B I2 and I1 = C V2 − D I2. From the z equations, A = z11/z21 = 30/20 = 1.5, B = Δz/z21 = 650/20 = 32.5 Ω, C = 1/z21 = 0.05 S and D = z22/z21 = 35/20 = 1.75. Check by short-circuiting port 2: V2 = 0 gives V1 = −B I2, where −I2 is the current leaving port 2. From the earlier result I2 = −0.5714 I1, and V1 = 18.571 I1, so B = 18.571/0.5714 = 32.5 Ω, and AD − BC = 2.625 − 1.625 = 1, confirming reciprocity.

Answer: B = 32.5 Ω

Problem 3 [A1-018] Interconnected two-ports and terminated two-ports

Three passive two-ports are connected in cascade, the output port of each joined directly to the input port of the next. Network N1 is a single series resistor of 50 Ω in the upper line. Network N2 is a single shunt conductor of 0.01 S between the upper line and the common line. Network N3 is a single series resistor of 25 Ω in the upper line. The common line runs unbroken through all three. The cascade is driven at its input by a source of 100 V open-circuit voltage with a 30 Ω source resistance, and the output is terminated in a load resistor RL = 200 Ω. Using ABCD (transmission) parameters, analyse the terminated cascade.

  1. (a) Find the overall ABCD parameter B of the cascade in ohms. [4]
  2. (b) Find the input resistance seen at the input port with the load connected, in ohms. [5]
  3. (c) Find the voltage gain Vo/Vin (load voltage over input-port voltage). [5]
  4. (d) Find the load voltage Vo, in volts, with the source resistance included. [6]
(a)

Cascaded networks multiply their ABCD matrices in order. A series resistor R has [1 R; 0 1], and a shunt conductor G has [1 0; G 1]. So T = [1 50; 0 1] × [1 0; 0.01 1] × [1 25; 0 1]. The first product is [1.5 50; 0.01 1]. Multiplying by [1 25; 0 1] gives A = 1.5, B = 1.5 × 25 + 50 = 87.5 Ω, C = 0.01 and D = 0.01 × 25 + 1 = 1.25. The determinant 1.5 × 1.25 − 87.5 × 0.01 = 1, as it must for a reciprocal network.

Answer: B = 87.5 Ω

(b)

For a terminated ABCD two-port, with V1 = A V2 + B I2′ and I1 = C V2 + D I2′ where I2′ is the current into the load, Zin = (A RL + B)/(C RL + D). Substituting RL = 200 Ω: numerator = 1.5 × 200 + 87.5 = 387.5, denominator = 0.01 × 200 + 1.25 = 3.25. So Zin = 387.5/3.25 = 119.23 Ω. A quick plausibility check: 25 + 200 = 225, in parallel with 100 Ω gives 69.2 Ω, plus 50 Ω gives 119.2 Ω, which agrees with the cascade.

Answer: Zin = 119.2 Ω

(c)

The voltage transfer ratio is V2/V1 = RL/(A RL + B) = 200/387.5 = 0.5161. This follows because V2 = RL I2′, and V1 = (A RL + B) I2′. A check by division: 200 into 225 total in the last section gives 0.8889 at the shunt node, and the node to input ratio is 69.23/119.23 = 0.5806, so 0.8889 × 0.5806 = 0.5161. The gain below one reflects the series losses in N1 and N3 and the loading of the shunt branch.

Answer: Vo/Vin = 0.5161

(d)

The source delivers 100 V through its 30 Ω resistance into Zin, so the port voltage is Vin = 100 × 119.23/(30 + 119.23) = 100 × 0.79897 = 79.90 V. The load voltage is then Vo = 0.5161 × 79.90 = 41.24 V. The load power is Vo²/RL = 41.24²/200 = 8.50 W. The input port draws 79.90²/119.23 = 53.5 W, so only about 16 percent reaches the load, the rest being dissipated in the 50 Ω, 100 Ω and 25 Ω paths.

Answer: Vo = 41.24 V

Problem 4 [A1-019] Mutual inductance and coupled circuits

Two magnetically coupled coils form a small isolation transformer without a core of high permeability. Coil 1 has self-inductance L1 = 0.5 H and coil 2 has L2 = 0.2 H, with coupling coefficient k = 0.8. A 120 V rms, 60 Hz (ω = 377 rad/s) source feeds coil 1 through a series resistor of 10 Ω. Coil 2 supplies a 50 Ω resistive load and is otherwise lossless. The dot convention places a dot at the upper terminal of each coil; the source current I1 enters coil 1 at its dotted terminal, and the secondary current I2 is defined as entering coil 2 at its dotted terminal. Take the source as the phasor reference at 0°.

  1. (a) Find the mutual inductance M in henrys. [3]
  2. (b) Find the rms primary current magnitude |I1| in amperes. [6]
  3. (c) Find the rms secondary current magnitude |I2| in amperes. [5]
  4. (d) Find the average power delivered to the 50 Ω load, in watts. [6]
(a)

The mutual inductance is M = k √(L1 L2) = 0.8 √(0.5 × 0.2) = 0.8 √0.1 = 0.8 × 0.31623 = 0.2530 H. The coefficient k = 0.8 is below one, so there is leakage flux. The reactances at 377 rad/s are ωL1 = 188.5 Ω, ωL2 = 75.4 Ω and ωM = 95.37 Ω, which are used in the loop equations. The sign of the coupling terms depends on the dots, which here make both loop equations carry +jωM times the other current.

Answer: M = 0.2530 H

(b)

Write the two mesh equations with both currents entering the dotted terminals: 120 = (10 + j188.5) I1 + jωM I2, and 0 = jωM I1 + (50 + j75.4) I2. From the second, I2 = −jωM I1/(50 + j75.4). Substitute into the first: 120 = I1[(10 + j188.5) + (ωM)²/(50 + j75.4)]. The reflected impedance is 9095/(50 + j75.4) = 9095(50 − j75.4)/(2500 + 5685) = 55.6 − j83.8 Ω, so Zin = 65.6 + j104.7 Ω, with magnitude 123.5 Ω. Then |I1| = 120/123.5 = 0.9713 A.

Answer: |I1| = 0.9713 A

(c)

From the second mesh equation, |I2| = ωM |I1| / |50 + j75.4|. The numerator is 95.37 × 0.9713 = 92.64 V, and the denominator is √(2500 + 5685) = 90.47 Ω. So |I2| = 92.64/90.47 = 1.024 A. The secondary current is slightly larger than the primary, which is allowed since the primary drives a mostly inductive loop of high impedance. The phase of I2 relative to I1 is −90° − arctan(75.4/50) = −146.4°, about 34° short of the 180° of an ideal transformer.

Answer: |I2| = 1.024 A

(d)

The average power in the 50 Ω load is P = |I2|² R = 1.024² × 50 = 1.0485 × 50 = 52.4 W. Using the more precise current 1.02397 A gives 1.04858 × 50 = 52.43 W. Check by power balance: input real power is |I1|² × Re(Zin) = 0.9434 × 65.6 = 61.9 W, of which 0.9434 × 10 = 9.43 W is lost in the series 10 Ω, leaving 52.4 W for the load, so the coupling itself dissipates nothing.

Answer: P = 52.4 W

Problem 5 [A1-020] Circuit design to meet a response specification and what-if parameter change

A tuned pickup for a 5 kHz telemetry tone is to be built as a series RLC loop driven by an ideal voltage source. The inductor is a ferrite coil of L = 10 mH with an internal winding resistance of 4.0 Ω, treated as a resistor in series with an ideal inductance. The designer adds an external series resistor Rx and a capacitor C so that the loop current peaks at exactly 5.0 kHz and the half-power (3 dB) bandwidth of the current response is 400 Hz. After the circuit is built, the capacitor value is found to be 5 percent larger than the design value because of tolerance and temperature drift. Use series resonance relations to size the parts and to find the effect of the drift on the response.

  1. (a) Find the design capacitance C in nanofarads. [4]
  2. (b) Find the external resistance Rx in ohms needed to meet the 400 Hz bandwidth, allowing for the 4.0 Ω coil resistance. [5]
  3. (c) With C 5 percent too large, find the new resonant frequency in hertz. [5]
  4. (d) With the drifted circuit, find the ratio of the loop current at 5.0 kHz to the current at the circuit's own resonance (dimensionless). [6]
(a)

Resonance requires ω0 = 1/√(LC), so C = 1/(ω0² L). With f0 = 5000 Hz, ω0 = 2π × 5000 = 31 416 rad/s and ω0² = 9.8696×10⁸ rad²/s². Then C = 1/(9.8696×10⁸ × 0.010) = 1.0132×10⁻⁷ F = 101.3 nF. The standard-value neighbours would be 100 nF or 110 nF, and 100 nF would shift f0 to 5033 Hz, so a trimmer or a series pair would be needed. The coil resistance has no influence on this choice, because resonance depends only on L and C.

Answer: C = 101.3 nF

(b)

For a series RLC circuit the half-power bandwidth is BW = R_total/(2πL) in hertz. Solving, R_total = 2π × 400 × 0.010 = 25.13 Ω. The quality factor is then Q = f0/BW = 5000/400 = 12.5, and a check gives ω0L/R = 314.16/25.13 = 12.5. The coil already supplies 4.0 Ω, so the added resistor must be Rx = 25.13 − 4.0 = 21.13 Ω. A smaller resistor would give a narrower, higher-Q response that is more sensitive to drift.

Answer: Rx = 21.13 Ω

(c)

The new capacitance is C′ = 1.05 × 101.32 nF = 106.39 nF. Resonance moves to f′ = 1/(2π√(LC′)). Because f ∝ 1/√C, f′ = 5000/√1.05 = 5000/1.02470 = 4879.5 Hz. The shift is −120.5 Hz, which is 30 percent of the 400 Hz bandwidth. The tone at 5 kHz is therefore above the new resonance, on the upper skirt of the response, and is no longer at the current peak. Resistance and inductance are unchanged, so the bandwidth in hertz is still R_total/(2πL) = 400 Hz, while Q becomes ω0′L/R = 12.2.

Answer: f0′ = 4880 Hz

(d)

The current ratio relative to the peak is 1/√(1 + Q′²(f/f0′ − f0′/f)²), where Q′ = ω0′L/R_total is the quality factor of the drifted circuit: Q′ = 12.5/1.02470 = 12.198. Take f = 5000, f0′ = 4879.5: f/f0′ = 1.02470, f0′/f = 0.97590, difference 0.04880. Then Q′ × 0.04880 = 0.5953 and the ratio is 1/√(1 + 0.3544) = 0.8593. The drift costs about 1.3 dB at the tone frequency. This is why a high-Q tuned circuit needs a trimmer capacitor or a temperature-stable dielectric: a 5 percent change in C moved the peak by only 2.4 percent of the frequency, yet it cut the received tone by about 14 percent in amplitude.

Answer: Current ratio = 0.859

A1 Practice Paper 5

Problem 1 [A1-021] Equivalent circuits, series-parallel reduction and source transformations

A two-terminal resistor network is built into a sensor interface. Between terminal a and terminal b it contains the following elements. A 30 Ω resistor R1 connects terminal a to an internal node m. A 60 Ω resistor R2 connects node m directly to terminal b. A third branch also runs from node m to terminal b and consists of a fixed 20 Ω resistor R3 in series with an adjustable trimming resistor Rx. The cable that will be attached to the interface requires the network to present an input resistance of exactly 50 Ω looking into terminals a and b. Later the interface is driven by dc sources connected with their positive terminals to terminal a and their negative terminals to terminal b.

  1. (a) Design the trimming resistor Rx so that the resistance seen between a and b is 50 Ω. [5]
  2. (b) An ideal 40 V source is connected across a and b. Find the power it delivers. [3]
  3. (c) For the same 40 V ideal source, find the power dissipated in the trimming resistor Rx. [4]
  4. (d) The 40 V source is now replaced by a practical source made of a 40 V ideal source in series with a 10 Ω internal resistance. Find the current in the 60 Ω resistor R2. [4]
  5. (e) Replace the practical source of part (d) by its Norton equivalent. State the Norton current source value. [4]
(a)

Rab = R1 + [R2 || (R3 + Rx)]. For Rab = 50 Ω the parallel combination must equal 50 − 30 = 20 Ω. Let y = R3 + Rx be the branch resistance. Then 60y/(60 + y) = 20, so 60y = 1200 + 20y and y = 1200/40 = 30 Ω. Since R3 = 20 Ω is fixed, Rx = 30 − 20 = 10 Ω. Check: 60 || 30 = 1800/90 = 20 Ω, and 30 + 20 = 50 Ω. The reduction works because the parallel combination of two resistors is always smaller than the smaller one, so the 30 Ω series resistor leaves only 20 Ω to be made up by the parallel pair.

Answer: Rx = 10 Ω

(b)

With the 40 V ideal source directly across a and b and Rab = 50 Ω, the source current is I = V/Rab = 40/50 = 0.8 A. The source delivers P = V·I = 40 × 0.8 = 32 W. Equivalently the power equals V²/Rab = 1600/50 = 32 W. This must equal the total dissipation in all four resistors, which is checked in part (c): R1 takes 0.8² × 30 = 19.2 W and the parallel pair takes 0.8² × 20 = 12.8 W, giving 32 W in total. The ideal source has no internal loss, so all of its power appears in the network.

Answer: 32 W

(c)

The current 0.8 A enters node m through R1. The voltage across the parallel pair is Vm = 0.8 × 20 = 16 V, since the pair has an equivalent resistance of 20 Ω. The branch containing R3 and Rx has a total resistance of 30 Ω, so its current is 16/30 = 0.5333 A (the remaining 16/60 = 0.2667 A flows in R2, and 0.5333 + 0.2667 = 0.8 A as required). The power in Rx is P = I²Rx = 0.5333² × 10 = 2.844 W. This is a current-divider result: the branch with the smaller resistance carries the larger share of the current, two thirds in this case.

Answer: 2.84 W

(d)

The source with its internal resistance is a series circuit: total resistance seen by the ideal 40 V source is 10 + 50 = 60 Ω, so the terminal current is 40/60 = 0.6667 A. The voltage at node m relative to b is the current times the parallel equivalent: Vm = 0.6667 × 20 = 13.333 V. The current in R2 is Vm/R2 = 13.333/60 = 0.2222 A. This could also be found by a current divider: the share to the 60 Ω branch is 0.6667 × 30/(60 + 30) = 0.2222 A, which agrees. The internal resistance reduces every current by the factor 50/60.

Answer: 0.222 A

(e)

A source transformation turns a voltage source Vs in series with Rs into a current source Is = Vs/Rs in parallel with the same Rs. Here Is = 40/10 = 4 A, in parallel with 10 Ω, with the arrow pointing toward terminal a. Check by short-circuiting the terminals: the Thevenin form gives 40/10 = 4 A and the Norton form gives 4 A, and the open-circuit voltage of the Norton form is 4 × 10 = 40 V, matching the Thevenin source. The two forms are identical at the terminals, but not inside: with the terminals open the Thevenin source dissipates no power while the Norton resistor dissipates 4² × 10 = 160 W.

Answer: 4 A

Problem 2 [A1-022] Nodal analysis of resistive circuits with dependent sources

A transducer front end is modelled with two non-reference nodes, 1 and 2, and a reference node (ground). An ideal 5 mA current source injects current into node 1 from ground. A 2 kΩ resistor connects node 1 to ground. A 4 kΩ resistor connects node 1 to node 2. A 1 kΩ resistor connects node 2 to ground. A voltage-controlled current source, controlled by the voltage V1 of node 1 with respect to ground, injects a current g·V1 into node 2 from ground, where the transconductance g is to be chosen by the designer. The design requirement is that the output voltage at node 2 equals 4.00 V with respect to ground. Use the passive sign convention and take node voltages positive relative to ground.

  1. (a) Find the voltage V1 that node 1 must have when V2 is 4.00 V. [3]
  2. (b) Design the transconductance g that achieves V2 = 4.00 V. [5]
  3. (c) With this g, find the power delivered to the circuit by the dependent source. [4]
  4. (d) Find the power delivered by the independent 5 mA source. [3]
  5. (e) A production unit has g reduced by 20 percent to 0.300 mS. Find the resulting V2. [5]
(a)

Write KCL at node 1 with the currents leaving the node: 5 mA enters from the source, so 5 mA = V1/2 kΩ + (V1 − V2)/4 kΩ. With V2 = 4 V and working in mA and kΩ, 5 = V1/2 + (V1 − 4)/4. Multiply by 4: 20 = 2V1 + V1 − 4, so 3V1 = 24 and V1 = 8 V. Node 1 does not contain the dependent source, so its equation does not involve g, which is why it can be solved first and used to find the design value in part (b). A design target on an output node often lets one equation be solved independently.

Answer: V1 = 8 V

(b)

KCL at node 2, writing the currents leaving through resistors on the left and the injected source on the right: (V2 − V1)/4 kΩ + V2/1 kΩ = g·V1. With V1 = 8 V and V2 = 4 V: (4 − 8)/4 + 4/1 = −1 + 4 = 3 mA. The right side is g × 8 V, so g = 3 mA/8 V = 0.375 mS. The positive result means the source does inject current into node 2 as drawn, which is needed because the 4 kΩ resistor delivers 1 mA into node 2 from node 1 (V1 is larger than V2) and the 1 kΩ resistor needs 4 mA. The dependent source supplies the remaining 3 mA.

Answer: g = 0.375 mS

(c)

The dependent source injects g·V1 = 0.375 mS × 8 V = 3 mA into node 2, and node 2 sits at V2 = 4 V above ground. The current leaves the source at its terminal connected to node 2, which is the positive-potential terminal, so the source delivers power P = V2 × (g·V1) = 4 V × 3 mA = 12 mW. A dependent source can deliver or absorb power just like an independent one, and here it is an active element supplying energy. Energy check: in mA and kΩ units the 2 kΩ resistor dissipates 8²/2 = 32 mW, the 4 kΩ resistor (8 − 4)²/4 = 4 mW and the 1 kΩ resistor 4²/1 = 16 mW, a total of 52 mW, which equals 40 mW from the independent source plus 12 mW from the dependent source.

Answer: 12 mW

(d)

The independent source drives 5 mA into node 1, whose potential is V1 = 8 V above ground, so it delivers P = 8 V × 5 mA = 40 mW. The system energy balance is a useful check on the whole solution: the resistors dissipate in 2 kΩ: V1²/2000 = 64/2000 = 32 mW; in 4 kΩ: (8 − 4)²/4000 = 4 mW; in 1 kΩ: 4²/1000 = 16 mW. The total is 52 mW, equal to the 40 mW from the independent source plus the 12 mW from the dependent source. Tellegen's theorem requires the sum of delivered powers to equal the sum of absorbed powers.

Answer: 40 mW

(e)

Now g = 0.3 mS. Node 2 equation in mA and kΩ units: (V2 − V1)/4 + V2 = 0.3 V1, so 1.25 V2 = 0.55 V1 and V2 = 0.44 V1. Node 1 equation: 5 = V1/2 + (V1 − V2)/4 = 0.75 V1 − 0.25 V2. Substituting V2 = 0.44 V1: 5 = 0.75 V1 − 0.11 V1 = 0.64 V1, so V1 = 7.8125 V and V2 = 0.44 × 7.8125 = 3.4375 V. A 20 percent change in g produced a drop in V2 of about 14 percent from 4.00 V, so the output is quite sensitive to g, and a designer would specify a tolerance on g of well under 5 percent to hold V2 within a few percent.

Answer: V2 = 3.44 V

Problem 3 [A1-023] Mesh analysis and supermesh

A planar resistive network has three meshes side by side, numbered 1, 2 and 3 from left to right. Assign clockwise mesh currents I1, I2 and I3 in amperes. Mesh 1 has a 40 V source in its left branch with the positive terminal at the top, and a 5 Ω resistor in its top branch. Meshes 1 and 2 share a vertical branch that contains only an ideal 2 A current source pointing upward. Mesh 2 has a 10 Ω resistor in its top branch, and shares a vertical branch with mesh 3 that contains a 4 Ω resistor. Mesh 3 has a 6 Ω resistor in its top branch, and in its right branch a variable resistor Rx in series with a 16 V source whose positive terminal is at the lower end. All bottom branches are ideal wires. Mesh 3 is to carry 1.75 A clockwise.

  1. (a) Using a supermesh around meshes 1 and 2, find the mesh current I2 that is required when I3 = 1.75 A. [5]
  2. (b) Design Rx so that I3 = 1.75 A. [6]
  3. (c) Find the power delivered by the 2 A current source. [5]
  4. (d) Find the power dissipated in Rx. [4]
(a)

The current source lies in a branch shared by meshes 1 and 2, so its voltage is unknown and a supermesh is formed by the outer loop of meshes 1 and 2. In the shared branch mesh 2 flows upward and mesh 1 downward, so the constraint is I2 − I1 = 2, giving I1 = I2 − 2. The supermesh KVL clockwise, with rises written as negatives, is −40 + 5I1 + 10I2 + 4(I2 − I3) = 0. Substitute: −40 + 5I2 − 10 + 10I2 + 4I2 − 4(1.75) = 0, so 19I2 = 50 + 7 = 57 and I2 = 3.00 A. Then I1 = 1.00 A, which is positive, so the 40 V source supplies current in the assumed direction.

Answer: I2 = 3.00 A

(b)

Mesh 3 clockwise: the left branch of mesh 3 carries I3 upward through the 4 Ω resistor against I2, so the drop across it is 4(I3 − I2). Going clockwise, the right branch is traversed downward, entering the source at its negative upper terminal and leaving at the positive lower terminal, so the 16 V source is a rise. KVL: 6I3 + Rx·I3 − 16 + 4(I3 − I2) = 0. Substitute I3 = 1.75 and I2 = 3.00: 10.5 + 1.75Rx − 16 + 4(−1.25) = 0, so 1.75Rx = 10.5, and Rx = 6.00 Ω. Check: (6 + 6 + 4) × 1.75 = 28 V, and 16 + 4 × 3 = 28 V, so the equation balances.

Answer: Rx = 6.00 Ω

(c)

The voltage across the current source is found from a mesh that contains it. Use mesh 1, whose clockwise path goes down through the shared branch. Writing the voltage drop v across the current source in the downward direction: −40 + 5I1 + v = 0, so v = 40 − 5(1) = 35 V. The downward drop of 35 V means the top terminal is 35 V above the bottom terminal. The 2 A current flows upward, leaving the source through its more positive terminal, so it delivers P = 35 × 2 = 70 W. Check with mesh 2 going up through the source: −35 + 10I2 + 4(I2 − I3) = −35 + 30 + 5 = 0, which confirms v.

Answer: 70 W

(d)

The current in Rx is the mesh 3 current, 1.75 A, so the power dissipated is P = I²Rx = 1.75² × 6 = 3.0625 × 6 = 18.375 W. The power balance confirms the whole solution: the sources deliver 40 × 1 = 40 W from the 40 V source plus 70 W from the current source, and the 16 V source supplies 16 × 1.75 = 28 W, a total of 138 W. The resistors absorb 5(1)² + 10(3)² + 4(1.25)² + 6(1.75)² + 18.375 = 5 + 90 + 6.25 + 18.375 + 18.375 = 138 W. Equal totals show the design is consistent.

Answer: 18.4 W

Problem 4 [A1-024] Thevenin and Norton equivalents and maximum power transfer

An instrument power stage feeds a variable load resistor RL across terminals a and b. Looking back from these terminals the circuit is as follows. A 60 V ideal source has its positive terminal connected through a 20 Ω resistor to terminal a, and its negative terminal connected to terminal b. A 30 Ω resistor connects terminal a to terminal b. An ideal 1.5 A current source is connected between b and a and drives its current from b into a. The load RL is connected between a and b. The load resistor can be chosen by the designer, and the loading specification is that the load must receive at least 50 W.

  1. (a) Find the open-circuit voltage Voc between a and b with the load removed. [4]
  2. (b) Find the Thevenin resistance Rth seen at a and b. [3]
  3. (c) Find the Norton (short-circuit) current from a to b. [3]
  4. (d) Find the maximum power that any load can receive and the matching load value. State the maximum power. [4]
  5. (e) The load must receive at least 50 W. Find the largest load resistance that still meets this specification. [6]
(a)

With the load removed, there is one non-reference node a. KCL at a, taking currents leaving through the resistors and the 1.5 A source entering: (Va − 60)/20 + Va/30 = 1.5. Multiply by 60: 3(Va − 60) + 2Va = 90, so 5Va = 270 and Va = 54 V. Since b is the reference, Voc = 54 V. This is less than 60 V because the 20 Ω and 30 Ω resistors divide the source, which would alone give 36 V, and the current source adds 1.5 A × 12 Ω = 18 V through the parallel combination, so 36 + 18 = 54 V, which agrees with superposition.

Answer: Voc = 54 V

(b)

To find Rth, deactivate the independent sources: replace the 60 V source with a short circuit and the ideal current source with an open circuit. The 20 Ω resistor is then connected from a to b through the short, in parallel with the 30 Ω resistor. Rth = 20 × 30/(20 + 30) = 600/50 = 12 Ω. No dependent sources are present, so this direct reduction is valid. A check follows in part (c): Voc/Isc should give the same Rth. A designer needs Rth because it fixes the optimum load and the way the delivered power varies with the load.

Answer: Rth = 12 Ω

(c)

Short-circuit terminals a and b. Then Va = 0, the 30 Ω resistor carries no current, and the current from the 60 V source through the 20 Ω resistor is 60/20 = 3 A from a toward b. The current source adds 1.5 A entering a, which also must leave through the short. The short-circuit current from a to b is 3 + 1.5 = 4.5 A. Check: Voc/Rth = 54/12 = 4.5 A, which matches. The Norton equivalent is therefore a 4.5 A current source in parallel with 12 Ω, equivalent to a 54 V Thevenin source in series with 12 Ω.

Answer: Isc = 4.5 A

(d)

Maximum power transfer to a variable resistive load occurs when RL = Rth = 12 Ω. At this load the voltage across RL is half of Voc, 27 V, and the load current is 54/(12 + 12) = 2.25 A. The power is P = Voc²/(4Rth) = 54²/(4 × 12) = 2916/48 = 60.75 W. At the matched condition the source resistance dissipates an equal 60.75 W, so the efficiency of the Thevenin source is only 50 percent. Matching is therefore used where signal power matters, not where energy efficiency matters, as in power distribution.

Answer: Pmax = 60.75 W at RL = 12 Ω

(e)

The load power for a Thevenin source is P = Voc²·RL/(Rth + RL)². Setting P = 50 W: 2916 RL = 50(12 + RL)², which gives 50RL² + 1200RL + 7200 − 2916 RL = 0, or 50RL² − 1716RL + 7200 = 0. Then RL = [1716 ± √(1716² − 4 × 50 × 7200)]/100 = [1716 ± √1 504 656]/100 = (1716 ± 1226.6)/100, giving RL = 29.43 Ω or 4.89 Ω. Because the load power exceeds 50 W for loads between these two values (it peaks at 12 Ω), the largest load meeting the specification is 29.4 Ω, and the smallest is 4.89 Ω.

Answer: RL(max) = 29.4 Ω

Problem 5 [A1-025] Superposition and linearity in circuits with several sources

A summing node X in a sensor readout is connected to ground (the reference) through a 12 kΩ resistor. A 12 V ideal source in series with a 4 kΩ resistor feeds node X. An ideal 2 mA current source injects its current into node X from ground. A third feeder consists of an adjustable ideal voltage source Vs in series with a 6 kΩ resistor, connected to node X, with Vs measured with respect to ground. The output is the node voltage Vx. The designer must choose Vs so that Vx = 16.0 V. Use the principle of superposition to build the answer, treating each source separately, and note that voltage sources are replaced by short circuits and current sources by open circuits when they are turned off.

  1. (a) Find the contribution to Vx of the 12 V source acting alone. [3]
  2. (b) Find the contribution to Vx of the 2 mA current source acting alone. [3]
  3. (c) Design Vs so that Vx = 16.0 V. [6]
  4. (d) With this design, find the current supplied by the Vs source. [4]
  5. (e) Find the power dissipated in the 12 kΩ resistor. Then explain why adding the powers from each single-source case gives a different, incorrect value. [4]
(a)

With only the 12 V source active, the 2 mA source is open and Vs is shorted. Node X sees the 12 kΩ and 6 kΩ resistors to ground in parallel, which is 4 kΩ, in a voltage divider with the 4 kΩ series resistor. Vx1 = 12 × 4/(4 + 4) = 6 V. A check by currents: the source current is 12 V/(4 + 4) kΩ = 1.5 mA, and the drop across the 4 kΩ parallel pair is 1.5 mA × 4 kΩ = 6 V, which agrees. Because the circuit is linear, this contribution is independent of the other sources and remains exactly 6 V when they are present.

Answer: 6 V

(b)

With only the current source active, both voltage sources are replaced by short circuits, so the 4 kΩ, 6 kΩ and 12 kΩ resistors all connect from X to ground in parallel. Their conductance is 0.25 + 0.1667 + 0.0833 = 0.5 mS, so the equivalent resistance is 2 kΩ. Vx2 = 2 mA × 2 kΩ = 4 V. The current source sets the current, not the voltage, so it is replaced by an open circuit when it is turned off in the other cases. This contribution is again independent of every other source in the linear circuit.

Answer: 4 V

(c)

With only Vs active, the 12 V source is shorted and the current source is open. The 4 kΩ and 12 kΩ resistors in parallel give 3 kΩ, so Vx3 = Vs × 3/(6 + 3) = Vs/3. Superposition gives Vx = 6 + 4 + Vs/3 = 10 + Vs/3. Setting Vx = 16 V: Vs/3 = 6, so Vs = 18 V. Check with a node equation in mA and kΩ: (Vx − 12)/4 + Vx/12 + (Vx − 18)/6 = 2 gives (4/4) + 16/12 + (−2/6) = 1 + 1.3333 − 0.3333 = 2.0 mA, which confirms the design.

Answer: Vs = 18 V

(d)

The current from the Vs source flows through the 6 kΩ resistor into node X, so it equals (Vs − Vx)/6 kΩ = (18 − 16)/6 = 0.3333 mA. This is positive, so Vs does supply current into the node and delivers 18 V × 0.3333 mA = 6 mW. For the other sources, the 12 V source supplies (12 − 16)/4 = −1 mA, meaning it absorbs current, and the current source supplies 2 mA. The currents entering X are −1 + 2 + 0.3333 = 1.3333 mA, which equals the current Vx/12 kΩ = 1.3333 mA leaving through the 12 kΩ resistor.

Answer: 0.333 mA

(e)

The actual voltage across the 12 kΩ resistor is Vx = 16 V, so P = Vx²/R = 256/12 000 = 21.33 mW. Using the single-source voltages 6 V, 4 V and 6 V, the powers would be 36/12 + 16/12 + 36/12 = 7.33 mW in the same units. The sum is wrong because power is quadratic in voltage: (6 + 4 + 6)² = 256, whereas 6² + 4² + 6² = 88. The cross terms 2(6 × 4 + 6 × 6 + 4 × 6) = 168 are missing. Superposition applies to linear quantities, voltage and current, but not to power, which must be calculated from the total voltage or current.

Answer: P = 21.3 mW

A1 Practice Paper 6

Problem 1 [A1-026] Ideal inductors and capacitors, energy storage and lumped models

An airport runway strobe uses a capacitor bank as its energy store. The bank is ideal and is charged to 330 V. Each flash discharges the bank through the lamp down to 270 V, and the energy released in one flash must be 40 J. After each flash the bank is recharged from 270 V back to 330 V by a charger that supplies a constant current of 0.50 A. The charger is a boost converter whose energy-transfer element is an ideal 5.0 mH inductor, fed from a 24 V supply. In each switching cycle the inductor current is ramped from zero to a peak of 40 A with the full 24 V across it, and then all of the stored inductor energy is passed to the capacitor bank without loss.

  1. (a) Design the capacitance C of the bank that releases 40 J when its voltage falls from 330 V to 270 V. [5]
  2. (b) Find the total energy stored in the bank at 330 V. [3]
  3. (c) Find the time needed for the 0.50 A constant-current charger to restore the voltage from 270 V to 330 V. [4]
  4. (d) Find the time for the inductor current to ramp from zero to 40 A with 24 V across it. [4]
  5. (e) Find the number of switching cycles needed to deliver the 40 J that replaces one flash, if each cycle transfers the full inductor energy. [4]
(a)

The energy stored in a capacitor is W = ½CV². The energy released between two voltages is ΔW = ½C(V1² − V2²) = ½C(330² − 270²) = ½C(108 900 − 72 900) = 18 000C joules, with C in farads. Setting 18 000C = 40 gives C = 40/18 000 = 2.222 × 10⁻³ F, which is 2.22 mF. Only part of the stored energy is used in each flash, because a capacitor discharging below about 80 percent of its voltage would make the lamp dim, so a bank sized for the full stored energy would be larger and more costly than the one required.

Answer: C = 2.22 mF

(b)

With C = 2.2222 mF, the energy at the full voltage is W = ½CV² = 0.5 × 2.2222 × 10⁻³ × 330² = 0.5 × 2.2222 × 10⁻³ × 108 900 = 121 J. The energy remaining after a flash is 0.5 × 2.2222 × 10⁻³ × 72 900 = 81 J. The difference, 121 − 81 = 40 J, is the energy of the flash, as the specification requires. The capacitor therefore holds 121 J in total but only one third of this is used per flash, which is a consequence of the voltage swing being limited to about 18 percent.

Answer: 121 J

(c)

The capacitor current is i = C dv/dt. For a constant current of 0.50 A the voltage rises linearly, so the charging time is t = C ΔV/I = 2.2222 × 10⁻³ × (330 − 270)/0.50 = 2.2222 × 10⁻³ × 60/0.5 = 0.2667 s. The average charging power is 40 J/0.2667 s = 150 W, which is the supply power that the converter must provide ideally. This also sets the maximum flash rate of the strobe at about 3.75 flashes per second, since the bank cannot be recharged faster with this constant current.

Answer: t = 0.267 s

(d)

For an ideal inductor v = L di/dt. With a constant 24 V across the inductor the current rises linearly from zero, so t = L I/V = 5 × 10⁻³ × 40/24 = 8.333 × 10⁻³ s = 8.33 ms. The energy stored at the peak is ½LI² = 0.5 × 5 × 10⁻³ × 40² = 4 J. At the end of the ramp the current is continuous, so when the converter opens the switch the inductor current of 40 A must flow into the capacitor bank. An inductor current cannot change instantly, which is the fact the converter depends on.

Answer: t = 8.33 ms

(e)

Each switching cycle transfers the full inductor energy, ½LI² = 4 J, as found in part (d). The flash removed 40 J, so the number of cycles to replace it is 40 J/4 J = 10. This takes 10 × 8.33 ms = 83 ms of ramp time, much shorter than the 0.267 s taken by the constant-current charger, so the inductor stage could recharge faster than the specified 0.50 A charger allows. In practice the cycle count is increased by about 10 to 20 percent to cover switch and diode losses, which were assumed zero here.

Answer: 10 cycles

Problem 2 [A1-027] First-order RC and RL transients with switching

A control relay coil is modelled as an ideal 0.80 H inductor in series with a 40 Ω winding resistance. It is energised from a 24 V dc supply through a series resistor Rs by closing a switch at t = 0, with zero initial current.
