This is the frequency at which the circuit would oscillate if R were zero. It sets the time scale of the response, and the damping ratio then determines how much of the ringing remains. The time for one undamped cycle is 2π/ω0 = 6.28 ms.

Answer: 1000 rad/s

(b)

The attenuation constant is α = R/(2L) = 10/(2 × 0.020) = 250 s⁻¹. The damping ratio is ζ = α/ω0 = 250/1000 = 0.250. Equivalently, ζ = (R/2)√(C/L) = 5 × √(50 × 10⁻⁶/0.020) = 5 × 0.05 = 0.25. Since ζ is less than 1, the response is underdamped, with a damped natural frequency ωd = ω0 √(1 - ζ²) = 968 rad/s, and the capacitor voltage will ring about its final value of 12 V. Each successive peak is smaller than the last by the factor e-2πζ/√(1-ζ²) = 0.197.

Answer: 0.250

(c)

For a second-order underdamped step response the fractional overshoot is Mp = exp(-π ζ/√(1 - ζ²)). With ζ = 0.25, √(1 - 0.0625) = 0.9682, so the exponent is -π × 0.25/0.9682 = -0.8112. Then Mp = e-0.8112 = 0.4443, which is 44.4 percent overshoot. The peak capacitor voltage is therefore 12 × 1.444 = 17.3 V, which may exceed the voltage rating of the capacitor or the load. This explains why the design engineer wants to see the overshoot before choosing R.

Answer: 44.4 percent

(d)

Overshoot of 20 percent means Mp = 0.20, so ζ = -ln(Mp)/√(π² + ln²(Mp)). With ln(0.2) = -1.6094, the numerator is 1.6094 and the denominator is √(9.8696 + 2.5903) = 3.5299, so ζ = 0.4559. Because ζ = (R/2)√(C/L) = R/40, the resistance is R = 40 ζ = 40 × 0.4559 = 18.2 Ω. The measured value therefore means the real circuit has about 8 Ω more series resistance than the nominal design, for example from a long cable or the winding resistance, and the engineer should account for it.

Answer: 18.2 Ω

(e)

Critical damping occurs at ζ = 1, which is the same as R = 2√(L/C). With L/C = 0.020/(50 × 10⁻⁶) = 400, the square root is 20 Ω, so R = 40.0 Ω. At this value the two roots coincide at s = -α = -1000 s⁻¹ and the step response has no overshoot while giving the fastest non-oscillatory rise. A resistance above 40 Ω gives an overdamped, slower response, while one below it rings, with the overshoot given by the formula used above.

Answer: 40.0 Ω

Problem 4 [A1-049] Sinusoidal steady state with phasors

A 120 V rms, 60 Hz source with phase angle 0° feeds a lighting panel through a feeder of 5.0 Ω resistance, from source terminal a to node b. At node b the load is two parallel branches connected to the return conductor, which is the reference. Branch 1 is a coil with resistance 20 Ω in series with an inductance of 30 mH. Branch 2 is a power-factor correction capacitor of 100 μF. The return conductor is ideal and the source is ideal. Voltages and currents are given as rms phasors. The electrician wants to know what the capacitor is doing to the feeder current, so each answer is compared with the case in which the capacitor is removed.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the impedance of the parallel combination at node b. [4]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the voltage at node b. [4]
  3. (c) Find the phase angle of the voltage at node b relative to the source. [3]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the feeder current. [4]
  5. (e) Find the feeder current magnitude if the capacitor is removed. [5]
(a)

At 60 Hz, ω = 2π × 60 = 376.99 rad/s. The coil impedance is Z1 = 20 + j ω L = 20 + j 11.31 Ω, and the capacitor impedance is Z2 = 1/(jωC) = -j 26.53 Ω. The admittances add: Y1 = 1/Z1 = (20 - j11.31)/527.9 = 0.03789 - j0.02143 S, and Y2 = j0.03770 S. The total is Y = 0.03789 + j0.01627 S, with magnitude 0.04123 S. So |Zp| = 1/0.04123 = 24.25 Ω, at an angle of about -23.2°, so the combination is capacitive (the capacitor current exceeds the coil's reactive current).

Answer: 24.25 Ω

(b)

The parallel impedance in rectangular form is Zp = 24.25 ∠-23.2° = 22.28 - j9.56 Ω. The total series impedance seen by the source is 5 + Zp = 27.28 - j9.56 Ω, with magnitude 28.91 Ω. The current is I = 120∠0°/28.91∠-19.3° = 4.150 ∠19.3° A. The voltage at b is Vb = I × Zp = 4.150 × 24.25 = 100.65 V. The voltage is lower than the source because of the drop in the feeder, which is why a voltage at b of about 100.7 V is expected.

Answer: 100.7 V

(c)

The phase of Vb is the phase of the current plus the phase of Zp. The total impedance angle is arctan(-9.56/27.28) = -19.3°, so the current leads the source voltage by 19.3°. Adding the angle of Zp, -23.2°, the phase of Vb is 19.3° - 23.2° = -3.9°, more exactly -3.91°. The load voltage lags the source slightly, because the feeder drop has a component in quadrature with the load voltage. Phase angles are measured relative to the source reference of 0°.

Answer: -3.91°

(d)

From part b the magnitude of the total impedance is |5 + Zp| = √(27.28² + 9.56²) = 28.91 Ω. The feeder current is the source voltage divided by this, so I = 120/28.91 = 4.15 A rms. A check by the power balance: the real power in the feeder is I² × 5 = 86.1 W, and the active power in the coil is I_coil² × 20, with I_coil = Vb/|Z1| = 100.65/22.98 = 4.38 A, so 383.6 W. The total of about 470 W matches 120 × 4.15 × cos(19.3°) = 470 W.

Answer: 4.15 A

(e)

Without the capacitor only the coil remains, so the total impedance is 5 + 20 + j11.31 = 25 + j11.31 Ω with magnitude √(625 + 127.9) = 27.44 Ω. The feeder current is 120/27.44 = 4.37 A, larger than the 4.15 A with the capacitor in place. The capacitor supplies part of the reactive current that the coil needs, so the feeder carries less current for the same real power, reducing the voltage drop and the feeder loss. The current falls about 5 percent, a modest improvement because 100 μF compensates only a part of the coil's reactive power.

Answer: 4.37 A

Problem 5 [A1-050] AC power, complex power and power factor correction

A machine shop in Ontario is fed from a single-phase 600 V, 60 Hz supply, treated as constant at the load terminals. The load draws 150 kW at a lagging power factor of 0.72. The feeder between the transformer and the load has a total resistance of 0.050 Ω and negligible reactance. The plant manager considers installing a capacitor bank across the load to raise the power factor to 0.95 lagging, and also expects the load to grow. Treat the load as a constant real power and constant reactive power, and ignore the loss in the capacitor bank itself. Keep three significant figures in the answers.

  1. (a) Find the reactive power of the load before correction. [3]
  2. (b) Find the reactive power rating of the capacitor bank needed for a power factor of 0.95 lagging. [4]
  3. (c) Find the capacitance of that bank at 600 V and 60 Hz. [4]
  4. (d) Find the reduction in feeder I²R loss that results from the correction. [4]
  5. (e) The real load later grows to 190 kW at the same 0.72 lagging power factor, with the bank from part b still in place. Find the new power factor. [5]
(a)

The power factor of 0.72 gives a phase angle θ = arccos(0.72) = 43.95°, and tan θ = 0.9639. The reactive power is Q = P tan θ = 150 × 0.9639 = 144.6 kvar. The apparent power is S = P/pf = 150/0.72 = 208.3 kVA. The complex power of the load is therefore S = 150 + j144.6 kVA. A lagging power factor means the load is inductive and absorbs reactive power, as expected for an induction-motor load in a machine shop.

Answer: 144.6 kvar

(b)

The target power factor of 0.95 gives θ2 = arccos(0.95) = 18.19°, with tan θ2 = 0.3287. The real power does not change, so the reactive power after correction is Q2 = 150 × 0.3287 = 49.3 kvar. The capacitor bank must supply the difference: Qc = 144.6 - 49.3 = 95.3 kvar. After correction the apparent power is S = 150/0.95 = 157.9 kVA, down from 208.3 kVA, so the transformer and feeder have capacity released for additional load.

Answer: 95.3 kvar

(c)

A capacitor bank across a voltage V supplies Qc = V² ω C, so C = Qc/(ω V²). With Qc = 95 275 var, ω = 2π × 60 = 376.99 rad/s and V² = 360 000 V², C = 95 275/(376.99 × 360 000) = 7.02 × 10⁻⁴ F = 702 μF. Its reactance is 1/(ωC) = 3.78 Ω, and the current drawn by the bank is 95 275/600 = 158.8 A. In a real installation, the bank would be split into switched steps, because a fixed bank would overcorrect when the motors are lightly loaded.

Answer: 702 μF

(d)

The feeder current before correction is I1 = P/(V pf) = 150 000/(600 × 0.72) = 347.2 A, so the feeder loss is I1² R = 347.2² × 0.050 = 6.03 kW. After correction the current is I2 = 150 000/(600 × 0.95) = 263.2 A, with loss 263.2² × 0.050 = 3.46 kW. The reduction is 6.03 - 3.46 = 2.57 kW. This is the saving on the feeder only, and it is paid for by the supply of reactive power locally rather than from the transformer. The loss falls by 42.6 percent, the square of the current ratio 0.72/0.95.

Answer: 2.57 kW

(e)

With the bank in place and unchanged, the net reactive power is the new load reactive power minus the bank rating. For 190 kW at pf 0.72, Q = 190 × 0.9639 = 183.1 kvar, and the net Q = 183.1 - 95.3 = 87.8 kvar. The apparent power is S = √(190² + 87.8²) = 209.3 kVA. The power factor is 190/209.3 = 0.908 lagging, a little lower than the 0.95 achieved at 150 kW. The bank no longer fully corrects the larger load, so a further step of about 25 kvar will be needed to restore 0.95.

Answer: 0.908 lagging

A1 Practice Paper 11

Problem 1 [A1-051] Frequency response, resonance and quality factor

A technician is troubleshooting the front-end filter of an intermediate-frequency stage in a portable receiver. The filter is a series RLC loop driven by a voltage source of negligible internal resistance, and the output is taken as the current in the loop (equivalently, the voltage across the resistor). The loop contains a coil of inductance L = 250 μH, a capacitor of C = 470 pF and a total series resistance R = 12 Ω that includes the coil losses. The bench shows the stage is slightly off tune and too broad. Treat all elements as ideal apart from the stated resistance, and use the exact series-resonance relations. The technician then tries two changes, one at a time, to see what each does to the response.

  1. (a) Find the resonant frequency f0, the quality factor Q and the half-power bandwidth for the circuit as built. [6]
  2. (b) The technician replaces the capacitor by one that is 10 percent larger (517 pF). Find how far the resonant frequency moves, as a positive shift in kHz. [6]
  3. (c) With the original capacitor restored, a corroded joint adds 8 Ω of series resistance. Find the new bandwidth in kHz. [8]
(a)

For a series RLC loop, resonance occurs when the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, so f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)). With L = 250 μH and C = 470 pF, LC = 1.175 × 10⁻¹³ s², so √(LC) = 3.428 × 10⁻⁷ s and f0 = 1/(2π × 3.428 × 10⁻⁷) = 464.3 kHz. The quality factor of a series circuit is Q = ω0 L / R, where ω0 = 2π f0 = 2.917 × 10⁶ rad/s. Then ω0 L = 729.3 Ω and Q = 729.3/12 = 60.8. The half-power bandwidth is B = f0/Q = 464.3/60.78 = 7.64 kHz. This is also R/(2πL), which is independent of C, a useful cross-check: 12/(2π × 250 × 10⁻⁶) = 7639 Hz.

Answer: f0 = 464.3 kHz, Q = 60.8, B = 7.64 kHz; answer for the part: f0 = 464.3 kHz

(b)

Because f0 varies as 1/√C, a 10 percent increase in C multiplies f0 by 1/√1.1 = 0.9535. The new resonant frequency is therefore 464.3 × 0.95346 = 442.7 kHz. The shift is 464.30 - 442.70 = 21.6 kHz downward. Note that the shift is slightly less than the 5 percent (23.2 kHz) that a first-order estimate (half the fractional change in C) would give, because the exact square-root dependence is used. Since the bandwidth is 7.64 kHz, this detuning of 21.6 kHz is nearly three bandwidths, which means a signal formerly at the filter centre would now sit far down the skirt of the response. The assumptions are an ideal capacitor with no extra loss and unchanged inductance and resistance.

Answer: 21.6 kHz

(c)

The bandwidth of a series resonant circuit is B = R/(2πL) in hertz, and it depends only on the total series resistance and the inductance, not on C. With the added corrosion the total resistance is R = 12 + 8 = 20 Ω. Then B = 20/(2π × 250 × 10⁻⁶) = 20/(1.5708 × 10⁻³) = 12.73 kHz. The resonant frequency is unchanged at 464.3 kHz because it does not depend on R, so the new quality factor is Q = 464.3/12.73 = 36.5. The extra loss therefore widens the passband by a factor 20/12 = 1.667 and lowers the peak current at resonance from V/12 to V/20. This explains the symptom of a broad, weak response and shows that a high-resistance contact is a loss mechanism, not a tuning error.

Answer: 12.73 kHz

Problem 2 [A1-052] Transfer functions and Bode magnitude of passive circuits

A sensor signal conditioner uses a passive RC network as an anti-alias filter. A source of voltage vs drives the input node through a series resistor R1 = 4.7 kΩ. At the output node, a capacitor C = 22 nF is connected between the output node and ground, and a load resistor RL is also connected between the output node and ground, so the capacitor and load are in parallel. The output voltage is the voltage across the load. The designer has computed the response with RL = 10 kΩ, but the circuit will now be connected to a different data-acquisition board whose input resistance is only 2.2 kΩ. Treat the source as ideal and the capacitor as lossless. Frequencies are in hertz and gains are expressed as voltage ratios in decibels, 20 log10 of the magnitude.

  1. (a) With RL = 10 kΩ, find the low-frequency (dc) gain in dB and the corner frequency in Hz of the transfer function Vout/Vs. Give the corner frequency as the answer. [7]
  2. (b) With RL = 2.2 kΩ, find the dc gain in dB. [5]
  3. (c) With RL = 2.2 kΩ, find the gain in dB at 2 kHz, using the exact magnitude of the transfer function. [8]
(a)

Replace the source, R1 and the load by a Thevenin view of the capacitor. The transfer function is H(s) = [RL/(R1+RL)] / (1 + sC·(R1‖RL)). With RL = 10 kΩ the dc gain is 10/(4.7+10) = 0.6803, which is 20 log10(0.6803) = -3.35 dB. The parallel resistance seen by the capacitor is R1‖RL = 4.7 × 10/14.7 = 3.197 kΩ. The corner (break) frequency is fc = 1/(2π × 3197 × 22 × 10⁻⁹) = 2263 Hz. Above fc the magnitude falls at 20 dB per decade, and the gain at fc is 3 dB below the dc value, so about -6.35 dB there. The corner is where the denominator real and imaginary parts are equal.

Answer: dc gain -3.35 dB; fc = 2263 Hz

(b)

With RL = 2.2 kΩ the divider ratio is RL/(R1+RL) = 2.2/(4.7+2.2) = 2.2/6.9 = 0.3188. The dc gain is 20 log10(0.3188) = -9.93 dB, which is 6.58 dB lower than the original design because the load now draws far more current through R1. At dc the capacitor is an open circuit, so only the resistive divider matters, and this is the first thing a candidate should check when a load changes. The consequence is a signal that is about 47 percent of its former amplitude (0.3188/0.6803 = 0.469) before any filtering action even begins.

Answer: -9.93 dB

(c)

The new parallel resistance is R1‖RL = 4.7 × 2.2/6.9 = 1.4986 kΩ. The corner frequency moves up to fc = 1/(2π × 1498.6 × 22 × 10⁻⁹) = 4828 Hz, so the filter is now wider, as well as weaker. The magnitude at f = 2000 Hz is |H| = 0.3188/√(1 + (f/fc)²) = 0.3188/√(1 + (2000/4828)²) = 0.3188/√(1.1716) = 0.3188/1.0824 = 0.2945. In decibels this is 20 log10(0.2945) = -10.62 dB. Compared with the old design at 2 kHz (about -5.85 dB) the signal is 4.8 dB smaller while the corner moved away from the alias band, so the new loading is bad on both counts.

Answer: -10.62 dB

Problem 3 [A1-053] Impulse response and convolution in circuits

A series RC circuit is used as a smoothing stage in a timing circuit. The input voltage vin(t) is applied across the series combination of a resistor R = 10 kΩ followed by a capacitor C = 2 μF, and the output vout(t) is taken across the capacitor. The capacitor is initially uncharged and the circuit is linear and time invariant. A single rectangular pulse of height 5 V and duration 30 ms starting at t = 0 is applied. A technician suspects the smoothing is too strong and proposes replacing the capacitor with a 0.5 μF unit. Use the impulse-response and convolution method to compare the two cases, and treat the voltage source as ideal with zero internal resistance.

  1. (a) Find the impulse response h(t) for the original circuit and state its value at t = 0+ in s⁻¹. [4]
  2. (b) Find the peak output voltage at the end of the pulse for the original 2 μF capacitor. [5]
  3. (c) Find the peak output voltage at the end of the pulse if the capacitor is replaced by 0.5 μF. [5]
  4. (d) For the original circuit, find the time after the pulse ends for the output to decay to 0.1 V, in ms. [6]
(a)

For the voltage across the capacitor, the transfer function is H(s) = 1/(1 + sRC), so the impulse response is h(t) = (1/τ) e-t/τ u(t) with τ = RC = 10 × 10³ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.020 s. The initial value is h(0+) = 1/τ = 1/0.020 = 50 s⁻¹. The units are 1/s because an impulse of area one volt-second applied to the circuit produces an output voltage, and the area under h(t) is one, which gives a dc gain of unity. This confirms the output eventually follows a long constant input, and shows that the time constant controls how quickly a pulse is smoothed.

Answer: h(t) = 50 e-50t u(t); h(0+) = 50 s⁻¹

(b)

The output is the convolution y(t) = ∫ x(λ) h(t - λ) dλ. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 0.03 s the input is a constant 5 V, so y(t) = 5 ∫₀ᵗ (1/τ) e-(t-λ)/τ dλ = 5(1 - e-t/τ). At the end of the pulse t = 0.03 s, t/τ = 1.5, so y(0.03) = 5(1 - e-1.5) = 5(1 - 0.22313) = 3.884 V. This is the peak value because for t beyond 30 ms the input is zero and the output can only decay. The result is also the step response of the circuit evaluated at 30 ms, which a candidate should recognise as a valid shortcut for a pulse that is long enough to start at t = 0.

Answer: 3.88 V

(c)

With C = 0.5 μF the time constant becomes τ = 10 × 10³ × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ = 5 ms. The same convolution result applies for 0 ≤ t ≤ 30 ms, y(t) = 5(1 - e-t/τ), but now t/τ = 30/5 = 6 at the end of the pulse. Then y(0.03) = 5(1 - e-6) = 5(1 - 0.002479) = 4.988 V. The output almost reaches the full 5 V pulse height. The conclusion is that the smaller capacitor smooths much less: the pulse is reproduced almost faithfully, with rise time of about 2.2τ = 11 ms instead of 44 ms, so if the aim is to preserve pulse shape the technician's suspicion is correct.

Answer: 4.99 V

(d)

After the pulse ends the input is zero and the capacitor discharges through R, so y(t) = y(0.03) e-(t - 0.03)/τ for t > 0.03 s, with the original τ = 20 ms and y(0.03) = 3.884 V. Set the output equal to 0.1 V: 0.1 = 3.884 e-Δt/τ, so Δt = τ ln(3.884/0.1) = 0.020 × ln(38.84) = 0.020 × 3.659 = 0.0732 s, or 73.2 ms. This is about 3.66 time constants. The result is the time the original circuit needs to settle to within 0.1 V, which is relevant if the next pulse is expected to arrive soon after the first, as leftover charge would add to the next pulse by superposition.

Answer: 73.2 ms

Problem 4 [A1-054] Differential equation formulation and solution for circuits

A series RLC circuit is used to drive a small solenoid driver and is switched onto a 24 V dc source at t = 0. The loop contains, in series, a switch, a resistor R, an inductor L = 50 mH and a capacitor C = 20 μF. The inductor current and capacitor voltage are both zero immediately before the switch closes. The output of interest is the capacitor voltage vc(t) for t > 0. The design resistance is R = 40 Ω, but field reports say the output rings badly, so the engineer wants to see what happens at other resistance values. Derive the differential equation for vc(t) from Kirchhoff's voltage law and use the standard second-order form, treating the source as ideal.

  1. (a) For R = 40 Ω find the damping ratio ζ and the damped natural frequency ωd in rad/s. Give ωd as the answer value. [5]
  2. (b) For R = 40 Ω find the percentage overshoot of the capacitor voltage in its step response. [5]
  3. (c) Find the resistance that gives critical damping. [4]
  4. (d) For R = 200 Ω, find the slower of the two real time constants of the response in ms. [6]
(a)

Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop gives L di/dt + R i + vc = Vs, and with i = C dvc/dt this becomes LC d²vc/dt² + RC dvc/dt + vc = Vs. Divide by LC to compare with d²v/dt² + 2α dv/dt + ω0² v = ω0² Vs. Then ω0 = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(0.05 × 20 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/√(10⁻⁶) = 1000 rad/s, and α = R/(2L) = 40/0.1 = 400 s⁻¹. The damping ratio is ζ = α/ω0 = 0.4. The circuit is underdamped, and the damped frequency is ωd = ω0 √(1 - ζ²) = 1000 √(1 - 0.16) = 1000 × 0.9165 = 916.5 rad/s.

Answer: ζ = 0.4; ωd = 916.5 rad/s

(b)

For an underdamped second-order step response the percentage overshoot depends only on the damping ratio: %OS = 100 exp(-π ζ/√(1 - ζ²)). With ζ = 0.4, ζ/√(1 - ζ²) = 0.4/0.9165 = 0.4364, and π × 0.4364 = 1.371. Then exp(-1.371) = 0.2538, so the overshoot is 25.4 percent. The peak capacitor voltage is therefore 24 × 1.254 = 30.1 V, well above the supply, which is why the ringing reported by the field staff might damage downstream parts rated just above 24 V. The overshoot occurs at tp = π/ωd = 3.43 ms.

Answer: 25.4 percent

(c)

Critical damping occurs when ζ = 1, that is when α = ω0. Since α = R/(2L), the condition is R/(2L) = 1/√(LC), which gives R = 2√(L/C). Evaluating, L/C = 0.05/(20 × 10⁻⁶) = 2500 Ω², so √(L/C) = 50 Ω and R = 2 × 50 = 100 Ω. At this value the response has a repeated root s = -1000 s⁻¹, there is no overshoot, and the response reaches the final value as fast as possible without ringing. Any resistance above 100 Ω is overdamped and slower, and any below is underdamped with some overshoot, so 100 Ω is the design target for a no-overshoot driver.

Answer: 100 Ω

(d)

With R = 200 Ω, α = R/(2L) = 200/0.1 = 2000 s⁻¹, which exceeds ω0 = 1000 rad/s, so the circuit is overdamped. The characteristic roots are s = -α ± √(α² - ω0²) = -2000 ± √(4 × 10⁶ - 10⁶) = -2000 ± 1732. They are s1 = -268 s⁻¹ and s2 = -3732 s⁻¹. The corresponding time constants are 1/268 = 3.73 ms and 1/3732 = 0.268 ms. The slower mode dominates the settling, so the response takes roughly 4 × 3.73 = 15 ms to settle within 2 percent. Raising R beyond critical damping removes the ringing but makes the output slower, which is the trade-off the engineer must weigh.

Answer: 3.73 ms

Problem 5 [A1-055] Laplace transform analysis of circuits with initial conditions

A source-free series RLC loop is analysed after a fault clears at t = 0. The loop consists of a resistor R = 30 Ω, an inductor L = 20 mH and a capacitor C = 50 μF connected in series. Immediately before t = 0 the inductor carries a current of 0.5 A in the reference direction of loop current i(t), and the capacitor holds a voltage vc(0) that is a drop in the same direction as i(t) (positive when the current would flow into the positive plate). Use the Laplace transform with the initial conditions entered as source terms. The question asks how the response changes if a different charge state was left on the capacitor by the fault, with the inductor current unchanged.

  1. (a) With vc(0) = 12 V, find the damped natural frequency ωd of the loop current in rad/s. [5]
  2. (b) With vc(0) = 12 V, find i(t) at t = 1 ms. [8]
  3. (c) With vc(0) = -12 V (reversed capacitor), find i(t) at t = 1 ms. [7]
(a)

Write KVL in the s-domain with initial-condition sources: R I(s) + L[s I(s) - i(0)] + I(s)/(sC) + vc(0)/s = 0. Collecting I(s): I(s) = [L i(0) - vc(0)/s] / [R + sL + 1/(sC)] = [i(0) s - vc(0)/L] / [s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC)]. The denominator is s² + 1500 s + 10⁶, with α = R/(2L) = 750 s⁻¹ and ω0² = 1/(LC) = 1/(20 × 10⁻³ × 50 × 10⁻⁶) = 10⁶. Then ωd = √(ω0² - α²) = √(10⁶ - 562 500) = √437 500 = 661.4 rad/s. The poles are s = -750 ± j661.4, so the loop is underdamped.

Answer: ωd = 661.4 rad/s

(b)

Using the numerator i(0) s - vc(0)/L with i(0) = 0.5 and vc(0)/L = 12/0.02 = 600, I(s) = (0.5 s - 600)/[(s + 750)² + 661.4²]. Rewrite the numerator about the pole real part: 0.5 s - 600 = 0.5(s + 750) - (375 + 600) = 0.5(s + 750) - 975. The inverse transform is i(t) = e-750t[0.5 cos ωd t - (975/661.4) sin ωd t] = e-750t[0.5 cos ωd t - 1.474 sin ωd t]. As a check, the initial slope is -α(0.5) + ωd(-1.474) = -375 - 975 = -1350 A/s, which equals -(R i0 + vc0)/L = -(15 + 12)/0.02, as KVL requires. At t = 1 ms, ωd t = 0.6614 rad, e-0.75 = 0.4724, cos = 0.7891 and sin = 0.6143, so i = 0.4724 × (0.3946 - 0.9055) = -0.2413 A. The current has already reversed.

Answer: -0.2413 A

(c)

Reversing the capacitor changes the source term in the numerator to i(0) s + 600, so I(s) = (0.5 s + 600)/[(s + 750)² + 661.4²]. Rewriting, 0.5 s + 600 = 0.5(s + 750) + (600 - 375) = 0.5(s + 750) + 225, so the sine coefficient is B = 225/661.4 = 0.3402 and the cosine coefficient stays 0.5 because the initial current is unchanged. Then i(t) = e-750t[0.5 cos ωd t + 0.3402 sin ωd t]. At t = 1 ms, with e-0.75 = 0.4724, cos = 0.7891 and sin = 0.6143, i = 0.4724 × (0.3946 + 0.2090) = 0.2851 A. The current remains positive because the reversed capacitor voltage now drives current in the same direction as the inductor current.

Answer: 0.2851 A

A1 Practice Paper 12

Problem 1 [A1-056] Transient response by Laplace with switching and sources

A solenoid coil is modelled as a resistance R = 8 Ω in series with an inductance L = 0.25 H. A 24 V dc source is connected across the coil by a switch at t = 0, and the coil already carries an initial current of 1.2 A from an earlier cycle, flowing in the direction that the source drives. At t = 0.1 s the switch moves to a second position that connects the coil terminals to a short circuit, so the applied voltage becomes zero and the coil current decays through the short. Model the applied voltage as v(t) = 24[u(t) - u(t - 0.1)] volts and solve with the Laplace transform. A designer then asks what would happen if a larger coil with L = 0.5 H and the same resistance were used in the same cycle.

  1. (a) Find the coil current at the end of the 0.1 s drive interval, for L = 0.25 H. [5]
  2. (b) Find the coil current at t = 0.15 s, for L = 0.25 H. [5]
  3. (c) For L = 0.5 H, find the current at t = 0.1 s. [5]
  4. (d) For L = 0.5 H, find the current at t = 0.15 s. [5]
(a)

In the s-domain, V(s) = 24(1 - e-0.1s)/s and the circuit equation is (R + sL) I(s) - L i(0) = V(s). Then I(s) = [L i(0) + V(s)]/(R + sL) = i(0)/(s + R/L) + (24/L)(1 - e-0.1s)/[s(s + R/L)]. With R/L = 32 s⁻¹, the first interval has the standard result i(t) = 3 + (1.2 - 3) e-32t, where the final value is 24/8 = 3 A. At t = 0.1 s, e-3.2 = 0.04076, so i = 3 - 1.8 × 0.04076 = 3 - 0.07337 = 2.927 A. The delayed term e-0.1s does not affect this interval since it only starts at t = 0.1 s.

Answer: 2.927 A

(b)

The delayed term e-0.1s cancels the source after 0.1 s. The total solution for t > 0.1 s is the first-interval formula minus the same step response delayed by 0.1 s: i(t) = [3 - 1.8e-32t] - 3[1 - e-32(t - 0.1)]. Simplifying, i(t) = 3e-32(t - 0.1) - 1.8 e-32t, and this is equivalent to i(0.1) e-32(t - 0.1). At t = 0.15 s, e-32 × 0.05 = e-1.6 = 0.2019. Then i(0.15) = 2.9266 × 0.2019 = 0.591 A. The current decays toward zero with time constant L/R = 31.25 ms, which is the response of a source-free RL loop starting from 2.927 A.

Answer: 0.591 A

(c)

For L = 0.5 H the time constant is τ = L/R = 0.5/8 = 62.5 ms and the exponent factor is 1/τ = 16 s⁻¹. The initial current and final value are unchanged at 1.2 A and 3 A. The drive-interval current is i(t) = 3 - 1.8 e-16t. At t = 0.1 s, e-1.6 = 0.2019, so i = 3 - 1.8 × 0.2019 = 3 - 0.3634 = 2.637 A. Compared with the 0.25 H coil the current rises more slowly and has not reached as high a value at the end of the pulse, because the larger inductance stores energy more slowly and holds the current closer to its initial value.

Answer: 2.637 A

(d)

After the switch moves to the short, the current obeys L di/dt + R i = 0 with initial value i(0.1) = 2.637 A, so i(t) = 2.637 e-(t - 0.1)/τ with τ = 62.5 ms. At t = 0.15 s the elapsed time is 0.05 s, so the exponent is 0.05/0.0625 = 0.8 and e-0.8 = 0.4493. Then i(0.15) = 2.6366 × 0.4493 = 1.185 A. This is twice the current obtained with the 0.25 H coil at the same instant (0.591 A), because the decay is slower. A solenoid using the larger coil therefore keeps its force longer after switch-off, which matters if release time is a design requirement.

Answer: 1.185 A

Problem 2 [A1-057] Two-port parameters (z, y, h, ABCD)

An audio line attenuator pad is a resistive T network used as a two-port. Port 1 is the input and port 2 is the output. A series resistor R1 = 10 Ω connects the port 1 high terminal to a central node, a series resistor R2 = 30 Ω connects the central node to the port 2 high terminal, and a shunt resistor R3 connects the central node to the common (lower) terminals of both ports. The nominal pad uses R3 = 20 Ω. The technician is diagnosing a level drop in a signal path and wants to see the effect of replacing R3 by a 40 Ω resistor that was fitted by mistake. Use the standard convention with both port currents defined as flowing into the two-port, and treat all resistors as ideal.

  1. (a) For the nominal pad (R3 = 20 Ω), find the open-circuit output impedance parameter z22. [4]
  2. (b) For the nominal pad, find the ABCD parameter B in ohms. [5]
  3. (c) For the nominal pad, find the h-parameter h21 (short-circuit forward current gain). [5]
  4. (d) With R3 = 40 Ω find the open-circuit voltage ratio V2/V1. [6]
(a)

For a T network the open-circuit impedance parameters are z11 = R1 + R3, z12 = z21 = R3 and z22 = R2 + R3. They follow from exciting one port with a current source while the other port is open: with port 1 driven and port 2 open, V2 is the voltage across R3 only, because no current flows in R2, so z21 = R3. With the nominal pad, z22 = R2 + R3 = 30 + 20 = 50 Ω. Similarly z11 = 10 + 20 = 30 Ω and z12 = z21 = 20 Ω. The network is reciprocal since z12 = z21, as expected for a passive resistive circuit without dependent sources.

Answer: z22 = 50 Ω

(b)

The ABCD parameters can be converted from the z parameters with A = z11/z21, B = (z11 z22 - z12 z21)/z21, C = 1/z21 and D = z22/z21. Using z11 = 30, z12 = z21 = 20 and z22 = 50, the determinant of z is Δz = 30 × 50 - 20 × 20 = 1500 - 400 = 1100 Ω². Then B = 1100/20 = 55 Ω. The other parameters are A = 30/20 = 1.5, C = 1/20 = 0.05 S and D = 50/20 = 2.5. A check is that AD - BC = 3.75 - 2.75 = 1, which must hold for any reciprocal two-port.

Answer: B = 55 Ω

(c)

The h parameter h21 is the ratio I2/I1 with the output port shorted (V2 = 0). From the z equations, V2 = z21 I1 + z22 I2 = 0, so I2 = -(z21/z22) I1 and h21 = -z21/z22. Using the nominal values, h21 = -20/50 = -0.4. The negative sign arises from the convention that I2 flows into port 2, so the real current delivered to a shorted load is 0.4 times I1 in magnitude. Physically, the input current splits between R3 and the shorted R2 branch, and R2 carries 20/(20 + 30) = 0.4 of it, a result that can be confirmed with the current divider rule.

Answer: h21 = -0.4

(d)

With R3 = 40 Ω the parameters become z11 = R1 + R3 = 50 Ω, z12 = z21 = 40 Ω and z22 = R2 + R3 = 70 Ω. With the output open, I2 = 0, so V1 = z11 I1 and V2 = z21 I1. The open-circuit voltage ratio is V2/V1 = z21/z11 = 40/50 = 0.800. For the nominal pad it was 20/30 = 0.667, so the wrong resistor raises the open-circuit gain by 20 percent, which would give a higher signal level, not a drop. The loss reported by the technician therefore suggests the loaded case matters, since a load on port 2 reduces V2 by the factor shown by z22.

Answer: V2/V1 = 0.800

Problem 3 [A1-058] Interconnected and terminated two-ports

A measurement link consists of two resistive two-port sections connected in cascade. Section X is a single series resistor of 100 Ω between its input and output terminals. Section Y is a single shunt conductance of 0.01 S connected across its terminals. The source has an open-circuit voltage of 20 V and a Thevenin resistance of 50 Ω, and the load is a resistor RL = 200 Ω. In the first arrangement the source feeds X, then X feeds Y, then Y feeds the load. A technician wonders whether reversing the order of the two sections (Y first, then X) would deliver more signal to the load. Use ABCD parameters, with A = V1/V2 for I2 = 0 and with the output current defined as leaving the two-port.

  1. (a) For the original order (X then Y), find the input impedance seen by the source. [5]
  2. (b) For the original order, find the load voltage V2. [5]
  3. (c) For the reversed order (Y then X), find the load voltage V2. [5]
  4. (d) Find the ratio of power delivered to the load in the reversed order to that in the original order. [5]
(a)

Section X has [A B; C D] = [1 100; 0 1] and section Y has [1 0; 0.01 1]. For a cascade, multiply the matrices in signal order: [1 100; 0 1] × [1 0; 0.01 1] = [1 + 100 × 0.01, 100; 0.01, 1] = [2 100; 0.01 1]. For a two-port terminated in RL, the input impedance is Zin = (A RL + B)/(C RL + D) = (2 × 200 + 100)/(0.01 × 200 + 1) = 500/3 = 166.7 Ω. The input impedance is therefore larger than the source resistance of 50 Ω, which determines the divider formed with the source. A check is that AD - BC = 2 - 1 = 1, as required for a reciprocal pair of resistive sections.

Answer: Zin = 166.7 Ω

(b)

The input voltage follows from the source divider: V1 = 20 × Zin/(Rs + Zin) = 20 × 166.67/216.67 = 15.385 V. For a load RL, the ABCD relation V1 = A V2 + B(-I2) with -I2 = V2/RL gives V1 = V2 (A + B/RL) = V2 (2 + 0.5) = 2.5 V2. Therefore V2 = 15.385/2.5 = 6.154 V. This is the voltage at the load in the original arrangement. As a cross-check, the shunt conductance and load together are 0.01 + 1/200 = 0.015 S, or 66.7 Ω, which in series with the 100 Ω resistor gives 166.7 Ω as found in part (a).

Answer: V2 = 6.154 V

(c)

With the order reversed the matrix is [1 0; 0.01 1] × [1 100; 0 1] = [1, 100; 0.01, 0.01 × 100 + 1] = [1 100; 0.01 2]. The input impedance is Zin = (1 × 200 + 100)/(0.01 × 200 + 2) = 300/4 = 75 Ω. The source divider gives V1 = 20 × 75/(50 + 75) = 12.0 V. The voltage ratio uses A + B/RL = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5, so V2 = 12/1.5 = 8.000 V. Physically, the shunt element now loads the source more (V1 falls to 12 V), but the load divider 200/(100 + 200) taken after it is far better than in the original arrangement, so V2 rises.

Answer: V2 = 8.000 V

(d)

Power in the load is V2²/RL. In the original order P = 6.154²/200 = 37.87/200 = 0.1893 W. In the reversed order P = 8.0²/200 = 64/200 = 0.3200 W. The ratio is 0.3200/0.1893 = 1.690, which is also (8/6.154)² = 1.300² = 1.690. The reversed order delivers about 69 percent more power for the same two parts, because the interconnection changes the impedances seen by the source and the load. Two-ports do not commute in general, and the ABCD matrix product shows exactly this with the unequal results, so the order of sections matters.

Answer: ratio 1.69

Problem 4 [A1-059] Mutual inductance and coupled circuits

Two coils are wound on a common laminated core and used as a series-connected inductive ballast. Coil 1 has self-inductance L1 = 0.4 H and resistance 10 Ω. Coil 2 has L2 = 0.9 H and resistance 20 Ω. The coupling coefficient is k = 0.8. The coils are connected in series across a 120 V, 60 Hz supply, and the technician expects the series-aiding connection (the same current direction through both windings produces flux in the same direction in the core). The measured current is much higher than the expected value, and the technician suspects one coil was connected the wrong way round. Treat the supply as ideal, the inductances as linear and use the rms magnitude of current.

  1. (a) Find the mutual inductance M. [4]
  2. (b) Find the supply current with the coils series-aiding. [5]
  3. (c) Find the supply current with the coils series-opposing. [5]
  4. (d) If the coupling coefficient fell to k = 0.5 and the coils were still series-opposing, find the current. [6]
(a)

The coupling coefficient is defined by k = M/√(L1 L2), so M = k √(L1 L2). Substituting, √(0.4 × 0.9) = √0.36 = 0.6 H, and M = 0.8 × 0.6 = 0.48 H. The value must not exceed √(L1 L2) = 0.6 H, which is the limit for perfect coupling, so this is a physically valid answer and corresponds to a tightly coupled pair. The mutual inductance sets how strongly current in one coil induces voltage in the other, and its effect adds to or subtracts from the self-inductance depending on whether the two fluxes aid or oppose each other.

Answer: M = 0.48 H

(b)

For series-aiding connection the equivalent inductance is Leq = L1 + L2 + 2M = 0.4 + 0.9 + 0.96 = 2.26 H. The series resistance is 10 + 20 = 30 Ω. At 60 Hz, ω = 2π × 60 = 377.0 rad/s, so X = ω Leq = 377.0 × 2.26 = 852.0 Ω. The impedance magnitude is |Z| = √(30² + 852.0²) = √(900 + 725 900) = 852.5 Ω. The current is I = 120/852.5 = 0.1408 A. This is the expected value, because the two fluxes add and the inductive reactance is high, which holds the current low.

Answer: I = 0.1408 A

(c)

For series-opposing connection the fluxes subtract and Leq = L1 + L2 - 2M = 1.3 - 0.96 = 0.34 H. The reactance is X = 377.0 × 0.34 = 128.2 Ω, and the impedance magnitude is |Z| = √(900 + 128.2²) = √(900 + 16 435) = 131.7 Ω. The current is I = 120/131.7 = 0.9116 A, which is 6.5 times the expected value. This matches the symptom of an unexpectedly high current, so the technician's suspicion of a reversed winding is consistent with the measurement. The remedy is to swap the leads of one coil, which converts the connection to series-aiding.

Answer: I = 0.9116 A

(d)

With k = 0.5, M = 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.3 H. For the opposing connection Leq = 1.3 - 2 × 0.3 = 0.7 H and X = 377.0 × 0.7 = 263.9 Ω. The impedance magnitude is |Z| = √(900 + 263.9²) = √(900 + 69 643) = 265.6 Ω. The current is I = 120/265.6 = 0.452 A. The current falls from 0.912 A to 0.452 A when the coupling weakens, because less of the self-inductance is cancelled by the mutual term. This also shows that a loosely coupled pair is less sensitive to the connection polarity, since the 2M term is smaller.

Answer: I = 0.452 A

Problem 5 [A1-060] Circuit design to meet a response specification and what-if parameter change

A second-order passive low-pass filter is to be built for a sensor output. The filter is a series connection of a resistor R, an inductor L = 4.7 mH and a capacitor C, driven by a voltage source of negligible internal resistance, with the output taken across the capacitor. The specification is an undamped natural frequency of 5 kHz and a damping ratio ζ = 0.5 (about 16 percent step overshoot). After the design is finished, the capacitors from the supplier turn out to have a tolerance of plus 20 percent. Use ω0 = 1/√(LC) and ζ = (R/2)√(C/L), and assume the inductor and resistor are exact and the capacitor is lossless.

  1. (a) Find the capacitance C needed for the natural frequency of 5 kHz, in nF. [5]
  2. (b) Find the resistance R needed for ζ = 0.5, using the exact C from part (a). [5]
  3. (c) If the actual capacitor is 20 percent above nominal, find the percentage change in the natural frequency (negative for a decrease). [5]
  4. (d) With the 20 percent larger capacitor and the R from part (b), find the percentage overshoot of the step response. [5]
(a)

The natural frequency is ω0 = 2π × 5000 = 31 416 rad/s, and ω0 = 1/√(LC), so C = 1/(ω0² L). Compute ω0² = 9.8696 × 10⁸ rad²/s², and ω0² L = 9.8696 × 10⁸ × 4.7 × 10⁻³ = 4.639 × 10⁶. Therefore C = 1/(4.639 × 10⁶) = 2.156 × 10⁻⁷ F = 215.6 nF. In practice one would pick the nearest standard value, 220 nF, which shifts f0 down to 4.95 kHz, so the question of component tolerance is worth examining next. The inductance is fixed so the capacitor is the free variable.

Answer: C = 215.6 nF

(b)

From ζ = (R/2)√(C/L), R = 2ζ √(L/C). With L = 4.7 mH and C = 215.58 nF, L/C = 4.7 × 10⁻³/2.1558 × 10⁻⁷ = 21 802 Ω², so √(L/C) = 147.65 Ω, which is the characteristic impedance of the filter. Then R = 2 × 0.5 × 147.65 = 147.7 Ω. The choice ζ = 0.5 means R equals the characteristic impedance exactly. A standard 150 Ω resistor would give ζ = 0.508, a negligible change, so the design is not sensitive to the resistor tolerance.

Answer: R = 147.7 Ω

(c)

Because ω0 varies as 1/√C, a capacitance 20 percent above nominal gives ω0' = ω0/√1.2 = ω0 × 0.91287. The new natural frequency is 31 416 × 0.91287 = 28 679 rad/s, or 4.564 kHz. The change is (0.91287 - 1) × 100 = -8.71 percent, so the cut-off moves down by 436 Hz. The shift is slightly less than half of the 20 percent change, since the square root dependence halves small fractional changes but not exactly for large ones. A filter that is 9 percent low may attenuate wanted signal near the band edge, which is the design risk this tolerance creates.

Answer: -8.71 percent

(d)

With R unchanged and C larger, ζ' = (R/2)√(C'/L) = ζ √1.2 = 0.5 × 1.0954 = 0.5477. The percentage overshoot for a second-order step is 100 exp(-π ζ/√(1 - ζ²)). Here √(1 - 0.5477²) = √(0.7000) = 0.8367, so π × 0.5477/0.8367 = 2.0564 and exp(-2.0564) = 0.1279. The overshoot is 12.8 percent, down from 16.3 percent in the nominal design. A larger capacitor therefore makes the filter slightly better damped but also slower, so the tolerance in this case helps the overshoot but moves the cut-off frequency, which is the more important error for a sensor band.

Answer: 12.8 percent

A1 Practice Paper 13

Problem 1 [A1-061] Equivalent circuits, series-parallel reduction and source transformations

A sensor interface is fed from a resistive network that must be reduced to a single equivalent source at terminals a and b. Node 1 is held at +36 V relative to the reference node 0 by an ideal voltage source, with its positive terminal at node 1. A 6 Ω resistor joins node 1 to node 2. A 12 Ω resistor joins node 2 to node 0. An ideal 2 A current source pushes current from node 0 into node 2. A 4 Ω resistor joins node 2 to terminal a, and terminal b is node 0. A variable load resistor RL will later be connected between a and b. All elements are ideal and linear.

  1. (a) Using source transformations and series-parallel reduction, find the open-circuit voltage Vab at the terminals. [4]
  2. (b) Find the equivalent resistance seen looking into terminals a and b with both independent sources set to zero. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum power that the network can deliver to a load RL and state the value of RL that gives it. [4]
  4. (d) A load of RL = 20 Ω is connected instead. Find the power absorbed by the load. [4]
  5. (e) With RL = 8 Ω connected, find the percentage of the total power delivered by the two independent sources that reaches the load. [4]
(a)

Transform the 36 V source in series with 6 Ω into a 6 A current source in parallel with 6 Ω. At node 2 this 6 A source and the 2 A source act in the same sense into the node, giving 8 A. The 6 Ω and the 12 Ω resistors to node 0 are in parallel, which is 4 Ω. With the terminals open, the 4 Ω series resistor carries no current, so Vab equals the node 2 voltage: V2 = 8 A × 4 Ω = 32 V. Check by nodal analysis: (36 - V2)/6 + 2 = V2/12 gives V2 = 32 V. Vab = 32 V, with a positive.

Answer: 32 V

(b)

Set the voltage source to a short circuit and the current source to an open circuit. From node 2 to node 0 the 6 Ω resistor, which now returns to node 0 through the shorted source, is in parallel with the 12 Ω resistor: 6 × 12/(6 + 12) = 4 Ω. This combination is in series with the 4 Ω resistor that leads to terminal a. Rth = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω. The 2 A source, being open, contributes nothing to the resistance. This value, with Vth from part (a), completes the Thevenin equivalent: a 32 V source in series with 8 Ω.

Answer: 8 Ω

(c)

Maximum power transfer from a linear source occurs when RL equals the Thevenin resistance, so RL = 8 Ω. At that point the load voltage is half of Vth, which is 16 V, and the current is Vth/(2 Rth) = 32/16 = 2 A. Pmax = Vth²/(4 Rth) = 32²/(4 × 8) = 1024/32 = 32 W. Check: I²RL = 2² × 8 = 32 W. The result applies to the load alone; the Thevenin equivalent dissipates another 32 W in its 8 Ω, but this is not the real internal loss, as part (e) shows.

Answer: 32 W

(d)

Use the Thevenin equivalent with RL = 20 Ω. The current is I = Vth/(Rth + RL) = 32/(8 + 20) = 1.1429 A. The power absorbed by the load is P = I² RL = (1.1429)² × 20 = 1.3061 × 20 = 26.12 W. This is below the 32 W maximum, as expected, because the load is mismatched. The load voltage is 22.86 V, so P = V²/RL = 22.86²/20 gives the same 26.12 W, which confirms the arithmetic.

Answer: 26.1 W

(e)

With RL = 8 Ω the terminal current is 2 A, so the 4 Ω series resistor drops 8 V and node 2 sits at 24 V. The voltage source supplies (36 - 24)/6 = 2 A at 36 V, which is 72 W. The current source delivers 2 A into a node at 24 V, which is 48 W. Total supplied power is 120 W. The load receives 32 W, so efficiency = 32/120 = 26.7 %. This shows that maximum power transfer is not maximum efficiency: only about a quarter of the total is delivered, since the source network wastes the rest.

Answer: 26.7 %

Problem 2 [A1-062] Nodal analysis of resistive circuits with dependent sources

A transistor stage is modelled by a linear network with reference node 0 and two other nodes, 1 and 2. An independent 5 mA current source drives current from node 0 into node 1. A 2 kΩ resistor joins node 1 to node 0. A 4 kΩ resistor joins node 1 to node 2. A 1 kΩ resistor joins node 2 to node 0. A voltage-controlled current source delivers a current of 2 mS times V1 from node 0 into node 2, where V1 is the voltage of node 1 with respect to node 0. The output terminals are node 2 and node 0. A load will later be connected across the output. Treat the model as linear and ideal.

  1. (a) Write nodal equations and find V1 with the output open-circuited. [3]
  2. (b) Find the open-circuit output voltage V2. [4]
  3. (c) Find the Thevenin resistance seen at the output terminals by applying a 1 mA test current source with the independent source set to zero. [5]
  4. (d) A 3 kΩ load is connected across the output. Find the load current. [4]
  5. (e) Find the power absorbed by the 3 kΩ load. [4]
(a)

Use units of kΩ, mA and V. Node 1: V1/2 + (V1 - V2)/4 = 5. Node 2: (V2 - V1)/4 + V2/1 = 2 V1, because the dependent source of 2 mS × V1 equals 2 V1 mA and enters node 2. Rearranged, node 1 gives 0.75 V1 - 0.25 V2 = 5, and node 2 gives -2.25 V1 + 1.25 V2 = 0. From node 2, V2 = 1.8 V1. Substituting into node 1: 0.75 V1 - 0.45 V1 = 0.30 V1 = 5, so V1 = 16.67 V. The dependent source is treated like any other current source, with its value written in terms of the node voltage.

Answer: 16.67 V

(b)

From the second equation of part (a), V2 = 2.25 V1/1.25 = 1.8 V1. With V1 = 16.667 V, V2 = 1.8 × 16.667 = 30.0 V. This is the open-circuit voltage between node 2 and node 0, so Vth = 30 V. A check using the node 1 equation: 16.667/2 + (16.667 - 30)/4 = 8.333 - 3.333 = 5.0 mA, which matches the independent source. The dependent source contributes 2 × 16.667 = 33.3 mA into node 2, balanced by the 30 mA in the 1 kΩ resistor and the 3.33 mA flowing back toward node 1.

Answer: 30 V

(c)

Switch off the 5 mA source (open circuit) but keep the dependent source, since its control quantity remains in the circuit. Inject Itest = 1 mA into node 2 and call the resulting voltages V1 and V2. Node 1: V1/2 + (V1 - V2)/4 = 0, so 0.75 V1 = 0.25 V2 and V1 = V2/3. Node 2: (V2 - V1)/4 + V2 = 2 V1 + 1. Substituting V1 = V2/3: 0.25 V2 - 0.0833 V2 + V2 = 0.6667 V2 + 1, which gives 0.5 V2 = 1 and V2 = 2 V for 1 mA. Rth = V2/Itest = 2 kΩ. A dependent source is never switched off when finding Rth this way.

Answer: 2 kΩ

(d)

Replace the network by its Thevenin equivalent, 30 V in series with 2 kΩ, and connect the 3 kΩ load. The load current is I = Vth/(Rth + RL) = 30 V/(2 kΩ + 3 kΩ) = 6 mA. The load voltage is 6 mA × 3 kΩ = 18 V. As a cross-check, the short-circuit current is Vth/Rth = 15 mA, and the load takes the share Rth/(Rth + RL) of it, which is 2/5 × 15 mA = 6 mA. The result holds because the circuit is linear, so the Thevenin model is valid for any load connected at the output.

Answer: 6 mA

(e)

The power absorbed by the load is P = I² RL = (6 mA)² × 3 kΩ = 36 × 10⁻⁶ A² × 3000 Ω = 0.108 W = 108 mW. Alternatively P = V²/RL = 18²/3000 = 0.108 W. For comparison, the maximum available power from this network would occur with a 2 kΩ load and equal Vth²/(4 Rth) = 900/8000 = 0.1125 W, so the 3 kΩ load receives about 96 percent of the maximum, a mild mismatch loss that a designer would accept for a voltage-driven stage.

Answer: 108 mW

Problem 3 [A1-063] Mesh analysis and supermesh

A resistive network has a reference node 0 and nodes 1, 2 and 3. An ideal 50 V source has its positive terminal at node 1 and its negative terminal at node 0. A 4 Ω resistor joins node 1 to node 2, a 6 Ω resistor joins node 2 to node 3, an 8 Ω resistor joins node 3 to node 0, and a 12 Ω resistor joins node 1 to node 3. An ideal 2 A current source is connected between node 0 and node 2 and drives current from node 0 into node 2. Analyse the circuit by the mesh method, treating the meshes that share the current source as a supermesh, and then check the power balance.

  1. (a) Find the current in the 4 Ω resistor, taken from node 1 to node 2. [4]
  2. (b) Find the current in the 12 Ω resistor, taken from node 1 to node 3. [4]
  3. (c) Find the power delivered by the 50 V source. [4]
  4. (d) Find the power delivered by the 2 A current source. [4]
  5. (e) Find the total power absorbed by the four resistors and confirm that it equals the total delivered. [4]
(a)

Take clockwise mesh currents ia through the 50 V source, 4 Ω resistor and current source, ib through the current source, 6 Ω and 8 Ω resistors, and ic around the 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 12 Ω loop. Meshes a and b share the current source, so they form a supermesh and the source constraint ib - ia = 2 A replaces one mesh equation. The mesh equations give the same branch currents as nodal analysis, which is used here for the arithmetic: node 2: (V2 - 50)/4 + (V2 - V3)/6 = 2; node 3: (V3 - V2)/6 + V3/8 + (V3 - 50)/12 = 0. Solving gives V2 = 47.73 V and V3 = 32.32 V. The current in the 4 Ω resistor, node 1 to node 2, is (50 - 47.73)/4 = 0.568 A.

Answer: 0.568 A

(b)

With V3 = 32.324 V from part (a), the current in the 12 Ω resistor from node 1 to node 3 is (50 - 32.324)/12 = 17.676/12 = 1.473 A. The current in the 6 Ω resistor from node 2 to node 3 is (47.730 - 32.324)/6 = 2.568 A. KCL at node 3 requires that the current leaving through the 8 Ω resistor equals 2.568 + 1.473 = 4.041 A, and indeed 32.324/8 = 4.041 A. This check shows that the mesh and nodal results are consistent. In mesh terms the 12 Ω current is a mesh current or a difference of two, since it lies on the boundary of the meshes.

Answer: 1.473 A

(c)

The source current leaves the positive terminal at node 1 and equals the sum of the currents into the 4 Ω and 12 Ω resistors: 0.5676 + 1.4730 = 2.0405 A. Power delivered = 50 V × 2.0405 A = 102.03 W. The sign is positive because the current leaves the positive terminal, so this source supplies energy. Its share is a little over half of the total, because the current source supplies the remainder. This value is used for the power balance in part (e), where the delivered and absorbed totals must agree.

Answer: 102.0 W

(d)

The voltage across the current source is the node 2 voltage with respect to node 0, which is 47.73 V, with node 2 positive. Its current of 2 A enters node 2, so the current leaves the source at its positive terminal and the source delivers power: P = 47.73 × 2 = 95.46 W. The source is ideal, so its terminal voltage is set by the rest of the network, not by the source. The supermesh method is needed precisely because this voltage is unknown and cannot be written as a simple mesh voltage drop.

Answer: 95.46 W

(e)

Powers in the resistors: 4 Ω: (0.5676)² × 4 = 1.289 W; 6 Ω: (2.5676)² × 6 = 39.55 W; 8 Ω: (4.0405)² × 8 = 130.61 W; 12 Ω: (1.4730)² × 12 = 26.04 W. The sum is 197.49 W. The sources deliver 102.03 + 95.46 = 197.49 W. The two totals agree to the rounding of the arithmetic, which confirms conservation of energy and that the solution is consistent with all branch relationships in the network. Because the 50 V source and the 2 A source both supply energy here, neither can be ignored in the balance.

Answer: 197.5 W

Problem 4 [A1-064] Thevenin and Norton equivalents and maximum power transfer

A bridge circuit is used to detect a small change in a sensor resistance. A 12 V ideal source has its positive terminal at node P and its negative terminal at node N. A 1.0 kΩ resistor joins P to node A and a 1.2 kΩ resistor joins A to N. A 2.2 kΩ resistor joins P to node B and a 1.5 kΩ resistor joins B to N. A detector of internal resistance 500 Ω is connected between A and B. Treat the source as ideal. The detector is to be analysed using Thevenin and Norton equivalents as seen from nodes A and B, and the bridge is then rebalanced by trimming the 1.2 kΩ arm.

  1. (a) Find the Thevenin voltage VA - VB with the detector removed. [4]
  2. (b) Find the Thevenin resistance seen between A and B with the source replaced by a short circuit. [4]
  3. (c) Find the detector current, in mA. [4]
  4. (d) Find the maximum power that the bridge could deliver to any detector resistance, in mW. [4]
  5. (e) Find the value of the 1.2 kΩ resistor that balances the bridge, so that no detector current flows. [4]
(a)

With the detector removed, each arm is a voltage divider. VA = 12 × 1.2/(1.0 + 1.2) = 6.545 V, and VB = 12 × 1.5/(2.2 + 1.5) = 4.865 V. The Thevenin voltage seen by the detector, with A as the positive terminal, is Vth = VA - VB = 6.545 - 4.865 = 1.681 V. Both dividers are unloaded, which is correct because the detector branch is the open circuit being studied. The positive sign means that node A sits above node B in potential.

Answer: 1.681 V

(b)

With the source replaced by a short circuit, P and N become the same node. Looking into A, the 1.0 kΩ and 1.2 kΩ resistors are in parallel: 1.0 × 1.2/2.2 = 0.5455 kΩ. Looking into B, the 2.2 kΩ and 1.5 kΩ resistors are in parallel: 2.2 × 1.5/3.7 = 0.8919 kΩ. These two parallel pairs are in series through the shorted node, so Rth = 0.5455 + 0.8919 = 1.4373 kΩ = 1437 Ω. The detector resistance does not affect Rth because the detector is the load connected across the terminals.

Answer: 1437 Ω

(c)

The detector current is Id = Vth/(Rth + Rd) = 1.6806/(1437.3 + 500) = 1.6806/1937.3 = 0.8675 mA. The Norton short-circuit current is Isc = Vth/Rth = 1.6806/1437.3 = 1.169 mA, with Rth as the parallel Norton resistance. The detector takes the fraction Rth/(Rth + Rd) = 0.742 of Isc, which is 0.8675 mA, so the Norton and Thevenin models agree. A detector that cannot tolerate this current would need a shunt resistor across it, or a series resistor to limit the current.

Answer: 0.867 mA

(d)

Maximum power transfer occurs when the load equals the Thevenin resistance, here 1437 Ω. The power is Pmax = Vth²/(4 Rth) = (1.6806)²/(4 × 1437.3) = 2.8244/5749.4 = 4.913 × 10⁻⁴ W = 0.491 mW. The actual 500 Ω detector receives I² Rd = (0.8675 mA)² × 500 = 0.376 mW, so it is mismatched by about 23 percent below the maximum, which is acceptable because a detector is designed for sensitivity, not for power transfer. Matching the detector to 1437 Ω would raise the power only slightly and would lower the sensitivity of the bridge.

Answer: 0.491 mW

(e)

The bridge is balanced when VA = VB, which requires R1/R2 = R3/R4, so R2 = R1 R4/R3 = 1000 × 1500/2200 = 681.8 Ω. At this value VA = 12 × 681.8/1681.8 = 4.865 V, equal to VB, and the Thevenin voltage is zero, so no current flows in the detector regardless of its resistance. The trimming from 1200 Ω to 682 Ω is large, which shows the original bridge is far from balance and would be used as a deflection bridge, not as a null instrument.

Answer: 682 Ω

Problem 5 [A1-065] Superposition and linearity in circuits with several sources

A filter output is driven by two sources acting at once. A single series source is the sum of a 12 V DC source and a sinusoidal source 8 cos(400 t) V, where t is in seconds. This combined source drives, in series, a 20 Ω resistor and a 50 mH inductor, ending at node X. From node X to the reference node, a 50 μF capacitor is connected in parallel with an 80 Ω resistor, and the output vo is the voltage across this parallel pair. The circuit has been connected long enough for all transients to have died away. Use superposition, treating the DC and sinusoidal components separately.

  1. (a) Find the DC component of vo. [3]
  2. (b) Find the amplitude of the sinusoidal component of vo. [5]
  3. (c) Find the phase angle of the sinusoidal component of vo relative to the cosine source, in degrees. [4]
  4. (d) Find the average power absorbed by the 80 Ω resistor. [4]
  5. (e) The DC source is doubled to 24 V and the sinusoidal amplitude is halved to 4 V. Find the new average power in the 80 Ω resistor. [4]
(a)

For the DC component the inductor is a short circuit and the capacitor is an open circuit. The 20 Ω and 80 Ω resistors then form a divider across 12 V. vo(DC) = 12 × 80/(20 + 80) = 9.6 V. The 50 mH and 50 μF elements store energy but carry no steady power at DC, so the answer is independent of them. Superposition is valid because the circuit is linear, which means the DC response can be found with the sinusoidal source set to zero, a short circuit for a voltage source.

Answer: 9.6 V

(b)

With the DC source shorted, use phasors at ω = 400 rad/s. The inductor impedance is jωL = j400 × 0.05 = j20 Ω. The capacitor impedance is 1/(jωC) = -j/(400 × 50 × 10⁻⁶) = -j50 Ω. The parallel branch is Zp = 1/(1/80 + j/50) = 1/(0.0125 + j0.02) = 22.47 - j35.96 Ω. The total series impedance is 20 + j20 + Zp = 42.47 - j15.96 Ω, of magnitude 45.37 Ω. The magnitude of Zp is 42.40 Ω, so the gain magnitude is 42.40/45.37 = 0.9345. The amplitude of the sinusoidal part of vo is 8 × 0.9345 = 7.476 V.

Answer: 7.476 V

(c)

The output phasor equals the source phasor times Zp/(20 + j20 + Zp). The angle of Zp = 22.47 - j35.96 is -57.99°. The angle of the denominator 42.47 - j15.96 is -20.59°. The output angle relative to the source is -57.99° - (-20.59°) = -37.40°. The source is 8 cos(400 t), a phasor of 8 at 0°, so vo(ac) = 7.476 cos(400 t - 37.4°) V. The output lags the source because the series inductor and the shunt capacitor both delay the response at this frequency, and the parallel branch is capacitive.

Answer: -37.4°

(d)

By superposition of power across different frequencies, average powers add because the cross term averages to zero. The DC part gives 9.6²/80 = 1.152 W. The AC part gives (7.476)²/(2 × 80) = 55.89/160 = 0.3493 W. The total is 1.152 + 0.349 = 1.501 W. Adding the voltages and squaring would be wrong in general for two components of different frequency, so the powers must be summed, not the voltages first. The result also equals the rms value squared of vo divided by 80.

Answer: 1.501 W

(e)

Linearity scales each component: the DC output becomes 2 × 9.6 = 19.2 V and the AC amplitude becomes 7.476/2 = 3.738 V, with unchanged phase. The new power is 19.2²/80 + 3.738²/(2 × 80) = 4.608 + 0.0873 = 4.695 W. The DC part dominates because power goes as the square of voltage. The answer shows that superposition applies to voltages and currents, not to power, since doubling one component and halving another changes the power by different factors.

Answer: 4.695 W

A1 Practice Paper 14

Problem 1 [A1-066] Ideal inductors and capacitors, energy storage and lumped models

Two storage elements are studied in a power-electronics bench. First, a 470 μF capacitor charged to 48 V is connected by a closing switch and a 0.5 Ω resistor in series to an initially uncharged 220 μF capacitor. Both capacitors are ideal and the switch is closed at t = 0 and left closed. Second, a coil with inductance 15 mH carries a current that rises linearly from 0 to 6 A in 4 ms. The real coil is modelled as the ideal 15 mH inductance in series with a winding resistance of 0.4 Ω. Take the passive sign convention for the coil, with current entering the terminal taken as positive.

  1. (a) Find the final common voltage across the two capacitors. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total energy dissipated in the 0.5 Ω resistor during the transient. [5]
  3. (c) Find the voltage across the ideal inductance during the 4 ms current ramp. [3]
  4. (d) Find the energy stored in the coil at the end of the ramp. [4]
  5. (e) Find the power lost in the winding resistance at the end of the ramp, when the current is 6 A. [4]
(a)

Charge is conserved when the two capacitors are joined, because no charge can leave through the ideal switch or resistor. The initial charge is Q = C1 V0 = 470 × 10⁻⁶ × 48 = 22.56 mC. After the transient the capacitors are in parallel at a common voltage, with total capacitance 470 + 220 = 690 μF. Vf = Q/Ctotal = 22.56 × 10⁻³/690 × 10⁻⁶ = 32.70 V. The resistor value does not appear, because it affects only how fast the voltage settles, not the final state.

Answer: 32.70 V

(b)

The initial energy is E0 = ½ C1 V0² = 0.5 × 470 × 10⁻⁶ × 48² = 0.5414 J. The final energy is Ef = ½ (C1 + C2) Vf² = 0.5 × 690 × 10⁻⁶ × 32.70² = 0.3688 J. The difference, 0.5414 - 0.3688 = 0.1726 J, is dissipated in the resistor. An equivalent formula is ½ [C1 C2/(C1 + C2)] V0² = 0.5 × 149.9 × 10⁻⁶ × 2304 = 0.1726 J. The loss is independent of the 0.5 Ω resistance: a smaller resistor gives a larger peak current over a shorter time, with the same total energy.

Answer: 0.1726 J

(c)

For an ideal inductor v = L di/dt. The current rises linearly, so di/dt = 6 A/(4 × 10⁻³ s) = 1500 A/s, which is constant. The voltage is v = 15 × 10⁻³ × 1500 = 22.5 V during the whole ramp, positive because the current enters the positive terminal and is increasing. The voltage is constant because the slope is constant. The winding resistance would add a further drop of up to 2.4 V at 6 A, which is not part of the voltage across the ideal inductance alone.

Answer: 22.5 V

(d)

The energy stored in an inductor depends only on the instantaneous current: w = ½ L i² = 0.5 × 15 × 10⁻³ × 6² = 0.5 × 0.015 × 36 = 0.27 J. This energy is stored in the magnetic field and is recoverable, unlike the energy dissipated in a resistor. It is of the same order as the 0.54 J stored initially in the 470 μF capacitor, so the coil and capacitor are comparable energy stores in this bench. The winding resistance does not change the stored energy, only the losses.

Answer: 0.27 J

(e)

In the lumped model the winding resistance carries the same current as the inductance, since they are in series. The power lost in it is p = i² R = 6² × 0.4 = 36 × 0.4 = 14.4 W at the end of the ramp. At the start of the ramp the loss is zero because the current is zero. Averaged over the 4 ms ramp, with the current proportional to time, the mean loss is one third of the peak, 4.8 W. The terminal voltage at 6 A is 22.5 + 2.4 = 24.9 V, so the real coil's terminals see more than the ideal inductance does.

Answer: 14.4 W

Problem 2 [A1-067] First-order RC and RL transients with switching

A relay coil is modelled as an inductance of 0.8 H in series with a resistance of 60 Ω. At t = 0 a switch connects the coil to an ideal 24 V DC supply, with the coil initially de-energised. The relay contacts pick up when the coil current reaches 0.25 A. After the current has reached steady state, a second operation takes place, taken as a new time zero: the supply is disconnected and, at the same instant, a 240 Ω freewheel resistor becomes connected across the coil terminals so that the coil current continues to flow through it. The relay drops out when the coil current falls to 0.10 A.

  1. (a) Find the final steady-state coil current after the supply is connected. [3]
  2. (b) Find the time after switch-on at which the relay picks up, in ms. [5]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the voltage across the freewheel resistor immediately after disconnection. [4]
  4. (d) Find the time after disconnection at which the relay drops out, in ms. [4]
  5. (e) Find the energy dissipated in the freewheel resistor during the whole decay. [4]
(a)

In steady state the inductor behaves as a short circuit, so only the 60 Ω coil resistance limits the current: I = V/R = 24/60 = 0.4 A. The time constant of the energising circuit is τ = L/R = 0.8/60 = 13.33 ms. The current is therefore i(t) = 0.4 (1 - e-t/τ) A. The steady value is reached, to within one percent, after about five time constants, which is 67 ms, and the problem states that the second operation happens after this.

Answer: 0.4 A

(b)

Solve 0.25 = 0.4 (1 - e-t/τ). Then 1 - e-t/τ = 0.625, so e-t/τ = 0.375. Taking the natural logarithm, t = -τ ln(0.375) = 13.33 ms × 0.9808 = 13.08 ms. The relay therefore picks up in about 13 ms, roughly one time constant. A higher supply voltage would shorten this time because the current would cross 0.25 A earlier on the steeper part of the exponential, and a series resistor with a higher supply is a standard way to speed up a relay.

Answer: 13.08 ms

(c)

The inductor current cannot change instantly, so at the instant of disconnection the 0.4 A that was flowing in the coil continues, and the only path is through the 240 Ω resistor. The voltage across that resistor is v = I R = 0.4 × 240 = 96 V in magnitude. Its polarity is reversed compared with the supply voltage, because the coil acts as a source while its field collapses. Without a freewheel path, the voltage would try to become very large, which is why the resistor is connected.

Answer: 96 V

(d)

After disconnection the coil, its 60 Ω winding and the 240 Ω resistor form a single series loop of 300 Ω with L = 0.8 H, so τ2 = 0.8/300 = 2.667 ms. The current decays as i(t) = 0.4 e-t/τ2. Setting this equal to 0.10 A, e-t/τ2 = 0.25, so t = τ2 ln 4 = 2.667 ms × 1.3863 = 3.697 ms. The decay is about five times faster than the build-up, because the loop resistance is five times larger, and a larger freewheel resistor gives faster release but a higher voltage.

Answer: 3.697 ms

(e)

The energy stored in the coil at the start of the decay is ½ L I² = 0.5 × 0.8 × 0.4² = 0.064 J. In the series loop of 300 Ω, this energy is divided between the coil winding and the freewheel resistor in proportion to their resistances, because they carry the same current. The share in the 240 Ω resistor is 240/300 = 0.8 of 0.064 J = 0.0512 J. The remaining 0.0128 J is dissipated in the 60 Ω winding resistance.

Answer: 0.0512 J

Problem 3 [A1-068] Second-order RLC natural and step response

A pulse-forming circuit consists of an ideal 50 V DC source in series with a switch, a 40 Ω resistor, a 10 mH inductor and a 10 μF capacitor, all in a single series loop. The output is the voltage vC across the capacitor. The switch closes at t = 0 and before that the inductor current and the capacitor voltage are both zero. The circuit is to be analysed for the step response, and the resistor is then redesigned so that the response has no overshoot. Treat all elements as ideal apart from the stated resistance and take time in seconds.

  1. (a) Find the damping coefficient α = R/(2L) in s⁻¹. [3]
  2. (b) Find the damped natural frequency ωd in rad/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the time of the first peak of vC, in ms. [4]
  4. (d) Find the peak value of vC. [5]
  5. (e) Find the resistance required for critical damping. [4]
(a)

The series RLC loop gives the characteristic equation s² + (R/L) s + 1/(LC) = 0. The damping coefficient is α = R/(2L) = 40/(2 × 0.010) = 2000 s⁻¹. The undamped natural frequency is ω0 = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(0.010 × 10 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/√(10⁻⁷) = 3162.3 rad/s. Because α is less than ω0, the roots are complex and the response is underdamped. The damping ratio is ζ = α/ω0 = 0.632, which is a moderate value that predicts visible but modest overshoot.

Answer: 2000 s⁻¹

(b)

For an underdamped circuit the roots are s = -α ± jωd, where ωd = √(ω0² - α²). Then ωd = √(3162.3² - 2000²) = √(10⁷ - 4 × 10⁶) = √(6 × 10⁶) = 2449.5 rad/s. This is the angular frequency of the ringing in the capacitor voltage, which gives a period of 2π/2449.5 = 2.565 ms. The envelope of the oscillation decays as e-2000 t, with a time constant of 0.5 ms, so the ringing dies out within a few milliseconds.

Answer: 2449.5 rad/s

(c)

The step response of the capacitor voltage is vC(t) = 50 [1 - e-αt (cos ωd t + (α/ωd) sin ωd t)] V. Setting the derivative to zero, the extremes occur where sin ωd t = 0, so the first peak is at tp = π/ωd = 3.1416/2449.5 = 1.2825 ms. Subsequent extremes are spaced by the same interval, alternately above and below the final value of 50 V. The peak time depends only on ωd, so it would be unchanged by a change in the source voltage, which only scales the whole response.

Answer: 1.2825 ms

(d)

At the first peak the exponential factor is e-α tp = e-2000 × 1.2825 × 10⁻³ = e-2.565 = 0.0769. At this instant cos ωd tp = -1 and sin ωd tp = 0, so vC = 50 [1 + 0.0769] = 53.85 V. The overshoot is 7.69 percent, equal to exp(-π α/ωd). This peak voltage is the stress the capacitor must withstand, so a 63 V rated capacitor would be the minimum choice, with a safety margin on top of it.

Answer: 53.85 V

(e)

Critical damping occurs when α = ω0, that is, R/(2L) = 1/√(LC), so R = 2 √(L/C). Here L/C = 0.010/(10 × 10⁻⁶) = 1000, so R = 2 × √1000 = 2 × 31.62 = 63.25 Ω. The resistor must therefore be increased by about 58 percent, from 40 Ω to 63.25 Ω. With this value, vC rises to 50 V with no overshoot in the fastest possible non-oscillatory way, and any larger resistance gives an overdamped, slower response.

Answer: 63.25 Ω

Problem 4 [A1-069] Sinusoidal steady state with phasors

A workshop is fed from a 60 Hz single-phase source of 240 V rms, taken as the phase reference, through a line of impedance 0.5 + j1.0 Ω. At the far end of the line two loads are connected in parallel across the same load bus. Load 1 has impedance Z1 = 12 + j9 Ω. Load 2 has impedance Z2 = 20 - j15 Ω. Use rms phasors throughout and the convention that a positive angle on current means the current leads the source voltage. Find the line current, the voltage at the load bus, the power absorbed by the loads and the loss in the line.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the line current. [4]
  2. (b) Find the angle of the line current relative to the source voltage, in degrees. [4]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the voltage at the load bus. [4]
  4. (d) Find the total average power absorbed by the two loads. [4]
  5. (e) Find the average power lost in the line impedance. [4]
(a)

First combine the loads in parallel: Zp = Z1 Z2/(Z1 + Z2). The product is (12 + j9)(20 - j15) = 240 - j180 + j180 + 135 = 375. The sum is 32 - j6. So Zp = 375/(32 - j6) = 375(32 + j6)/(32² + 6²) = 375(32 + j6)/1060 = 11.32 + j2.12 Ω. The total impedance is 0.5 + j1.0 + 11.32 + j2.12 = 11.82 + j3.12 Ω, of magnitude 12.22 Ω. The line current magnitude is 240/12.22 = 19.63 A.

Answer: 19.63 A

(b)

The angle of the total impedance is arctan(3.12/11.82) = 14.80°, positive because the total reactance is inductive. The current phasor is the source phasor, 240 at 0°, divided by the impedance, so its angle is -14.80°. The current lags the source voltage by 14.80°, which is expected for a net inductive circuit. The load bus therefore sees a lagging current, although load 2 is capacitive on its own, because load 1 and the line inductance dominate. The result is a power factor angle of 14.80° seen from the source, so the source also supplies reactive power to the line and to load 1.

Answer: -14.80°

(c)

The load bus voltage is the current times the parallel impedance. The magnitude of Zp is √(11.32² + 2.12²) = 11.52 Ω. Then |Vl| = 19.63 × 11.52 = 226.1 V. This is 13.9 V lower than the 240 V source, a drop of 5.8 percent caused by the line impedance. The phase of Vl is -14.80° + 10.62° = -4.18°, so the bus voltage lags the source slightly, as the current has the angle of -14.80° and Zp has an angle of +10.62°.

Answer: 226.1 V

(d)

The branch currents follow from the bus voltage: |I1| = 226.1/|12 + j9| = 226.1/15 = 15.07 A and |I2| = 226.1/|20 - j15| = 226.1/25 = 9.04 A. The average power is the sum of the resistive losses, P = 15.07² × 12 + 9.04² × 20 = 2726 + 1636 = 4362 W. Load 1 absorbs 2726 W and load 2 absorbs 1636 W. The reactive power is 817.9 var lagging in total, so the apparent power is 4438 VA and the load power factor is 0.983 lagging.

Answer: 4362 W

(e)

The average power lost in the line is the resistive part only: P = |I|² R = 19.63² × 0.5 = 385.3 × 0.5 = 192.7 W. The source delivers 240 × 19.63 × cos 14.80° = 4555 W. Check: 4362 + 192.7 = 4555 W. The line loss is 4.2 percent of the delivered power. Improving the power factor at the load bus would lower the line current and therefore this loss, since the loss varies with the square of the current. Note also that the load bus voltage is not equal to the source voltage, so any rating based on 240 V would overstate the load power.

Answer: 192.7 W

Problem 5 [A1-070] AC power, complex power and power factor correction

A 600 V, 60 Hz single-phase industrial feeder supplies a load of 180 kW at a power factor of 0.72 lagging. The feeder conductors have a total resistance of 0.05 Ω in the go-and-return path, and the source behind the plant bus is modelled as an inductance of 0.25 mH. A capacitor bank is to be connected across the load to raise the power factor to 0.95 lagging. Take the load voltage as 600 V rms before and after correction, and take the real power as constant. Assume the capacitor bank is lossless and that the feeder loss is due to its resistance only.

  1. (a) Find the reactive power that the capacitor bank must supply, in kvar. [4]
  2. (b) Find the capacitance required, in μF. [4]
  3. (c) Find the feeder current after correction. [3]
  4. (d) Find the reduction in feeder loss, in kW. [4]
  5. (e) The capacitor bank resonates with the source inductance. Find the harmonic order of this parallel resonance, as a multiple of 60 Hz, and state in one sentence why a value near a characteristic harmonic is a concern. [5]
(a)

The initial angle is φ1 = arccos 0.72 = 43.95°, with tan φ1 = 0.9639. The final angle is φ2 = arccos 0.95 = 18.19°, with tan φ2 = 0.3287. The real power is unchanged, so the bank supplies Qc = P (tan φ1 - tan φ2) = 180 × (0.9639 - 0.3287) = 180 × 0.6352 = 114.3 kvar. The load still draws its reactive power, but the capacitors now supply that amount locally, so the source supplies only the remainder, about 59.2 kvar.

Answer: 114.3 kvar

(b)

The reactive power of a capacitor at voltage V is Qc = ω C V², so C = Qc/(ω V²). With ω = 2π × 60 = 376.99 rad/s and V = 600 V, C = 114.33 × 10³/(376.99 × 360 000) = 114 330/135.7 × 10⁶ = 842.4 × 10⁻⁶ F = 842 μF. In practice a bank of standard units in parallel would be chosen, and the nearest standard size would give a power factor close to, but not exactly, 0.95. The capacitor voltage rating must exceed 600 V.

Answer: 842.4 μF

(c)

After correction the real power is still 180 kW but the current is smaller. I = P/(V pf) = 180 000/(600 × 0.95) = 315.8 A. Before correction I = 180 000/(600 × 0.72) = 416.7 A. The current falls by about 24 percent, which also frees capacity in the feeder, so the same conductors can carry more real load. The correction works because the capacitor current, leading by 90°, cancels part of the lagging reactive component of the load current.

Answer: 315.8 A

(d)

The feeder loss is I² R. Before correction it is 416.7² × 0.05 = 173 611 × 0.05 = 8.68 kW. After correction it is 315.8² × 0.05 = 99 723 × 0.05 = 4.99 kW. The reduction is 8.68 - 4.99 = 3.69 kW, a saving of about 43 percent of the feeder loss. Over a year of continuous operation this is about 32 MWh, which is a typical justification for correction, since utilities also may charge penalties for a low power factor.

Answer: 3.694 kW

(e)

Seen from the load bus, the capacitor and the source inductance form a parallel resonant circuit at f = 1/(2π √(L C)) = 1/(2π √(0.25 × 10⁻³ × 842.4 × 10⁻⁶)). The product is 2.106 × 10⁻⁷, its square root is 4.589 × 10⁻⁴, and f = 1/(2.883 × 10⁻³) = 346.8 Hz. The harmonic order is 346.8/60 = 5.78. This is close to the 5th and 7th harmonics, which are common from rectifier loads, so harmonic currents may be amplified by the resonance and overload the capacitors.

Answer: 5.78

A1 Practice Paper 15

Problem 1 [A1-071] Frequency response, resonance and quality factor

A medium-wave receiver front end is modelled as a series loop made of an ideal voltage source of 2.00 mV rms (the signal induced in the antenna coil), a coil of inductance 250 μH with a total winding resistance of 12.0 Ω, and a variable tuning capacitor C. All three elements are in one series loop, and the receiver output is taken as the voltage across the capacitor. The station to be received broadcasts at 990 kHz. Treat the coil resistance as the only loss in the circuit and treat the source as having zero internal impedance. Work with rms phasors and use ω = 2πf throughout.

  1. (a) Find the capacitance, in pF, to which the tuning capacitor must be set for resonance at 990 kHz. [5]
  2. (b) Find the quality factor Q of the loop at resonance and the half-power bandwidth in kHz. [5]
  3. (c) Find the rms voltage across the capacitor, in mV, when the source is exactly at 990 kHz. [5]
  4. (d) The source frequency is now 1.000 MHz with the capacitor unchanged. Find the capacitor voltage in mV and state how this compares with the 990 kHz result. [5]
(a)

At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, so ω0²LC = 1. With ω0 = 2π × 990 × 10³ = 6.2204 × 10⁶ rad/s, ω0² = 3.8694 × 10¹³ rad²/s². Then C = 1/(ω0²L) = 1/(3.8694 × 10¹³ × 250 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/(9.6736 × 10⁹) = 1.0338 × 10⁻¹⁰ F. This is 103.4 pF, a value well inside the range of a typical air-spaced tuning capacitor. The method is simply the resonance condition for a series RLC loop, where the net reactance is zero and the impedance is purely the coil resistance of 12 Ω. Checking the answer: 1/(ω0C) = 1/(6.2204 × 10⁶ × 103.4 × 10⁻¹²) = 1555 Ω, equal to ω0L = 1555 Ω.

Answer: 103.4 pF

(b)

For a series loop, Q = ω0L/R. Here ω0L = 6.2204 × 10⁶ × 250 × 10⁻⁶ = 1555.1 Ω, so Q = 1555.1/12.0 = 129.6. The half-power (3 dB) bandwidth is the frequency span between the two points where the current magnitude falls to 1/√2 of its peak, and for a series resonant circuit it is B = f0/Q = ω0/(2πQ) = R/(2πL). Substituting, B = 990 kHz/129.6 = 7.64 kHz. The same figure follows from R/(2πL) = 12/(2π × 250 × 10⁻⁶) = 7639 Hz. A bandwidth of 7.6 kHz is narrow enough to separate stations spaced 10 kHz apart, which is the design purpose of the tuned stage.

Answer: Q = 129.6, bandwidth 7.64 kHz

(c)

At resonance the loop current is limited only by R, so I = Vs/R = 2.00 mV/12.0 Ω = 166.7 μA rms. The capacitor voltage magnitude is the current times the capacitive reactance, Vc = I/(ω0C) = 166.7 × 10⁻⁶ × 1555.1 = 0.2592 V. Equivalently Vc = Q Vs = 129.6 × 2.00 mV = 259.2 mV, which shows the voltage magnification of a series resonant circuit: the output across C is Q times larger than the source. Here the transfer function from source to capacitor voltage has magnitude 1/(ω C |Z|), and at ω0 it equals Q. This passive voltage gain, with no active device, is why a resonant input stage helps a weak signal.

Answer: 259 mV

(d)

At ω = 2π × 1.000 × 10⁶ = 6.2832 × 10⁶ rad/s the inductive reactance is ωL = 1570.8 Ω and the capacitive reactance is 1/(ωC) = 1/(6.2832 × 10⁶ × 103.38 × 10⁻¹²) = 1539.5 Ω. The net reactance is X = 1570.8 − 1539.5 = 31.3 Ω, so |Z| = √(12² + 31.3²) = 33.5 Ω. The current is I = 2.00 mV/33.5 Ω = 59.7 μA, and the capacitor voltage is Vc = I × 1539.5 = 0.0920 V = 92.0 mV. This is 92.0/259.2 = 0.355 of the resonant value, a drop of about 9.0 dB.
