The filter is linear and time-invariant, with transfer function H(jω) = 1/(1 + jωRC). The three components are a DC offset, a 100 Hz structural-vibration tone and a 1 kHz interference tone. Treat steady state only, and take phase as the angle of the output relative to the input, negative for lag. Report angles in degrees.

  1. (a) Find the cutoff (3 dB) frequency of the filter, in Hz. [5]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the frequency response |H| at 1 kHz. [5]
  3. (c) Find the phase angle of H at 1 kHz, in degrees (give a negative number for a lag). [5]
  4. (d) Find the mean-square value of the steady-state output voltage, in V², including the DC term and both tones. [5]
(a)

For a first-order RC low-pass the magnitude is |H| = 1/√(1 + (ωRC)²), which falls to 1/√2 when ωRC = 1. The time constant is RC = 2000 × 0.1×10⁻⁶ = 2.00×10⁻⁴ s. The cutoff angular frequency is ωc = 1/RC = 5000 rad/s, and the cutoff in hertz is fc = ωc/2π = 5000/6.2832 = 796 Hz. The 100 Hz vibration tone lies well below this and will pass almost unattenuated, while the 1 kHz interference lies above cutoff and will be reduced. Because there is no load, the capacitor voltage is the output and the above expression holds exactly.

Answer: 796 Hz

(b)

At 1 kHz, ω = 2π × 1000 = 6283.2 rad/s. Then ωRC = 6283.2 × 2.0×10⁻⁴ = 1.2566. The magnitude is |H| = 1/√(1 + 1.2566²) = 1/√(1 + 1.5791) = 1/√2.5791 = 1/1.6060 = 0.6227. So the 1 kHz component is reduced to about 62 percent of its input amplitude, a reduction of 4.1 dB. A single RC section gives only a gentle attenuation just above cutoff, so a designer who needs the interference at least 20 dB down would need a higher-order filter or a lower cutoff frequency.

Answer: 0.623

(c)

The phase of H(jω) = 1/(1 + jωRC) is −arctan(ωRC). At 1 kHz, ωRC = 1.2566, so the phase is −arctan(1.2566) = −51.49°. The negative sign means the output lags the input. At the cutoff frequency the lag would be exactly 45°, and as frequency increases the lag approaches 90°, so 51.5° is slightly beyond the corner as expected. This lag corresponds to a time delay of 51.49/360 of the 1 ms period, about 0.143 ms. Phase information matters if the filtered signal is later compared in timing with another channel.

Answer: -51.5°

(d)

The output is the sum of three components, each scaled by the gain at its own frequency. DC: gain 1, so 2 V and mean square 4.000. The 100 Hz tone: ωRC = 628.32 × 2.0×10⁻⁴ = 0.12566, gain = 1/√(1 + 0.01579) = 0.99220, amplitude 3 × 0.9922 = 2.9766 V, mean square = 2.9766²/2 = 4.430. The 1 kHz tone: amplitude 1.5 × 0.6227 = 0.9340 V, mean square = 0.9340²/2 = 0.4362. Because the components are at different frequencies, their cross terms average to zero, so the total is 4.000 + 4.430 + 0.436 = 8.87 V². The input had 4 + 4.5 + 1.125 = 9.625 V².

Answer: 8.87 V²

Problem 5 [A3-005] Sampling and the Nyquist theorem, aliasing

A vibration monitor on a pump at a Windsor water plant digitizes a signal x(t) = cos(2π·3000t) + 0.5cos(2π·7000t) with t in seconds. The data acquisition card samples at fs = 10 kHz and the samples are then converted back to an analog voltage with an ideal reconstruction low-pass filter that passes all frequencies below fs/2 and blocks all frequencies above. The designer originally assumed the 7 kHz tone was far enough above the signal of interest to be harmless, so no anti-alias filter was fitted before the sampler. Both tones start with zero phase, and the sampled values are x[n] = x(n/fs). Frequencies of aliased components are to be reported as the apparent frequency in the range 0 to fs/2.

  1. (a) Find the Nyquist rate for this signal, in kHz, as the minimum sampling rate that avoids aliasing of both tones. [5]
  2. (b) Find the apparent (aliased) frequency of the 7 kHz tone after sampling at 10 kHz, in kHz. [5]
  3. (c) After ideal reconstruction, find the amplitude of the 3 kHz component in the output voltage, in volts. [5]
  4. (d) The card is changed to fs = 12 kHz with the same reconstruction filter (pass below 6 kHz). Find the apparent frequency of the 7 kHz tone, in kHz. [5]
(a)

The Nyquist theorem requires the sampling rate to exceed twice the highest frequency component in the signal. The highest tone is at 7 kHz, so the Nyquist rate is 2 × 7 = 14 kHz. Sampling at exactly the Nyquist rate is the borderline case, and in practice one samples somewhat above it. The card in use runs at 10 kHz, which is below 14 kHz, so aliasing must occur. The 3 kHz tone alone would need only 6 kHz, and is correctly sampled at 10 kHz. It is the 7 kHz tone that violates the criterion, since its frequency exceeds fs/2 = 5 kHz.

Answer: 14 kHz

(b)

Sampling at fs maps a tone at f onto f_alias = |f − k·fs| for the integer k that brings the result into 0 to fs/2. For f = 7 kHz and fs = 10 kHz, take k = 1: |7 − 10| = 3 kHz, which lies below 5 kHz. We can check with the samples: cos(2π × 7000 × n/10000) = cos(2π × 0.7 n) = cos(2π × (0.7 − 1) n) = cos(2π × 0.3 n), which is the sample sequence of a 3 kHz cosine. The 7 kHz tone therefore lands exactly on top of the genuine 3 kHz signal and cannot be told apart from it afterwards.

Answer: 3 kHz

(c)

The reconstruction filter passes everything below 5 kHz, so the reconstructed output contains only a 3 kHz cosine. The original 3 kHz tone has amplitude 1.0 and, from the previous part, the 7 kHz tone is aliased into cos(2π × 0.3 n) with its amplitude 0.5, with no phase change because both are cosines starting at zero phase and the sign of the cosine argument does not matter. These two sequences add in phase, giving an output amplitude of 1.0 + 0.5 = 1.50 V. The measurement is therefore 50 percent too large, and the error cannot be corrected after the fact. An analog anti-alias filter ahead of the sampler is the only cure.

Answer: 1.50 V

(d)

At fs = 12 kHz the folding frequency is 6 kHz, and 7 kHz is still above it, so aliasing persists. The apparent frequency is |7 − 12| = 5 kHz, which lies within 0 to 6 kHz. The sample sequence is cos(2π × 7000 n/12000) = cos(2π × (7/12) n) = cos(2π × (−5/12) n) = cos(2π × (5/12) n), a 5 kHz cosine. Although the alias no longer coincides with the 3 kHz tone, so the 3 kHz measurement is now correct at 1.0 V, a spurious 5 kHz line of amplitude 0.5 V appears in the output. Raising the rate above 14 kHz is the only way to remove it.

Answer: 5 kHz

A3 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A3-006] Reconstruction and quantization noise

An energy-metering project at a Mississauga substation uses a 10-bit analog-to-digital converter whose input range is −2.50 V to +2.50 V, a total span of 5.00 V. The converter is a uniform mid-tread quantizer with 210 levels, and the quantization error is assumed uniformly distributed over one step with zero mean and independent of the signal. The signal is a sinusoidal voltage of amplitude 2.00 V, so it does not use the whole range. Answers use the standard model in which the quantization step is Δ = span/2N, and the noise power is Δ²/12 into a 1 Ω reference. The signal power is also referred to 1 Ω. Report noise in millivolts rms and SNR in decibels.

  1. (a) Find the quantization step Δ, in millivolts. [5]
  2. (b) Find the rms quantization noise voltage, in millivolts. [5]
  3. (c) Find the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio for the 2.00 V amplitude sinusoid, in decibels. [5]
  4. (d) The metering specification demands at least 72 dB SNR for this same 2.00 V amplitude on the same 5.00 V span. Find the smallest whole number of bits N that satisfies it. [5]
(a)

The span is 5.00 V divided into 210 = 1024 equal steps, so Δ = 5.00/1024 = 4.8828×10⁻³ V = 4.88 mV. This is the voltage resolution of the converter, the smallest change in input that can move the output code by one level. Because the quantizer rounds to the nearest level, the error never exceeds ±Δ/2 = ±2.44 mV for an in-range input. Each added bit halves the step size, so an 11-bit converter on the same range would have a step of 2.44 mV.

Answer: 4.88 mV

(b)

For an error uniformly distributed over (−Δ/2, +Δ/2), the mean-square error is Δ²/12, derived from the integral (1/Δ)∫ e² de over that interval. Hence the rms noise is Δ/√12 = 4.8828 mV/3.4641 = 1.4095 mV. The result is independent of the signal as long as the signal is large and busy enough to make the uniform-error assumption valid. At a sampling rate fs this noise power is spread evenly over 0 to fs/2, so oversampling could reduce the noise density within a narrow signal band, although this question does not require it.

Answer: 1.41 mV

(c)

The signal power of a sine with amplitude 2.00 V is A²/2 = 4.00/2 = 2.00 V² (on 1 Ω). The noise power is Δ²/12 = (4.8828×10⁻³)²/12 = 1.987×10⁻⁶ V². The ratio is 2.00/1.987×10⁻⁶ = 1.0066×10⁶, and in decibels SNR = 10 log10(1.0066×10⁶) = 60.03 dB. A full-range sine would give 6.02N + 1.76 = 61.96 dB, so using only 80 percent of the range costs 20 log10(0.8) = 1.94 dB. This illustrates why the input gain should be set to fill the converter range without clipping.

Answer: 60.0 dB

(d)

For a sine of amplitude A on a span S, SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 + 20 log10(2A/S), where 2A/S is the fraction of the full-scale peak-to-peak span used. Here 2A/S = 4/5 = 0.8, so the last term is −1.94 dB. We need 6.02N + 1.76 − 1.94 ≥ 72, so 6.02N ≥ 72.18 and N ≥ 11.99. The smallest whole number is N = 12 bits. At 11 bits the SNR would be 6.02(11) + 1.76 − 1.94 = 66.0 dB, falling short, while 12 bits gives 6.02(12) + 1.76 − 1.94 = 72.1 dB, which just passes. The margin is thin, so a designer might still choose a better converter.

Answer: 12 bits

Problem 2 [A3-007] Discrete-time systems and difference equations

A temperature controller in an Oshawa plastics plant smooths sensor readings x[n] with a second-order recursive filter implemented in a PLC. The output is given by the difference equation y[n] = 0.6 y[n−1] − 0.08 y[n−2] + x[n], with all initial conditions (y[−1] = y[−2] = 0 and x[n] = 0 for n < 0) equal to zero, so the system starts at rest. The input is applied at n = 0. The system is linear and time-invariant. Part of the exercise uses the unit impulse δ[n] and the unit step u[n] as test inputs. Use the characteristic polynomial z² − 0.6z + 0.08 to discuss pole locations. Sample values are in degrees Celsius normalized to a unit input, so no units are attached to the filter outputs.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the pole with the largest magnitude of the system. [5]
  2. (b) Find the impulse response value h[3]. [5]
  3. (c) Find the unit step response value y[3] for x[n] = u[n]. [5]
  4. (d) Find the steady-state (DC) gain of the filter, that is the final value of y[n] for a unit step input. [5]
(a)

The poles are the roots of the characteristic polynomial z² − 0.6z + 0.08 = 0. By the quadratic formula, z = (0.6 ± √(0.36 − 0.32))/2 = (0.6 ± 0.2)/2, giving z = 0.4 and z = 0.2. Both poles are real and lie inside the unit circle, so the system is stable (bounded input gives bounded output). The larger pole at 0.4 dominates the slow part of the response, since 0.4n decays more slowly than 0.2n. The magnitude of the dominant pole is therefore 0.400, which implies the transient decays by a factor of about 0.4 per sample.

Answer: 0.400

(b)

For x[n] = δ[n] the recursion gives h[0] = x[0] = 1 (since the earlier outputs are zero). Then h[1] = 0.6 h[0] − 0.08 h[−1] = 0.6. Next h[2] = 0.6 h[1] − 0.08 h[0] = 0.36 − 0.08 = 0.28. Finally h[3] = 0.6 h[2] − 0.08 h[1] = 0.168 − 0.048 = 0.120. As a check, the closed form with the poles 0.4 and 0.2 is h[n] = 2(0.4)n − (0.2)n, which at n = 3 gives 2(0.064) − 0.008 = 0.120, matching the recursion.

Answer: 0.120

(c)

Run the recursion with x[n] = 1 for n ≥ 0. At n = 0: y[0] = 0 + 0 + 1 = 1. At n = 1: y[1] = 0.6(1) − 0.08(0) + 1 = 1.6. At n = 2: y[2] = 0.6(1.6) − 0.08(1) + 1 = 0.96 − 0.08 + 1 = 1.88. At n = 3: y[3] = 0.6(1.88) − 0.08(1.6) + 1 = 1.128 − 0.128 + 1 = 2.000. Alternatively the step response is the running sum of h[n]: 1 + 0.6 + 0.28 + 0.12 = 2.00, which agrees. The output is climbing toward its steady-state value, which is requested in the next part.

Answer: 2.00

(d)

For a stable system the DC gain is the sum of the impulse response, equivalently the transfer function evaluated at z = 1. Setting y[n] = y[n−1] = y[n−2] = y_ss and x[n] = 1 in the difference equation gives y_ss = 0.6 y_ss − 0.08 y_ss + 1, so y_ss (1 − 0.6 + 0.08) = 1 and y_ss = 1/0.48 = 2.0833. Since y[3] = 2.000 is already within 4 percent of this, the settling is quick, consistent with the dominant pole of 0.4. A unit change in the sensor input therefore ends up as a 2.083 change in the smoothed output, so the filter has gain above unity at DC.

Answer: 2.083

Problem 3 [A3-008] The Z-transform and region of convergence

A sampled-data model of a heat exchanger in a Sarnia refinery has a causal impulse response h[n] = (0.7)n u[n] + 2(−0.5)n u[n], where n is the sample index. Use the one-sided definition H(z) = Σ h[n] z−n and the standard pair an u[n] ↔ z/(z − a) valid for |z| > |a|. The system is causal, so the region of convergence (ROC) of the sum is the intersection of the individual regions, lying outside a circle in the z-plane. The unit circle is |z| = 1, and the frequency response exists when the ROC includes it. Evaluate the transform only at points inside its ROC, and treat all quantities as dimensionless sample values.

  1. (a) State the radius of the circle outside which the ROC lies (|z| > r) and give r. [5]
  2. (b) Evaluate H(z) at z = 2, a point inside the ROC. [5]
  3. (c) Find the sum of all impulse response samples, Σ h[n], using H(z). [5]
  4. (d) Find the sample value h[4] of the impulse response. [5]
(a)

H(z) = z/(z − 0.7) + 2z/(z + 0.5). The first term converges for |z| > 0.7 and the second for |z| > 0.5. For a sum, the ROC is the intersection of the two regions, which is |z| > 0.7, the larger of the two radii. So r = 0.700. Since 0.7 < 1, the unit circle lies inside the ROC, so the system has a frequency response and is BIBO stable. The poles of H(z) are at z = 0.7 and z = −0.5, and the ROC always lies outside the outermost pole for a causal sequence.

Answer: 0.700

(b)

Substitute z = 2 into each term: the first term is 2/(2 − 0.7) = 2/1.3 = 1.5385. The second term is 2 × 2/(2 + 0.5) = 4/2.5 = 1.6000. The sum is H(2) = 1.5385 + 1.6000 = 3.1385. The point z = 2 satisfies |z| > 0.7, so the series Σ h[n] 2−n converges and equals this value. A quick check from the series: h[0] = 3, h[1] = 0.7 − 1 = −0.3, h[2] = 0.49 + 0.5 = 0.99; the partial sum 3 − 0.15 + 0.2475 + ... heads toward 3.14, consistent with the closed form.

Answer: 3.14

(c)

The sum of all samples is H evaluated at z = 1, valid because the unit circle is inside the ROC. H(1) = 1/(1 − 0.7) + 2/(1 + 0.5) = 1/0.3 + 2/1.5 = 3.3333 + 1.3333 = 4.6667. This is also the DC gain of the system, the steady-state output for a unit step input. Check with the geometric series: Σ 0.7n = 1/(1 − 0.7) = 3.3333, and Σ 2(−0.5)n = 2/(1 + 0.5) = 1.3333, which total 4.6667, agreeing exactly. A DC gain of 4.67 means a steady unit disturbance produces a final output 4.67 times larger.

Answer: 4.67

(d)

Evaluate the time-domain expression directly at n = 4. The first term is 0.74 = 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.2401. The second term is 2(−0.5)4 = 2 × 0.0625 = 0.1250, since an even power makes the negative base positive. Then h[4] = 0.2401 + 0.1250 = 0.3651. Alternatively, h[4] is the coefficient of z−4 in the series expansion of H(z). The pole at −0.5 makes the odd-indexed samples smaller, because (−0.5)n alternates in sign. The sequence therefore decays but with a small alternating component, which matters for any ringing in the response.

Answer: 0.365

Problem 4 [A3-009] Inverse Z-transform and system response

A digital equalizer in a Kingston telephone exchange has the transfer function H(z) = (1 + 0.5 z⁻¹)/((1 − 0.5 z⁻¹)(1 − 0.25 z⁻¹)), and it is causal and initially at rest. Its input is the unit impulse δ[n], so the output y[n] is the impulse response and the transform of the output is Y(z) = H(z). Use partial fractions on Y(z)/z or on the equivalent z⁻¹ form to write y[n] = A(0.5)n + B(0.25)n for n ≥ 0, and use the standard pair an u[n] ↔ 1/(1 − a z⁻¹) for |z| > |a|. All quantities are dimensionless sample values. The region of convergence is |z| > 0.5, which includes the unit circle.

  1. (a) Find the coefficient A of the (0.5)n term. [5]
  2. (b) Find the coefficient B of the (0.25)n term (give the signed value). [5]
  3. (c) Find the output sample y[5] for the impulse input. [5]
  4. (d) Find the sum of all output samples, Σ y[n], which is the DC gain of the equalizer. [5]
(a)

Write Y(z) = z(z + 0.5)/((z − 0.5)(z − 0.25)). Dividing by z gives Y(z)/z = (z + 0.5)/((z − 0.5)(z − 0.25)). The residue at z = 0.5 is A = (0.5 + 0.5)/(0.5 − 0.25) = 1.0/0.25 = 4.00. The coefficient A multiplies the pole at 0.5 in the output, since multiplying a partial fraction A/(z − 0.5) by z yields Az/(z − 0.5), whose inverse transform is A(0.5)n u[n]. Cover-up is used: delete the factor (z − 0.5) from the denominator and evaluate the rest at z = 0.5.

Answer: 4.00

(b)

The residue at z = 0.25 is B = (0.25 + 0.5)/(0.25 − 0.5) = 0.75/(−0.25) = −3.00. Together with A = 4, the impulse response is y[n] = 4(0.5)n − 3(0.25)n for n ≥ 0. A check at n = 0 gives 4 − 3 = 1, which must equal h[0] = 1 since the numerator and denominator are both monic in z⁰. At n = 1 the formula gives 2 − 0.75 = 1.25, which matches the direct long division: H(z) = 1 + 1.25 z⁻¹ + ..., so the partial fraction is confirmed.

Answer: -3.00

(c)

Use y[n] = 4(0.5)n − 3(0.25)n. At n = 5, 0.55 = 0.03125 and 0.255 = 0.0009766. Then y[5] = 4 × 0.03125 − 3 × 0.0009766 = 0.12500 − 0.0029297 = 0.12207. The response is dominated by the slower pole at 0.5 by this stage, because the faster 0.25n term has nearly disappeared (its contribution is only 2.3 percent of the total). The output decays by roughly a factor of two per sample, as expected from the dominant pole. We can also verify with the recursion y[n] = 0.75 y[n−1] − 0.125 y[n−2] + δ[n] + 0.5 δ[n−1], which gives the same value.

Answer: 0.122

(d)

Because the ROC |z| > 0.5 contains the unit circle, the sum of the impulse response equals H(z) at z = 1. H(1) = (1 + 0.5)/((1 − 0.5)(1 − 0.25)) = 1.5/(0.5 × 0.75) = 1.5/0.375 = 4.00. Checking with the closed-form samples: Σ 4(0.5)n = 4/(1 − 0.5) = 8 and Σ 3(0.25)n = 3/(1 − 0.25) = 4, so the total is 8 − 4 = 4.00, which agrees. The equalizer therefore has a DC gain of 4, and a constant input of unit size will settle to an output of 4, which the line designer must allow for when setting amplifier headroom.

Answer: 4.00

Problem 5 [A3-010] Discrete-time frequency response and stability

A resonant digital filter in a vibration analyzer built in Waterloo has the transfer function H(z) = 1/(1 − 1.2 z⁻¹ + 0.72 z⁻²), implemented at a sampling frequency fs = 8 kHz. The filter is causal. The frequency response is H(ejω) with ω the digital frequency in rad/sample, and the real frequency is f = ω fs/(2π). The denominator can be written as (1 − r ejθ z⁻¹)(1 − r e−jθ z⁻¹), a complex-conjugate pole pair at z = r e±jθ. A causal filter is stable when all poles lie strictly inside the unit circle. Angles are requested in degrees and magnitudes as plain numbers.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude r of the complex-conjugate poles. [5]
  2. (b) Find the pole angle θ in degrees. [5]
  3. (c) Find the DC gain |H(ej0)|. [5]
  4. (d) Find the gain |H(ejπ/4)| at the pole angle, which corresponds to 1 kHz. [5]
(a)

The product of the pole pair is r², and it equals the constant term of the denominator polynomial z² − 1.2z + 0.72. Hence r² = 0.72 and r = √0.72 = 0.8485. Since r < 1, both poles lie inside the unit circle, so the filter is stable. The closer r is to 1, the sharper the resonance, so r = 0.85 gives a moderately sharp peak. The magnitude of 0.849 also sets the decay rate of the impulse response, which falls as rn = 0.849n and takes about 14 samples to drop to 10 percent.

Answer: 0.849

(b)

For the pole pair, the sum of the poles is 2r cos θ, which equals the coefficient 1.2 in z² − 1.2z + 0.72. So cos θ = 1.2/(2 × 0.8485) = 1.2/1.6971 = 0.7071, giving θ = 45.0°, which is π/4 rad. At a sampling frequency of 8 kHz this corresponds to a real frequency of 8000 × 45/360 = 1000 Hz, so the filter resonates near 1 kHz. A pole pair with an angle of 45° gives an impulse response h[n] = rn sin((n+1)θ)/sin θ, an exponentially damped sinusoid that rings at about 1 kHz.

Answer: 45.0°

(c)

At ω = 0, z = 1, so the denominator is 1 − 1.2 + 0.72 = 0.52. The DC gain is |H| = 1/0.52 = 1.9231. This is the final value of the step response, since the poles are inside the unit circle. The gain at DC is larger than unity because the denominator is less than 1, which is expected for a resonant filter with positive-real-part poles. The step response will overshoot above 1.92 and ring at about 1 kHz before settling, since the poles are complex. The DC gain alone does not reveal this ringing.

Answer: 1.92

(d)

At ω = π/4, z⁻¹ = e−jπ/4 = 0.7071 − j0.7071 and z⁻² = e−jπ/2 = −j. The denominator is 1 − 1.2(0.7071 − j0.7071) + 0.72(−j) = 1 − 0.8485 + j0.8485 − j0.72 = 0.1515 + j0.1285. Its magnitude is √(0.1515² + 0.1285²) = √(0.02295 + 0.01651) = √0.03946 = 0.1987. Therefore |H| = 1/0.1987 = 5.03. This is the peak of the resonance, about 2.6 times the DC gain, or 14.0 dB versus 5.7 dB. The filter strongly amplifies the 1 kHz component, which suits a tuned vibration detector.

Answer: 5.03

A3 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A3-011] AM modulation and demodulation, bandwidth and efficiency

A regional broadcaster transmits conventional double-sideband AM with a large carrier on 1.2 MHz. The unmodulated carrier is 40 V peak across a 50 Ω resistive antenna load. The message is the sum of two tones: m(t) = 0.5 cos(2π × 2000 t) + 0.3 cos(2π × 5000 t), so the modulated signal is s(t) = 40[1 + m(t)] cos(2π × 1.2×10⁶ t) volts. A student plans to demodulate with a diode envelope detector driven by an ideal source, followed by an RC load. Treat the sidebands as exactly the components that the two tones produce and ignore any distortion products.

  1. (a) Find the transmission bandwidth of the signal in kilohertz. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total power in the sidebands in watts, dissipated in the 50 Ω load. [5]
  3. (c) Find the power efficiency of the transmission, the sideband power as a percentage of the total power. [5]
  4. (d) For the 5 kHz tone alone, with its modulation index of 0.3, find the largest RC time constant in microseconds for which the envelope detector can still follow the envelope without diagonal clipping. [6]
(a)

The spectrum contains the carrier plus a pair of sidebands for each tone, at fc ± 2 kHz and fc ± 5 kHz. The highest message frequency is therefore 5 kHz, and DSB AM occupies twice that, from fc − 5 kHz to fc + 5 kHz. So B = 2 × fm,max = 2 × 5 kHz = 10 kHz. The 2 kHz tone lies entirely inside this band and adds no extra bandwidth. Note that the bandwidth depends only on the highest message frequency, not on the modulation indices of the tones or on the carrier amplitude, which only set how the transmitted power is divided between carrier and sidebands.

Answer: B = 10 kHz

(b)

The carrier power is Pc = Ac²/(2R) = 40²/(2 × 50) = 1600/100 = 16 W. For a tone of modulation index μ each of the two sidebands has amplitude μAc/2, so the pair carries Pc μ²/2. With two tones the sideband powers add because the tones are at different frequencies: Ps = Pc(μ₁² + μ₂²)/2 = 16 × (0.25 + 0.09)/2 = 16 × 0.34/2 = 2.72 W. I assume the two tones produce no intermodulation, which is true for ideal linear AM. The total transmitted power is Pc + Ps = 18.72 W.

Answer: Ps = 2.72 W

(c)

Efficiency is the fraction of total power that sits in the sidebands, because only the sidebands carry the message. η = Ps/(Pc + Ps) = 2.72/(16 + 2.72) = 2.72/18.72 = 0.1453, or 14.5 percent. The remaining 85.5 percent of the transmitted power is carrier, which carries no information but allows a cheap envelope detector in the receiver. Efficiency rises with modulation depth, and for a single tone at μ = 1 it would reach only 33.3 percent, so a typical speech signal with a small average depth is quite inefficient. This is the price of simple receivers.

Answer: η = 14.5 %

(d)

The detector capacitor discharges through R with time constant RC, and it follows the envelope only if the discharge slope is no steeper than the envelope fall. For a tone the condition is RC ≤ √(1 − μ²)/(μ ωm). Here μ = 0.3 and ωm = 2π × 5000 = 31416 rad/s. Then √(1 − 0.09) = 0.9539 and μ ωm = 0.3 × 31416 = 9424.8 rad/s, so RC ≤ 0.9539/9424.8 = 1.012×10⁻⁴ s, about 101 μs. The carrier period (0.83 μs) is far shorter than this, so ripple is small. A larger RC would clip the falling edge of the envelope.

Answer: RC(max) ≈ 101 μs

Problem 2 [A3-012] DSB-SC, SSB and envelope detection

A suppressed-carrier link carries a single-tone test message m(t) = 2 cos(2π × 4000 t) volts on a carrier of frequency fc = 900 kHz with carrier amplitude factor Ac = 5, so the double-sideband suppressed-carrier signal is s(t) = Ac m(t) cos(2π fc t). The receiver multiplies the received signal by a local oscillator cos(2π fc t + φ) of unit amplitude and low-pass filters the product to remove the components near 2fc. The signal is developed across a 50 Ω load for power calculations. Later the transmitter is changed to send only the upper sideband of the same message with the same Ac, and the receiver oscillator develops a frequency error of 100 Hz.

  1. (a) For the DSB-SC system with φ = 25° and no frequency error, find the amplitude of the recovered 4 kHz tone in volts. [5]
  2. (b) Find the phase error φ in degrees at which the recovered amplitude falls to half of its value at φ = 0. [4]
  3. (c) Find the average power of the single-sideband (upper) transmitted signal in milliwatts across the 50 Ω load. [6]
  4. (d) For the SSB signal, with the receiver oscillator at fc + 100 Hz and no phase error assumption, find the frequency in hertz of the recovered audio tone. [5]
(a)

Multiplying s(t) by cos(2πfc t + φ) gives Ac m(t)[cos(φ) + cos(4πfc t + φ)]/2. The low-pass filter removes the 2fc term, leaving y(t) = (Ac/2) m(t) cos φ. For the tone, the amplitude is (Ac/2) × 2 × cos φ = 5 × cos 25° = 5 × 0.9063 = 4.532 V. With φ = 0 the amplitude would be 5 V, so a 25° phase error costs about 9 percent of the amplitude. I assume the filter has unity gain at 4 kHz and the oscillator amplitude is exactly one.

Answer: 4.53 V

(b)

The output scales with cos φ, so half of the φ = 0 value requires cos φ = 0.5. Hence φ = arccos(0.5) = 60°. At φ = 90° the output vanishes completely, because the oscillator is in quadrature with the carrier. This sensitivity to phase is the main disadvantage of coherent detection of DSB-SC, and it is why a pilot tone or a phase-locked loop such as a Costas loop is used. If the phase wanders in time, the recovered tone fades up and down, which is audible as a slow amplitude variation.

Answer: φ = 60°

(c)

The upper-sideband signal for a tone is a single component at fc + 4 kHz. The DSB-SC signal Ac m cos(ωct) is 5 × 2 cos(ωmt) cos(ωct) = 10 cos(ωmt) cos(ωct) = 5 cos((ωc + ωm)t) + 5 cos((ωc − ωm)t). Each sideband therefore has amplitude 5 V. The SSB signal keeps only one of them, amplitude 5 V, so its average power in 50 Ω is P = 5²/(2 × 50) = 25/100 = 0.25 W = 250 mW. The DSB-SC signal has twice this, 500 mW, for the same message but twice the bandwidth.

Answer: P(SSB) = 250 mW

(d)

The upper sideband is at fc + fm = 904 kHz. The oscillator at fc + 100 Hz = 900.1 kHz mixes with it to give a difference component at 904 − 900.1 = 3.9 kHz, which passes through the low-pass filter. So the recovered tone is at fm − Δf = 4000 − 100 = 3900 Hz. A frequency error in SSB shifts every audio component by the same number of hertz, which makes speech sound like a changed pitch (Donald Duck effect). Unlike DSB-SC, there is no fading, only a shift, and for 100 Hz speech remains intelligible.

Answer: f = 3900 Hz

Problem 3 [A3-013] Angle modulation: FM and PM, Carson bandwidth

A narrowband land-mobile transmitter is being compared with a phase modulator on the same test tone. The frequency modulator has frequency sensitivity kf = 15 kHz per volt, so the instantaneous frequency is fi(t) = fc + kf m(t). The test message is m(t) = 3 cos(2π × 5000 t) volts. The phase modulator has phase sensitivity kp radians per volt, so the instantaneous phase deviation is kp m(t). The carrier amplitude is the same in both systems. Use Carson's rule, B = 2(Δf + fm), for the bandwidth of each signal. Throughout, a tone of frequency fm and amplitude Am is applied, and the quoted tone is changed in part c and part d only.

  1. (a) Find the modulation index β of the FM signal for the 5 kHz tone. [4]
  2. (b) Find the Carson bandwidth of the FM signal in kilohertz. [4]
  3. (c) The tone frequency is raised to 10 kHz with the amplitude unchanged at 3 V. Find the new FM Carson bandwidth in kilohertz. [5]
  4. (d) The phase modulator is set so that its peak frequency deviation for the original 5 kHz, 3 V tone equals that of the FM system. With the same 3 V amplitude at 10 kHz, find the PM Carson bandwidth in kilohertz. [7]
(a)

For FM with a tone, the peak frequency deviation is Δf = kf Am = 15 kHz/V × 3 V = 45 kHz. The modulation index is the deviation divided by the tone frequency, β = Δf/fm = 45 kHz/5 kHz = 9. A β of 9 is wideband FM, far from the β < 0.5 narrowband case, so the spectrum contains many significant sidebands spaced fm apart. I take Am = 3 V as the peak value of the message. The deviation depends on message amplitude only, not on message frequency, for FM.

Answer: β = 9

(b)

Carson's rule gives the bandwidth containing about 98 percent of the signal power: B = 2(Δf + fm) = 2(45 + 5) kHz = 100 kHz. This is approximately 2fm(β + 1). The bandwidth is far larger than the 10 kHz that DSB AM would need for the same tone, which is the cost of the noise advantage of wideband FM. The carrier power is unaffected by the modulation, since the amplitude is constant, so all this bandwidth uses the same total power as the unmodulated carrier.

Answer: B = 100 kHz

(c)

For FM the deviation Δf = kf Am depends only on the message amplitude, so it stays at 45 kHz when the tone frequency changes. Now B = 2(45 + 10) = 110 kHz, and β falls to 4.5. The bandwidth grows only slightly, from 100 kHz to 110 kHz, because the deviation term dominates the bracket. This weak dependence on message frequency is why Carson's rule is useful for design with speech or music, where the highest frequency varies but the peak amplitude is controlled by a limiter or compressor.

Answer: B = 110 kHz

(d)

For PM, the phase deviation is Δφ = kp Am, and the peak frequency deviation is Δφ × fm because frequency is the derivative of phase. At 5 kHz and 3 V the FM deviation is 45 kHz, so Δφ = β = 9 rad and kp = 9/3 = 3 rad/V. At 10 kHz with 3 V the phase deviation is still 9 rad, so the frequency deviation is 9 × 10 kHz = 90 kHz. Carson gives B = 2(90 + 10) = 200 kHz. The PM bandwidth grows almost in proportion to fm, while the FM bandwidth hardly changed.

Answer: B(PM) = 200 kHz

Problem 4 [A3-014] FM demodulation and noise performance basics

A telemetry receiver for a wideband FM signal uses a limiter-discriminator demodulator. The transmitted signal is frequency modulated by a sinusoidal tone of frequency 15 kHz with a modulation index β = 5. At the receiver input the carrier power is 2.0 nW and the noise is white with one-sided power spectral density N0 = 1.0×10⁻¹⁷ W/Hz. The receiver has an ideal bandpass filter of width equal to the Carson bandwidth for this signal, followed by the ideal demodulator and an ideal low-pass filter of bandwidth 15 kHz. Assume operation above the FM threshold, so the standard output signal-to-noise ratio result for tone modulation applies: SNRout = (3/2) β² × (carrier power)/(N0 W), where W is the message bandwidth.

  1. (a) Find the Carson bandwidth of the FM signal in kilohertz. [3]
  2. (b) Find the carrier-to-noise ratio at the discriminator input, within the Carson bandwidth, in dB. [4]
  3. (c) Find the demodulated output signal-to-noise ratio in dB. [6]
  4. (d) Explain in words why increasing β raises the output SNR, what it costs, and what happens to the output when the input carrier-to-noise ratio is lowered below the threshold. [7]
(a)

The peak deviation is Δf = β fm = 5 × 15 kHz = 75 kHz. Carson's rule is B = 2(Δf + fm) = 2(75 + 15) kHz = 180 kHz. This is the width of the bandpass filter that precedes the limiter, and it sets how much noise power enters the demodulator. The filter must be at least this wide so that the signal sidebands are passed, otherwise the demodulated tone would be distorted. A narrower filter would reduce noise but at the cost of distortion in the output tone, and is therefore not used here.

Answer: B = 180 kHz

(b)

The noise power in the filter is N = N0 B = 1.0×10⁻¹⁷ × 1.8×10⁵ = 1.8×10⁻¹² W. The carrier power is 2.0×10⁻⁹ W, so the ratio is C/N = 2.0×10⁻⁹/1.8×10⁻¹² = 1111. In decibels, 10 log₁₀(1111) = 30.46 dB. This is comfortably above the usual FM threshold of about 10 dB, which is why the standard output result may be used. The ratio is calculated in the full 180 kHz band, not the 15 kHz message band, and the two give different numbers, so state which one is meant.

Answer: CNR = 30.5 dB

(c)

The reference carrier-to-noise ratio in the message bandwidth is Pc/(N0 W) = 2.0×10⁻⁹/(1.0×10⁻¹⁷ × 1.5×10⁴) = 2.0×10⁻⁹/1.5×10⁻¹³ = 13 333. The output SNR is (3/2)β² × 13 333 = 1.5 × 25 × 13 333 = 5.0×10⁵. In decibels, 10 log₁₀(5.0×10⁵) = 56.99 dB. Compared with a baseband transmission of the same power, the factor (3/2)β² = 37.5 is an improvement of 15.7 dB, obtained by spending bandwidth. The result assumes the input noise is white and the tone is the only message, and that the discriminator is working above threshold, so no clicks are present in the output.

Answer: SNRout = 57.0 dB

(d)

The deviation sets how far the instantaneous frequency moves for a given message amplitude, while the noise at the discriminator output is a fixed frequency fluctuation. Increasing β increases the signal deviation without increasing the noise per hertz, so SNRout rises as β², a square-law gain, at the cost of bandwidth that grows roughly in proportion to β by Carson's rule. This is a trade of bandwidth for SNR. When the input carrier-to-noise ratio falls below the threshold, about 10 dB, noise spikes begin to cause phase jumps of 2π in the carrier, which the discriminator turns into clicks. The output SNR then falls much faster than the usual formula predicts, and the improvement is lost.

Answer: Explained

Problem 5 [A3-015] Superheterodyne receiver and mixing

A portable AM broadcast-band superheterodyne receiver covers 540 kHz to 1600 kHz. Its intermediate frequency is 455 kHz and the local oscillator is tuned above the incoming signal frequency (high-side injection). The receiver is set to a station at 980 kHz. The RF stage before the mixer contains a single tuned circuit with a loaded quality factor Q = 60 that is tuned to the wanted station. Image rejection of a single tuned circuit is given by α = √(1 + Q²ρ²), where ρ = (f_image/f_s) − (f_s/f_image). The local oscillator uses a fixed inductor and a variable capacitor, and its resonant frequency equals the oscillator frequency, so f_LO = 1/(2π√(LC)).

  1. (a) Find the local oscillator frequency in kilohertz for the 980 kHz station. [3]
  2. (b) Find the image frequency in kilohertz. [4]
  3. (c) Find the image rejection of the RF tuned circuit in dB. [7]
  4. (d) Find the ratio Cmax/Cmin of the oscillator capacitor needed to tune the whole band 540 kHz to 1600 kHz with the same fixed inductor. [6]
(a)

With high-side injection the oscillator is above the signal by the intermediate frequency, f_LO = f_s + f_IF = 980 + 455 = 1435 kHz. The mixer produces the difference frequency f_LO − f_s = 455 kHz, which passes through the IF filter that sets the selectivity of the receiver. The sum frequency, 2415 kHz, is rejected by that filter. The IF is fixed, so all later gain and filtering can be designed once for 455 kHz, which is the main advantage of the superheterodyne principle over a tuned radio frequency receiver.

Answer: f_LO = 1435 kHz

(b)

An unwanted signal at the image frequency also mixes down to the IF, because it lies on the opposite side of the oscillator at the same distance. The image is f_image = f_s + 2 f_IF = 980 + 910 = 1890 kHz, and indeed f_image − f_LO = 1890 − 1435 = 455 kHz. Once converted, the image cannot be separated from the wanted signal, so it must be rejected before the mixer, by the RF stage. A higher IF would push the image further from the station and make rejection easier.

Answer: f_image = 1890 kHz

(c)

First evaluate ρ = 1890/980 − 980/1890 = 1.92857 − 0.51852 = 1.41005. Then Qρ = 60 × 1.41005 = 84.60, and α = √(1 + 84.60²) = √(1 + 7158) = 84.61. In decibels, 20 log₁₀(84.61) = 38.55 dB. A single tuned circuit therefore gives only 38.5 dB of image rejection at this tuning, which is adequate for strong stations only; practical receivers use two or more tuned stages to achieve more. The rejection is worst at the high end of the band, where the image is closer to the signal in relative terms, so the design is checked there.

Answer: α = 38.5 dB

(d)

The oscillator tunes from 540 + 455 = 995 kHz to 1600 + 455 = 2055 kHz. Because f_LO = 1/(2π√(LC)) with L fixed, C is proportional to 1/f², so Cmax/Cmin = (f_max/f_min)² = (2055/995)² = (2.0653)² = 4.27. The oscillator capacitor needs a range of 4.27 to 1, whereas a tuned circuit with no IF offset would need (1600/540)² = 8.78 to 1. This smaller ratio is an additional practical benefit of the high-side injection, which is the reason it is used in AM broadcast receivers. A low-side oscillator would have to run from 85 kHz to 1145 kHz, a ratio of 13.5 in frequency and 181 in capacitance, which is impractical.

Answer: Cmax/Cmin = 4.27

A3 Practice Paper 4

Problem 1 [A3-016] Noise in analog communication, SNR

An engineer compares the noise performance of three analog amplitude-modulation schemes for a speech link. The message has bandwidth W = 5 kHz. The received signal power is PR = 2.0×10⁻⁸ W and the channel adds white noise of one-sided power spectral density N0 = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ W/Hz. Define the baseband reference SNR as γ = PR/(N0 W). Ideal coherent demodulation is used for suppressed-carrier schemes and an ideal envelope detector, operating well above threshold, is used for conventional AM. Take the output SNR of conventional AM with a single tone of modulation index μ as η γ with η = μ²/(2 + μ²), and the output SNR of DSB-SC with coherent detection as γ.

  1. (a) Find the baseband reference SNR γ in dB. [4]
  2. (b) Find the output SNR in dB of conventional AM with a single tone of modulation index μ = 0.8. [5]
  3. (c) Find the baseband SNR γ in dB that would be needed to reach 40 dB output SNR with tone modulation at μ = 1. [6]
  4. (d) For the DSB-SC system, the local oscillator has a constant phase error of 20°. Find the output SNR in dB. [5]
(a)

The noise power in the message bandwidth is N0 W = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ × 5×10³ = 5.0×10⁻¹¹ W. Then γ = PR/(N0 W) = 2.0×10⁻⁸/5.0×10⁻¹¹ = 400. In decibels this is 10 log₁₀(400) = 26.02 dB. This is the SNR that an ideal baseband system would obtain with the same received power, and it is the benchmark against which the modulation schemes are compared. It is called the channel signal-to-noise ratio, as it uses the message bandwidth, not the transmission bandwidth.

Answer: γ = 26.0 dB

(b)

For μ = 0.8, η = μ²/(2 + μ²) = 0.64/2.64 = 0.2424. The output SNR is η γ = 0.2424 × 400 = 96.97, or 10 log₁₀(96.97) = 19.87 dB. Conventional AM loses 6.2 dB relative to the baseband reference, because most of the transmitted power is carrier, which carries no information. Even at full modulation μ = 1 the loss would be 4.8 dB, since η would be 1/3. This is the efficiency penalty for the simple envelope detector.

Answer: SNR = 19.9 dB

(c)

At μ = 1 the figure η = 1/(2 + 1) = 1/3. A 40 dB output SNR means a ratio of 10⁴, so we need η γ = 10⁴ and γ = 3 × 10⁴. In decibels, 10 log₁₀(30 000) = 44.77 dB. This is 4.77 dB above the output requirement, the cost of the carrier. Compared with the present 26.02 dB the link would need an increase of 18.75 dB in received power, a factor of about 75, or a much narrower message bandwidth. Remember that μ = 1 is the most favourable case for AM, so real speech does worse.

Answer: γ = 44.8 dB

(d)

A phase error φ in the local oscillator multiplies the recovered message by cos φ. The signal power then falls by cos²φ, while the noise in the in-phase channel is unchanged for white noise. So SNR = γ cos²φ = 400 × cos²20° = 400 × 0.8830 = 353.2, which is 25.48 dB. The loss is 10 log₁₀(0.8830) = −0.54 dB. A 20° error is modest, but at φ near 90° the output would vanish, which is why carrier recovery is needed in the receiver of a suppressed-carrier system.

Answer: SNR = 25.5 dB

Problem 2 [A3-017] Digital baseband and pulse shaping, intersymbol interference

A telemetry system sends data over a bandlimited baseband channel using pulse amplitude modulation with raised-cosine pulses, designed so that intersymbol interference is zero at the sampling instants. The raised-cosine spectrum has roll-off factor α, and its absolute bandwidth is B = (1 + α)/(2T), where 1/T is the symbol rate. The first design uses binary polar signalling at a bit rate of 64 kb/s with α = 0.35. The second design uses the same bit rate but four-level PAM. The third design is for a different channel of absolute bandwidth 50 kHz that must carry 128 kb/s using four-level PAM. Assume every level pattern is equally likely and symbols are independent.

  1. (a) Find the theoretical minimum (Nyquist) bandwidth in kilohertz for the first design with binary signalling. [4]
  2. (b) Find the absolute bandwidth of the first design with α = 0.35, in kilohertz. [4]
  3. (c) Find the absolute bandwidth of the second design, four-level PAM at 64 kb/s with α = 0.35, in kilohertz. [5]
  4. (d) For the third design, find the largest roll-off factor α that fits in the 50 kHz channel. [7]
(a)

Nyquist showed that zero ISI is possible with bandwidth equal to half the symbol rate, B = 1/(2T). For binary signalling each symbol carries one bit, so the symbol rate is 64 kbaud and the minimum bandwidth is 64/2 = 32 kHz. This corresponds to the ideal sinc pulse with α = 0, which cannot be built exactly because it is of infinite duration and has a very high sensitivity to timing error. A real system must use a positive roll-off to make timing error tolerable.

Answer: B(min) = 32 kHz

(b)

The raised-cosine pulse has an excess bandwidth fraction α beyond the Nyquist value, so B = (1 + α)/(2T) = (1 + α) Rs/2. With Rs = 64 kbaud and α = 0.35 this gives B = 1.35 × 32 kHz = 43.2 kHz. A raised cosine pulse is a compromise: the tails fall off as 1/t³ so a timing error in the sampler causes much less ISI than with the sinc pulse. The price is the 35 percent extra bandwidth, which is 11.2 kHz here.

Answer: B = 43.2 kHz

(c)

With four levels each symbol carries log₂4 = 2 bits, so the symbol rate falls to 64 kb/s ÷ 2 = 32 kbaud. The bandwidth is then B = (1 + α) Rs/2 = 1.35 × 16 kHz = 21.6 kHz. The bandwidth is halved relative to the binary design at the same bit rate. The cost is a smaller spacing between the levels for the same peak amplitude, which lowers the noise margin, so a higher SNR is needed for the same error probability.

Answer: B = 21.6 kHz

(d)

The bit rate of 128 kb/s with four-level PAM gives a symbol rate of 128/2 = 64 kbaud. The bandwidth limit gives (1 + α) × 64/2 ≤ 50 kHz, so (1 + α) ≤ 50/32 = 1.5625 and α ≤ 0.5625. The largest roll-off is therefore 0.5625. A designer would choose a smaller value in practice, for example 0.35 for B = 43.2 kHz, to leave guard room for the channel edges. A larger roll-off is gentler on timing error and filter design, so the largest allowable value is attractive from that viewpoint.

Answer: α(max) = 0.5625

Problem 3 [A3-018] ASK, FSK and PSK modulation

A modem on a 70 MHz intermediate frequency carries data at 2 Mb/s using one of several digital modulations, all with rectangular symbol pulses so that each signal component has a spectrum of the form sinc² with its main lobe extending a distance equal to the symbol rate either side of its centre frequency. Use null-to-null bandwidth, the total width of the main lobe, as the measure of bandwidth. For binary FSK, take the two tone frequencies to be separated by Δf = 2 MHz (equal to the bit rate), so the full signal spectrum extends from the lower null of the lower tone to the upper null of the upper tone. Assume no coding or filtering of any kind.

  1. (a) Find the null-to-null bandwidth of binary PSK in megahertz. [4]
  2. (b) Find the null-to-null bandwidth of QPSK in megahertz. [4]
  3. (c) Find the null-to-null bandwidth of binary FSK in megahertz with the stated 2 MHz tone separation. [6]
  4. (d) Find the null-to-null bandwidth in megahertz if 8-PSK is used for the same 2 Mb/s. [6]
(a)

In binary PSK each bit is one symbol, so the symbol rate is Rs = Rb = 2 Mbaud. The PSK signal is a carrier with a rectangular baseband multiplier, so the main lobe is centred on the carrier and extends ±Rs. The null-to-null bandwidth is B = 2Rs = 2 × 2 MHz = 4 MHz. About 90 percent of the power lies within this main lobe, and the side lobes fall off slowly, which is why transmit filtering is normally added in practice. Here we ignore that. The spectrum is symmetrical about 70 MHz, from 68 MHz to 72 MHz.

Answer: B = 4 MHz

(b)

QPSK sends two bits per symbol, so the symbol rate is Rs = Rb/2 = 1 Mbaud. The main lobe is the same shape, extending ±Rs about the carrier, so B = 2Rs = 2 × 1 MHz = 2 MHz. QPSK therefore needs half the bandwidth of BPSK at the same bit rate, with the same bit error probability for the same Eb/N0 if coherent detection is used. The saving comes from two orthogonal bit streams on the in-phase and quadrature carriers, which share the same spectrum.

Answer: B = 2 MHz

(c)

The binary FSK signal is two ASK-like components with Rs = 2 Mbaud each, with the lobes extending ±2 MHz about their centres. The two centre frequencies are 2 MHz apart. The lower null of the lower tone is 2 MHz below f1 and the upper null of the upper tone is 2 MHz above f2. Then B = Δf + 2Rs = 2 + 2 × 2 = 6 MHz. That is 50 percent more than BPSK. The wide tone separation makes the tones easy to separate, but binary FSK is the least bandwidth-efficient choice of the schemes listed here.

Answer: B = 6 MHz

(d)

In 8-PSK each symbol carries log₂8 = 3 bits, so Rs = 2 Mb/s ÷ 3 = 0.6667 Mbaud. The null-to-null bandwidth is B = 2Rs = 1.3333 MHz. The bandwidth saving over BPSK is a factor of three. The price is paid in power: the eight phases are only 45° apart, so a much larger Eb/N0 is needed for a given error rate, about 3.6 dB more than QPSK for a bit error rate of 10⁻⁵. The choice therefore trades bandwidth against power.

Answer: B = 1.33 MHz

Problem 4 [A3-019] Digital demodulation, matched filter and bit error probability

A baseband binary antipodal link sends a 1 as a rectangular pulse of amplitude +A and a 0 as −A, each of duration Tb = 10 μs, with A = 1.5 mV. The channel adds white Gaussian noise of one-sided power spectral density N0 = 4.0×10⁻¹² V²/Hz, so that signal energy is computed on a 1 Ω reference resistance. The receiver is a filter matched to the rectangular pulse, sampled at the end of each bit interval, with the decision threshold at zero. The two symbols are equally likely. The bit error probability of this receiver is Pe = Q(√(2Eb/N0)), where Q is the Gaussian tail probability.

  1. (a) Find the energy per bit Eb in picojoules, with Eb = A² Tb on a 1 Ω reference. [4]
  2. (b) Find Eb/N0 in dB. [4]
  3. (c) Find the bit error probability, giving the value multiplied by 10⁴ (that is, the number of errors per 10 000 bits). [6]
  4. (d) Find the Eb/N0 in dB needed for a bit error probability of 10⁻⁶. [6]
(a)

The pulse amplitude is A = 1.5×10⁻³ V and its duration is Tb = 10×10⁻⁶ s. The energy on a 1 Ω resistance is Eb = A² Tb = (1.5×10⁻³)² × 10×10⁻⁶ = 2.25×10⁻⁶ × 10⁻⁵ = 2.25×10⁻¹¹ J, that is 22.5 pJ. Both symbols have the same energy because they differ only in sign, so the average energy per bit is also 22.5 pJ. Both symbols give the same result, so the average energy per bit is unchanged by the data. The units here are V²s, equal to joules on 1 Ω, matching N0 given in V²/Hz.

Answer: Eb = 22.5 pJ

(b)

The ratio is Eb/N0 = 2.25×10⁻¹¹/4.0×10⁻¹² = 5.625. In decibels this is 10 log₁₀(5.625) = 7.50 dB. The noise N0 is quoted for a 1 Ω reference, which keeps the units consistent. This is the standard figure of merit for comparing digital systems, because it does not depend on the bit rate chosen or on the filter bandwidth. The matched filter maximises the peak output SNR at the sampling instant, and that maximum equals 2Eb/N0 = 11.25, or 10.5 dB.

Answer: Eb/N0 = 7.5 dB

(c)

With the matched filter, Pe = Q(√(2Eb/N0)) = Q(√11.25) = Q(3.354). Using Pe = Q(x) with x = 3.354, and the Gaussian tail value Q(3.354) from a table or calculator, the probability is 3.98×10⁻⁴. So about four bits in every ten thousand are in error, a value of 3.98 when expressed per 10⁴ bits. This is an uncoded error rate that is acceptable for some voice links but not for data, which would need either coding or a further increase of roughly 3 dB in Eb/N0 to reach 10⁻⁶.

Answer: Pe = 3.98×10⁻⁴

(d)

We need Q(x) = 10⁻⁶ with x = √(2Eb/N0). The inverse tail gives x = 4.753. Then Eb/N0 = x²/2 = 22.59/2 = 11.30, and in decibels 10 log₁₀(11.30) = 10.53 dB, the standard figure for a bit error rate of one in a million with coherent antipodal signalling. The present link has 7.50 dB, so it needs another 3.03 dB, a factor of 2.0 in energy, which could be provided by doubling the pulse energy through a longer pulse or a higher amplitude, or by halving N0 through a better receiver. The matched filter is assumed ideal and the timing of the sampler is assumed perfect.

Answer: Eb/N0 = 10.5 dB

Problem 5 [A3-020] Link design combining bandwidth, SNR and modulation choice

A 6 GHz point-to-point microwave link in northern Ontario connects two towers 120 km apart. The transmitter delivers 1 W. Each antenna has a gain of 25 dBi. Branching, feeder and rain-fade allowances total 6 dB. The receiver system noise temperature is 600 K. Boltzmann's constant is 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K, the speed of light is 3×10⁸ m/s, and free-space path loss is 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ). The link carries 100 Mb/s using QPSK with root-raised-cosine pulses of roll-off 0.25, and coherent detection has Pe = Q(√(2Eb/N0)) for QPSK. The target is Pe = 10⁻⁶, which needs an Eb/N0 of 10.53 dB.

  1. (a) Find the free-space path loss in dB. [4]
  2. (b) Find the received power in dBm after the antenna gains and the 6 dB allowance. [4]
  3. (c) Find the received Eb/N0 in dB. [5]
  4. (d) Find the link margin in dB over the 10.53 dB required for Pe = 10⁻⁶. [4]
  5. (e) Find the occupied bandwidth in megahertz of the QPSK signal. [3]
(a)

The wavelength is λ = c/f = 3×10⁸/6×10⁹ = 0.05 m. The distance is d = 120 000 m. The path loss is 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ) = 20 log₁₀(4π × 120 000/0.05) = 20 log₁₀(3.016×10⁷) = 20 × 7.4794 = 149.59 dB. The loss grows by 6 dB for each doubling of distance or of frequency. This ignores atmospheric absorption and ground reflection effects, which are covered here by the 6 dB allowance, and assumes the path is clear of obstructions with clearance of the first Fresnel zone.

Answer: L = 149.6 dB

(b)

The transmit power of 1 W is 30 dBm. Adding the two antenna gains gives 30 + 25 + 25 = 80 dBm of effective radiated and captured power, before the loss. Subtracting the path loss and the allowance gives Pr = 80 − 149.59 − 6 = −75.59 dBm, which is 2.8×10⁻⁸ mW (2.8×10⁻¹¹ W). This is the carrier power at the receiver input. It is a very small signal, so the receiver front end must be a low noise design, which is the reason for the system noise temperature specification of 600 K.

Answer: Pr = −75.6 dBm

(c)

The noise density is N0 = kT = 1.380649×10⁻²³ × 600 = 8.284×10⁻²¹ W/Hz, which is −200.82 dBW/Hz or −170.82 dBm/Hz. Then C/N0 = Pr − N0 = −75.59 + 170.82 = 95.23 dB-Hz. The bit rate of 100 Mb/s is 80 dB-Hz, so Eb/N0 = C/N0 − 10 log₁₀(Rb) = 95.23 − 80 = 15.23 dB. Dividing the received power per second by the bit rate gives the energy per bit, so this is the natural figure of merit for the link and does not depend on the bandwidth chosen.

Answer: Eb/N0 = 15.2 dB

(d)

For QPSK with coherent detection Pe = Q(√(2Eb/N0)), the required Eb/N0 for 10⁻⁶ is 10.53 dB, as given. The margin is the available figure minus the required figure: 15.23 − 10.53 = 4.70 dB. A margin of 4.7 dB means the link can tolerate 4.7 dB more attenuation, for example a heavier rain fade than the 6 dB already allowed, before the error rate exceeds 10⁻⁶. A margin of at least 3 dB is typical of a good design, and it also absorbs equipment ageing and small pointing errors of the dish antennas.

Answer: Margin = 4.7 dB

(e)

QPSK carries two bits per symbol, so the symbol rate is Rs = 100/2 = 50 Mbaud. A root-raised-cosine pulse with roll-off α occupies B = (1 + α) Rs = 1.25 × 50 = 62.5 MHz. This is the bandwidth that the filter and the channel allocation must accommodate. Using BPSK would double the symbol rate and require 125 MHz, and 16-QAM would halve the bandwidth to 31.25 MHz, but would need about 4 dB more Eb/N0, which would just fit inside our margin of 4.7 dB but leave almost nothing for further fades.

Answer: B = 62.5 MHz

A3 Practice Paper 5

Problem 1 [A3-021] Fourier series coefficients and spectra of periodic signals

A gate-drive circuit for a power converter produces a periodic rectangular pulse train v(t). In each period T = 100 μs the voltage is A = 5 V for 0 ≤ t < τ and 0 V for τ ≤ t < T, where the pulse width τ is adjustable. The waveform is applied to a 1 Ω resistor for the purpose of power calculations. The designer wants the third harmonic of the switching frequency to be absent from the spectrum, because a resonant element in the converter is tuned to 3/T and would otherwise ring. Use the exponential Fourier series v(t) = Σ c_n ej2πnt/T, with c_n computed over one period starting at t = 0, and note that the magnitude |c_n| is all that matters for this problem.

  1. (a) Find the pulse width τ (the smallest positive value) that makes the third harmonic coefficient zero. [5]
  2. (b) With this τ, find the DC component of v(t). [3]
  3. (c) With this τ, find the amplitude of the fundamental sinusoidal component, which equals 2|c1|. [6]
  4. (d) With this τ, find the percentage of the total average power in the pulse train that is carried by the DC component plus the first two harmonics (n = 1 and n = 2, counting both positive and negative frequencies). [6]
(a)

For a rectangular pulse of width τ and height A over period T, c_n = (A/(jπn))·(...) and its magnitude is |c_n| = A (τ/T) |sin(πnτ/T)/(πnτ/T)|. This is zero whenever nτ/T is a non-zero integer. For n = 3 the smallest positive solution is 3τ/T = 1, so τ = T/3 = 100 μs / 3 = 33.33 μs. Any smaller τ would leave sin(3πτ/T) non-zero, since the argument would be below π. The duty ratio is then exactly one third. Note also that every multiple of three harmonic (6, 9, ...) is removed by the same condition, which is why this choice is common in converters sensitive to triplen harmonics.

Answer: 33.33 μs

(b)

The DC term is c_0 = (1/T)∫v dt = A τ/T. Substituting A = 5 V and τ/T = 1/3 gives c_0 = 5 × 0.3333 = 1.667 V. This is simply the average of the waveform, equal to the area under one pulse (5 V × 33.33 μs = 166.7 μV·s) divided by the period of 100 μs. A moving-coil meter on this waveform would read 1.667 V. The result does not depend on the delay of the pulse within the period, only on its area, which is a useful check on any Fourier series calculation of this kind before the harmonics are considered.

Answer: 1.667 V

(c)

For n = 1, |c1| = A (τ/T) |sin(π/3)/(π/3)| = 5 × (1/3) × 0.8660/1.0472 = 1.378 V. Equivalently |c1| = A sin(π/3)/π = 5 × 0.8660/3.1416 = 1.378 V. For a real signal the sinusoid at the fundamental has amplitude 2|c1| because the positive and negative frequency terms are complex conjugates and combine, so amplitude = 2 × 1.378 = 2.757 V. The fundamental is at 1/T = 10 kHz. As a sanity check, this is more than the DC value of 1.667 V, which is expected for a pulse train with one third duty, since its energy is concentrated near the low harmonics.

Answer: 2.757 V

(d)

By Parseval, the average power in 1 Ω is P = (1/T)∫v² dt = A² τ/T = 25/3 = 8.333 W. The power in each harmonic pair is |c_n|² + |c_-n|² = 2|c_n|². DC power is c_0² = 1.667² = 2.778 W. For n = 1 the pair carries 2 × 1.378² = 3.798 W. For n = 2, |c2| = A sin(2π/3)/(2π) = 5 × 0.8660/6.2832 = 0.6891 V, so the pair carries 2 × 0.4749 = 0.9497 W. The total is 2.778 + 3.798 + 0.950 = 7.526 W, which is 7.526/8.333 = 90.3 % of the total. The remaining 9.7 % is in harmonics 4, 5, 7 and above, with the third, sixth and ninth missing by design.

Answer: 90.3 %

Problem 2 [A3-022] Fourier transform pairs and properties

A pulsed radar transmitter in an air traffic surveillance system sends a burst x(t) = A rect(t/τ) cos(2π f0 t), where rect(t/τ) equals 1 for |t| < τ/2 and 0 otherwise, A = 3 V, and the carrier frequency is f0 = 10 MHz. The existing design uses a pulse width τ = 2 μs. Treat the Fourier transform as X(f) = ∫ x(t) e-j2πft dt in V·s, and assume f0 is large enough compared with 1/τ that the positive-frequency and negative-frequency lobes of the spectrum do not overlap. The spectrum regulator for the band requires the null-to-null width of the main lobe to be no more than 400 kHz, so the pulse width must be increased. The following refers first to the existing design and then to the redesigned pulse.

  1. (a) For the existing design (τ = 2 μs), find the magnitude of X(f) at f = f0, in μV·s. [4]
  2. (b) For the existing design, find the null-to-null width of the main lobe around the carrier, in MHz. [3]
  3. (c) Find the minimum pulse width τ that makes the null-to-null width no more than 400 kHz, in μs. [6]
  4. (d) For the redesigned pulse (the τ from part c), find the magnitude of X(f) at f = f0 + 300 kHz, in μV·s, neglecting the negative-frequency lobe. [7]
(a)

Start from the pair rect(t/τ) ↔ τ sinc(fτ), where sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu). Multiplication by cos(2πf0 t) shifts the spectrum to ±f0 and halves each copy, by the modulation property, so X(f) = (Aτ/2)[sinc((f−f0)τ) + sinc((f+f0)τ)]. At f = f0 the first term is sinc(0) = 1, and the second is negligible because it is centred at −f0 and its argument is about 40 for this pulse. So |X(f0)| = Aτ/2 = 3 × 2×10⁻⁶ / 2 = 3×10⁻⁶ V·s = 3 μV·s. This equals half the area of the envelope A·τ.

Answer: 3 μV·s

(b)

The main lobe of sinc((f−f0)τ) extends between the first nulls where (f−f0)τ = ±1, that is f = f0 ± 1/τ. The null-to-null width is therefore 2/τ. For τ = 2 μs this is 2/(2×10⁻⁶) = 1×10⁶ Hz = 1.0 MHz, so the band occupied is 9.5 MHz to 10.5 MHz. This is the standard time-bandwidth trade-off of the scaling property: a pulse narrower in time has a spectrum wider in frequency by the same factor. The existing design is therefore 2.5 times wider than the regulator permits, which motivates the redesign requested in part c.

Answer: 1.0 MHz

(c)

Require 2/τ ≤ 400 kHz, so τ ≥ 2/(400×10³) = 5×10⁻⁶ s. The minimum pulse width is τ = 5 μs. Any wider pulse also meets the limit but delivers more energy per burst at the cost of range resolution, since resolution c·τ/2 grows with pulse length: at 5 μs the range cell is about 750 m against 300 m before. So the regulator limit imposes a direct penalty on resolution. The designer should state this trade-off, and in practice a chirped pulse would be used to recover resolution, but that goes beyond this problem and is not needed for the answer.

Answer: 5 μs

(d)

With τ = 5 μs the peak envelope is Aτ/2 = 3 × 5×10⁻⁶/2 = 7.5×10⁻⁶ V·s. At a frequency offset of 300 kHz from the carrier the sinc argument is 300×10³ × 5×10⁻⁶ = 1.5. Then sinc(1.5) = sin(1.5π)/(1.5π) = (−1)/4.712 = −0.2122, so the magnitude is 7.5×10⁻⁶ × 0.2122 = 1.59×10⁻⁶ V·s = 1.59 μV·s. The sign is negative, which means this point lies in the first sidelobe, between the first null at 200 kHz and the second null at 400 kHz. It is about 21 percent of the peak value, or −13.5 dB, which agrees with the familiar −13.3 dB first sidelobe level of a rectangular pulse.

Answer: 1.59 μV·s

Problem 3 [A3-023] Energy, power and spectra, Parseval's theorem

A sensor transient in a protection relay is modelled as the decaying exponential pulse x(t) = A e−at u(t), with A = 4 V and a = 2000 s⁻¹, where u(t) is the unit step. The pulse is dissipated in a 1 Ω reference resistor, so energy is computed as the integral of x(t)² over all time. The signal is an energy signal, so its energy spectral density is |X(f)|² with X(f) = ∫ x(t) e−j2πft dt, and its two-sided spectrum is symmetric in f. A designer wants to choose a low-pass bandwidth for the relay input stage that preserves most of the pulse energy while rejecting noise, and also wants to know how much energy an existing 1 kHz ideal low-pass filter would pass. Work in hertz for frequencies, and use ω = 2πf where needed.

  1. (a) Find the total energy of the pulse in the time domain, in mJ. [4]
  2. (b) Find the energy spectral density |X(f)|² at f = 0, in μJ/Hz. [3]
  3. (c) Find the bandwidth W in hertz such that an ideal low-pass filter of cutoff W passes 90 percent of the pulse energy. [7]
  4. (d) Find the energy, in mJ, at the output of an ideal 1 kHz low-pass filter driven by this pulse. [6]
(a)

In the time domain E = ∫₀^∞ A² e−2at dt = A²/(2a). Substituting A = 4 V and a = 2000 s⁻¹ gives E = 16/4000 = 4×10⁻³ J = 4 mJ in the 1 Ω resistor. Parseval's theorem says the same value must be obtained by integrating the energy spectral density over all frequencies, which is the check used in the later parts. The units are V²·s, which equals joules when the reference resistance is 1 Ω. The result is the total available energy against which the filter fractions in parts c and d are measured.

Answer: 4 mJ

(b)

The transform is X(f) = A/(a + j2πf), so |X(f)|² = A²/(a² + (2πf)²). At f = 0 this is A²/a² = 16/(2000)² = 16/4×10⁶ = 4×10⁻⁶ V²·s² per hertz, that is 4 μJ/Hz. The spectrum is largest at DC and falls as 1/f² at high frequency. It falls to half at (2πf) = a, that is f = a/2π = 318 Hz, which is the 3 dB frequency of the pulse spectrum. This is a quick test of whether a given bandwidth is meaningful for the pulse.

Answer: 4 μJ/Hz

(c)

The energy in |f| ≤ W is E(W) = ∫_{−W}W A²/(a² + (2πf)²) df. Evaluating, E(W) = (A²/(π a)) arctan(2πW/a), and as W → ∞ this tends to A²/(2a), so the fraction is (2/π) arctan(2πW/a). Setting it to 0.90 gives arctan(2πW/a) = 0.45π, so 2πW/a = tan(0.45π) = 6.314. Then W = 6.314 × 2000/(2π) = 2010 Hz. About two kilohertz is enough for 90 percent of the energy even though the spectrum technically extends to infinity, so the relay input stage need not be wideband to preserve the pulse.

Answer: 2010 Hz

(d)

For a 1 kHz ideal low-pass filter, the passed fraction is (2/π) arctan(2π × 1000/2000) = (2/π) arctan(3.1416). Since arctan(3.1416) = 1.2626 rad, the fraction is 0.6366 × 1.2626 = 0.8038. The output energy is 0.8038 × 4 mJ = 3.215 mJ, so the filter removes about 19.6 percent of the pulse energy. Compare with part c: 1 kHz is about half the 2010 Hz needed for 90 percent, yet it still passes 80 percent, which shows how much of the energy is concentrated at low frequency.

Answer: 3.215 mJ

Problem 4 [A3-024] LTI filtering of signals and frequency response

A data logger on a strain gauge bridge receives the voltage x(t) = 2 + 0.5 cos(2π·1000 t) + 0.8 cos(2π·8000 t) volts, where the DC term is the wanted measurement, the 1 kHz term is a slow mechanical vibration to be passed, and the 8 kHz term is switching noise from a nearby inverter. The signal is filtered by a first-order passive RC low-pass filter with transfer function H(jω) = 1/(1 + jωRC), driven from an ideal voltage source and unloaded. The designer wants the 8 kHz noise to be reduced to exactly 10 percent of its input amplitude, and has available a capacitor of C = 10 nF. Use steady-state sinusoidal analysis and the superposition of the three components. Report phase as a lag magnitude in degrees where asked.

  1. (a) Find the time constant RC that reduces the 8 kHz component to 10 percent of its input amplitude, in μs. [5]
  2. (b) Find the resistance R needed with C = 10 nF, in kΩ. [3]
  3. (c) Find the amplitude of the 1 kHz component at the output, in volts. [6]
  4. (d) Find the phase lag of the 1 kHz component at the output, in degrees. [6]
(a)

The magnitude of the response is |H(jω)| = 1/√(1 + (ωRC)²). Setting |H| = 0.1 at ω = 2π × 8000 = 50265 rad/s gives 1 + (ωRC)² = 100, so ωRC = √99 = 9.950. Then RC = 9.950/50265 = 1.979×10⁻⁴ s = 197.9 μs. The corner frequency of this filter is 1/(2πRC) = 804 Hz, so the 8 kHz noise is about a decade above the corner and is attenuated by 20 dB, consistent with the −20 dB per decade roll-off of a single pole. The DC component is unaffected because |H(0)| = 1.

Answer: 197.9 μs

(b)

With the time constant fixed by part a and C = 10 nF = 10×10⁻⁹ F, R = RC/C = 1.979×10⁻⁴ / 10⁻⁸ = 1.979×10⁴ Ω = 19.79 kΩ. In practice the nearest standard value is 20 kΩ, which would give an 8 kHz attenuation of 1/√(1 + (50265 × 2×10⁻⁴)²) = 0.0990, still very close to the target. The source impedance and any load must be much smaller and much larger than R respectively, otherwise the effective RC differs from the design value, which is why the problem states an ideal source and an unloaded output.

Answer: 19.79 kΩ

(c)

At 1 kHz, ωRC = 2π × 1000 × 1.979×10⁻⁴ = 1.2437. The gain is |H| = 1/√(1 + 1.2437²) = 1/√2.547 = 0.6267. The input amplitude is 0.5 V, so the output amplitude is 0.5 × 0.6267 = 0.3133 V. The DC term passes unchanged at 2 V, and the 8 kHz term becomes 0.8 × 0.1 = 0.08 V. The 1 kHz vibration is therefore attenuated by 4 dB, a side effect of choosing the corner so low. If the vibration data were important, a second-order or higher-corner design would be needed.

Answer: 0.313 V

(d)

The phase of the response is ∠H(jω) = −arctan(ωRC). At 1 kHz this is −arctan(1.2437) = −51.2°, which is a lag of 51.2 degrees. The corresponding time delay is 51.2/360 × 1 ms = 0.142 ms. The output at 1 kHz is therefore 0.3133 cos(2π·1000 t − 51.2°) V. A lag arises because the capacitor voltage lags the current. Since the phase is not proportional to frequency, the three components are delayed by different amounts, so the waveform shape changes slightly, which matters if the logger needs waveform fidelity.

Answer: 51.2 degrees

Problem 5 [A3-025] Sampling and the Nyquist theorem, aliasing

A voice-band telephone interface digitises a speech signal whose useful content extends up to 3.4 kHz. A line-frequency whine at 5.5 kHz is also sometimes present on the input. The designer is comparing two sampling rates, fs = 8 kHz and fs = 12 kHz, with an analogue anti-alias filter in front of the sampler. The anti-alias filter is a Butterworth low-pass with cutoff (3 dB) frequency 3.4 kHz and magnitude-squared response |H(f)|² = 1/(1 + (f/3.4 kHz)2n), where n is the integer order. The requirement is that any component that could fold into the 0 to 3.4 kHz band must be attenuated by at least 40 dB, measured at the lowest frequency that would fold onto 3.4 kHz, namely fs − 3.4 kHz. Answer with the sampling theorem for an ideal sampler.

  1. (a) Find the minimum sampling rate, in kHz, at which the speech band is theoretically free of aliasing. [4]
  2. (b) With fs = 8 kHz, find the frequency, in kHz, within the 0 to fs/2 range at which the 5.5 kHz whine appears after sampling. [3]
  3. (c) With fs = 12 kHz, find the minimum Butterworth order n that gives at least 40 dB attenuation at fs − 3.4 kHz. [5]
  4. (d) For that order, find the actual attenuation, in dB, at fs − 3.4 kHz. [6]
  5. (e) Briefly explain why a higher sampling rate relaxes the anti-alias filter even though the signal bandwidth is unchanged. [2]
(a)

The sampling theorem states that a band-limited signal with highest frequency fmax is recoverable if fs > 2 fmax. For fmax = 3.4 kHz this gives fs > 6.8 kHz, so the Nyquist rate is 6.8 kHz. This value assumes an ideal, infinitely sharp reconstruction filter and an ideal brick-wall anti-alias filter, neither of which is physical. The standard telephone rate of 8 kHz therefore leaves a guard band of 1.2 kHz in total, from 3.4 to 4.6 kHz, which is the transition band that the real anti-alias filter has to fit into, as used in part c.

Answer: 6.8 kHz

(b)

Sampling at 8 kHz repeats the spectrum around multiples of fs, so a tone at f appears at |f − k fs| for the integer k that brings it into 0 to fs/2 = 4 kHz. For f = 5.5 kHz, 5.5 is above the Nyquist limit of 4 kHz, so k = 1 and the alias frequency is |5.5 − 8| = 2.5 kHz. That lies inside the speech band, so the whine would be indistinguishable from a genuine 2.5 kHz speech component after sampling, and it cannot be removed digitally. This is the reason for the analogue anti-alias filter placed before the sampler.

Answer: 2.5 kHz

(c)

With fs = 12 kHz, the lowest frequency that folds to 3.4 kHz is 12 − 3.4 = 8.6 kHz. The attenuation required is 10 log₁₀(1 + (8.6/3.4)2n) ≥ 40, so (2.529)2n ≥ 9999. Taking logs, 2n ln(2.529) ≥ ln(9999) = 9.2102. With ln(2.529) = 0.9278, 2n ≥ 9.2102/0.9278 = 9.927, so n ≥ 4.96. The next integer is n = 5. An order of 4 would give only about 32 dB, which fails the requirement, so the designer must round up, never down.

Answer: 5

(d)

For n = 5 and fs = 12 kHz, (8.6/3.4)10 = (2.529)10 = e9.278 = 1.07×10⁴. Then the attenuation is 10 log₁₀(1 + 1.07×10⁴) = 10 × 4.0302 = 40.3 dB. This slightly exceeds the 40 dB requirement, because the order has to be an integer and the exact requirement was 4.96. At 8 kHz sampling the same specification would need the edge at 4.6 kHz and a ratio of only 1.353, which would call for order 16, impractical for an analogue filter.

Answer: 40.3 dB

(e)

Raising the sampling rate moves the first alias edge fs − 3.4 kHz farther from the 3.4 kHz band edge, so the transition band the filter must cover is wider. A Butterworth response falls as (f/fc)−n, so a wider ratio gives the same stop-band attenuation at a much lower order, as parts c and d show (order 5 at 12 kHz against about 16 at 8 kHz). The cost is a higher data rate and more computation downstream, so converters use oversampling followed by digital decimation.

Answer: Wider transition band gives a lower order filter

A3 Practice Paper 6

Problem 1 [A3-026] Reconstruction and quantization noise

A portable instrument digitises a sinusoidal sensor output with a uniform mid-tread quantizer. The converter input range is ±1.5 V, spanning 2N levels over the 3 V total range, and a full-scale sinusoid has peak amplitude 1.5 V. Treat quantization error as uniformly distributed over one step Δ, giving noise power Δ²/12 into a 1 Ω reference resistance, and ignore clipping and all other noise sources. The specification requires a signal-to-quantization-noise ratio (SQNR) of at least 70 dB for a full-scale sinusoid. The converter output is reconstructed by a zero-order-hold (ZOH) digital-to-analogue converter at the sampling rate fs = 8 kHz, whose frequency response magnitude is |sinc(f/fs)| with sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu), and the highest signal frequency of interest is 3.4 kHz.

  1. (a) Find the minimum number of bits N that meets the 70 dB requirement for a full-scale sinusoid. [4]
  2. (b) For that N, find the step size Δ, in mV. [3]
  3. (c) For that N, find the rms quantization noise voltage, in μV. [3]
  4. (d) The input signal is actually only 0.15 V peak. Find the SQNR in dB at the N from part a. [5]
  5. (e) Find the ZOH droop at 3.4 kHz, as a loss in dB, when fs = 8 kHz. [5]
(a)

For a full-scale sinusoid with a uniform N-bit quantizer, the signal power is (V_FS)²/2 and the noise power is Δ²/12 with Δ = 2V_FS/2N, giving SQNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB. Setting 6.02N + 1.76 ≥ 70 gives N ≥ 68.24/6.02 = 11.34, so N = 12 bits. An 11-bit converter would reach only 67.98 dB, which misses the requirement by about 2 dB. A 12-bit converter reaches 74.0 dB, providing a margin of 4 dB for converter non-idealities such as differential non-linearity.

Answer: 12 bits

(b)

The range is 3 V over 212 = 4096 levels, so Δ = 3/4096 = 7.324×10⁻⁴ V = 0.7324 mV. The least significant bit therefore corresponds to about 0.73 mV, which is the smallest change the instrument can resolve. This is also the width of the uniform distribution over which quantization error is spread, from −Δ/2 to +Δ/2, which is the assumption behind the Δ²/12 noise formula used in the next part. The result should be compared with the sensor's own noise floor before specifying the converter.

Answer: 0.732 mV

(c)

The noise power is Δ²/12, so the rms noise voltage is Δ/√12 = 0.7324 mV/3.4641 = 0.2114 mV = 211.4 μV. This is the standard deviation of a uniformly distributed error of width Δ. It can be checked against the SQNR of part a: the signal rms is 1.5/√2 = 1.0607 V, and 20 log₁₀(1.0607/211.4×10⁻⁶) = 74.0 dB, which agrees with the formula 6.02 × 12 + 1.76. The noise is independent of the signal amplitude, a property used in the next part.

Answer: 211.4 μV

(d)

The noise power is unchanged because it depends only on Δ: (0.7324×10⁻³)²/12 = 4.47×10⁻⁸ V². The signal power is 0.15²/2 = 0.01125 V². Hence SQNR = 10 log₁₀(0.01125/4.47×10⁻⁸) = 10 log₁₀(2.517×10⁵) = 54.0 dB. This is 20 dB below the 74 dB of a full-scale input, since the amplitude is a tenth of full scale and the signal power a hundredth. The specification of 70 dB would be violated at this level, so either the gain must be increased ahead of the converter or more bits are needed.

Answer: 54.0 dB

(e)

The ZOH holds each sample for one sampling period, so its response magnitude is |sinc(f/fs)|. At 3.4 kHz with fs = 8 kHz, f/fs = 0.425. Then sin(π × 0.425) = sin(1.3352) = 0.9724, and π × 0.425 = 1.3352, so |sinc| = 0.7283. The loss is −20 log₁₀(0.7283) = 2.75 dB. This high-frequency droop is a deterministic distortion rather than noise, and it is usually corrected by an inverse-sinc equaliser, either digital before the converter or analogue after it, so that the passband is flat to within the specification.

Answer: 2.75 dB

Problem 2 [A3-027] Discrete-time systems and difference equations

A battery management unit smooths a cell-temperature reading x[n], sampled at 100 Hz, using the first-order recursive filter y[n] = a y[n−1] + (1 − a) x[n], where 0 < a < 1 and the filter is initially at rest, y[−1] = 0. A unit step in temperature, x[n] = u[n] (that is, 1 for n ≥ 0), is applied at n = 0. The engineer wants the output to have risen to at least 95 percent of its final value by the sample n = 19, the 20th sample, and wants the largest a, that is the heaviest smoothing, that still achieves this. Take the output to be exactly 0.95 at n = 19 for the design. The unit-step response is y[n] = 1 − an+1, and the filter is later used on white measurement noise of unit variance.

  1. (a) Find the value of a that gives exactly 95 percent of the final value at n = 19. [5]
  2. (b) With that a, find the step response value y[5]. [4]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the frequency response |H(ejω)| at 10 Hz (ω = 2π × 10/100 rad/sample). [5]
  4. (d) Find the factor by which the filter reduces the variance of white noise of unit variance at its input, that is the sum of the squared impulse response. [6]
(a)

Setting y[19] = 1 − a20 = 0.95 gives a20 = 0.05, so a = 0.051/20 = exp(ln 0.05/20) = exp(−2.9957/20) = exp(−0.14979) = 0.8609. Any larger a would smooth more but respond more slowly, failing the 95 percent requirement at n = 19, so this is the largest a that meets the response time and, by the statement, the design value. The sample period is 10 ms, so 20 samples is 0.2 s. The time constant of the filter is −1/ln a = 6.7 samples, about 67 ms, and 95 percent is reached after about three time constants.

Answer: 0.8609

(b)

Use the step response given in the problem statement with n = 5: y[5] = 1 − a6. With a = 0.8609, a6 = exp(6 × (−0.14979)) = exp(−0.8987) = 0.4071. So y[5] = 1 − 0.4071 = 0.593. The filter has therefore risen to about 59 percent after six samples including the first at n = 0, equal to 50 ms after the step. This can also be checked recursively: y[0] = 0.1391, y[1] = 0.1391 × 0.8609 + 0.1391 = 0.2589, and so on, matching the closed form at each step.

Answer: 0.593

(c)

Taking the z-transform of the difference equation gives H(z) = (1 − a)/(1 − a z−1). At z = ejω with ω = 2π × 0.1 = 0.6283 rad/sample, |1 − a e−jω|² = 1 − 2a cos ω + a² = 1 − 2(0.8609)(0.8090) + 0.7411 = 1 − 1.3929 + 0.7411 = 0.3482. The magnitude of the denominator is √0.3482 = 0.5901. Then |H| = (1 − 0.8609)/0.5901 = 0.1391/0.5901 = 0.2357. A 10 Hz variation is therefore reduced to under a quarter of its size, and DC passes with gain exactly 1.

Answer: 0.2357

(d)

The impulse response is h[n] = (1 − a) an for n ≥ 0. White noise of variance σ² at the input produces output variance σ² Σ h[n]² = σ² (1 − a)² Σ a2n = σ² (1 − a)²/(1 − a²) = σ² (1 − a)/(1 + a). With a = 0.8609, (1 − a)/(1 + a) = 0.1391/1.8609 = 0.0748. The noise variance is therefore reduced by a factor of about 13.4, which is a 11.3 dB improvement. The price paid is the slower step response of parts a and b, which is the standard trade-off of a recursive smoother.

Answer: 0.0748

Problem 3 [A3-028] The Z-transform and region of convergence

A discrete-time control loop around a rotary encoder has the system function H(z) = 1/(1 − a z−1 − 0.21 z−2), where the real feedback coefficient a is set by the firmware gain. The system is implemented as a causal difference equation y[n] = a y[n−1] + 0.21 y[n−2] + x[n]. For the purposes of this problem, bounded-input bounded-output stability of a causal system requires all poles of H(z) to lie strictly inside the unit circle. Poles are the roots of z² − a z − 0.21 = 0. The engineer first determines the stable range of a and then examines the design a = 0.5. State the region of convergence (ROC) assumptions used where relevant, and treat the system as causal unless told otherwise.

  1. (a) Find the largest positive value of a for which the causal system is stable. [6]
  2. (b) For a = 0.5, find the magnitude of the pole of largest magnitude. [4]
  3. (c) For a = 0.5, find the number of samples n at which the envelope of the impulse response, decaying as (largest pole magnitude)n, falls to 1 percent of its starting value. [5]
  4. (d) For a = 0.5, find the DC gain H(z) at z = 1. [5]
(a)

For z² − a z − 0.21 = 0, the product of the roots is −0.21 and their sum is a. For real roots one is positive and one negative. The larger magnitude root is z₁ = (a + √(a² + 0.84))/2 and the stability limit is z₁ = 1. Substituting z = 1 into the polynomial gives 1 − a − 0.21 = 0, so a = 0.79. For a larger a, the root exceeds 1 and the system is unstable. This agrees with the Jury triangle condition |a| < 1 + (−0.21) = 0.79 for the polynomial z² − a z − 0.21. So the largest stable a is 0.79.

Answer: 0.79

(b)

With a = 0.5, the polynomial is z² − 0.5 z − 0.21 = 0. The discriminant is 0.25 + 0.84 = 1.09, with square root 1.0440. The roots are z = (0.5 ± 1.0440)/2, that is z₁ = 0.7720 and z₂ = −0.2720.
