The result is the root-sum-square of the tone indices, not their arithmetic sum of 0.7. The arithmetic sum is the peak envelope excursion, which matters for overmodulation in part (e), while the root-sum-square value governs the power.

Answer: μ = 0.50

(b)

Total power for an AM wave is the carrier power plus the sideband power: Pt = Pc(1 + μ²/2). With Pc = 20 kW and μ² = 0.25, the sidebands carry Pc μ²/2 = 20 × 0.125 = 2.5 kW. Therefore Pt = 20 + 2.5 = 22.5 kW. Check by summing per tone: tone 1 gives 20 × 0.16/2 = 1.6 kW and tone 2 gives 20 × 0.09/2 = 0.9 kW, which add to 2.5 kW, confirming the independent-sideband assumption. The carrier power is unchanged by modulation in conventional AM, which is why the carrier occupies most of the power budget.

Answer: 22.5 kW

(c)

Efficiency is the useful sideband power divided by total power, η = Ps/Pt = (μ²/2)/(1 + μ²/2). Substituting μ² = 0.25 gives η = 0.125/1.125 = 0.1111, which is 11.1 percent. Equivalently 2.5 kW divided by 22.5 kW. Only the sidebands carry information, so 88.9 percent of the transmitted power is spent on the carrier, which is the price paid for the simple, cheap envelope-detector receiver. Even at 100 percent single-tone modulation the efficiency could not exceed one third, and with a speech-like programme it is usually below 10 percent.

Answer: 11.1 %

(d)

Diagonal clipping is avoided when the capacitor discharge curve is no steeper than the steepest fall of the envelope. The envelope is 1 + μ cos(ωm t), whose maximum negative slope relative to its value is μ ωm sin(ωm t)/(1 + μ cos ωm t). The worst case gives the condition RC ≤ √(1 − μ²)/(μ ωm). With μ = 0.3 and ωm = 2π × 3000 = 18850 rad/s, μ ωm = 5655 s⁻¹ and √(1 − 0.09) = 0.9539. Then RC ≤ 0.9539/5655 = 1.687 × 10⁻⁴ s = 168.7 µs. The lower bound is RC much greater than 1/fc = 1.67 µs, so the carrier ripple is smoothed. A value near 100 µs satisfies both limits.

Answer: RC ≤ 168.7 µs

(e)

The envelope is Ac[1 + 0.4 cos(ω1 t) + 0.3 cos(ω2 t)]. Its smallest value occurs when both cosines equal −1 at the same instant, which for commensurate tones at 1 kHz and 3 kHz does occur (at t = 0.5 ms the two phases are π and 3π). The minimum is 1 − 0.4 − 0.3 = 0.30, so the envelope bottoms out at 0.30 Ac. This is positive, so the envelope never crosses zero and never reverses phase. The wave is therefore not overmodulated, and an envelope detector recovers the message without distortion from this cause, although the peak excursion of 0.7 leaves 30 percent headroom.

Answer: 0.30 Ac, not overmodulated

Problem 2 [A3-072] DSB-SC, SSB and envelope detection

A double-sideband suppressed-carrier signal s(t) = Ac m(t) cos(2π fc t) with Ac = 4 V is sent from a field sensor node, where m(t) is a message limited to W = 4 kHz with mean-square value 0.25 V² (take the load as 1 Ω, so power is volts squared). The receiver multiplies the received signal by a local oscillator signal cos(2π fc t + φ) and passes the product through an ideal low-pass filter that rejects the double-frequency term. Channel noise is white with two-sided power spectral density N0/2, where N0 = 2 × 10⁻⁹ W/Hz, and it is band-limited by an ideal predetection filter of width 2W. The designer also wants to compare the DSB-SC choice with a single-sideband alternative and with envelope detection.

  1. (a) Find the transmitted power of the DSB-SC signal in W. [4]
  2. (b) With a phase error φ = 30° at the local oscillator, find the demodulated message power in W at the low-pass filter output. [4]
  3. (c) Find the phase error φ in degrees at which the demodulated message power falls to half of its value at φ = 0 (the 3 dB point). [3]
  4. (d) With φ = 0, find the output signal-to-noise ratio in dB of the coherent DSB-SC receiver. Use SNR_out = Ac²⟨m²⟩/(2 N0 W). [5]
  5. (e) Explain in two or three sentences why an envelope detector cannot recover m(t) from this DSB-SC wave, even with a phase-perfect receiver, and what is sent in conventional AM to make it work. [4]
(a)

The mean power of s(t) = Ac m(t) cos(2π fc t) is the average of Ac² m²(t) cos²(2π fc t). Since the carrier is much faster than the message, cos² averages to one half independently of m(t), so Pt = (Ac²/2)⟨m²⟩. With Ac = 4 V and ⟨m²⟩ = 0.25 V², Pt = (16/2) × 0.25 = 2.0 W. There is no carrier term, so all of this power is carried by the two sidebands. This is the total power for the SNR comparison of part (d), where the ratio of this power to N0 W sets the output signal-to-noise ratio.

Answer: 2.0 W

(b)

The product of s(t) and the oscillator is Ac m(t) cos(ωc t) cos(ωc t + φ) = (Ac/2) m(t)[cos φ + cos(2ωc t + φ)]. The low-pass filter removes the double-frequency term and leaves y(t) = (Ac/2) cos φ · m(t). Its mean power is (Ac²/4) cos²φ ⟨m²⟩. With Ac = 4 V, (Ac²/4) = 4, ⟨m²⟩ = 0.25 and cos²30° = 0.75, the power is 4 × 0.25 × 0.75 = 0.75 W. At φ = 0 the output power would be 1.0 W, so a 30 degree phase error costs 25 percent of the signal power, which is 1.25 dB.

Answer: 0.75 W

(c)

The output power is proportional to cos²φ. Setting cos²φ = 0.5 gives cos φ = 1/√2, so φ = 45°. In terms of the powers found above, 1.0 W × 0.5 = 0.5 W. A fixed phase error only attenuates the output, but a phase error that drifts with time, as happens when the carrier is recovered poorly, makes the output fade in and out, and at φ = 90° the signal vanishes entirely. This quadrature null is why DSB-SC systems need a phase-locked loop or Costas loop for carrier recovery.

Answer: φ = 45°

(d)

For a coherent DSB-SC receiver, the detected message power is Ac²⟨m²⟩/4. The output noise power after the detector and low-pass filter works out, with the detector scaling included, to give SNR_out = Ac²⟨m²⟩/(2 N0 W), which equals Pt/(N0 W) because Pt = Ac²⟨m²⟩/2. Substituting Ac²⟨m²⟩ = 16 × 0.25 = 4 W and N0 W = 2 × 10⁻⁹ × 4000 = 8 × 10⁻⁶ W gives SNR_out = 4/(2 × 8 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.5 × 10⁵. In decibels, 10 log10(2.5 × 10⁵) = 53.98 dB. A single-sideband system with the same transmitted power and the same message bandwidth would give the same figure, using only W of channel bandwidth instead of 2W.

Answer: 54.0 dB

(e)

The envelope of Ac m(t) cos(ωc t) is Ac|m(t)|, the magnitude of the message. Whenever m(t) changes sign the carrier phase reverses by 180 degrees, but an envelope detector responds only to amplitude and cannot see phase, so the output is the full-wave rectified message, which is badly distorted and contains frequency doubling. Conventional AM avoids this by adding a carrier term so the waveform is Ac[1 + μ m(t)] cos(ωc t) with μ|m(t)| at most 1. The envelope is then always positive and equals the scaled message plus a DC offset that a coupling capacitor removes. The cost is the carrier power, as seen in the efficiency figure for AM.

Answer: Envelope follows |m(t)|, so sign is lost; AM adds a carrier large enough that the envelope never goes negative.

Problem 3 [A3-073] Angle modulation: FM and PM, Carson bandwidth

An FM transmitter on a carrier of 98.1 MHz carries a single-tone message m(t) = Am cos(2π fm t) with Am = 2 V and fm = 5 kHz. The frequency modulator has a sensitivity kf = 12 kHz per volt, so the instantaneous frequency deviation is kf m(t). The unmodulated carrier power into the 50 Ω antenna load is 500 W. A phase modulator on the same carrier has a phase sensitivity kp = 2 rad per volt. For the Bessel function of the first kind, J0(4.8) = −0.2404, and the first zero of J0 occurs at an argument of 2.405. Use these values rather than a table.

  1. (a) Find the Carson-rule bandwidth in kHz of the FM wave for the given message. [4]
  2. (b) Find the power remaining in the carrier frequency component in W. [4]
  3. (c) Find the smallest message amplitude Am in volts for which the carrier component vanishes, with fm and kf unchanged. [4]
  4. (d) The message is changed to Am = 2 V at fm = 10 kHz. Find the Carson bandwidth in kHz of the PM wave from the phase modulator, with phase deviation kp Am. [5]
  5. (e) Find the Carson bandwidth in kHz of the original FM wave when fm is raised to 10 kHz with Am = 2 V. [3]
(a)

The peak frequency deviation is Δf = kf Am = 12 kHz/V × 2 V = 24 kHz, and the modulation index is β = Δf/fm = 24/5 = 4.8. Carson's rule estimates the bandwidth containing about 98 percent of the power as B = 2(Δf + fm) = 2(24 + 5) = 58 kHz. Equivalently B = 2 fm(β + 1) = 2 × 5 × 5.8 = 58 kHz. With β of 4.8 the wave is wideband FM, and the bandwidth is about 11.6 times the message frequency, far wider than the 10 kHz that an AM wave of the same tone would need.

Answer: 58 kHz

(b)

FM with a constant-amplitude envelope has constant total power, equal to the unmodulated carrier power of 500 W. The spectrum of a tone-modulated FM wave is a set of lines at fc ± n fm with amplitudes Ac Jn(β). The carrier line has amplitude Ac J0(4.8), so its share of the power is J0²(4.8) of the total. Then Pcarrier = 500 × (−0.2404)² = 500 × 0.05779 = 28.9 W. The remaining 471.1 W is carried by the sideband lines. Because the total is fixed, modulation merely moves power out of the carrier into the sidebands, unlike AM where sidebands add to the carrier power.

Answer: 28.9 W

(c)

The carrier line vanishes when J0(β) = 0. The first zero of J0 is at β = 2.405. Since β = kf Am/fm, Am = β fm/kf = 2.405 × 5 kHz/12 kHz per volt = 1.002 V. At this amplitude all of the power is in the sidebands, and the spectrum has no component at 98.1 MHz. This property is used in practice to calibrate frequency deviation, by raising the tone amplitude until the carrier on a spectrum analyser first disappears and then reading off the known β. Further carrier nulls appear at β = 5.520 and 8.654.

Answer: Am = 1.00 V

(d)

For phase modulation with θ(t) = kp m(t), the peak phase deviation is β = kp Am = 2 × 2 = 4 rad, independent of the tone frequency. The instantaneous frequency deviation is the derivative of the phase divided by 2π, so the peak frequency deviation is Δf = β fm = 4 × 10 kHz = 40 kHz. Carson's rule then gives B = 2(Δf + fm) = 2(40 + 10) = 100 kHz. For the earlier case at 5 kHz the PM bandwidth would have been 2(20 + 5) = 50 kHz, so doubling fm doubles the PM bandwidth, a major difference between PM and FM.

Answer: 100 kHz

(e)

For FM the deviation depends on amplitude only, Δf = kf Am = 24 kHz regardless of fm. Carson's rule gives B = 2(24 + 10) = 68 kHz. Compare with the 58 kHz found for fm = 5 kHz, an increase of only 17 percent, while the PM bandwidth at the same change doubled to 100 kHz. The FM modulation index drops to β = 2.4 when fm doubles, whereas the PM index stays at 4. This is the reason FM bandwidth grows slowly with message frequency while PM bandwidth grows almost in proportion, and the reason FM is the usual choice for broadcast audio.

Answer: 68 kHz

Problem 4 [A3-074] FM demodulation and noise performance basics

A broadcast FM link is being designed. The received FM signal at the discriminator has a carrier power of Pc = 3.0 × 10⁻¹³ W at the detector input. Receiver noise is white with two-sided power spectral density N0/2, where N0 = 4 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz. The message has a bandwidth W = 15 kHz, a mean-square value of 0.2 V² and a peak magnitude of 1 V. The frequency modulator has sensitivity kf = 75 kHz per volt. Use the standard result for an FM discriminator above threshold, SNR_out = 3 kf² ⟨m²⟩ Pc/(N0 W³), and define the carrier-to-noise ratio in a given bandwidth B as Pc/(N0 B). A de-emphasis filter with time constant 75 µs is available.

  1. (a) Find the carrier-to-noise ratio in dB measured in the message bandwidth W. [3]
  2. (b) Find the output signal-to-noise ratio in dB of the FM discriminator without de-emphasis. [5]
  3. (c) Find the carrier-to-noise ratio in dB at the discriminator input, using the Carson bandwidth for a peak deviation set by the 1 V peak message. [4]
  4. (d) With a de-emphasis time constant of 75 µs, find the SNR improvement in dB from pre-emphasis and de-emphasis, using I = (W/f0)³/(3[(W/f0) − arctan(W/f0)]) with f0 = 1/(2π τ). [5]
  5. (e) Find the smallest carrier power at the detector input in fW (10⁻¹⁵ W) that holds the predetection CNR at the 20 dB level used as the design threshold. [3]
(a)

The noise power in the message bandwidth is N0 W = 4 × 10⁻²¹ × 15000 = 6 × 10⁻¹⁷ W. The carrier-to-noise ratio is Pc/(N0 W) = 3 × 10⁻¹³/(6 × 10⁻¹⁷) = 5000. In decibels, 10 log10(5000) = 36.99 dB. This is a convenient reference figure, since SNR figures for baseband and AM systems are quoted against the same quantity, but it is not the ratio at the discriminator input, where the signal and noise occupy the much wider Carson bandwidth computed in part (c).

Answer: 37.0 dB

(b)

Using SNR_out = 3 kf² ⟨m²⟩ Pc/(N0 W³), rewrite it as 3 (kf/W)² ⟨m²⟩ × [Pc/(N0 W)]. The ratio kf/W = 75/15 = 5, so (kf/W)² = 25. Then 3 × 25 × 0.2 = 15. Multiplying by the carrier-to-noise ratio of 5000 from part (a) gives SNR_out = 15 × 5000 = 75000. In decibels, 10 log10(75000) = 48.75 dB. The FM output exceeds the carrier-to-noise ratio by 11.76 dB, the noise-reduction gain bought by spending bandwidth. A baseband or DSB-SC link at the same carrier-to-noise ratio would give 36.99 dB.

Answer: 48.8 dB

(c)

The peak frequency deviation is Δf = kf × 1 V = 75 kHz, and Carson's rule gives BT = 2(Δf + W) = 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz. The noise power in this predetection bandwidth is N0 BT = 4 × 10⁻²¹ × 180000 = 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ W. Then CNR = 3 × 10⁻¹³/7.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ = 416.7, which is 10 log10(416.7) = 26.2 dB. The detector threshold effect makes FM noise performance collapse when this predetection CNR falls below about 10 to 12 dB, so 26.2 dB leaves a margin of roughly 14 dB and the formula of part (b) is valid.

Answer: 26.2 dB

(d)

The de-emphasis corner frequency is f0 = 1/(2π × 75 × 10⁻⁶) = 2122 Hz. Then W/f0 = 15000/2122 = 7.069. The arctan term is arctan(7.069) = 1.4297 rad. The improvement factor is I = 7.069³/(3 × (7.069 − 1.4297)) = 353.2/(3 × 5.639) = 20.88. In decibels, 10 log10(20.88) = 13.2 dB. It works because FM output noise has a parabolic spectrum that is largest at the high audio frequencies, where speech and music energy is small, so a matched pre-emphasis and de-emphasis pair reduces the noise a great deal while leaving the message flat. The output SNR would become 48.75 + 13.2 = 61.95 dB.

Answer: 13.2 dB

(e)

A 20 dB design threshold means the predetection CNR must be 100. The required carrier power is Pc = 100 × N0 × BT = 100 × 4 × 10⁻²¹ × 180000 = 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ W, which equals 72 fW. The present carrier power of 300 fW therefore has a margin of 300/72 = 4.17, about 6.2 dB. Check against part (c): 26.2 − 20 = 6.2 dB. Below this power the discriminator starts producing clicks, and a power drop of more than 6 dB, for example from fading, would collapse the output SNR.

Answer: 72 fW

Problem 5 [A3-075] Superheterodyne receiver and mixing

A portable AM broadcast receiver uses a superheterodyne architecture with an intermediate frequency of 455 kHz and a local oscillator that tunes above the signal (high-side injection). It must cover the broadcast band from 530 kHz to 1600 kHz. The RF stage is a single tuned circuit with loaded quality factor Q = 60, followed by a low-noise amplifier with gain 15 dB and noise figure 3 dB, then a mixer with noise figure 9 dB. Listeners often complain about a whistle when tuned to a station at 1020 kHz, and the designer suspects the image channel. Assume the standard single-tuned-circuit image rejection expression √(1 + Q²ρ²) with ρ = fim/fs − fs/fim, and a variable capacitor tuning the local oscillator inductor.

  1. (a) Find the local oscillator frequency in kHz when the receiver is tuned to 1020 kHz. [3]
  2. (b) Find the image frequency in kHz for the 1020 kHz station. [3]
  3. (c) Find the image rejection ratio in dB provided by the single tuned RF circuit when tuned to 1020 kHz. [5]
  4. (d) Find the noise figure in dB of the LNA followed by the mixer, using the cascade (Friis) formula. [4]
  5. (e) The local oscillator must tune from 985 kHz to 2055 kHz. Find the ratio of maximum to minimum capacitance of the tuning capacitor needed, with a fixed inductor. [5]
(a)

With high-side injection the local oscillator is above the wanted signal by exactly the intermediate frequency, fLO = fs + fIF = 1020 + 455 = 1475 kHz. The mixer produces sum and difference products, and the 455 kHz difference term fLO − fs passes through the narrow IF filter, where nearly all of the receiver selectivity is provided. Because the IF is fixed, the same filter and amplifier serve every station, which is the main advantage of the superheterodyne architecture compared with a tuned-radio-frequency receiver whose bandwidth would change across the dial.

Answer: 1475 kHz

(b)

The image frequency is the other input frequency that mixes down to the same IF, and with high-side injection it lies above the local oscillator by one IF: fim = fLO + fIF = fs + 2 fIF = 1020 + 910 = 1930 kHz. Any signal at 1930 kHz produces fim − fLO = 455 kHz at the mixer output, which is indistinguishable from the wanted signal after the mixer. This is why a whistle or a second station is heard in the background: no later filter can separate the two once they share the IF, so the rejection must come from the RF stage ahead of the mixer.

Answer: 1930 kHz

(c)

First compute ρ = fim/fs − fs/fim = 1930/1020 − 1020/1930 = 1.8922 − 0.5285 = 1.3637. Then Qρ = 60 × 1.3637 = 81.82. The image rejection ratio is α = √(1 + (Qρ)²) = √(1 + 6694.7) = 81.83. In decibels, 20 log10(81.83) = 38.26 dB. A single tuned circuit therefore gives only about 38 dB, which may not suffice when a strong local station sits at 1930 kHz, so designers add a second tuned stage, or raise the IF so that fim moves further from the signal. The rejection also worsens at the high end of the band (34.9 dB at 1600 kHz versus 43.0 dB at 530 kHz), where the image is closer in relative terms.

Answer: 38.3 dB

(d)

Convert to linear values. The LNA has F1 = 100.3 = 1.995 and G1 = 101.5 = 31.62. The mixer has F2 = 100.9 = 7.943. The cascade noise factor is F = F1 + (F2 − 1)/G1 = 1.995 + 6.943/31.62 = 1.995 + 0.2196 = 2.215. In decibels, 10 log10(2.215) = 3.45 dB. The mixer's poor noise figure of 9 dB raises the cascade by only 0.45 dB, since the LNA gain of 15 dB suppresses its contribution. The first stage dominates the noise performance, which is why a low-noise first stage is spent on the weakest-signal link.

Answer: 3.45 dB

(e)

The oscillator frequency is f = 1/(2π√(LC)), so with L fixed C is proportional to 1/f². The band edges give fLO,min = 530 + 455 = 985 kHz and fLO,max = 1600 + 455 = 2055 kHz. The frequency ratio is 2055/985 = 2.0863, so the capacitance ratio is Cmax/Cmin = (2.0863)² = 4.353. Compare a tuned oscillator without an IF offset, which would need (1600/530)² = 9.11. The offset at high-side injection narrows the frequency ratio and therefore the capacitor ratio, a practical advantage of high-side over low-side injection for this band.

Answer: 4.35

A3 Practice Paper 16

Problem 1 [A3-076] Noise in analog communication, SNR

A rural AM broadcast link carries a tone-modulated conventional AM signal with modulation index μ = 0.8, so the mean-square normalized message is 0.5 and the figure of merit of an envelope-detected AM receiver is μ²P/(1 + μ²P), where P = 0.5. The transmitter power is 500 W, the total path loss is 140 dB, and the message bandwidth is W = 5 kHz. The receiver front end is characterised by noise figure 6 dB at a reference temperature T0 = 290 K, for which kT0 = 4.0 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz. Take the noise power in the message bandwidth as N0 W, with N0 = kT0 F, and treat the channel signal-to-noise ratio as the received power divided by N0 W. Receiver gain does not affect any of these ratios.

  1. (a) Find the received signal power in dBm. [3]
  2. (b) Find the channel signal-to-noise ratio in dB. [4]
  3. (c) Find the output signal-to-noise ratio in dB of the envelope-detected AM receiver. [5]
  4. (d) Find the extra transmit power in dB that AM needs, compared with DSB-SC, to reach the same output SNR. [4]
  5. (e) If the modulation index is raised to the maximum μ = 1 for the same tone message (P = 0.5), find the best-case output SNR in dB at the same received power. [4]
(a)

The path loss of 140 dB is a power ratio of 10¹⁴, so the received power is Pr = 500/10¹⁴ = 5 × 10⁻¹² W. In dBm, 10 log10(5 × 10⁻¹²/10⁻³) = 10 log10(5 × 10⁻⁹) = −83.01 dBm. Equivalently, the transmitter at 500 W is 56.99 dBm, and subtracting 140 dB gives −83.01 dBm. The calculation treats the path loss as a single lumped quantity including antenna gains and propagation, so Pr is the power delivered at the receiver input terminals before any gain.

Answer: −83.0 dBm

(b)

The noise figure of 6 dB is F = 100.6 = 3.981, so the effective noise density is N0 = kT0 F = 4.0 × 10⁻²¹ × 3.981 = 1.592 × 10⁻²⁰ W/Hz. The noise power in the message bandwidth is N0 W = 1.592 × 10⁻²⁰ × 5000 = 7.96 × 10⁻¹⁷ W. The channel SNR is Pr/(N0 W) = 5 × 10⁻¹²/7.96 × 10⁻¹⁷ = 6.28 × 10⁴. In decibels, 10 log10(62800) = 47.98 dB. This is the SNR a baseband or DSB-SC system would deliver at the receiver output for the same received power, so it is the reference against which AM is compared.

Answer: 48.0 dB

(c)

For envelope-detected AM above threshold, SNR_out = [μ²P/(1 + μ²P)] × (channel SNR). With μ = 0.8 and P = 0.5, μ²P = 0.64 × 0.5 = 0.32, and the figure of merit is 0.32/1.32 = 0.2424. Multiplying by the channel SNR of 62800 gives SNR_out = 15224. In decibels, 10 log10(15224) = 41.83 dB. Equivalently the output SNR is the channel SNR of 47.98 dB less the figure-of-merit loss of 6.15 dB. The loss exists because 76 percent of the transmitted power is spent on the carrier, which contributes nothing to the detected message.

Answer: 41.8 dB

(d)

A coherent DSB-SC receiver gives SNR_out equal to the channel SNR, with a figure of merit of 1. AM has a figure of merit of 0.2424, so to reach the same output SNR the AM transmit power must be raised by the factor 1/0.2424 = 4.125. In decibels, 10 log10(4.125) = 6.15 dB. In power terms the 500 W transmitter would have to become 2.06 kW. This penalty is what a broadcaster accepts in exchange for receivers that are cheap and need no carrier recovery circuit, because each listener has a simple diode detector rather than a coherent demodulator.

Answer: 6.15 dB

(e)

With μ = 1 and P = 0.5, the figure of merit is μ²P/(1 + μ²P) = 0.5/1.5 = 0.3333, which is the maximum for a tone. Multiplying by the channel SNR of 62800 gives 20933, which in decibels is 10 log10(20933) = 43.21 dB. This is 1.38 dB above the μ = 0.8 case of 41.83 dB. A figure of merit of one third, a loss of 4.77 dB, is the theoretical best for single-tone AM, and a real speech signal, which has a high peak-to-average ratio and so must run at a lower average index, does worse.

Answer: 43.2 dB

Problem 2 [A3-077] Digital baseband and pulse shaping, intersymbol interference

A leased-line data modem sends 4-level PAM, so each symbol carries 2 bits, with symbols shaped by a raised-cosine pulse p(t) = sinc(t/Ts) cos(π α t/Ts)/[1 − (2 α t/Ts)²], where Ts is the symbol period and sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx). The bit rate is 19.2 kbit/s and the roll-off factor is α = 0.35. The channel is an ideal low-pass line. A second link uses the same pulse family with α = 0.25 on a line of 8 kHz bandwidth. Timing jitter in the symbol clock can move the sampling instant away from the ideal point by a fraction of Ts, and the engineer wants to check the resulting intersymbol interference.

  1. (a) Find the minimum channel bandwidth in kHz needed for the 19.2 kbit/s link with α = 0.35. [4]
  2. (b) For the 8 kHz line with α = 0.25, find the highest bit rate in kbit/s that can be sent with 4-level PAM without intersymbol interference at ideal sampling. [4]
  3. (c) For α = 0.35, find the value of the pulse p(t) at t = Ts/4, normalized to p(0) = 1. [4]
  4. (d) With a sampling error of τ = 0.1 Ts and α = 0.35, find the worst-case total ISI, the sum over all other symbol positions of |p(τ − kTs)| for k ≠ 0, as a fraction of the main-pulse sample p(τ). Sum k from −200 to 200. [5]
  5. (e) Explain in two or three sentences why a designer would not choose α = 0 even though it needs the least bandwidth. [3]
(a)

With 4-level PAM, each symbol carries log2(4) = 2 bits, so the symbol rate is Rs = 19200/2 = 9600 symbols per second, giving Ts = 104.2 µs. A raised-cosine spectrum has a one-sided bandwidth B = (1 + α)/(2 Ts) = Rs(1 + α)/2. Substituting, B = 9600 × 1.35/2 = 6480 Hz = 6.48 kHz. This is 35 percent more than the Nyquist minimum of 4.8 kHz, which is the price of a practical roll-off that makes the pulse tails decay quickly and lets the receiver tolerate timing errors.

Answer: 6.48 kHz

(b)

For a given channel bandwidth B, the largest ISI-free symbol rate with raised-cosine pulses satisfies B = Rs(1 + α)/2, so Rs = 2B/(1 + α) = 16000/1.25 = 12800 symbols per second. With 2 bits per symbol, the bit rate is 2 × 12800 = 25600 bit/s = 25.6 kbit/s. The result is 80 percent of the 2B = 16 kBd limit for an ideal rectangular spectrum. A lower roll-off would give more rate but a longer, more jitter-sensitive pulse, so α = 0.25 is a typical compromise between rate and timing tolerance.

Answer: 25.6 kbit/s

(c)

Evaluate at t/Ts = 0.25. The sinc factor is sin(π × 0.25)/(π × 0.25) = 0.7071/0.7854 = 0.9003. The cosine factor is cos(π × 0.35 × 0.25) = cos(0.2749) = 0.9624. The denominator is 1 − (2 × 0.35 × 0.25)² = 1 − 0.03063 = 0.9694. Then p = 0.9003 × 0.9624/0.9694 = 0.8938, about 0.894. At a sampling error of one quarter of a symbol, the main-pulse amplitude is reduced by about 11 percent, and the lost margin plus ISI from the neighbouring pulses reduce the noise tolerance of the eye.

Answer: 0.894

(d)

Sampled at t = τ, the main pulse gives p(0.1) and each neighbour k contributes p(0.1 − k) multiplied by its symbol amplitude. For worst-case alignment the contributions all add in magnitude, so the ISI is D = Σ|p(0.1 − k)| for k ≠ 0, then normalized by p(0.1). The main sample is p(0.1) = 0.9836 × 0.9940/0.9951 = 0.9825. Neighbours k = ±1 give magnitudes of about 0.099 and 0.078 and the tails drop as 1/k³, so the sum of the remaining terms is small. Numerical summation gives D = 0.2660, and D/p(0.1) = 0.2707. The eye opening is therefore about 1 − 0.27 = 0.73 of the main sample for a binary pulse, quite a large loss from a 10 percent timing error.

Answer: 0.271

(e)

With α = 0 the pulse is p(t) = sinc(t/Ts) whose tails decay only as 1/t. A timing error then lets every neighbouring symbol leak a contribution of order 1/k, and the sum of these terms diverges logarithmically, so even a small timing error can close the eye if many symbols line up. A raised-cosine pulse with α > 0 decays as 1/t³, which makes the sum converge to a small number, as in part (d). Also, the rectangular spectrum needed for α = 0 cannot be realised by a physical filter, and the sharp cutoff causes long ringing in the transmit and receive filters.

Answer: Sinc tails decay as 1/t, so timing jitter makes ISI sum large and unbounded; practical filters cannot realize the brick-wall spectrum.

Problem 3 [A3-078] ASK, FSK and PSK modulation

A telemetry designer must send 56 kbit/s over a 100 kHz channel allocation and is comparing carrier-modulation options. Option 1 is on-off keying (binary ASK) using rectangular pulses. Option 2 is binary FSK with tones at fc − Rb/2 and fc + Rb/2, so the tone spacing equals the bit rate Rb, again with rectangular pulses; take its bandwidth as the null-to-null width of the combined main lobes. Option 3 is QPSK with raised-cosine pulses of roll-off α = 0.3. Option 4 is 8-PSK with raised-cosine pulses of roll-off α = 0.25 on the same channel. For rectangular-pulse binary signals use the null-to-null bandwidth of 2Rb for the single main lobe, and for raised-cosine passband signals use Rs(1 + α).

  1. (a) Find the null-to-null bandwidth in kHz of Option 1, OOK with rectangular pulses at 56 kbit/s, and say whether it fits the 100 kHz allocation (give the number). [3]
  2. (b) Find the null-to-null bandwidth in kHz of Option 2, binary FSK with tone spacing Rb. [4]
  3. (c) Find the bandwidth in kHz of Option 3, QPSK with raised-cosine pulses, α = 0.3, at 56 kbit/s. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest bit rate in kbit/s for Option 4, 8-PSK with α = 0.25 filling the whole 100 kHz. [5]
  5. (e) Explain in two or three sentences why a designer might still choose binary FSK despite its worse spectral efficiency. [4]
(a)

For binary ASK or PSK with rectangular pulses of duration Tb = 1/Rb, the baseband spectrum is a sinc-squared shape with its first nulls at ±Rb. Translating to the carrier fc, the main lobe runs from fc − Rb to fc + Rb, so the null-to-null bandwidth is 2Rb = 2 × 56 = 112 kHz. This exceeds the 100 kHz allocation, so the rectangular-pulse OOK signal does not fit without filtering and some of the sidelobes would spill into adjacent channels. A pulse-shaping filter would reduce the bandwidth, which is the motivation for Option 3.

Answer: 112 kHz

(b)

Each FSK tone is a rectangular-pulse carrier whose spectrum has a main lobe of null-to-null width 2Rb centred on its tone frequency. The tones sit at fc − Rb/2 and fc + Rb/2, a spacing of Rb. The combined spectrum runs from the lower edge of the lower lobe, fc − Rb/2 − Rb, to the upper edge of the upper lobe, fc + Rb/2 + Rb, so the total width is 2Rb + Rb = 3Rb = 3 × 56 = 168 kHz. This is wider than the OOK figure because two lobes are used, so the cost of FSK is bandwidth, in return for a constant carrier envelope and tolerance to nonlinear amplifiers.

Answer: 168 kHz

(c)

QPSK carries 2 bits per symbol, so the symbol rate is Rs = 56000/2 = 28000 symbols per second. A raised-cosine passband signal occupies Rs(1 + α) = 28 × 1.3 = 36.4 kHz. This is well inside the 100 kHz allocation, with 63.6 kHz to spare, which could hold a second signal or a guard band. The spectral efficiency is 56/36.4 = 1.54 bit/s/Hz. Compared with binary PSK on rectangular pulses at 112 kHz, which has 0.5 bit/s/Hz, QPSK with shaping is more than three times as efficient.

Answer: 36.4 kHz

(d)

The signal bandwidth is Rs(1 + α), so the largest symbol rate in 100 kHz is Rs = 100/1.25 = 80 kilosymbols per second. 8-PSK carries log2(8) = 3 bits per symbol, so the bit rate is 3 × 80 = 240 kbit/s. The spectral efficiency is 2.4 bit/s/Hz. The 56 kbit/s requirement needs only 23 percent of this capacity, so a designer could instead run 8-PSK at a lower symbol rate or add error-correction coding. The price is a smaller spacing between constellation points, so 8-PSK needs about 3.6 dB more Eb/N0 than QPSK for the same bit error rate.

Answer: 240 kbit/s

(e)

FSK has a constant envelope, so the transmitter can use a saturated, power-efficient Class C amplifier without the spectral regrowth that distorts amplitude-varying signals such as QPSK or 8-PSK. This matters for battery-powered telemetry nodes, where each milliwatt of DC power counts. FSK can also be demodulated noncoherently with a pair of band-pass filters and envelope detectors, so the receiver needs no carrier-phase recovery and tolerates phase noise, oscillator drift and fading. The cost is the 168 kHz bandwidth found in part (b) and a worse bit-error performance than coherent PSK at the same Eb/N0.

Answer: Constant envelope allows efficient nonlinear amplifier; noncoherent detection is simple and robust to phase and fading.

Problem 4 [A3-079] Digital demodulation, matched filter and bit error probability

A coherent BPSK receiver in a remote sensor gateway receives data at Rb = 2 Mbit/s with equiprobable bits over an additive white Gaussian noise channel. The received signal power at the input of the matched filter is −97 dBm. The receiver noise figure is 4 dB referred to T0 = 290 K, Boltzmann's constant is k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, and the noise power spectral density is N0 = kT0 F (two-sided density N0/2). The bit error probability of coherent BPSK is Pb = Q(√(2Eb/N0)) with Q(x) = ½ erfc(x/√2), and that of noncoherent binary FSK is Pb = ½ exp(−Eb/(2N0)). The matched filter is matched to a rectangular bit pulse.

  1. (a) Find Eb/N0 in dB at the matched filter output for the stated received power. [3]
  2. (b) Find the bit error probability for coherent BPSK at this Eb/N0. [5]
  3. (c) Find the bit error probability for noncoherent binary FSK at the same Eb/N0. [4]
  4. (d) Find the received power in dBm needed for coherent BPSK to reach Pb = 10⁻⁶. Use that Q(4.753) = 10⁻⁶. [5]
  5. (e) An implementation loss of 1.5 dB, from imperfect timing and filtering, reduces the effective Eb/N0. Find the bit error probability of coherent BPSK with that loss. [3]
(a)

The received power is −97 dBm = 10−9.7 × 10⁻³ W = 1.995 × 10⁻¹³ W. The energy per bit is Eb = Pr/Rb = 1.995 × 10⁻¹³/(2 × 10⁶) = 9.98 × 10⁻²⁰ J. The noise density is N0 = kT0 F, with kT0 = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 290 = 4.002 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz and F = 100.4 = 2.512, so N0 = 1.005 × 10⁻²⁰ W/Hz. Then Eb/N0 = 9.98 × 10⁻²⁰/1.005 × 10⁻²⁰ = 9.924, which is 9.97 dB. The matched filter is optimum because it maximises the peak output SNR at the sampling instant, and that SNR depends only on Eb/N0, not on the pulse shape.

Answer: 9.97 dB

(b)

The argument of the Q function is √(2 Eb/N0) = √(2 × 9.924) = √19.85 = 4.455. The tail probability is Q(4.455) = ½ erfc(4.455/√2) = ½ erfc(3.150). For large argument, erfc(3.150) = 8.38 × 10⁻⁶, so Pb = 4.19 × 10⁻⁶. In a stream of 2 Mbit/s this is an average of about 8.4 errors per second before any error-correction coding. The result is steeply dependent on Eb/N0, so a drop of 1 dB would raise the error rate by about an order of magnitude, which is why a link margin is built in.

Answer: 4.2 × 10⁻⁶

(c)

The noncoherent FSK expression is Pb = ½ exp(−Eb/(2N0)). With Eb/N0 = 9.924, the exponent is −9.924/2 = −4.962. Then exp(−4.962) = 6.998 × 10⁻³ and Pb = 3.50 × 10⁻³. This is about 830 times worse than coherent BPSK at the same Eb/N0. To match the BPSK error rate, noncoherent FSK would need Eb/N0 of about 2 × ln(1/(2 × 4.19 × 10⁻⁶)) = 23.4, which is 13.7 dB, instead of 9.97 dB, so noncoherent FSK needs about 3.7 dB more power than coherent BPSK.

Answer: 3.5 × 10⁻³

(d)

For Pb = 10⁻⁶, √(2Eb/N0) = 4.753, so Eb/N0 = 4.753²/2 = 11.30, which is 10.53 dB. The required received power is Pr = (Eb/N0) × N0 × Rb = 11.30 × 1.005 × 10⁻²⁰ × 2 × 10⁶ = 2.27 × 10⁻¹³ W, which in dBm is 10 log10(2.27 × 10⁻¹⁰) = −96.44 dBm. The present −97 dBm is 0.56 dB short of this level. A fade margin of a few dB would therefore be needed in a real design to hold 10⁻⁶ on a fading channel.

Answer: −96.4 dBm

(e)

The effective Eb/N0 is reduced by 1.5 dB, a factor of 10−0.15 = 0.7079, so Eb/N0 = 9.924 × 0.7079 = 7.025. The argument of Q is √(2 × 7.025) = 3.748. Then Pb = Q(3.748) = ½ erfc(2.650) = 8.9 × 10⁻⁵. The error probability rose by a factor of about 21 for a 1.5 dB loss. This sensitivity is why imperfect carrier phase, a timing error or filter mismatch must be budgeted at design time, and why the matched filter, which has no loss at ideal timing, is preferred to a simple low-pass filter.

Answer: 8.9 × 10⁻⁵

Problem 5 [A3-080] Link design combining bandwidth, SNR and modulation choice

A point-to-point microwave link in northern Ontario must carry 12 Mbit/s of telemetry and video within a 5 MHz allocated channel. The designer considers 16-QAM with raised-cosine pulses of roll-off α = 0.25. For Gray-coded 16-QAM use Ps = 3 Q(√(Es/(5 N0))) for the symbol error probability and Pb ≈ Ps/4 for the bit error probability. The receiver has a system noise temperature of 500 K, Boltzmann's constant is k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, and N0 = kT. The path loss is 148 dB, and the transmit and receive antennas each have 30 dBi gain. The channel must reach Pb = 10⁻⁶, and Q(4.695) = 1.333 × 10⁻⁶. Cable and other losses are included in the path loss.

  1. (a) Find the Shannon minimum SNR in dB needed to carry 12 Mbit/s in the 5 MHz channel. [3]
  2. (b) Find the bit rate in Mbit/s that the 16-QAM system can carry in the 5 MHz channel. [3]
  3. (c) Find the Es/N0 in dB needed for Pb = 10⁻⁶ with 16-QAM. [5]
  4. (d) Find the required received signal power in dBm at the demodulator. [5]
  5. (e) Find the transmitter power in dBm needed to provide an 8 dB fade margin on top of the required received power. [4]
(a)

The required spectral efficiency is Rb/B = 12/5 = 2.4 bit/s/Hz. Shannon's capacity C = B log2(1 + SNR) must be at least 12 Mbit/s, so SNR ≥ 22.4 − 1 = 5.278 − 1 = 4.278. In decibels, 10 log10(4.278) = 6.31 dB. This is the theoretical limit, reached only by ideal coding with infinite complexity, and a practical uncoded system needs much more, as parts (c) and (d) show. The gap between this figure and the uncoded 16-QAM requirement is the potential gain from error-correction coding.

Answer: 6.31 dB

(b)

A raised-cosine signal occupies Rs(1 + α), so the highest symbol rate in 5 MHz is Rs = 5/1.25 = 4 Msymbol/s. 16-QAM carries log2(16) = 4 bits per symbol, so Rb = 4 × 4 = 16 Mbit/s. This exceeds the required 12 Mbit/s by 33 percent. The spare capacity can be used for error-correction overhead, or the symbol rate can be reduced to 3 Msymbol/s to match 12 Mbit/s exactly, narrowing the signal to 3.75 MHz. The design retains the full 4 Msymbol/s here, so the receiver bandwidth is 4 MHz matched.

Answer: 16 Mbit/s

(c)

Pb ≈ Ps/4 = 10⁻⁶ gives Ps = 4 × 10⁻⁶. With Ps = 3 Q(x), x = √(Es/(5 N0)), so Q(x) = 4 × 10⁻⁶/3 = 1.333 × 10⁻⁶. The given value Q(4.695) = 1.333 × 10⁻⁶ gives x = 4.695. Then Es/N0 = 5x² = 5 × 22.04 = 110.2. In decibels, 10 log10(110.2) = 20.42 dB. Compare with QPSK, which needs Es/N0 of about 13.6 dB for the same Pb. The 6.8 dB difference is the price paid for fitting 4 bits per symbol rather than 2 in the same bandwidth.

Answer: 20.4 dB

(d)

Received power Pr = Es Rs, where Es is the symbol energy. Es = (Es/N0) × N0, and N0 = kT = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 500 = 6.9 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz. Then Es = 110.2 × 6.9 × 10⁻²¹ = 7.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and Pr = Es × Rs = 7.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 4 × 10⁶ = 3.04 × 10⁻¹² W. In dBm, 10 log10(3.04 × 10⁻¹²/10⁻³) = −85.17 dBm. A margin to cover fading is added in part (e). Note that only the symbol rate matters here, not the bit rate, because the symbol energy is multiplied by the symbol rate.

Answer: −85.2 dBm

(e)

The net link loss is the path loss less the two antenna gains: 148 − 30 − 30 = 88 dB. The received power must be the required −85.17 dBm plus an 8 dB margin, which is −77.17 dBm. The link budget in dB is Pt = Pr + net loss, so Pt = −77.17 + 88 = 10.83 dBm. In linear terms this is 12.1 mW. This is a low power, as expected with two 30 dBi dishes. A real design would also include feeder loss, rain fade and an allowance for interference, but the point stands that the modulation choice, which sets the Es/N0, links directly to the transmitter size.

Answer: 10.8 dBm

A3 Practice Paper 17

Problem 1 [A3-081] Fourier series coefficients and spectra of periodic signals

A gate-drive controller outputs a periodic rectangular pulse train v(t) for a small solenoid driver. The waveform has amplitude 5 V during each pulse and 0 V otherwise, a period T of 2.0 ms and a pulse width τ of 0.50 ms. The pulse is centred on t = 0, so it occupies −0.25 ms to +0.25 ms in every period and the waveform is an even function of time. Use the exponential Fourier series v(t) = Σ c_n ej2πnf0t with f0 = 1/T. The 1 Ω normalised power of the signal is the mean of v(t)². A designer must decide how much bandwidth a filter and a cable need to carry so that the distortion of the pulse train stays small.

  1. (a) Find the dc component of v(t). [4]
  2. (b) Find the amplitude of the third harmonic term, 2|c_3|, in the cosine form of the series. [5]
  3. (c) Use Parseval's theorem to find the fraction of the total normalised power that lies in the dc term and harmonics 1 to 7. [5]
  4. (d) The designer requires at least 97 percent of the total normalised power. Find the smallest number N of harmonics that must pass, and the bandwidth N·f0 needed. [6]
(a)

The dc component is the average of the waveform over one period. The pulse has height A = 5 V and lasts τ = 0.5 ms out of T = 2 ms, so c_0 = Aτ/T = 5 × 0.5/2 = 1.25 V. This is the same as the duty ratio, 0.25, multiplied by the pulse height, which is a quick check that the result is believable. A meter with a low-pass response would read 1.25 V, not 5 V.

Answer: 1.25 V

(b)

For a centred rectangular pulse train the coefficients are real: c_n = (Aτ/T) sinc(nτ/T) with sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx). Here τ/T = 0.25, so c_3 = 1.25 × sin(3π/4)/(3π/4) = 1.25 × 0.7071/2.3562 = 0.3751 V. In the cosine form each harmonic amplitude is 2|c_n| because the terms at +n and −n combine, giving 2 × 0.3751 = 0.750 V. The sign of c_n only affects the phase, 0 or 180 degrees, not the amplitude. The third harmonic sits at 1.5 kHz, three times f0, and its amplitude is about 60 percent of the 1.25 V dc level, which shows the spectrum decays slowly. Always state the form, cosine or exponential, because the factor of two between them is a common marking error.

Answer: 0.750 V

(c)

Parseval's theorem for a periodic signal gives the total power as the sum of |c_n|² over all n, and it equals the mean of v² in the time domain: P = A²τ/T = 25 × 0.25 = 6.25 W (1 Ω basis). The power up to harmonic 7 is c_0² + 2Σ_{n=1..7}|c_n|², using the symmetry c_{−n} = c_n. Evaluating the terms: c_0² = 1.5625 and the harmonic coefficients c_1 to c_7 are 1.1254, 0.7958, 0.3751, 0, −0.2251, −0.2653 and −0.1608, whose squares sum to 2.1875. The total is 1.5625 + 2 × 2.1875 = 5.9375 W, so the fraction is 5.9375/6.25 = 0.950, which is 95.0 percent. The n = 4 term vanishes because sinc(1) = 0.

Answer: 95.0 percent

(d)

Repeat the power sum, adding harmonics until the running total reaches 0.97 × 6.25 = 6.0625 W. The nulls of sinc fall at multiples of 4 (n = 4, 8, 12), so those harmonics add nothing, and the sum passes 97 percent only when n = 14 is included: the fraction is 0.973 at N = 14 and 0.9688 at N = 13. The bandwidth is N f0 = 14 × 500 Hz = 7.0 kHz, because f0 = 1/2 ms = 500 Hz. Notice the tail beyond the first null is slow to decay, which is why sharp pulses need wide cable bandwidth.

Answer: N = 14, bandwidth 7.0 kHz

Problem 2 [A3-082] Fourier transform pairs and properties

A radar altimeter transmits a rectangular RF burst x(t) = A rect(t/τ) cos(2π f_c t), where rect(t/τ) equals 1 for |t| < τ/2 and 0 elsewhere. The amplitude A is 2.0 V, the burst length τ is 10 μs and the carrier frequency f_c is 1.0 MHz, so there are ten carrier cycles in each burst. Take the Fourier transform as X(f) = ∫ x(t) e−j2πft dt and treat the voltage as appearing across 1 Ω. A receiver channel must be chosen to pass most of the burst energy while rejecting out-of-band interference. Because f_c τ = 10, the overlap between the positive-frequency and negative-frequency spectral lobes is negligible and may be ignored in the numerical parts.

  1. (a) Using the modulation property, find the magnitude of the spectrum at f = f_c, in μV per hertz (μV/Hz). [4]
  2. (b) Find the null-to-null width of the main lobe around f_c. [4]
  3. (c) Find the total energy of the burst, in μJ, using Parseval's theorem or the time-domain integral. [4]
  4. (d) Find the percentage of the burst energy that lies inside the main lobe. [4]
  5. (e) A receiver channel is centred on f_c with total width 150 kHz. Find the percentage of the burst energy it passes, and decide whether widening to the main-lobe width is worth the added noise. [4]
(a)

A rectangular pulse A rect(t/τ) has transform Aτ sinc(fτ). Multiplying by cos(2πf_c t) shifts and halves it: X(f) = (Aτ/2)[sinc((f − f_c)τ) + sinc((f + f_c)τ)]. At f = f_c the first term is sinc(0) = 1 and the second is negligible, so |X(f_c)| = Aτ/2 = 2.0 × 10×10⁻⁶ / 2 = 1.0×10⁻⁵ V·s, which is 10 μV/Hz. The factor of one half arises because the cosine splits the energy equally between the positive and negative frequency lobes. The units come from the transform of a voltage: volts multiplied by seconds is volts per hertz. Quote the answer in μV/Hz as asked, and note that the same peak would appear at −f_c by symmetry for a real signal, with equal magnitude.

Answer: 10 μV/Hz

(b)

The main lobe of sinc((f − f_c)τ) is bounded by the first zeros where (f − f_c)τ = ±1, that is f − f_c = ±1/τ = ±100 kHz. The null-to-null width is therefore 2/τ = 2/(10×10⁻⁶ s) = 200 kHz. A shorter burst gives a wider lobe, which is the time-bandwidth trade-off of the transform pair: halving τ would double the main-lobe width to 400 kHz while halving the peak spectral density. As a check on the numbers, ten carrier cycles per burst means the burst is about ten periods long, so a bandwidth of roughly a tenth of the carrier frequency is reasonable for a 1 MHz carrier.

Answer: 200 kHz

(c)

The energy over 1 Ω is E = ∫ x(t)² dt = A² ∫ cos²(2πf_c t) dt over the burst. Since cos² averages to one half over ten whole carrier cycles, E = A² τ / 2 = 4 × 10×10⁻⁶ / 2 = 2.0×10⁻⁵ J, which is 20 μJ. By Parseval's theorem the same value results from integrating |X(f)|² over all frequencies, which provides a useful cross-check for the spectral peak found in part (a). A marker looks for the average of cos² being one half and for the correct conversion of microseconds, so show both steps. Energy in joules over 1 Ω is numerically equal to the volt-squared-second integral.

Answer: 20 μJ

(d)

Near f_c the energy spectral density is |X|² = (Aτ/2)² sinc²((f − f_c)τ). Integrating over the whole positive lobe gives half the total energy, 10 μJ, and the negative lobe holds the other half. With u = (f − f_c)τ, the main-lobe fraction of the positive-lobe energy is the integral of sinc²(u) from −1 to 1, since the sinc² integral over all u equals 1. Numerical integration gives 0.9028, so 90.3 percent of the burst energy is inside the main lobe, about 18.1 μJ in total.

Answer: 90.3 percent

(e)

A 150 kHz channel covers f − f_c from −75 kHz to +75 kHz, that is u = (f − f_c)τ from −0.75 to +0.75. The fraction passed is the integral of sinc²(u) from −0.75 to 0.75, which is 0.8888, or 88.9 percent. Widening from 150 kHz to 200 kHz raises the passed energy by only 1.4 percentage points, while noise power grows in proportion to bandwidth, a 33 percent increase. The narrower channel gives the better signal to noise ratio, so it is the sensible choice.

Answer: 88.9 percent

Problem 3 [A3-083] Energy, power and spectra, Parseval's theorem

A bench power supply feeds a 15 Ω resistive load from a full-wave rectifier connected to the 60 Hz mains, with no smoothing capacitor. The load voltage is v(t) = |V_p sin(2π·60 t)| with V_p = 10 V, so it repeats at 120 Hz. Its Fourier series is v(t) = 2V_p/π − Σ_{k=1}∞ [4V_p/(π(4k² − 1))] cos(2π·120k·t). A technician wants to know how the average power divides between the dc term and the ripple, in order to choose a filter. Use Parseval's theorem for periodic signals, and take the series as given. Power values are average power dissipated in the 15 Ω load unless stated as normalised (1 Ω).

  1. (a) Find the dc component of the load voltage. [4]
  2. (b) Find the average power dissipated in the 15 Ω load, using the mean-square value of v(t) in the time domain. [4]
  3. (c) Use the series to find the fraction of the total power carried by the dc term and the 120 Hz harmonic together. [4]
  4. (d) Find the ripple factor, defined as the rms of the ac part divided by the dc component. [4]
  5. (e) Of the ac power only, find the fraction carried by the 120 Hz component, and say what this implies for the filter design. [4]
(a)

The dc term of the series is 2V_p/π = 20/π = 6.366 V. This is the average of one half-cycle of a sine of peak 10 V, namely (1/π) times the integral of V_p sin θ from 0 to π, which gives 2V_p/π. A dc voltmeter across the load would therefore read 6.37 V, noticeably less than the 7.07 V rms value of the underlying sine. The result is the area under half a sine divided by its base, so it can be checked against the mean of a sine, 0.637 of its peak. This dc term is the useful output of an unfiltered rectifier, and it is the part a moving-coil meter would respond to.

Answer: 6.37 V

(b)

Squaring a rectified sine gives the same square as the original sine, so the mean-square value is V_p²/2 = 50 V². The rms load voltage is √50 = 7.071 V. The average power in the 15 Ω resistor is P = V_rms²/R = 50/15 = 3.333 W. Parseval's theorem says the same total comes from summing the powers of all the Fourier components, which parts (c) and (e) use as a cross-check on the series coefficients. Do not use the dc value alone: a power calculation from 6.366 V gives only 2.70 W, which would understate the heating because the ripple also dissipates power in the resistor.

Answer: 3.33 W

(c)

The normalised (1 Ω) powers are: dc term (6.366)² = 40.53 V², and the 120 Hz harmonic of amplitude 4V_p/(3π) = 4.244 V contributes 4.244²/2 = 9.006 V², since a cosine of amplitude a has mean square a²/2. Their sum is 49.54 V². The total mean square is 50 V², so the fraction is 49.54/50 = 0.9907, or 99.1 percent. The remaining 0.46 V² is spread over 240 Hz and higher harmonics. Note that the powers of different harmonics add directly because sinusoids at different frequencies are orthogonal over a period, which is exactly the content of Parseval's theorem for a Fourier series.

Answer: 99.1 percent

(d)

The ac part has mean square equal to the total minus the dc part: 50 − 40.53 = 9.47 V², so its rms is √9.47 = 3.077 V. The ripple factor is 3.077/6.366 = 0.483. A value of 0.48 means the unsmoothed output has ripple nearly half as large as its dc level, which is unacceptable for most electronics and shows why a smoothing capacitor or an LC filter is needed. The result can also be written as √(V_rms²/V_dc² − 1) = √(1.2337 − 1) = 0.483, a handy cross-check on the ripple factor of a full-wave rectifier, which depends only on the waveform shape and not on V_p or R.

Answer: 0.483

(e)

The ac power (normalised) is 9.47 V². The 120 Hz harmonic holds 9.006 V² of it, so the fraction is 9.006/9.47 = 0.951, or 95.1 percent. Because nearly all the ripple sits at 120 Hz, a filter only needs to attenuate that one frequency strongly; the higher harmonics are already about twenty times smaller in power. A single-stage low-pass section with its corner well below 120 Hz would therefore remove almost all the ripple. The next harmonic at 240 Hz has amplitude 0.8488 V and carries only 0.36 V², about 3.8 percent of the ac power, which confirms that a filter designed around 120 Hz does most of the work.

Answer: 95.1 percent

Problem 4 [A3-084] LTI filtering of signals and frequency response

A strain-gauge amplifier output contains a wanted 1.0 kHz tone of amplitude 2.0 V and a switching-supply interference tone at 20 kHz of amplitude 1.0 V. A passive first-order RC low-pass filter is to be placed between the amplifier and a data logger. The filter is a series resistor R followed by a shunt capacitor C, with the output taken across C, so H(jω) = 1/(1 + jωRC) and the corner (−3 dB) frequency is f_c = 1/(2πRC). The specification limits the loss of the wanted tone to exactly 1.0 dB. Capacitors are available in the preferred value C = 47 nF. Decide the filter corner and judge whether the interference is suppressed enough for a logger that needs the interference below −20 dB relative to the wanted tone at its input.

  1. (a) Find the corner frequency f_c for which the 1 kHz tone is attenuated by exactly 1.0 dB. [5]
  2. (b) Find the attenuation, in dB, that this filter gives to the 20 kHz interference (give the magnitude as a positive number). [4]
  3. (c) Find the resistor R needed with C = 47 nF. [4]
  4. (d) Find the phase shift of the wanted tone at 1 kHz. [3]
  5. (e) Find the interference-to-signal ratio at the filter output, in dB, and decide whether the −20 dB requirement is met. [4]
(a)

The magnitude is |H| = 1/√(1 + (f/f_c)²). A 1.0 dB loss means |H| = 10−1/20 = 0.8913. Then (f/f_c)² = 1/0.8913² − 1 = 1.2589 − 1 = 0.2589, so f/f_c = 0.5088 and f_c = 1000/0.5088 = 1965 Hz. A larger corner would lose less of the wanted tone but would also reduce the suppression of the interference, so this is the highest-attenuation design that still meets the 1 dB limit. The same calculation can be done in decibels without a calculator for the square root by noting that a 1 dB loss at f/f_c = 0.509 is a standard first-order result, and that the 3 dB point is where f = f_c.

Answer: 1.97 kHz

(b)

At 20 kHz the ratio f/f_c is 20000/1965.2 = 10.18, so |H| = 1/√(1 + 103.6) = 1/10.23 = 0.0978. In decibels this is 20 log₁₀(0.0978) = −20.2 dB, so the interference is attenuated by 20.2 dB. A first-order section rolls off at 20 dB per decade well above the corner, and 20 kHz is a little more than one decade above 1.97 kHz, which agrees with the answer. Always quote the attenuation as a positive number of decibels when asked for attenuation, and as a negative gain if asked for the gain. Here the −20.2 dB gain is the same fact as a 20.2 dB attenuation.

Answer: 20.2 dB

(c)

With f_c = 1965.2 Hz and C = 47 nF the resistor follows from f_c = 1/(2πRC): R = 1/(2π × 1965.2 × 47×10⁻⁹) = 1/(5.803×10⁻⁴) = 1723 Ω. The nearest E96 value is 1.72 kΩ, which moves f_c by less than 0.2 percent. The amplifier output resistance and logger input resistance are assumed negligible against this R and C load, since otherwise they would shift the corner. Rounding the resistor to the standard value shifts the corner slightly, so the designer should recompute the 1 dB loss at 1 kHz with the actual parts. With 1.72 kΩ and 47 nF the corner becomes 1969 Hz.

Answer: 1.72 kΩ

(d)

The phase of H(jω) is −arctan(f/f_c) = −arctan(1000/1965.2) = −arctan(0.5088) = −27.0 degrees. The negative sign means the output lags the input. A lag of 27 degrees at 1 kHz corresponds to a time delay of (27.0/360) × 1 ms = 75 μs, which is harmless for a slowly varying strain signal but would matter in a control loop that shares the same sensor signal. Phase should be quoted with its sign. A pure delay of 75 μs would give the same phase at 1 kHz but a phase proportional to frequency at all frequencies, whereas the RC filter only approaches that delay at low frequencies.

Answer: −27.0 degrees

(e)

At the output the wanted tone is 2.0 × 0.8913 = 1.783 V and the interference is 1.0 × 0.0978 = 0.0978 V. Their ratio is 0.0978/1.783 = 0.0549, which is 20 log₁₀(0.0549) = −25.2 dB. The input ratio was 1/2, or −6 dB, so the filter improves it by 19.2 dB. The result of −25.2 dB is below −20 dB, so the specification is met with a 5.2 dB margin. Decibel ratios of signal amplitudes are 20 log₁₀ of the amplitude ratio. Subtracting the input ratio from the output ratio, −25.2 − (−6.0) = −19.2 dB, gives the extra rejection provided by the filter, which agrees with 20.2 − 1.0.

Answer: −25.2 dB

Problem 5 [A3-085] Sampling and the Nyquist theorem, aliasing

A condition-monitoring unit on a pump records a vibration signal that contains tones at 300 Hz, 1.1 kHz and 2.3 kHz. A first prototype samples the raw sensor voltage at f_s = 2.0 kHz with no anti-alias filter. A redesign will sample at f_s = 6.0 kHz and place a Butterworth low-pass anti-alias filter ahead of the converter. The band of interest is 0 to 1 kHz, so any interference that folds into that band after sampling is unwanted. The filter has its −3 dB corner at 1.0 kHz and a magnitude response |H(f)|² = 1/(1 + (f/1000)2n), where n is the filter order. The redesign must give at least 40 dB of attenuation at f_s − 1 kHz, the lowest frequency that would alias onto 1 kHz.

  1. (a) For the prototype with f_s = 2.0 kHz, find the apparent frequency in hertz of the 1.1 kHz tone after sampling. [3]
  2. (b) For the prototype, find the apparent frequency of the 2.3 kHz tone after sampling. [3]
  3. (c) Explain why the 2.3 kHz tone cannot be separated from the genuine 300 Hz tone in software. [3]
  4. (d) Find the minimum integer filter order n for the redesign. [5]
  5. (e) Find the attenuation in dB that the order found in part (d) gives at 5.0 kHz. [6]
(a)

A real tone at frequency f appears after sampling at the alias |f − k f_s| with the integer k chosen to place the result in 0 to f_s/2. With f_s = 2000 Hz the Nyquist frequency is 1000 Hz, and 1100 Hz lies above it. Taking k = 1 gives |1100 − 2000| = 900 Hz, which lies in the range 0 to 1000 Hz. The 1.1 kHz tone therefore shows up as a false 900 Hz component, which a technician might mistake for a real fault frequency.

Answer: 900 Hz

(b)

For 2300 Hz take k = 1: |2300 − 2000| = 300 Hz, which is below the Nyquist frequency of 1000 Hz. The tone therefore appears at exactly 300 Hz. Once samples are taken, the sample values at the instants t = m/f_s are identical in form for the real 300 Hz tone and the 2300 Hz tone, because 2300 − 300 = 2000 = f_s. No later processing can tell them apart, so the damage is permanent. The same fold-back rule gives the alias of any frequency: subtract the nearest integer multiple of the sampling rate. Here 2300 is closest to 2000, leaving a remainder of 300 Hz, which is inside the baseband.

Answer: 300 Hz

(c)

Sampling maps every frequency f + k f_s onto the same discrete-time frequency, so the sample sequences of a 300 Hz cosine and a 2300 Hz cosine are the same numbers, differing only in a phase and amplitude that add. The record contains one combined 300 Hz term whose size depends on the relative phase. Any software, however clever, receives only those numbers and has no information that distinguishes the sources. The only remedy is to remove the 2.3 kHz energy before sampling with an analogue filter, or to sample faster than 4.6 kHz.

Answer: Both tones appear at 300 Hz

(d)

The requirement is |H(5000)|² ≤ 10−4, since 40 dB is a power ratio of 10⁴. With f/f_c = 5 we need 1/(1 + 52n) ≤ 10⁻⁴, so 52n ≥ 9999. Taking logs, 2n ≥ ln(9999)/ln 5 = 9.210/1.609 = 5.723, so n ≥ 2.86. The order must be an integer, so n = 3. A second-order filter would give 10 log₁₀(1 + 5⁴) = 28.0 dB, which falls short of the 40 dB target. The Butterworth response is maximally flat, so the formula holds at all frequencies, and the 40 dB figure applies at the lowest frequency that could alias onto the 1 kHz band edge, f_s − 1000 = 5000 Hz.

Answer: n = 3

(e)

For n = 3 the attenuation at 5 kHz is A = 10 log₁₀(1 + (5000/1000)6) = 10 log₁₀(1 + 15625) = 10 log₁₀(15626) = 41.94 dB. This exceeds the 40 dB requirement by about 1.9 dB, so the design has a small margin. A fourth-order filter would give 56 dB but costs more components, extra phase shift and a longer settling time, so the third-order choice is the economical one. The −3 dB corner at 1 kHz also means the wanted band edge is attenuated by 3 dB, so the designer should choose a corner a little higher if the passband must be flat to 1 kHz, accepting the lower stopband rejection that follows.

Answer: 41.9 dB

A3 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A3-086] Reconstruction and quantization noise

A data acquisition board has a bipolar input range of ±2.5 V, so the converter span is 5.0 V, and it uses a uniform mid-tread quantizer with N bits. The input is a sine wave of amplitude 0.80 V (peak), which does not use the full range. Quantization error is assumed uniform over one step Δ and independent of the signal, so its rms value is Δ/√12. The first prototype uses N = 14 bits. The customer needs a signal to quantization noise ratio of at least 90 dB for this input level. Two alternatives are being compared: a converter with more bits, or oversampling with a 14-bit converter and an ideal digital low-pass filter (noise spread uniformly over the sampled bandwidth). The converter output is also reconstructed by a zero-order-hold DAC.

  1. (a) Find the rms quantization noise voltage for the 14-bit converter, in μV. [4]
  2. (b) Find the signal to quantization noise ratio in dB for the 0.80 V sine with N = 14. [4]
  3. (c) Find the smallest whole number of bits that reaches 90 dB for this input. [4]
  4. (d) Find the oversampling ratio needed to reach 90 dB with the 14-bit converter, using the white-noise assumption. [4]
  5. (e) The reconstruction DAC is a zero-order hold with response |sin(πf/f_s)/(πf/f_s)|. Find its droop in dB at f = 0.4 f_s. [4]
(a)

The step size is Δ = 5.0 V / 214 = 5.0/16384 = 3.052×10⁻⁴ V, which is 305 μV. The rms quantization noise is Δ/√12 = 305.2 μV / 3.464 = 88.1 μV. This noise is independent of the signal amplitude under the stated assumption, which is why a small signal on a large range suffers a worse signal to noise ratio. Quote the answer in microvolts as asked. The same figure can be found as 5 V divided by 214 and by 3.464, and the quantizer is assumed to be uniform, mid-tread and not overloaded by the 0.8 V peak signal.

Answer: 88.1 μV

(b)

The rms of a sine of peak 0.80 V is 0.80/√2 = 0.5657 V. The ratio is SQNR = 20 log₁₀(0.5657/88.1×10⁻⁶) = 20 log₁₀(6421) = 76.2 dB. A full-scale 2.5 V sine would give 6.02 × 14 + 1.76 = 86.0 dB, so using only 0.8 V of the 2.5 V peak range costs about 9.9 dB, which is 20 log₁₀(2.5/0.8). The result depends on the signal level, not just the number of bits. The familiar 6.02N + 1.76 dB formula applies only to a full-scale sine wave, which is 86.0 dB for 14 bits, so a lower signal level loses decibel for decibel.

Answer: 76.2 dB

(c)

Each extra bit halves Δ and adds 6.02 dB. Starting at 76.15 dB for N = 14, the gains are 82.17 dB at N = 15, 88.19 dB at N = 16 and 94.21 dB at N = 17. Since N = 16 gives 88.2 dB, below the 90 dB limit, and N = 17 gives 94.2 dB, the answer is 17 bits. This also leaves 4 dB of margin, useful because real converters lose some effective bits to thermal noise.

Answer: 17 bits

(d)

Oversampling by a factor M spreads the fixed quantization noise power over M times the bandwidth, and an ideal digital filter keeps only the signal band, so noise power falls by M and the SQNR rises by 10 log₁₀ M dB. The required gain is 90 − 76.15 = 13.85 dB, so M = 101.385 = 24.3. In practice M = 32 would be chosen as a power of two, which also gives margin. This simple scheme gains only about 3 dB per doubling, 0.5 bit, so noise shaping is much more efficient.

Answer: 24.3

(e)

The zero-order hold has response |H| = |sin(πx)/(πx)| with x = f/f_s. At x = 0.4, sin(0.4π) = 0.9511 and πx = 1.2566, so |H| = 0.7568. In decibels, 20 log₁₀(0.7568) = −2.42 dB. This droop at 0.4 f_s can be corrected by a digital pre-equalizer or an analogue inverse-sinc stage, otherwise high-frequency components in the signal band are reproduced too weakly. The droop is a deterministic loss of gain, not noise, and can be compensated exactly in the digital domain. The same formula at f = 0.5 f_s gives 3.92 dB, the usual limit that makes a 2 or 4 times oversampled DAC attractive.

Answer: −2.42 dB

Problem 2 [A3-087] Discrete-time systems and difference equations

A weigh-scale controller smooths its load-cell readings with a first-order recursive filter that obeys the difference equation y[n] = 0.90 y[n−1] + 0.10 x[n], where x[n] is the raw sample, y[n] is the filtered output and n counts samples. The filter is initially at rest, y[−1] = 0, and the sample rate is f_s = 100 Hz. A product is dropped on the scale at n = 0, so the input is a unit step x[n] = u[n], with a step height of 1 unit used for the working. The operator is asked whether the filter settles quickly enough for a packing line that allows about 1.5 s for a reading. The designer wants numbers for the final value, the transient and the noise bandwidth.

  1. (a) Find the final value of y[n] for a unit step input. [3]
  2. (b) Find y[5] for the unit step, using the closed-form step response. [4]
  3. (c) Find the time constant of the filter in samples, defined as the n for which the pole term 0.9n falls to e−1. [4]
  4. (d) Find the −3 dB frequency in hertz of the frequency response H(ejω) at f_s = 100 Hz. [5]
  5. (e) Find the smallest n for which y[n] is within 2 percent of the final value, and decide whether 1.5 s is enough. [4]
(a)

Taking the z-transform with zero initial state gives Y(z)(1 − 0.9z⁻¹) = 0.1 X(z), so H(z) = 0.1/(1 − 0.9z⁻¹). The dc gain is H(1) = 0.1/(1 − 0.9) = 1.0. For a unit step input the final value theorem confirms y[∞] = H(1) × 1 = 1.00. Because the pole at z = 0.9 lies inside the unit circle, the filter is stable and the output does settle. The final-value theorem applies because all poles of (z − 1)Y(z) lie inside the unit circle. Check it with the time-domain result y[n] = 1 − 0.9n+1, whose limit as n grows is 1, which also confirms there is no steady-state error in the weight reading.

Answer: 1.00

(b)

With a unit step, y[n] = 0.9 y[n−1] + 0.1. Iterating: y[0] = 0.1, y[1] = 0.19, y[2] = 0.271 and so on, which fits y[n] = 1 − 0.9n+1 for n ≥ 0. Then y[5] = 1 − 0.96 = 1 − 0.5314 = 0.4686. The output has reached less than half the final value after 6 samples, showing that the heavy smoothing (a pole near 1) comes at the cost of speed. Check the closed form against the recursion: y[1] = 0.9 × 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.19, and 1 − 0.9² = 0.19. The first sample y[0] = 0.1 is not zero because the 0.1 x[n] term acts immediately on the step.

Answer: 0.469

(c)

The transient is the pole term 0.9n = en ln 0.9. Setting the exponent to −1 gives n = −1/ln(0.9) = 1/0.10536 = 9.49 samples. At f_s = 100 Hz that corresponds to 94.9 ms. The result matches the usual rule that a pole at z = e−1/τ has time constant τ samples, with 0.9 ≈ e−0.105. A time constant in samples is converted to seconds by dividing by f_s, so at 100 Hz it is 0.0949 s. Settling to 2 percent takes about four time constants, which is consistent with the 38 samples found in part (e).

Answer: 9.49 samples

(d)

The frequency response is H(ejω) = 0.1/(1 − 0.9e−jω), so |H|² = 0.01/(1.81 − 1.8 cos ω). Setting |H|² = 0.5 (half power, since the dc gain is 1) gives 1.81 − 1.8 cos ω = 0.02, so cos ω = 1.79/1.8 = 0.99444 and ω = 0.10546 rad per sample. Then f = ω f_s/(2π) = 0.10546 × 100/6.2832 = 1.678 Hz. The filter passes only very slow weight changes. The −3 dB frequency is far below the 50 Hz Nyquist frequency, which is why the pole near z = 1 gives heavy smoothing. For small ω the formula reduces to ω ≈ (1 − 0.9)/0.9 = 0.111 rad, close to the exact 0.105.

Answer: 1.68 Hz

(e)

The step response is within 2 percent of 1 when 0.9n+1 ≤ 0.02, so (n + 1) ≥ ln(0.02)/ln(0.9) = (−3.912)/(−0.10536) = 37.13. Therefore n + 1 = 38 and n = 37, since n = 36 gives 0.937 = 0.0203 which is just above 0.02. The settling time is 38 samples at 10 ms, which is 0.38 s. That is well inside the 1.5 s allowed by the packing line, so the filter is fast enough. The packing line needs the filter to be settled within 1.5 s, which is 150 samples at 100 Hz. The 38 samples needed leave a factor of about four of safety, so the pole could even be moved to 0.95 for extra noise reduction.

Answer: n = 37

Problem 3 [A3-088] The Z-transform and region of convergence

A digital resonator in a motor controller has transfer function H(z) = z/((z − 0.6)(z + 0.8)), with the input and output both sampled signals. The designer is told that the same algebraic H(z) can describe three different systems depending on the region of convergence (ROC) chosen, and must decide which one is physically usable. The usable system must be causal, meaning the output depends only on present and past inputs, and bounded-input bounded-output stable. The impulse response h[n] is the inverse z-transform of H(z), and the unit circle is |z| = 1. Do the working with partial fractions on H(z)/z, and keep four significant figures. The following parts check poles, response, gain and the ROC choice.

  1. (a) State the largest pole magnitude of H(z). [3]
  2. (b) Find the impulse response sample h[3] for the causal ROC. [5]
  3. (c) Find the dc gain, that is H(z) evaluated at z = 1. [4]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the gain at the Nyquist frequency, z = −1. [4]
  5. (e) Explain which of the three possible ROCs gives a causal and stable system, and why the others do not. [4]
(a)

The poles are the roots of the denominator: z = 0.6 and z = −0.8. Their magnitudes are 0.6 and 0.8, so the largest is 0.8. For a causal system the ROC lies outside the outermost pole, so the causal ROC is |z| > 0.8. Since 0.8 < 1, the unit circle lies inside that ROC, which is the stability test for a causal system. The zero at z = 0 does not affect stability and is not a pole. A marker looks for both poles being found and compared with the unit circle, since the largest magnitude decides the stability of a causal system.

Answer: 0.8

(b)

Write H(z)/z = 1/((z − 0.6)(z + 0.8)) = A/(z − 0.6) + B/(z + 0.8). Then A = 1/(0.6 + 0.8) = 0.7143 and B = 1/(−0.8 − 0.6) = −0.7143. Hence H(z) = 0.7143[z/(z − 0.6) − z/(z + 0.8)], and for the causal ROC h[n] = 0.7143[0.6n − (−0.8)n] u[n]. At n = 3, 0.6³ = 0.216 and (−0.8)³ = −0.512, so h[3] = 0.7143 × 0.728 = 0.52. The recursion h[n] = −0.2h[n−1] + 0.48h[n−2] gives the same: h[3] = −0.2(−0.2) + 0.48(1) = 0.52.

Answer: 0.52

(c)

Set z = 1 in the transfer function: H(1) = 1/((1 − 0.6)(1 + 0.8)) = 1/(0.4 × 1.8) = 1/0.72 = 1.389. This is only valid because z = 1 lies inside the ROC |z| > 0.8, so the dc gain exists and equals the sum of all impulse response samples. A unit step input would therefore settle to 1.389. The dc gain exceeds 1 because the pole at 0.6 gives positive gain at dc while the pole at −0.8 reduces its contribution. Always check that z = 1 is inside the ROC before evaluating, otherwise the sum of h[n] does not converge.

Answer: 1.389

(d)

The Nyquist frequency corresponds to z = ejπ = −1. Then H(−1) = (−1)/((−1 − 0.6)(−1 + 0.8)) = (−1)/((−1.6)(−0.2)) = −1/0.32 = −3.125. The magnitude is 3.125, about 9.9 dB, so this resonator strongly amplifies components at half the sampling rate, a sign of the pole at −0.8 close to the unit circle at z = −1. The large gain at z = −1 is the visible effect of a pole near −1, which acts as a resonance at the Nyquist frequency. If this is unwanted the designer would move the pole closer to the origin or add a zero at z = −1.

Answer: 3.125

(e)

Three ROCs are possible because the poles split the plane into |z| < 0.6, 0.6 < |z| < 0.8 and |z| > 0.8. The outer ROC |z| > 0.8 is causal and includes the unit circle, so it is stable. The inner ROC |z| < 0.6 gives a purely left-sided (anticausal) response, so it is not causal, and it excludes the unit circle, so the frequency response does not exist. The middle annulus gives a two-sided response that also excludes the unit circle, because the pole at 0.8 would then be treated as left-sided while 0.6 is right-sided, and a real-time controller cannot implement it. Only |z| > 0.8 gives both properties.

Answer: |z| > 0.8

Problem 4 [A3-089] Inverse Z-transform and system response

A digital smoothing stage in a sensor node has transfer function H(z) = (1 + z⁻¹)/(1 − 0.5z⁻¹) and is initially at rest. A calibration routine injects the decaying test sequence x[n] = (0.25)n u[n], so x[0] = 1, x[1] = 0.25, and so on, and records the output y[n]. The technician must predict the response without running the filter, check that the output dies away quickly enough for the next calibration pulse, and compare it with the response to a constant input. Use partial fractions in powers of z⁻¹ to invert Y(z) = H(z)X(z), and check the first two samples against the difference equation y[n] = 0.5y[n−1] + x[n] + x[n−1] before trusting the closed form.

  1. (a) Find the partial fraction coefficient A of the pole at z = 0.5 in Y(z) = A/(1 − 0.5z⁻¹) + B/(1 − 0.25z⁻¹). [4]
  2. (b) Find y[4] from the closed-form inverse transform. [4]
  3. (c) Find the sum of all output samples, the sum over n from 0 to infinity of y[n]. [4]
  4. (d) Find the smallest n for which y[n] < 0.01, to decide how many samples to wait before the next pulse. [4]
  5. (e) Find the steady-state output for a constant input of 1 unit, using H(1). [4]
(a)

Multiply out: Y(z) = (1 + z⁻¹)/((1 − 0.5z⁻¹)(1 − 0.25z⁻¹)). The coefficient of the 0.5 pole is found by evaluating (1 + z⁻¹)/(1 − 0.25z⁻¹) at z⁻¹ = 1/0.5 = 2: the numerator is 1 + 2 = 3 and the denominator is 1 − 0.5 = 0.5, so A = 3/0.5 = 6. For the second pole at z⁻¹ = 4 the numerator is 5 and the other factor is 1 − 2 = −1, giving B = −5. Check at n = 0: A + B = 1, matching y[0] = x[0] = 1.

Answer: A = 6

(b)

The inverse transform of each fraction is a causal geometric sequence, so y[n] = 6(0.5)n − 5(0.25)n for n ≥ 0. First verify with the difference equation: y[0] = 1 and y[1] = 0.5(1) + 0.25 + 1 = 1.75, and the formula gives 3 − 1.25 = 1.75, so the inversion is correct. At n = 4, 6/16 = 0.375 and 5/256 = 0.01953, so y[4] = 0.375 − 0.01953 = 0.3555. A common mistake is to forget that the 0.25 term is subtracted with a factor of 5, not 1. Always test the first two samples against the recursion before trusting the closed form, as the problem statement advised.

Answer: 0.3555

(c)

The sum of a sequence equals its z-transform evaluated at z = 1, provided the unit circle lies in the ROC. Here the ROC is |z| > 0.5, which includes z = 1. Then Y(1) = (1 + 1)/((1 − 0.5)(1 − 0.25)) = 2/(0.5 × 0.75) = 2/0.375 = 5.333. As a check, summing the closed form gives 6/(1 − 0.5) − 5/(1 − 0.25) = 12 − 6.667 = 5.333, in agreement. The sum is also the dc component of the response to a unit impulse train of long period, and it is bounded here because both poles lie inside the unit circle. It is larger than the input sum 1/(1 − 0.25) = 1.333 by the dc gain of 4.

Answer: 5.333

(d)

The 0.5n term decays more slowly than 0.25n, so it dominates later. Tabulating y[n] = 6(0.5)n − 5(0.25)n: y[8] = 0.02344 − 0.00008 = 0.02336, y[9] = 0.01172 − 0.00002 = 0.01170, and y[10] = 0.005859 − 0.000005 = 0.005854. The output first drops below 0.01 at n = 10, since y[9] = 0.0117 is still above the limit. The technician should wait at least 11 samples, including n = 0, before the next pulse. The test is on the sampled values, so no interpolation is needed. A quicker estimate uses only the slow term: 6(0.5)n < 0.01 gives n > 9.2, so n = 10, in agreement with the table of values.

Answer: n = 10

(e)

For a constant (dc) input the steady-state output equals H(1) times the input, because z = 1 lies in the ROC and the pole at 0.5 is inside the unit circle. H(1) = (1 + 1)/(1 − 0.5) = 2/0.5 = 4.0. The filter therefore has a dc gain of 4, so a constant 1 unit input settles to an output of 4.0 units, four times the input, which could saturate a converter with small headroom. The filter has a zero at z = −1, so it blocks components at the Nyquist frequency, but its dc gain is high. A designer wanting unity dc gain would scale the numerator by 0.25, which gives (1 + z⁻¹)/4 as the numerator.

Answer: 4.0

Problem 5 [A3-090] Discrete-time frequency response and stability

A resonant digital notch-sensing filter in an audio test set has transfer function H(z) = 1/(1 − 1.2z⁻¹ + 0.72z⁻²) and runs at a sampling rate of 8.0 kHz. The designer is concerned about sensitivity to coefficient rounding in a fixed-point processor. A second version of the filter changes only the last coefficient, giving H₂(z) = 1/(1 − 1.2z⁻¹ + 1.05z⁻²). The poles of a second-order section with denominator 1 + a₁z⁻¹ + a₂z⁻² are the roots of z² + a₁z + a₂. Use the pole radius and angle to judge stability, resonance and growth, and evaluate the frequency response on the unit circle where needed.

  1. (a) Find the pole radius of the original filter H(z). [4]
  2. (b) Find the resonant frequency in hertz implied by the pole angle. [4]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude |H(ejω)| at the pole angle ω = π/4 rad per sample. [5]
  4. (d) Find the pole radius of the second version H₂(z) and state, with a reason, whether it is stable. [4]
  5. (e) If an impulse is applied to the second filter, find the number of samples over which the envelope of the response doubles. [3]
(a)

The denominator is z² − 1.2z + 0.72. Its roots are z = [1.2 ± √(1.44 − 2.88)]/2 = 0.6 ± j0.6. The magnitude of each pole is √(0.6² + 0.6²) = √0.72 = 0.8485, which is also √a₂ for a complex pair. The radius is below 1, so both poles are inside the unit circle and the causal filter is stable. The margin to the unit circle is 0.151. The radius for a complex pair equals the square root of the constant coefficient, so a₂ = 0.72 gives 0.8485. This shortcut avoids computing the roots, and it shows how a₂ alone controls the distance of both poles from the origin.

Answer: 0.8485

(b)

The pole angle is arctan(0.6/0.6) = 45 degrees = π/4 rad per sample. A discrete frequency ω corresponds to f = ω f_s/(2π) = (π/4)(8000)/(2π) = 1000 Hz. The magnitude response peaks close to this frequency, so the filter resonates at about 1.0 kHz; the exact peak is slightly shifted because the poles are not on the unit circle and because of the conjugate partner. Because the radius is 0.85 the response peak is lower and broader than for a pole on the circle. The sampling rate of 8 kHz sets the scale, and the pole angle of 45 degrees is one eighth of the full circle.

Answer: 1000 Hz

(c)

Evaluate the denominator at ω = π/4 with e−jω = 0.7071 − j0.7071 and e−j2ω = −j. Then D = 1 − 1.2(0.7071 − j0.7071) + 0.72(−j) = 1 − 0.8485 + j0.8485 − j0.72 = 0.1515 + j0.1285. Its magnitude is √(0.1515² + 0.1285²) = √(0.02295 + 0.01651) = 0.1987, so |H| = 1/0.1987 = 5.03. The gain is about 14 dB at resonance, compared with a dc gain of 1/(1 − 1.2 + 0.72) = 1.92. The magnitude at resonance is far larger than at dc, which shows the filter is selective. Any rounding of the coefficients changes the denominator at ω = π/4 directly, so the gain here is sensitive to fixed-point word length.

Answer: 5.03

(d)

For the second filter the poles satisfy z² − 1.2z + 1.05 = 0, so the radius is √1.05 = 1.0247 for the complex conjugate pair, since the product of the roots is 1.05. A radius above 1 places the poles outside the unit circle, so the causal filter is unstable. The impulse response grows without bound, as 1.0247n times a sinusoid. A change of the coefficient a₂ from 0.72 to 1.05 shows how little margin a second-order section has: stability requires a₂ < 1.

Answer: 1.0247, unstable

(e)

The envelope of the impulse response grows by the pole radius each sample, rn = 1.0247n. It doubles when n ln(1.0247) = ln 2, so n = 0.6931/0.02440 = 28.4 samples. At 8 kHz this is 3.55 ms, so the output would saturate within a few milliseconds of any disturbance. The fixed-point design must therefore keep a₂ comfortably below 1 after rounding. The doubling time depends only on the pole radius, so it is independent of the pole angle. A radius only 2.5 percent above 1 already makes the output double in 28 samples, which is why stability margins matter in recursive filters.

Answer: 28.4 samples

A3 Practice Paper 19

Problem 1 [A3-091] AM modulation and demodulation, bandwidth and efficiency

A regional medium-wave broadcaster operates a double-sideband large-carrier AM transmitter into a matched antenna load. With no modulation the carrier power is 25 kW. During commissioning a single 5 kHz test tone is applied and the modulation index is set to 0.8. In normal service the programme is compressed speech, which may be modelled as a message m(t) with peak magnitude 1 and mean-square value 0.1. The modulator has amplitude sensitivity ka = 0.9, so the envelope is Ac[1 + ka m(t)]. The station engineer must judge how much of the transmitted power actually carries programme, and what carrier power is needed if the sideband power in normal service must reach 5 kW.

  1. (a) Find the total transmitted power during the 0.8 tone test, in kilowatts. [3]
  2. (b) Find the transmission efficiency (fraction of total power in the sidebands) for the tone test, as a percentage. [4]
