Hardware then stacks the context and fetches the vector, taking 12 cycles. The interrupt service routine (ISR) for a sensor sampling every 200 microseconds executes 150 cycles of code and returns in 10 cycles. A higher-priority communications interrupt occurs less often, but one occurrence in the worst case takes 300 cycles in total, including its own entry and exit. Assume the sensor ISR is not interrupted by anything except that one occurrence of the communications interrupt, and that interrupts are otherwise always enabled.

  1. (a) Find the worst-case interrupt latency, from request to the first ISR instruction, in microseconds. [4]
  2. (b) Find the time for the sensor ISR body plus return, in microseconds. [4]
  3. (c) Find the percentage of CPU time consumed by the sensor interrupt, counting entry, body and return. [5]
  4. (d) Find the worst-case time from the sensor request to completion of its return when one communications interrupt strikes just before the sensor ISR would start. [7]
(a)

Latency is the sum of the time to finish the instruction in progress and the hardware entry sequence. Worst case = 12 + 12 = 24 cycles. At 48 MHz one cycle lasts 1 ÷ 48 × 106 s = 20.83 ns. Latency = 24 × 20.83 ns = 500 ns = 0.5 µs. This is the worst case, because the long instruction began just before the request arrived. The best case would be only the 12-cycle entry. Real-time deadlines must be met against this worst value, not against the average latency.

Answer: 0.5 µs

(b)

The ISR body takes 150 cycles and the return sequence takes 10 cycles, a total of 160 cycles. Converting at 20.83 ns per cycle, 160 × 20.83 ns = 3333 ns = 3.333 µs. This is the time the sensor handler spends running once it has started. It must be much shorter than the 200 µs sampling period, which it is, so the sensor interrupt cannot fall behind by itself. The figure excludes the latency of part (a), which is the time spent before the handler begins.

Answer: 3.333 µs

(c)

Each sensor interrupt costs the entry 12 cycles, the body 150 cycles and the return 10 cycles, a total of 172 cycles. The sampling period is 200 µs, a rate of 5 kHz. Cycles used per second = 5000 × 172 = 860 000. The CPU supplies 48 × 106 cycles each second. Utilisation = 860 000 ÷ 48 000 000 = 0.017917, which is 1.792 percent. The instruction-in-progress wait is not counted, since it is part of other code that still runs. The remaining 98.2 percent is available to the main program and other interrupts.

Answer: 1.792 %

(d)

The worst case adds the delays in order. First the current instruction finishes, 12 cycles. The communications interrupt, which has higher priority, has already begun and takes its full 300 cycles. Then the sensor interrupt is serviced: entry 12, body 150 and return 10 cycles. Total = 12 + 300 + 12 + 150 + 10 = 484 cycles. Time = 484 × 20.83 ns = 10 083 ns = 10.083 µs. This is only about 5 percent of the 200 µs period, so the schedule is safe, but the figure shows why a long higher-priority ISR directly enlarges the worst-case latency of lower-priority work.

Answer: 10.083 µs

Problem 2 [A4-097] Serial and parallel interfacing (UART, SPI, I2C)

A battery-powered environmental sensor node in northern Ontario uses three serial links. A UART link to a radio runs at 115 200 baud with 8 data bits, no parity, 1 start bit and 1 stop bit. An SPI link at an 8 MHz clock reads a 16-bit sample from an ADC: the master sends one command byte then clocks in two data bytes, so each read takes 24 clock cycles, and the chip-select setup and hold add 1.0 µs per transaction. An I2C bus runs at 400 kHz; a register read transaction sends one address byte and receives two data bytes. Each byte takes 9 bit times including its acknowledge, and the start and stop conditions together add 2 bit times. The I2C bus capacitance is 100 pF and the specification limits the rise time (30 to 70 percent of supply) to 300 ns.

  1. (a) Find the time to send a 64-byte packet over the UART, in milliseconds. [5]
  2. (b) Find the maximum SPI sample rate, in samples per second, if samples are read back to back. [5]
  3. (c) Find the duration of one I2C read transaction, in microseconds. [5]
  4. (d) The 30 to 70 percent rise time of an RC pull-up is 0.8473 RC. Find the largest pull-up resistance, in ohms, that meets the rise-time limit. [5]
(a)

Each UART frame carries 8 data bits plus 1 start bit and 1 stop bit, so 10 bits per byte of payload. At 115 200 baud the bit time is 1 ÷ 115 200 = 8.68 µs. The packet of 64 bytes needs 64 × 10 = 640 bit times. Time = 640 ÷ 115 200 = 5.556 ms. The effective data rate is 11 520 bytes per second, which is 80 percent of the baud rate because of the framing overhead. Any gaps the radio inserts between bytes would add to this figure, but none are assumed.

Answer: 5.556 ms

(b)

One SPI read uses 24 clock cycles at 8 MHz, each lasting 125 ns, so the data phase takes 24 × 125 ns = 3.0 µs. The chip-select setup and hold overhead adds 1.0 µs, giving 4.0 µs per sample. Back-to-back reads therefore give a rate of 1 ÷ 4.0 µs = 250 000 samples per second. The SPI clock alone would allow 8 × 106 ÷ 24 = 333 333 samples per second, so the select overhead costs 25 percent of the throughput. The ADC conversion time is assumed hidden or shorter than this interval.

Answer: 250 000 samples/s

(c)

Count the bit times on the bus. The address byte and the two data bytes are three bytes, each with its acknowledge: 3 × 9 = 27 bit times. The start and stop conditions add 2 bit times, for a total of 29 bit times. At 400 kHz one bit time is 2.5 µs, so the transaction lasts 29 × 2.5 µs = 72.5 µs. This is about 18 times longer than the SPI read for the same two bytes, which is the cost of the addressing, acknowledgement and open-drain signalling that I2C provides in exchange for needing only two wires shared by many devices.

Answer: 72.5 µs

(d)

The pull-up resistor charges the bus capacitance, so the 30 to 70 percent rise time is t = 0.8473 R C. The limit is 300 ns with C = 100 pF. Solve for R: R = t ÷ (0.8473 C) = 300 × 10-9 ÷ (0.8473 × 100 × 10-12) = 300 × 10-9 ÷ 84.73 × 10-12 = 3541 Ω. Any resistor at or below about 3.5 kΩ meets the timing. A lower value gives a faster edge but draws more current when the line is held low, which matters on a battery-powered node, so the largest allowed value is normally chosen.

Answer: 3541 Ω

Problem 3 [A4-098] Memory-mapped I/O, timers and DMA

A data logger for a wastewater plant uses a 24 MHz microcontroller. Its ADC is read through a memory-mapped data register. A general-purpose timer is driven by the 24 MHz clock through a prescaler that divides by 24; the timer counts from 0 up to an auto-reload value ARR and then returns to 0, so its period is (ARR + 1) timer clocks. The timer must generate an update event at 2 kHz, which triggers one ADC conversion. In a first design every conversion raises an interrupt whose handler takes 240 CPU cycles. In a second design a DMA controller moves each result into a buffer of 256 samples; each DMA transfer steals 4 bus cycles, and after every full buffer one interrupt handler of 300 CPU cycles runs.

  1. (a) Find the ARR value that gives the 2 kHz update rate. [5]
  2. (b) Find the CPU load of the interrupt-per-sample design, as a percentage. [4]
  3. (c) Find the CPU load of the DMA design, as a percentage. [5]
  4. (d) Find the factor by which DMA reduces the CPU load, and then the percentage of bus cycles the DMA transfers steal. [6]
(a)

The prescaler divides 24 MHz by 24, so the timer clock is 1 MHz, a tick every 1 µs. For a 2 kHz update the period is 1 ÷ 2000 = 500 µs, which is 500 timer ticks. Because the counter counts 0 to ARR inclusive, the period is ARR + 1 ticks. Setting ARR + 1 = 500 gives ARR = 499. If ARR were set to 500 the period would be 501 ticks, a rate of 1.996 kHz, a small but real error that would show up as a timing drift in the sampled signal.

Answer: 499

(b)

Each conversion produces one interrupt with a handler of 240 cycles. At 2000 interrupts per second the CPU spends 2000 × 240 = 480 000 cycles per second. The CPU provides 24 × 106 cycles per second. Load = 480 000 ÷ 24 000 000 = 0.02, which is 2.0 percent. This ignores the entry and exit costs unless they are included in the 240 cycles, which is the stated assumption. The load is small, but each interrupt also adds latency jitter to the main program and disturbs its cache and pipeline state.

Answer: 2.0 %

(c)

With DMA the CPU is interrupted only after each full buffer of 256 samples. The buffer interrupt rate is 2000 ÷ 256 = 7.8125 per second. Each handler uses 300 cycles, so the CPU uses 7.8125 × 300 = 2343.75 cycles per second. Load = 2343.75 ÷ 24 000 000 = 9.766 × 10-5, which is 0.009766 percent. The DMA controller itself does the memory-mapped data register read and the buffer write without executing CPU instructions. The only costs are the handler and the bus cycles that DMA steals, treated in part (d).

Answer: 0.009766 %

(d)

The reduction factor is the ratio of the loads: 2.0 ÷ 0.009766 = 204.8, which equals 480 000 ÷ 2343.75. The DMA also uses the bus. Each transfer steals 4 cycles, so per second 2000 × 4 = 8000 cycles are taken, which is 8000 ÷ 24 × 106 = 0.0333 percent of bus time. This is far less than the CPU saved, so DMA is clearly beneficial here, though the CPU must wait during a stolen cycle if it needs the bus at the same moment.

Answer: 204.8 times

Problem 4 [A4-099] Instruction set and assembly-level reasoning

A teaching processor has 32-bit words and a load-store instruction set with registers r0 to r15, where r0 always reads as 0. LW rd,off(rs) loads the word at address rs + off. ADD rd,rs,rt adds registers. ADDI rd,rs,imm adds a signed immediate. BNE rs,rt,label branches to label if rs is not equal to rt. Addresses are in bytes, and one word is 4 bytes. At the start r1 = 0x2000, r2 = 6, r3 = 0, and the six words stored from address 0x2000 are 5, -3, 12, 7, -8, 20. The loop is: loop: LW r4,0(r1); ADD r3,r3,r4; ADDI r1,r1,4; ADDI r2,r2,-1; BNE r2,r0,loop. The processor runs at 100 MHz without pipelining and takes 5 cycles for a load, 4 cycles for ADD or ADDI and 3 cycles for a branch.

  1. (a) Find the value left in r3 when the loop ends. [5]
  2. (b) Find the number of instructions executed by the loop. [4]
  3. (c) Find the execution time of the loop in microseconds. [5]
  4. (d) The loop is unrolled by 3: the body holds three loads at offsets 0, 4 and 8, three ADDs, one ADDI r1,r1,12, one ADDI r2,r2,-3 and one BNE, run for 2 passes. Find the percentage reduction in cycles. [6]
(a)

The loop adds each word to the running total r3, stepping r1 by 4 bytes per pass and counting r2 down from 6. The six words are summed in order: 5 + (-3) = 2, then 2 + 12 = 14, then 14 + 7 = 21, then 21 + (-8) = 13, then 13 + 20 = 33. After the sixth pass r2 reaches 0, so BNE r2,r0 falls through and the loop ends. Final r3 = 33. At the end r1 = 0x2000 + 6 × 4 = 0x2018, which points just past the array.

Answer: 33

(b)

The loop body contains five instructions: LW, ADD, ADDI r1, ADDI r2 and BNE. The counter r2 starts at 6 and the branch is taken while r2 is not zero, so the body runs exactly 6 times; on the last pass the branch is not taken but is still executed. Instructions executed = 5 × 6 = 30. The setup that loaded r1, r2 and r3 before the loop is not counted. A smaller body would reduce this number, which is the idea behind loop unrolling in part (d).

Answer: 30

(c)

Cycles per pass = LW 5 + ADD 4 + ADDI 4 + ADDI 4 + BNE 3 = 20 cycles. For 6 passes the total is 6 × 20 = 120 cycles. At 100 MHz one cycle takes 10 ns, so the loop time is 120 × 10 ns = 1200 ns = 1.2 µs. We assume the branch costs 3 cycles whether or not it is taken and that no instruction fetch stalls occur. Execution of a different instruction mix would change the cycle count but the method of summing cycle counts remains the same.

Answer: 1.2 µs

(d)

One unrolled pass has 3 loads, 3 ADDs, 2 ADDIs and 1 BNE. Cycles = 3 × 5 + 3 × 4 + 2 × 4 + 3 = 15 + 12 + 8 + 3 = 38 cycles. With 6 elements and 3 per pass, 2 passes are needed, so total = 76 cycles. The original used 120 cycles. Reduction = (120 − 76) ÷ 120 = 0.3667, that is 36.67 percent. The saving comes from removing eight ADDI instructions and four branches (8 × 4 + 4 × 3 = 44 cycles). The price is a larger code size and the requirement that the element count be a multiple of 3, otherwise clean-up code is needed.

Answer: 36.67 %

Problem 5 [A4-100] System design trade-offs combining CPU, memory and I/O

An Ontario smart-meter gateway uses a 100 MHz processor with an average CPI of 1.3. Three tasks run. A sampling interrupt fires 7680 times per second (128 samples per 60 Hz cycle) and executes 1400 instructions each time. A communications task executes 2 000 000 instructions every second. A logging task executes 60 000 000 instructions every 10 seconds. The sample buffer holds 6 channels of 16-bit samples for 128 samples per cycle and keeps 12 cycles in a ring buffer. A log record of 48 bytes is written every 10 seconds into a circular log that occupies a single 4096-byte erase sector of flash, rated for 100 000 erase cycles for that sector. A day is 86 400 seconds and a year is 365 days. Designers want the CPU load not to exceed 70 percent.

  1. (a) Find the CPU load at 100 MHz, as a percentage. [5]
  2. (b) Find the size of the sample ring buffer in bytes. [4]
  3. (c) Find the flash lifetime in years, assuming the log area is erased evenly sector by sector and exactly one sector worth of data is written per erase. [5]
  4. (d) Find the lowest clock frequency, in megahertz, that keeps the CPU load at or below 70 percent. [6]
(a)

Instructions per second from each task: sampling 7680 × 1400 = 10 752 000; communications 2 000 000; logging 60 000 000 ÷ 10 = 6 000 000. The total is 18 752 000 instructions per second. Multiplying by CPI 1.3 gives 24 377 600 cycles per second. The processor supplies 100 × 106 cycles per second, so the load = 24 377 600 ÷ 100 000 000 = 0.2438, which is 24.38 percent. Most of the load comes from the sampling interrupt at 57 percent of the total, so it is the task to optimise first.

Answer: 24.38 %

(b)

Each sample is 16 bits = 2 bytes and there are 6 channels, so one sample instant needs 12 bytes. One 60 Hz cycle holds 128 sample instants, which is 128 × 12 = 1536 bytes. The ring buffer keeps 12 cycles, so the size is 12 × 1536 = 18 432 bytes, exactly 18 KiB. This memory must be fast and is best placed in on-chip SRAM, as the sampling interrupt writes it at 7680 times per second and the communications and logging tasks read from it.

Answer: 18 432 bytes

(c)

Log data written per day = (86 400 ÷ 10) records × 48 bytes = 8640 × 48 = 414 720 bytes. With 4096-byte sectors this fills 414 720 ÷ 4096 = 101.25 sector-erases per day when wear is spread evenly. Each sector survives 100 000 erases, and each sector in the area is erased once per pass, so the area lasts 100 000 ÷ 101.25 = 987.65 days. In years this is 987.65 ÷ 365 = 2.706 years. A larger log area or wear-levelling over more sectors would extend the life in proportion to the number of sectors, since the day count is fixed.

Answer: 2.706 years

(d)

Cycles needed per second are fixed at 24 377 600, independent of the clock. Load = cycles per second ÷ clock frequency. To keep load ≤ 0.70 the clock must satisfy f ≥ 24 377 600 ÷ 0.70 = 34 825 143 Hz, which is 34.83 MHz. A real design would choose the next standard oscillator or divider setting above this, and keep a margin for interrupt latency and bursts. Running slower saves power, since dynamic power falls roughly with frequency and with voltage, but the 70 percent ceiling leaves little spare capacity for added features.

Answer: 34.83 MHz

Exam A5: Electronics

A5 Practice Paper 1

Problem 1 [A5-001] Diode circuits, clippers and rectifiers

A small bench supply for a sensor board in an Ontario laboratory is fed from a 120 V rms, 60 Hz outlet through a 10:1 step-down transformer, so the secondary open-circuit voltage is 12 V rms. The secondary drives a single silicon diode in series with a load resistor R = 220 Ω. A capacitor C = 2200 μF is connected directly across the load, from the diode cathode to the secondary return, to smooth the output. Model the diode as an ideal diode in series with a constant 0.70 V forward drop, and neglect the transformer winding resistance. The capacitor is large enough that the load voltage ripple can be treated as a linear discharge at constant load current between charging peaks.

  1. (a) Find the peak load voltage. [4]
  2. (b) Find the peak-to-peak ripple voltage, assuming the capacitor discharges at constant current for a full period T = 1/60 s. [6]
  3. (c) Find the average load current, taking the average load voltage as the peak value minus half the ripple. [5]
  4. (d) Find the peak inverse voltage that the diode must withstand, and state in one sentence why the filter capacitor makes it larger than for a resistive load with no capacitor. [5]
(a)

The secondary peak voltage is the rms value times √2, so Vs,pk = 12 × √2 = 16.97 V. The capacitor charges through the diode at the instant the secondary reaches its positive peak, so the diode conducts and drops 0.70 V. The assumption is that the constant-drop model holds at the peak, where the current is highest, and that the transformer is ideal with no regulation. Then the peak load voltage is Vo,pk = Vs,pk − VD = 16.97 − 0.70 = 16.27 V. This is the voltage to which the capacitor is charged each cycle and it is the maximum value of the load voltage waveform. The marker looks for the use of the peak value, not the rms value, and for the subtraction of the diode drop.

Answer: 16.27 V

(b)

For a half-wave rectifier the capacitor discharges for nearly one whole period, because it is recharged only once per cycle. Assume constant discharge current equal to the peak load current, Io ≈ Vo,pk/R = 16.27/220 = 73.95 mA. The ripple is the charge lost over one period divided by capacitance, Vr = Io T/C = Io/(f C). Substituting, Vr = 0.07395/(60 × 2200×10⁻⁶) = 0.07395/0.132 = 0.560 V. This equals Vo,pk/(f R C) = 16.27/(60 × 220 × 0.0022) = 16.27/29.04 = 0.560 V, which confirms the result. The ripple is about 3.4 percent of the peak, small enough that the constant-current assumption is reasonable and the answer can be quoted to three figures.

Answer: 0.560 V

(c)

The average output voltage of a ripple waveform that falls linearly from the peak is approximately the peak minus half the peak-to-peak ripple, so Vo,avg = 16.27 − 0.560/2 = 16.27 − 0.280 = 15.99 V. The average load current then follows from Ohm's law applied to the average voltage, Io,avg = Vo,avg/R = 15.99/220 = 0.07268 A, which is 72.7 mA. This is slightly below the peak load current of 73.95 mA found in part (b), as it must be. Because the same current flows through the diode only during short charging pulses, the diode current while conducting is much larger than this average, which is the point examined in part (d).

Answer: 72.7 mA

(d)

When the secondary is at its negative peak the diode cathode is held near the capacitor voltage, which is close to +Vo,pk because the capacitor barely discharges. The reverse voltage across the diode is therefore the secondary negative peak plus the capacitor voltage: PIV = Vs,pk + Vo,pk = 16.97 + 16.27 = 33.24 V. Without the capacitor the cathode would sit near zero when the diode is off, so the PIV would only be Vs,pk = 16.97 V. The capacitor stores the positive peak and adds it to the reversed secondary voltage, which nearly doubles the stress. A diode rated at 50 V or more would be selected with margin for line surges.

Answer: 33.2 V

Problem 2 [A5-002] Zener regulators and power supply filtering

A 9 V reference rail for an instrumentation amplifier is made from an unregulated supply that varies between 21 V and 27 V, using a series resistor Rs and a Zener diode in shunt with the load. The Zener is modelled as a voltage source Vz0 = 8.90 V in series with a dynamic resistance rz = 5.0 Ω, valid for any Zener current at or above 5.0 mA, which is the minimum current needed to stay in regulation. The load draws a current IL that varies from 10 mA to 60 mA. Treat the unregulated input as an ideal voltage source of the stated value, and ignore temperature effects. Rs is first designed for the worst case and then a standard value of 180 Ω is fitted for the remaining parts.

  1. (a) Find the largest value of Rs that keeps the Zener at or above 5.0 mA under the worst case. [5]
  2. (b) With Rs = 180 Ω, find the Zener power dissipation at the other extreme, Vin = 27 V and IL = 10 mA. [5]
  3. (c) Find the change in output voltage caused by the full 6 V swing of the input, with the load current held constant. [5]
  4. (d) Find the change in output voltage when the load current steps from 10 mA to 60 mA at a fixed input voltage. [5]
(a)

The worst case for keeping the Zener in regulation is the lowest input voltage, 21 V, with the highest load current, 60 mA. At the 5.0 mA limit the Zener terminal voltage is Vz = Vz0 + rz Iz = 8.90 + 5.0 × 0.005 = 8.925 V. The current through Rs must supply both the Zener and the load, so Is = 5 + 60 = 65 mA. Applying Ohm's law to the series resistor, Rs = (Vin,min − Vz)/Is = (21 − 8.925)/0.065 = 12.075/0.065 = 185.8 Ω. Any larger resistance would reduce Is below 65 mA and drop the Zener out of regulation at that corner. The next standard value below this is 180 Ω, which is therefore a valid choice and is used from here on.

Answer: 185.8 Ω

(b)

The Zener carries the most current when the input is highest and the load lightest. Write the node equation at the Zener cathode: (Vin − Vz)/Rs = Iz + IL, with Vz = Vz0 + rz Iz. Substituting gives (Vin − Vz0 − rz Iz)/Rs = Iz + IL, so Iz = (Vin − Vz0 − Rs IL)/(Rs + rz) = (27 − 8.90 − 180 × 0.010)/185 = 16.3/185 = 88.1 mA. The Zener voltage is Vz = 8.90 + 5 × 0.0881 = 9.340 V. The dissipation is P = Vz Iz = 9.340 × 0.0881 = 0.823 W. A 1 W part would run hot at this corner, so a 1.3 W device or a lower input range is the safer selection.

Answer: 0.823 W

(c)

With constant load current, a small change in input voltage divides between Rs and rz seen in series, because the Zener branch behaves like rz in series with a fixed source. The line regulation is therefore ΔVo/ΔVin = rz/(Rs + rz) = 5.0/(180 + 5.0) = 0.02703. For the full swing ΔVin = 27 − 21 = 6 V, so ΔVo = 0.02703 × 6 = 0.162 V. This is the peak-to-peak change of the 9 V rail, about 1.8 percent, which comes almost entirely from the Zener dynamic resistance. A Zener with lower rz, or a second regulation stage, would reduce the figure in proportion.

Answer: 0.162 V

(d)

A load current step draws current from the node that the source Rs and the Zener branch both feed. The Thévenin resistance seen at the output with the input held fixed is Rs in parallel with rz, so the output falls by ΔVo = −ΔIL (Rs ∥ rz). Compute Rs ∥ rz = (180 × 5.0)/(180 + 5.0) = 900/185 = 4.865 Ω. The load step is ΔIL = 60 − 10 = 50 mA, giving ΔVo = 0.050 × 4.865 = 0.243 V in magnitude, a drop. Most of the current change is taken from the Zener, whose current falls by almost 50 mA, which is why the Zener current must never reach zero. This confirms that the 5 mA minimum was chosen sensibly.

Answer: 0.243 V

Problem 3 [A5-003] Thyristors, SCR and TRIAC circuits

A 120 V rms, 60 Hz single-phase supply feeds a 15 Ω resistive heating element through a single SCR that is gated to give half-wave phase control. The SCR is fired at a delay angle α = 60° measured from the positive-going zero crossing of the supply voltage, and it turns off naturally when the load current falls to zero. Treat the SCR as ideal, with no forward drop and no gate-circuit losses, and assume the gate current is large enough to latch it on at the firing instant. The supply is an ideal sinusoid and the element resistance does not change with temperature. All results refer to the steady state, with the SCR firing in every positive half cycle.

  1. (a) Find the time delay between the zero crossing and the firing instant. [3]
  2. (b) Find the average load voltage. [5]
  3. (c) Find the rms load voltage and the average power delivered to the element. [7]
  4. (d) Find the supply power factor, taking the supply current to be the load current. [5]
(a)

The delay angle is converted to time using the period T = 1/f = 1/60 = 16.667 ms, which corresponds to 360° of the supply. The firing delay is t = (α/360°) T = (60/360) × 16.667 ms = 2.778 ms. The assumption is that the gate pulse is timed from the exact positive-going zero crossing, for instance by a synchronising comparator. After this delay the supply is at Vm sin 60° = 169.7 × 0.866 = 147.0 V, so the full voltage is applied suddenly across the load when the SCR latches. This step is the reason phase control produces harmonic currents and radio noise.

Answer: 2.78 ms

(b)

The peak supply voltage is Vm = 120√2 = 169.7 V. For half-wave control the load voltage equals the supply from α to π and is zero otherwise, so Vavg = (1/2π) ∫ from α to π of Vm sin θ dθ = (Vm/2π)(1 + cos α). Substituting α = 60°, cos α = 0.5, gives Vavg = (169.7/6.283) × 1.5 = 27.01 × 1.5 = 40.51 V. For comparison a fully conducting half-wave rectifier would give Vm/π = 54.0 V, and the 60° delay reduces the average to 75 percent of that value. This is the quantity read by a moving-coil meter across the element and used to set the heater power level.

Answer: 40.5 V

(c)

The heating power depends on the rms load voltage, which follows from integrating the square of the voltage over the conducting interval: Vrms = (Vm/2) √(1 − α/π + sin 2α/(2π)). With α = π/3, α/π = 0.3333 and sin 120° = 0.8660, so the bracket is 1 − 0.3333 + 0.8660/6.283 = 0.8045. Its square root is 0.8969, hence Vrms = 84.85 × 0.8969 = 76.10 V. The average power in the resistance is P = Vrms²/R = 76.10²/15 = 5791/15 = 386.1 W. The full-wave sinusoidal power at 120 V would be 960 W, so half-wave control at 60° delivers about 40 percent of it, a fact worth comparing with the 50 percent (480 W) that a simple half-wave diode would give.

Answer: 76.1 V rms and 386 W

(d)

The supply current is the load current, with rms value Irms = Vrms/R = 76.10/15 = 5.073 A. The apparent power drawn from the 120 V source is S = Vs Irms = 120 × 5.073 = 608.8 VA. The real power is the 386.1 W found in part (c), so the power factor is PF = P/S = 386.1/608.8 = 0.634. This equals Vrms/Vs = 76.10/120 and is low, even though the load is a pure resistance, because the delay distorts the current waveform and introduces harmonics, and because the fundamental of the delayed current also lags the supply voltage. Both the displacement angle of that fundamental and the harmonic distortion therefore lower the power factor, even though the load is purely resistive. This is a standard disadvantage of phase-controlled heating.

Answer: 0.634

Problem 4 [A5-004] BJT bias circuits and operating point

A silicon NPN transistor is used in a voltage-divider bias circuit for a low-level audio preamplifier powered from a 12 V supply. The base is connected to the supply through R1 = 47 kΩ and to ground through R2 = 10 kΩ. The collector is connected to the supply through RC = 2.2 kΩ and the emitter to ground through RE = 1.0 kΩ. Assume the transistor is in the forward active region with VBE = 0.70 V, a current gain β = 120 and negligible leakage current and Early effect. Ignore coupling capacitors, which are open circuits at DC. The designer wants to check the quiescent point and then estimate the sensitivity to a transistor replacement.

  1. (a) Find the collector current at the quiescent point. [6]
  2. (b) Find VCE and confirm the transistor is in the active region. [4]
  3. (c) The transistor is replaced by one with β = 240. Find the new collector current. [6]
  4. (d) Express the change in collector current as a percentage of the original value. [4]
(a)

Replace the divider by its Thévenin equivalent at the base. VTH = 12 × 10/(47 + 10) = 2.105 V and RTH = 47 ∥ 10 = 8.246 kΩ. The base loop equation is VTH = IB RTH + VBE + IE RE with IE = (β + 1) IB. Solving gives IB = (VTH − VBE)/(RTH + (β + 1) RE) = (2.105 − 0.70)/(8.246 kΩ + 121 × 1 kΩ) = 1.405/129.25 kΩ = 10.87 μA. The collector current is IC = β IB = 120 × 10.87 μA = 1.304 mA. The assumption of active-region operation is verified in part (b).

Answer: 1.30 mA

(b)

The emitter current is IE = (β + 1) IB = 121 × 10.87 μA = 1.315 mA. Writing the collector-emitter loop, VCE = VCC − IC RC − IE RE = 12 − 1.304 mA × 2.2 kΩ − 1.315 mA × 1.0 kΩ = 12 − 2.869 − 1.315 = 7.81 V. Because VCE is well above the saturation value of about 0.2 V, and VBE is positive, the forward-active assumption is confirmed. The point is near the middle of the supply, leaving a collector swing of about 7 V before cutoff or saturation, which is adequate for a preamplifier stage handling millivolt signals.

Answer: 7.81 V

(c)

The Thévenin voltage and resistance do not depend on the transistor, so VTH = 2.105 V and RTH = 8.246 kΩ remain. Recompute the base current with β = 240: IB = (2.105 − 0.70)/(8.246 kΩ + 241 × 1 kΩ) = 1.405/249.25 kΩ = 5.637 μA. Then IC = 240 × 5.637 μA = 1.353 mA. Doubling β has raised IC by only a few hundredths of a milliampere, because the emitter resistor feeds back almost all of the base-current change. The result shows why divider bias with an emitter resistor is preferred over fixed-base bias, where IC would have doubled.

Answer: 1.35 mA

(d)

The percentage change is (IC,new − IC,old)/IC,old × 100. Using the unrounded values from the calculations above, IC,old = 1.3045 mA and IC,new = 1.3529 mA, so the change is (1.3529 − 1.3045)/1.3045 × 100 = 3.71 percent. A 100 percent increase in β therefore gives about 3.7 percent change in the collector current, so the stability is good. The reason is that RTH is small compared with (β + 1) RE, so the current is set mainly by VTH, VBE and RE. A rule of thumb is to choose RTH at most about a tenth of (β + 1) RE, and here the ratio is 8.2/121, close to that rule.

Answer: 3.71 percent

Problem 5 [A5-005] BJT small-signal model and common-emitter amplifier

A common-emitter amplifier stage is biased at a collector current IC = 1.5 mA. The transistor has β = 150, Early voltage VA = 80 V, and the thermal voltage is taken as VT = 25 mV. The bias network presents a parallel resistance RB = R1 ∥ R2 = 10 kΩ at the base. The collector resistor is RC = 3.3 kΩ and the emitter resistor is fully bypassed at signal frequencies. A load RL = 4.7 kΩ is capacitor-coupled to the collector, and the signal source has an internal resistance Rsig = 1.0 kΩ, coupled through a large capacitor to the base. All coupling and bypass capacitors are short circuits in the midband, and the hybrid-π model is to be used with ro included.

  1. (a) Find the small-signal parameters gm, rπ and ro, and report rπ. [4]
  2. (b) Find the midband voltage gain from base to collector, vo/vb. [6]
  3. (c) Find the input resistance seen by the source after the coupling capacitor. [4]
  4. (d) Find the overall voltage gain vo/vsig including the source resistance. [6]
(a)

The transconductance is gm = IC/VT = 1.5 mA/25 mV = 60 mS. The base-emitter resistance is rπ = β/gm = 150/0.060 = 2500 Ω = 2.50 kΩ. The output resistance due to the Early effect is ro = VA/IC = 80/0.0015 = 53.3 kΩ. These three values form the hybrid-π model at this bias point. The assumption is that the small-signal model uses the quiescent collector current, which is valid for signal amplitudes of a few millivolts at the base. The thermal voltage of 25 mV corresponds to a temperature of about 290 K, close enough to room temperature for design work.

Answer: 2.50 kΩ

(b)

At the collector, the signal current gm vb flows into three resistances in parallel: ro, RC and RL, because the supply is an AC ground and the load is coupled through a short-circuit capacitor. The effective load is RL' = ro ∥ RC ∥ RL. First RC ∥ RL = 3.3 × 4.7/(3.3 + 4.7) = 1.939 kΩ. Combining with ro: 1/RL' = 1/1.939 + 1/53.3 = 0.5158 + 0.01876 = 0.5345 mS⁻¹, so RL' = 1.871 kΩ. The inverting gain is vo/vb = −gm RL' = −0.060 × 1871 = −112.3 V/V. The minus sign shows phase inversion. The gain is large because the transconductance at 1.5 mA is high.

Answer: −112

(c)

Looking into the coupling capacitor, the source sees the bias network resistance RB and the transistor input resistance rπ in parallel, because the bypassed emitter leaves no feedback resistance in the base circuit. Therefore Rin = RB ∥ rπ = 10 × 2.5/(10 + 2.5) = 25/12.5 = 2.00 kΩ. The Early-effect resistance does not appear in the input resistance when the load is taken to be small compared with ro. This value will form a divider with the source resistance, so the input resistance of 2.00 kΩ is crucial in part (d), and a larger bias resistance would improve it only up to rπ.

Answer: 2.00 kΩ

(d)

The source resistance and the input resistance form a voltage divider at the input, so vb/vsig = Rin/(Rin + Rsig) = 2.00/(2.00 + 1.0) = 0.6667. The overall gain is the product of this divider ratio and the base-to-collector gain from part (b): vo/vsig = 0.6667 × (−112.3) = −74.84 V/V. Roughly one third of the available signal is lost across the 1 kΩ source resistance. To improve this, a designer could raise rπ by reducing the bias current, but that would also lower gm and the gain, so a compromise is needed. The result is assumed to hold across the midband only.

Answer: −74.8

A5 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A5-006] Common-collector and common-base stages

A transistor with β = 100 is biased at IC = 2.0 mA and its small-signal behaviour is described by the hybrid-π model with thermal voltage VT = 25 mV and Early effect neglected. In the first circuit it is used as an emitter follower: the signal source of resistance Rs = 5.0 kΩ drives the base directly, the emitter has a bias resistor RE = 2.0 kΩ, and a load RL = 1.0 kΩ is capacitor-coupled to the emitter. Bias components at the base are large and are ignored. In the second circuit, the same device is used as a common-base stage with collector resistor RC = 3.0 kΩ and a load of 3.0 kΩ coupled to the collector, driven at the emitter by a source of resistance 50 Ω.

  1. (a) For the emitter follower, find the resistance looking into the base. [5]
  2. (b) Find the voltage gain from the base to the output of the follower. [4]
  3. (c) Find the output resistance looking back into the follower from the load, including RE and the source resistance. [5]
  4. (d) For the common-base circuit, find the overall voltage gain from the source voltage to the output across the 3.0 kΩ load, using the exact input resistance. [6]
(a)

The transconductance is gm = 2.0 mA/25 mV = 80 mS, so rπ = β/gm = 100/0.080 = 1.25 kΩ. The signal resistance at the emitter is RE in parallel with RL, so Re' = 2.0 ∥ 1.0 = 0.6667 kΩ. The resistance looking into the base is reflected up by (β + 1): Rib = rπ + (β + 1) Re' = 1.25 kΩ + 101 × 0.6667 kΩ = 1.25 + 67.33 = 68.58 kΩ. This high value is the main benefit of the emitter follower, since it loads a weak source lightly. The Early resistance would lower this slightly but is neglected as stated.

Answer: 68.6 kΩ

(b)

The base-emitter junction and the emitter-side resistance form a divider from the base to the output: vo/vb = (β + 1) Re'/(rπ + (β + 1) Re'). The numerator is 101 × 0.6667 kΩ = 67.33 kΩ, and the denominator is 1.25 kΩ + 67.33 kΩ = 68.58 kΩ. The gain is therefore 67.33/68.58 = 0.9818. This is just under unity and positive, so the output follows the input without inversion. Gain slightly below unity arises because a small fraction of the base signal appears across the rπ junction, so that vbe is nonzero and drives the output current.

Answer: 0.982

(c)

Remove the load and the signal and look into the emitter. The resistance seen into the emitter of a transistor driven from a base circuit of resistance Rs is (Rs + rπ)/(β + 1) = (5000 + 1250)/101 = 61.88 Ω. The bias resistor RE appears in parallel with it, so Rout = 2000 ∥ 61.88 = 2000 × 61.88/2061.88 = 60.02 Ω. The follower thus transforms the 5 kΩ source into an output resistance near 60 Ω, which is why this stage is used as a buffer ahead of low-resistance loads. Without the load removed the figure would be unchanged because the load is the external element.

Answer: 60.0 Ω

(d)

The input resistance at the emitter of a common-base stage is re = VT/IE, where IE = IC (β + 1)/β = 2.0202 mA, so re = 25 mV/2.0202 mA = 12.375 Ω (equal to rπ/(β + 1) = 12.38 Ω). The collector load is RC ∥ RL = 1.5 kΩ, and the gain from emitter to output is gm RC' = 0.080 × 1500 = 120 V/V, positive because there is no inversion. The source resistance of 50 Ω divides the input: ve/vs = 12.375/(12.375 + 50) = 0.1984. The overall gain is 120 × 0.1984 = 23.81 V/V. A low input resistance means the stage is poorly matched to high-resistance sources, so it is used with low-impedance sources or as a cascode.

Answer: 23.8 V/V

Problem 2 [A5-007] MOSFET bias and operating regions

An n-channel enhancement MOSFET is used in a four-resistor bias circuit powered from VDD = 10 V. The gate is held by a divider from VDD, with 3.0 MΩ to VDD and 2.0 MΩ to ground, and draws no current. The source is connected to ground through RS = 2.0 kΩ and the drain connects to VDD through RD = 3.0 kΩ. The device has threshold voltage Vt = 1.0 V and obeys the saturation-region square law ID = (kn/2)(VGS − Vt)², with kn = 2.0 mA/V² and zero channel-length modulation. The designer needs the bias point and the largest drain resistor for which the device remains in saturation. Neglect the body effect.

  1. (a) Find the drain current. [7]
  2. (b) Find VDS and verify that the device is in saturation. [4]
  3. (c) Find the small-signal transconductance gm at this bias point. [3]
  4. (d) Find the largest value of RD that keeps the device in saturation, with all other values unchanged. [6]
(a)

The gate voltage is set by the divider, VG = 10 × 2.0/(3.0 + 2.0) = 4.0 V, with no gate current. The gate-source voltage is VGS = VG − ID RS = 4.0 − 2000 ID. Put the square law in mA: ID = (2.0/2)(VGS − 1)² = (3 − 2 ID)², using ID in mA and RS in kΩ. Expanding gives 4 ID² − 12 ID + 9 = ID, so 4 ID² − 13 ID + 9 = 0. The roots are ID = (13 ± √(169 − 144))/8 = (13 ± 5)/8, which is 2.25 mA or 1.00 mA. The 2.25 mA root would give VGS = 4 − 4.5 = −0.5 V, below threshold, so it is rejected. Therefore ID = 1.00 mA.

Answer: 1.00 mA

(b)

With ID = 1.00 mA, VGS = 4.0 − 1.0 × 2.0 = 2.0 V, and the overdrive is VGS − Vt = 1.0 V. The drain-source voltage follows from the drain loop: VDS = VDD − ID (RD + RS) = 10 − 1.00 mA × (3.0 + 2.0) kΩ = 5.00 V. Saturation requires VDS ≥ VGS − Vt, that is 5.00 V ≥ 1.0 V, which is satisfied with a large margin. The square-law assumption used in part (a) is therefore valid. The device sits comfortably in the saturation region, so it can amplify small signals at the drain without clipping until the drain swing is about 4 V.

Answer: 5.00 V

(c)

In saturation the transconductance is gm = dID/dVGS = kn (VGS − Vt) = 2.0 mA/V² × 1.0 V = 2.0 mS. An equivalent expression is gm = 2 ID/(VGS − Vt) = 2 × 1.0 mA/1.0 V = 2.0 mS, and the two agree, confirming consistency. Channel-length modulation is neglected, so ro is infinite. This transconductance is much smaller than that of a bipolar transistor at the same current, which would give about 40 mS, and this is why MOSFET stages generally give lower gain per unit current.

Answer: 2.00 mS

(d)

Raising RD lowers VDS and, since VGS and ID are unaffected as long as the device stays in saturation, the limit is reached when VDS = VGS − Vt = 1.0 V. The drain loop gives VDD − ID (RD + RS) = 1.0, so 10 − 1.00 × (RD + 2.0) = 1.0, with RD in kΩ and ID in mA. This gives RD + 2.0 = 9.0, therefore RD,max = 7.0 kΩ. Beyond this value the device enters the triode region and the current falls below the square-law prediction. In practice a margin is kept so that the output can swing, so a drain resistor of 3 kΩ, as used here, is a sensible design.

Answer: 7.00 kΩ

Problem 3 [A5-008] MOSFET small-signal amplifiers

A common-source amplifier uses an n-channel MOSFET biased at ID = 0.50 mA. The process transconductance parameter times aspect ratio is kn = 4.0 mA/V², so the saturation current is ID = (kn/2)(VGS − Vt)², and the channel-length modulation parameter is λ = 0.020 V⁻¹. The drain resistor is RD = 10 kΩ and a load RL = 10 kΩ is capacitor-coupled to the drain. A source resistor RS = 500 Ω is present. In part (b) it is completely bypassed by a large capacitor, and in parts (c) and (d) it is not bypassed at all. Coupling capacitors are short circuits at signal frequencies and the body effect is neglected. Ignore ro in the degenerated cases, as stated in those parts.

  1. (a) Find gm for the device. [4]
  2. (b) With RS bypassed, find the midband voltage gain, including ro. [5]
  3. (c) With RS unbypassed and ro neglected, find the midband voltage gain. [6]
  4. (d) With RS unbypassed, find the percentage change in the gain magnitude if gm increases by 20 percent, and compare with the bypassed case. [5]
(a)

In saturation gm = √(2 kn ID) = √(2 × 4.0 mA/V² × 0.50 mA) = √4.0 mS² = 2.0 mS, using milliamps and milli-siemens consistently. The same result follows from gm = kn (VGS − Vt), because the overdrive is √(2 ID/kn) = √(2 × 0.5/4.0) = 0.50 V, and 4.0 × 0.50 = 2.0 mS. The output resistance is ro = 1/(λ ID) = 1/(0.020 × 0.5 mA) = 100 kΩ, which is required in part (b). These are the two parameters of the small-signal model, and both depend on the bias current.

Answer: 2.00 mS

(b)

With the source at signal ground the drain sees ro, RD and RL in parallel. RD ∥ RL = 5.0 kΩ, and including ro = 100 kΩ gives 1/Ro' = 1/5 + 1/100 = 0.21 mS, so Ro' = 4.762 kΩ. The gain of the common-source stage is Av = −gm Ro' = −2.0 mS × 4.762 kΩ = −9.524 V/V. The negative sign indicates phase inversion. The effect of ro is small here because RD ∥ RL is far lower than ro, reducing the gain by only about 5 percent compared with −10. This is the highest gain available at this bias current and these resistors.

Answer: −9.52 V/V

(c)

Without the bypass capacitor the source resistor carries the signal current and provides negative feedback. With ro neglected, the gain of the degenerated stage is Av = −gm (RD ∥ RL)/(1 + gm RS). Substituting, RD ∥ RL = 5.0 kΩ and gm RS = 2.0 mS × 0.5 kΩ = 1.0, so Av = −2.0 × 5.0/(1 + 1.0) = −10/2 = −5.0 V/V. The source resistor has halved the gain compared with the ideal −10. This trade of gain for linearity and stability is the purpose of degeneration: the gain now depends mainly on the resistor ratio, not on gm.

Answer: −5.00 V/V

(d)

A 20 percent increase gives gm = 2.4 mS, so gm RS = 1.2. The new gain magnitude is 2.4 × 5.0/(1 + 1.2) = 12/2.2 = 5.4545. The original magnitude was 5.0, so the change is (5.4545 − 5.0)/5.0 = 9.09 percent. In the bypassed case, with ro neglected, the gain is proportional to gm and would change by the full 20 percent. Degeneration has therefore cut the sensitivity to the device parameter by more than half, here by the factor 1/(1 + gm RS) = 0.455. This desensitisation is why the unbypassed source resistor makes the stage tolerant to temperature and device spread.

Answer: 9.09 percent

Problem 4 [A5-009] Multistage amplifiers and loading effects

Two voltage amplifier stages are cascaded to drive a 1.0 kΩ load from a 20 kΩ source. Each stage is described by its input resistance, open-circuit voltage gain and output resistance. Stage 1 has Rin1 = 100 kΩ, Avo1 = −50 V/V and Ro1 = 5.0 kΩ. Stage 2 has Rin2 = 2.0 kΩ, Avo2 = −100 V/V and Ro2 = 200 Ω. All elements are purely resistive in the midband, so every gain is a real number. The source is an ideal voltage vs in series with Rs = 20 kΩ. Each stage is treated as a Thévenin equivalent at its output, and loading at each interface follows from simple voltage division.

  1. (a) Find the overall voltage gain vo/vs of the two-stage amplifier. [6]
  2. (b) Express the overall gain in decibels. [3]
  3. (c) Find the overall current gain io/is, where is is the current delivered by the signal source to Stage 1 and io is the current in the load. [5]
  4. (d) A unity-gain buffer with Rin = 500 kΩ and Ro = 100 Ω is inserted between the two stages. Find the new overall voltage gain. [6]
(a)

Treat each interface as a voltage divider. At the input, vi1/vs = Rin1/(Rin1 + Rs) = 100/120 = 0.8333. Stage 1 produces an open-circuit voltage Avo1 vi1, which divides between Ro1 and Rin2: vi2/(Avo1 vi1) = 2.0/(2.0 + 5.0) = 0.2857. Stage 2 produces Avo2 vi2, which divides between Ro2 and RL: vo/(Avo2 vi2) = 1.0/(1.0 + 0.2) = 0.8333. The overall gain is the product: 0.8333 × (−50) × 0.2857 × (−100) × 0.8333 = 992.1 V/V. Both gains are negative, so the cascade is non-inverting and the product is positive.

Answer: 992 V/V

(b)

The voltage gain in decibels is 20 log10 of the magnitude of the ratio. With |vo/vs| = 992.1, log10(992.1) = 2.9965, so the gain is 20 × 2.9965 = 59.93 dB. The open-circuit gains alone would give 50 × 100 = 5000 V/V, which is 74.0 dB, so the three loading divisions have cost 14.1 dB. This shows how large the loading losses are when the resistances are not well matched: a good cascade has input resistances much larger than the preceding output resistances. The positive sign of the gain does not affect the decibel value.

Answer: 59.9 dB

(c)

The source current is is = vs/(Rs + Rin1) = vi1/Rin1, so is = vi1/100 kΩ. The load current is io = vo/RL = vo/1.0 kΩ. The gain from vi1 to vo is the overall gain divided by the input divider: 992.1/0.8333 = 1190.5. Therefore io/is = (vo/RL)/(vi1/Rin1) = 1190.5 × Rin1/RL = 1190.5 × 100 kΩ/1.0 kΩ = 1.1905 × 10⁵. The current gain is much larger than the voltage gain because the amplifier takes current from a high-resistance port and delivers it into a low-resistance one. Power gain combines both ratios for the stage.

Answer: 1.19 × 10⁵

(d)

The buffer has unity open-circuit gain, so it only changes the loading at the two interfaces. Stage 1 now drives 500 kΩ: 500/(500 + 5) = 0.9901. The buffer, with Ro = 100 Ω, drives Rin2 = 2.0 kΩ: 2.0/(2.0 + 0.1) = 0.9524. The input and output dividers are unchanged, 0.8333 each. The new overall gain is 0.8333 × (−50) × 0.9901 × 1 × 0.9524 × (−100) × 0.8333 = 3274 V/V. The buffer improves the gain by a factor of 3.3, about 10.4 dB, because it removes the heavy interstage loss of 0.2857 and replaces it with 0.9430.

Answer: 3270 V/V

Problem 5 [A5-010] Frequency response of amplifiers, poles and Miller effect

A common-emitter amplifier stage is driven by a source of resistance Rsig = 1.0 kΩ, and the bias network resistances are large enough to ignore. The transistor hybrid-π parameters at the operating point are gm = 40 mS, rπ = 2.5 kΩ, Cπ = 20 pF and Cμ = 2.0 pF, with rx and ro neglected. The effective collector load is RL' = 2.0 kΩ. All coupling and bypass capacitors are short circuits across the frequencies of interest. The high-frequency response is to be found with the Miller approximation, which replaces the bridging capacitor Cμ by a capacitor at the input, and the output pole is assumed to lie far above the input pole and is ignored.

  1. (a) Find the midband voltage gain vo/vsig. [5]
  2. (b) Find the Miller multiplication of Cμ and the total input capacitance. [5]
  3. (c) Find the upper −3 dB frequency fH. [5]
  4. (d) The transistor is replaced by one with Cμ = 4.0 pF, other parameters unchanged. Find the new fH. [5]
(a)

At midband the capacitors are open circuits, so the input divider is vπ/vsig = rπ/(rπ + Rsig) = 2.5/(2.5 + 1.0) = 0.7143. The collector current gm vπ flows in RL', giving vo = −gm RL' vπ. The gain from base to collector is −gm RL' = −0.040 × 2000 = −80 V/V. The overall gain is therefore vo/vsig = 0.7143 × (−80) = −57.14 V/V. The 1 kΩ source resistance costs 29 percent of the signal. This is the low-frequency asymptote from which the bandwidth is measured, and it is the number against which the −3 dB point is defined.

Answer: −57.1 V/V

(b)

The capacitor Cμ bridges the input and the output, where the voltage gain is K = −gm RL' = −80. By the Miller approximation, the equivalent capacitance at the input is Cμ (1 − K) = Cμ (1 + gm RL') = 2.0 pF × 81 = 162 pF. The total input capacitance adds Cπ in parallel: Cin = 20 + 162 = 182 pF. The small bridging capacitance has therefore become the dominant one, which is the Miller effect. The approximation is valid when the output pole is far higher than the input pole, as stated, and when the gain is taken at midband.

Answer: 182 pF

(c)

The input pole is set by the resistance seen by Cin, which is Rsig in parallel with rπ: R = 1.0 ∥ 2.5 = 0.7143 kΩ. The upper −3 dB radian frequency is ωH = 1/(R Cin) = 1/(714.3 × 182×10⁻¹²) = 1/(1.3000×10⁻⁷) = 7.692×10⁶ rad/s. Converting to hertz, fH = ωH/(2π) = 7.692×10⁶/6.2832 = 1.224 MHz. Above this frequency the gain falls at 20 dB per decade, since a single dominant pole is assumed. Reducing the source resistance or using a cascode would extend the bandwidth.

Answer: 1.22 MHz

(d)

The Miller capacitance becomes 4.0 pF × 81 = 324 pF, so Cin = 20 + 324 = 344 pF. The resistance seen by Cin is unchanged at 714.3 Ω. The new pole is fH = 1/(2π × 714.3 × 344×10⁻¹²) = 1/(1.5438×10⁻⁶) = 647.7 kHz. Doubling Cμ nearly halved the bandwidth, from 1.224 MHz to 0.648 MHz, because the Miller term accounts for 162 of the 182 pF originally. The midband gain is not affected, so the gain-bandwidth product falls by the same factor. This shows why a small collector-base capacitance is the key parameter in high-frequency amplifier selection.

Answer: 648 kHz

A5 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A5-011] Differential amplifiers and current mirrors

A bipolar differential amplifier for a thermocouple front end runs from +12 V and -12 V supplies. The emitters of matched transistors Q1 and Q2 join at one node that connects to the collector of Q4. Q4 is the output transistor of a two-transistor current mirror: Q3 is diode-connected (its base and collector are tied together), Q3 and Q4 have bases joined and emitters both at -12 V. The collector of Q3 connects to the +12 V supply through a reference resistor Rref = 22.6 kΩ. Each of Q1 and Q2 has a collector resistor RC = 10 kΩ to +12 V; the bases are the two inputs. All transistors have β = 100, VBE = 0.7 V when conducting, thermal voltage VT = 25 mV and Early voltage VA = 100 V. Use the exact base-current relation for the mirror, and in part (b) neglect the Early effect on the mirror ratio.

  1. (a) Find the reference current in Q3. [4]
  2. (b) Find the tail current delivered by Q4, including the effect of finite β in the mirror. [4]
  3. (c) With the output taken differentially between the two collectors, find the differential voltage gain, using gm of each transistor at its bias point. [6]
  4. (d) The output resistance of Q4 limits common-mode rejection. Taking the tail resistance as VA divided by the tail current, find the CMRR in dB when the output is taken single-ended from one collector (differential gain Ad/2 against single-ended common-mode gain RC/(2 Ro)). [6]
(a)

Q3 is diode-connected, so its base-emitter drop is 0.7 V and its collector sits at -12 + 0.7 = -11.3 V. The reference resistor connects the +12 V supply to that collector, so the voltage across it is 12 - (-11.3) = 23.3 V. Applying Ohm's law, Iref = 23.3 V / 22.6 kΩ = 1.031 mA. This current is the input of the mirror: it flows through Q3 and also supplies the base currents of Q3 and Q4, which is accounted for in part (b). The sign convention is that currents flow down the branch from +12 V toward the negative rail.

Answer: Iref = 1.031 mA

(b)

In the mirror, Q3 and Q4 share the same VBE so their collector currents are equal when the base currents are ignored. The reference current supplies Q3's collector current plus the two base currents: Iref = IC + 2IB = IC(1 + 2/β). With β = 100, IC = Iref/(1.02) = 1.031 mA / 1.02 = 1.0108 mA. Q4 conducts the same collector current, so the tail current is Io = 1.011 mA. The error from finite β is 2 percent, which is acceptable here but would grow for a low-β device. We neglect the Early effect on the mirror ratio as instructed in part (b); the Q3 and Q4 collectors sit about 10 V apart, so applying VA = 100 V would change the ratio by roughly 10 percent.

Answer: Io = 1.011 mA

(c)

The tail current splits equally between Q1 and Q2 by symmetry, so each emitter current is Io/2 = 0.5054 mA, and the collector current is IC = α IE = (100/101) × 0.5054 = 0.5004 mA. The transconductance is gm = IC/VT = 0.5004 mA / 25 mV = 20.02 mS. For a differential input and differential output, each collector swings by gm RC times half the input, so the differential gain magnitude is Ad = gm RC = 20.02 mS × 10 kΩ = 200. The sign is negative at the collector of Q1 and positive at the other when measured per input polarity, but the magnitude is 200 V/V.

Answer: |Ad| = 200 V/V

(d)

The tail output resistance is Ro = VA/Io = 100 V / 1.0108 mA = 98.9 kΩ. For a common-mode input each half sees a source resistance of 2Ro in its emitter, so the single-ended common-mode gain is Acm = RC/(2Ro) = 10 kΩ / 197.9 kΩ = 0.0505. The single-ended differential gain is Ad/2 = 100.1. Then CMRR = (Ad/2)/Acm = 100.1/0.0505 = 1980, which is 20 log10(1980) = 65.9 dB. A larger Ro, for example from a Wilson or cascode mirror, would raise the CMRR directly.

Answer: CMRR = 65.9 dB

Problem 2 [A5-012] Op-amp inverting and non-inverting circuits

A load-cell signal conditioner uses two ideal-style op-amp stages in cascade. Stage 1 is an inverting amplifier: the input source connects through R1 = 10 kΩ to the inverting input of op-amp U1, whose non-inverting input is grounded, with feedback resistor Rf1 = 47 kΩ from the output of U1 to its inverting input. The output of U1 feeds directly the non-inverting input of op-amp U2. U2 is a non-inverting amplifier: R3 = 2.2 kΩ connects the inverting input of U2 to ground, and R4 = 33 kΩ connects the output of U2 to its inverting input. Both op-amps saturate at ±13 V. Unless stated otherwise treat the op-amps as ideal with infinite open-loop gain.

  1. (a) Find the overall voltage gain vo/vin. [5]
  2. (b) Find the input resistance seen by the source. [3]
  3. (c) If U1 has a finite open-loop gain of 5000, find the actual voltage gain of stage 1 alone. [6]
  4. (d) Taking both stages ideal, find the largest peak input amplitude, in volts, that can be applied before the output of U2 clips. [6]
(a)

With the non-inverting input grounded, the inverting input of U1 is a virtual ground, so the stage-1 gain is -Rf1/R1 = -47/10 = -4.7. U2 sees this output at its non-inverting input and has gain 1 + R4/R3 = 1 + 33/2.2 = 16. The two stages are cascaded with the ideal U1 output having zero resistance, so no loading occurs and gains multiply: Av = -4.7 × 16 = -75.2. The negative sign means the output is 180 degrees out of phase with the input at all frequencies in the ideal case.

Answer: Av = -75.2

(b)

The inverting input of U1 is held at virtual ground by the negative feedback, so the voltage across R1 is the full input voltage and the current drawn from the source is vin/R1. The input resistance is therefore vin divided by that current, Rin = R1 = 10 kΩ. This is independent of Rf1. It matters for the load cell, because its source resistance would add directly to R1 and change the gain, so a source resistance of 100 Ω would cause a 1 percent gain error.

Answer: Rin = 10 kΩ

(c)

For an inverting stage with finite open-loop gain A the exact closed-loop gain is G = -(Rf/R1) / (1 + (1 + Rf/R1)/A). Here Rf/R1 = 4.7, so 1 + Rf/R1 = 5.7 and 5.7/5000 = 0.00114. Then G = -4.7 / 1.00114 = -4.6946. The gain error is 0.114 percent. This follows from writing the node equation at the inverting terminal with v- = -vo/A. A gain of 5000 is far lower than the 10⁵ typical for a general-purpose op-amp, which is why the error is visible at all.

Answer: G1 = -4.695

(d)

Clipping occurs when the output magnitude reaches 13 V. With the ideal overall gain of 75.2, the largest peak input is vin,max = 13/75.2 = 0.1729 V. Check that stage 1 does not clip first: its output peak is 4.7 × 0.1729 = 0.812 V, well below 13 V, so U2 is the limiting stage. Beyond 0.1729 V peak the output flattens at ±13 V and harmonic distortion appears. If the load-cell signal could reach 0.25 V, the gain would have to be reduced, for example by lowering R4.

Answer: vin,max = 0.1729 V

Problem 3 [A5-013] Op-amp summing, integrating, differentiating and filters

An analogue computer element is built around an ideal op-amp. Two sources feed the inverting input of the op-amp through separate resistors: source V1 = +2.0 V dc through R1 = 10 kΩ, and source V2 = -0.5 V dc through R2 = 20 kΩ. The non-inverting input is grounded. A capacitor C = 100 nF connects the op-amp output to the inverting input, and nothing else is in the feedback path. The capacitor is uncharged at t = 0 when both sources are switched on together. Part (d) later adds a 1 MΩ resistor Rf in parallel with C. Take the output limits as ±12 V, and assume ideal behaviour apart from the saturation limits.

  1. (a) Find the rate of change of the output voltage, in V/s, after t = 0. [5]
  2. (b) Find the time, in milliseconds, for the output to reach -10 V. [4]
  3. (c) Replace both sources by a single sine source of 1 V peak at 1 kHz applied through R1 only (V2 removed). Find the peak output amplitude of the integrator, in volts. [5]
  4. (d) With the 1 MΩ resistor Rf in parallel with C and the single sine source of part (c), find the corner frequency in hertz above which the circuit behaves as an integrator. [6]
(a)

The inverting input is a virtual ground, so the input current is the sum I = V1/R1 + V2/R2 = 2/10 kΩ + (-0.5)/20 kΩ = 200 μA - 25 μA = 175 μA. All of it flows into the capacitor, so dvc/dt = I/C and the output is vo = -vc, giving dvo/dt = -I/C = -175 μA / 100 nF = -1750 V/s. The output ramps negative because the net input current is positive. Initial output is zero. The ramp slope is the weighted sum of the two inputs, which is why this circuit is called a summing integrator.

Answer: dvo/dt = -1750 V/s

(b)

The output is a linear ramp, vo(t) = -1750 t, because the capacitor was uncharged and the input current is constant. Setting vo = -10 V gives t = 10/1750 = 5.714 ms. This is within the ±12 V saturation limit so the ramp is valid up to this point. The output would saturate at -12 V after t = 12/1750 = 6.857 ms and remain there, since a pure integrator has no mechanism to stop a dc imbalance. This runaway behaviour is exactly what part (d) addresses.

Answer: t = 5.714 ms

(c)

For a sinusoidal input at angular frequency ω, the ideal integrator has transfer function Vo/Vi = -1/(jωR1C). Its magnitude is 1/(ωR1C). With ω = 2π × 1000 = 6283.2 rad/s, R1 = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF, R1C = 1.0 ms, so ωR1C = 6.283 and the gain magnitude is 0.1592. For a 1 V peak input the output peak is 0.1592 V. The output is a cosine lagging the inversion by 90 degrees, which matches the integral of a sine. At lower frequency the gain grows as 1/ω.

Answer: Vo,peak = 0.1592 V

(d)

With Rf across C the feedback impedance is Rf in parallel with 1/(sC), and the transfer function becomes -(Rf/R1)/(1 + sRfC), a low-pass response. The corner frequency is fc = 1/(2π Rf C) = 1/(2π × 10⁶ × 100×10⁻⁹) = 1/(0.6283) = 1.592 Hz. Above fc the circuit integrates; below it the gain is limited to Rf/R1 = 100, so dc offsets no longer ramp to saturation. The cost is that signals below roughly ten times fc, about 16 Hz, are not integrated accurately.

Answer: fc = 1.592 Hz

Problem 4 [A5-014] Feedback in amplifiers: gain, bandwidth and stability

A non-inverting voltage amplifier is built from an operational amplifier whose open-loop gain is A(f) = A0 / ((1 + j f/f1)(1 + j f/f2)), with A0 = 10⁵, dominant pole f1 = 10 Hz and second pole f2 = 250 kHz. The feedback network is a resistive divider that returns a fraction β = 0.10 of the output voltage to the inverting input, independent of frequency, so the loop gain is Aβ. The input is applied to the non-inverting input. Treat the amplifier as having infinite input resistance and zero output resistance. Later parts ask what happens when the open-loop dc gain changes by -20 percent because of supply or temperature change, with β unchanged.

  1. (a) Find the closed-loop dc gain. [4]
  2. (b) Find the frequency, in kilohertz, at which the magnitude of the loop gain Aβ equals one. [5]
  3. (c) Find the phase margin, in degrees, at that frequency. [6]
  4. (d) Find the change in the closed-loop dc gain, in parts per million, when A0 falls by 20 percent. [5]
(a)

The closed-loop gain of a feedback amplifier is Af = A/(1 + Aβ). At dc A = A0 = 10⁵ and β = 0.10, so Aβ = 10⁴ and Af = 10⁵/(1 + 10⁴) = 9.999. This is almost exactly 1/β = 10, which shows that the gain is set by the divider and not by the op-amp. The shortfall of 0.01 percent is the ideal-gain error 1/(1 + Aβ). The result applies at frequencies well below the first pole movement of the loop.

Answer: Af = 9.999

(b)

The loop gain magnitude is |Aβ| = A0β / (√(1 + (f/f1)²) √(1 + (f/f2)²)). We want it equal to 1. With A0β = 10⁴, f1 = 10 Hz and f2 = 250 kHz, a first estimate that ignores the second pole gives f ≈ A0β f1 = 10⁴ × 10 = 100 kHz. Including the second pole factor √(1 + (f/250 kHz)²), solved numerically, gives a slightly lower crossover f = 93.65 kHz. At this frequency the first factor is 9365 and the second factor is 1.067, and 10⁴/(9365 × 1.067) = 1.00. The crossover is therefore 93.65 kHz.

Answer: fx = 93.65 kHz

(c)

The phase of the loop gain at fx is -arctan(fx/f1) - arctan(fx/f2). With fx = 93.65 kHz: arctan(93650/10) = 89.99 degrees and arctan(93.65/250) = 20.54 degrees. The total phase is -110.53 degrees. The phase margin is PM = 180 - 110.53 = 69.5 degrees. A margin above about 60 degrees gives a well-damped closed-loop step response with little overshoot, so this amplifier is comfortably stable for β = 0.10. A smaller β, which increases closed-loop gain, would move fx lower and increase the margin further, while a larger β would worsen it.

Answer: PM = 69.5 degrees

(d)

A fall of 20 percent gives A0 = 8×10⁴, so Aβ = 8000 and Af = 8×10⁴/(1 + 8000) = 9.99875. Relative to the original 9.99900, the change is (9.99875 - 9.99900)/9.99900 = -2.5×10⁻⁵, which is -25 ppm. This is a reduction of the sensitivity by the factor 1/(1 + Aβ) = 1/10001 compared with the open-loop change of -20 percent. This desensitisation is the main reason to use negative feedback; the price is the gain reduction from 10⁵ to 10.

Answer: -25.0 ppm

Problem 5 [A5-015] Comparators, Schmitt triggers and oscillators

An inverting Schmitt trigger for a float-switch sensor uses an op-amp whose output saturates at +12 V and -12 V. The input voltage vin is applied to the inverting input. A resistive divider provides positive feedback: R2 = 47 kΩ connects the output to the non-inverting input, and R1 = 10 kΩ connects the non-inverting input to ground. No other resistor loads either node. The op-amp is otherwise ideal and the output switches instantly when the two inputs cross. Part (c) removes the external input and instead connects a resistor R = 22 kΩ from the output to the inverting input, with a capacitor C = 47 nF from the inverting input to ground, using the same divider, to form a relaxation oscillator.

  1. (a) Find the upper threshold voltage of the trigger, in volts. [4]
  2. (b) Find the width of the hysteresis band, in volts. [4]
  3. (c) Find the oscillation frequency, in hertz, of the relaxation oscillator described. [6]
  4. (d) In the trigger circuit of parts (a) and (b), a 5 V peak, 60 Hz sine wave is applied as vin. Find the time after the positive-going zero crossing at which the output first switches, in milliseconds. [6]
(a)

When the output sits at +12 V, the positive-feedback divider gives the non-inverting input voltage V+ = 12 × R1/(R1 + R2) = 12 × 10/57 = 2.105 V. Because vin drives the inverting input, the output stays at +12 V until vin rises above this value, at which point V- exceeds V+ and the output flips to -12 V. So the upper threshold is VTH = +2.105 V. The feedback fraction is β = R1/(R1 + R2) = 0.1754, which sets both thresholds by symmetry.

Answer: VTH = +2.105 V

(b)

With the output at -12 V, the same divider gives V+ = -12 × 0.1754 = -2.105 V, so the lower threshold is VTL = -2.105 V. The output returns to +12 V only when vin falls below this value. The hysteresis width is VH = VTH - VTL = 2.105 - (-2.105) = 4.211 V, equal to 2βVsat. Noise on the sensor line smaller than 4.21 V peak-to-peak cannot cause chatter. If the divider R2 were reduced, β would rise and the band would widen.

Answer: VH = 4.211 V

(c)

In the relaxation oscillator the capacitor charges toward the output voltage through R until it reaches the threshold ±βVsat set by the divider. With β = 0.1754 the capacitor swings between -2.105 V and +2.105 V. The half period is t = RC ln((1 + β)/(1 - β)) = 22 kΩ × 47 nF × ln(1.1754/0.8246) = 1.034 ms × 0.3544 = 0.3666 ms. The full period is T = 2t = 0.7332 ms, so f = 1/T = 1364 Hz. The waveform at the output is a symmetric square wave, and the duty cycle is 50 percent because the two thresholds are equal and opposite.

Answer: f = 1364 Hz

(d)

The output flips to -12 V when the rising sine reaches vin = VTH. The sine is vin = 5 sin(2π × 60 t), so we need sin(θ) = 2.105/5 = 0.4211, giving θ = arcsin(0.4211) = 24.90 degrees = 0.4346 rad. The time is t = θ/ω = 0.4346/(2π × 60) = 0.4346/376.99 = 1.153 ms after the zero crossing. The sine period is 16.67 ms, so the delay is about 6.9 percent of the cycle. Because of hysteresis, the falling edge occurs at the corresponding point shifted by 180 degrees.

Answer: t = 1.153 ms

A5 Practice Paper 4

Problem 1 [A5-016] Power amplifiers, efficiency and heat dissipation

A class B push-pull emitter-follower output stage drives a loudspeaker in an Ontario public-address cabinet. An npn transistor connects the +15 V rail to the output node and a matched pnp transistor connects the -15 V rail to the output node, with their bases driven so that each conducts on alternate half-cycles. The speaker is a resistor RL = 8 Ω from the output node to ground. Ignore crossover distortion and the base drive power, and take the transistor saturation voltage as zero. The output is a sine wave of peak voltage 12 V. For the heat-sink part, each transistor has junction-to-case thermal resistance 1.5 °C/W, case-to-sink resistance 0.5 °C/W, a maximum junction temperature of 150 °C, and the ambient temperature is 40 °C.

  1. (a) Find the average power delivered to the load, in watts. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total average power drawn from both supplies, in watts. [4]
  3. (c) Find the efficiency, in percent. [4]
  4. (d) Find the maximum average power dissipated in each transistor over all possible output amplitudes, in watts. [4]
  5. (e) Find the largest allowable heat-sink-to-ambient thermal resistance for each transistor, in °C/W, so that the worst-case junction temperature just reaches 150 °C. [4]
(a)

With a sinusoidal output of peak value Vp = 12 V across RL = 8 Ω, the load power is PL = Vp²/(2RL) = 144/16 = 9.00 W. This is average power, since the rms voltage is Vp/√2 = 8.485 V and 8.485²/8 gives the same result. The peak load current is 12/8 = 1.5 A, which both transistors must be rated to carry on their conducting half-cycles. The output peak of 12 V is 80 percent of the supply rail, so the stage is not near clipping.

Answer: PL = 9.00 W

(b)

Each supply delivers current only on its half-cycle: the average of a half-wave rectified sine of peak Vp/RL is (Vp/RL)/π. Each supply supplies Vcc × Vp/(π RL) = 15 × 12/(π × 8) = 7.162 W, so two supplies give Ps = 2 × 7.162 = 14.32 W. This is equivalent to Ps = 2VccVp/(π RL). The supplies deliver much more power than the load receives, and the difference is dissipated as heat in the transistors. The calculation assumes the quiescent current is zero, which is the ideal class B condition.

Answer: Ps = 14.32 W

(c)

Efficiency is the ratio of load power to supply power, η = PL/Ps = 9.00/14.32 = 0.628, or 62.8 percent. The same result follows from η = (π/4)(Vp/Vcc) = 0.7854 × 0.8 = 0.628. At the theoretical maximum swing Vp = Vcc, the efficiency would be 78.5 percent, still far above the 25 percent limit of a class A stage with a resistive load. The actual figure is lower than that maximum because the swing is only 80 percent of the supply.

Answer: η = 62.8 percent

(d)

The total dissipation in the two transistors is PD = Ps - PL = 2VccVp/(π RL) - Vp²/(2RL). Setting dPD/dVp = 0 gives 2Vcc/(π RL) = Vp/RL, so Vp = 2Vcc/π = 9.549 V. Substituting, the total maximum dissipation is 2Vcc²/(π² RL) = 2 × 225/(9.8696 × 8) = 5.699 W. By symmetry each transistor dissipates half, 2.850 W. This is the worst-case value, and note that it occurs at a lower output level than the 12 V used in parts (a) to (c), where each transistor dissipates only 2.66 W.

Answer: PD,max = 2.850 W

(e)

The thermal path from junction to ambient has total resistance θja = θjc + θcs + θsa. The allowed temperature rise is 150 - 40 = 110 °C, and the worst-case dissipation is 2.850 W, so θja,max = 110/2.850 = 38.60 °C/W. Subtracting the 1.5 and 0.5 °C/W already used gives θsa,max = 38.60 - 2.0 = 36.6 °C/W. A sink with a rating of 36.6 °C/W or lower is required, and a real design would choose one with a margin, since the junction would be exactly at its limit.

Answer: θsa,max = 36.6 °C/W

Problem 2 [A5-017] BJT and MOSFET as switches

A 5 V logic output must switch a 12 V relay coil of resistance 120 Ω, connected between the +12 V supply and the collector of an npn transistor whose emitter is grounded. The logic output connects to the base through a resistor RB. Transistor data: minimum β = 80, VBE(on) = 0.75 V and VCE(sat) = 0.2 V when saturated. The designer wants an overdrive factor of 3, meaning base current is three times the minimum needed. A second design replaces the BJT by an n-channel enhancement MOSFET with its source grounded and its gate driven directly at 5 V, with threshold Vt = 2 V and process-and-geometry constant K = μnCox(W/L) = 0.2 A/V², where triode current is iD = K[(vGS - Vt) vDS - vDS²/2].

  1. (a) Find the base resistance RB, in ohms, for the BJT design. [6]
  2. (b) Find the total power dissipated in the BJT in the on state, in milliwatts. [4]
  3. (c) For the MOSFET design, find the on-resistance for small vDS, in ohms, taking 1/[K(vGS - Vt)]. [4]
  4. (d) Find the power dissipated in the MOSFET when it carries the coil current, in milliwatts, using that on-resistance in series with the 120 Ω coil. [6]
(a)

The saturated collector current is IC = (12 - 0.2)/120 = 98.33 mA. The minimum base current to support this is IC/β = 98.33 mA/80 = 1.229 mA, and with an overdrive factor of 3 the actual base current is IB = 3.6875 mA. The base resistor sees the logic voltage minus the base-emitter drop: RB = (5 - 0.75)/3.6875 mA = 4.25/0.0036875 = 1153 Ω. A standard 1.2 kΩ resistor would give about 3.5 mA, which still exceeds the minimum 1.229 mA by a factor of nearly 3. The extra drive guarantees saturation across β spread.

Answer: RB = 1153 Ω

(b)

In the on state the transistor dissipates the collector term VCE(sat) IC plus the base term VBE IB. The collector term is 0.2 × 98.33 mA = 19.67 mW, and the base term is 0.75 × 3.6875 mA = 2.766 mW. The total is 22.43 mW. That is tiny compared with the 1.16 W absorbed by the coil, so no heat sink is needed. The base-drive term is small but nonzero, and it grows if the overdrive factor is increased.

Answer: P = 22.4 mW

(c)

With the gate at 5 V the overdrive is vGS - Vt = 3 V. For small vDS the triode current is approximately iD = K(vGS - Vt)vDS, so the channel behaves as a resistor rDS = 1/[K(vGS - Vt)] = 1/(0.2 × 3) = 1.667 Ω. This value is valid only when vDS is much smaller than the overdrive, which we verify in part (d). A larger W/L would reduce this resistance proportionally, which is how power MOSFETs reach milliohm values.

Answer: rDS = 1.667 Ω

(d)

The series loop has resistance 120 + 1.667 = 121.667 Ω, so the current is iD = 12/121.667 = 98.63 mA. The voltage across the MOSFET is vDS = iD rDS = 0.1644 V, which is much less than the 3 V overdrive, so the triode and small-vDS assumptions hold. The MOSFET dissipation is iD² rDS = (0.09863)² × 1.667 = 16.2 mW. Because no gate current flows in steady state, no drive power is needed, unlike the BJT's base term. The two devices carry nearly the same current, but the MOSFET dissipates less.

Answer: P = 16.2 mW

Problem 3 [A5-018] CMOS inverter and logic gate design

A static CMOS inverter is designed for a 3.3 V supply. The n-channel transistor has threshold Vtn = +0.6 V and conduction parameter Kn = μnCox(W/L)n = 400 μA/V². The p-channel transistor has threshold Vtp = -0.7 V and Kp = 150 μA/V². In saturation the drain current of either transistor is ½K(|vGS| - |Vt|)². Channel-length modulation is neglected. The inverter input and output are tied together for the switching-threshold calculation, so that both transistors are saturated at VM. A NAND2 gate is also to be derived from this inverter in part (d), where the inverter's nMOS device has (W/L) = 4 and its pMOS device has (W/L) = 10.

  1. (a) Find the switching threshold VM of this inverter, in volts. [5]
  2. (b) Find the Kp, in μA/V², required for the switching threshold to be exactly VDD/2 with Kn unchanged. [5]
  3. (c) For that redesigned inverter, find the peak (short-circuit) current drawn from the supply at the switching threshold, in microamperes. [5]
  4. (d) A two-input NAND gate must have the same worst-case pull-down and pull-up strengths as the original inverter. Find the required (W/L) of each series nMOS transistor. [5]
(a)

At the switching threshold vin = vout = VM and both devices are saturated with equal currents, so Kn(VM - Vtn)² = Kp(VDD - VM - |Vtp|)². Taking square roots gives √Kn (VM - Vtn) = √Kp (VDD - VM - |Vtp|). Define r = √(Kp/Kn) = √(150/400) = 0.6124. Solving, VM = [r(VDD - |Vtp|) + Vtn]/(1 + r) = [0.6124 × 2.6 + 0.6]/1.6124 = 2.1922/1.6124 = 1.360 V. This is below VDD/2 = 1.65 V because the n device is stronger, so the transfer curve is shifted toward the low side.

Answer: VM = 1.360 V

(b)

Setting VM = 1.65 V in the same relation gives √Kn(1.65 - 0.6) = √Kp(3.3 - 1.65 - 0.7), or √Kn × 1.05 = √Kp × 0.95. Then √(Kp/Kn) = 1.05/0.95 = 1.1053 and Kp/Kn = 1.2216. With Kn = 400 μA/V², Kp = 488.6 μA/V². The p device must therefore be stronger than the n device by 22 percent, which is possible since the p-device mobility is lower and the pMOS must be about 2.5 times wider in W/L at equal mobility ratios. The threshold voltages are unequal in magnitude, which is why the ratio is not simply set by mobility.

Answer: Kp = 488.6 μA/V²

(c)

At VM both devices carry the same current, which is also the peak short-circuit current. Using the nMOS side: Ipeak = ½Kn(VM - Vtn)² = 0.5 × 400 μA/V² × (1.65 - 0.6)² = 200 μA/V² × 1.1025 V² = 220.5 μA. The pMOS side gives ½ × 488.6 × (0.95)² = 220.5 μA, the same value, which checks the algebra. This short-circuit current flows briefly during each transition and contributes to the dynamic power of the gate in addition to the load-charging power.

Answer: Ipeak = 220.5 μA

(d)

In a NAND2 gate the two nMOS transistors are in series, so for the worst-case pull-down (both on) the combined resistance doubles unless each device is made twice as strong. Keeping the pull-down strength equal to the inverter's requires each series nMOS device to have twice the inverter value: (W/L) = 2 × 4 = 8. The two pMOS transistors are in parallel, and the worst-case pull-up has only one pMOS on, so each keeps (W/L) = 10. The NAND2 therefore costs more area than the inverter, a factor of about (8 + 8 + 10 + 10)/(4 + 10) = 2.6 in transistor width.

Answer: (W/L)n = 8

Problem 4 [A5-019] Propagation delay and power in CMOS

A CMOS inverter in a 1.8 V process drives a total load capacitance CL = 50 fF, which includes wiring and the input capacitance of the next gate. The nMOS device has conduction parameter Kn = μnCox(W/L)n = 500 μA/V² and the pMOS device has Kp = 250 μA/V². Use the approximate delay models tPHL = 1.6 CL/(Kn VDD) and tPLH = 1.6 CL/(Kp VDD), which are valid for this process. The inverter belongs to a chain in a controller whose clock is 200 MHz, and the average switching activity is 0.15 transitions of the output per clock cycle taken as full charge-discharge cycles. Part (d) considers a ring oscillator made of 11 identical inverters, each with the same load and the average delay found in part (b).

  1. (a) Find the high-to-low propagation delay tPHL, in picoseconds. [5]
  2. (b) Find the low-to-high propagation delay tPLH, in picoseconds. [4]
  3. (c) Find the average dynamic power for the inverter in microwatts, using P = α CL VDD² f. [5]
  4. (d) Find the oscillation frequency of the 11-stage ring oscillator, in megahertz, using the average of tPHL and tPLH as the delay of each stage. [6]
(a)

The pull-down delay is tPHL = 1.6 CL/(Kn VDD) = 1.6 × 50×10⁻¹⁵ F/(500×10⁻⁶ A/V² × 1.8 V). The numerator is 80×10⁻¹⁵ and the denominator is 9×10⁻⁴, so tPHL = 8.889×10⁻¹¹ s = 88.9 ps. The expression is the time for the nMOS device, supplying a roughly constant average current, to remove half the load charge CL VDD/2, scaled by a factor that accounts for the triode portion. A faster fall needs a larger Kn, a smaller load capacitance, or a higher supply.

Answer: tPHL = 88.9 ps

(b)

The pull-up delay uses the pMOS device, with Kp = 250 μA/V² being half of Kn. Substituting, tPLH = 1.6 × 50 fF/(250 μA/V² × 1.8 V) = 80×10⁻¹⁵/4.5×10⁻⁴ = 1.778×10⁻¹⁰ s = 177.8 ps. The delay is twice tPHL because the pMOS device is only half as strong, which is why equal-sized transistors give unequal rise and fall times. Widening the pMOS device by a factor of 2 would equalise the delays at 88.9 ps, at the cost of larger input capacitance for the driving stage.

Answer: tPLH = 177.8 ps

(c)

Each full output cycle charges and discharges CL through the supply, drawing energy CL VDD² from it. At activity α = 0.15 and clock f = 200 MHz, the power is P = α CL VDD² f = 0.15 × 50×10⁻¹⁵ × (1.8)² × 200×10⁶. With (1.8)² = 3.24, 0.15 × 50×10⁻¹⁵ = 7.5×10⁻¹⁵, times 3.24 gives 2.43×10⁻¹⁴, times 2×10⁸ gives 4.86×10⁻⁶ W. So the dynamic power is 4.86 μW per inverter. The power falls with the square of the supply voltage, so a reduction to 1.2 V would cut it by 56 percent.

Answer: P = 4.86 μW

(d)

The average stage delay is tp = (88.89 + 177.78)/2 = 133.33 ps. In a ring of N = 11 inverters a transition travels around the ring twice per period, so T = 2 N tp = 2 × 11 × 133.33 ps = 2933 ps, and f = 1/T = 340.9 MHz. N must be odd for the ring to oscillate, which is why 11 is chosen. The measured frequency of a fabricated ring is often used to extract tp for the process, since the ring needs no external clock or input signal.

Answer: f = 341 MHz

Problem 5 [A5-020] Amplifier design to meet a specification, comparing topologies

A preamplifier for a piezo vibration sensor must give an overall voltage gain from source to load of at least 40 V/V in magnitude. The source has resistance Rs = 5 kΩ, the load is RL = 10 kΩ, and the collector (or drain) resistor is 4.7 kΩ in each candidate, with the output taken across the load through a large coupling capacitor that is a short at signal frequencies. Option 1 is a common-emitter BJT stage biased at IC = 1.2 mA with β = 150, VA = 100 V and VT = 25 mV, with the emitter bypassed and the source coupled to the base.
