Option 2 is a common-source MOSFET stage biased at ID = 1.2 mA with K = μnCox(W/L) = 4 mA/V² (iD = ½K Vov²) and VA = 50 V, source bypassed, gate coupled to the source with no dc path loss.

  1. (a) Find the overall voltage gain vo/vs of Option 1, including the source resistance and ro. [6]
  2. (b) Find the overall voltage gain vo/vs of Option 2, including ro. [6]
  3. (c) Find the transconductance, in mS, that Option 2 would need to match the gain magnitude of Option 1, keeping the same ro as in part (b). [4]
  4. (d) For that transconductance and the given K, find the drain current needed, in mA, neglecting the resulting change in ro. [4]
(a)

At IC = 1.2 mA the BJT has gm = IC/VT = 1.2 mA/25 mV = 48 mS, rπ = β/gm = 150/48 mS = 3125 Ω and ro = VA/IC = 100/1.2 mA = 83.3 kΩ. The effective collector load is RC || RL || ro = 4.7 k || 10 k || 83.3 k = 3079 Ω. The input divider gives vπ/vs = rπ/(Rs + rπ) = 3125/8125 = 0.3846. The overall gain is vo/vs = -0.3846 × gm × 3079 = -0.3846 × 0.048 × 3079 = -56.85 V/V. The magnitude exceeds 40, so Option 1 meets the specification even though the source loses 62 percent of its signal at the input.

Answer: Av1 = -56.85 V/V

(b)

For the MOSFET, Vov = √(2ID/K) = √(2 × 1.2 mA/4 mA/V²) = 0.7746 V and gm = 2ID/Vov = 2.4 mA/0.7746 V = 3.098 mS. The output resistance is ro = VA/ID = 50/1.2 mA = 41.7 kΩ. The effective load is 4.7 k || 10 k || 41.7 k = 2969 Ω. The gate draws no current at signal frequencies, so there is no input loss and vo/vs = -gm × 2969 = -3.098 mS × 2969 = -9.20 V/V. This is far below the 40 V/V requirement, because the MOSFET at this current has a much lower transconductance than the BJT.

Answer: Av2 = -9.20 V/V

(c)

To reach the gain magnitude of 56.85 with no input-divider loss, the required gm is gm = |Av|/R'L = 56.85/2969 Ω = 19.14 mS. This is about 6.2 times the 3.098 mS available at 1.2 mA. For the BJT, gm = IC/VT is linear in current, while for a MOSFET gm = √(2KID) rises only as the square root of current, so the MOSFET must be pushed much harder, or made wider, to compete at the same current and supply voltage.

Answer: gm = 19.14 mS

(d)

From gm = √(2K ID), ID = gm²/(2K) = (19.14×10⁻³)²/(2 × 4×10⁻³) = 3.664×10⁻⁴/8×10⁻³ = 45.8 mA. This is 38 times the 1.2 mA assumed for the BJT, and the power at a 12 V supply would be more than half a watt, which is unreasonable for a sensor preamplifier. The better route is a larger K, for example a wider device, which reduces the current needed. A designer would choose the BJT for this gain target, or a MOSFET with a much larger W/L ratio at the same current.

Answer: ID = 45.8 mA

A5 Practice Paper 5

Problem 1 [A5-021] Diode circuits, clippers and rectifiers

A small workshop charger for a 12.6 V lead-acid battery is built from a 60 Hz step-down transformer feeding a four-diode bridge rectifier. The transformer secondary delivers 18.0 V rms, sinusoidal and open-circuit, and its winding resistance may be neglected. Each diode is modelled as an ideal diode in series with a constant 0.70 V drop. The battery is modelled as an ideal 12.6 V source in series with an internal resistance of 0.20 Ω, and a separate series resistor R is wired between the bridge output and the battery. The positive output terminal of the bridge connects through R to the battery positive terminal, and the bridge negative terminal connects directly to the battery negative terminal. Initially R = 1.00 Ω. There is no filter capacitor, so current flows only while the rectified voltage exceeds the battery voltage plus the two diode drops.

  1. (a) Find the peak charging current with R = 1.00 Ω. [5]
  2. (b) Find the total conduction angle per half-cycle of the supply, in degrees. [4]
  3. (c) Find the average charging current with R = 1.00 Ω. [6]
  4. (d) The battery manufacturer asks for an average charging current of exactly 3.00 A. Find the series resistance R required. [5]
(a)

Two diodes conduct at any instant, so the diode drops add to 1.40 V. The secondary peak is Vp = 18.0√2 = 25.46 V. At the peak, the net driving voltage is Vp − 1.40 − 12.60 = 11.46 V, and it acts across the total loop resistance Rt = R + 0.20 = 1.20 Ω (diodes treated as ideal apart from the constant drop). Peak current is Ipk = 11.46 / 1.20 = 9.55 A. Assumption: the transformer is stiff, so its secondary voltage stays sinusoidal even while the charger draws current. Check: this peak is well below the 30 A or so a typical small bridge package can carry for a single cycle, so the model is physically reasonable.

Answer: 9.55 A

(b)

Current flows only when Vp sinθ exceeds the threshold Vo = 12.60 + 1.40 = 14.00 V. The turn-on angle is θ1 = asin(14.00 / 25.456) = asin(0.5500) = 33.37 degrees. By symmetry, conduction ends at 180 − 33.37 = 146.63 degrees. The conduction angle per half-cycle is therefore 146.63 − 33.37 = 113.27 degrees, which is 0.63 of the half-cycle. Reasoning: because the threshold is more than half of the peak, the diodes are off for nearly 37 percent of every half-cycle, and all the charge is delivered in a short, tall pulse. This is why an unfiltered bridge into a battery produces a high peak-to-average current ratio.

Answer: 113.3 degrees

(c)

Average current over the rectified waveform has period π, so Iavg = (1/π)∫(Vp sinθ − Vo)/Rt dθ from θ1 to π − θ1. The integral gives (1/(π Rt))[2Vp cosθ1 − Vo(π − 2θ1)]. Here cosθ1 = √(1 − 0.55²) = 0.8352 and θ1 = 0.5824 rad, so π − 2θ1 = 1.9768 rad. Then 2Vp cosθ1 = 2(25.456)(0.8352) = 42.52 V, and Vo(π − 2θ1) = 14.00(1.9768) = 27.68 V. The difference is 14.84 V. Dividing by πRt = π(1.20) = 3.770 Ω gives Iavg = 3.94 A. This is the figure the charger actually delivers on average to the battery, about 41 percent of the 9.55 A peak.

Answer: 3.94 A

(d)

The average-current expression is a decreasing function of the total resistance Rt, because the peak current (Vp − Vo)/Rt falls as Rt rises, while the conduction angle stays fixed at 113.3 degrees since Vo and Vp do not depend on R. Because the bracket is independent of R, the expression inverts directly: Iavg = (1/(π Rt))[2Vp cosθ1 − Vo(π − 2θ1)] where the bracket is the fixed quantity 14.84 V. Since θ1 depends only on Vo and Vp, the bracket does not change with R. Therefore Rt = 14.84 / (π × 3.00) = 1.575 Ω and R = 1.575 − 0.20 = 1.375 Ω. Check: with this R the peak current is 11.46 / 1.575 = 7.28 A, lower than before, as expected. Choose the nearest standard value, 1.4 Ω, in practice.

Answer: 1.37 Ω

Problem 2 [A5-022] Zener regulators and power supply filtering

A 9 V rail for a sensor interface is produced by a Zener shunt regulator fed from a full-wave bridge rectifier and a reservoir capacitor, running from the 60 Hz mains. The Zener diode is modelled by a battery of 8.90 V in series with a dynamic resistance of 6.0 Ω, valid for Zener currents above a minimum of 4.0 mA. A series resistor Rs connects the capacitor output to the cathode of the Zener, and the load connects across the Zener. The load current varies between 0 and 50 mA. The unregulated voltage across the reservoir capacitor, measured at its average value, varies with mains conditions between 12.0 V and 16.0 V. The sensor interface requires the regulated output to stay within the Zener model limits throughout. Assume the Zener power rating must be checked at the worst case only.

  1. (a) Find the largest series resistance Rs that keeps the Zener above its minimum current at worst-case input and load. [6]
  2. (b) A standard 56 Ω resistor is chosen. Find the worst-case Zener power dissipation. [5]
  3. (c) The filter capacitor supplies an average current of 70 mA and the peak-to-peak ripple on it is limited to 1.5 V. Find the capacitance, using the full-wave ripple formula with a 120 Hz ripple frequency. [5]
  4. (d) Estimate the peak-to-peak ripple at the regulated output with the 56 Ω resistor, assuming the load current is constant. [4]
(a)

The worst case for the Zener minimum current is the lowest input, 12.0 V, with maximum load, 50 mA. At the knee the Zener current is 4.0 mA, so the regulated output is Vo = 8.90 + 6.0 × 0.004 = 8.924 V. The current through Rs is the load plus the Zener current, 50 + 4 = 54 mA. Writing the voltage drop, Rs = (12.0 − 8.924) / 0.054 = 56.96 Ω. Any larger Rs would let the Zener current fall below 4 mA at that corner, taking it out of regulation. So Rs must not exceed about 57 Ω, and the nearest lower standard value of 56 Ω is a sensible selection.

Answer: 57.0 Ω

(b)

The worst case for Zener power is the highest input, 16.0 V, with the load removed, so all the current flows through the Zener. The loop equation is 16.0 = Iz Rs + 8.90 + 6.0 Iz, hence Iz = (16.0 − 8.90) / (56 + 6.0) = 7.10 / 62 = 0.11452 A. The Zener voltage is Vz = 8.90 + 6.0 × 0.11452 = 9.587 V. The power is P = Vz Iz = 9.587 × 0.11452 = 1.098 W. A 1 W part would be overstressed, so a 2 W Zener or a bigger heat-sinked device is needed. Reasoning: the worst-case power occurs when the load is lightest, which is the opposite corner from the worst-case regulation.

Answer: 1.10 W

(c)

For a full-wave rectifier with a reservoir capacitor, the capacitor discharges for nearly one ripple period T = 1/(2f) = 1/120 s = 8.33 ms between peaks. The charge drawn in that time is ΔQ = I T and the ripple is ΔV = ΔQ/C, which rearranges to C = I / (2 f ΔV). Substituting I = 0.070 A, f = 60 Hz and ΔV = 1.5 V, C = 0.070 / (120 × 1.5) = 0.070 / 180 = 3.889 × 10⁻⁴ F, so C = 389 µF. In practice the next larger standard value, 470 µF, is used, which leaves margin for capacitor tolerance and ageing, and the diode conduction interval, which was ignored here, is short.

Answer: 389 µF

(d)

The ripple at the capacitor appears across the divider formed by Rs and the Zener dynamic resistance rz, with the load current assumed constant so that it contributes no ripple. The ripple transfer ratio is rz / (Rs + rz) = 6.0 / (56 + 6.0) = 0.09677. The output ripple is therefore 1.5 V × 0.09677 = 0.1452 V peak to peak. This is a reduction of about 10.3 times, or 20.3 dB. A smaller dynamic resistance, or a larger Rs fed from a higher unregulated voltage, would improve the rejection. Assumption: the small-signal model of the Zener is linear over the ripple excursion and the load is a constant-current drain.

Answer: 0.145 V

Problem 3 [A5-023] Thyristors, SCR and TRIAC circuits

A 2.40 kW resistive electric heater is supplied from a 240 V rms, 60 Hz single-phase source through a TRIAC phase-angle controller. The heater resistance is constant at 24.0 Ω. The TRIAC is triggered at the same firing delay angle α in each half-cycle, measured from the preceding zero crossing of the supply voltage, and it turns off at each current zero. The TRIAC on-state voltage drop is negligible. The process engineer wants the heater to deliver only 800 W, one third of its rating, for a slow warm-up stage of an industrial oven. The controller must be commissioned by entering the firing delay as a time rather than an angle.

  1. (a) Find the firing angle α, in degrees, that produces an average power of 800 W in the heater. [7]
  2. (b) Find the rms load current at this setting. [4]
  3. (c) Find the power factor at the supply terminals. [5]
  4. (d) Find the firing delay from each zero crossing in milliseconds. [4]
(a)

For a resistive load with full-wave phase control, the rms load voltage satisfies Vrms,load² = Vs² [1 − α/π + sin(2α)/(2π)], where Vs is the supply rms voltage. The power is P = Vrms,load² / R, so P = (Vs²/R)[1 − α/π + sin(2α)/(2π)]. The full-conduction power is 240² / 24.0 = 2400 W, so the bracket must equal 800/2400 = 0.3333. This transcendental equation has no closed form, so solve it numerically: at α = 90 degrees the bracket is 0.500, and at α = 105.36 degrees (1.8389 rad) it gives 1 − 0.5854 + sin(3.6778)/(6.2832) = 0.4146 − 0.0813 = 0.3333. Thus α = 105.4 degrees.

Answer: 105.4 degrees

(b)

The load is resistive, so the rms current follows directly from the delivered power: P = Irms² R, which gives Irms = √(P/R) = √(800/24.0) = √33.33 = 5.774 A. This takes account of the full non-sinusoidal waveform because the power and rms voltage formulas of part (a) already use the true rms value. Check: the rms load voltage is Irms R = 5.774 × 24.0 = 138.6 V, which is 57.7 percent of the supply, consistent with the square root of the 0.3333 conduction fraction. The peak instantaneous current occurs right after firing and equals 339.4 sin(105.36 degrees) / 24.0 = 13.6 A, which the TRIAC must be rated to carry repetitively.

Answer: 5.77 A

(c)

The power factor is the real power divided by the apparent power at the supply terminals, PF = P / (Vs Irms). The TRIAC controller is in series with the heater, so the supply current equals the load current. The apparent power is S = 240 × 5.774 = 1385.6 VA, and the real power is 800 W. PF = 800 / 1385.6 = 0.577. The result also equals √(P / P_full) = √0.3333 for a resistive load, which is a useful check. The low power factor is caused by the distortion of the current waveform and the displacement of its fundamental, not by any reactive element. Utilities in Ontario penalise poor power factor on larger industrial loads, so this matters.

Answer: 0.577

(d)

The firing delay time is the fraction of a supply period corresponding to α. One period at 60 Hz is 1/60 = 16.667 ms, so 360 degrees corresponds to 16.667 ms. The delay is t = (α / 360) × 16.667 ms = (105.36 / 360) × 16.667 = 4.878 ms. Equivalently, t = α / (2π f) with α in radians: t = 1.8389 / (2π × 60) = 1.8389 / 376.99 = 4.878 ms. Because the TRIAC fires in both half-cycles, the same delay is applied after every zero crossing, giving a symmetric waveform with no DC component in the supply current. The commissioning entry is therefore about 4.9 ms. Assume the controller times from a clean zero-crossing detector.

Answer: 4.88 ms

Problem 4 [A5-024] BJT bias circuits and operating point

An engineer must design a four-resistor (voltage-divider) bias network for a silicon NPN transistor in a common-emitter stage powered from a single 15.0 V supply. The nominal current gain is β = 120 and VBE = 0.700 V in the active region. The divider R1 runs from the supply to the base and R2 from the base to ground. RC connects the supply to the collector, and RE connects the emitter to ground. Design targets: collector current IC = 2.00 mA, emitter voltage VE = 2.00 V, and collector-emitter voltage VCE = 6.00 V. The divider current is to be set at ten times the nominal base current. Use IE = IC (β + 1)/β for the emitter resistor and treat the collector current as flowing wholly through RC. Resistor values are to be left unrounded for the later check.

  1. (a) Find RE. [4]
  2. (b) Find RC. [3]
  3. (c) Find R2, with the divider current equal to ten times the base current. [4]
  4. (d) Find R1. [5]
  5. (e) The transistor is replaced by one with β = 300. Using the unrounded resistor values and a Thévenin equivalent of the divider, find the new collector current. [4]
(a)

The emitter current is IE = IC (β + 1)/β = 2.00 mA × 121/120 = 2.0167 mA. The emitter resistor must drop the specified 2.00 V at this current, so RE = VE / IE = 2.00 / 2.0167 × 10³ = 991.7 Ω. A standard 1.0 kΩ resistor would be close enough in practice, moving the bias point by well under one percent. The reasoning behind choosing VE as a fixed fraction of the supply is to make the bias less sensitive to β: a larger VE gives more negative feedback through RE, but it also costs headroom for the output swing. Here 2.0 V is about 13 percent of the supply.

Answer: 992 Ω

(b)

The collector voltage is VC = VE + VCE = 2.00 + 6.00 = 8.00 V. The drop across RC is 15.0 − 8.00 = 7.00 V, and it carries the collector current of 2.00 mA. Hence RC = 7.00 / 0.00200 = 3500 Ω, or 3.50 kΩ. Check the active region: VCB = VC − VB = 8.00 − 2.70 = 5.30 V, which is positive, so the collector-base junction is reverse biased and the transistor is in the active region as assumed. The quiescent point sits at 6 V of VCE out of 13 V available after RE, leaving room for symmetric swing of several volts on the output in each direction.

Answer: 3.50 kΩ

(c)

The base voltage is VB = VE + VBE = 2.00 + 0.700 = 2.700 V. The base current is IB = IC / β = 2.00 mA / 120 = 16.67 µA. The divider current is ten times this, I2 = 166.7 µA. All of that current flows through R2, so R2 = VB / I2 = 2.700 / 166.7 × 10⁻⁶ = 16 200 Ω = 16.2 kΩ. The factor of ten is a standard rule of thumb: it makes the base voltage 'stiff', meaning that it changes by only a few percent when IB changes with β, while avoiding an excessively low input resistance that would load the signal source in an amplifier stage.

Answer: 16.2 kΩ

(d)

R1 carries the divider current plus the base current, since the base current branches off at the base node: I1 = I2 + IB = 166.7 + 16.67 = 183.3 µA. The voltage across R1 is the supply minus the base voltage, 15.0 − 2.700 = 12.30 V. Hence R1 = 12.30 / 183.3 × 10⁻⁶ = 67 091 Ω = 67.1 kΩ. A student who forgets the base current would use only I2 and get 73.8 kΩ, which would lower the base voltage and shift the whole bias point. The parallel combination R1 || R2 = 13.06 kΩ is the resistance the Thévenin source presents to the base in the next part.

Answer: 67.1 kΩ

(e)

Replace the divider by its Thévenin equivalent: VTH = 15.0 × R2 / (R1 + R2) = 15.0 × 16.2 / 83.29 = 2.917 V, and RTH = R1 || R2 = 13.04 kΩ. The base loop equation is VTH = IB RTH + VBE + IE RE with IE = (β + 1) IB, so IB = (VTH − VBE) / (RTH + (β + 1) RE) = (2.917 − 0.700) / (13 040 + 301 × 991.7) = 2.217 / 311 540 = 7.116 µA. The collector current is IC = β IB = 300 × 7.116 µA = 2.135 mA. Although β rose by 150 percent, IC rose by only about 7 percent, which shows the benefit of the stiff divider and emitter degeneration.

Answer: 2.14 mA

Problem 5 [A5-025] BJT small-signal model and common-emitter amplifier

A common-emitter amplifier uses an NPN transistor biased at IC = 1.50 mA, with β = 150, Early voltage VA = 100 V and thermal voltage VT = 25.0 mV. The emitter resistor is fully bypassed at signal frequencies, and all coupling capacitors are short circuits. The signal source has open-circuit voltage vs and series resistance Rs = 2.00 kΩ. The bias divider presents an equivalent resistance RB = R1 || R2 = 20.0 kΩ from base to signal ground. The collector resistor is RC = 4.70 kΩ and the load resistor RL = 10.0 kΩ is capacitively coupled to the collector. Use the hybrid-π model with rπ = β/gm and ro = VA/IC, and neglect the base spreading resistance and rμ.

  1. (a) Find rπ. [3]
  2. (b) Find the input resistance seen by the source. [3]
  3. (c) Find the overall voltage gain vo/vs, including ro, as a signed number. [6]
  4. (d) The designer wants the overall gain magnitude reduced to 40 by leaving an unbypassed emitter resistor RE1 in the emitter circuit. Neglecting ro for this part, find RE1. [8]
(a)

The transconductance is gm = IC / VT = 1.50 mA / 25.0 mV = 0.0600 S, or 60 mS. The small-signal base-emitter resistance is rπ = β / gm = 150 / 0.0600 = 2500 Ω = 2.50 kΩ. For completeness, ro = VA / IC = 100 / 1.50 mA = 66.67 kΩ, which is used in part (c). Reasoning: rπ is the slope of the base-emitter input characteristic, and it depends on the bias current, not on the supply or the resistors, so it can be computed directly from the transistor data and the chosen operating point.

Answer: 2.50 kΩ

(b)

With the emitter bypassed, the resistance looking into the base is rπ alone. The bias divider presents RB = 20.0 kΩ in parallel with this, because both connect from the base to signal ground. The input resistance seen by the source is Rin = RB || rπ = (20 000 × 2500) / (20 000 + 2500) = 50 000 000 / 22 500 = 2222 Ω = 2.22 kΩ. Observation: the base-circuit resistance rπ dominates, so the divider does not load the input badly. Since the source resistance is of a similar size, about half of the source voltage appears at the base, which affects the overall gain in the next part.

Answer: 2.22 kΩ

(c)

The voltage gain from base to output is −gm (ro || RC || RL), because the collector current gm vbe flows in the parallel of ro, RC and RL. First RC || RL = 4.70 × 10.0 / 14.70 = 3.197 kΩ. Including ro, the effective load is 1 / (1/66.67 + 1/3.197) kΩ = 3.051 kΩ. The base-to-output gain is therefore −0.0600 × 3051 = −183.1. The input voltage divider factor is Rin / (Rin + Rs) = 2222 / 4222 = 0.5263. The overall gain is vo/vs = −183.1 × 0.5263 = −96.3. The negative sign shows phase inversion. Neglecting ro would have given −101.0, a difference of about 4.8 percent, which is acceptable in hand design.

Answer: -96.3

(d)

With an unbypassed RE1 and ro neglected, the resistance into the base is Rb = rπ + (β + 1) RE1, and the base-to-output gain is −β (RC || RL) / Rb. The overall gain magnitude is |A| = [Ri / (Ri + Rs)] × β (RC || RL) / Rb, where Ri = RB || Rb. With RC || RL = 3.197 kΩ, setting |A| = 40 and solving numerically gives RE1 = 43.6 Ω. Check: Rb = 2500 + 151 × 43.6 = 9083 Ω, Ri = 20 000 × 9083 / 29 083 = 6246 Ω, factor 6246 / 8246 = 0.7575, base-to-output gain 150 × 3197 / 9083 = 52.8, and the product is 40.0. The price of the gain reduction is a much higher input resistance and better gain stability against β.

Answer: 43.6 Ω

A5 Practice Paper 6

Problem 1 [A5-026] Common-collector and common-base stages

A sensor with open-circuit voltage vs and Thévenin resistance Rs = 10.0 kΩ must drive a 200 Ω actuator. An emitter follower is placed between them. The NPN transistor is biased at IC = 5.00 mA with β = 100 and thermal voltage VT = 25.0 mV; neglect ro and base spreading resistance. The emitter resistor is RE = 2.00 kΩ, and the actuator RL = 200 Ω is capacitively coupled to the emitter, so signal current divides between RE and RL. The bias network presents RB = 60.0 kΩ from the base to signal ground. The coupling capacitors are short circuits at the signal frequency. In the last part, a separate common-base stage is analysed: it is biased at IC = 2.00 mA, has α = β/(β + 1) with β = 100, a collector resistor RC = 4.00 kΩ and a load RL2 = 12.0 kΩ, with the base at signal ground.

  1. (a) Find the resistance seen by the source looking into the follower stage, including RB. [5]
  2. (b) Find the overall voltage gain vo/vs of the follower with the 10.0 kΩ source resistance. [5]
  3. (c) Find the output resistance seen by the actuator looking back into the follower (including RE in parallel). [5]
  4. (d) For the common-base stage, find the voltage gain from the emitter terminal to the output. [5]
(a)

The small-signal parameters are gm = 5.00 mA / 25.0 mV = 0.200 S and rπ = β / gm = 100 / 0.200 = 500 Ω. The emitter load seen by the signal is RE || RL = 2000 × 200 / 2200 = 181.8 Ω. The resistance looking into the base is Rb = rπ + (β + 1)(RE || RL) = 500 + 101 × 181.8 = 18 864 Ω. The bias network RB = 60 kΩ is in parallel with this, so Rin = 60 000 × 18 864 / (60 000 + 18 864) = 14 352 Ω ≈ 14.35 kΩ. Observation: the follower multiplies its emitter load by (β + 1), so the stage presents a resistance roughly seventy-five times larger than the 200 Ω load that it drives.

Answer: 14.35 kΩ

(b)

The voltage division at the input is Rin / (Rin + Rs) = 14 352 / 24 352 = 0.5893. The gain from base to emitter output is (β + 1)(RE || RL) / [rπ + (β + 1)(RE || RL)] = 18 364 / 18 864 = 0.9735. The overall gain is vo/vs = 0.5893 × 0.9735 = 0.5737. Without the follower, connecting the 10 kΩ source directly to the 200 Ω load would give 200 / 10 200 = 0.0196, so the follower improves the gain by a factor of about 29. The reasoning is the same as impedance matching in buffer use: the stage transforms a high source resistance down to a level comparable with the load. The output is in phase with the input.

Answer: 0.574

(c)

Looking back from the output, the resistance at the emitter is the source-side resistance divided by (β + 1). The source-side resistance at the base is Rs || RB = 10 000 × 60 000 / 70 000 = 8571 Ω. Adding rπ gives 9071 Ω, and dividing by β + 1 = 101 gives 89.8 Ω looking into the emitter. This is in parallel with RE = 2000 Ω, so Rout = 89.8 × 2000 / 2089.8 = 86.0 Ω. The load of 200 Ω is therefore driven from about 86 Ω, a much better match than the 10 kΩ source alone. Assumption: ro is infinite, which is consistent with the problem statement and slightly underestimates the output resistance of a real device.

Answer: 86.0 Ω

(d)

In a common-base stage the signal is applied at the emitter and the output is taken at the collector. With IC = 2.00 mA, gm = 2.00 mA / 25.0 mV = 0.0800 S, and the emitter current is IE = IC / α. The resistance looking into the emitter is re = VT / IE = α / gm. The collector current is α ie, and it flows into RC || RL2 = 4.00 × 12.0 / 16.0 = 3.00 kΩ, so the gain is vo/ve = α (RC || RL2) / re = gm (RC || RL2) = 0.0800 × 3000 = 240. The α factors cancel exactly. The output is in phase with the input, and the emitter input resistance is only about 12.4 Ω, so the stage suits current-source or high-frequency use.

Answer: 240

Problem 2 [A5-027] MOSFET bias and operating regions

An n-channel enhancement MOSFET is used as a source-degenerated common-source stage from a single 12.0 V supply. In saturation its drain current obeys ID = (Kn/2)(VGS − Vt)², with Kn = 2.00 mA/V² and threshold Vt = 0.800 V, and channel-length modulation is ignored. The gate is held by a resistive divider from the 12.0 V supply to ground, with R1 on the supply side and R2 to ground, and the gate draws no current. The source resistor RS connects the source to ground and the drain resistor RD connects the drain to the supply. Design targets: ID = 1.50 mA, source voltage VS = 1.50 V and drain voltage VD = 7.00 V. The divider must have a total resistance R1 + R2 = 1.50 MΩ so that it presents a high input resistance.

  1. (a) Find the gate voltage VG required. [4]
  2. (b) Find RD. [3]
  3. (c) Find R2. [4]
  4. (d) Find R1. [3]
  5. (e) A replacement part has Vt = 1.20 V with the same Kn. Using the resistors above, find the new drain current, and state whether it remains in saturation. [6]
(a)

In saturation, 1.50 mA = (2.00 mA/V² / 2)(VOV)², where VOV = VGS − Vt. So VOV² = 1.50 / 1.00 = 1.50 V² and VOV = 1.2247 V. Then VGS = Vt + VOV = 0.800 + 1.2247 = 2.0247 V. The gate sits above the source by VGS, so VG = VS + VGS = 1.50 + 2.0247 = 3.525 V. The source resistor sets VS, and the divider must hold the gate at this voltage. Check the saturation condition at the design point: VDS = VD − VS = 7.00 − 1.50 = 5.50 V, which exceeds VOV = 1.22 V, so the device is in saturation as assumed and the square-law model applies.

Answer: 3.525 V

(b)

The drain resistor carries the whole drain current of 1.50 mA, because the gate current is zero, and it must drop the difference between the supply and the drain voltage: 12.0 − 7.00 = 5.00 V. Therefore RD = 5.00 / 1.50 × 10⁻³ = 3333 Ω = 3.33 kΩ. For completeness the source resistor is RS = VS / ID = 1.50 / 1.50 × 10⁻³ = 1000 Ω, which is used in part (e). The drain at 7.00 V is roughly midway between the supply and the edge of triode (VS + VOV = 2.72 V), so the output can swing about 4 V up and 4 V down before leaving saturation.

Answer: 3.33 kΩ

(c)

With the total divider resistance fixed at 1.50 MΩ, the divider current is I = 12.0 / 1.50 × 10⁶ = 8.00 µA. The gate voltage is the voltage across R2, so R2 = VG / I = 3.5247 / 8.00 × 10⁻⁶ = 440 593 Ω ≈ 441 kΩ. Equivalent form: VG = 12.0 × R2 / (R1 + R2), so R2 / 1.50 MΩ = 3.5247 / 12.0 = 0.29373 and R2 = 440.6 kΩ. Since the gate current is zero (insulated gate), the divider current is the same through both resistors, which makes the MOSFET design simpler than the BJT divider, where the base current has to be accounted for.

Answer: 441 kΩ

(d)

The two divider resistors sum to 1.50 MΩ, so R1 = 1.50 MΩ − R2 = 1 500 000 − 440 593 = 1 059 407 Ω ≈ 1.06 MΩ. Check: the voltage across R1 is 8.00 µA × 1.0594 MΩ = 8.475 V, and 12.0 − 8.475 = 3.525 V, which agrees with the required gate voltage. The Thévenin resistance of the divider seen by the gate is R1 || R2 = 311.5 kΩ, which does not affect the DC bias because the gate current is zero, but sets the low-frequency input resistance of the amplifier stage when the signal is applied through a coupling capacitor.

Answer: 1.06 MΩ

(e)

The gate voltage is unchanged at 3.525 V because the divider does not depend on the transistor. The loop equation is VG = VGS + ID RS, with VGS = Vt + √(2 ID / Kn). Writing ID = (Kn/2)(VG − ID RS − Vt)² with Vt = 1.20 V, RS = 1000 Ω and Kn = 2.00 mA/V², and solving the quadratic by choosing the root with VOV > 0, gives ID = 1.220 mA, VOV = 1.105 V and VGS = 2.305 V. Then VD = 12.0 − 1.220 × 3.333 = 7.93 V and VS = 1.22 V, so VDS = 6.71 V, which exceeds VOV, and the device remains in saturation. The current falls by about 19 percent for a 50 percent rise in Vt, because RS provides negative feedback.

Answer: 1.22 mA, still saturated

Problem 3 [A5-028] MOSFET small-signal amplifiers

A common-source amplifier uses an n-channel MOSFET biased at ID = 0.500 mA with Kn = 1.00 mA/V² (so ID = (Kn/2) VOV² in saturation) and channel-length modulation parameter λ = 0.0200 V⁻¹. The signal source has open-circuit voltage vs and series resistance Rsig = 100 kΩ. A gate resistor RG = 2.00 MΩ connects the gate to signal ground, and the gate draws no signal current. The drain resistor RD is to be chosen, and a load resistor RL = 30.0 kΩ is capacitively coupled to the drain. The source is fully bypassed to signal ground. Use the small-signal model with gm = 2 ID / VOV and ro = 1/(λ ID), and treat all capacitors as short circuits. The designer wants an overall gain vo/vs of −8.00.

  1. (a) Find the transconductance gm. [3]
  2. (b) Find the output resistance ro of the transistor. [3]
  3. (c) Find the value of RD that gives vo/vs = −8.00. [8]
  4. (d) Find the output resistance of the amplifier, looking into the drain with RL removed. [3]
  5. (e) With RD = 13.2 kΩ, an unbypassed source resistor RS1 = 500 Ω is added. Neglecting ro, find the magnitude of the new overall gain. [3]
(a)

In saturation, ID = (Kn/2) VOV², so VOV = √(2 ID / Kn) = √(2 × 0.500 / 1.00) = 1.00 V. The transconductance is gm = 2 ID / VOV = 2 × 0.500 mA / 1.00 V = 1.00 mS. This is also gm = Kn VOV = 1.00 mA/V² × 1.00 V = 1.00 mS, which is a useful cross-check. Note that gm is lower than the value a BJT would give at the same current: a BJT at 0.5 mA has gm = 20 mS, which is why MOSFET stages need higher load resistances to reach the same gain. The result depends only on the bias point and Kn, not on the resistors in the signal path.

Answer: 1.00 mS

(b)

The output resistance caused by channel-length modulation is ro = 1 / (λ ID) = 1 / (0.0200 V⁻¹ × 0.500 mA) = 1 / (1.00 × 10⁻⁵ S) = 100 000 Ω = 100 kΩ. Equivalently ro = VA / ID with Early voltage VA = 1/λ = 50 V. Because ro is large compared with the practical drain resistances in this stage, it has a modest effect: it appears in parallel with RD and RL and lowers the effective load only slightly. Note that ro depends on the bias current and falls if ID is increased, a point that matters in designs that need higher gain.

Answer: 100 kΩ

(c)

The gate draws no current, so the input divider factor is RG / (RG + Rsig) = 2.00 / 2.10 = 0.9524. The overall gain is vo/vs = −0.9524 × gm (ro || RD || RL). Setting this equal to −8.00 gives gm (ro || RD || RL) = 8.00 / 0.9524 = 8.40, so the effective load is 8.40 / 1.00 mS = 8.40 kΩ. Then 1/RD = 1/8400 − 1/100 000 − 1/30 000 = 1.1905 × 10⁻⁴ − 1.000 × 10⁻⁵ − 3.333 × 10⁻⁵ = 7.571 × 10⁻⁵ S, so RD = 13.21 kΩ. Check the bias: ID RD = 6.6 V, so the supply must exceed this plus the source voltage and the swing allowance, say 15 V or more.

Answer: 13.2 kΩ

(d)

The output resistance of the amplifier is found by turning off the signal source and looking into the drain with the load removed. In the small-signal model the controlled current source gm vgs becomes zero because vgs = 0 when the input is grounded through the source resistance, leaving ro in parallel with RD. So Rout = ro || RD = 100 × 13.21 / 113.21 = 11.67 kΩ. This is much higher than a source follower would give, which is why a common-source stage is poor at driving low-resistance loads without a buffer. With the 30 kΩ load, the loaded output resistance matters for gain, as used in part (c).

Answer: 11.7 kΩ

(e)

With an unbypassed source resistor RS1 and ro neglected, the gain from gate to drain becomes −gm (RD || RL) / (1 + gm RS1) because the source resistor carries feedback. Here RD || RL = 13.21 × 30.0 / 43.21 = 9.171 kΩ, and 1 + gm RS1 = 1 + 1.00 mS × 500 Ω = 1.50. The gate-to-output gain is −1.00 mS × 9171 / 1.50 = −6.114. The input divider factor is unchanged at 0.9524, so the overall gain is −6.114 × 0.9524 = −5.82, with magnitude 5.82. The gain has fallen by about 27 percent relative to −8.00 (which included ro), but is now far less sensitive to variations in gm.

Answer: 5.82

Problem 4 [A5-029] Multistage amplifiers and loading effects

A microphone preamplifier chain is made from two voltage-amplifier stages followed by a load. The source has open-circuit voltage vs and series resistance Rs = 2.00 kΩ. Stage 1 has input resistance Ri1 = 8.00 kΩ, open-circuit voltage gain Avo1 = −90.0 V/V and output resistance Ro1 = 4.00 kΩ. Stage 2 has input resistance Ri2 = 50.0 kΩ, open-circuit voltage gain Avo2 = −30.0 V/V and output resistance Ro2 = 1.50 kΩ. The load is a 600 Ω line driver input. A designer considers inserting a unity-gain buffer between stage 2 and the load, with input resistance 200 kΩ, open-circuit gain +0.980 and output resistance 100 Ω. All stages are linear and unilateral, so each stage's gain and resistances are independent of what follows it. Treat the signals as sinusoids.

  1. (a) Find the overall voltage gain vo/vs, as a magnitude, with the load connected directly to stage 2. [5]
  2. (b) Find the overall voltage gain magnitude with the buffer inserted. [5]
  3. (c) Find the improvement in gain in dB caused by the buffer. [4]
  4. (d) For a source peak voltage of 0.500 mV, find the average power delivered to the 600 Ω load with the buffer in place. [6]
(a)

Each stage is treated as a Thévenin source of open-circuit gain times its input voltage, with a resistor divider at each interface. At the input, the divider is Ri1 / (Ri1 + Rs) = 8.00 / 10.00 = 0.800. Stage 1 to stage 2: Ri2 / (Ri2 + Ro1) = 50.0 / 54.0 = 0.9259. Stage 2 to load: RL / (RL + Ro2) = 600 / 2100 = 0.2857. The overall gain is the product of all three dividers and both open-circuit gains: 0.800 × (−90.0) × 0.9259 × (−30.0) × 0.2857 = +571.4. The magnitude is 571, and the sign is positive because there are two inversions. Note that the load divider alone loses 71 percent of the available voltage.

Answer: 571

(b)

With the buffer, the interface between stage 2 and the buffer is 200 / (200 + 1.50) = 0.9926, much closer to unity than before because the buffer input resistance is far larger than Ro2. The buffer has an open-circuit gain of 0.980. The interface between the buffer and the load is 600 / (600 + 100) = 0.8571. The overall gain becomes 0.800 × 90.0 × 0.9259 × 30.0 × 0.9926 × 0.980 × 0.8571 = 1667.5 in magnitude. The low output resistance of the buffer makes the load divider nearly 0.86 instead of 0.29, which is where nearly all of the improvement comes from, while the buffer's high input resistance costs only 0.7 percent at the stage 2 output.

Answer: 1667

(c)

The improvement in dB is 20 log10 of the ratio of the two voltage gains: 20 log10(1667.5 / 571.4) = 20 log10(2.918) = 20 × 0.4651 = 9.30 dB. The voltage-gain ratio of 2.92 is the product of the output-divider improvement, 0.8571 × 0.9926 × 0.980 / 0.2857 = 2.918, the quantity actually accounting for the change. Conclusion: a unity-gain buffer can raise the delivered signal by nearly 10 dB when a high-output-resistance stage must drive a low-resistance load, even though the buffer itself provides no voltage gain. This is the standard justification for buffers in multistage design, and it costs one extra transistor stage.

Answer: 9.30 dB

(d)

With a source peak of 0.500 mV, the output peak voltage is 0.500 mV × 1667.5 = 0.8338 V. For a sinusoid across a resistive load, the average power is P = Vpk² / (2 RL) = 0.8338² / (2 × 600) = 0.6952 / 1200 = 5.794 × 10⁻⁴ W = 0.579 mW. The equivalent rms voltage is 0.8338 / √2 = 0.5896 V, and 0.5896² / 600 gives the same answer, which provides a useful check. Without the buffer, the peak output would be 0.2857 V and the power only 0.0681 mW, so the buffer raises the delivered power by a factor of 8.5, which is 18.6 dB in power terms, twice the voltage figure.

Answer: 0.579 mW

Problem 5 [A5-030] Frequency response of amplifiers, poles and Miller effect

A common-source amplifier uses a MOSFET with gm = 4.00 mS. The drain is loaded by an effective resistance R'L = 5.00 kΩ (the drain resistor in parallel with the load and ro), and the gate is driven from a source with resistance Rsig = 50.0 kΩ through a very large gate bias resistor that may be ignored. The device capacitances are Cgs = 2.00 pF and Cgd = 0.500 pF, and a load capacitance CL = 3.00 pF is connected from the drain to ground. Assume the midband gain is −gm R'L and that the input pole is dominant. Use the Miller approximation for the effect of Cgd on the input node and treat the output pole separately using the drain-node capacitance Cgd + CL and resistance R'L. Coupling and bypass capacitors are short circuits throughout.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the midband voltage gain. [3]
  2. (b) Find the Miller-effect input capacitance seen at the gate. [4]
  3. (c) Find the upper 3 dB frequency from the input pole for Rsig = 50.0 kΩ. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest source resistance that gives an upper 3 dB frequency of at least 1.00 MHz. [4]
  5. (e) Find the output pole frequency and comment on whether the dominant-input-pole assumption holds. [5]
(a)

With the midband gain given by −gm R'L, the magnitude is 4.00 mS × 5.00 kΩ = 20.0. The gate bias resistor is ignored, so the input divider factor is unity and the overall gain equals the gain from the gate to the drain. The sign is negative, showing phase inversion, which matters for the Miller effect in part (b), since the capacitor Cgd bridges an inverting amplifier. In decibels the gain is 20 log10(20.0) = 26.0 dB. This is the low-frequency (midband) value, valid when all internal capacitances are open circuits and all external coupling capacitances are short circuits.

Answer: 20.0

(b)

The Miller theorem replaces the bridging capacitor Cgd by an input-side capacitor Cgd (1 + gm R'L) and an output-side capacitor Cgd (1 + 1/(gm R'L)). The gain magnitude is 20.0, so the input-side term is 0.500 pF × (1 + 20.0) = 10.5 pF. Adding the gate-source capacitance gives the total Cin = Cgs + Cgd (1 + gm R'L) = 2.00 + 10.5 = 12.5 pF. Observation: although Cgd is only a quarter of Cgs, the multiplication by the gain makes it five times larger than Cgs at the input. This is the Miller effect, and it is the reason that high-gain stages have such poor high-frequency response from a high-resistance source.

Answer: 12.5 pF

(c)

The input node is a first-order low-pass network formed by the source resistance and the total input capacitance. The pole frequency is f = 1 / (2π Rsig Cin) = 1 / (2π × 50 000 × 12.5 × 10⁻¹²) = 1 / (3.927 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.546 × 10⁵ Hz = 254.6 kHz. This is the upper 3 dB frequency if the input pole dominates. The time constant is τ = Rsig Cin = 0.625 µs. At this frequency the gain has fallen to 20.0 / √2 = 14.1, or 23.0 dB. The gain-bandwidth product of this stage is 20.0 × 254.6 kHz = 5.09 MHz. It is limited by the high source resistance, not by the transistor.

Answer: 255 kHz

(d)

The upper 3 dB frequency requirement of 1.00 MHz fixes the maximum value of the time constant: Rsig Cin = 1 / (2π × 1.00 × 10⁶) = 1.592 × 10⁻⁷ s. With Cin = 12.5 pF (unchanged, since the gain is unchanged), Rsig,max = 1.592 × 10⁻⁷ / 12.5 × 10⁻¹² = 12 732 Ω ≈ 12.7 kΩ. So the source resistance must be reduced by a factor of 3.9 from the original value, for instance by placing a source follower or a lower-impedance buffer ahead of the stage. Alternatively, a cascode connection holds the gain across Cgd near unity and removes most of the Miller multiplication, which would permit a larger Rsig.

Answer: 12.7 kΩ

(e)

The output node sees the drain capacitance Cgd + CL (the Miller output term Cgd (1 + 1/20) is almost Cgd, so the output capacitance is approximately 0.500 + 3.00 = 3.50 pF) in parallel with R'L = 5.00 kΩ. The pole is f = 1 / (2π R'L Cout) = 1 / (2π × 5000 × 3.50 × 10⁻¹²) = 9.095 × 10⁶ Hz = 9.09 MHz. This is 35.7 times the input pole at 254.6 kHz, so the input pole is indeed dominant and the first-order assumption holds well. Above about 2 MHz the output pole starts to affect the phase and the 1 MHz result of part (d) would then be slightly in error.

Answer: 9.09 MHz

A5 Practice Paper 7

Problem 1 [A5-031] Differential amplifiers and current mirrors

A discrete differential amplifier uses two matched NPN transistors Q1 and Q2 with β = 200, VBE = 0.70 V and Early voltage VA = 100 V. The emitters are joined and connected to the collector of Q5, which is the output transistor of a simple two-transistor current mirror (Q5 and a matched diode-connected transistor Q6, with the bases of Q5 and Q6 tied together and both emitters at the negative supply). The supplies are +12 V and −12 V. A resistor Rref runs from +12 V to the collector of Q6. Each of Q1 and Q2 has a collector resistor RC = 10 kΩ to +12 V, and the output is taken differentially between the two collectors. Take VT = 25 mV and treat the tail current as splitting equally between Q1 and Q2.

  1. (a) Choose Rref so that the tail current in Q5 is 1.00 mA, allowing for the finite β of the mirror transistors. [6]
  2. (b) Find the differential voltage gain Vod/Vid of the amplifier, ignoring ro of Q1 and Q2 in the collector loads. [5]
  3. (c) Find the differential input resistance seen between the two bases. [4]
  4. (d) The output is now taken single-ended from the collector of Q2 only. Using the output resistance of the Q5 mirror to find the common-mode gain, calculate the common-mode rejection ratio in dB. [5]
(a)

The diode-connected transistor Q6 sets VBE = 0.70 V, so the reference current is Iref = (12 − 0.70 − (−12))/Rref = 23.3 V/Rref. In a simple mirror the collector current of Q5 equals Iref reduced by the base currents of both mirror transistors: Iref = IC5 + 2IB, with IB = IC5/β. Therefore IC5 = Iref/(1 + 2/β). Rearranging for a tail current of 1.00 mA gives Iref = 1.00 mA × (1 + 2/200) = 1.01 mA. Then Rref = 23.3 V/1.01 mA = 23.07 kΩ. A ratio of 1% between ideal and actual reference current is the usual size of the β error for β = 200. The nearest standard value of 23.2 kΩ would be adequate in practice.

Answer: 23.1 kΩ

(b)

Each transistor carries IC = 0.5 mA (the base-current difference is neglected as stated). The transconductance is gm = IC/VT = 0.5 mA/25 mV = 20 mS. For a balanced differential input vid, the emitter junction is a virtual ground for the half circuits, so each transistor sees vid/2 across its base-emitter junction. The collector voltages swing by ±gm(vid/2)RC in opposite directions, so the differential output is vod = gm RC vid. With RC = 10 kΩ the gain is Ad = 0.020 S × 10 000 Ω = 200 V/V. The sign depends on which output terminal is defined as positive. Ignoring ro is acceptable since ro = VA/IC = 200 kΩ is much larger than RC.

Answer: 200 V/V

(c)

For differential drive each base sees a small-signal resistance rπ looking into it, because the emitters are at signal ground and the two input junctions are in series between the input terminals. First rπ = β/gm = 200/0.020 S = 10 kΩ. The differential input resistance is the sum of the two series resistances: Rid = 2rπ = 20 kΩ. This is the resistance a source driving the pair differentially would see. The result confirms that the pair presents a modest input resistance, so a high impedance source would lose gain by division. If higher Rid were needed, emitter resistors or Darlington input stages would be added. Rid scales directly with β and inversely with the bias current.

Answer: 20 kΩ

(d)

The tail source has small-signal output resistance Ro = VA/IC5 = 100 V/1.00 mA = 100 kΩ. For a common-mode input, the pair acts as two identical half circuits each with 2Ro in the emitter, so the single-ended common-mode gain is approximately Acm = −RC/(2Ro) = −10 kΩ/200 kΩ = −0.05. The single-ended differential gain is half of the differential-output gain: Ad,se = 200/2 = 100 V/V. The rejection ratio is CMRR = |Ad,se/Acm| = 100/0.05 = 2000, which is 20 log10(2000) = 66.0 dB. Improving CMRR requires a larger Ro, for example a cascode or Wilson mirror in the tail, or a larger gm with the same RC.

Answer: 66.0 dB

Problem 2 [A5-032] Op-amp inverting and non-inverting circuits

A strain-gauge bridge produces a signal of 0 to 12 mV that must be amplified by a two-stage op-amp circuit running from ±5 V supplies. The output of each op-amp can swing to at most ±3.6 V before it clips. Stage 1 is a non-inverting amplifier built with R1 = 2.0 kΩ from the inverting input to ground and Rf = 118 kΩ from the output back to the inverting input; the bridge signal drives the non-inverting input. Stage 2 is an inverting amplifier with an input resistor of 10 kΩ from the output of stage 1 to its inverting input, a feedback resistor of 47 kΩ, and the non-inverting input grounded. The op-amps are identical with a gain-bandwidth product of 1.0 MHz, and a dc open-loop gain of 2 × 10⁴ in the real case.

  1. (a) Find the ideal closed-loop gain of stage 1 and the ideal overall gain of the two stages, and report the magnitude of the overall gain. [4]
  2. (b) Stage 1 has a real dc open-loop gain of 2 × 10⁴. Find the percentage gain error of stage 1 relative to its ideal gain of 60. Report the magnitude of the error. [5]
  3. (c) Using the constant gain-bandwidth product, find the −3 dB bandwidth of stage 1. [4]
  4. (d) Using the ideal gains, find the largest bridge signal amplitude, in mV, that can be amplified before the output of stage 2 reaches its +/-3.6 V clipping limit. State also whether the full 12 mV range can be used and explain the consequence. [7]
(a)

For a non-inverting amplifier with an ideal op-amp, the voltage at the inverting input equals the input, and the divider R1, Rf gives Vo/Vin = 1 + Rf/R1. With 118 kΩ and 2.0 kΩ, stage 1 has a gain of 1 + 59 = 60 V/V. Stage 2 is an inverting amplifier with gain −Rf2/Rin2 = −47 kΩ/10 kΩ = −4.7 V/V. The two stages are in cascade, and since the first stage output is a low-impedance source of an ideal op-amp, there is no loading, so the overall gain is 60 × (−4.7) = −282 V/V. The magnitude is 282 V/V. The negative sign means the overall output is inverted with respect to the bridge signal.

Answer: 282 V/V

(b)

The feedback factor of the non-inverting stage is β = R1/(R1 + Rf) = 2.0/120 = 1/60. The loop gain is Aβ = 20 000/60 = 333.3. The exact closed-loop gain of a non-inverting amplifier with finite A is G = A/(1 + Aβ) = 20 000/334.33 = 59.82 V/V. The ideal gain 1/β is 60, so the error is (59.82 − 60)/60 = −0.299 percent, which has magnitude 0.299 percent. Equivalently the error is about 1/(1 + Aβ) = 0.30 percent. A gain this close to ideal confirms that the open-loop gain is large enough for a strain-gauge instrument needing about 0.5 percent accuracy, though temperature drift in A would add to this.

Answer: 0.299 %

(c)

The op-amp behaves as a single-pole amplifier, so the product of closed-loop gain and closed-loop bandwidth is constant and equal to the gain-bandwidth product. For a non-inverting stage the gain is 60, so f3dB = GBW/G = 1.0 MHz/60 = 16.67 kHz. This holds because the closed-loop bandwidth equals the open-loop corner frequency multiplied by (1 + Aβ), and the unity-gain frequency is A0 times that corner. Stage 2 has a noise gain of 1 + 47/10 = 5.7 and a bandwidth of 175 kHz, so stage 1 is the limiting stage and sets the overall bandwidth near 16.7 kHz. For a strain-gauge signal that changes slowly, this is more than adequate.

Answer: 16.7 kHz

(d)

The stage 2 output is limited to 3.6 V in magnitude. With a total gain of 282 V/V, the largest input is Vin,max = 3.6 V/282 = 12.77 mV. At 12 mV the output would be 12 mV × 282 = 3.384 V, which is inside the limit, so the full 0 to 12 mV range can be used with a margin of about 0.216 V (6 percent). The margin must also cover the offset voltages of both stages, which the gain of 282 multiplies: an input offset of 1 mV would give 0.28 V at the output, enough to push the 12 mV signal into clipping. If the bridge signal could rise above 12.8 mV, the gain split would have to be reduced. The check of the stage 1 output is also needed: 12 mV × 60 = 0.72 V, which is comfortable.

Answer: 12.8 mV

Problem 3 [A5-033] Op-amp summing, integrating, differentiating and filters

An ideal op-amp is connected as an inverting summing low-pass filter for combining two sensor signals V1 and V2 in an Ontario water-treatment plant. Input V1 reaches the inverting node through R1 = 15 kΩ and input V2 reaches the same node through R2 = 30 kΩ. The feedback network between the output and the inverting node is a resistor Rf = 60 kΩ in parallel with a capacitor Cf. The non-inverting input is grounded. The filter is required to have a −3 dB corner frequency of 2.0 kHz for the V1 channel. Treat both input channels as having the same feedback impedance, so each channel has the same corner frequency, and assume the signals are sinusoidal in steady state unless the text says dc.

  1. (a) Find the capacitance Cf, in nF, that gives a corner frequency of 2.0 kHz. [5]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the gain from V1 to the output at 10 kHz. [5]
  3. (c) With dc inputs V1 = +0.50 V and V2 = −0.30 V, find the steady-state dc output voltage. [5]
  4. (d) Find the phase of the output relative to the input V1 at 10 kHz, expressed as the additional lag, in degrees, beyond the 180 degrees of inversion. [5]
(a)

The feedback impedance is Rf in parallel with Cf, so Zf = Rf/(1 + jωRfCf). The corner frequency occurs where ωRfCf = 1, which gives fc = 1/(2πRfCf). Solving for the capacitor, Cf = 1/(2π Rf fc) = 1/(2π × 60 000 Ω × 2000 Hz). The product 2π × 60 000 × 2000 is 7.540 × 10⁸, so Cf = 1.326 × 10⁻⁹ F, or 1.33 nF. The nearest standard value is 1.3 nF, which moves the corner to 2.04 kHz, a change of 2 percent. The corner frequency depends only on the feedback components and not on R1 or R2, because the virtual ground makes each input current independent of Zf.

Answer: 1.33 nF

(b)

For the V1 channel the transfer function is Vo/V1 = −Zf/R1 = −(Rf/R1)/(1 + jf/fc). At dc this gives a gain of −60/15 = −4, so the dc gain magnitude is 4. At f = 10 kHz and fc = 2 kHz, the ratio f/fc is 5. The magnitude of the gain is 4/√(1 + 5²) = 4/√26 = 4/5.099 = 0.7845 V/V. This is about 20 log10(0.7845) = −2.1 dB, compared with +12 dB at dc, so the filter has dropped the gain by 14.1 dB at five times the corner frequency. A first-order roll-off gives −20 dB per decade above the corner, and the calculation confirms about −14 dB for a factor of five.

Answer: 0.784 V/V

(c)

At dc the capacitor is an open circuit, so only Rf is in the feedback path. With a virtual ground at the inverting node, the currents from the two inputs add: I = V1/R1 + V2/R2 = 0.50/15 000 + (−0.30)/30 000 = 33.33 μA − 10.00 μA = 23.33 μA. This entire current flows through Rf, so Vo = −I Rf = −23.33 μA × 60 kΩ = −1.40 V. Alternatively, Vo = −(Rf/R1 V1 + Rf/R2 V2) = −(4 × 0.50 + 2 × (−0.30)) = −(2.00 − 0.60) = −1.40 V. The weights of 4 and 2 show that the summing amplifier lets each channel have its own gain without interaction, a key advantage of the virtual ground.

Answer: −1.40 V

(d)

The complex transfer function is Vo/V1 = −4/(1 + j f/fc). The minus sign gives a constant 180 degree shift. The denominator contributes a phase of −arctan(f/fc). At 10 kHz, f/fc is 5, so the additional lag is arctan(5) = 78.69 degrees. The total phase is therefore 180° − 78.69° = 101.3° (or equivalently −258.7° if lag is measured continuously). This extra lag is the phase typical of a first-order low-pass filter well above its corner, approaching 90 degrees at high frequency. At the corner frequency itself the lag would be exactly 45 degrees, so the response at 10 kHz is much closer to the asymptotic value. A designer using this filter in a control loop would need to include this lag in the loop phase budget.

Answer: 78.7 degrees

Problem 4 [A5-034] Feedback in amplifiers: gain, bandwidth and stability

A voltage amplifier has a dc open-loop gain A0 = 5000 and a single dominant pole giving an open-loop −3 dB bandwidth of 2.0 kHz. Its open-loop input resistance is 10 kΩ. A resistive network samples the output voltage and feeds back a fraction β of it in series with the input (voltage-series, or series-shunt, feedback), where β is frequency independent and the network does not load the amplifier. The designer first uses β = 0.020. Later, the designer must set β so the closed-loop dc gain equals exactly 25. Assume the open-loop response stays single-pole, so the product of gain and bandwidth is maintained, and ignore the loading of the feedback network on the input and output.

  1. (a) Find the closed-loop dc gain when β = 0.020. [4]
  2. (b) With β = 0.020, find the closed-loop −3 dB bandwidth. [4]
  3. (c) Find the value of β that gives a closed-loop dc gain of exactly 25. [5]
  4. (d) With the design β from part (c), the open-loop gain falls by 20 percent to 4000 because of ageing. Find the percentage change in closed-loop gain, reporting its magnitude. [7]
(a)

For negative feedback the closed-loop gain is Af = A/(1 + Aβ). With A0 = 5000 and β = 0.020 the loop gain is Aβ = 100, so Af = 5000/(1 + 100) = 5000/101 = 49.50 V/V. This is close to the ideal value 1/β = 50, because the loop gain is much larger than one; the shortfall of 0.99 percent equals 1/(1 + Aβ). The feedback factor 1 + Aβ = 101 is also the desensitivity factor that appears in the bandwidth, the input resistance and the sensitivity to changes in A. The closed-loop gain therefore depends mostly on the passive network and only weakly on the active device.

Answer: 49.5 V/V

(b)

A single-pole amplifier with feedback has its corner frequency multiplied by the same factor that reduces the gain: fHf = fH(1 + Aβ). With fH = 2.0 kHz and 1 + Aβ = 101, the closed-loop bandwidth is 2.0 kHz × 101 = 202 kHz. The gain-bandwidth product stays constant: 5000 × 2 kHz = 10 MHz and 49.5 × 202 kHz = 10.0 MHz. Feedback therefore trades gain for bandwidth at a fixed rate. For a single-pole system there is also no stability problem, because the loop phase shift never reaches 180 degrees. With two or more poles inside the loop the same increase in loop gain would reduce the phase margin.

Answer: 202 kHz

(c)

The closed-loop gain is Af = A0/(1 + A0β). Setting Af = 25 gives 1 + A0β = A0/25 = 5000/25 = 200. Then A0β = 199 and β = 199/5000 = 0.0398. Note this differs from the ideal 1/25 = 0.0400 by 0.5 percent, because the finite open-loop gain reduces the gain below 1/β; a designer who used β = 1/25 directly would get Af = 5000/(1 + 200) = 24.88, an error of 0.5 percent. With the corrected β, the loop gain is 199 and the closed-loop bandwidth becomes 2.0 kHz × 200 = 400 kHz. The choice of β therefore sets the gain and the bandwidth simultaneously.

Answer: 0.0398

(d)

With β = 0.0398 and A = 5000, the nominal closed-loop gain is exactly 25.000. When A falls to 4000 the loop gain is Aβ = 4000 × 0.0398 = 159.2, so Af = 4000/(1 + 159.2) = 4000/160.2 = 24.969 V/V. The change is (24.969 − 25.000)/25.000 = −0.1248 percent, so the magnitude is 0.125 percent. Compare this with the 20 percent change in A: the closed-loop gain changed by a factor 1/(1 + Aβ) of the relative change in A, roughly 20/160 = 0.125 percent. This is the desensitivity property of negative feedback, and it is the reason precision amplifiers use large loop gain. The price is a reduction in gain from 5000 to 25, a factor of 200.

Answer: 0.125 %

Problem 5 [A5-035] Comparators, Schmitt triggers and oscillators

An inverting Schmitt trigger is built from an op-amp whose output saturates at +12 V and −12 V. A resistor R1 is connected from the output to the non-inverting input, and a resistor R2 is connected from the non-inverting input to ground. The input signal is applied to the inverting input. The designer wants the switching thresholds to be symmetric at ±2.0 V and chooses R2 = 10 kΩ. The same op-amp is then rearranged as a relaxation oscillator: the input signal is removed, a resistor R = 22 kΩ is connected from the output to the inverting input, and a capacitor C = 47 nF is connected from the inverting input to ground, while the R1, R2 network is retained. Assume ideal saturation levels and ideal switching.

  1. (a) Find the value of R1 that gives thresholds of ±2.0 V. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total hysteresis width of the trigger, in volts. [3]
  3. (c) For the relaxation oscillator, find the oscillation frequency using β = 1/6. [7]
  4. (d) In the Schmitt trigger of the first stage, the bottom of R2 is now returned to a reference voltage of +1.2 V instead of ground. Find the new upper threshold voltage. [6]
(a)

With the output saturated at ±Vsat, the voltage at the non-inverting input is the divider output β Vsat where β = R2/(R1 + R2). The output switches when the input crosses this voltage, so the thresholds are ±β Vsat. Requiring β × 12 V = 2.0 V gives β = 1/6. Then R2/(R1 + R2) = 1/6, which means R1 = 5 R2 = 5 × 10 kΩ = 50 kΩ. The two resistors therefore form a 60 kΩ divider with the junction at one sixth of the output. The negative-feedback path is absent in this stage; the feedback goes to the non-inverting terminal, so the circuit is regenerative and the output has two stable states rather than a linear value.

Answer: 50 kΩ

(b)

The upper threshold is VTH = +β Vsat = +2.0 V, which is the input level at which the output goes from high to low. The lower threshold is VTL = −β Vsat = −2.0 V, at which the output returns from low to high. The hysteresis width is the difference VTH − VTL = 2β Vsat = 2 × 2.0 = 4.0 V. Any noise on the input smaller than 4.0 V peak to peak, centred on a point between the thresholds, cannot cause the output to chatter. A wider band means more noise immunity but a larger input change before switching. The design choice of 4.0 V therefore suits signals whose swing is at least a few volts.

Answer: 4.0 V

(c)

The capacitor charges through R toward the output level and the output flips each time the capacitor voltage reaches ±β Vsat. Starting at −βVsat with the output at +Vsat, the capacitor voltage rises toward +Vsat with time constant RC: v(t) = Vsat − (Vsat + βVsat)e−t/RC. It reaches +βVsat when e−t/RC = (1 − β)/(1 + β), so the half period is T/2 = RC ln((1 + β)/(1 − β)). With β = 1/6 the ratio is (7/6)/(5/6) = 1.4 and ln 1.4 = 0.3365. Also RC = 22 000 × 47 × 10⁻⁹ = 1.034 ms, so T = 2 × 1.034 ms × 0.3365 = 0.6958 ms. The frequency is f = 1/T = 1437 Hz. The result does not depend on Vsat, only on β, R and C.

Answer: 1437 Hz

(d)

With the lower end of R2 at Vref = 1.2 V, the non-inverting input voltage follows from superposition of the output through R1 and the reference through R2. The weights are R2/(R1 + R2) = 1/6 for the output and R1/(R1 + R2) = 5/6 for the reference. Thus V+ = (1/6)Vo + (5/6)(1.2 V). When Vo = +12 V, V+ = 2.0 + 1.0 = 3.0 V, which is the new upper threshold. When Vo = −12 V, V+ = −2.0 + 1.0 = −1.0 V, the new lower threshold. The hysteresis width is still 4.0 V, but the centre of the band moved from 0 to +1.0 V, which is (5/6)Vref. This is the standard method of shifting the trip point without altering the hysteresis.

Answer: 3.0 V

A5 Practice Paper 8

Problem 1 [A5-036] Power amplifiers, efficiency and heat dissipation

A class B complementary emitter-follower output stage drives an 8.0 Ω loudspeaker from supplies of +15 V and −15 V. The stage has no crossover distortion in this idealization and the transistors saturate at zero collector-emitter voltage, so the output can swing up to the full supply. The amplifier is to deliver an average sinusoidal power of 10 W to the load. The output transistors are identical, each in a package with a junction-to-case thermal resistance of 2.0 °C/W, and a thermal pad between case and heat sink with 0.5 °C/W. The maximum junction temperature is 150 °C and the ambient air temperature at the heat sink is 50 °C. Ignore quiescent current and treat the supply power as the average of the rectified collector currents.

  1. (a) Find the peak output voltage needed to deliver 10 W to the load. [4]
  2. (b) Find the efficiency of the amplifier at this output power. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum power dissipation of each transistor as Vp is varied and give the value in watts. [5]
  4. (d) Find the largest heat-sink-to-ambient thermal resistance, in °C/W, for each transistor if its junction must not exceed 150 °C at the maximum dissipation. [6]
(a)

The average power of a sinusoid in a resistive load is P = Vp²/(2RL). Solving for the peak value, Vp = √(2 P RL) = √(2 × 10 W × 8.0 Ω) = √160 = 12.65 V. This is below the supply of 15 V, so the stage is not driven into clipping, and the headroom of 15 − 12.65 = 2.35 V is available for the transistor saturation drop and the emitter resistors in a practical circuit. The corresponding peak load current is Ip = Vp/RL = 12.65/8.0 = 1.581 A. The stage must be able to supply this peak current with the chosen transistors, which in practice means a current rating of at least 2 to 3 A.

Answer: 12.65 V

(b)

Each supply provides the half-wave rectified load current from its own transistor, so the average current drawn from one supply is Ip/π. The total supply power is Pdc = 2 × VCC × Ip/π = 2 × 15 V × 1.581 A/π = 15.10 W. The efficiency is the ratio of load power to supply power: η = 10 W/15.10 W = 0.662, or 66.2 percent. At full swing (Vp = 15 V) the ideal class B limit is π/4 = 78.5 percent, so this stage sits about 12 points below the maximum at the chosen output. The difference between the supply power and the load power, 5.10 W, is dissipated as heat in the two output transistors.

Answer: 66.2 %

(c)

The dissipation per transistor equals half the total heat: PD = (1/2)(2VCC Vp/(πRL) − Vp²/(2RL)). Setting the derivative with respect to Vp to zero gives 2VCC/(πRL) = Vp/RL, so the worst case is Vp = 2VCC/π = 9.55 V. Substituting, the maximum per-transistor dissipation is PDmax = VCC²/(π² RL) = 225/(9.870 × 8.0) = 2.85 W. At the operating point of 10 W the dissipation was 5.10 W/2 = 2.55 W, which is lower than the maximum. The designer must size the heat sink for 2.85 W, not for the 10 W condition, because the speaker will often play at the output level at which dissipation peaks.

Answer: 2.85 W

(d)

The steady-state junction temperature is Tj = Ta + PD(θjc + θcs + θsa). Solving for the sink thermal resistance gives θsa = (Tjmax − Ta)/PD − θjc − θcs. With Tjmax = 150 °C, Ta = 50 °C and PD = 2.85 W, the total allowed resistance from junction to ambient is 100/2.85 = 35.09 °C/W. Subtracting 2.0 °C/W and 0.5 °C/W gives θsa = 35.09 − 2.50 = 32.59 °C/W. This is a fairly modest requirement, a small extruded aluminum sink. In practice the designer would aim for a margin, for example 25 °C/W, so that the junction stays below about 130 °C and the reliability is better. Both transistors may share one sink only if they are electrically insulated.

Answer: 32.6 °C/W

Problem 2 [A5-037] BJT and MOSFET as switches

A 5 V logic output (VOH = 5.0 V) must switch a 12 V relay whose coil resistance is 240 Ω. The coil is connected between the +12 V rail and the switching device, which is on the low side, with its emitter or source grounded. In the bipolar design an NPN transistor with VCE(sat) = 0.20 V and VBE(sat) = 0.80 V is driven through a base resistor Rb from the logic output, and the designer chooses a forced current gain of 10 for hard saturation. In the MOSFET alternative, an n-channel enhancement device with threshold voltage Vt = 2.0 V and process transconductance parameter k = 0.10 A/V² (ID = k[(VGS − Vt)VDS − VDS²/2] in the triode region) is driven directly from the 5 V gate drive. Ignore the diode across the coil.

  1. (a) Find the collector current in the BJT design when the transistor is saturated. [4]
  2. (b) Find the base resistor Rb that gives the forced current gain of 10. [5]
  3. (c) Find the total power dissipated in the BJT while it is on, from the collector and base terminals, in mW. [5]
  4. (d) In the MOSFET design with VGS = 5.0 V, find the drain-source voltage VDS in the on state, noting that the device is in the triode region. Give the answer in volts. [6]
(a)

In saturation the collector-emitter voltage is fixed at VCE(sat) = 0.20 V, so the entire remainder of the supply drops across the coil. The voltage on the coil is 12 − 0.20 = 11.8 V. With a coil resistance of 240 Ω, the collector current is IC = 11.8 V/240 Ω = 49.17 mA. This value does not depend on the transistor gain, because in saturation the external circuit sets the current. The transistor must have a collector current rating well above this value, and a gain at 50 mA of at least the forced gain of 10 or the design will not saturate. The relay will operate reliably if its pull-in voltage is below 11.8 V.

Answer: 49.2 mA

(b)

The forced gain of 10 means the base current is IB = IC/10 = 49.17 mA/10 = 4.917 mA. This base current flows from the logic output at 5.0 V through Rb into the base, with the base-emitter junction at VBE(sat) = 0.80 V. The voltage across Rb is therefore 5.0 − 0.80 = 4.20 V. Rb = 4.20 V/4.917 mA = 854 Ω. A standard 820 Ω resistor would give 5.12 mA, a forced gain of 9.6, still safely in saturation. The selected forced gain is lower than the datasheet β of a typical small-signal transistor (100 to 300), which guarantees saturation over the temperature and device spread. Check that the logic gate can source 5 mA.

Answer: 854 Ω

(c)

The power in a saturated transistor is the sum of the collector-circuit loss and the base-circuit loss: P = VCE(sat) IC + VBE(sat) IB. The collector term is 0.20 V × 49.17 mA = 9.83 mW. The base term is 0.80 V × 4.917 mA = 3.93 mW. The total is 9.83 + 3.93 = 13.77 mW. This is very small, so no heat sink is needed. The coil, in comparison, dissipates 11.8 V × 49.17 mA = 580 mW. Most of the power loss in a switch occurs during the switching transitions if the load is inductive, which here is controlled by the diode across the coil that the problem told us to ignore, and in a real design the diode is mandatory.

Answer: 13.8 mW

(d)

The overdrive is VGS − Vt = 3.0 V. For the triode region, ID = 0.10 (3.0 VDS − VDS²/2). The load line from the coil is ID = (12 − VDS)/240. Equating the two gives 0.10(3.0 VDS − 0.5 VDS²) = (12 − VDS)/240. Expanding, 0.3 VDS − 0.05 VDS² = 0.05 − VDS/240, which gives 0.05 VDS² − 0.30417 VDS + 0.05 = 0 and VDS = [0.30417 − √(0.09252 − 0.01)]/(0.1) = 0.169 V. The triode assumption is valid since VDS = 0.169 V is less than VGS − Vt = 3.0 V. The drain current is 49.3 mA, matching the BJT. The on-state loss is only 8.3 mW, with no gate current at dc.

Answer: 0.169 V

Problem 3 [A5-038] CMOS inverter and logic gate design

A 1.8 V CMOS process has threshold voltages Vtn = 0.50 V and Vtp = −0.50 V, process transconductance parameters kn′ = 300 μA/V² for NMOS and kp′ = 100 μA/V² for PMOS, a drawn channel length of 0.18 μm for every transistor, and a gate oxide capacitance per unit area Cox = 8.5 fF/μm². The saturation current is ID = (k′/2)(W/L)(VGS − Vt)². A reference inverter is to have its switching threshold VM at VDD/2 and uses (W/L)n = 4. Later the same drive strength is required of logic gates built in the same process. Neglect channel-length modulation and body effect throughout the problem, and treat the transistors as being matched in length.

  1. (a) Find the PMOS-to-NMOS ratio (W/L)p/(W/L)n that places VM at VDD/2 = 0.90 V. [4]
  2. (b) A layout engineer uses equal widths for both transistors by mistake, so (W/L)p = (W/L)n. Find the new switching threshold VM, in volts. [5]
  3. (c) A three-input NOR gate must have the same pull-up and pull-down strength as the reference inverter of (W/L)n = 4 and (W/L)p = 12. Find the (W/L) of each PMOS transistor in the NOR3 gate. [5]
  4. (d) Find the total input gate capacitance seen by one input of the NOR3 gate (one NMOS plus one PMOS, using Cox L (Wn + Wp)), in fF. [6]
(a)

At the switching threshold both transistors are in saturation with equal currents. For VM = VDD/2 and symmetric thresholds, the overdrive voltages are equal: VM − Vtn = 0.40 V and VDD − VM − |Vtp| = 0.40 V. Equal currents then require kn = kp, that is kn′(W/L)n = kp′(W/L)p. Therefore (W/L)p/(W/L)n = kn′/kp′ = 300/100 = 3. The PMOS must be three times as wide as the NMOS because holes have about one third of the mobility of electrons. With (W/L)n = 4 the PMOS has (W/L)p = 12, so Wn = 0.72 μm and Wp = 2.16 μm.

Answer: 3

(b)

With equal drive currents at VM, the general result is VM = [Vtn + r(VDD − |Vtp|)]/(1 + r), where r = √(kp/kn). For equal widths kp/kn = kp′/kn′ = 1/3, so r = 0.5774. Then VM = [0.50 + 0.5774 × (1.8 − 0.5)]/(1 + 0.5774) = (0.50 + 0.7506)/1.5774 = 0.7928 V. The threshold has moved down by 0.107 V from the ideal 0.90 V because the weaker PMOS pull-up needs the input to be lower to win against the NMOS. The shifted threshold reduces the noise margin on the high side and makes the rise delay longer than the fall delay.

Answer: 0.793 V

(c)

In a NOR gate the NMOS transistors are in parallel, so each NMOS can be the same size as the inverter NMOS, (W/L)n = 4, for the worst case in which only one is on. The PMOS transistors are three in series. A series stack of N identical devices has N times the resistance of one, so to equal the inverter pull-up each device must be N times as wide: (W/L)p = 3 × 12 = 36. The pull-up path from three series devices of 36 has a conductance equal to that of one device of 12. In practice the stack of three PMOS is the largest and slowest part of the gate, which is why NOR gates with many inputs are avoided in fast logic.

Answer: 36

(d)

The gate capacitance of a transistor is approximately Cox W L. For the NOR3 input, the NMOS has (W/L) = 4 so Wn = 4 × 0.18 μm = 0.72 μm, and the PMOS has (W/L) = 36 so Wp = 36 × 0.18 = 6.48 μm. The total width at one input is 0.72 + 6.48 = 7.20 μm. The input capacitance is C = Cox L (Wn + Wp) = 8.5 fF/μm² × 0.18 μm × 7.20 μm = 11.02 fF. The reference inverter has an input capacitance of only 8.5 × 0.18 × 2.88 = 4.41 fF, so the NOR3 loads its driver 2.5 times as much for the same drive. This is the cost in delay and area of a wide series stack.

Answer: 11.0 fF

Problem 4 [A5-039] Propagation delay and power in CMOS

A CMOS inverter in a 1.2 V logic family drives a load capacitance CL = 50 fF made up of wiring and the input capacitance of the next gate. The equivalent switching resistance of the NMOS pull-down is Rn = 8.0 kΩ and that of the PMOS pull-up is Rp = 12 kΩ. Use the RC model in which the 50 percent delay of a step response is 0.69 times the equivalent resistance times the load capacitance. The inverter is part of a bus driver that switches at a clock frequency of 250 MHz with an activity factor of 0.20 (that is, the output makes a 0-to-1 transition in 20 percent of the clock cycles). A second, larger load of 2.0 pF must later be driven from a minimum inverter whose input capacitance is 5.0 fF, using a chain of inverters sized by logical effort, with τ = 15 ps and parasitic delay p = 1 for each inverter.

  1. (a) Find the high-to-low propagation delay tpHL in ps. [4]
  2. (b) Find the average propagation delay tp of the inverter in ps. [4]
  3. (c) Find the average dynamic power of the load capacitor at 250 MHz with activity factor 0.20, in μW. [5]
  4. (d) For the 2.0 pF load driven from the 5.0 fF minimum inverter, use the optimum integer number of stages with each stage having equal effort. Find the total delay of the chain, in ps, using each stage delay of (f + p) τ. [7]
(a)

When the input rises, the NMOS pulls the output from VDD down through its equivalent resistance, so the output follows an exponential decay with time constant RnCL. The time to reach half of VDD is tpHL = 0.69 Rn CL. The time constant is 8000 Ω × 50 × 10⁻¹⁵ F = 400 ps. Multiplying by 0.69 gives tpHL = 276 ps. The result does not depend on VDD in this model, because the 50 percent point scales with VDD. In a real transistor the equivalent resistance does depend on the supply, so a lower supply means a larger Rn and a longer delay. For this inverter, the fall delay is shorter than the rise delay since the NMOS is the stronger device.

Answer: 276 ps

(b)

The low-to-high delay is tpLH = 0.69 Rp CL = 0.69 × 12 000 Ω × 50 fF. The RC product is 600 ps, so tpLH = 414 ps. The average propagation delay is the mean of the two edges: tp = (tpHL + tpLH)/2 = (276 + 414)/2 = 345 ps. This is also equal to 0.69 × (Rn + Rp)/2 × CL = 0.69 × 10 kΩ × 50 fF = 345 ps. The asymmetry between the two edges is 138 ps, which can distort the duty cycle of a clock signal passing through many stages. Widening the PMOS by a factor 1.5 would equalize the two delays at the price of a larger load on the previous stage.

Answer: 345 ps

(c)

The dynamic power is the energy taken from the supply per charging event multiplied by the rate of those events. Each 0-to-1 transition draws CL VDD² from the supply, and half of this is stored on the capacitor while half is lost in the pull-up resistance; the stored energy is lost on the discharge. So the average power is P = α CL VDD² f. Substituting α = 0.20, CL = 50 × 10⁻¹⁵ F, VDD² = 1.44 V² and f = 250 × 10⁶ Hz, we find P = 0.20 × 50 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 1.44 × 250 × 10⁶ = 3.6 × 10⁻⁶ W, which is 3.6 μW. The result is independent of the transistor resistance. Reducing the supply to 1.0 V would reduce this power by 31 percent.

Answer: 3.6 μW

(d)

The overall electrical effort is F = CL/Cin = 2.0 pF/5.0 fF = 400. The best stage effort is about 4, so the number of stages is N = ln 400/ln 4 = 4.32, which rounds to N = 4 stages. With four stages the effort per stage is f = 4001/4 = 4.472, a value close to the ideal 4. Each stage then has a delay of (f + p)τ = (4.472 + 1) × 15 ps = 82.08 ps. The total delay is D = 4 × 82.08 ps = 328.3 ps. A single inverter driving the load directly would have a delay of (400 + 1) × 15 ps = 6.0 ns, so the chain is about 18 times faster. The size of the successive inverters grows by 4.47 at each stage.

Answer: 328 ps

Problem 5 [A5-040] Amplifier design to meet a specification, comparing topologies

A small-signal amplifier is needed between a microphone source and a 5.0 kΩ load. The source has an open-circuit voltage vs and a series resistance Rs = 1.0 kΩ. A single NPN transistor is biased at IC = 1.0 mA with β = 150, VT = 25 mV and an output resistance ro so large that it is neglected (treat ro as infinite). The collector resistor is RC = 5.0 kΩ, and the load RL = 5.0 kΩ is coupled to the collector through a large capacitor, so the signal sees RC in parallel with RL. In topology A the emitter is bypassed to ground (common-emitter). In topology B an unbypassed emitter resistor RE is added, and its value is to be chosen so that the overall voltage gain from vs to the load is 30 V/V in magnitude. Use the T-equivalent relation Ri = rπ + (β + 1)RE for the base input resistance.

  1. (a) For topology A, find the magnitude of the overall voltage gain vo/vs, including the loss at the source. [5]
  2. (b) For topology B, find the emitter resistor RE that makes the overall gain magnitude 30 V/V. [6]
  3. (c) Find the input resistance seen at the base of topology B. [4]
  4. (d) The transistor is replaced by a unit with β = 100 at the same IC. Find the percentage reduction in the magnitude of the overall gain of topology B, using the same RE. [5]
(a)

First find gm = IC/VT = 1.0 mA/25 mV = 40 mS and rπ = β/gm = 150/0.040 S = 3.75 kΩ. The load seen by the collector is RC∥RL = 5.0 kΩ∥5.0 kΩ = 2.5 kΩ, so the gain from base to output is −gm × 2.5 kΩ = −100 V/V. The source drives the base through a divider formed by Rs and Ri = rπ = 3.75 kΩ, so the fraction reaching the base is 3.75/(1.0 + 3.75) = 0.7895. The overall gain is therefore −100 × 0.7895 = −78.95 V/V, with magnitude 78.9 V/V. Because the gain depends on β through rπ, a different transistor will change this value, which is the motivation for degeneration.

Answer: 78.9 V/V

(b)

With an unbypassed RE, the gain from the source to the output is vo/vs = −β(RC∥RL)/[Rs + rπ + (β + 1)RE]. The numerator is 150 × 2.5 kΩ = 375 kΩ. Setting the magnitude to 30 gives a denominator of 375 000/30 = 12 500 Ω. Subtracting Rs = 1000 Ω and rπ = 3750 Ω leaves (β + 1)RE = 7750 Ω. Dividing by 151, RE = 51.32 Ω. A standard 51 Ω resistor gives a gain of 30.1, well inside the tolerance. The emitter resistor is small enough that the dc bias point is only slightly affected, but it must be accounted for in the bias calculation (about 51 mV at 1 mA).

Answer: 51.3 Ω

(c)

The input resistance at the base is Ri = rπ + (β + 1)RE, since the emitter resistor is reflected to the base multiplied by (β + 1). With rπ = 3.75 kΩ and RE = 51.32 Ω, the reflected term is 151 × 51.32 Ω = 7.75 kΩ. Therefore Ri = 3.75 + 7.75 = 11.5 kΩ. This is about three times that of topology A at 3.75 kΩ, so the amplifier loads the microphone less, which is part of the reason the gain from the source falls less than the gain from the base. The divider fraction in topology B is 11.5/(1.0 + 11.5) = 0.92 compared with 0.79 in topology A.

Answer: 11.5 kΩ

(d)

With β = 100, rπ = β/gm = 100/0.040 S = 2.5 kΩ. The new numerator is β RC∥RL = 100 × 2.5 kΩ = 250 kΩ. The denominator is Rs + rπ + (β + 1)RE = 1000 + 2500 + 101 × 51.32 = 8683 Ω. The gain is 250 000/8683 = 28.79 V/V, compared with 30.0 before, a reduction of (30 − 28.79)/30 = 4.04 percent. For topology A, the same change gives −100 × 2.5/(1.0 + 2.5) = −71.4, a 9.5 percent drop from 78.9. Thus degeneration roughly halves the sensitivity to β, at the cost of cutting the gain from 79 to 30. The designer chooses B when gain accuracy matters more than gain.

Answer: 4.0 %

A5 Practice Paper 9

Problem 1 [A5-041] Diode circuits, clippers and rectifiers

A bench power supply for a 150 Ω load uses a 60 Hz transformer with a 18 V rms secondary feeding a four-diode bridge rectifier. The output is smoothed by a single 2200 μF capacitor connected directly across the load. Each silicon diode drops 0.7 V when conducting, and the transformer is ideal with negligible winding resistance. Use the usual approximation that the capacitor discharges into the load at a constant current equal to the peak load current for the whole interval between charging peaks, so the peak-to-peak ripple is ΔV = Vp/(fr R C), where fr is the ripple frequency. A technician notices the output hum has dropped in pitch and the ripple has grown. She suspects that one diode of the bridge has failed open circuit, which turns the bridge into a half-wave rectifier.

  1. (a) Find the peak output voltage Vp with all four diodes healthy. [4]
  2. (b) Find the peak-to-peak ripple voltage with the healthy full-wave bridge. [5]
  3. (c) With one bridge diode open, find the new peak-to-peak ripple. Assume the peak voltage reaching the load is unchanged. [5]
  4. (d) Find the average load current after the fault, taking the average output voltage as Vp minus half the ripple. [3]
