  5. (e) Explain in two or three sentences why the diodes in the faulty supply also see higher stress than the technician might expect, naming the quantity that most limits the life of the remaining diodes. [3]
(a)

With the bridge healthy, current flows through two diodes in series on each half cycle, so two diode drops of 0.7 V are lost from the secondary peak. The secondary peak is Vs,peak = 18 × √2 = 25.46 V. The peak across the load is therefore Vp = 25.46 − 2 × 0.7 = 25.46 − 1.40 = 24.06 V. The capacitor charges to this value on every peak of the rectified waveform. We assume the transformer is ideal, so there is no extra drop from winding resistance, and we take each diode drop as constant at 0.7 V, which is the stated model. This value is the starting point for every later part because both the ripple and the average load voltage are measured relative to it.

Answer: 24.06 V

(b)

For a full-wave bridge, the capacitor is recharged twice per mains cycle, so the ripple frequency is fr = 2 × 60 = 120 Hz. The ripple formula is ΔV = Vp/(fr R C). Substituting the numbers gives ΔV = 24.06 / (120 × 150 × 2200×10⁻⁶). The product in the denominator is 120 × 150 = 18 000, and 18 000 × 2200×10⁻⁶ = 39.6. Therefore ΔV = 24.06 / 39.6 = 0.607 V peak to peak. The constant-current discharge assumption slightly overestimates the true ripple because the real discharge is exponential, but with a ripple of about 2.5 percent of Vp the error is small. The result tells us the average output voltage will sit about half of this ripple below the peak.

Answer: 0.607 V

(c)

With one diode open circuit, the bridge conducts only on alternate half cycles, so the capacitor is recharged once per mains cycle and the ripple frequency falls to fr = 60 Hz. The peak charging path still contains two diode drops on the conducting half cycle, so Vp stays at 24.06 V, as the question allows. Then ΔV = Vp/(fr R C) = 24.06 / (60 × 150 × 2200×10⁻⁶) = 24.06 / 19.8 = 1.215 V peak to peak. This is exactly double the healthy value because the capacitor has twice as long to discharge into the same load current between recharging peaks. The lower pitch of the hum matches the halving of the ripple frequency from 120 Hz to 60 Hz that the technician heard.

Answer: 1.215 V

(d)

The average output voltage is approximated by the peak minus half of the peak-to-peak ripple, because the waveform swings roughly symmetrically about its mean. After the fault, Vavg = 24.06 − 1.215/2 = 24.06 − 0.607 = 23.45 V. The average load current follows from Ohm's law on the 150 Ω resistor: Iavg = Vavg / R = 23.45 / 150 = 0.1563 A, or about 156 mA. Before the fault, the average voltage was 24.06 − 0.304 = 23.75 V and the current 158 mA, so the average current barely changes. This is why the fault is easy to miss on a DC voltmeter and is found only with an oscilloscope or by listening to the hum.

Answer: 0.1563 A

(e)

With only one diode pair now able to conduct, the capacitor must be recharged in half as many conduction intervals, and because the ripple has doubled it loses twice the charge per cycle. The conduction angle stays short, so the charging current pulses carry twice the charge in each pulse and the repetitive peak current in the remaining diodes roughly doubles, on top of the large surge current at switch on when the capacitor is empty. The mean current is about the same as before, so heating from average current does not change much, but the peak repetitive and surge currents are what limit diode life. The diode current rating, in particular its repetitive peak rating, should therefore be checked against this fault condition.

Answer: Higher peak surge current in the remaining conducting diodes

Problem 2 [A5-042] Zener regulators and power supply filtering

A 12 V ideal Zener diode (zero dynamic resistance, knee current 5 mA) regulates the supply to a sensor board. The unregulated input is a nominal 24 V DC with negligible internal resistance, delivered through a series resistor Rs = 220 Ω to the Zener, and the load is connected in parallel with the Zener. The load is first a 1 kΩ resistor. Later the sensor board is swapped for a heavier unit presented as a 330 Ω load, and the supply is also seen to sag during motor starts elsewhere in the plant. Treat the Zener as holding exactly 12 V while its current stays above the knee value, and as an open circuit with the load and Rs forming a divider when it does not.

  1. (a) Find the Zener current with the 1 kΩ load and a 24 V input. [4]
  2. (b) Find the Zener current when the 330 Ω load replaces the 1 kΩ load, with the input still 24 V. [4]
  3. (c) With the 330 Ω load connected, find the lowest input voltage at which the output is still held at 12 V. [5]
  4. (d) During a motor start the input falls to 18 V with the 330 Ω load still connected. Find the output voltage. [4]
  5. (e) With the load disconnected entirely and the input at 24 V, find the power dissipated in the Zener. [3]
(a)

The series resistor carries the total current, which is Is = (24 − 12) / 220 = 12 / 220 = 54.55 mA. The load current is IL = 12 V / 1000 Ω = 12 mA, because the Zener holds the load at 12 V. Kirchhoff's current law at the junction of Rs, the Zener and the load gives the Zener current as the difference: Iz = Is − IL = 54.55 − 12 = 42.55 mA. This is well above the 5 mA knee, so the Zener is regulating as assumed. The same junction equation will be used in each later part, with the only change being the load current and the input voltage, so it is worth writing in this general form.

Answer: 42.5 mA

(b)

The series current is unchanged at 54.55 mA because the voltage across Rs is still 24 − 12 = 12 V, provided the Zener keeps regulating. The new load current is IL = 12 / 330 = 36.36 mA. Applying the junction equation: Iz = 54.55 − 36.36 = 18.18 mA. This is still above the 5 mA knee, so regulation holds, but the margin has shrunk from 37.5 mA to 13.2 mA above the knee. This shows the effect of the heavier load: the Zener absorbs less of the supply current and the headroom against a falling input voltage is greatly reduced. A designer would flag this as a marginal arrangement because the load is changing by a factor of three.

Answer: 18.2 mA

(c)

Regulation is just maintained when the Zener current falls to the knee value of 5 mA. At that point the series current is Is = IL + Iz,min = 36.36 + 5 = 41.36 mA. The voltage drop across Rs is then 220 × 41.36×10⁻³ = 9.10 V. The input voltage must supply this drop plus the 12 V across the Zener: Vs,min = 12 + 9.10 = 21.10 V. The supply may therefore sag by only 2.9 V, or about 12 percent below nominal, before the output starts to fall. A voltage dip of that size is common during motor starts, which explains the intermittent resets on the sensor board when this heavier load is used.

Answer: 21.1 V

(d)

At 18 V the input is below the 21.1 V minimum, so the Zener has dropped below its knee and carries essentially no current. It behaves as an open circuit, leaving Rs and the load as a simple voltage divider. The output is Vo = 18 × 330 / (220 + 330) = 18 × 0.6 = 10.8 V. We check the assumption: 10.8 V is below the 12 V Zener voltage, so the Zener is indeed not conducting, and the result is self-consistent. The output is therefore 1.2 V low, which on a logic or sensor supply is enough to cause brown-out resets. The remedy is a lower Rs, a higher input voltage margin, or a series-pass or switching regulator.

Answer: 10.8 V

(e)

With the load removed, all of the series current flows through the Zener. The series current is still Is = (24 − 12)/220 = 54.55 mA, since the Zener holds 12 V while conducting. The power dissipated in the Zener is Pz = Vz × Iz = 12 × 54.55×10⁻³ = 0.6545 W. This is the worst case for the Zener, because the load normally takes part of the current away. The device chosen therefore needs a power rating comfortably above about 0.65 W, such as a 1.3 W part, and the designer should also check that the input does not rise above its stated nominal value, since the Zener power increases directly with the current in Rs.

Answer: 0.655 W

Problem 3 [A5-043] Thyristors, SCR and TRIAC circuits

A 12 Ω resistive heating element in an Ontario greenhouse is supplied from a 120 V rms, 60 Hz single-phase source through a single SCR in series with the element, so the heater receives only the positive half cycles. The SCR is triggered at a firing angle α = 60°, measured from the positive-going zero crossing, and conducts until the current falls to zero at 180°. Assume an ideal SCR with no forward drop and an ideal gating circuit. For half-wave phase control of a resistor, the rms load voltage is Vrms = (Vm/2) √(1 − α/π + sin 2α/(2π)), and the average load voltage is Vm(1 + cos α)/(2π), where Vm is the peak source voltage. Later, the owner asks what happens if the control is turned down or if the SCR is replaced by a TRIAC.

  1. (a) Find the average load voltage at α = 60°. [4]
  2. (b) Find the average power delivered to the heater at α = 60°. [5]
  3. (c) The owner wants the heater to dissipate only 250 W using the SCR. Find the firing angle required, in degrees. [5]
  4. (d) The SCR is replaced by a TRIAC firing at the same α = 60° in each half cycle. Find the heater power. [3]
  5. (e) With the original SCR, find the heater power if the control is turned down to α = 120°. [3]
(a)

The source peak is Vm = 120 × √2 = 169.7 V. The average load voltage for half-wave phase control of a resistive load is Vavg = Vm (1 + cos α)/(2π). With α = 60°, cos α = 0.5, so Vavg = 169.7 × 1.5 / 6.2832 = 254.6 / 6.2832 = 40.51 V. The average is found by integrating the positive half sine from α to π and dividing by the full period 2π, because the negative half cycle contributes nothing. The average current would be 40.51/12 = 3.38 A, which is what a DC moving-coil meter in series with the element would read, although the heating depends on the rms value, not on this average.

Answer: 40.5 V

(b)

Heating power depends on the rms voltage, so we evaluate the bracket in the given formula. With α = π/3 = 1.0472 rad, α/π = 0.3333 and sin 2α = sin 120° = 0.8660. The bracket is 1 − 0.3333 + 0.8660/(2π) = 0.6667 + 0.1378 = 0.8045. The square root is 0.8969. With Vm/2 = 84.85 V, Vrms = 84.85 × 0.8969 = 76.1 V. The power is P = Vrms²/R = 76.1² / 12 = 5792 / 12 = 482.7 W. For comparison, uncontrolled half-wave conduction would give 120²/(2 × 12) = 600 W, so firing at 60° passes about 80 percent of the full half-wave power.

Answer: 483 W

(c)

We need Vrms = √(P R) = √(250 × 12) = √3000 = 54.77 V. Dividing by Vm/2 = 84.85 V gives the ratio 0.6455, and its square is 0.4167. The firing angle must satisfy the equation 1 − α/π + sin 2α/(2π) = 0.4167. This is transcendental, so we solve it numerically. At α = 90° the bracket is 0.5 + 0 = 0.5, too high. At α = 100° (1.7453 rad) it is 1 − 0.5556 + sin 200°/(2π) = 0.4444 − 0.0544 = 0.3900, too low. Interpolating and refining gives α ≈ 97.5°. The firing angle is past the peak of the sine wave, where the supply voltage is already falling, which is why power drops quickly in this region of the control range.

Answer: 97.5°

(d)

A TRIAC conducts on both half cycles, with the same firing angle in each, so the negative half cycle now repeats the positive one with reversed polarity. The load voltage waveform over a full cycle has twice the energy of the half-wave case at the same angle, while the load resistance is unchanged. The power is therefore exactly double: P = 2 × 482.7 = 965.4 W. Equivalently, the rms voltage becomes (Vm/√2) × 0.8969 = 107.6 V, and 107.6²/12 = 965 W. The TRIAC also removes the DC component from the supply current, which matters because a DC component can saturate upstream transformers, so it is the preferred choice for a heating load of this size.

Answer: 965 W

(e)

At α = 120° = 2π/3 rad, α/π = 0.6667 and sin 2α = sin 240° = −0.8660, so the term sin 2α/(2π) = −0.1378. The bracket is 1 − 0.6667 − 0.1378 = 0.1955, with square root 0.4421. Then Vrms = 84.85 × 0.4421 = 37.5 V, and the power is P = 37.5²/12 = 1407/12 = 117.3 W. Moving from 60° to 120° therefore cuts the power by a factor of more than four, from 483 W to 117 W, although the angle only doubled. The relationship between firing angle and power is strongly nonlinear, so a linear dial would feel very sensitive at low settings.

Answer: 117 W

Problem 4 [A5-044] BJT bias circuits and operating point

A silicon NPN transistor is used in a voltage-divider biased common-emitter stage powered from a 15 V supply. The divider is R1 = 47 kΩ from the supply to the base and R2 = 10 kΩ from the base to ground. The collector resistor is RC = 2.2 kΩ and the emitter resistor is RE = 1 kΩ. Take VBE = 0.7 V in the active region, VCE(sat) = 0.2 V and a current gain β = 100. A repair technician replaces the original transistor with a part of the same type but with β = 300, and later a joint fails so that R2 opens. Use IE = (β + 1)IB and IC = βIB, and write IE ≈ IC only where a part says so.

  1. (a) Find the collector current IC with the original β = 100 transistor. [5]
  2. (b) Find the collector-emitter voltage VCE of the original circuit and state whether the transistor is in the active region. [3]
  3. (c) Find the collector current with the replacement β = 300 transistor. [4]
  4. (d) Find the collector current at the edge of saturation for the original circuit, taking VCE = 0.2 V and IE ≈ IC. [4]
  5. (e) The joint fails so that R2 is open circuit. Find the collector current the active-region equations would predict, and decide whether it exceeds IC(sat). [4]
(a)

Replace the divider by its Thevenin equivalent. Vth = 15 × 10/(47 + 10) = 2.632 V and Rth = 47 k ∥ 10 k = 8.246 kΩ. The base loop equation is Vth = IB Rth + VBE + IE RE with IE = (β + 1)IB. Solving for the base current gives IB = (Vth − VBE) / (Rth + (β + 1)RE) = (2.632 − 0.7) / (8.246 + 101 × 1) kΩ = 1.932 / 109.25 mA = 17.68 μA. The collector current is IC = βIB = 100 × 17.68 μA = 1.768 mA. This is the dc bias current that sets the operating point for the stage, and the transistor is in the active region as we check in the next part.

Answer: 1.77 mA

(b)

The emitter current is IE = (β + 1)IB = 101 × 17.68 μA = 1.786 mA. Around the collector-emitter loop, VCE = VCC − IC RC − IE RE = 15 − 1.768 × 2.2 − 1.786 × 1 = 15 − 3.890 − 1.786 = 9.324 V. Since VCE is far above the saturation value of 0.2 V, and the base current is positive, the transistor is in the forward-active region and the assumed model is valid. The Q point of about 1.77 mA and 9.3 V leaves ample room for symmetrical output swing, since half of 15 V is 7.5 V and the Q point sits slightly above that, favouring a little more swing on the negative side.

Answer: 9.32 V

(c)

The Thevenin values are unchanged, so IB = (2.632 − 0.7) / (8.246 + 301 × 1) kΩ = 1.932 / 309.25 mA = 6.248 μA. The collector current is IC = 300 × 6.248 μA = 1.874 mA. A tripling of β has raised the collector current by only 6 percent, from 1.768 mA to 1.874 mA. The reason is that the emitter resistor and the stiff divider set the emitter voltage, and therefore the current, almost independently of β, because (β + 1)RE is much larger than Rth. This is the point of using the divider bias with emitter degeneration: the operating point is stable against transistor replacement, which is useful in repair work.

Answer: 1.874 mA

(d)

At the edge of saturation, the supply is shared across the collector resistor, the transistor and the emitter resistor. With IE ≈ IC, VCC = IC (RC + RE) + VCE(sat), so IC(sat) = (15 − 0.2) / (2.2 + 1) kΩ = 14.8 / 3.2 = 4.625 mA. This is the largest collector current the external circuit can carry. Any base drive that would try to push the collector current beyond this value cannot succeed, and the transistor saturates with VCE pinned near 0.2 V and the ratio IC/IB falling below β. The result will be compared with the current the base drive could demand after the fault in the next part.

Answer: 4.625 mA

(e)

With R2 open, the base network is just R1 from the supply, so Vth = 15 V and Rth = 47 kΩ. The active-region base current would be IB = (15 − 0.7) / (47 + 101 × 1) kΩ = 14.3 / 148 mA = 96.6 μA. The predicted collector current is IC = 100 × 96.6 μA = 9.66 mA. This is more than twice the 4.625 mA that the circuit can supply, so the active-region assumption is false and the transistor must be saturated. The true collector current is limited to about 4.6 mA, VCE falls to about 0.2 V, and the measured collector voltage sits near 15 − 4.6 × 2.2 = 4.8 V. A technician measuring the near-zero VCE would immediately suspect an open R2.

Answer: 9.66 mA, which exceeds 4.625 mA, so the transistor saturates

Problem 5 [A5-045] BJT small-signal model and common-emitter amplifier

A common-emitter stage in a microphone preamplifier uses an NPN transistor biased at IC = 1.5 mA with β = 150 and Early voltage VA = 80 V. Take the thermal voltage VT = 25 mV. The emitter is bypassed to ground at signal frequencies. The base bias network presents an equivalent resistance of 20 kΩ to ground at the base, which appears in parallel with the transistor input. The collector resistor is 3.3 kΩ and the load, capacitively coupled, is 10 kΩ. The source has an internal resistance of 1 kΩ. Use the hybrid-π model with gm = IC/VT, rπ = β/gm and ro = VA/IC. A designer then asks what happens to the gain if the bypass capacitor is removed, leaving an unbypassed emitter resistor of 200 Ω.

  1. (a) Find the transconductance gm in mS. [3]
  2. (b) Find the input resistance seen by the source, including the 20 kΩ bias network. [3]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the overall voltage gain vo/vs with the emitter bypassed, including the effect of ro. [5]
  4. (d) The bypass capacitor is removed so that the emitter has an unbypassed 200 Ω resistor. Neglecting ro, find the magnitude of vo/vs. [6]
  5. (e) Find the factor by which the overall gain magnitude falls when the bypass capacitor is removed. [3]
(a)

The transconductance of a BJT at a bias current IC is gm = IC / VT, because the exponential collector current law gives dIC/dVBE = IC/VT. Substituting the stated values, gm = 1.5 mA / 25 mV = 60 mA/V, which is 60 mS. This is the small-signal gain parameter of the device and does not depend on β or on the Early voltage. From it the other hybrid-π parameters follow: rπ = β/gm = 150 / 0.060 = 2.5 kΩ, and ro = VA/IC = 80 / 1.5 mA = 53.3 kΩ. Those two values are used in the input resistance and in the voltage gain calculations that follow, so they should be recorded here.

Answer: 60 mS

(b)

With the emitter fully bypassed, the resistance looking into the base is rπ = 2.5 kΩ. The bias network presents 20 kΩ in parallel at the same node, so Rin = 20 k ∥ 2.5 k = (20 × 2.5)/(20 + 2.5) kΩ = 50/22.5 = 2.222 kΩ. The bias resistors therefore load the signal source only slightly, since they are eight times larger than rπ, and the input resistance is dominated by the transistor itself. This value controls how much of the 1 kΩ source resistance forms a divider with the stage, which is needed for the overall gain in the next part.

Answer: 2.22 kΩ

(c)

The ac load on the collector is RC, RL and ro in parallel: RC ∥ RL = 3.3 × 10/13.3 = 2.481 kΩ, and with ro = 53.33 kΩ the total is 1/(1/2.481 + 1/53.33) = 2.371 kΩ. The gain from base to output is vo/vπ = −gm × 2.371 kΩ = −0.060 × 2371 = −142.3. The input divider between the 1 kΩ source and Rin = 2.222 kΩ gives vπ/vs = 2.222/(2.222 + 1) = 0.6897. Hence vo/vs = −142.3 × 0.6897 = −98.1, so the magnitude is 98.1. The negative sign indicates the 180 degree phase inversion typical of the common-emitter amplifier.

Answer: 98.1

(d)

With an unbypassed emitter resistor, the resistance into the base is Rb,in = rπ + (β + 1)RE = 2500 + 151 × 200 = 32 700 Ω. In parallel with the 20 kΩ bias network, Rin = 20 k ∥ 32.7 k = 12.41 kΩ. The collector load is RC ∥ RL = 2.481 kΩ since ro is neglected. The base-to-output gain is −βR'L / Rb,in = −150 × 2481/32 700 = −11.38. The input divider is Rin/(Rin + Rs) = 12.41/(12.41 + 1) = 0.9254. Therefore vo/vs = −11.38 × 0.9254 = −10.53, magnitude 10.5. The gain has collapsed because the 200 Ω resistor introduces local negative feedback, the price paid for linearity and stability of gain.

Answer: 10.5

(e)

The factor is the ratio of the bypassed gain magnitude to the unbypassed gain magnitude. Using the values from the earlier parts, 98.1 / 10.53 = 9.31. The gain therefore falls by a factor of about 9.3, roughly 19.4 dB. Part of the loss comes from the base-to-output gain, which fell from 142.3 to 11.4, and part is partially offset by the improvement in the input divider, which rose from 0.690 to 0.925 because the input resistance increased. This tradeoff, lower gain in exchange for higher input resistance and gain that depends mainly on resistor ratios instead of on gm and β, is the usual reason for leaving some emitter resistance unbypassed.

Answer: 9.3

A5 Practice Paper 10

Problem 1 [A5-046] Common-collector and common-base stages

An emitter follower is used to isolate a 5 kΩ sensor from a 330 Ω data-logger input. The transistor has β = 120 and is biased at IC = 4 mA. Take VT = 25 mV and neglect ro. The emitter bias resistor RE is 1 kΩ, connected from the emitter to the negative supply, and the base bias network is represented by a single 100 kΩ resistor in parallel with the transistor input at the base. The load is capacitively coupled to the emitter, so at signal frequencies RE and RL are in parallel. The source resistance is Rs = 5 kΩ. Use the hybrid-π model with gm = IC/VT and rπ = β/gm. A colleague proposes swapping the follower for a common-base stage using the same transistor and bias, and later the data logger is replaced by one with a 50 Ω input.

  1. (a) Find the input resistance seen by the source at the base node, including the 100 kΩ bias resistor. [5]
  2. (b) Find the overall voltage gain vo/vs, including the source resistance of 5 kΩ. [5]
  3. (c) Find the output resistance seen by the 330 Ω load, including RE and the effect of the source. [4]
  4. (d) The logger is replaced by one with a 50 Ω input. Find the new overall gain vo/vs. [3]
  5. (e) Explain briefly why a common-base stage, with the same transistor and bias, would not be a suitable replacement as a buffer between this 5 kΩ source and the logger, quoting the order of magnitude of its input resistance. [3]
(a)

First gm = 4 mA/25 mV = 160 mS and rπ = β/gm = 120/0.160 = 750 Ω. The signal emitter load is RE ∥ RL = 1000 × 330/1330 = 248.1 Ω. Reflecting this to the base gives the resistance looking into the base of the transistor: Rb,in = rπ + (β + 1)(RE ∥ RL) = 750 + 121 × 248.1 = 750 + 30 023 = 30 773 Ω. The bias resistor of 100 kΩ is in parallel at the base node, so Rin = 100 k ∥ 30.77 k = 23.53 kΩ. This is far larger than the 330 Ω load, which is the first advantage of the follower: it presents a light load to the source.

Answer: 23.5 kΩ

(b)

The gain from the base to the emitter output is a voltage divider within the transistor model: vo/vb = (β + 1)(RE ∥ RL) / (rπ + (β + 1)(RE ∥ RL)) = 30 023 / 30 773 = 0.9756. The source divider at the input is Rin/(Rin + Rs) = 23.53/(23.53 + 5) = 0.8248. The overall gain is therefore vo/vs = 0.9756 × 0.8248 = 0.8047. The gain is positive, so there is no phase inversion, and it is below unity. The loss comes mainly from the 5 kΩ source driving the 23.5 kΩ input, not from the transistor itself, which is nearly an ideal buffer at this bias current and load.

Answer: 0.805

(c)

Looking back into the emitter, the base circuit resistance is the source in parallel with the bias resistor: Rs ∥ 100 k = 5 × 100/105 = 4.762 kΩ. This resistance is divided by (β + 1) when seen from the emitter and added to the intrinsic emitter resistance: Rout,transistor = (rπ + 4762)/(β + 1) = (750 + 4762)/121 = 45.55 Ω. The emitter bias resistor RE = 1000 Ω is in parallel with this at the output, so Rout = 45.55 ∥ 1000 = 43.57 Ω. The follower therefore delivers its signal from a source of only 43.6 Ω, much smaller than the 5 kΩ source resistance, which is the impedance-transforming action that makes it a buffer.

Answer: 43.6 Ω

(d)

With RL = 50 Ω, the signal emitter load becomes RE ∥ RL = 1000 × 50/1050 = 47.62 Ω. The resistance looking into the base is rπ + 121 × 47.62 = 750 + 5762 = 6512 Ω. In parallel with 100 kΩ this gives Rin = 6113 Ω. The base-to-emitter gain is 5762/6512 = 0.8848, and the source divider is 6113/(6113 + 5000) = 0.5501. The overall gain is vo/vs = 0.8848 × 0.5501 = 0.4867. This is a drop from 0.805, because both the transistor stage and the input divider lose gain, since a heavy load reflects a much lower resistance to the base. The heavier load therefore costs about 40 percent of the gain, which a follower can only avoid by using a larger bias current.

Answer: 0.487

(e)

A common-base stage presents an input resistance of about re = α/gm, which at this bias is 0.992/0.160 = 6.2 Ω, in parallel with the emitter bias resistor. Almost all of the signal from a 5 kΩ source would be lost across the source resistance, giving an input divider of about 6/5006, near 0.001. The stage has a good voltage gain for a high-resistance collector load and excellent high-frequency behaviour, and a current gain just below unity, but those are the wrong properties for isolating a high-impedance source from a low-impedance load. The follower is the correct choice here because it has high input resistance, low output resistance and a voltage gain near unity.

Answer: Its input resistance is only about re, roughly 6 Ω, which would load the 5 kΩ source heavily

Problem 2 [A5-047] MOSFET bias and operating regions

An n-channel enhancement MOSFET is biased with a resistive divider from a 12 V supply: R1 = 1 MΩ from the supply to the gate and R2 = 500 kΩ from the gate to ground, so no gate current flows. The source resistor is RS = 2 kΩ and the drain resistor is RD = 3.3 kΩ. The device parameters are Vt = 1 V and K = 2 mA/V², with channel length modulation neglected. In saturation, ID = (K/2)(VGS − Vt)². In the triode region, ID = K[(VGS − Vt)VDS − VDS²/2]. A later repair uses a drain resistor of 10 kΩ by mistake, and the designer also wants to know what source resistor would give a lower bias current.

  1. (a) Find the drain current ID in the original circuit, assuming saturation. [5]
  2. (b) Find VDS in the original circuit and confirm the saturation assumption. [3]
  3. (c) The 10 kΩ drain resistor is fitted by mistake. Find the new drain current, deciding first whether the device remains in saturation. [6]
  4. (d) For the 10 kΩ drain resistor, find VDS. [3]
  5. (e) With RD = 3.3 kΩ and the same gate divider, find the source resistor RS that would lower the bias current to 0.5 mA. [3]
(a)

The gate voltage is VG = 12 × 500 k/(1 M + 500 k) = 4 V, and since the gate current is zero, VGS = VG − ID RS = 4 − 2 ID with ID in mA and RS in kΩ. With saturation, ID = (K/2)(VGS − Vt)² = 1 × (VGS − 1)² mA. Let x = VGS − 1 = 3 − 2 ID. Then ID = x² gives x = 3 − 2x², or 2x² + x − 3 = 0. The positive root is x = (−1 + √(1 + 24))/4 = 1.00 V, so VGS = 2 V and ID = 1.00 mA. The other root is negative, meaning VGS would fall below Vt, which is not physically acceptable. The operating region must now be checked.

Answer: 1.00 mA

(b)

The drain-source voltage is VDS = VDD − ID(RD + RS) = 12 − 1.00 × (3.3 + 2) = 6.7 V. For saturation of an enhancement NMOS we require VDS ≥ VGS − Vt = 2 − 1 = 1 V. Since 6.7 V is well above 1 V, the transistor is saturated and the assumption used in part a is justified. The device has about 5.7 V of headroom beyond the saturation boundary, so it will tolerate a drain voltage swing of this size before leaving the saturation region, an important point if the stage is later used as an amplifier.

Answer: 6.7 V

(c)

Try saturation first: it would again give ID = 1.00 mA with VGS = 2 V, so VDS = 12 − 1 × (10 + 2) = 0 V, which is below VGS − Vt = 1 V. The device cannot be saturated, so it is in the triode region. The unknowns satisfy VGS = 4 − 2 ID and VDS = 12 − 12 ID, with ID = K[(VGS − Vt)VDS − VDS²/2]. Substituting gives ID = 2[(3 − 2 ID)(12 − 12 ID) − (12 − 12 ID)²/2]. Solving numerically, ID = 0.951 mA gives VGS = 2.099 V and VDS = 0.592 V, and checking, 2[(1.099)(0.592) − 0.175] = 0.951 mA, which satisfies the equation. The current is hardly changed, because RS, not RD, dominates the current.

Answer: 0.951 mA

(d)

From the solution of part c, ID = 0.9506 mA. The drain-source voltage follows from the drain loop: VDS = VDD − ID(RD + RS) = 12 − 0.9506 × 12 = 12 − 11.41 = 0.592 V. This is smaller than the overdrive VGS − Vt = 1.099 V, which confirms the triode assumption. The transistor is acting as a resistor of about VDS/ID = 0.592/0.9506 = 623 Ω rather than as a current source. In an amplifier this would be a serious fault, since the output signal would be clipped heavily and the gain would collapse.

Answer: 0.592 V

(e)

For saturation at ID = 0.5 mA, (K/2)(VGS − Vt)² = 0.5, so (VGS − 1)² = 0.5 and VGS − 1 = 0.7071 V, giving VGS = 1.7071 V. The gate stays at 4 V, so the source resistor must drop VS = 4 − 1.7071 = 2.2929 V at 0.5 mA: RS = 2.2929 / 0.5 mA = 4.586 kΩ. We can check that the device remains saturated: VDS = 12 − 0.5 × (3.3 + 4.586) = 8.06 V, far above the 0.707 V overdrive. A larger source resistor lowers the current and also reduces its sensitivity to variations in Vt between devices, so the design is more stable.

Answer: 4.59 kΩ

Problem 3 [A5-048] MOSFET small-signal amplifiers

A common-source amplifier uses an n-channel MOSFET biased in saturation at ID = 0.5 mA. The device has K = 4 mA/V² in ID = (K/2)(VGS − Vt)², threshold Vt = 0.8 V, and channel length modulation λ = 0.02 V⁻¹, so ro = 1/(λ ID). The drain resistor is RD = 10 kΩ and a capacitively coupled load RL = 20 kΩ is attached. The gate bias resistor is 1 MΩ and the source has an internal resistance of 50 kΩ. The source terminal is bypassed to ground in the first configuration. In a second configuration an unbypassed source resistor of 500 Ω is left in the signal path. Neglect ro when an unbypassed source resistor is present.

  1. (a) Find the transconductance gm at the stated bias point, in mS. [3]
  2. (b) With the source bypassed, find the magnitude of the voltage gain vo/vgs, including ro. [4]
  3. (c) With the source bypassed, find the magnitude of the overall gain vo/vs including the 50 kΩ source resistance and the 1 MΩ gate resistor. [3]
  4. (d) Now leave the 500 Ω source resistor unbypassed and neglect ro. Find the magnitude of the voltage gain from the gate to the output, taking the input voltage as that applied between gate and ground. [5]
  5. (e) Find the value of unbypassed source resistor that would limit the gain magnitude to 4, using the same approximation. [5]
(a)

In saturation the overdrive is found from ID = (K/2)VOV². Therefore VOV = √(2 ID/K) = √(2 × 0.5/4) = √0.25 = 0.5 V, and VGS = Vt + VOV = 1.3 V. The transconductance is gm = ∂ID/∂VGS = K VOV = 4 × 0.5 = 2 mS. Equivalently gm = 2 ID/VOV = 2 × 0.5 mA/0.5 V = 2 mS. We have neglected the small effect of λ on gm. The output resistance is ro = 1/(0.02 × 0.5 mA) = 100 kΩ, which will be needed in the gain calculation with the bypassed source, where ro is included.

Answer: 2 mS

(b)

The small-signal load seen by the drain current source is RD, RL and ro in parallel. RD ∥ RL = 10 × 20/30 = 6.667 kΩ, and with ro = 100 kΩ the total is 1/(1/6.667 + 1/100) = 6.25 kΩ. The gain is vo/vgs = −gm (RD ∥ RL ∥ ro) = −2 mS × 6.25 kΩ = −12.5. The magnitude is 12.5. The minus sign shows that the common-source stage inverts the signal. Including ro lowers the gain by 6 percent compared with neglecting it, which would give 13.3, and this is the correct size of correction when ro is 15 times larger than the parallel load.

Answer: 12.5

(c)

The input resistance of the stage is the 1 MΩ bias resistor, since the gate draws no signal current. The source divider is Rin/(Rin + Rsig) = 1000/(1000 + 50) = 0.9524. The overall voltage gain magnitude is therefore |vo/vs| = 12.5 × 0.9524 = 11.9. The high input resistance of the MOSFET stage means the 50 kΩ source resistance costs only about 5 percent of the signal, whereas a BJT stage with an input resistance of a few kilohms would lose most of it. This is the main advantage of the MOSFET for amplifying signals from high-impedance sources.

Answer: 11.9

(d)

With an unbypassed source resistor RS, the gain from gate to drain is vo/vi = −gm R'L/(1 + gm RS), with R'L = RD ∥ RL = 6.667 kΩ since ro is neglected. The term gm RS = 2 mS × 0.5 kΩ = 1. So vo/vi = −2 × 6.667/(1 + 1) = −13.33/2 = −6.667, magnitude 6.67. The source resistor produces local series feedback: part of the output signal appears as a voltage across RS in opposition to the input, so the gain is reduced by the factor 1 + gm RS = 2, and the effective transconductance is halved to 1 mS. The reduction comes in return for a gain that depends more on resistor values and less on the device parameters.

Answer: 6.67

(e)

Set the gain magnitude equal to 4: gm R'L/(1 + gm RS) = 4, with gm R'L = 2 × 6.667 = 13.33. Then 1 + gm RS = 13.33/4 = 3.333, so gm RS = 2.333 and RS = 2.333/2 mS = 1.1667 kΩ = 1167 Ω. As a check, 13.33/(1 + 2 × 1.1667) = 13.33/3.333 = 4. This resistor must also be used consistently in the dc bias design, where its drop of 0.5 mA × 1.1667 kΩ = 0.583 V changes the required gate voltage by that amount. In practice the nearest standard value, 1.2 kΩ, would give a gain magnitude of 3.9, which is acceptable for a design target of 4.

Answer: 1167 Ω

Problem 4 [A5-049] Multistage amplifiers and loading effects

A two-stage voltage amplifier is built from two common-emitter stages in cascade. Each stage is characterised by its open-circuit voltage gain, input resistance and output resistance. Stage 1 has open-circuit gain Avo1 = −120, input resistance Rin1 = 2.0 kΩ and output resistance Ro1 = 3.0 kΩ. Stage 2 has Avo2 = −200, Rin2 = 1.5 kΩ and Ro2 = 1.2 kΩ. The source resistance is Rs = 600 Ω and the load is RL = 2.4 kΩ, and the stages are coupled with capacitors that are large enough to be treated as short circuits at signal frequencies. A technician finds the measured gain is far below the product of the individual open-circuit gains and wants to see how an emitter-follower buffer inserted between the stages would help. The buffer has open-circuit gain 0.98, input resistance 100 kΩ and output resistance 60 Ω.

  1. (a) Find the loaded voltage gain of stage 1 when it drives the input of stage 2. [3]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the overall gain vo/vs of the two-stage amplifier. [5]
  3. (c) Express the overall gain magnitude in decibels. [2]
  4. (d) The buffer is inserted between stage 1 and stage 2. Find the magnitude of the overall gain vo/vs. [6]
  5. (e) Find the ratio of the buffered gain to the unbuffered gain. [4]
(a)

The output of stage 1 forms a voltage divider between its own output resistance and the input resistance of stage 2. The loaded gain is Av1 = Avo1 × Rin2/(Rin2 + Ro1) = −120 × 1.5/(1.5 + 3.0) = −120 × 0.3333 = −40. Two thirds of the signal produced by stage 1 are lost across its own output resistance, because stage 2 has an input resistance only half as large as that output resistance. This is the loading effect: the open-circuit gain would be available only if the following stage drew no current. The product of open-circuit gains, 24 000, is therefore grossly misleading for the real amplifier.

Answer: -40

(b)

The overall gain is the product of the input divider and the loaded gains of the two stages. The input divider is Rin1/(Rin1 + Rs) = 2.0/(2.0 + 0.6) = 0.7692. The loaded gain of stage 1 is −40 from part a. The loaded gain of stage 2 with the load is Av2 = Avo2 × RL/(RL + Ro2) = −200 × 2.4/(2.4 + 1.2) = −133.3. The product is 0.7692 × (−40) × (−133.3) = +4103. The two inversions cancel, so the overall gain is positive, with magnitude 4103. Only 17 percent of the 24 000 open-circuit product reaches the output, because loading occurs at three interfaces.

Answer: 4103

(c)

The gain in decibels is 20 log10 of the voltage gain ratio. Using the result of part b, 20 log10(4103) = 20 × 3.613 = 72.26 dB. The value 3.613 is found from log10(4103) = log10(4.103) + 3 = 0.6131 + 3. This is the voltage gain, which is the quantity relevant for amplifiers that have different input and output resistances, and no assumption is made about power gain. Each stage and each interface contributes to the total: the input divider costs 2.3 dB, stage 1 contributes 32.0 dB, and stage 2 contributes 42.5 dB, and these sum to the same 72.3 dB, with the sign neglected.

Answer: 72.3 dB

(d)

With the buffer, stage 1 drives a 100 kΩ input instead of 1.5 kΩ, so its loaded gain is −120 × 100/(100 + 3) = −116.5. The buffer drives stage 2, so its loaded gain is 0.98 × 1.5/(1.5 + 0.06) = 0.98 × 0.9615 = 0.9423. Stage 2 and the input divider are unchanged: −133.3 and 0.7692. The overall gain is 0.7692 × (−116.5) × 0.9423 × (−133.3) = +11 260. The buffer loses only a few percent at each of its own interfaces, whereas the direct connection between stages lost two thirds of the signal. The buffer is thus a good investment even though it contributes no voltage gain of its own.

Answer: 11 260

(e)

The ratio is found by dividing the buffered gain by the gain found in part b: 11 260 / 4103 = 2.745. The buffer improves the gain by a factor of 2.74, or 8.8 dB, without any change to either amplifying stage. The improvement arises entirely from replacing the loading between stages: the divider at that interface changed from 0.3333 to 0.9709 (from 1.5 over 4.5, to 100 over 103), which is a factor of 2.91, partly offset by the 0.9423 loss through the buffer itself. 2.91 × 0.9423 = 2.745, which agrees with the ratio. This shows the method for diagnosing multistage loading: examine each interface divider separately.

Answer: 2.74

Problem 5 [A5-050] Frequency response of amplifiers, poles and Miller effect

A common-emitter stage in a sensor amplifier has gm = 40 mS, rπ = 3.75 kΩ, Cπ = 15 pF and Cμ = 2 pF. The transistor is driven from a source of resistance Rs = 1 kΩ, and the bias resistors may be neglected. The collector load in the signal path is RL' = 2.5 kΩ (the collector resistor in parallel with the load, ro neglected), and the base spreading resistance is neglected. Use the Miller approximation: the capacitor Cμ between base and collector appears at the input as Cμ(1 + gm RL'), and the output-side pole is ignored. The dominant high-frequency pole is set by the Thevenin resistance seen by the input capacitance, which is Rs in parallel with rπ. Later the designer lowers the load to RL' = 1 kΩ to see the effect on bandwidth.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the midband voltage gain vo/vs. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total input capacitance Cin using the Miller approximation, in pF. [4]
  3. (c) Find the upper 3 dB frequency fH of the stage in kHz. [4]
  4. (d) The load is reduced to RL' = 1 kΩ. Find the new upper 3 dB frequency in kHz. [4]
  5. (e) Find the ratio of the gain-bandwidth product (midband gain magnitude times fH) for the 1 kΩ load to that of the 2.5 kΩ load. [4]
(a)

At midband the capacitors are open circuits. The base-to-output gain is −gm RL' = −0.040 × 2500 = −100. The input divider formed by the source resistance and rπ gives vπ/vs = rπ/(rπ + Rs) = 3.75/(3.75 + 1) = 0.7895. The midband gain is therefore Am = −100 × 0.7895 = −78.95, magnitude 78.95. The minus sign again indicates inversion. This value is the starting point for the bandwidth: the midband gain and the high-frequency pole will be multiplied to give a gain-bandwidth product, which indicates how much bandwidth is available per unit of gain.

Answer: 78.9

(b)

The Miller multiplication factor is 1 + gm RL' = 1 + 100 = 101. The feedback capacitor Cμ = 2 pF therefore appears at the input as 2 × 101 = 202 pF. This adds to the base-emitter capacitance Cπ = 15 pF in parallel, so Cin = 15 + 202 = 217 pF. The Miller effect dominates: 93 percent of the input capacitance comes from the 2 pF feedback capacitor, because the voltage across it is 101 times the input signal. This explains why a transistor with a very small Cμ can still have a bandwidth that is limited by that capacitance, and why reducing the gain is an effective way of extending bandwidth.

Answer: 217 pF

(c)

The resistance seen by Cin is the Thevenin resistance Rs ∥ rπ = 1000 × 3750/4750 = 789.5 Ω. The pole frequency is fH = 1/(2π R Cin) = 1/(2π × 789.5 × 217×10⁻¹²). The product is 789.5 × 217×10⁻¹² = 1.713×10⁻⁷ s, and 2π times this is 1.0765×10⁻⁶ s. Therefore fH = 1/1.0765×10⁻⁶ = 929 kHz. The stage is thus useful for audio and for signals up to a few hundred kilohertz with limited droop, but not for video or RF work. This pole is the dominant one if the output-side pole lies well above it.

Answer: 929 kHz

(d)

The Miller factor becomes 1 + 0.040 × 1000 = 41, so the Miller capacitance is 2 × 41 = 82 pF and Cin = 15 + 82 = 97 pF. The Thevenin resistance is unchanged at 789.5 Ω, because only the load has changed. The new pole is fH = 1/(2π × 789.5 × 97×10⁻¹²) = 1/(4.812×10⁻⁷) = 2078 kHz. Reducing the load resistance by a factor of 2.5 has increased the bandwidth by a factor of 2.24. The midband gain has dropped to 40 × 1 × 0.7895 = 31.6 at the same time, so the designer has traded gain for bandwidth, as expected for a stage whose bandwidth is limited by the Miller effect.

Answer: 2078 kHz

(e)

The gain-bandwidth product for the 2.5 kΩ load is 78.95 × 929 kHz = 73.3 MHz. For the 1 kΩ load it is 31.58 × 2078 kHz = 65.6 MHz. The ratio is 65.6/73.3 = 0.895. The product is not constant, as it would be for an op-amp with a single pole, because the Miller capacitance includes the fixed 17 pF term of Cπ plus Cμ, which does not scale with load. If Cπ were zero the product would be nearly constant. The gain-bandwidth product falls about 10.5 percent when the load is reduced, so trading gain for bandwidth is not completely free in this stage.

Answer: 0.895

A5 Practice Paper 11

Problem 1 [A5-051] Differential amplifiers and current mirrors

A bench prototype of an instrumentation front end uses a BJT differential pair running from supplies of +12 V and -12 V. Q1 and Q2 are identical NPN transistors with β = 150, VBE = 0.7 V when conducting and thermal voltage VT = 25 mV. Each collector connects to ground through its own 10 kΩ resistor, and the differential output is taken between the two collectors. The emitters join at a common node fed by a tail current source: Q4 is an NPN with its collector on that node and its emitter at -12 V. Q3 is diode connected (base tied to collector), is matched to Q4, shares its base, and has its emitter at -12 V. A resistor Rref connects ground to the collector of Q3 and sets the reference current. Rref is 22.6 kΩ. Ignore the Early effect on all DC currents, but use VA = 100 V for the output resistance of Q4. A technician notices the measured differential gain is twice the value expected from the design sheet.

  1. (a) Find the tail current delivered by Q4, allowing for the finite base currents of Q3 and Q4 in the mirror, in mA. [4]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the differential voltage gain Ad (differential output) for the design as intended. Assume each of Q1 and Q2 carries half of the tail current. [4]
  3. (c) Find the common-mode rejection ratio in dB when the output is taken single-endedly from one collector, using the output resistance of Q4 as the common-mode emitter resistance. [4]
  4. (d) The technician finds that a 11.3 kΩ resistor was fitted in place of Rref. Find the new differential gain magnitude. [4]
  5. (e) Explain, without further calculation, why the single-ended CMRR in part (c) is the same for the wrong resistor as for the correct one, and state the physical quantity that sets it. [4]
(a)

The reference current flows from ground through Rref into the diode connected Q3, whose base-emitter voltage is 0.7 V above the -12 V rail. So Iref = (0 - (-12) - 0.7)/22.6 kΩ = 11.3/22.6 kΩ = 0.500 mA. This current splits into the collector current of Q3 and the base currents of both Q3 and Q4: Iref = IC + 2IB = IC(1 + 2/β). Because the two transistors are matched with the same VBE, the collector current of Q4 equals the collector current of Q3, so Itail = Iref/(1 + 2/150) = 0.500/1.01333 = 0.4934 mA. The finite β therefore reduces the tail current by about 1.3 percent compared with the ideal mirror.

Answer: Itail = 0.4934 mA

(b)

Each device of the pair carries IC = 0.4934/2 = 0.2467 mA, so gm = IC/VT = 0.2467 mA/25 mV = 9.868 mS. With a differential output taken between the collectors and the emitter node acting as a virtual ac ground for a differential input, the gain magnitude of the pair is Ad = gm RC = 9.868 mS × 10 kΩ = 98.7. The sign is negative for the output defined as the collector of Q2 relative to the collector of Q1 against the input defined as the base of Q2 relative to the base of Q1, so only the magnitude is asked. This is the value the design sheet would show, so the technician expects about 98.7, or 39.9 dB.

Answer: |Ad| = 98.7

(c)

For a single-ended output the differential gain is gm RC/2 and the common-mode gain is approximately -RC/(2 Ro), where Ro is the small-signal output resistance of the tail source. Q4 has Ro = VA/Itail = 100 V/0.4934 mA = 202.7 kΩ. The ratio gives CMRR = (gm RC/2)/(RC/(2 Ro)) = gm Ro = 9.868 mS × 202.7 kΩ = 2000. In decibels this is 20 log10(2000) = 66.0 dB. Note that RC cancels completely, so the collector resistors play no role in the rejection, only the tail source and the transistor transconductance matter.

Answer: CMRR = 66.0 dB

(d)

With 11.3 kΩ in place, the reference current doubles: Iref = 11.3/11.3 kΩ = 1.000 mA. The mirror gives Itail = 1.000/1.01333 = 0.9868 mA, so each pair transistor carries 0.4934 mA and gm = 0.4934 mA/25 mV = 19.74 mS. The differential gain magnitude is then gm RC = 19.74 mS × 10 kΩ = 197.4, exactly twice the intended value. This matches the technician's observation and identifies the resistor as the fault, because gain in a bipolar pair is proportional to the tail current when the collector resistors are fixed.

Answer: |Ad| = 197.4

(e)

For the single-ended output, CMRR = gm Ro. The transconductance is proportional to the tail current, since gm = Itail/(2 VT), and the tail source output resistance is inversely proportional to it, since Ro = VA/Itail. In the product the tail current cancels, leaving CMRR = VA/(2 VT) = 100/(2 × 0.025) = 2000, or 66.0 dB. So doubling the tail current doubles the gain but halves the common-mode resistance, and the rejection is unchanged. The quantity that sets it is the Early voltage of the tail transistor relative to the thermal voltage. To improve rejection one would have to raise the effective output resistance with a cascode or Wilson mirror, not simply choose a different bias current.

Answer: CMRR = VA/(2VT), independent of tail current

Problem 2 [A5-052] Op-amp inverting and non-inverting circuits

A data-acquisition card uses an inverting amplifier built from a general purpose op-amp powered from +12 V and -12 V. The input resistor R1 is 10 kΩ from the signal source to the inverting terminal, and the feedback resistor Rf is 100 kΩ from the output back to the inverting terminal, with the non-inverting terminal at ground. The design sheet quotes a closed-loop gain of -10, but a technician measuring the board with a precise signal source obtains a gain of magnitude 9.950 at low frequency. The op-amp is modelled as an ideal voltage amplifier with finite open-loop DC gain A, infinite input resistance and zero output resistance. The output can swing only to ±10.5 V before clipping. The technician proposes swapping Rf for a 470 kΩ resistor to obtain a gain near -47 without changing anything else.

  1. (a) Find the open-loop gain A of the installed op-amp implied by the measured gain magnitude of 9.950. [5]
  2. (b) Find the largest input amplitude, in volts, that the circuit as built can accept before the output clips. [4]
  3. (c) Find the input resistance seen by the signal source for the circuit as built, in kΩ, keeping the finite open-loop gain. [4]
  4. (d) Find the closed-loop gain magnitude with Rf = 470 kΩ and the same op-amp, and the percentage by which it falls short of the ideal value of 47. [4]
  5. (e) Explain in two or three sentences why the gain error grows as the ideal closed-loop gain is raised while A is held fixed. [3]
(a)

For an inverting stage with finite open-loop gain A, the closed-loop gain magnitude is G = (Rf/R1)/(1 + (1 + Rf/R1)/A). Here Rf/R1 = 10, so G = 10/(1 + 11/A). Setting G = 9.950 gives 1 + 11/A = 10/9.950 = 1.005025, so 11/A = 0.005025 and A = 11/0.005025 = 2189. This is far lower than the 100 000 or more of a good op-amp at DC, and it points to a weak or damaged device, or to a part whose gain has collapsed because the output stage is loaded. The result is only as precise as the 0.5 percent gain deficit, so A is accurate to a few percent.

Answer: A = 2189

(b)

The ideal output is clipped at 10.5 V in magnitude. With the actual gain magnitude of 9.950 the largest allowable input amplitude is Vin,max = 10.5/9.950 = 1.055 V. If the engineer had used the ideal gain of 10 the answer would have been 1.050 V, so the finite gain makes only a tiny difference in this part. The more important design point is that a sensor signal above about 1.05 V peak would be flattened by the amplifier. The same limit would apply for positive and negative half cycles because the supplies are symmetrical.

Answer: Vin,max = 1.055 V

(c)

The source sees R1 in series with the impedance looking into the summing node. By the Miller relation, the feedback resistor joins the summing node to an output that is A times larger in magnitude and opposite in sign, so it appears across the summing node as Rf/(1 + A). The input resistance is therefore Rin = R1 + Rf/(1 + A). With A = 2189, Rf/(1 + A) = 100 kΩ/2190 = 45.7 Ω. Therefore Rin = 10 000 + 45.7 = 10 046 Ω, or 10.05 kΩ. The virtual-earth approximation (Rin = R1) is thus accurate to under half of one percent here, because the loop gain is large compared with unity.

Answer: Rin = 10.05 kΩ

(d)

With Rf = 470 kΩ the ideal gain magnitude is 47, and the closed-loop expression is G = 47/(1 + 48/A) = 47/(1 + 48/2189) = 47/1.02193 = 45.99. The shortfall from ideal is (47 - 45.99)/47 = 2.15 percent. Note that the error is more than four times the 0.5 percent seen with Rf = 100 kΩ, so the swap would worsen accuracy even though it is a simple resistor change. The technician should either replace the op-amp first or accept the larger error.

Answer: G = 45.99, error 2.15 percent

(e)

The fractional gain error of an inverting amplifier is approximately (1 + Rf/R1)/A, which is the reciprocal of the loop gain scaled by the noise gain. The noise gain 1 + Rf/R1 rises from 11 to 48 when Rf is increased, while A has not changed, so the loop gain A/(1 + Rf/R1) falls from about 199 to about 46. The feedback therefore has less excess gain available to force the summing node to ground, and the output departs further from the ideal value. The cure is a higher open-loop gain or a lower gain per stage.

Answer: Error ≈ noise gain/A

Problem 3 [A5-053] Op-amp summing, integrating, differentiating and filters

An analogue integrator for a flow-metering instrument uses an op-amp with a 100 kΩ input resistor R from the signal source to the inverting terminal and a 10 nF capacitor C connected from the output back to the inverting terminal. The non-inverting terminal is grounded. The op-amp runs from ±12 V supplies and saturates at ±10.5 V. Its input offset voltage is 3.0 mV, and you may take all other non-idealities (bias current, finite gain) as negligible. At time t = 0 the capacitor is discharged. The designer's lab notebook reports that with the input grounded the output slowly drifts into saturation, so a 1.0 MΩ resistor Rf is proposed in parallel with the capacitor. Use the offset voltage as an equivalent source in series with the non-inverting input.

  1. (a) With Rf absent and the capacitor discharged, a constant input of +0.40 V is applied at t = 0 and the op-amp offset is neglected. Find the time in milliseconds for the output to reach -10.5 V. [4]
  2. (b) With the input grounded, no Rf and the 3.0 mV offset present, find the magnitude of the output drift rate in V/s. [4]
  3. (c) With Rf = 1.0 MΩ in parallel with C, find the steady DC output error in mV caused by the offset. [4]
  4. (d) Find the corner frequency of the modified circuit in Hz. [4]
  5. (e) Find the magnitude of the voltage gain of the modified circuit at 1.00 kHz, and compare it to the gain 1/(ωRC) of the ideal integrator. [4]
(a)

For an ideal inverting integrator, vo(t) = -(1/RC)∫vin dt. With a constant input of 0.40 V, vo = -(0.40/(RC)) t where RC = 100 kΩ × 10 nF = 1.0 ms. So the slope is -0.40 V/1.0 ms = -400 V/s. The output reaches -10.5 V when t = 10.5/400 = 0.02625 s = 26.25 ms. After that instant the op-amp saturates and the integrator no longer behaves as designed. This shows how short the usable interval is: a sustained DC input of only a few tenths of a volt exhausts the output range in a few tens of milliseconds.

Answer: t = 26.25 ms

(b)

With the input grounded, the offset voltage Vos appears as a DC input at the non-inverting terminal. The inverting terminal is held at Vos by feedback, so the resistor R carries a current of -Vos/R (flowing from the inverting node to ground) and the capacitor must supply it. The output therefore ramps at dvo/dt = Vos/(RC) in magnitude, which is 3.0 mV/1.0 ms = 3.0 V/s. It would reach the 10.5 V limit in 3.5 s. This matches the observation that the integrator slowly drifts into saturation even with a grounded input, and shows why a DC path around the capacitor is needed.

Answer: drift 3.0 V/s

(c)

With Rf in parallel with C, the DC gain for the offset is the non-inverting gain 1 + Rf/R = 1 + 1 MΩ/100 kΩ = 11, because the capacitor is open at DC. The offset appears as an equivalent input at the non-inverting terminal, so the DC output error is Vos(1 + Rf/R) = 3.0 mV × 11 = 33 mV. This is a fixed offset, no longer a ramp, and is small compared with the ±10.5 V range. The price of the added resistor is that the circuit is only a true integrator above the corner frequency set by Rf and C.

Answer: 33 mV

(d)

The feedback impedance is Rf parallel C, so the circuit is an inverting first-order low-pass with a transfer function -(Rf/R)/(1 + jωRfC). The corner is at ωc = 1/(RfC) = 1/(1.0 MΩ × 10 nF) = 100 rad/s, so fc = 100/(2π) = 15.92 Hz. Below this frequency the gain is flat at Rf/R = 10, and above it the magnitude falls at 20 dB per decade and approximates an integrator. The designer must therefore operate the signals of interest well above 16 Hz or accept integration error at lower frequencies.

Answer: fc = 15.92 Hz

(e)

At f = 1.00 kHz, ω = 2π × 1000 = 6283 rad/s and ωRfC = 6283 × 0.01 = 62.83. The gain magnitude is (Rf/R)/√(1 + (ωRfC)²) = 10/√(1 + 3947.8) = 10/62.84 = 0.1591. The ideal integrator has 1/(ωRC) = 1/(6283 × 0.001) = 0.1592. The two agree to within 0.1 percent, which confirms that at 1 kHz, about 63 times the corner frequency, the modified circuit behaves as an integrator. The phase lag of the low-pass is arctan(62.8) = 89.1°, within one degree of the ideal integrator value of 90°, so the circuit integrates accurately at this frequency.

Answer: |H| = 0.1591

Problem 4 [A5-054] Feedback in amplifiers: gain, bandwidth and stability

An operational amplifier macro-model used in a precision loop has an open-loop gain A(s) = A0/((1 + s/ωp1)(1 + s/ωp2)). The DC gain is A0 = 100 000, the dominant pole is at fp1 = 10 Hz and a second pole lies at fp2 = 200 kHz. There are no other poles or zeros. The amplifier is placed in a negative-feedback loop with a frequency-independent feedback factor β, so that the loop gain is Aβ. The designer is comparing two uses of the same device: a non-inverting amplifier with β = 0.01 (closed-loop gain about 100) and a unity-gain follower with β = 1. Phase margin is defined as 180° minus the magnitude of the loop phase lag at the frequency where the loop-gain magnitude is unity. Use the exact transfer function, not the single-pole approximation, when finding crossover.

  1. (a) Find the DC closed-loop gain when β = 0.01. [3]
  2. (b) Find the phase margin in degrees when β = 0.01. [4]
  3. (c) Find the loop-gain crossover frequency in kHz for the unity-gain follower (β = 1). [4]
  4. (d) Find the phase margin in degrees for the unity-gain follower. [4]
  5. (e) Explain why the follower, with the lowest closed-loop gain, is the least stable configuration, and state what the phase margin implies about the step response. [5]
(a)

The closed-loop DC gain of a negative-feedback amplifier is A0/(1 + A0 β). With A0 = 100 000 and β = 0.01, A0 β = 1000, so the gain is 100 000/1001 = 99.9. This is within 0.1 percent of the ideal value 1/β = 100, because the loop gain at DC is large. In the exam setting one would note that the loop gain, not the open-loop gain alone, decides the accuracy. Here the fractional error equals 1/(1 + A0β) = 0.0999 percent.

Answer: 99.9

(b)

The crossover frequency fc satisfies |Aβ| = 1: A0β/√((1 + (fc/10)²)(1 + (fc/200 000)²)) = 1 with A0β = 1000. Solving numerically gives fc = 9988 Hz, almost exactly the 10 kHz given by gain-bandwidth/closed-loop-gain = 1 MHz/100. The phase lag of the loop is arctan(fc/10) + arctan(fc/200 000) = 89.99° + 2.86° = 92.85°, so the phase margin is 180° - 92.85° = 87.2°. This is very comfortable: the second pole is twenty times above crossover and costs less than 3° of margin, so the closed loop is nearly a first-order system.

Answer: PM = 87.2°

(c)

For β = 1 the loop gain is A(s) itself, with magnitude 100 000/√((1 + (f/10)²)(1 + (f/200 000)²)). The magnitude reaches unity at f where 1010 = (1 + (f/10)²)(1 + (f/200 000)²). Solving numerically gives f = 425.4 kHz. A single-pole estimate would say 1 MHz (the gain-bandwidth product), but the second pole pulls the magnitude down faster beyond 200 kHz, so the true crossover is less than half of that. This is the key difference from the β = 0.01 case, where crossover was far below the second pole.

Answer: fc = 425.4 kHz

(d)

At fc = 425.4 kHz the phase lag from the dominant pole is arctan(425 400/10) = 89.99°, and from the second pole arctan(425.4/200) = arctan(2.127) = 64.8°. The total lag is 154.8°, so the phase margin is 180° - 154.8° = 25.2°. This is well below the 45° to 60° normally required for a well-damped response, so the follower made from this macro-model would show heavy peaking and ringing in its step response, and would be at risk if any extra pole (such as a capacitive load) were added.

Answer: PM = 25.2°

(e)

The crossover frequency is approximately β A0 fp1, so raising β moves crossover higher. The second pole contributes a phase lag arctan(fc/fp2) that grows quickly as fc approaches fp2, and the dominant pole already contributes almost 90°. With β = 1 the crossover lies at twice the second-pole frequency and the lag from that pole is about 65°, leaving a phase margin of only 25°. A small margin means a lightly damped closed-loop pole pair: the step response overshoots by well over 40 percent and rings for many cycles, and the closed-loop gain shows a peak near fc. Lower β (higher closed-loop gain) keeps crossover below fp2 and gives a stable, well-damped response.

Answer: Higher β pushes crossover toward fp2

Problem 5 [A5-055] Comparators, Schmitt triggers and oscillators

A relaxation oscillator is built around a single op-amp that saturates at ±11 V from its ±12 V supplies. The output is fed back to the non-inverting input through a voltage divider formed by R1 = 10 kΩ from the non-inverting input to ground and R2 = 15 kΩ from the output to the non-inverting input. The output also charges a capacitor C = 22 nF through a resistor R = 47 kΩ connected from the output to the inverting input, with the capacitor connected from the inverting input to ground. Assume the capacitor starts discharged, the op-amp is otherwise ideal, and the steady-state output is a symmetrical square wave. During repair a technician fits a 33 kΩ resistor in place of R2 by mistake, and notices the frequency has risen.

  1. (a) Find the positive threshold voltage at the non-inverting input (the upper trip point) for the original circuit, in volts. [3]
  2. (b) Find the oscillation frequency of the original circuit in Hz. [5]
  3. (c) Find the oscillation frequency in Hz after the 33 kΩ resistor replaces R2. [4]
  4. (d) With R2 still 33 kΩ, find the value of R in kΩ that would restore the original frequency. [4]
  5. (e) Find the peak-to-peak voltage across the capacitor in the faulty circuit (R2 = 33 kΩ, R = 47 kΩ), in volts. [4]
(a)

The non-inverting input sees the divider R1/(R1 + R2) of the output. The feedback fraction is β = 10/(10 + 15) = 0.40. When the output is at +Vsat = +11 V, the voltage at the non-inverting input is βVsat = 0.40 × 11 = 4.4 V, and this is the level the capacitor voltage must reach for the comparator to flip. The lower threshold, with the output at -11 V, is -4.4 V. The hysteresis band is therefore 8.8 V wide, which sets how far the capacitor has to swing in each half cycle.

Answer: +4.4 V

(b)

Each half period is the time for the capacitor to move from -βVsat to +βVsat while charging towards +Vsat (or the reverse). The capacitor voltage is vc(t) = Vsat - (Vsat + βVsat)e-t/RC, and setting vc = βVsat gives t = RC ln((1 + β)/(1 - β)). With β = 0.40, ln(1.4/0.6) = ln(2.3333) = 0.8473. RC = 47 kΩ × 22 nF = 1.034 ms, so each half period is 0.8761 ms and T = 2 × 0.8761 = 1.752 ms. The frequency is f = 1/T = 570.7 Hz. The result is independent of the supply value, which only scales the voltages.

Answer: f = 570.7 Hz

(c)

With R2 = 33 kΩ the feedback fraction becomes β = 10/(10 + 33) = 0.2326. The half-period factor is ln((1 + β)/(1 - β)) = ln(1.2326/0.7674) = ln(1.6061) = 0.4738. The period is T = 2RC × 0.4738 = 2 × 1.034 ms × 0.4738 = 0.9798 ms, so f = 1/T = 1020.6 Hz. The frequency has nearly doubled because the smaller hysteresis band (±2.56 V instead of ±4.4 V) means the capacitor has a shorter distance to travel in each half cycle, and the time constant has not changed. This explains the technician's observation.

Answer: f = 1020.6 Hz

(d)

The original period was 1.752 ms. With the new β the factor is 0.4738, so the required time constant satisfies 2RC × 0.4738 = 1.752 ms, giving RC = 1.752 ms/(0.9476) = 1.849 ms. With C = 22 nF, R = 1.849 ms/22 nF = 84.05 kΩ. In practice the technician would use the nearest standard value, 82 kΩ or 82 kΩ plus a small trimmer. Note that restoring the frequency this way would not restore the original capacitor swing, which is set by the divider and remains ±2.56 V, so the amplitude of the ramp would still be smaller.

Answer: R = 84.05 kΩ

(e)

The capacitor voltage swings between the two threshold voltages ±βVsat, so the peak-to-peak value is 2βVsat. With β = 10/43 = 0.2326 and Vsat = 11 V, this is 2 × 0.2326 × 11 = 5.12 V. In the correct circuit the swing was 2 × 0.40 × 11 = 8.8 V. A smaller swing together with a higher frequency also means a smaller triangle amplitude at the inverting input, which would be noticeable if the capacitor voltage were used as a triangle output. The square wave amplitude at the op-amp output is unchanged at ±11 V.

Answer: 5.12 V peak-to-peak

A5 Practice Paper 12

Problem 1 [A5-056] Power amplifiers, efficiency and heat dissipation

A bench audio amplifier is a Class B complementary push-pull stage using one NPN and one PNP power transistor, driving an 8 Ω loudspeaker through a direct connection. The supplies are +15 V and -15 V, each transistor has VCE(sat) = 1.0 V and the crossover distortion is negligible. The output is a sine wave. During a burn-in test at an ambient temperature of 55 °C the heat sink became too hot to touch while the amplifier drove a sine of 12 V peak. Each transistor has a maximum junction temperature of 150 °C, a junction-to-case thermal resistance of 1.8 °C/W and a case-to-sink resistance of 0.6 °C/W. Assume the two transistors are on separate but identical heat sinks, and quiescent dissipation is negligible.

  1. (a) Find the efficiency of the stage in percent when the output sine has a 12 V peak. [4]
  2. (b) Find the average power dissipated in each transistor for the 12 V peak output, in watts. [4]
  3. (c) Find the largest average power that either transistor can be made to dissipate, over all sine amplitudes below clipping, in watts. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest permissible sink-to-ambient thermal resistance, in °C/W, so that neither junction exceeds 150 °C at the worst-case dissipation of part (c) with ambient 55 °C. [4]
  5. (e) Find the efficiency in percent at the maximum undistorted output allowed by VCE(sat). [4]
(a)

The load power for a sine of peak Vp across RL is PL = Vp²/(2RL) = 12²/(2 × 8) = 9.00 W. Each supply delivers current only on the half cycle in which its transistor conducts, with average current Vp/(πRL), so the total power drawn from the two supplies is Ps = 2 Vcc Vp/(πRL) = 2 × 15 × 12/(π × 8) = 14.32 W. The efficiency is η = PL/Ps = 9.00/14.32 = 0.628, or 62.8 percent. This agrees with the general result η = (π/4)(Vp/Vcc) = 0.7854 × 0.8 = 0.628. The remaining 5.32 W is dissipated as heat in the two output transistors.

Answer: η = 62.8 percent

(b)

The total dissipation is the supply power minus the power delivered to the load, which is 14.32 - 9.00 = 5.32 W. The two transistors are identical and conduct on alternate half cycles, so each dissipates half of this: PD = 5.32/2 = 2.66 W (2.662 W with more digits retained). A designer would use this figure to compare against the rating of each device. Note that it is a long-term average over the cycle, since the instantaneous dissipation peaks higher but only for part of a half cycle.

Answer: PD = 2.662 W

(c)

The dissipation in each transistor is PD(Vp) = (1/2)[2 Vcc Vp/(πRL) - Vp²/(2RL)] = Vcc Vp/(πRL) - Vp²/(4RL). Setting the derivative to zero gives Vcc/(πRL) = Vp/(2RL), so Vp = 2Vcc/π = 9.549 V. Substituting, PD,max = Vcc²/(π² RL) = 225/(9.8696 × 8) = 2.850 W. The maximum occurs at a moderate output, not at full output: the amplifier is hottest at about 64 percent of its peak voltage swing, which is why a 12 V peak output (part b) is slightly cooler than the worst case.

Answer: PD,max = 2.850 W

(d)

The junction temperature is Tj = Ta + PD(θjc + θcs + θsa). Setting Tj = 150 °C with Ta = 55 °C and PD = 2.850 W gives θjc + θcs + θsa = (150 - 55)/2.850 = 33.33 °C/W. Subtracting θjc + θcs = 1.8 + 0.6 = 2.4 °C/W leaves θsa = 30.93 °C/W (30.94 with unrounded power). Any heat sink with a thermal resistance lower than about 31 °C/W is therefore adequate. That is a small sink, so the claim that the sink was too hot to touch suggests either a much smaller sink than this, or a hotter ambient than assumed.

Answer: θsa = 30.94 °C/W

(e)

The largest undistorted peak is Vcc - VCE(sat) = 15 - 1.0 = 14 V. The load power is 14²/(2 × 8) = 12.25 W. The efficiency is η = (π/4)(Vp/Vcc) = 0.7854 × 14/15 = 0.733, or 73.3 percent. This is lower than the ideal 78.5 percent of a Class B stage that reaches the rails, because the saturation voltage of each transistor wastes part of the supply swing. In operation, the amplifier is most efficient when it is driven hardest, and the 62.8 percent of part (a) is lower only because 12 V peak is below the clipping limit.

Answer: η = 73.3 percent

Problem 2 [A5-057] BJT and MOSFET as switches

A 5 V logic output drives an NPN transistor that switches a 12 V relay coil of resistance 240 Ω, connected between the 12 V supply and the transistor collector, with the emitter at ground. The base resistor RB joins the logic output to the base. The transistor datasheet gives a minimum current gain β = 80 in saturation, VBE = 0.8 V and VCE(sat) = 0.2 V when saturated. Ignore the relay inductance and flyback diode currents for this analysis. In production, the board was built with RB = 4.7 kΩ. A field return reports that the relay does not pull in reliably when the 5 V logic rail is replaced by a 3.3 V rail on a newer microcontroller board, and the transistor was warm to the touch.

  1. (a) Find the collector current, in mA, when the transistor is saturated. [4]
  2. (b) Find the value of RB, in ohms, that would give a forced β of 10 when driven from 5 V. [4]
  3. (c) For the as-built RB = 4.7 kΩ driven from 5 V, find the overdrive factor, defined as actual base current divided by the base current just needed for saturation with β = 80. [4]
  4. (d) With the logic high level of only 3.3 V and RB = 4.7 kΩ, assume the transistor is not saturated and operates in its active region with β = 80. Find the collector-emitter voltage in volts. [4]
  5. (e) Find the power dissipated in the transistor in the situation of part (d), in mW. [4]
(a)

When the transistor is saturated, VCE = 0.2 V, so the voltage across the 240 Ω coil is 12 - 0.2 = 11.8 V. The collector current is IC = 11.8/240 = 0.04917 A = 49.17 mA. This is the current that the relay coil draws when the transistor is a closed switch. It is the highest current the transistor can carry in this circuit, since the load fixes it: no more base current will increase it. The transistor must be rated for at least this collector current with a suitable margin.

Answer: IC(sat) = 49.17 mA

(b)

A forced β of 10 means the base current is IC/10 = 49.17 mA/10 = 4.917 mA. The base resistor drops the logic voltage minus VBE: RB = (5 - 0.8)/4.917 mA = 4.2/0.004917 = 854 Ω. This is a heavy overdrive, since the real β of the transistor is at least 80, so about 8 times the minimum base current is supplied. A forced β of 10 is a common design rule for fast and reliable switching, at the cost of a slower turn-off from stored charge and more logic output current.

Answer: RB = 854 Ω

(c)

With RB = 4.7 kΩ and a 5 V drive the base current is IB = (5 - 0.8)/4.7 kΩ = 4.2/4700 = 0.8936 mA. The base current required just to saturate with β = 80 is IC/β = 49.17 mA/80 = 0.6146 mA. The overdrive factor is therefore 0.8936/0.6146 = 1.454. This is a modest margin (about 45 percent) but it does saturate the transistor at 5 V even with the worst-case minimum β, so the original design works adequately on a 5 V supply. It is less generous than a forced β of 10 rule would give.

Answer: overdrive = 1.454

(d)

With a 3.3 V logic high, the base current is IB = (3.3 - 0.8)/4.7 kΩ = 2.5/4700 = 0.5319 mA. This is below the 0.6146 mA needed for saturation, so the transistor stays in its active region with IC = βIB = 80 × 0.5319 mA = 42.55 mA. The voltage across the coil is 240 × 0.04255 = 10.21 V, leaving VCE = 12 - 10.21 = 1.787 V. This is greater than 0.2 V, so the active-region assumption is consistent. The coil now sees only 10.2 V instead of 11.8 V, so its pull-in force is reduced, and the relay may fail to operate reliably.

Answer: VCE = 1.787 V

(e)

The transistor dissipation is P = VCE IC = 1.787 V × 42.55 mA = 76.05 mW. When properly saturated the dissipation would have been VCE(sat) IC = 0.2 × 49.17 mA = 9.8 mW. So the partly-on transistor dissipates nearly eight times more heat, which explains why the transistor was warm. The cure is to lower RB so that the base current is above IC/β at the lowest logic level, for example by using a 3.3 V design with RB near (3.3 - 0.8)/(49.17 mA/10) = 508 Ω, or to change to a logic-level MOSFET.

Answer: P = 76.05 mW

Problem 3 [A5-058] CMOS inverter and logic gate design

A standard-cell library uses a 3.3 V CMOS process with the following square-law parameters: nMOS threshold Vtn = 0.6 V, pMOS threshold Vtp = -0.7 V, process transconductance k'n = 110 μA/V² and k'p = 45 μA/V². Channel-length modulation is negligible. The reference inverter has an nMOS device of aspect ratio (W/L)n = 4 and a pMOS device of (W/L)p = 10. The switching threshold VM is the input voltage at which the input equals the output, with both devices saturated. A layout error halves the pMOS width in one cell. A designer also proposes a two-input NAND built from the same process, with its inputs tied together for a worst-case analysis of the switching point.

  1. (a) Find the switching threshold VM of the reference inverter in volts. [4]
  2. (b) Find VM in volts for the faulty cell in which (W/L)p is halved to 5, with (W/L)n unchanged. [4]
  3. (c) A two-input NAND has two series nMOS devices, each of (W/L) = 8, and two parallel pMOS devices, each of (W/L) = 10. With both inputs tied together, find its switching threshold in volts. [5]
  4. (d) With (W/L)p = 10, find the (W/L)n that places the inverter's VM exactly at VDD/2 = 1.65 V. [4]
  5. (e) Explain why the tied-input NAND's switching point sits above that of the reference inverter, and say what that does to its noise margins. [3]
(a)

With both devices saturated at VM, the currents are equal: (kn/2)(VM - Vtn)² = (kp/2)(VDD + Vtp - VM)², where kn = k'n(W/L)n = 110 × 4 = 440 μA/V² and kp = k'p(W/L)p = 45 × 10 = 450 μA/V². Taking the square root, with r = √(kp/kn) = √(450/440) = 1.0113, gives VM - Vtn = r(VDD + Vtp - VM), so VM = (Vtn + r(VDD + Vtp))/(1 + r) = (0.6 + 1.0113 × 2.6)/2.0113 = (0.6 + 2.629)/2.0113 = 1.606 V. This is slightly below VDD/2 = 1.65 V, so the reference inverter is close to symmetric.

Answer: VM = 1.606 V

(b)

Halving the pMOS width halves kp to 225 μA/V², so r = √(225/440) = 0.7151. The switching point becomes VM = (0.6 + 0.7151 × 2.6)/(1 + 0.7151) = (0.6 + 1.859)/1.7151 = 1.434 V. The weaker pull-up means the input must be lower for the pMOS to win, so VM moves down by 0.17 V. A cell with a threshold 0.2 V below the centre has a reduced low-level noise margin (NML) and a larger NMH, and the gate would respond too early to a rising input. The layout error would be caught in a corner simulation.

Answer: VM = 1.434 V

(c)

With the two inputs tied, both series nMOS devices turn on together, forming an equivalent device of aspect ratio 8/2 = 4, so kn,eff = 110 × 4 = 440 μA/V². Both parallel pMOS devices are on together and act as a single device of aspect ratio 20, so kp,eff = 45 × 20 = 900 μA/V². Then r = √(900/440) = 1.430, and VM = (0.6 + 1.430 × 2.6)/(2.430) = (0.6 + 3.718)/2.430 = 1.777 V. The nMOS width of 8 was chosen so that the pull-down matches the inverter, but when both pMOS devices are on the pull-up is twice as strong.

Answer: VM = 1.777 V

(d)

Solve the threshold equation for r: r = (VM - Vtn)/(VDD + Vtp - VM) = (1.65 - 0.6)/(2.6 - 1.65) = 1.05/0.95 = 1.1053. Since r² = kp/kn, kn = kp/r² = 450/1.2216 = 368.4 μA/V². The aspect ratio is (W/L)n = kn/k'n = 368.4/110 = 3.35. The nMOS device is narrower than the 4 of the reference inverter, which shifts VM up slightly from 1.606 V to 1.65 V. The width ratio between the devices is then 10/3.35 = 2.99, rather than the usual 2 to 3 estimate based on mobility alone.

Answer: (W/L)n = 3.35

(e)

Switching threshold increases with the strength of the pMOS pull-up relative to the nMOS pull-down. With the inputs tied, the NAND has two pMOS devices in parallel (twice the pull-up strength of one) while the series nMOS stack was only sized to match one inverter, so the pull-up wins the contest earlier and the output stays high for a larger input voltage. VM therefore moves up, from 1.606 V to 1.777 V. A higher VM shrinks the noise margin for a high input (NMH) and gives more tolerance of low-level noise (a larger NML), so the gate is skewed. In practice the single-input switching point differs again, because only one of the two pMOS devices is on.

Answer: VM rises; NMH shrinks, NML grows

Problem 4 [A5-059] Propagation delay and power in CMOS

A CMOS logic gate in a 1.8 V process is modelled by an equivalent switch resistance when driving a capacitive load: Rn = 3.2 kΩ when the nMOS network discharges the load, and Rp = 5.4 kΩ when the pMOS network charges it. The 50 percent propagation delay of an RC transition is taken as 0.69 RC. The gate drives a total load capacitance of 0.35 pF. Its output toggles with an activity factor α = 0.2 transitions per clock cycle (counting each 0 to 1 transition as one) at a clock frequency of 100 MHz. During review a new fan-out of three identical gates is added, each presenting 0.12 pF of input capacitance. The designer also wants to know the power saving if the supply is lowered to 1.2 V. Neglect leakage and short-circuit power.

  1. (a) Find the average propagation delay of the gate, (tpHL + tpLH)/2, for the 0.35 pF load, in ns. [4]
  2. (b) Find the dynamic power of the gate at 1.8 V, in μW, using P = α C VDD² f. [4]
  3. (c) Find the new average propagation delay after the fan-out of three gates is added to the original load, in ns. [4]
  4. (d) A path of ten such gates in series with the loading of part (c) must complete within one clock period. Find the maximum clock frequency in MHz. [4]
  5. (e) Find the percentage reduction in dynamic power from lowering the supply from 1.8 V to 1.2 V at the same load, activity and frequency. [4]
(a)

For a falling output, tpHL = 0.69 Rn C = 0.69 × 3200 × 0.35 pF = 0.773 ns. For a rising output, tpLH = 0.69 Rp C = 0.69 × 5400 × 0.35 pF = 1.304 ns. The average is (0.773 + 1.304)/2 = 1.038 ns. The pMOS network is slower because holes have a lower mobility, which makes the rising transition 69 percent slower than the falling one. A designer would normally widen the pMOS devices to even these out, but the cost is more input capacitance and more dynamic power.

Answer: tp = 1.038 ns

(b)

The dynamic power comes from charging and discharging the load capacitance: P = α C VDD² f. With α = 0.2, C = 0.35 pF, VDD = 1.8 V and f = 100 MHz we get P = 0.2 × 0.35 × 10⁻¹² × 3.24 × 10⁸ = 2.268 × 10⁻⁵ W = 22.68 μW. Each charging event takes CVDD² from the supply and half of that is dissipated in the pull-up network, while the other half is stored and then dissipated in the pull-down network during discharge. The result is therefore independent of the switch resistances.

Answer: P = 22.68 μW

(c)

The total load becomes 0.35 pF + 3 × 0.12 pF = 0.71 pF. With the same switch resistances the average resistance is (3200 + 5400)/2 = 4300 Ω, so the average delay is 0.69 × 4300 × 0.71 pF = 2.107 ns. The delay has roughly doubled, because it scales directly with the load capacitance in this model, and the added load is slightly more than the original. This shows why a gate must be sized or buffered when its fan-out grows, since each added input slows every transition.

Answer: tp = 2.107 ns

(d)

Ten gates in series give a path delay of 10 × 2.107 ns = 21.07 ns. The clock period must be at least this, ignoring set-up time and clock skew, so fmax = 1/21.07 ns = 4.747 × 10⁷ Hz = 47.47 MHz. The original 100 MHz clock (period 10 ns) would be violated by such a path. The remedy is to pipeline the path, to speed up the gates by widening them (accepting the power cost), or to reduce the fan-out so that the capacitance per stage falls back toward the original 0.35 pF.

Answer: fmax = 47.47 MHz

(e)

Dynamic power scales with VDD², so the ratio of powers is (1.2/1.8)² = 0.4444. The reduction is 1 - 0.4444 = 0.5556, or 55.6 percent. For the 0.71 pF load, the powers would be 46.0 μW at 1.8 V and 20.4 μW at 1.2 V. The saving is large because of the squared dependence on the supply, but the model resistances would in practice rise at lower supply, since the transistors have less gate overdrive, so the delay would increase and the speed would decrease, offsetting part of the benefit.

Answer: reduction 55.6 percent
