Problem 5 [A5-060] Amplifier design to meet a specification, comparing topologies

A designer must meet this specification for a small-signal common-emitter stage: the overall voltage gain magnitude |vo/vs| from a signal source of resistance Rs = 2 kΩ must be at least 30 for every transistor with current gain β between 100 and 200, and the spread (maximum minus minimum) divided by the mean of the gains at β = 100 and β = 200 must not exceed 15 percent. The transistor is biased at IC = 1.0 mA (held constant for all β by the bias network), with VT = 25 mV, gm = IC/VT and rπ = β/gm. Ignore the Early effect and base spreading resistance. The collector resistor is RC = 4.7 kΩ and the load is RL = 10 kΩ, coupled by a large capacitor. The bias divider presents 60 kΩ (R1 in parallel with R2) from base to ground at signal frequencies. An emitter resistor RE, if present, is unbypassed. All coupling capacitors are large. Review the plain stage first, then the effect of adding RE.

  1. (a) Find |vo/vs| for the stage with no emitter resistor and β = 100. [4]
  2. (b) Find the spread of the gain over the β range 100 to 200 for the stage with no emitter resistor, as a percentage of the mean. [4]
  3. (c) Find |vo/vs| at β = 100 when an unbypassed RE of 47 Ω is added. [4]
  4. (d) Find the spread of the gain over the β range for the stage with RE = 47 Ω, as a percentage of the mean. [4]
  5. (e) Find the largest value of RE, in ohms, for which the gain at β = 100 still meets the 30 minimum. [4]
(a)

Without RE, the gain from base to output is -gm(RC ∥ RL), where gm = 1 mA/25 mV = 40 mS and RC ∥ RL = 4.7 kΩ × 10 kΩ/14.7 kΩ = 3.197 kΩ. So the stage gain is 40 mS × 3.197 kΩ = 127.9. For β = 100, rπ = 100/40 mS = 2.5 kΩ. The input resistance seen from the source is Rin = 60 kΩ ∥ 2.5 kΩ = 2.400 kΩ. The source divider is Rin/(Rin + Rs) = 2.400/4.400 = 0.5455. So |vo/vs| = 127.9 × 0.5455 = 69.76. The gain meets the minimum of 30 easily, but the input loading is heavy.

Answer: |vo/vs| = 69.76

(b)

At β = 200, rπ = 5 kΩ, so Rin = 60 kΩ ∥ 5 kΩ = 4.615 kΩ and the divider is 4.615/6.615 = 0.6977. The overall gain is 127.9 × 0.6977 = 89.23. The spread is (89.23 - 69.76) = 19.47, and the mean is (89.23 + 69.76)/2 = 79.49, so the spread is 19.47/79.49 = 24.5 percent. This exceeds the 15 percent limit. The reason is that the stage gain is independent of β (gm is fixed by IC) but the input loading depends on rπ, which is proportional to β, so the signal reaching the base varies strongly with the transistor.

Answer: spread 24.5 percent

(c)

With RE the resistance looking into the base is Rib = rπ + (β + 1)RE = 2500 + 101 × 47 = 7247 Ω. The voltage gain from base to collector output is -β(RC ∥ RL)/Rib = 100 × 3197/7247 = 44.1. The source sees Rin = 60 kΩ ∥ 7.247 kΩ = 6.467 kΩ, so the divider is 6.467/8.467 = 0.7638. The overall gain is 44.1 × 0.7638 = 33.70. The degeneration has lowered the gain from 69.8 to 33.7, but this still meets the minimum of 30 at β = 100. The cost is gain, the benefit is the reduced β sensitivity checked next.

Answer: |vo/vs| = 33.70

(d)

At β = 200, rπ = 5 kΩ and Rib = 5000 + 201 × 47 = 14 447 Ω. The base-to-output gain is 200 × 3197/14 447 = 44.26, and Rin = 60 kΩ ∥ 14.447 kΩ = 11.65 kΩ, so the divider is 11.65/13.65 = 0.8535. The overall gain is 44.26 × 0.8535 = 37.77. The spread is 37.77 - 33.70 = 4.07 and the mean is 35.74, so the spread is 11.4 percent, within the 15 percent limit. With RE = 47 Ω both specifications are met: the minimum gain is 33.7 and the spread is 11.4 percent.

Answer: spread 11.4 percent

(e)

The minimum gain over the β range occurs at β = 100. The overall gain is G(RE) = [100 × 3197/(2500 + 101 RE)] × Rin/(Rin + 2000), with Rin = 60 000 ∥ (2500 + 101 RE). Setting G = 30 and solving numerically gives RE = 58.2 Ω. Check: Rib = 2500 + 101 × 58.2 = 8378 Ω, base gain = 319 700/8378 = 38.16, Rin = 60 000 ∥ 8378 = 7351 Ω, divider = 7351/9351 = 0.786, product = 30.0. A larger RE would break the minimum gain, though the spread would improve further. A designer would choose a standard value such as 47 Ω to leave a margin of over 10 percent.

Answer: RE,max = 58.2 Ω

A5 Practice Paper 13

Problem 1 [A5-061] Diode circuits, clippers and rectifiers

A sensor-conditioning stage protects an input pin with a two-sided diode clipper. The source is vs = 12 sin(2π·60t) V in series with a resistor R = 1.00 kΩ. The other end of R is the output node X, and nothing else is connected to X except the clipping branches. Branch 1: diode D1 has its anode on X and its cathode on node P, and a 3.30 V battery sits between P (positive terminal) and ground. Branch 2: diode D2 has its cathode on X and its anode on node N, and a 1.30 V battery sits between N (negative terminal) and ground, so the positive terminal of that battery is grounded. Model each diode as a 0.70 V constant drop with zero resistance when conducting and an open circuit otherwise. Take t = 0 as the instant vs crosses zero going positive.

  1. (a) Find the positive clipping level of vX. [3]
  2. (b) Find the negative clipping level of vX (give the signed value). [2]
  3. (c) Find the conduction angle of D1 in each cycle, in degrees. [4]
  4. (d) Find the average current in D1 over one cycle. [5]
  5. (e) Find the average power dissipated in R over one cycle, counting both clipping branches. [6]
(a)

D1 starts to conduct when the anode voltage vX exceeds the cathode voltage plus the diode drop. The cathode sits at the battery voltage, 3.30 V, because the positive terminal of that battery is on P. So conduction needs vX > 3.30 + 0.70 = 4.00 V. While D1 conducts, vX is held at that level and the excess source voltage appears across R. While D1 is off, no current flows in R (the output is unloaded), so vX follows vs exactly. The positive clipping level is therefore 4.00 V, and because the source peak of 12 V is higher than this, clipping does occur on every positive half cycle. D2 is reverse biased in this region, since its cathode is at X, which is positive.

Answer: 4.00 V

(b)

D2 has its cathode on X and its anode on N. The battery has its negative terminal on N and its positive terminal on ground, so vN = -1.30 V. D2 conducts when vN - vX > 0.70 V, that is when vX < -1.30 - 0.70 = -2.00 V. Below this value the diode clamps vX at -2.00 V and the rest of the source swing drops across R. The source minimum is -12 V, well below the clip level, so clipping occurs on the negative peaks. The output signal is therefore confined to the window between -2.00 V and +4.00 V, asymmetrical because the two batteries differ. Assumption: ideal constant drop diodes, no reverse leakage.

Answer: -2.00 V

(c)

D1 conducts while vs > 4.00 V. Set 12 sin θ = 4.00, so sin θ1 = 1/3 and θ1 = asin(0.3333) = 19.47 degrees. The source stays above 4.00 V from θ1 up to 180 - θ1 by the symmetry of the sine about 90 degrees. The conduction angle is therefore 180 - 2×19.47 = 141.06 degrees per cycle. This is 39.2 percent of the 360 degree period. Equivalently the diode is off for 218.9 degrees. The conduction angle matters because it sets how long each cycle the battery is being charged or discharged, and it controls the peak and average currents that the diode and battery must be rated for.

Answer: 141.1 degrees

(d)

While D1 conducts the current is i = (vs - 4.00)/R, because vX is held at 4.00 V. The average over a full 2π cycle is Iavg = (1/(2πR)) ∫ (12 sin θ - 4) dθ from θ1 to π - θ1. Integrating gives (1/(2πR)) [ -12 cos θ - 4θ ] between those limits = (1/(2πR)) [ 24 cos θ1 - 4(π - 2θ1) ]. With cos θ1 = √(1 - 1/9) = 0.9428 and θ1 = 0.33984 rad: 24×0.9428 = 22.627 and 4×(3.14159 - 0.67967) = 9.848. The bracket is 12.779. Divide by 2π×1000 = 6283.2 to get 2.034 mA. The peak current is (12 - 4)/1000 = 8.0 mA, so the average is only about a quarter of the peak.

Answer: 2.03 mA

(e)

With the output unloaded, current flows in R only while a diode conducts, and then i = (|vs| - Vclip)/R, with Vclip = 4.00 V for D1 and 2.00 V for D2 (the magnitude of the negative clip level). Power in R is the mean of i²R = (excess voltage)²/R. For D1: ∫ (12 sin θ - 4)² dθ from 0.33984 to 2.80176 rad = 80.884 V²·rad, giving 80.884/(2π×1000) = 12.87 mW. For D2 the level is 2.00 V, θ0 = asin(2/12) = 0.16745 rad, and the integral is 142.316 V²·rad, giving 22.65 mW. The sum is 12.87 + 22.65 = 35.52 mW. The negative branch dissipates more because its clip level is closer to zero, so the diode conducts for longer and with larger excess voltage.

Answer: 35.5 mW

Problem 2 [A5-062] Zener regulators and power supply filtering

A bench supply for a 9 V sensor board uses a 120 V to 18 V rms transformer (full secondary voltage 18 V rms at 60 Hz) feeding a four-diode bridge rectifier, a filter capacitor C, and a Zener shunt regulator. Each conducting diode pair drops 1.40 V in total. The capacitor feeds a series resistor R = 150 Ω, and the node after R carries the Zener diode to ground in parallel with the load RL = 300 Ω. The Zener is modelled as a 9.00 V source in series with a dynamic resistance rz = 5.0 Ω in the breakdown region. The filter capacitor is to be chosen so that the peak-to-peak ripple across it is 1.50 V. Use the usual approximation that the capacitor voltage averages the peak value minus half the ripple, and that the capacitor discharges at the constant average current drawn through R.

  1. (a) Find the peak voltage across the capacitor with no ripple considered. [3]
  2. (b) Find the capacitance needed for 1.50 V peak-to-peak ripple. [6]
  3. (c) Find the Zener current at the average capacitor voltage. [4]
  4. (d) Find the peak-to-peak ripple at the load. [4]
  5. (e) With the load disconnected, find the Zener power dissipation, keeping the capacitor average voltage unchanged. [3]
(a)

The secondary voltage is 18 V rms, so its peak is 18√2 = 25.456 V. In a bridge rectifier the current path passes through two diodes at any instant, which costs 1.40 V in total as stated. The capacitor therefore charges up to Vp = 25.456 - 1.40 = 24.06 V on each half cycle. This is the highest value the capacitor voltage reaches. The ripple then makes the voltage fall below this value between peaks, and the average is lower than Vp by half the peak-to-peak ripple. Assumption: ideal transformer with negligible winding resistance, and the diode drops constant at 0.70 V each.

Answer: 24.06 V

(b)

The average capacitor voltage is Vdc = Vp - Vr/2 = 24.056 - 0.75 = 23.306 V. The regulator network is R in series with the Zener in parallel with RL. Write VL = 9.00 + 5Iz and the node equation Iz = (Vdc - VL)/R - VL/RL. Substituting and multiplying by 300 gives 300 Iz = 2(Vdc - 9 - 5Iz) - (9 + 5Iz), so 315 Iz = 2Vdc - 27 = 19.612 and Iz = 62.26 mA. Then VL = 9.311 V and the current out of the capacitor is IR = (23.306 - 9.311)/150 = 93.30 mA. With full-wave rectification the capacitor recharges twice per cycle so the discharge time is about 1/(2f). Vr = IR/(2fC), so C = 0.09330/(2×60×1.50) = 518 µF. A standard 560 µF part would be chosen in practice.

Answer: 518 µF

(c)

The Zener current follows from the node equation solved in part b. Using Vdc = 23.306 V: 315 Iz = 2(23.306) - 27 = 19.612, so Iz = 0.06226 A = 62.26 mA. The load voltage is VL = 9.00 + 5.0×0.06226 = 9.311 V, and the load current is 9.311/300 = 31.04 mA. The resistor current is the sum 62.26 + 31.04 = 93.30 mA, which agrees with (Vdc - VL)/R. This Zener current is far above any knee current, so the Zener is well inside the breakdown region and the linear model is valid. The Zener keeps about 2/3 of the series current, so it carries most of the burden at this load.

Answer: 62.3 mA

(d)

The ripple at the capacitor appears at the load through a divider formed by R and the parallel combination of rz and RL. For small signals the Zener is rz = 5.0 Ω, and RL = 300 Ω is in parallel: rp = 5×300/305 = 4.918 Ω. The divider ratio is rp/(R + rp) = 4.918/(150 + 4.918) = 0.03175. The load ripple is 1.50 V × 0.03175 = 47.6 mV peak to peak. So the regulator attenuates the input ripple by a factor of about 31.5, or 30 dB. This is the line-rejection benefit of the shunt regulator, and the ripple at the load of 47.6 mV is about 0.5 percent of 9.3 V. A lower rz or a larger R would improve it further.

Answer: 47.6 mV

(e)

With RL removed, the only path is R in series with the Zener. Iz = (Vdc - 9.00)/(R + rz) = (23.306 - 9.00)/(150 + 5.0) = 14.306/155 = 92.30 mA. The Zener power is the dissipation in the source and resistance parts: P = 9.00×0.09230 + 5.0×0.09230² = 0.8307 + 0.0426 = 0.873 W. A 1 W Zener is therefore loaded to 87 percent, which leaves little margin when the line voltage rises 10 percent. The design must either use a 2 W or 5 W Zener or guarantee that the load cannot be removed. In practice the capacitor voltage also rises at light load, which makes the result worse than computed here.

Answer: 0.873 W

Problem 3 [A5-063] Thyristors, SCR and TRIAC circuits

An industrial oven element of resistance R = 20.0 Ω is supplied from a 240 V rms, 60 Hz single-phase source. Initially the heater is controlled by a single SCR in series with the heater (half-wave control), fired at a delay angle α = 60 degrees measured from the positive-going zero crossing of the supply. The SCR conducts only while the supply is positive. Treat the SCR as an ideal switch with no forward drop and assume the gate is triggered by a pulse that is exactly at the stated angle. Later, the SCR is replaced by a TRIAC (full-wave control) so that both half cycles are controlled with the same delay angle α. The heater is purely resistive, so the current turns off at the supply zero crossings.

  1. (a) With the SCR at α = 60 degrees, find the average voltage across the heater. [4]
  2. (b) Find the rms voltage across the heater with the SCR at α = 60 degrees. [4]
  3. (c) Find the average power delivered to the heater in the SCR circuit. [3]
  4. (d) Find the power factor seen by the source in the SCR circuit. [3]
  5. (e) With the TRIAC, find the delay angle that gives exactly 1200 W in the heater, in degrees. [6]
(a)

The supply peak is Vm = 240√2 = 339.41 V. The SCR is gated at α and then conducts until the supply reaches zero at π, so the load voltage is Vm sin θ for α to π and zero otherwise. Vavg = (1/2π) ∫ Vm sin θ dθ from α to π = (Vm/2π)(1 + cos α). With α = 60 degrees, cos α = 0.5, so the factor is 1.5. Vavg = 339.41×1.5/6.2832 = 81.03 V. The average is lower than the 108 V (0.318 Vm) that a plain half-wave diode would give because conduction starts at 60 degrees instead of 0 degrees. The heater responds to the rms value rather than the average, but the average matters for any transformer or choke in the supply path because it is a DC component.

Answer: 81.0 V

(b)

For a resistive load, heating depends on the rms voltage. Vrms² = (1/2π) ∫ (Vm sin θ)² dθ from α to π = (Vm²/2π)[(π - α)/2 + sin 2α/4]. Equivalently Vrms = Vm √[(π - α)/(4π) + sin 2α/(8π)]. With α = 60 degrees = 1.0472 rad: (π - α)/(4π) = 2.0944/12.566 = 0.16667 and sin 120 degrees/(8π) = 0.86603/25.133 = 0.03446. The sum is 0.20112 and its square root is 0.44847. So Vrms = 339.41×0.44847 = 152.2 V. Check: at α = 0 the same formula gives Vm/2 = 169.7 V, the half-wave limit, so 152.2 V at 60 degrees is sensible, being lower but not far below.

Answer: 152.2 V

(c)

Power in a purely resistive load is Vrms²/R. P = 152.22²/20.0 = 23,171/20.0 = 1158 W. For comparison, at α = 0 the half-wave circuit would deliver (169.7)²/20.0 = 1440 W, which is half of the 2880 W (240²/20.0) the heater draws on the full supply. So at 60 degrees the SCR delivers 80.4 percent of its own maximum. The heater therefore can never exceed 1440 W with this single SCR, no matter how early it is fired. That limit is important when sizing the element, and it is the reason why the TRIAC is considered for the second part of the problem, where the available range extends to the full 2880 W.

Answer: 1158 W

(d)

The source current equals the heater current, because the circuit is a simple series loop. Irms = Vrms/R = 152.22/20.0 = 7.611 A. The apparent power seen by the source is S = Vs,rms × Irms = 240×7.611 = 1826.6 VA. The real power is P = 1158 W. The power factor is P/S = 1158/1826.6 = 0.634. The load is resistive, so this low value does not come from a phase lag of a smooth sine current. It comes from the current waveform being a chopped partial half sine, which contains a DC component and harmonics. The fundamental of the current also lags the voltage a little because the pulse starts late in the cycle. This is a typical drawback of phase control.

Answer: 0.634

(e)

The required heater rms voltage is Vt = √(P R) = √(1200×20.0) = 154.92 V. For full-wave control with the same delay angle in each half cycle, Vrms = Vm √[(π - α)/(2π) + sin 2α/(4π)]. Set (Vt/Vm)² = (154.92/339.41)² = 0.20833 = (π - α)/(2π) + sin 2α/(4π). This is transcendental, so solve numerically. At α = 97.54 degrees (1.7025 rad): (π - α)/(2π) = 0.22905 and sin 2α/(4π) = sin(195.09 degrees)/(4π) = -0.26024/12.566 = -0.02071. The sum is 0.20834, in agreement with 0.20833. Thus α ≈ 97.5 degrees. Note the first-order trap: α = 90 degrees is the mid-point and gives 0.250, which is too much power.

Answer: 97.5 degrees

Problem 4 [A5-064] BJT bias circuits and operating point

A discrete silicon NPN transistor is biased by a four-resistor network from VCC = +15.0 V. Resistor R1 = 47.0 kΩ connects VCC to the base node, resistor R2 = 10.0 kΩ connects the base node to ground, resistor RC = 2.20 kΩ connects VCC to the collector, and resistor RE = 1.00 kΩ connects the emitter to ground. Take VBE = 0.700 V and β = 120 in the forward active region, and use a thermal voltage of 25.0 mV. The emitter is bypassed to ground at signal frequencies by a large capacitor, and the collector drives a 4.70 kΩ load through a large coupling capacitor. Neglect the output resistance of the transistor and base spreading resistance.

  1. (a) Find the collector current at the quiescent point. [4]
  2. (b) Find the collector-emitter voltage at the quiescent point. [3]
  3. (c) A replacement transistor has β = 250. Find the percentage increase in collector current compared with part a. [3]
  4. (d) At high temperature VBE falls to 0.620 V with β = 120. Find the increase in collector current compared with part a. [4]
  5. (e) Find the magnitude of the small-signal voltage gain from base to the load output, using the quiescent current of part a. [6]
(a)

Replace the divider by its Thevenin equivalent: Vth = 15.0×10.0/57.0 = 2.632 V and Rth = 47.0∥10.0 = 8.246 kΩ. Write the base loop: Vth = IB Rth + VBE + IE RE with IE = (β + 1) IB. So IB = (Vth - VBE)/(Rth + (β + 1) RE) = (2.632 - 0.700)/(8246 + 121×1000) = 1.932/129,246 = 14.95 µA. The collector current is IC = β IB = 120×14.95 µA = 1.793 mA. The large (β + 1) RE term dominates the denominator, so IC is set mostly by the divider and RE, which is the goal of this four-resistor bias scheme. The emitter current is 1.808 mA.

Answer: 1.793 mA

(b)

The collector-emitter voltage follows from the output loop: VCE = VCC - IC RC - IE RE. With IC = 1.7934 mA and IE = (121/120) IC = 1.8084 mA: IC RC = 1.7934e-3×2200 = 3.945 V and IE RE = 1.8084e-3×1000 = 1.808 V. Then VCE = 15.00 - 3.945 - 1.808 = 9.246 V. This is greater than the saturation value of about 0.2 V, so the forward active assumption holds. The collector sits at 15.00 - 3.945 = 11.05 V, and the supply voltage is divided about 26 percent across RC, 12 percent across RE and 62 percent across the transistor, a comfortable allocation for symmetrical swing.

Answer: 9.25 V

(c)

Repeat the bias calculation with β = 250. IB = 1.932/(8246 + 251×1000) = 1.932/259,246 = 7.452 µA, so IC = 250×7.452 µA = 1.863 mA. The relative increase is (1.8627 - 1.7934)/1.7934 = 0.0386 = 3.86 percent. The transistor β more than doubled (a 108 percent increase) but IC rose by under 4 percent. This is the stability benefit of the emitter resistor: the base current term (β + 1)RE in the denominator is much larger than Rth, so the current is set mainly by the stiff divider. Without RE, IC would nearly track β, which would shift the Q-point completely.

Answer: 3.86 percent

(d)

The reduced VBE raises the numerator in the base-loop equation. IB = (2.632 - 0.620)/(8246 + 121000) = 2.012/129,246 = 15.56 µA with β = 120, so IC = 1.8677 mA. The increase is 1.8677 - 1.7934 = 0.0743 mA, which is 4.1 percent. This corresponds to a fall of 80 mV in VBE, and in a silicon transistor this represents about 40 degrees C of temperature rise at about -2 mV per degree. The sensitivity is ΔIC/ΔVBE = β/(Rth + (β + 1)RE) = 120/129,246 = 0.93 mA per volt, so 80 mV gives 0.074 mA, consistent. Thermal runaway is not an issue because the stability is good.

Answer: 0.0743 mA

(e)

At the quiescent point gm = IC/VT = 1.7934 mA/25.0 mV = 71.74 mS. The emitter is bypassed, so there is no signal degeneration, and ro is neglected. The signal sees RC in parallel with the 4.70 kΩ load: RL' = 2.20×4.70/6.90 = 1.4986 kΩ. The gain from the base-emitter voltage to the output is vo/vπ = -gm RL' = -0.07174×1498.6 = -107.5. Its magnitude is 107.5, and the sign shows the 180 degree phase inversion of the common-emitter stage. The gain is large because the bypassed emitter leaves the full gm in action. If the bypass were removed, the unbypassed RE would reduce the gain to about RL'/RE = 1.5, showing how bias and gain are separate design choices.

Answer: 107.5

Problem 5 [A5-065] BJT small-signal model and common-emitter amplifier

A common-emitter amplifier uses VCC = 12.0 V, a base divider of R1 = 33.0 kΩ (to VCC) and R2 = 6.80 kΩ (to ground), a collector resistor RC = 3.30 kΩ, and a total emitter resistance split as RE1 = 100 Ω (unbypassed) in series with RE2 = 1.20 kΩ (bypassed for signals by a large capacitor). The transistor has β = 150, VBE = 0.700 V and Early voltage VA = 80.0 V, and VT = 25.0 mV. A signal source with series resistance Rs = 1.00 kΩ drives the base through a large coupling capacitor, and a 10.0 kΩ load is connected to the collector through another coupling capacitor. Use the hybrid-π model with rπ = β/gm.

  1. (a) Find the quiescent collector current. [4]
  2. (b) Find rπ at this operating point. [3]
  3. (c) Find the input resistance seen by the source (the divider in parallel with the resistance looking into the base). [4]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the overall gain vo/vs, neglecting ro in this part. [6]
  5. (e) Find the output resistance seen by the 10.0 kΩ load, including ro and RC (use VCE from the quiescent point for ro). [3]
(a)

Thevenin equivalent of the base network: Vth = 12.0×6.80/39.8 = 2.050 V and Rth = 33.0∥6.80 = 5.638 kΩ. Only the dc emitter total RE = 100 + 1200 = 1300 Ω counts for bias, because RE2 is bypassed only for signals. Base loop: IB = (Vth - VBE)/(Rth + (β + 1)RE) = (2.050 - 0.700)/(5638 + 151×1300) = 1.350/201,938 = 6.686 µA. Then IC = βIB = 150×6.686 µA = 1.003 mA. The emitter current is 1.010 mA. The quiescent VCE follows: 12.0 - 1.003 mA×3.30 kΩ - 1.010 mA×1.30 kΩ = 12.0 - 3.310 - 1.313 = 7.378 V, in the active region.

Answer: 1.003 mA

(b)

The transconductance is gm = IC/VT = 1.003 mA/25.0 mV = 40.12 mS. The base-emitter small-signal resistance is rπ = β/gm = 150/0.04012 = 3.739 kΩ. For completeness, the output resistance is ro = (VA + VCE)/IC = (80.0 + 7.378)/1.003 mA = 87.1 kΩ, used in part e. The input resistance of the bare junction is thus 3.74 kΩ, but with the unbypassed 100 Ω resistor in the emitter it will appear larger by the factor (β + 1) applied to RE1, as calculated in part c. The value of rπ is the same whether the emitter is bypassed or not, since it only depends on the dc current.

Answer: 3.74 kΩ

(c)

Looking into the base, the resistance is Rib = rπ + (β + 1)RE1 = 3739 + 151×100 = 18,839 Ω, since RE2 is bypassed and ro is neglected. This is in parallel with the bias divider Rth = 5638 Ω: Rin = 5638×18,839/(5638 + 18,839) = 106.21e6/24,477 = 4339 Ω. The bias network therefore dominates the input resistance, loading the source more than the transistor does. A larger divider resistance would raise Rin but would also make the bias less stable, as seen in the previous problem on stability. The input coupling capacitor is treated as a short at midband frequencies, so it does not appear in the result.

Answer: 4.34 kΩ

(d)

The source divider gives vb/vs = Rin/(Rin + Rs) = 4339/(4339 + 1000) = 0.8127. The gain from the base to the collector with RE1 unbypassed and ro neglected is -β RL'/Rib, where RL' = RC∥RL = 3.30×10.0/13.3 = 2.481 kΩ. This is equal to -gm RL'/(1 + gm RE1(1 + 1/β)) in another form. Numerically -150×2481/18,839 = -19.76. The overall gain is vo/vs = 0.8127×(-19.76) = -16.05, so the magnitude is 16.05. Without RE1 the gain would be -gm RL' = -99.5 but the input loading and distortion would be worse; the 100 Ω resistor trades gain for linearity and bandwidth.

Answer: 16.05

(e)

Output resistance is found by turning the source off (vs = 0), removing the load and looking back into the collector node. The transistor collector resistance with an emitter resistor RE1 is approximately ro[1 + gm RE1 rπ/(rπ + Rb + RE1)], where Rb = Rs∥Rth = 849 Ω is the resistance seen from the base to ground. Numerically gm RE1 rπ/(rπ + Rb + RE1) = 0.04012×100×3739/(3739 + 849 + 100) = 3.200. So Rtrans = 87.1 kΩ × 4.200 = 365.9 kΩ. In parallel with RC = 3.30 kΩ: Rout = 3.30×365.9/(369.2) = 3.27 kΩ. The collector resistance of the transistor is much greater than RC, so the output resistance is only slightly below RC.

Answer: 3.27 kΩ

A5 Practice Paper 14

Problem 1 [A5-066] Common-collector and common-base stages

An emitter-follower buffer uses VCC = 12.0 V (the collector is tied directly to VCC), a base divider of R1 = 47.0 kΩ to VCC and R2 = 47.0 kΩ to ground, and an emitter resistor RE = 2.20 kΩ to ground. The transistor has β = 100 and VBE = 0.700 V, with VT = 25.0 mV. A source of series resistance Rs = 5.00 kΩ is coupled to the base through a large capacitor, and a 1.00 kΩ load is coupled to the emitter through a large capacitor. Neglect ro. Separately, a second transistor (β = 100) biased at IC = 2.00 mA is used as a common-base stage with a source of Rs2 = 75.0 Ω at the emitter, a collector resistor of 3.90 kΩ and a 10.0 kΩ load on the collector, all signal-coupled by large capacitors.

  1. (a) Find the emitter-follower quiescent collector current. [3]
  2. (b) Find the input resistance seen by the source in the emitter follower (including the bias divider). [4]
  3. (c) Find the overall voltage gain vo/vs of the emitter follower. [5]
  4. (d) Find the output resistance seen by the 1.00 kΩ load in the emitter follower, with the source turned off. [4]
  5. (e) Find the voltage gain vo/vs of the common-base stage. [4]
(a)

The divider is 47.0 kΩ and 47.0 kΩ from 12.0 V, so Vth = 6.00 V and Rth = 23.5 kΩ. The base-loop equation, with the collector at VCC, is Vth = IB Rth + VBE + (β + 1) IB RE. So IB = (6.00 - 0.700)/(23,500 + 101×2200) = 5.300/245,700 = 21.57 µA. Then IC = βIB = 100×21.57 µA = 2.157 mA, and IE = 2.179 mA. The emitter sits at 2.179 mA×2.20 kΩ = 4.79 V, so VCE = 12.0 - 4.79 = 7.21 V, comfortably in the active region. The small-signal parameters follow: gm = 2.157/25.0 = 86.3 mS and rπ = 100/0.0863 = 1.159 kΩ.

Answer: 2.157 mA

(b)

At signal frequencies the load RL = 1.00 kΩ is in parallel with RE: RE' = 2.20×1.00/3.20 = 0.6875 kΩ. Looking into the base, Rib = rπ + (β + 1)RE' = 1159 + 101×687.5 = 70,596 Ω. The bias divider (Rth = 23.5 kΩ) is in parallel with this: Rin = 23,500×70,596/(23,500 + 70,596) = 17,631 Ω = 17.6 kΩ. The emitter follower multiplies the load resistance by about β + 1, so the input resistance is high, but the bias network now sets the limit. A bootstrapped bias network would raise it further, though this is not needed here.

Answer: 17.6 kΩ

(c)

Two voltage dividers appear in series. At the input: vb/vs = Rin/(Rin + Rs) = 17,631/(17,631 + 5000) = 0.7791. Inside the follower, the gain from base node to output is (β + 1)RE'/Rib = 101×687.5/70,596 = 0.9836, which is less than one because rπ drops some signal. The overall gain is vo/vs = 0.7791×0.9836 = 0.7663. The follower has near-unity voltage gain and no inversion. The loss is dominated by the 5.00 kΩ source resistance against the 17.6 kΩ input, which is a reminder that the buffer does not eliminate source loading, only reduces it compared with driving the 1 kΩ load directly.

Answer: 0.766

(d)

With the source off, the resistance seen from the base to ground is Rb = Rs∥Rth = 5.00×23.5/28.5 = 4.123 kΩ. Looking into the emitter, the transistor presents (Rb + rπ)/(β + 1) = (4123 + 1159)/101 = 52.30 Ω. This is in parallel with RE = 2.20 kΩ: Rout = 52.30×2200/(52.30 + 2200) = 51.08 Ω. The load itself is not included, since the output resistance is what the load sees. So a 1.00 kΩ load would form a divider with 51 Ω, causing about 4.9 percent signal loss at the output, which is already inside the gain figure from part c. The low output resistance is the main purpose of the follower.

Answer: 51.1 Ω

(e)

For the common-base stage IC = 2.00 mA, so IE = 2.00×101/100 = 2.02 mA and the emitter resistance is re = VT/IE = 25.0/2.02 = 12.38 Ω. The current gain from emitter to collector is α = β/(β + 1) = 0.990. The collector load is RC∥RL = 3.90×10.0/13.9 = 2.806 kΩ. The input current is vs/(Rs2 + re), so vo/vs = α RL'/(Rs2 + re) = 0.990×2806/(75.0 + 12.38) = 2778/87.38 = 31.79. The output is in phase with the input, unlike the common-emitter stage. The input resistance is only re = 12.4 Ω, so a low-impedance source is needed. Its main advantages are the wide bandwidth and the absence of Miller multiplication.

Answer: 31.8

Problem 2 [A5-067] MOSFET bias and operating regions

An n-channel enhancement MOSFET is biased from VDD = 12.0 V using a gate divider of R1 = 470 kΩ (to VDD) and R2 = 270 kΩ (to ground), a drain resistor RD = 3.30 kΩ and a source resistor RS = 2.00 kΩ. The gate draws no current. In saturation the drain current is ID = ½ k (VGS - Vt)², with k = 2.00 mA/V² and threshold voltage Vt = 1.20 V. Channel-length modulation is neglected. A large capacitor bypasses RS for small signals, and the drain is coupled to a high-impedance load. The transistor remains in saturation as long as VDS ≥ VGS - Vt. The circuit is the first stage of a sensor preamplifier whose operating point must be proved before any signal gain is quoted.

  1. (a) Find the gate voltage VG. [3]
  2. (b) Find the quiescent drain current ID. [5]
  3. (c) Find VDS at the quiescent point. [3]
  4. (d) Find the largest RD that keeps the transistor in saturation, with all other values unchanged. [4]
  5. (e) Find the magnitude of the small-signal voltage gain with RS bypassed, using the original RD. [5]
(a)

The gate draws no current, so the divider is unloaded: VG = VDD R2/(R1 + R2) = 12.0×270/(470 + 270) = 12.0×0.36486 = 4.378 V. This fixes the gate-to-ground voltage independent of the transistor. The gate-source voltage then equals VG minus the voltage drop across RS, which depends on the drain current, so the bias is self-adjusting: any rise in ID raises the source voltage and reduces VGS. That negative feedback is the same idea as emitter degeneration in a BJT stage, and it is what makes the quiescent point stable against variations in k and Vt between devices.

Answer: 4.378 V

(b)

Write VGS = VG - ID RS and let Vov = VGS - Vt. Then Vov = (4.378 - 1.200) - ID×2.00 kΩ = 3.178 - 2ID with ID in mA. Saturation gives ID = ½×2.00×Vov² = Vov² mA. Substitute: Vov = 3.178 - 2Vov², so 2Vov² + Vov - 3.178 = 0. The positive root is Vov = (-1 + √(1 + 25.43))/4 = (-1 + 5.141)/4 = 1.0352 V. Then ID = 1.0352² = 1.0716 mA. The other root is negative and is rejected because it would imply VGS < Vt. The gate-source voltage is VGS = 2.235 V, safely above the threshold of 1.20 V, so the device is on.

Answer: 1.072 mA

(c)

The drain-source voltage is the supply minus the drops across RD and RS: VDS = VDD - ID(RD + RS) = 12.0 - 1.0716 mA×5.30 kΩ = 12.0 - 5.679 = 6.321 V. The saturation requirement is VDS ≥ Vov = 1.035 V. Since 6.32 V exceeds this by a wide margin, the transistor is in saturation and the square-law equation used in part b is valid. The drain voltage relative to ground is VD = 12.0 - 1.0716×3.30 = 8.46 V and the source is at 2.14 V. The remaining headroom for output swing is about 5.3 V on the way down to the saturation edge, which is sufficient for a small-signal preamplifier.

Answer: 6.32 V

(d)

The saturation limit is reached when VDS = Vov. With the drain current unchanged (it is set by the gate-source loop and not by RD while in saturation): VDD - ID RS - ID RD,max = Vov. So RD,max = (VDD - ID RS - Vov)/ID = (12.0 - 1.0716×2.00 - 1.0352)/1.0716 = (12.0 - 2.1432 - 1.0352)/1.0716 = 8.8216/1.0716 = 8.232 kΩ. The original 3.30 kΩ is therefore well inside the limit, with a ratio of about 2.5. If RD were raised above 8.23 kΩ, the transistor would enter the triode region, and the drain current would no longer follow the square law, so the analysis would have to be redone with the triode equation.

Answer: 8.23 kΩ

(e)

For the square-law device gm = k Vov = 2.00 mA/V²×1.0352 V = 2.070 mS. Equivalently gm = 2ID/Vov = 2×1.0716/1.0352 = 2.070 mS. With RS bypassed for small signals, the source is at signal ground and the voltage gain of the common-source stage is Av = -gm RD = -2.070 mS×3.30 kΩ = -6.83. The magnitude is 6.83. The gain is modest because the transconductance of a MOSFET at about 1 mA is small compared with a BJT at the same current (about 40 mS). The unloaded drain assumption holds since the load is stated to be high impedance, so the 6.83 figure is the open-circuit voltage gain.

Answer: 6.83

Problem 3 [A5-068] MOSFET small-signal amplifiers

A common-source amplifier uses an n-channel MOSFET with kn = 1.60 mA/V² and Vt = 0.800 V, biased at VGS = 1.60 V. Take the quiescent drain current as ID = ½ kn (VGS - Vt)², ignoring channel-length modulation in the dc current, and use λ = 0.030 V⁻¹ so that ro = 1/(λ ID) for small-signal purposes. The drain resistor is RD = 10.0 kΩ and the load coupled through a capacitor is RL = 20.0 kΩ. The source has a total bias resistance split as RS1 = 500 Ω (unbypassed) in series with a large bypassed resistor RS2. The gate is biased through RG = 1.00 MΩ to a dc voltage, and the signal source has resistance Rsig = 200 kΩ coupled to the gate through a large capacitor. All capacitors are short circuits at midband.

  1. (a) Find the transconductance gm at the bias point. [3]
  2. (b) Find the small-signal output resistance ro of the transistor. [2]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the voltage gain from gate to output, including ro, RS1, and the parallel load RD∥RL. [6]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the overall gain vo/vsig, including the input divider of Rsig and RG. [5]
  5. (e) Explain in words why the unbypassed RS1 reduces the sensitivity of the gain to the value of gm, and state the gain limit as RS1 becomes large. [4]
(a)

First the overdrive voltage: Vov = VGS - Vt = 1.60 - 0.80 = 0.80 V. The quiescent current is ID = ½×1.60 mA/V²×0.80² = 0.512 mA, which is used below for ro. The small-signal transconductance for a square-law device is gm = kn Vov = 1.60 mA/V²×0.80 V = 1.28 mS. As a check, gm = 2ID/Vov = 2×0.512/0.80 = 1.28 mS, the same value. A higher bias current or a larger W/L (hence kn) would raise gm, but the first costs power and the second costs gate capacitance, which limits bandwidth. The value of 1.28 mS will be used for all later parts.

Answer: 1.28 mS

(b)

The output resistance due to channel-length modulation is ro = 1/(λ ID) = 1/(0.030 V⁻¹×0.512 mA) = 1/(1.536e-5) = 65.1 kΩ. This resistance appears between drain and source in the small-signal model, in parallel with the controlled current source gm vgs. Its value is large compared with RD = 10 kΩ and with RL' = 6.67 kΩ, so it will only trim the gain slightly (the ratio of RL' to ro is about 10 percent). A longer channel gives a smaller λ and thus a larger ro, which is the reason analog designs use longer devices than digital designs.

Answer: 65.1 kΩ

(c)

The signal load is RL' = RD∥RL = 10.0×20.0/30.0 = 6.667 kΩ. For a source resistor RS1 with output resistance ro the exact gain is Av = -gm ro RL'/[RL' + ro + RS1(1 + gm ro)]. Compute gm ro = 1.28 mS×65.10 kΩ = 83.33. Numerator: 83.33×6667 = 555,560 Ω. Denominator: 6667 + 65,104 + 500×(1 + 83.33) = 6667 + 65,104 + 42,167 = 113,938 Ω. So Av = -555,560/113,938 = -4.876. The magnitude is 4.88. This is lower than the simple -gm RL' = -8.53 because the unbypassed RS1 degenerates the stage, and lower still than -gm(ro∥RL') = -7.74, because ro also loads the drain.

Answer: 4.88

(d)

The gate draws no current, so the input resistance at the gate is just RG = 1.00 MΩ. The input divider is vg/vsig = RG/(RG + Rsig) = 1.00 MΩ/(1.00 MΩ + 200 kΩ) = 0.8333. The overall gain is vo/vsig = 0.8333×(-4.876) = -4.063, so the magnitude is 4.06. Loss in the input divider is about 17 percent. Since a MOSFET gate has essentially infinite input resistance at low frequency, the only way to reduce this loss is to raise RG, which is limited by gate leakage and by noise considerations. At high frequency the gate capacitance starts to matter, but it is not included in this midband analysis.

Answer: 4.06

(e)

The unbypassed source resistor carries the drain current, so the voltage across it, id RS1, subtracts from the applied vg to give vgs. This is series-series negative feedback. For a large loop gain the effective transconductance becomes Gm = gm/(1 + gm RS1) = 1.28/(1 + 0.64) = 0.78 mS, so an error of ten percent in gm changes Gm by only about 6 percent. This is the desensitisation. As RS1 grows, gm RS1 dominates and the gain tends to -RL'/RS1 (ignoring ro), which depends only on two resistors and not on the transistor. The price paid is lower gain and a higher output resistance, which for the stage here is ro(1 + gm RS1) + RS1.

Answer: Negative feedback; gain tends to RL'/RS1.

Problem 4 [A5-069] Multistage amplifiers and loading effects

A two-stage amplifier for a microphone preamplifier uses a common-emitter first stage followed by an emitter-follower buffer. Stage 1: gm1 = 40.0 mS, β1 = 100, collector resistor Rc1 = 4.70 kΩ, with a base bias resistance of Rb = 30.0 kΩ to ground in parallel with the base. Stage 2 is directly signal-coupled to the collector of stage 1 through a capacitor and has rπ2 = 1.30 kΩ, β2 = 100 and emitter resistor Re2 = 3.30 kΩ, driving a load RL = 2.20 kΩ by a capacitor. The microphone has source resistance Rs = 2.00 kΩ. Neglect ro in both stages and ignore the bias network of stage 2 (assume its resistors are very large). All capacitors are short circuits at midband, and the emitter of stage 1 is fully bypassed.

  1. (a) Find the input resistance of stage 2 (looking into its base with the load connected). [3]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the loaded voltage gain of stage 1 (collector voltage divided by its own base voltage). [4]
  3. (c) Find the voltage gain of stage 2. [3]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the overall gain vo/vs of the cascade. [6]
  5. (e) Without stage 2, the load RL is connected straight to the collector of stage 1. Find the improvement in overall gain provided by the buffer, in dB. [4]
(a)

Stage 2 is an emitter follower. At signal frequencies the emitter load is Re2 in parallel with RL: Re2' = 3.30×2.20/5.50 = 1.32 kΩ. Looking into its base, the resistance is Rin2 = rπ2 + (β2 + 1)Re2' = 1300 + 101×1320 = 1300 + 133,320 = 134,620 Ω = 134.6 kΩ. The factor (β + 1) multiplies the emitter-side resistance, so the buffer presents a very light load to stage 1. This is the reason emitter followers are inserted between a high-gain stage and a heavy load. Note the bias network of stage 2 is neglected as stated, which in practice would limit the real input resistance to its parallel value.

Answer: 134.6 kΩ

(b)

The load on the collector of stage 1 is Rc1 in parallel with Rin2: Rl1 = 4.70×134.62/(4.70 + 134.62) = 632.7/139.32 = 4.541 kΩ. With the emitter bypassed and ro neglected, the gain is Av1 = -gm1 Rl1 = -0.0400×4541 = -181.7. The magnitude is 181.7. Because Rin2 is about 29 times larger than Rc1, the loading by stage 2 reduces the gain by only 3.4 percent compared with the unloaded value -gm1 Rc1 = -188. The sign shows inversion, which carries through to the overall gain. The parameter rπ1 = β1/gm1 = 100/0.0400 = 2.50 kΩ is used in the input resistance below.

Answer: 181.7

(c)

The emitter follower gain from its base to the output is Av2 = (β2 + 1)Re2'/[rπ2 + (β2 + 1)Re2'] = 133,320/134,620 = 0.9903. The gain is slightly below unity because a little signal is lost across rπ2. This follower has no phase inversion. The voltage gain is essentially one, and the benefit of the stage is not gain but the impedance transformation: it presents 134.6 kΩ at its input, and the output resistance it offers to the load is of the order of (Rc1 + rπ2)/(β2 + 1) = 59.4 Ω (in parallel with Re2). This explains why the overall gain stays close to the first stage gain.

Answer: 0.990

(d)

First the input divider. The base of stage 1 sees rπ1 = 2.50 kΩ in parallel with the bias resistance Rb = 30.0 kΩ, so Rin1 = 2.50×30.0/32.5 = 2.308 kΩ. The signal fraction at the base is vb1/vs = 2.308/(2.308 + 2.00) = 0.5357. The overall gain is the product of the three factors: vo/vs = 0.5357×(-181.66)×0.9903 = -96.38. The magnitude is 96.4. Most of the loss is at the input, where the 2.00 kΩ source is comparable with the 2.31 kΩ input resistance of the first stage, and this loss cannot be recovered by the buffer. A larger bias resistance or a lower-impedance microphone would raise the overall gain further.

Answer: 96.4

(e)

Without the buffer the load on the collector is Rc1∥RL = 4.70×2.20/6.90 = 1.4986 kΩ. The unbuffered gain is -gm1×1498.6 = -59.94 and the overall gain is 0.5357×(-59.94) = -32.11. With the buffer the overall gain is 96.38 in magnitude. The ratio is 96.38/32.11 = 3.002, which in decibels is 20 log10(3.002) = 9.55 dB. The buffer therefore triples the gain delivered to the 2.20 kΩ load. The input divider is the same in both cases, so the improvement equals the ratio of the loaded gains of stage 1, 181.66×0.9903 over 59.94, which equals 3.002 as well.

Answer: 9.55 dB

Problem 5 [A5-070] Frequency response of amplifiers, poles and Miller effect

A common-emitter stage drives a 2.00 kΩ effective collector load RL' (the collector resistor in parallel with the load). The transistor is biased at gm = 40.0 mS with rπ = 2.50 kΩ, and its high-frequency model has Cπ = 18.0 pF and Cμ = 2.50 pF. Neglect the base spreading resistance and ro. The source resistance is Rs = 1.00 kΩ and the source is coupled to the base through an input coupling capacitor Cc = 1.00 µF. Treat the upper cut-off as set by the single input-side pole produced by Cπ plus the Miller-multiplied Cμ, and the lower cut-off as set by Cc alone with the emitter fully bypassed. The Miller multiplier uses the midband base-to-collector gain.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the midband gain vo/vs. [4]
  2. (b) Find the Miller-multiplied equivalent of Cμ at the input. [3]
  3. (c) Find the upper 3 dB frequency. [5]
  4. (d) Find the lower 3 dB frequency due to Cc. [4]
  5. (e) The source is replaced by one with Rs = 100 Ω. Find the new upper 3 dB frequency. [4]
(a)

At midband all capacitors are open (the internal ones) or short (the coupling one). The input divider is vπ/vs = rπ/(rπ + Rs) = 2.50/(2.50 + 1.00) = 0.7143. The output voltage is vo = -gm vπ RL', so the gain from vπ to output is -gm RL' = -0.0400×2000 = -80.0. The overall midband gain is vo/vs = 0.7143×(-80.0) = -57.14, and its magnitude is 57.14. The gain from base to collector (80.0) is the value to be used in the Miller effect, while the 57.14 is the gain from the source. The negative sign reflects the 180 degree phase shift of the common-emitter stage.

Answer: 57.14

(b)

The capacitor Cμ connects base to collector, across which the voltage gain is -80.0. By the Miller theorem the capacitance seen at the input is Cμ(1 + gm RL') = 2.50 pF×(1 + 80.0) = 2.50×81.0 = 202.5 pF. This is about 11 times the value of Cπ = 18.0 pF, so the Miller effect is by far the dominant input capacitance. At the output the Miller capacitance is Cμ(1 + 1/80) = 2.53 pF, which is neglected here because the output pole is much higher in frequency. This large multiplication is the central limitation of the common-emitter stage, and it motivates the cascode circuit.

Answer: 202.5 pF

(c)

The total input capacitance is Cin = Cπ + Cm = 18.0 + 202.5 = 220.5 pF. The resistance driving this capacitance is the source resistance in parallel with rπ (the Thevenin resistance seen by the capacitor): Rth = 1.00×2.50/3.50 = 0.7143 kΩ. The pole is at fH = 1/(2π Rth Cin) = 1/(2π×714.3×220.5e-12) = 1/(9.896e-7) = 1.0105 MHz. So the upper 3 dB frequency is 1.01 MHz. The gain-bandwidth product of the stage from the source is 57.14×1.0105 MHz = 57.7 MHz, which is useful to compare with the transistor's transition frequency to see whether the Miller effect is the limit.

Answer: 1.01 MHz

(d)

At low frequency the coupling capacitor Cc is in series with Rs and the input resistance rπ (the bias network is neglected, since it is not given). The corner frequency is fL = 1/(2π (Rs + rπ) Cc) = 1/(2π×3500×1.00e-6) = 1/(0.021991) = 45.47 Hz. The bypass capacitor is assumed large enough that its pole is far lower and so does not matter here. Since the upper corner is 1.01 MHz and the lower corner is 45.5 Hz, the midband span is more than four decades, which suffices for audio use. If the bias resistors were present they would lower the effective input resistance a little and raise fL slightly.

Answer: 45.5 Hz

(e)

With Rs = 100 Ω the resistance driving the input capacitance falls to Rth = 100×2500/2600 = 96.15 Ω. The Miller multiplier is the base-to-collector gain, which is unchanged at 80.0, so Cin is still 220.5 pF. Then fH = 1/(2π×96.15×220.5e-12) = 1/(1.3321e-7) = 7.507 MHz. Lowering the source resistance by a factor of 10 raised the bandwidth by 7.4 times, not 10, because rπ in parallel does not drop in proportion. The midband gain also changes to 0.9615×80.0 = 76.9, so the product of gain and bandwidth rises to 577 MHz, well above the transistor limit in practice, where other poles take over.

Answer: 7.51 MHz

A5 Practice Paper 15

Problem 1 [A5-071] Differential amplifiers and current mirrors, with BJT small-signal analysis

A bipolar differential amplifier runs from supplies of +12 V and -12 V. Its two identical npn transistors Q1 and Q2 have emitters joined at a common node. That node is fed from the collector of npn transistor Q4, which is the output side of a current mirror. Q3 is the diode-connected reference transistor, with its base and collector tied together; a resistor of 23.3 kΩ runs from +12 V to the Q3 collector, and the emitters of Q3 and Q4 both connect to -12 V. The emitter area of Q4 is twice that of Q3. Every transistor has β = 100, VBE = 0.70 V when conducting, thermal voltage VT = 25.0 mV and Early voltage VA = 80 V. Q1 and Q2 each have a collector resistor of 8.00 kΩ to +12 V. Take the collector current of each pair transistor as half the tail current, and use α = 1 for small-signal parameters.

  1. (a) Find the tail current delivered by Q4, including the base-current error of the mirror, and then the transconductance gm of each pair transistor. [7]
  2. (b) Find the differential voltage gain Ad (magnitude) when the output is taken between the two collectors, and the differential input resistance. [7]
  3. (c) The output is now taken single-ended from one collector. Find the common-mode rejection ratio in dB, using the mirror output resistance ro4 = VA/Io as the tail resistance and CMRR = gm·REE for a single-ended output. [6]
(a)

The reference current is Iref = (12 - (-12) - 0.70) / 23.3 kΩ = 23.3 V / 23.3 kΩ = 1.000 mA. For a mirror with area ratio m = 2, the collector current of Q4 is Io = m·Iref / (1 + (1 + m)/β), because the two bases draw (1 + m) times the base current of Q3 away from the reference node. Substituting, Io = 2 × 1.000 mA / (1 + 3/100) = 2.000 mA / 1.03 = 1.942 mA. Each pair transistor carries Ic = Io/2 = 0.9709 mA. The transconductance is gm = Ic/VT = 0.9709 mA / 0.0250 V = 38.83 mS. Note the tail current is 2.9 percent below the ideal value of 2 mA, which is the finite-β error.

Answer: Io = 1.942 mA, gm = 38.83 mS

(b)

For the balanced output between the collectors, a differential input vd makes the pair collector currents change by ±gm·vd/2, so the output between collectors is vo = -gm·RC·vd. The magnitude is therefore |Ad| = gm RC = 38.83 mS × 8.00 kΩ = 310.7 V/V. This neglects the transistor output resistance ro, which is large compared with 8 kΩ (about 82 kΩ at this current) and would reduce the gain by about 9 percent if included; the problem says to use the simple relation. The differential input resistance is the series sum of the two base-emitter resistances, Rid = 2 rπ = 2β/gm = 2 × 100 / 38.83 mS = 5.15 kΩ. The input resistance is set by β and the bias current, not by the load.

Answer: |Ad| = 310.7, Rid = 5.15 kΩ

(c)

The tail resistance is the output resistance of Q4: REE = ro4 = VA/Io = 80 V / 1.942 mA = 41.2 kΩ. For a single-ended output, the differential gain is gm RC/2 and the common-mode gain magnitude is approximately RC/(2 REE) when REE is much greater than 1/gm, so their ratio is CMRR = gm REE. Substituting, CMRR = 38.83 mS × 41.2 kΩ = 1600. In decibels this is 20 log10(1600) = 20 × 3.204 = 64.1 dB. The result shows the mirror output resistance, not the pair itself, limits common-mode rejection. A Wilson or cascode mirror would raise REE by a factor close to β/2 and lift the CMRR by about 34 dB.

Answer: CMRR = 64.1 dB

Problem 2 [A5-072] Op-amp inverting and non-inverting circuits, with gain-bandwidth limits

A sensor signal conditioner uses two identical op-amps in cascade, each with a unity-gain bandwidth (gain-bandwidth product) of 1.00 MHz, a very high open-loop DC gain, and output slew rate of 0.500 V/µs. Stage 1 is non-inverting: the input signal goes to the non-inverting terminal, a 47.0 kΩ feedback resistor joins the output to the inverting terminal, and a 4.70 kΩ resistor joins the inverting terminal to ground. Stage 2 is inverting: the output of stage 1 passes through a 10.0 kΩ resistor to the inverting terminal of the second op-amp, a 100 kΩ feedback resistor joins its output to that terminal, and its non-inverting terminal is grounded. The input is a sine wave of 15.0 mV rms. Assume single-pole op-amp behaviour and that only the final stage output is slew-rate limited.

  1. (a) Find the rms output voltage at a frequency low enough for the ideal gain to apply. [5]
  2. (b) Find the overall -3 dB bandwidth of the cascade in kHz, using the closed-loop bandwidth of each stage from the gain-bandwidth product. [8]
  3. (c) Find the highest frequency at which the full 1.65 V rms output can be delivered without slew-rate distortion. [7]
(a)

Stage 1 is a non-inverting amplifier with gain 1 + Rf/Rg = 1 + 47.0/4.70 = 11.0. Stage 2 is an inverting amplifier with gain -Rf/Rin = -100/10.0 = -10.0. The overall gain of the cascade is the product, 11.0 × (-10.0) = -110. The negative sign only means a 180 degree phase inversion, so the output magnitude is 110 × 15.0 mV = 1.65 V rms. The peak value is 1.65 × √2 = 2.33 V, which is well inside the output swing of a typical op-amp on ±12 V supplies. At very high open-loop gain the inverting input is a virtual short, which is why each stage gain depends only on resistor ratios in this part of the analysis.

Answer: 1.65 V rms

(b)

For a single-pole op-amp the closed-loop bandwidth is the gain-bandwidth product divided by the noise gain, which is 1 + Rf/Rg, the same factor as for the non-inverting configuration. Stage 1 has noise gain 11.0, so f1 = 1 MHz / 11.0 = 90.9 kHz. Stage 2, although inverting, has noise gain 1 + 100/10 = 11.0, so f2 = 90.9 kHz as well. Two identical first-order low-pass responses in cascade give an overall magnitude 1/(1 + (f/fp)²), which equals 1/√2 when (f/fp)² = √2 - 1. Hence f(-3 dB) = fp √(√2 - 1) = 90.91 kHz × 0.6436 = 58.5 kHz. Cascading two stages shrinks the bandwidth to 64 percent of a single stage, a standard result.

Answer: 58.5 kHz

(c)

A sine wave v = Vp sin(2π f t) has maximum slope 2π f Vp. Distortion begins when this equals the slew rate SR. The peak output is Vp = 1.65 V × √2 = 2.333 V. The full-power frequency is therefore f = SR / (2π Vp) = 0.500 V/µs / (2π × 2.333 V). Converting SR to 0.500 × 10⁶ V/s gives f = 5.00 × 10⁵ / 14.66 = 3.41 × 10⁴ Hz = 34.1 kHz. This is well below the small-signal bandwidth of 58.5 kHz, so for this output level the slew rate, not the gain-bandwidth product, limits the useful range. Reducing the output amplitude raises the slew-limited frequency in inverse proportion.

Answer: 34.1 kHz

Problem 3 [A5-073] Op-amp summing amplifier followed by an active low-pass filter

Two ideal op-amps run from ±15 V supplies. Op-amp 1 is an inverting summer: the inverting terminal is joined to source V1 through 10.0 kΩ and to source V2 through 22.0 kΩ, a 47.0 kΩ resistor joins its output to the inverting terminal, and the non-inverting terminal is grounded. The output of op-amp 1 drives op-amp 2 through a 20.0 kΩ resistor to the inverting terminal of op-amp 2. A parallel combination of a 51.0 kΩ resistor and a 1.50 nF capacitor joins the output of op-amp 2 to its inverting terminal, and its non-inverting terminal is grounded. Op-amp 2 therefore forms a first-order active low-pass filter. In the first test both inputs are constant DC levels, V1 = +0.800 V and V2 = -0.300 V. In the second test V1 is a 1.00 kHz sine wave of 0.500 V peak and V2 = 0.

  1. (a) Find the DC output voltage of op-amp 2 for the first test. [7]
  2. (b) Find the cutoff frequency of the filter formed by op-amp 2. [5]
  3. (c) For the second test, find the peak amplitude of the output of op-amp 2. [8]
(a)

The inverting summer gives V_s = -Rf(V1/R1 + V2/R2) = -47.0 kΩ × (0.800/10.0 kΩ + (-0.300)/22.0 kΩ). The two currents are 80.0 µA and -13.64 µA, so their sum is 66.36 µA and V_s = -47.0 kΩ × 66.36 µA = -3.119 V. At DC the capacitor is an open circuit, so op-amp 2 is a simple inverting amplifier of gain -51.0/20.0 = -2.55. Then Vout = -2.55 × (-3.119 V) = +7.954 V. This is within the ±15 V supply minus the usual 1 to 2 V of headroom, so neither stage saturates. The virtual-ground at each inverting input is what makes the input currents add independently, so changing V2 never changes the current set by V1.

Answer: +7.95 V

(b)

For an inverting stage with a feedback impedance Zf = Rf in parallel with C, the transfer function is H(s) = -(Rf/Rin) / (1 + s Rf C). It is a first-order low-pass response with a DC gain of -Rf/Rin and a corner at ωc = 1/(Rf C). The corner frequency is fc = 1 / (2π × 51.0 kΩ × 1.50 nF). The product Rf C = 51.0 × 10³ × 1.50 × 10⁻⁹ = 76.5 µs, so fc = 1 / (2π × 76.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 1 / (4.807 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.080 kHz. Note that the input resistor Rin sets only the gain and not the corner frequency in this configuration, which lets a designer change the gain without moving the cutoff.

Answer: 2.08 kHz

(c)

With V2 = 0 the summer output has peak amplitude (47.0/10.0) × 0.500 V = 2.350 V, with inversion that does not matter for amplitude. The magnitude of the second-stage gain at 1.00 kHz is |H| = (51.0/20.0) / √(1 + (f/fc)²), where f/fc = 1000 / 2080.5 = 0.4807. The square root is √(1 + 0.2310) = 1.1095. So |H| = 2.550 / 1.1095 = 2.298. The output peak is 2.350 V × 2.298 = 5.40 V. The sine wave is attenuated by about 0.9 dB relative to the DC gain and delayed by arctan(0.4807) = 25.7 degrees in phase beyond the two inversions. The peak is far below the supply voltage so the output is undistorted.

Answer: 5.40 V peak

Problem 4 [A5-074] Feedback in amplifiers: gain, desensitivity and phase margin

A voltage amplifier built on a single chip has a low-frequency open-loop gain A0 = 2000 V/V and two real poles in its open-loop response: A(s) = A0 / [(1 + s/ωp1)(1 + s/ωp2)], with fp1 = 50.0 kHz and fp2 = 8.00 MHz. A resistive feedback network samples the output voltage and returns a fraction β = 0.0500 to the input, forming a series-shunt (voltage-series) negative feedback connection with a frequency-independent β and negligible loading of the amplifier by the network. The loop gain is T(s) = β A(s). Because of ageing and temperature, A0 can fall by 20 percent from the nominal 2000 V/V. Work with the ideal feedback equation for midband gain, and use the loop gain with both poles for the stability check.

  1. (a) Find the nominal closed-loop midband gain. [5]
  2. (b) Find the closed-loop midband gain after A0 has fallen by 20 percent, to show the desensitising effect of the feedback. [5]
  3. (c) For the nominal amplifier, find the phase margin in degrees at the frequency where the magnitude of T(jω) is unity. Solve for the crossover frequency numerically if needed. [10]
(a)

For a negative feedback amplifier with the loop gain T0 = β A0 the closed-loop gain is Af = A0 / (1 + β A0). The loop gain at midband is T0 = 0.0500 × 2000 = 100, so the amount of feedback is 1 + T0 = 101. Then Af = 2000 / 101 = 19.80 V/V, which is close to the ideal limit 1/β = 20.0 V/V. The difference between 19.80 and 20.0 is the finite-gain error, equal to 1/(1 + T0) of the ideal value, about 1 percent. The feedback therefore makes the gain depend mainly on the passive network, and the amplifier gain A0 matters only through the small correction term. This is the first and most useful property of negative feedback: gain stability.

Answer: 19.80 V/V

(b)

The aged open-loop gain is A0' = 0.800 × 2000 = 1600 V/V. The loop gain becomes β A0' = 0.0500 × 1600 = 80, so the amount of feedback is 81. The closed-loop gain is Af' = 1600 / 81 = 19.753 V/V. Compared with the nominal 19.802 V/V, the closed-loop gain has fallen by only 0.049 V/V, or 0.25 percent, while A0 fell by 20 percent. The ratio of the two fractional changes, 20/0.25 = 81, equals the amount of feedback at the aged condition, which is the desensitivity D = 1 + βA. The result shows that a 20 percent drift in the active device becomes a quarter of a percent drift in the overall gain, which is why feedback amplifiers are used when precision matters.

Answer: 19.75 V/V

(c)

The loop-gain magnitude is |T(jf)| = 100 / [√(1 + (f/50 kHz)²) × √(1 + (f/8 MHz)²)]. Setting this equal to 1 and solving, with a numerical root finder, gives a crossover frequency of about fx = 4.384 MHz. A check: at this frequency the first factor is √(1 + 87.7²) ≈ 87.7 and the second factor is √(1 + 0.3004) = 1.1404, so the product is 100.0, confirming |T| = 1. The phase of T is -arctan(f/fp1) - arctan(f/fp2) = -arctan(87.69) - arctan(0.548) = -89.35° - 28.72° = -118.07°. The phase margin is PM = 180° + (-118.07°) = 61.9°. A phase margin above 60 degrees gives a closed-loop response with little peaking, so the amplifier is comfortably stable with this β. A larger β would raise the crossover frequency and the phase lag, shrinking the margin.

Answer: Phase margin = 61.9 degrees

Problem 5 [A5-075] Schmitt trigger and op-amp relaxation oscillator

A relaxation oscillator is built from an op-amp powered from ±12 V whose output saturates at ±11.0 V. A 10.0 kΩ resistor R1 joins the non-inverting terminal to ground, and a 22.0 kΩ resistor R2 joins the output to the non-inverting terminal, giving positive feedback. A timing resistor R = 33.0 kΩ joins the output to the inverting terminal, and a capacitor C = 10.0 nF joins the inverting terminal to ground. The capacitor charges and discharges exponentially toward the output level, and the output flips whenever the capacitor voltage reaches the voltage at the non-inverting terminal. Assume ideal switching, a symmetric output swing, and that the circuit is already in steady oscillation. Express voltages in volts, time in microseconds and frequencies in hertz as the parts request.

  1. (a) Find the positive switching threshold of the Schmitt trigger formed by R1, R2 and the op-amp. [5]
  2. (b) Find the oscillation frequency in hertz. [8]
  3. (c) The designer wants the oscillator to run at 5.00 kHz with the same R and C by changing only R2. Find the new value of R2 in kΩ, keeping R1 = 10.0 kΩ. [7]
(a)

The non-inverting terminal sees the divider formed by R2 from the output and R1 to ground, with no load current taken. The fraction fed back is β = R1/(R1 + R2) = 10.0 / (10.0 + 22.0) = 0.3125. When the output is at +Vsat = +11.0 V, the voltage at the non-inverting terminal is the upper threshold VT+ = β Vsat = 0.3125 × 11.0 V = 3.4375 V. With the output at -11.0 V, the lower threshold is VT- = -3.4375 V. The width of the hysteresis band is 6.875 V. The capacitor voltage must travel across this entire band between flips, so the thresholds directly set the charge time along with the RC product.

Answer: +3.44 V

(b)

After a flip to +Vsat, the capacitor charges from VT- toward +Vsat and the output flips again when it reaches VT+. The time to move from -βVsat to +βVsat is t = RC ln[(Vsat + βVsat)/(Vsat - βVsat)] = RC ln[(1 + β)/(1 - β)]. The two half periods are equal for a symmetric swing, so the period is T = 2 RC ln[(1 + β)/(1 - β)]. Here RC = 33.0 kΩ × 10.0 nF = 330 µs and (1 + β)/(1 - β) = 1.3125/0.6875 = 1.9091, with a natural logarithm of 0.6466. Then T = 2 × 330 µs × 0.6466 = 426.8 µs, and f = 1/T = 2343 Hz. The frequency does not depend on Vsat because it cancels from the ratio, but it does depend on β.

Answer: 2.34 kHz = 2343 Hz

(c)

A frequency of 5.00 kHz corresponds to a period of 200 µs. From T = 2 RC ln[(1 + β)/(1 - β)] we get ln[(1 + β)/(1 - β)] = T/(2RC) = 200 µs / 660 µs = 0.3030. Taking the exponential, (1 + β)/(1 - β) = e0.3030 = 1.3541. Solving for β, β = (1.3541 - 1)/(1.3541 + 1) = 0.3541/2.3541 = 0.1504. Because β = R1/(R1 + R2), we have R2 = R1 (1/β - 1) = 10.0 kΩ × (6.649 - 1) = 56.5 kΩ. Using a smaller β narrows the hysteresis band to ±1.65 V, so the capacitor has less distance to travel and the frequency rises. Check: with R2 = 56.5 kΩ, β = 0.1504 and T = 660 µs × ln(1.1504/0.8496) = 200 µs.

Answer: R2 = 56.5 kΩ

A5 Practice Paper 16

Problem 1 [A5-076] Class B power amplifier, efficiency and heat sink design

A class B complementary push-pull emitter-follower output stage drives an 8.00 Ω loudspeaker from supply rails of +15.0 V and -15.0 V. Treat the transistors as ideal, with no crossover distortion and no saturation voltage loss, so the output swings fully toward the rails if needed. The input is a sine wave. Each output transistor is a power device in a TO-247 package, with junction-to-case thermal resistance of 3.00 °C/W and a mounting washer with case-to-sink thermal resistance of 0.500 °C/W. The maximum permitted junction temperature is 150 °C and the worst-case ambient is 40.0 °C. Each transistor is mounted on its own identical heat sink, and there is no thermal derating applied beyond the limit stated. The stage must deliver an average power of 6.00 W to the load.

  1. (a) Find the peak output voltage needed for 6.00 W average load power. [5]
  2. (b) Find the total power drawn from the two supplies and the efficiency at this output level. [7]
  3. (c) The heat sink must be sized for the worst-case signal level, which for class B gives a maximum dissipation per transistor of VCC²/(π² RL). Find the largest heat-sink thermal resistance to ambient, in °C/W, that keeps the junction at 150 °C. [8]
(a)

For a sinusoidal output of peak value Vp across a resistor RL the average load power is P = Vp² / (2 RL). Solving for the peak voltage gives Vp = √(2 P RL) = √(2 × 6.00 W × 8.00 Ω) = √96.0 = 9.798 V. The peak load current is then Ip = Vp / RL = 9.798 / 8.00 = 1.225 A. The required peak voltage is only about two thirds of the 15.0 V rail, so the stage has headroom and is operating below its full-power condition. At the full rail swing of 15.0 V the load power would reach 14.1 W, so the 6.00 W requested here is well within the amplifier capability.

Answer: 9.80 V

(b)

In a class B stage each transistor conducts for half a cycle, so each supply delivers a half-wave rectified current with average value Ip/π. The two supplies together deliver Ps = 2 × VCC × Ip/π = 2 × 15.0 V × 1.225 A / π = 36.74 / 3.1416 = 11.70 W. The efficiency is the load power divided by the supply power: η = 6.00 W / 11.70 W = 0.513, which is 51.3 percent. The theoretical maximum for class B is π/4 = 78.5 percent, reached only at the full rail swing. At lower output levels the efficiency falls in proportion to Vp, which is why a class B amplifier is acceptable for music with a high crest factor. The remaining 5.70 W is dissipated as heat in the two transistors.

Answer: Efficiency = 51.3 percent

(c)

The maximum device dissipation in class B occurs at Vp = 2VCC/π, not at full swing, and is Pd,max = VCC² / (π² RL) = 15.0² / (9.870 × 8.00) = 225 / 78.96 = 2.850 W per transistor. The thermal circuit is a series chain from junction to ambient: Tj - Ta = Pd (θjc + θcs + θsa). Rearranging, the total allowed resistance is (150 - 40.0) °C / 2.850 W = 38.60 °C/W. Subtracting the known resistances, θsa = 38.60 - 3.00 - 0.500 = 35.1 °C/W. A heat sink with a rating of 35 °C/W or lower is required, and in practice a designer would choose a lower value, such as 20 °C/W, to leave a margin so that the junction runs well below 150 °C.

Answer: θsa = 35.1 °C/W

Problem 2 [A5-077] BJT and MOSFET as relay-driver switches

A 12.0 V relay coil of resistance 200 Ω must be switched from a logic gate whose high output level is 4.80 V. The coil is connected between the +12.0 V rail and the switch, and a diode is connected across the coil to carry the coil current when the switch opens. In design 1, the switch is an npn transistor with its emitter grounded and its collector joined to the lower end of the coil; the gate drives its base through a resistor Rb. In saturation use VCE(sat) = 0.200 V and VBE = 0.750 V, and drive the transistor at a forced current gain of 10 so that it is firmly saturated. In design 2, the switch is an n-channel MOSFET, fully enhanced by the 4.80 V gate level, with on-resistance of 0.400 Ω, which is joined between the lower end of the coil and ground. The gate current of the MOSFET is negligible.

  1. (a) Find the base resistor Rb for design 1. [7]
  2. (b) Find the ratio of the power dissipated in the transistor of design 1, including the base-emitter junction, to the power dissipated in the MOSFET of design 2. [7]
  3. (c) Explain in words what would happen to the switch if the diode across the coil were omitted, and why the diode fixes it. [6]
(a)

In saturation the coil current is set almost entirely by the coil: Ic = (12.0 - 0.200) V / 200 Ω = 59.0 mA. A forced current gain of 10 means the base current is Ib = Ic / 10 = 5.90 mA. The voltage across the base resistor is the gate output minus the base-emitter drop, 4.80 - 0.750 = 4.05 V. Applying Ohm's law, Rb = 4.05 V / 5.90 mA = 686 Ω. The nearest preferred value, 680 Ω, gives a base current of 5.96 mA and keeps the transistor deeply saturated. A forced gain of 10 is common practice because the data-sheet β may be 100 or more, and the extra base drive ensures VCE(sat) stays low for every unit and at high temperature.

Answer: Rb = 686 Ω

(b)

For the BJT, the power is the sum of the collector-emitter and base-emitter contributions: P = VCE(sat) Ic + VBE Ib = 0.200 × 59.0 mA + 0.750 × 5.90 mA = 11.80 mW + 4.425 mW = 16.23 mW. For the MOSFET, the coil current is I = 12.0 V / (200 + 0.400) Ω = 59.88 mA. The conduction loss is P = I² RDS(on) = (0.05988)² × 0.400 = 1.434 mW. The gate draws no steady current, so there is no gate loss. The ratio is 16.23 / 1.434 = 11.3. The MOSFET dissipates roughly a tenth as much and needs no base resistor. At 60 mA neither device needs a heat sink, but in a high-current load the MOSFET advantage would be very large.

Answer: Ratio = 11.3

(c)

A relay coil is an inductor storing energy ½ L I² while it carries current. When the switch opens, the current cannot change instantly, and the inductor generates a voltage v = L di/dt of whatever size is needed to keep current flowing. Without the diode, this voltage appears as a large positive spike on the switch node, many times the 12.0 V supply, easily reaching hundreds of volts. This can exceed the VCE rating of the transistor or the drain-source rating of the MOSFET and destroy the device by avalanche breakdown. With the diode in place, the spike is clamped at one diode drop above the supply, and the coil current recirculates through the diode and decays through the coil resistance. The cost is slower relay release, since the energy is dissipated slowly.

Answer: Explanation: the coil's stored energy drives a large voltage spike across the switch when it opens.

Problem 3 [A5-078] CMOS inverter design and NAND gate sizing with propagation delay

A digital cell library uses a 3.30 V CMOS process with minimum channel length L = 0.350 µm. The long-channel parameters are: nMOS threshold Vtn = 0.600 V and pMOS threshold magnitude |Vtp| = 0.700 V; process transconductance parameters kn' = µnCox = 180 µA/V² and kp' = µpCox = 60.0 µA/V². The designer wants an inverter whose switching threshold VM, the input voltage at which both transistors are in saturation and carry equal current, equals VDD/2. Use the saturation-region square-law model, Id = ½ k' (W/L)(VGS - Vt)², and neglect channel-length modulation. Inverter loads are lumped capacitances. When estimating a delay, assume the transistor delivers its constant saturation current while the output moves through half the supply, so t = CL (VDD/2) / Idsat.

  1. (a) Find the ratio Wp/Wn that gives VM = VDD/2 = 1.65 V. [8]
  2. (b) The inverter uses Wn/L = 2.00. Find the high-to-low propagation delay tpHL for a load capacitance of 50.0 fF. [5]
  3. (c) The inverter is replaced by a two-input NAND gate whose pMOS devices each keep the inverter geometry (Wp/L = 3.665 × 2.00) and are connected in parallel, with the nMOS devices in series. For the worst case in which only one pMOS conducts, find the low-to-high delay tpLH for the same 50.0 fF load. [7]
(a)

At the switching threshold both transistors are saturated and carry the same current, so kn' (Wn/L)(VM - Vtn)² = kp' (Wp/L)(VDD - VM - |Vtp|)². Taking the square root of the ratio, define r = √(kp' Wp / (kn' Wn)). Then VM - Vtn = r (VDD - VM - |Vtp|), which gives VM = (Vtn + r (VDD - |Vtp|)) / (1 + r). Setting VM = 1.65 V: 1.65 (1 + r) = 0.600 + r × 2.600, so 1.05 = 0.950 r and r = 1.1053. Squaring, r² = 1.2216 = (60/180)(Wp/Wn), so Wp/Wn = 1.2216 × 3 = 3.665. The pMOS must be about 3.7 times wider than the nMOS to compensate for its lower mobility, so rise and fall behaviours match.

Answer: Wp/Wn = 3.66

(b)

For the pull-down, the nMOS has VGS = VDD = 3.30 V at the start of the transition, so its overdrive is 3.30 - 0.600 = 2.70 V. Its saturation current is Idsat,n = ½ × 180 µA/V² × 2.00 × (2.70 V)² = 0.5 × 180 × 10⁻⁶ × 2.00 × 7.29 = 1.312 mA. The delay estimate with the half-swing charge removal is tpHL = CL (VDD/2) / Idsat = 50.0 fF × 1.65 V / 1.312 mA = 82.5 × 10⁻¹⁵ / 1.312 × 10⁻³ = 62.9 ps. This simple model overestimates the current, as the device leaves saturation when VDS drops below the overdrive, so a real simulation would show a slightly longer delay.

Answer: tpHL = 62.9 ps

(c)

In a NAND gate the two pMOS transistors are in parallel, so when only one input falls, one pMOS alone charges the load. Its geometry is Wp/L = 3.665 × 2.00 = 7.330. The overdrive is VDD - |Vtp| = 3.30 - 0.700 = 2.60 V. The saturation current is Idsat,p = ½ × 60.0 µA/V² × 7.330 × (2.60 V)² = 0.5 × 60 × 10⁻⁶ × 7.330 × 6.76 = 1.486 mA. The delay is tpLH = CL (VDD/2) / Idsat,p = 50.0 fF × 1.65 V / 1.486 mA = 55.5 ps. If both inputs fall together, both pMOS devices conduct and the delay halves to about 27.7 ps, so the gate delay depends on the input pattern. Designers always quote the worst case, the one-input transition, for timing sign-off.

Answer: tpLH = 55.5 ps

Problem 4 [A5-079] CMOS propagation delay and dynamic power of a buffer chain

A clock distribution buffer must drive a 4.00 pF load from a minimum-size inverter whose input capacitance is Cin = 5.00 fF. The designer inserts a chain of N inverters, each one larger than the previous by the same fan-out factor f, so that the first inverter has input capacitance Cin and the last drives the 4.00 pF load. Use the delay model tp = N tp0 (1 + f/γ) for the chain, where tp0 = 12.0 ps is the unloaded delay of one inverter and γ = 1 for the process. The chain runs from a 1.20 V supply with a clock frequency of 250 MHz, and every node in the chain switches once per clock cycle in each direction (activity factor 1). The total switched capacitance is the sum of the input capacitances of all N inverters plus the load.

  1. (a) For N = 4 inverters, find the fan-out f per stage and the total propagation delay in picoseconds. [7]
  2. (b) Find the total propagation delay if the designer uses N = 6 inverters instead. [6]
  3. (c) For the N = 4 chain, find the dynamic power dissipated at 250 MHz from the 1.20 V supply, counting the load capacitance and all inverter input capacitances. [7]
(a)

The overall fan-out is F = CL/Cin = 4.00 pF / 5.00 fF = 800. With N equal stages each stage has f = F1/N = 8001/4 = 5.318. The delay of the chain is tp = N tp0 (1 + f/γ) = 4 × 12.0 ps × (1 + 5.318) = 48.0 ps × 6.318 = 303.3 ps. The sizes of the four inverters, as input capacitance, are 5.00 fF, 26.6 fF, 141 fF and 752 fF, each 5.318 times the one before. The final stage drives 4.00 pF, so 752 fF × 5.318 = 4.00 pF, which closes the chain. Using an even number of inverters keeps the clock polarity unchanged from input to output.

Answer: f = 5.32, tp = 303 ps

(b)

With N = 6 stages, the fan-out per stage becomes f = 8001/6. Taking natural logarithms, ln 800 = 6.6846, so ln f = 6.6846 / 6 = 1.1141 and f = 3.047. The delay is tp = 6 × 12.0 ps × (1 + 3.047) = 72.0 ps × 4.047 = 291.4 ps. Increasing the number of stages from four to six reduces the delay by 11.9 ps, about 4 percent. The gain is small because the fan-out per stage is already near its optimum range of 3 to 5, where the added delay of extra stages (the N tp0 term) nearly balances the benefit of a smaller f. A larger N would increase both area and power for little speed gain.

Answer: tp = 291 ps

(c)

The input capacitances of the four inverters are Cin(1 + f + f² + f³) with f = 5.318: 1 + 5.318 + 28.28 + 150.4 = 185.0, so the sum is 5.00 fF × 185.0 = 925 fF = 0.925 pF. Adding the 4.00 pF load gives the total switched capacitance Ctot = 4.925 pF. With activity factor 1 and the chosen clock, the dynamic power is P = Ctot VDD² fclk = 4.925 × 10⁻¹² F × (1.20 V)² × 250 × 10⁶ Hz = 4.925 × 10⁻¹² × 1.44 × 2.5 × 10⁸ = 1.773 mW. The load capacitance accounts for 81 percent of the power, so the buffer chain overhead is only 19 percent. Power depends on VDD squared, so dropping the supply to 1.0 V would cut the power by 31 percent.

Answer: P = 1.77 mW

Problem 5 [A5-080] Amplifier design to a gain specification: common-emitter versus common-source

An amplifier must be designed for a microphone source with a Thevenin resistance of 10.0 kΩ driving a 10.0 kΩ load, from a 15.0 V supply. Two candidate stages are compared at the same bias current of 1.00 mA. Both are single-transistor common-emitter or common-source stages with coupling capacitors that are short circuits at signal frequencies, with the drain or collector resistor to the supply and the load capacitively coupled to the output. The BJT has β = 150, thermal voltage 25.0 mV and output resistance ro = 100 kΩ. The MOSFET has the transconductance parameter kn'(W/L) = 4.00 mA/V², output resistance ro = 50.0 kΩ, and its gate draws no current. Each stage has a collector or drain resistor of 4.70 kΩ. The signal voltage gain is measured from the source open-circuit voltage vs to the output, so source loading is included.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the overall gain vo/vs of the BJT common-emitter stage. [6]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the overall gain vo/vs of the common-source MOSFET stage. [6]
  3. (c) The specification is |vo/vs| ≥ 50. Find the collector resistor RC (in kΩ) that makes the BJT stage just meet it, keeping the same bias current. Comment on whether the bias point still leaves a collector headroom. [8]
(a)

At Ic = 1.00 mA the transconductance is gm = Ic/VT = 1.00 mA / 25.0 mV = 40.0 mS and the base-emitter input resistance is rπ = β/gm = 150 / 40.0 mS = 3.75 kΩ. The output side sees RC = 4.70 kΩ, RL = 10.0 kΩ and ro = 100 kΩ in parallel: 1/R = 1/4.70 + 1/10.0 + 1/100 in kΩ⁻¹ = 0.2128 + 0.1000 + 0.0100 = 0.3228, so R = 3.098 kΩ. The unloaded-by-source gain is gm R = 40.0 mS × 3.098 kΩ = 123.9. The source divider multiplies it by rπ / (Rs + rπ) = 3.75 / 13.75 = 0.2727. The overall gain magnitude is 123.9 × 0.2727 = 33.8 (an inverting gain). Loss in the input divider costs a factor of 3.7.

Answer: |vo/vs| = 33.8

(b)

For a square-law MOSFET, Id = ½ kn'(W/L) Vov², so gm = √(2 kn'(W/L) Id) = √(2 × 4.00 mA/V² × 1.00 mA) = √(8.00 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.828 mS. The gate draws no current, so the input divider has no loss and vgs = vs. The output resistance seen by the transistor is RD || RL || ro: 1/R = 1/4.70 + 1/10.0 + 1/50.0 in kΩ⁻¹ = 0.2128 + 0.1000 + 0.0200 = 0.3328, so R = 3.005 kΩ. The gain magnitude is gm R = 2.828 mS × 3.005 kΩ = 8.50. The MOSFET gives only a quarter of the gain of the BJT at the same current because its transconductance (2.83 mS) is 14 times smaller than the BJT value (40.0 mS), partly offset by having no input loss.

Answer: |vo/vs| = 8.50

(c)

The source-divider factor stays 0.2727 and gm = 40.0 mS, so the required effective load is R = 50 / (0.2727 × 40.0 mS) = 4.583 kΩ. This is the parallel combination of RC, RL and ro. Then 1/RC = 1/4.583 - 1/10.0 - 1/100 in kΩ⁻¹ = 0.2182 - 0.1000 - 0.0100 = 0.1082, so RC = 9.24 kΩ. At Ic = 1.00 mA, the DC voltage across RC is 9.24 V, so VC = 15.0 - 9.24 = 5.76 V and VCE is about 5.1 V if the emitter is at 0.65 V, comfortably above saturation for the signal swing, although the output swing is limited by cutoff to about 4.6 V (1 mA times the 4.58 kΩ ac load), with the saturation limit near 4.9 V. The gain of 50 is met exactly, with no margin to spare.

Answer: RC = 9.24 kΩ

A5 Practice Paper 17

Problem 1 [A5-081] Diode circuits, clippers and rectifiers

A small instrumentation cabinet needs a smoothed DC rail. A transformer with a 24 V rms secondary (60 Hz, treat it as ideal with zero winding resistance) feeds a full-wave bridge made of four identical silicon diodes. Use the constant-drop model: each conducting diode drops 0.7 V and a reverse-biased diode is an open circuit. The bridge output connects to a filter capacitor C in parallel with a resistive load of 50 Ω. Initially C = 2200 μF. The designer must decide whether this capacitor is adequate when the rail feeds a sensor that tolerates no more than 1.0 V of peak-to-peak ripple. Use the standard approximation that the capacitor discharges linearly at the load current for a full half-cycle of the 60 Hz supply.

  1. (a) Find the peak DC rail voltage across the load. [4]
  2. (b) Find the peak-to-peak ripple voltage with C = 2200 μF. [5]
  3. (c) Find the peak reverse voltage that each non-conducting diode must withstand. [4]
  4. (d) Find the smallest capacitance that keeps the ripple at or below 1.0 V peak to peak, and state whether the 2200 μF part is adequate. [7]
(a)
