Two diodes conduct on each half-cycle, so the load sees the secondary peak minus two diode drops. The secondary peak is Vs,pk = 24√2 = 33.94 V. Then Vp = 33.94 − 2(0.7) = 33.94 − 1.40 = 32.54 V. The transformer is ideal, so there is no further drop. The model assumes the diodes switch instantly and that the capacitor charges to the peak at each crest. This is the voltage at the top of each ripple cycle, which is also the upper envelope of the load voltage.

Answer: 32.5 V

(b)

In a full-wave circuit the capacitor recharges every half-cycle, so the discharge time is T/2 = 1/(2f) = 1/120 s = 8.33 ms. The load current is approximately Vp/R = 32.54/50 = 0.6508 A. The capacitor loses charge ΔQ = I·(1/2f), so Vr = I/(2fC) = 0.6508/(2 × 60 × 2.2×10⁻³) = 0.6508/0.264 = 2.465 V peak to peak. Equivalently Vr = Vp/(2fRC) = 32.54/13.2 = 2.465 V. The assumption of a constant discharge current slightly overstates the ripple because the true discharge is exponential, so the figure is a conservative estimate.

Answer: 2.47 V

(c)

When the bridge conducts, the capacitor holds the output at about Vp = 32.54 V. A diode that is reverse biased has its cathode at the output terminal and its anode tied, through a conducting diode, to the opposite end of the secondary. Take the worst case at the secondary crest: the reverse diode sees the secondary peak minus one conducting drop, so PIV = Vs,pk − 0.7 = 33.94 − 0.7 = 33.24 V. A 50 V or higher rated diode gives a comfortable margin, and common 1N400x parts exceed this by a wide factor.

Answer: 33.2 V

(d)

Set the ripple limit Vr = 1.0 V in Vr = Vp/(2fRC) and solve for C: C = Vp/(2fR·Vr) = 32.54/(2 × 60 × 50 × 1.0) = 32.54/6000 = 5.42×10⁻³ F, so C ≈ 5420 μF. The existing 2200 μF capacitor gives 2.47 V of ripple, about two and a half times the permitted amount, so it is not adequate. A designer would choose the next standard value, 6800 μF, and check its voltage rating (at least 50 V) and ripple-current rating. A linear post-regulator would be an alternative if the capacitor size is a problem.

Answer: 5420 μF

Problem 2 [A5-082] Zener regulators and power supply filtering

A 9 V instrument rail is derived from an unregulated supply by a series resistor R feeding a Zener diode in parallel with the load. Model the Zener in breakdown as a 9.00 V source in series with a dynamic resistance rz = 4.0 Ω, valid for Zener currents above 5.0 mA. The unregulated input varies between 15.0 V and 21.0 V, and the load current varies between 0 and 40 mA. The Zener is rated for 1.3 W maximum dissipation. The designer picks a standard series resistor R = 120 Ω and wants to know whether it meets the requirement, how well the output is held, and how much hum on the input appears on the 9 V rail. Neglect the load's own impedance variation beyond the stated current range.

  1. (a) Find the largest series resistance that keeps the Zener current at or above 5.0 mA under the worst input and load conditions. [5]
  2. (b) With R = 120 Ω, find the Zener power dissipation at the highest input voltage and no load, and judge it against the 1.3 W rating. [5]
  3. (c) Find the change in output voltage when the load current steps from 0 to 40 mA at a fixed input. [5]
  4. (d) The input carries 2.0 V peak-to-peak ripple from a poorly filtered rectifier. Find the ripple that appears on the output. [5]
(a)

The worst case is the lowest input of 15.0 V with the largest load of 40 mA. At the minimum Zener current of 5.0 mA the Zener voltage is Vz = 9.00 + 4.0 × 0.005 = 9.02 V. The resistor carries the sum of load and Zener current, 40 + 5 = 45 mA. Then Rmax = (15.0 − 9.02)/0.045 = 5.98/0.045 = 132.9 Ω. Any larger resistor would let the Zener drop out of breakdown at low line and full load, and the output would sag. The chosen 120 Ω is below this limit, so it passes.

Answer: 133 Ω

(b)

With no load all of the resistor current flows in the Zener. At Vin = 21.0 V the current is I = (21.0 − 9.00)/(120 + 4.0) = 12.0/124 = 96.77 mA. The Zener voltage is Vz = 9.00 + 4.0 × 0.09677 = 9.387 V, so the dissipation is P = Vz × I = 9.387 × 0.09677 = 0.908 W. This is below the 1.3 W rating, a margin of about 30 percent. Note that heat sinking and a rise in ambient temperature reduce the rating, so the margin is not generous for an enclosed cabinet.

Answer: 0.908 W

(c)

For a fixed input the output moves by the parallel combination of R and rz times the change in load current, because the load current is taken from the Zener. rz ∥ R = (4.0 × 120)/(124) = 3.871 Ω. Then ΔVo = 3.871 × 0.040 = 0.1548 V, so the output drops by about 155 mV when the load goes from 0 to 40 mA, 1.7 percent of 9 V. The sign is a decrease because extra load current reduces the Zener current and its voltage falls by rz times that change. Load regulation is therefore about 3.9 mV per mA.

Answer: 0.155 V

(d)

Treat the ripple as a small signal. The divider formed by R and rz gives ΔVo/ΔVin = rz/(R + rz) = 4.0/124 = 0.03226, equal to 32.3 mV per volt of line change. For 2.0 V peak to peak of input ripple the output ripple is 2.0 × 0.03226 = 0.0645 V, which is 64.5 mV peak to peak. The load is assumed to draw constant current for this small-signal step. The result shows that a Zener with low dynamic resistance suppresses ripple by roughly 30 to 1, but a larger filter capacitor is still needed upstream if 64 mV is too much for the instruments.

Answer: 64.5 mV

Problem 3 [A5-083] Thyristors, SCR and TRIAC circuits

A resistive immersion heater of 20 Ω is controlled by a single SCR in series with it, fed from a 120 V rms, 60 Hz supply. The SCR is an ideal switch with zero on-state drop that conducts from the firing angle α until the load current reaches zero at 180°, with no gate current needed afterwards. The operator wants smooth control between about 250 W and the maximum available power. First the designer examines the circuit at α = 60°. Later the heater thermostat calls for exactly 250 W, and the supply company asks what the half-wave controlled circuit does to the power factor seen at the source. Take the supply voltage as vs = 120√2 sin ωt and measure α from the positive-going zero crossing.

  1. (a) Find the average load voltage when α = 60°. [4]
  2. (b) Find the load power when α = 60°. [5]
  3. (c) Find the power factor at the source when α = 60°. [4]
  4. (d) Find the firing angle that gives exactly 250 W, in degrees. [7]
(a)

The SCR conducts only on the positive half-cycle from α to π, so the average output is Vavg = (1/2π) ∫ from α to π of Vm sin θ dθ = Vm(1 + cos α)/(2π). With Vm = 120√2 = 169.7 V and α = 60°, cos α = 0.5, so Vavg = 169.7 × 1.5/6.283 = 40.51 V. The average current would be 40.51/20 = 2.03 A. The half-wave circuit therefore passes only a small DC component of supply current, which matters when sizing the supply transformer.

Answer: 40.5 V

(b)

Power depends on the rms load voltage: Vrms = Vm √[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/(4π)], where the divisor 4π (not 2π) reflects that only the positive half-cycle conducts. With α = 60° = 1.0472 rad, π − α = 2.0944 and ½ sin 120° = 0.4330. The bracket is (2.0944 + 0.4330)/(4π) = 2.5274/12.5664 = 0.20112, whose square root is 0.4485. So Vrms = 169.7 × 0.4485 = 76.11 V. Then P = Vrms²/R = 76.11²/20 = 289.6 W. The load is resistive, so voltage and current are in phase while the SCR conducts, and this expression gives the real power directly.

Answer: 290 W

(c)

The source delivers the same current as the load, Irms = Vrms/R = 76.11/20 = 3.805 A. The apparent power is S = Vs Irms = 120 × 3.805 = 456.6 VA and the real power is P = 289.6 W. The power factor is P/S = 289.6/456.6 = 0.634, which also equals Vrms/Vs = 76.11/120. The factor is below 1 even though the load is purely resistive, because the chopped current waveform carries harmonic content that transfers no average power. The low factor comes mainly from distortion, and because the lag is not a simple sinusoidal displacement, capacitors do not correct it.

Answer: 0.634

(d)

Require P = 250 W, so Vrms² = 250 × 20 = 5000 and Vrms = 70.71 V. The condition is 70.71 = 169.7 √[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/(4π)], which gives (π − α + ½ sin 2α) = 4π (70.71/169.7)² = 4π × 0.17361 = 2.1817. This cannot be solved in closed form, so iterate. At α = 60° the bracket is 2.5274 and at 90° it is 1.5708, so the root lies between them, near 72°. Refining gives α = 71.9° (1.2551 rad), where the bracket is 2.1817. This is only a little later than the 60° case of part (b), which gave 289.6 W, so the power falls from about 290 W to 250 W over a modest change of firing angle, and the control is nonlinear.

Answer: 71.9°

Problem 4 [A5-084] BJT bias circuits and operating point

A silicon NPN transistor is biased with a voltage divider and an emitter resistor from a 12.0 V supply. R1 = 33 kΩ runs from the supply to the base, R2 = 6.8 kΩ runs from the base to ground, the collector resistor is RC = 2.2 kΩ and the emitter resistor to ground is RE = 1.0 kΩ. Use VBE = 0.70 V in the active region and neglect leakage. The datasheet gives current gain β between 100 and 300, and production parts will fall anywhere in that range. A technician proposes accepting the circuit if the collector current stays within 5 percent of its value for the minimum-β part. Assess the circuit using Thevenin's theorem at the base and state whether the proposal is satisfied across the range.

  1. (a) Find the collector current for β = 100. [5]
  2. (b) Find the collector-emitter voltage for β = 100 and confirm the transistor is in the active region. [5]
  3. (c) Find the collector current for β = 300. [5]
  4. (d) Find the percentage rise in collector current from β = 100 to β = 300, and decide whether the 5 percent requirement is met. [5]
(a)

Replace the divider by its Thevenin equivalent: VBB = 12 × 6.8/(33 + 6.8) = 2.050 V and RB = 33 ∥ 6.8 = 5.638 kΩ. The base-emitter loop gives VBB = IB RB + VBE + IE RE with IB = IE/(β + 1). So IE = (VBB − VBE)/(RE + RB/(β + 1)) = 1.350/(1.0 + 5.638/101) = 1.350/1.0558 = 1.279 mA. Then IC = β/(β + 1) × IE = 0.9901 × 1.279 = 1.266 mA. The base current is only 12.7 μA, small compared with the divider current of about 0.3 mA, so the divider is fairly stiff.

Answer: 1.27 mA

(b)

Apply Kirchhoff's voltage law around the collector-emitter path: VCE = VCC − IC RC − IE RE = 12.0 − 1.266 × 2.2 − 1.279 × 1.0 = 12.0 − 2.786 − 1.279 = 7.936 V. The transistor is active if VCE exceeds VCE,sat of about 0.2 V and the collector is more positive than the base. The base sits at VB = 0.70 + 1.279 = 1.98 V, while the collector is at 12.0 − 2.786 = 9.21 V, so the collector junction is firmly reverse biased. The device is active, with the operating point near the middle of the 12 V supply, giving good swing.

Answer: 7.94 V

(c)

Repeat the Thevenin calculation with β = 300. The base-circuit term is RB/(β + 1) = 5.638/301 = 0.01873 kΩ, so IE = 1.350/(1.0 + 0.01873) = 1.350/1.01873 = 1.3254 mA. Then IC = (300/301) × 1.3254 = 0.99668 × 1.3254 = 1.3210 mA. Even though β tripled, IC rose only slightly because the emitter resistor and the stiff divider hold the emitter current near (VBB − VBE)/RE. This is the reason the voltage-divider arrangement is used in preference to fixed-base-current bias.

Answer: 1.32 mA

(d)

The change is (1.3210 − 1.2662)/1.2662 = 0.0548/1.2662 = 0.0434, a rise of 4.3 percent. The proposal asks for no more than 5 percent, so the requirement is met, but with little room: only 0.7 percentage points. Temperature drift of VBE (about −2 mV per kelvin) would shift VBB − VBE by a few percent as well, and resistor tolerances add more, so a careful designer would reduce RB, for example by halving both divider resistors, or increase RE. The cost would be a larger standing divider current and lower input resistance for signals.

Answer: 4.3 percent

Problem 5 [A5-085] BJT small-signal model and common-emitter amplifier

A common-emitter stage uses an NPN transistor biased at IC = 2.00 mA. Take VT = 25 mV, β = 150 and Early voltage VA = 100 V. The emitter is bypassed for signals. The bias network presents a total Thevenin resistance of 12 kΩ to ground at the base. A signal source of internal resistance 1.0 kΩ drives the base through a large coupling capacitor, the collector resistor is 3.3 kΩ and a 10 kΩ load is capacitively coupled to the collector. All capacitors are short circuits at signal frequencies. The designer is deciding whether to leave the emitter fully bypassed or to add an unbypassed emitter resistor of 100 Ω to trade gain for stability. Use the hybrid-π model, and for the degenerated case neglect ro.

  1. (a) Find rπ for the transistor. [4]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the voltage gain from base to output with the emitter fully bypassed (include ro). [5]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the overall gain vo/vs with the emitter bypassed. [5]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the overall gain vo/vs when a 100 Ω emitter resistor is left unbypassed, and say what has improved as a result. [6]
(a)

The transconductance is gm = IC/VT = 2.00 mA/25 mV = 0.0800 S. The base-emitter small-signal resistance is rπ = β/gm = 150/0.0800 = 1875 Ω. For later use ro = VA/IC = 100/0.002 = 50 kΩ. These values hold only at the quiescent current of 2 mA, so any change of bias current shifts every small-signal parameter. The result rπ = 1.875 kΩ means the base looks like a fairly low resistance, and it will form a significant divider with the 1 kΩ source resistance.

Answer: 1875 Ω

(b)

With the emitter bypassed, the output sees RC, RL and ro in parallel: 3.3 k ∥ 10 k = 2.481 kΩ, and 2.481 k ∥ 50 k = 2.364 kΩ. The gain from base to output is Av = −gm (RC ∥ RL ∥ ro) = −0.0800 × 2364 = −189.1. The magnitude is 189.1, and the negative sign shows 180 degree phase inversion. Neglecting ro would give −198.5, an error of about 5 percent, so including the Early effect matters at the level of accuracy a designer would expect here.

Answer: 189

(c)

The input resistance at the base is Rin = 12 kΩ ∥ rπ = 1.621 kΩ. The signal source divides against this: vb/vs = Rin/(Rin + Rs) = 1621.6/(1621.6 + 1000) = 0.6185. The overall gain is therefore vo/vs = 0.6185 × (−189.1) = −116.98, magnitude about 117. The source resistance throws away over a third of the signal, which is a typical drawback of a bypassed common-emitter stage fed from a modest source. A lower-impedance source or a preceding buffer would recover some of it.

Answer: 117

(d)

With RE = 100 Ω unbypassed and ro neglected, the load RL′ = 3.3 k ∥ 10 k = 2.481 kΩ. The gain from base is Av = −β RL′/(rπ + (β + 1) RE) = −150 × 2481/(1875 + 151 × 100) = −372,180/16,975 = −21.93. The input resistance rises to 12 k ∥ 16.975 k = 7.03 kΩ, so vb/vs = 7030/8030 = 0.8755 and vo/vs = 0.8755 × (−21.93) = −19.2. Gain has fallen by a factor of about 6, but gain now depends mainly on the resistor ratio, not on gm or β, and input resistance has more than quadrupled. Distortion also falls.

Answer: 19.2

A5 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A5-086] Common-collector and common-base stages

A sensor with a Thevenin source resistance of 5.0 kΩ must drive a 1.0 kΩ load. A designer considers inserting an emitter follower between them. The transistor has β = 100 and is biased at IC = 5.0 mA with VT = 25 mV, so gm = 0.200 S and rπ = 500 Ω. The emitter bias resistor is RE = 2.0 kΩ to the negative rail, and the bias network contributes 40 kΩ in parallel with the transistor's input resistance at the base. The load is capacitively coupled to the emitter. Neglect ro and treat all capacitors as short circuits at signal frequency. The sensor amplitude is 100 mV peak. Compare the buffered arrangement with connecting the sensor directly to the load.

  1. (a) Find the input resistance seen by the source, including the 40 kΩ bias resistance. [4]
  2. (b) Find the overall voltage gain vo/vs of the follower. [4]
  3. (c) Find the output resistance of the follower looking into the emitter, including RE. [4]
  4. (d) Find the average power in the load for the 100 mV peak sensor with the buffer in place. [4]
  5. (e) Find the ratio of load power with the buffer to the load power when the sensor drives the load directly. [4]
(a)

The effective load at the emitter is RL′ = RE ∥ RL = 2.0 k ∥ 1.0 k = 667 Ω. The resistance looking into the base is rb = rπ + (β + 1) RL′ = 500 + 101 × 667 = 67.83 kΩ. The 40 kΩ bias resistance appears in parallel at the input node, so Rin = 40 k ∥ 67.83 k = 25.16 kΩ. The bias network, not the transistor, is now the main limit on input resistance. Raising the bias resistors would help but would make the bias less stable against β variation.

Answer: 25.2 kΩ

(b)

The voltage gain from the base to the emitter is Ae = (β + 1) RL′/(rπ + (β + 1) RL′) = 67,333/67,833 = 0.9926. The source divider is Rin/(Rin + Rs) = 25.16/(25.16 + 5.0) = 0.8343. Multiplying gives vo/vs = 0.8343 × 0.9926 = 0.828. A gain below 1 looks unattractive, but the follower is used for impedance transformation, not voltage gain: it takes a 5 kΩ source that would otherwise be loaded by 1 kΩ and presents a much higher input resistance.

Answer: 0.828

(c)

Looking back into the emitter, the source and bias resistances are reflected through the transistor reduced by (β + 1). First Rs ∥ 40 k = 5.0 k ∥ 40 k = 4.444 kΩ. The resistance at the emitter terminal is (rπ + 4444)/(β + 1) = 4944/101 = 48.95 Ω. RE = 2.0 kΩ appears in parallel at the output node, so Rout = 2000 ∥ 48.95 = 47.79 Ω. The load of 1 kΩ is not included, since output resistance is a property of the stage itself. The result of under 50 Ω compares with the 5 kΩ source it replaces.

Answer: 47.8 Ω

(d)

The load voltage amplitude is vo,pk = 0.828 × 0.100 V = 0.08281 V. The average power in a resistor for a sinusoid is P = Vpk²/(2 RL) = (0.08281)²/(2 × 1000) = 6.857×10⁻³/2000 = 3.43×10⁻⁶ W. So the buffered load receives 3.43 μW. The follower itself consumes DC power, 5 mA from the rail, which is thousands of times larger than this signal power, but that is the price of impedance conversion and does not count against the signal power ratio here.

Answer: 3.43 μW

(e)

Without the buffer the source divides against the load: vL = 100 mV × 1000/(5000 + 1000) = 16.67 mV peak. The power is (0.016667)²/(2 × 1000) = 1.389×10⁻⁷ W = 0.139 μW. The ratio of buffered to direct power is 3.4286/0.13889 = 24.7, about 13.9 dB. The follower therefore lets the load receive nearly 25 times as much signal power, justifying its use even though its voltage gain is below unity. The same comparison would favour a follower less strongly if the source resistance were lower, since the direct connection would already be well matched.

Answer: 24.7

Problem 2 [A5-087] MOSFET bias and operating regions

An n-channel enhancement MOSFET is biased from a 10.0 V supply with a resistive divider and a source resistor. The gate divider is R1 = 1.5 MΩ from the supply to the gate and R2 = 1.0 MΩ from the gate to ground, so no DC gate current flows. The source resistor is RS = 2.0 kΩ and the drain resistor is RD = 3.0 kΩ. In saturation the drain current is ID = ½ k (VGS − Vt)² with k = 2.0 mA/V² and threshold voltage Vt = 0.80 V; neglect channel-length modulation. A process change may shift the threshold. The designer must verify that the transistor is saturated, find how much drain resistance is tolerable and assess the sensitivity of the bias point to the threshold.

  1. (a) Find the drain current, taking the root that is consistent with the device being on. [6]
  2. (b) Find VDS and state the operating region. [4]
  3. (c) Find the largest RD that keeps the device in saturation. [5]
  4. (d) The threshold shifts to 1.00 V. Find the percentage change in drain current. [5]
(a)

The gate voltage is VG = 10.0 × 1.0/(1.5 + 1.0) = 4.00 V and VGS = VG − ID RS = 4.00 − 2.0 ID (ID in mA, RS in kΩ). Substituting into ID = ½(2.0)(VGS − 0.8)² = (3.2 − 2.0 ID)² gives 4 ID² − 12.8 ID + 10.24 = ID, or 4 ID² − 13.8 ID + 10.24 = 0. The roots are ID = (13.8 ± 5.157)/8 = 1.080 mA or 2.37 mA. The larger root gives VGS = 4 − 4.74 < 0, below threshold, so it is rejected. Hence ID = 1.080 mA and VGS = 1.839 V.

Answer: 1.08 mA

(b)

The source is at VS = ID RS = 1.0803 × 2.0 = 2.161 V, and the drain is at VD = 10.0 − ID RD = 10.0 − 1.0803 × 3.0 = 6.759 V. So VDS = 6.759 − 2.161 = 4.598 V. The overdrive is VOV = VGS − Vt = 1.839 − 0.80 = 1.039 V. Saturation needs VDS ≥ VOV; here 4.60 V exceeds 1.04 V by a wide margin, so the transistor operates in saturation. The state is consistent with the square-law relation used in part (a), which confirms the original assumption was right.

Answer: 4.60 V

(c)

In saturation ID does not depend on RD, so the drain current stays at 1.0803 mA as RD is increased until the boundary VDS = VOV is reached. At that limit VDD − ID(RD + RS) = VOV, so RD + RS = (10.0 − 1.0394)/1.0803 = 8.295 kΩ. Subtracting RS = 2.0 kΩ gives RD(max) = 6.295 kΩ. The present RD = 3.0 kΩ is under half of that, which gives generous headroom for signal swing at the drain. Larger RD would raise voltage gain but push the transistor to the triode region on negative-going swings.

Answer: 6.29 kΩ

(d)

With Vt = 1.00 V the equation becomes ID = (3.0 − 2.0 ID)², or 4 ID² − 12 ID + 9 = ID, so 4 ID² − 13 ID + 9 = 0. The discriminant is 169 − 144 = 25, giving ID = (13 − 5)/8 = 1.000 mA (the other root, 2.25 mA, makes VGS negative). The change is (1.000 − 1.0803)/1.0803 = −0.0743, a fall of 7.4 percent for a 25 percent shift in threshold. The source resistor supplies negative feedback that desensitises the bias. Without RS, with the gate held at 4.00 V, the current would scale as (4.0 − Vt)² and fall from 10.24 to 9.00 in these units, a change of about −12 percent.

Answer: −7.4 percent

Problem 3 [A5-088] MOSFET small-signal amplifiers

A common-source amplifier uses an NMOS transistor biased at ID = 0.500 mA. The device has k = μnCox(W/L) = 1.00 mA/V² (so ID = ½ k VOV² in saturation) and channel-length modulation λ = 0.020 V⁻¹. The drain resistor is RD = 10 kΩ and a 20 kΩ load is capacitively coupled to the drain. The source is bypassed to ground for signals, and the gate is driven by an ideal signal source. A colleague suggests inserting a 1.0 kΩ unbypassed source resistor to make the gain less sensitive to the transistor parameters. Use the small-signal model, take ro = 1/(λ ID), and for the degenerated case neglect ro for simplicity. All capacitors are signal short circuits.

  1. (a) Find the transconductance gm. [4]
  2. (b) Find ro. [3]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the voltage gain with the source bypassed. [5]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the voltage gain with the 1.0 kΩ source resistor unbypassed. [4]
  5. (e) Find the output resistance of the bypassed stage as seen by the load. [4]
(a)

In saturation ID = ½ k VOV², so VOV = √(2 ID/k) = √(2 × 0.5/1.0) = 1.0 V. The transconductance is gm = k VOV = 1.00 × 1.0 = 1.00 mA/V. The same result follows from gm = √(2 k ID) = √(2 × 1.0 × 0.5) = 1.00 mA/V, or from gm = 2 ID/VOV = 2 × 0.5/1.0 = 1.00 mA/V. Note that a large overdrive of 1 V is used, which costs headroom but improves linearity. The transconductance is much less than that of a BJT at the same current, which would be about 20 mA/V.

Answer: 1.00 mA/V

(b)

The output resistance of the transistor itself arises from channel-length modulation. ro = 1/(λ ID) = 1/(0.020 × 0.5×10⁻³) = 1/(1.0×10⁻⁵) = 100 kΩ. This is much larger than RD and RL, so it will have a small effect on the gain. Strictly the formula uses ID at the edge of saturation without the (1 + λ VDS) term, an approximation that is accurate to a few percent for λ = 0.02 V⁻¹. A longer-channel device, with smaller λ, would give even higher ro and gain.

Answer: 100 kΩ

(c)

With the source bypassed, the signal at the drain sees RD, RL and ro in parallel: 10 k ∥ 20 k = 6.667 kΩ, and 6.667 k ∥ 100 k = 6.25 kΩ. The gain magnitude is |Av| = gm (RD ∥ RL ∥ ro) = 1.00 mS × 6.25 kΩ = 6.25. The output is inverted, so Av = −6.25. This modest gain is typical for a MOSFET stage biased at low current with moderate resistors; to increase it one would raise RD, accept a lower drain voltage, or use a higher-gm device.

Answer: 6.25

(d)

With an unbypassed source resistor Rs = 1.0 kΩ the gain drops to Av = −gm RL′/(1 + gm Rs) where RL′ = RD ∥ RL = 6.667 kΩ and ro is neglected. Then gm Rs = 1.0 and Av = −1.00 × 6.667/(1 + 1.0) = −3.33. The magnitude is 3.33. Gain has fallen by about 47 percent, but if gm Rs ≫ 1 the gain would approach −RL′/Rs, set only by resistors. Here gm Rs = 1 gives only partial desensitisation, so a larger Rs would be needed to obtain real insensitivity to device variation.

Answer: 3.33

(e)

For the bypassed stage the output resistance looking into the drain node is the parallel of ro and RD, since the source is grounded for signals and the gate source is ideal. Rout = RD ∥ ro = 10 k ∥ 100 k = 9.091 kΩ. The load is not included, since output resistance excludes it. This value is far larger than RL would like for good voltage transfer; with RL = 20 kΩ it is already costing the gain a factor RL/(RL + Rout) = 0.69. A source follower following the stage would cure the loading problem.

Answer: 9.09 kΩ

Problem 4 [A5-089] Multistage amplifiers and loading effects

A signal chain has a sensor with source resistance 10 kΩ driving a two-stage amplifier made of a voltage-gain stage and an emitter-follower output stage. Stage 1 has input resistance 50 kΩ, open-circuit voltage gain −120 and output resistance 4.0 kΩ. Stage 2, the follower, has input resistance 60 kΩ, open-circuit voltage gain +0.98 and output resistance 40 Ω. The load is a 300 Ω actuator coil driver input. Treat each stage as a two-port with these parameters and take the load as purely resistive. A junior engineer asks whether the follower is worth its cost, and the answer must be given with numbers by comparing the cascade with stage 1 driving the 300 Ω load directly.

  1. (a) Find the loaded voltage gain of stage 1 when it drives stage 2. [4]
  2. (b) Find the overall gain magnitude |vo/vs| of the full cascade with the follower. [6]
  3. (c) Find the overall gain magnitude |vo/vs| when stage 1 drives the 300 Ω load directly. [5]
  4. (d) Find the improvement from the follower in decibels. [5]
(a)

Stage 2 loads stage 1 through its 60 kΩ input resistance, forming a divider with the 4.0 kΩ output resistance of stage 1. The loaded gain is Av1 = Avo1 × Rin2/(Rin2 + Rout1) = −120 × 60/(60 + 4.0) = −120 × 0.9375 = −112.5. Loading has therefore cost only 6 percent of the gain. The assumption is that the input resistance of stage 2 does not depend on the load of stage 2; for a real follower it does, so a designer should quote Rin2 for the actual 300 Ω load, which is what the given figure represents.

Answer: −112.5

(b)

Three divider factors multiply. The source division is Rin1/(Rin1 + Rs) = 50/(50 + 10) = 0.8333. Stage 1 loaded gain is −112.5 from part (a). The output stage delivers Avo2 × RL/(RL + Rout2) = 0.98 × 300/(300 + 40) = 0.98 × 0.8824 = 0.8647. The overall gain is 0.8333 × (−112.5) × 0.8647 = −81.07, so the magnitude is 81.1. The three-factor chain shows that gain is lost at every interface, and the best-conditioned interfaces are those where the receiving input resistance is much greater than the driving output resistance.

Answer: 81.1

(c)

Remove stage 2. Stage 1 now drives the 300 Ω load directly, so its loaded gain is −120 × 300/(300 + 4000) = −120 × 0.06977 = −8.372. The source divider is still 0.8333. The overall gain is 0.8333 × (−8.372) = −6.977, magnitude 6.98. The 4.0 kΩ output resistance of stage 1 is more than thirteen times the load resistance, so about 93 percent of the signal is dropped inside the stage. This is the classic loading problem that a low-output-resistance follower is meant to solve.

Answer: 6.98

(d)

The gain ratio is 81.07/6.977 = 11.62. In decibels the improvement is 20 log10(11.62) = 20 × 1.0653 = 21.3 dB. The follower is therefore worth including on voltage-gain grounds alone: it raises gain by a factor of nearly twelve without adding voltage gain of its own, only by fixing the impedance mismatch. Its cost is one transistor, a bias network, extra supply current and a small loss of linearity, which are modest. The recommendation to the junior engineer is to keep it unless the load can be raised above about 40 kΩ.

Answer: 21.3 dB

Problem 5 [A5-090] Frequency response of amplifiers, poles and Miller effect

A common-emitter amplifier is driven by a source of resistance Rs = 500 Ω. The transistor small-signal parameters at the operating point are gm = 40 mS, rπ = 2.5 kΩ, Cπ = 20 pF and Cμ = 2.0 pF; ro and rx are negligible. The total collector load for signals, including the bias resistor and the next stage, is RL′ = 3.0 kΩ. Ignore the output pole and coupling capacitors, and treat the bias network as having negligible effect at the base. The team wants to know the upper cutoff frequency set by the input pole, and then judges whether replacing the stage by a cascode, which fixes the Miller multiplier at about 2 but leaves the midband gain unchanged, is worth the extra transistor.

  1. (a) Find the midband gain magnitude |vo/vs|. [4]
  2. (b) Find the Miller-equivalent input capacitance contributed by Cμ. [4]
  3. (c) Find the upper cutoff frequency set by the input pole. [5]
  4. (d) Find the upper cutoff frequency with a cascode input stage, where the Miller multiplier is 2. [4]
  5. (e) Find the gain-bandwidth product of the original stage. [3]
(a)

At midband the capacitors are open circuits. The base-emitter voltage is vπ = vs × rπ/(rπ + Rs) = vs × 2500/3000 = 0.8333 vs. The output is vo = −gm vπ RL′, so the gain is vo/vs = −0.8333 × (0.040 × 3000) = −0.8333 × 120 = −100. The magnitude is 100 (40 dB). Here the base-to-output gain gm RL′ = 120 sets the Miller multiplier in the next parts, so this number should be kept distinct from the overall gain that includes the source divider.

Answer: 100

(b)

Cμ bridges the input and output nodes of an inverting stage with gain −gm RL′ = −120 from base to collector. Miller's theorem gives an equivalent input capacitance CM = Cμ(1 + gm RL′) = 2.0 × (1 + 120) = 242 pF. This is twelve times the 20 pF of Cπ and dominates the input capacitance, so Cin = Cπ + CM = 20 + 242 = 262 pF. The output-side Miller capacitance, about Cμ, is much smaller and is ignored here. Physically the small capacitor is magnified because the voltage across it changes 121 times as much as the input does.

Answer: 242 pF

(c)

The resistance driving the input capacitance is the Thevenin resistance seen by Cin: Rs ∥ rπ = 500 ∥ 2500 = 416.7 Ω. The pole is at fH = 1/(2π Rth Cin) = 1/(2π × 416.7 × 262×10⁻¹²). The product is 2π × 416.7 = 2618 and 2618 × 262×10⁻¹² = 6.860×10⁻⁷ s, so fH = 1.458×10⁶ Hz = 1.46 MHz. This is far below the transistor's transition frequency, so bandwidth is limited entirely by the Miller effect and the source resistance, not by the device.

Answer: 1.46 MHz

(d)

In a cascode the collector of the input transistor is held near a constant voltage by the common-base transistor, so the first transistor sees a gain of about −1, giving a Miller multiplier of (1 + 1) = 2. Then Cin = Cπ + 2Cμ = 20 + 4 = 24 pF. The pole becomes fH = 1/(2π × 416.7 × 24×10⁻¹²) = 1/(6.283×10⁻⁸) = 1.59×10⁷ Hz = 15.9 MHz. This is nearly eleven times the bandwidth of part (c), 1.46 MHz,, obtained without losing midband gain, since the common-base stage passes the collector current to the 3.0 kΩ load unchanged.

Answer: 15.9 MHz

(e)

The gain-bandwidth product for a single dominant pole is the midband gain magnitude times the cutoff frequency: 100 × 1.458 MHz = 145.8 MHz. For the cascode the product is 100 × 15.9 MHz = 1.59 GHz in principle, though other poles from the stage's own capacitances would then take over and limit it. The original product of 146 MHz is the quantity the designer trades: with a single-pole response, doubling the gain would halve the bandwidth, which is why gain is bought with bandwidth in simple stages.

Answer: 146 MHz

A5 Practice Paper 19

Problem 1 [A5-091] Differential amplifiers and current mirrors

A bench instrument front end uses an NPN differential pair Q1 and Q2 powered from +12 V and -12 V. The two emitters join at one node, and a simple two-transistor NPN current mirror sinks the tail current from that node to the -12 V rail. The mirror reference transistor is diode connected and is fed from ground through a 23.3 kΩ resistor, so its base-emitter drop of 0.7 V sits above -12 V. Each collector of the pair connects to ground through RC = 10 kΩ, and the output is taken differentially between the two collectors. For every transistor take β = 200, VA = 100 V and VT = 25 mV. Neglect the output resistance of Q1 and Q2 and neglect Q1 and Q2 base currents when finding common-mode gain.

  1. (a) Find the tail current delivered by the mirror, including the finite-β error of the mirror (matched transistors, Early effect ignored for this part). [3]
  2. (b) Find the transconductance gm of each transistor of the pair at balance. [3]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the differential voltage gain Ad = vo,diff / vid with the output taken between the two collectors. [4]
  4. (d) Taking the output single-ended at the collector of Q2, find the common-mode rejection ratio CMRR in dB, using the tail output resistance Rt = VA / Itail from the mirror output transistor. [5]
  5. (e) A colleague proposes doubling Iref to improve the CMRR because 'more current means more gm'. Explain whether this works, using the expression for CMRR, and say what physical change would raise it. [5]
(a)

The reference branch is a 23.3 kΩ resistor in series with the diode-connected transistor across the full 24 V between the rails, so Iref = (24 - 0.7) / 23.3 kΩ = 23.3 V / 23.3 kΩ = 1.000 mA. In a two-transistor mirror the reference device must also supply the two base currents, each Iout/β, so Iref = Iout (1 + 2/β). Therefore Iout = Iref / (1 + 2/β) = 1.000 mA / (1 + 2/200) = 1.000 mA / 1.01 = 0.990 mA. This is the tail current Itail. Each side of the pair carries half of it, 0.495 mA, when the input is balanced. The 1 percent shortfall is the mirror's systematic β error and it is why a designer treats Iref as an upper bound when sizing the tail.

Answer: 0.990 mA

(b)

At balance the tail current divides equally, so Ic1 = Ic2 = Itail / 2 = 0.990 mA / 2 = 0.495 mA. For a BJT in the forward active region gm = Ic / VT. Substituting, gm = 0.495 mA / 25 mV = 19.8 mS. The corresponding base-emitter dynamic resistance would be rπ = β / gm = 200 / 19.8 mS = 10.1 kΩ, which is not needed for the next parts but confirms the transistors are not starved of base drive. We assume Ic is equal to Ie, since β = 200 makes the base current error below 0.5 percent.

Answer: 19.8 mS

(c)

For a differential input vid the half-circuit method applies: the emitter node is a virtual ground for differential signals, so each transistor acts as a common-emitter stage with collector load RC and transconductance gm. Each collector voltage swing is ±gm RC vid / 2. Taking the output between collectors doubles the single-ended swing, so |Ad| = gm RC = 19.8 mS × 10 kΩ = 198. The output resistance of Q1 and Q2 is neglected by instruction. Without that approximation the gain would fall by about RC / ro, with ro = VA / Ic = 100 V / 0.495 mA = 202 kΩ, giving roughly a 5 percent reduction, which shows the neglect is acceptable to first order.

Answer: 198

(d)

The tail resistance is Rt = VA / Itail = 100 V / 0.990 mA = 101 kΩ. For a common-mode input both emitters move together, so the half-circuit has an emitter resistance of 2 Rt, and with β large the single-ended common-mode gain is Acm ≈ - RC / (2 Rt) = -10 kΩ / (202 kΩ) = -0.0495. The single-ended differential gain is half of the differential-output value, Ad,se = gm RC / 2 = 99. Then CMRR = |Ad,se / Acm| = 99 / 0.0495 = 2000. Equivalently CMRR = gm Rt = 19.8 mS × 101 kΩ = 2000. In decibels this is 20 log10(2000) = 66.0 dB.

Answer: 66.0 dB

(e)

From part d, CMRR = gm Rt. With gm = Itail / (2 VT) and Rt = VA / Itail, the tail current cancels: CMRR = VA / (2 VT) = 100 V / 50 mV = 2000, the same 66 dB at any bias. Doubling Iref doubles gm but halves Rt, so the gain in differential gain is exactly offset by a rise in common-mode gain, and the CMRR does not move. The only things that change it are the Early voltage of the tail device or the structure of the current source. A cascode or Wilson mirror raises the output resistance from ro to about β ro / 2, so the same arithmetic gives a CMRR near 100 times higher, about 106 dB. A longer-channel or higher-VA device helps in proportion. So the colleague's proposal wastes 1 mA of power and leaves the CMRR unchanged.

Answer: No: CMRR = gm Rt = VA/(2 VT) is independent of tail current; use a mirror with higher output resistance (cascode or Wilson) instead.

Problem 2 [A5-092] Op-amp inverting and non-inverting circuits

A biomedical sensor produces a signal of 10 mV amplitude with content up to 5 kHz, and the signal must be raised to 1 V amplitude before it enters a data converter. The designer is choosing between a single non-inverting amplifier of gain 100 and two cascaded non-inverting amplifiers of gain 10 each. Every amplifier uses an op-amp with a DC open-loop gain A0 = 2 × 105 and a gain-bandwidth product GBW = 1 MHz, modelled as a single-pole amplifier. The single-stage version uses R1 = 1 kΩ from the inverting input to ground and Rf = 99 kΩ from the output to the inverting input. The two-stage version uses R1 = 1 kΩ and Rf = 9 kΩ in each stage. Treat each closed-loop stage as a single-pole response whose -3 dB frequency is GBW divided by the ideal gain.

  1. (a) Find the actual DC closed-loop gain of the single-stage amplifier when the finite open-loop gain A0 is included. [3]
  2. (b) Find the -3 dB bandwidth of the single-stage amplifier. [3]
  3. (c) Find the percentage gain error of the single-stage amplifier at 5 kHz, relative to its DC gain of 100. [4]
  4. (d) Find the percentage gain error at 5 kHz for the two-stage cascade of gain 10 per stage. [4]
  5. (e) If the single-stage design is kept, find the minimum GBW needed (in MHz) for the gain error at 5 kHz to be no more than 1 percent. [6]
(a)

The ideal gain is 1 + Rf / R1 = 1 + 99 kΩ / 1 kΩ = 100, so the feedback fraction is β = R1 / (R1 + Rf) = 1 kΩ / 100 kΩ = 0.01. For a non-inverting amplifier with finite open-loop gain, the closed-loop gain is G = A0 / (1 + A0 β). Substituting, G = 2 × 105 / (1 + 2 × 105 × 0.01) = 2 × 105 / 2001 = 99.95. The gain error from finite A0 is therefore only 0.05 percent, which is negligible compared with the resistor tolerance. The loop gain A0 β = 2000 is large, which is what justifies using the ideal formula in the remaining parts.

Answer: 99.95

(b)

For a single-pole op-amp the closed-loop bandwidth equals the gain-bandwidth product divided by the closed-loop gain, fc = GBW / G. With GBW = 1 MHz and the ideal gain of 100, fc = 1 × 106 / 100 = 10 kHz. This follows because the gain-bandwidth product is constant for a voltage-feedback amplifier with a single dominant pole: raising the gain by a factor lowers the bandwidth by the same factor. Equivalent reasoning with β gives fc = β × GBW = 0.01 × 1 MHz = 10 kHz. The bandwidth is therefore only twice the highest signal frequency of 5 kHz, which hints at a problem with amplitude accuracy at the top of the band.

Answer: 10 kHz

(c)

With the single-pole closed-loop model, the gain magnitude at frequency f is |G(f)| = G0 / √(1 + (f / fc)²). At f = 5 kHz with fc = 10 kHz and G0 = 100, |G| = 100 / √(1 + 0.25) = 100 / 1.1180 = 89.44. The gain error relative to 100 is (100 - 89.44) / 100 = 0.1056, that is 10.56 percent. The signal amplitude at 5 kHz would arrive at the converter as 0.894 V rather than 1 V. For a measurement chain that needs 1 percent accuracy this single-stage design is clearly unacceptable even though its DC gain is exact.

Answer: 10.56 %

(d)

Each stage has an ideal gain of 10 and so a -3 dB frequency of fc = 1 MHz / 10 = 100 kHz. At 5 kHz each stage gives 10 / √(1 + (5 / 100)²) = 10 / √1.0025 = 9.9875. The two stages multiply, so the overall gain is 9.9875² = 99.75, compared with the ideal 100. The error is (100 - 99.75) / 100 = 0.249 percent, roughly 40 times smaller than the single-stage error. The cascade needs one extra op-amp and one extra resistor pair, but its loop gain per stage is also higher in relative terms at the signal frequency, which is why it holds its gain flat.

Answer: 0.25 %

(e)

A gain error of 1 percent means |G(5 kHz)| / G0 ≥ 0.99. So 1 / √(1 + (f / fc)²) = 0.99, giving (f / fc)² = 1 / 0.9801 - 1 = 0.02030 and f / fc = 0.1425. Hence the needed corner frequency is fc = 5 kHz / 0.1425 = 35.09 kHz. Since fc = GBW / G0 with G0 = 100, GBW = 35.09 kHz × 100 = 3.509 MHz. This is 3.5 times the 1 MHz part chosen. A designer therefore either buys a faster and usually more expensive op-amp, or accepts the cascade of two cheaper 1 MHz parts. The cascade is usually the cheaper route when GBW cost rises faster than linearly with speed.

Answer: 3.51 MHz

Problem 3 [A5-093] Op-amp summing, integrating, differentiating and filters

A technician builds an inverting integrator for a vibration sensor. The op-amp inverting input connects to the signal source through R = 10 kΩ, a capacitor C = 10 nF connects from the output to the inverting input, and the non-inverting input is grounded. The op-amp has an input offset voltage of 3 mV (modelled as a DC source in series with the non-inverting input) and the output saturates at ±13 V. Bias currents are negligible. With the input grounded, the output drifts into saturation. To fix this, the technician places a resistor Rf = 1 MΩ in parallel with the capacitor, creating a lossy integrator. The signal is a 1 kHz sine of 100 mV peak. Assume the op-amp is otherwise ideal and the output starts from 0 V.

  1. (a) For the original pure integrator with the input grounded, find the output ramp rate caused by the offset voltage. [4]
  2. (b) Find the time for the output of the pure integrator to reach the 13 V saturation limit. [4]
  3. (c) With Rf = 1 MΩ in place, find the steady DC output offset with the signal grounded. [4]
  4. (d) Find the corner frequency of the lossy integrator, below which it stops integrating. [3]
  5. (e) Find the peak output amplitude produced by the 100 mV, 1 kHz sine, and comment by a number on how close this is to an ideal integrator. [5]
(a)

With the input grounded the inverting input sits at the offset voltage Vos, so the resistor R carries a current Vos / R from the input node to ground, and the whole current flows into the capacitor. The offset appears at the integrator input exactly like a DC signal of 3 mV, giving a constant capacitor current I = Vos / R = 3 mV / 10 kΩ = 0.3 µA. The capacitor charges so the output ramps at dVo/dt = I / C = 0.3 µA / 10 nF = 30 V/s. Equivalently the rate is Vos / (R C) = 0.003 / (104 × 10-8) = 30 V/s. The sign is set by the offset polarity, and it is the reason a pure integrator without reset cannot be left unattended.

Answer: 30 V/s

(b)

The output starts from 0 V and ramps linearly at 30 V/s, so the time to reach the 13 V rail is t = 13 V / 30 V/s = 0.4333 s. Because an offset-driven ramp is linear in time and no signal is present, this is simple division; with a real signal present the ramp adds to the useful integral and saturation comes even sooner if the signal has a DC component. About 0.43 s means that even a tiny 3 mV offset renders the circuit unusable within half a second, which motivates a DC feedback path. The same estimate shows why integrators in instruments are reset or paired with a DC-restoring loop.

Answer: 0.433 s

(c)

At DC the capacitor is open, so the circuit is an ordinary amplifier of the offset voltage with non-inverting gain 1 + Rf / R. The DC output offset is Vo = Vos (1 + Rf / R) = 3 mV × (1 + 1 MΩ / 10 kΩ) = 3 mV × 101 = 0.303 V. This is a stable value that sits comfortably within the ±13 V swing, unlike the ramp of the pure integrator. The price paid is a DC gain of magnitude Rf / R = 100 for real signals, and the circuit behaves as an integrator only above the corner frequency found next. The 0.303 V offset would be visible on a scope as a baseline shift of about 0.3 V.

Answer: 0.303 V

(d)

The feedback impedance is Rf in parallel with C. The transfer function of the inverting stage is Vo/Vi = -(Rf / R) / (1 + j ω Rf C). The pole is at ω = 1 / (Rf C), so the corner frequency is fc = 1 / (2π Rf C) = 1 / (2π × 106 × 10-8) = 1 / 0.06283 = 15.92 Hz. Above this frequency the response falls at 20 dB per decade, which is integrator behaviour, and below it the gain is flat at Rf / R = 100. The chosen signal frequency of 1 kHz is about 63 times higher than the corner, so the circuit should integrate faithfully there, as the next part confirms numerically.

Answer: 15.9 Hz

(e)

The magnitude of the gain at ω = 2π × 1000 = 6283 rad/s is |G| = (Rf / R) / √(1 + (ω Rf C)²). Here ω Rf C = 6283 × 106 × 10-8 = 62.83, so |G| = 100 / √(1 + 62.83²) = 100 / 62.84 = 1.5913. The peak output is 0.100 V × 1.5913 = 0.1591 V. An ideal integrator would give 0.1 V / (ω R C) = 0.1 / (6283 × 104 × 10-8) = 0.1 / 0.6283 = 0.15915 V. The difference is about 0.013 percent, and the phase differs from 90 degrees by atan(1 / 62.83) = 0.91 degrees. So the 1 MΩ resistor cures the drift and costs almost no accuracy at 1 kHz.

Answer: 0.1591 V

Problem 4 [A5-094] Feedback in amplifiers: gain, bandwidth and stability

A voltage amplifier has an open-loop gain A(s) = A0 / [(1 + s/ω1)(1 + s/ω2)] with A0 = 104, a first pole at f1 = 1 kHz and a second pole at f2 = 5 MHz. It is used in a negative-feedback loop with a purely resistive, frequency-independent feedback fraction β, so the loop gain is βA(s). The designer wants to know how much feedback the amplifier can tolerate before the phase margin becomes unacceptable, given that the second pole is only a factor of 5000 above the first and no third pole is present. Use magnitudes |A(f)| = A0 / [√(1 + (f/f1)²) √(1 + (f/f2)²)] and phase = -atan(f/f1) - atan(f/f2). Phase margin is defined as 180° plus the loop phase at the frequency where |βA| = 1.

  1. (a) For β = 0.1, find the DC closed-loop gain. [3]
  2. (b) For β = 0.1, find the loop crossover frequency at which |βA| = 1 (answer in kHz). [4]
  3. (c) For β = 0.1, find the phase margin in degrees. [4]
  4. (d) Find the smallest closed-loop ideal gain 1/β for which the phase margin is still at least 45 degrees. [5]
  5. (e) For a unity-gain buffer (β = 1), find the phase margin in degrees, and say whether the amplifier is usable as a follower. [4]
(a)

The closed-loop gain of a negative-feedback amplifier is Acl = A0 / (1 + β A0). With A0 = 104 and β = 0.1, β A0 = 1000, so Acl = 104 / 1001 = 9.990. This is very close to the ideal value 1 / β = 10, with an error of about 0.1 percent, which is expected when the loop gain at DC is as high as 1000. The statement that the amplifier has high loop gain at DC says nothing yet about stability, which depends on the phase at the loop crossover frequency, found in the next part by solving the magnitude condition numerically.

Answer: 9.990

(b)

The crossover satisfies 0.1 × 104 / [√(1 + (f/1 kHz)²) √(1 + (f/5 MHz)²)] = 1, that is √(1 + (f/f1)²) √(1 + (f/f2)²) = 1000. Because f is far above f1, the first square root is about f / f1, so a first guess is f ≈ 1000 f1 = 1 MHz. At 1 MHz the second root is √(1 + 0.04) = 1.0198 and the first is 1000.0005, giving a product 1019.8, a little over 1000, so the crossover is slightly lower. Solving numerically gives f = 981.3 kHz. That is below the second pole at 5 MHz, so the second pole contributes only a modest phase lag at crossover, as the next part will show.

Answer: 981 kHz

(c)

At the crossover f = 981.3 kHz, the loop phase is -atan(f/f1) - atan(f/f2). The first term is atan(981.3) = 89.94 degrees. The second term is atan(981.3 kHz / 5 MHz) = atan(0.1963) = 11.10 degrees. The total phase is -(89.94 + 11.10) = -101.04 degrees. The phase margin is 180 - 101.04 = 78.96 degrees, which rounds to 78.95. A phase margin near 79 degrees is very comfortable: the closed-loop step response would show almost no overshoot. This is typical of a modest amount of feedback applied to an amplifier whose second pole is well above the crossover.

Answer: 78.95°

(d)

As β rises towards 1 the crossover moves up toward the second pole and the phase margin falls. Setting the phase margin equal to 45 degrees means the loop phase is -135 degrees, which needs atan(f/f1) + atan(f/f2) = 135 degrees. Since atan(f/f1) is essentially 90 degrees, atan(f/f2) must be about 45 degrees, so the crossover is at about f = f2 = 5 MHz. Solving the magnitude and phase conditions together numerically gives β = 0.7075 with a crossover of 5.002 MHz. The smallest allowed gain is 1/β = 1.413. Any gain lower than 1.41 (more feedback) gives a phase margin below 45 degrees and a ringing step response.

Answer: 1.413

(e)

With β = 1 the crossover is where |A(f)| = 1. Solving 104 / [√(1 + (f/1 kHz)²) √(1 + (f/5 MHz)²)] = 1 numerically gives f = 6.248 MHz. At that frequency the phase is -atan(6248) - atan(6.248 MHz / 5 MHz) = -89.99 - 51.33 = -141.32 degrees. The phase margin is 180 - 141.32 = 38.68 degrees. This is below the 45 degrees guideline found in part d, so the unity-gain follower will show noticeable overshoot of about 25 percent in its step response. The amplifier is marginally usable for slow signals but would normally be compensated, for example by lowering the first pole, before it is used as a follower.

Answer: 38.7°

Problem 5 [A5-095] Comparators, Schmitt triggers and oscillators

An op-amp with output saturation levels of +10.5 V and -10.5 V is used in an inverting Schmitt trigger for a heater thermostat. The signal Vin goes to the inverting input. The non-inverting input node P connects through R1 = 4.7 kΩ to a reference of Vref = +2.00 V and through R2 = 47 kΩ to the op-amp output. The sensor signal carries switching noise, and the designer wants to know how much noise the comparator tolerates. Later the same op-amp is reused as an astable multivibrator: the reference is replaced by ground (so R1 = 4.7 kΩ goes from P to ground, R2 = 47 kΩ from P to the output), the inverting input connects to ground through C = 47 nF and to the output through R = 22 kΩ, and the circuit free-runs between the saturation levels. Take the op-amp as ideal apart from saturation.

  1. (a) Find the upper threshold voltage VTH of the Schmitt trigger (the value of Vin at which the output switches from high to low). [4]
  2. (b) Find the lower threshold voltage VTL. [3]
  3. (c) Find the hysteresis width, and hence the largest peak-to-peak noise on Vin that the circuit can ignore without chattering. [3]
  4. (d) In the astable configuration, find the oscillation period T. [5]
  5. (e) Keeping R, C and R1 unchanged, find the value of R2 (in kΩ) that makes the oscillation frequency exactly 5 kHz. [5]
(a)

The node P voltage is set by superposition of the reference and the output through the divider formed by R1 and R2. With the reference as one source and the output as the other, VP = Vref + (Vo - Vref) × R1 / (R1 + R2). Define β = R1 / (R1 + R2) = 4.7 / 51.7 = 0.09091. When the output is high, Vo = +10.5 V, so VP = 2.00 + 0.09091 × (10.5 - 2.00) = 2.00 + 0.7727 = 2.7727 V. The output stays high until Vin rises to this value, then the comparator flips, so VTH = 2.773 V. The thermostat therefore turns the heater off only when the sensor voltage rises above 2.773 V.

Answer: 2.773 V

(b)

After the output falls to Vo = -10.5 V the node P voltage changes to VP = Vref + (Vo - Vref) β = 2.00 + 0.09091 × (-10.5 - 2.00) = 2.00 - 1.1364 = 0.8636 V. The comparator output stays low until the sensor voltage Vin drops below this value, at which point the output switches high again. So VTL = 0.864 V. Note that the thresholds are not symmetric about zero because the 2.00 V reference shifts the whole window. With symmetric saturation levels the window is centred on Vref (1 - β) = 2.00 × 0.9091 = 1.818 V, and it extends 0.955 V either side of that centre.

Answer: 0.864 V

(c)

The hysteresis is the difference of the two thresholds, VH = VTH - VTL = 2.7727 - 0.8636 = 1.909 V. It equals β × (Vsat+ - Vsat-) = 0.09091 × 21 V = 1.909 V, a quick check. A noise signal superimposed on Vin that stays within the hysteresis window cannot cause both thresholds to be crossed within one noise cycle once the output has switched, so the largest peak-to-peak noise the trigger tolerates is just under 1.909 V. The practical margin should be less than this because the thresholds shift if the supply or the saturation voltage moves, so a designer would target noise below perhaps half the window.

Answer: 1.909 V

(d)

In the astable circuit the non-inverting node threshold is ±β Vsat with β = R1 / (R1 + R2) = 0.09091. The capacitor charges through R toward the output level until it crosses the threshold, then the output flips and the charging reverses. Starting from -β Vsat and charging toward +Vsat, the time to reach +β Vsat is t = R C ln[(Vsat + β Vsat) / (Vsat - β Vsat)] = R C ln[(1 + β) / (1 - β)]. Here (1 + β) / (1 - β) = 1.09091 / 0.90909 = 1.2, so ln 1.2 = 0.18232. The half period is 22 kΩ × 47 nF × 0.18232 = 1.034 ms × 0.18232 = 0.1885 ms, so T = 2 × 0.1885 = 0.377 ms and f = 2.65 kHz.

Answer: 0.377 ms

(e)

The period for 5 kHz is T = 0.2 ms. The astable period is T = 2 R C ln[(1 + β) / (1 - β)] and with β = R1 / (R1 + R2) the ratio simplifies to (1 + β) / (1 - β) = (R2 + 2 R1) / R2. Since 2 R C = 2 × 22 kΩ × 47 nF = 2.068 ms, we need ln[(R2 + 2 R1) / R2] = 0.2 / 2.068 = 0.09671, so (R2 + 2 R1) / R2 = e0.09671 = 1.10154. Then 2 R1 / R2 = 0.10154, giving R2 = 2 × 4.7 kΩ / 0.10154 = 92.57 kΩ. A smaller β means a smaller threshold so the capacitor swings less and the oscillation is faster, which is why R2 had to rise from 47 kΩ.

Answer: 92.6 kΩ

A5 Practice Paper 20

Problem 1 [A5-096] Power amplifiers, efficiency and heat dissipation

A class AB push-pull audio output stage drives an 8 Ω loudspeaker from supplies of +24 V and -24 V. The two output transistors are identical, and the stage is biased with a quiescent current of Iq = 20 mA in each device. Treat the stage as an ideal class B stage plus the quiescent power, with a sinusoidal output and no crossover distortion and ignoring saturation voltages. The supply current of an ideal class B stage at output peak voltage Vp averaged over a cycle is 2 Vp / (π RL) from each pair, so the total supply power is 2 Vcc Vp / (π RL) plus 2 Vcc Iq for the biasing. At a typical listening level the output peak is Vp = 20 V. Each transistor has Tj,max = 150 °C and θJC = 1.5 °C/W. The case is mounted to the heatsink with an insulator of θCS = 0.5 °C/W, and the enclosure ambient is 40 °C.

  1. (a) Find the average power delivered to the load at Vp = 20 V. [3]
  2. (b) Find the efficiency of the stage at Vp = 20 V including the quiescent power. [4]
  3. (c) Find the power dissipated in each output transistor at Vp = 20 V. [3]
  4. (d) Find the worst-case dissipation per transistor over all output amplitudes, and decide whether it occurs at full power. [5]
  5. (e) The designer limits the junction to 125 °C for reliability. Find the largest allowable heatsink-to-ambient thermal resistance θSA per transistor, assuming each transistor has its own heatsink and uses the worst-case dissipation. [5]
(a)

For a sinusoidal output, the load power is Pout = Vp² / (2 RL). With Vp = 20 V and RL = 8 Ω, Pout = 400 / 16 = 25.0 W. This is the average power over one cycle, because the RMS voltage is Vp / √2 = 14.14 V and Pout = Vrms² / RL = 200 / 8 = 25 W. The result is below the maximum available from these supplies: with a peak limited to about 24 V by the rails, the maximum is 24² / 16 = 36 W, so the stage is working at about 70 percent of its full-power capability when producing 25 W.

Answer: 25.0 W

(b)

The supply power is Ps = 2 Vcc Vp / (π RL) + 2 Vcc Iq. Substituting, 2 × 24 × 20 / (π × 8) = 960 / 25.133 = 38.20 W. The quiescent term is 2 × 24 × 0.020 = 0.96 W. So Ps = 38.20 + 0.96 = 39.16 W. The efficiency is η = Pout / Ps = 25.0 / 39.16 = 0.6385, which is 63.8 percent. For comparison, an ideal class B stage at the same level would reach 25.0 / 38.20 = 65.4 percent, so the quiescent bias costs only about 1.6 percentage points here. Class A stage would be limited to a maximum of 25 percent, which is why class AB is used.

Answer: 63.8 %

(c)

The total power lost in the two transistors is the difference between the supply power and the load power: Pd,total = Ps - Pout = 39.16 - 25.0 = 14.16 W. The two devices are identical and share the loss equally because the load current alternates between them, so each dissipates Pd = 14.16 / 2 = 7.08 W. Note that this includes the 0.48 W per device of quiescent dissipation. The figure is a time average, and the instantaneous power can peak much higher, but the junction responds to the average because the thermal time constants are far longer than the audio period.

Answer: 7.08 W

(d)

The total dissipation as a function of Vp is Pd(Vp) = 2 Vcc Vp / (π RL) - Vp² / (2 RL) + 2 Vcc Iq. Differentiating with respect to Vp and setting to zero gives 2 Vcc / (π RL) = Vp / RL, so Vp = 2 Vcc / π = 15.28 V. The quiescent term does not depend on Vp so it does not change the location. The maximum is Pd,max = 2 Vcc² / (π² RL) + 2 Vcc Iq = 1152 / 78.96 + 0.96 = 14.59 + 0.96 = 15.55 W, so each device sees 7.78 W. This occurs at 15.28 V peak, about 14.6 W of load power, not at full power, so a designer must size the heatsink for a moderate listening level, not for maximum volume.

Answer: 7.78 W

(e)

Each device has its own heatsink, so the thermal path is junction to case, case to sink and sink to ambient in series. The temperature rise allowed is Tj - Ta = 125 - 40 = 85 °C. With the worst-case dissipation of 7.775 W, the total thermal resistance must be at most θJA = 85 / 7.775 = 10.93 °C/W. Subtracting the known parts gives θSA = θJA - θJC - θCS = 10.93 - 1.5 - 0.5 = 8.93 °C/W. A heatsink with a rating of 8 °C/W or lower would be selected. Using the 150 °C limit instead would allow 12.2 °C/W, which shows how much margin the derating buys.

Answer: 8.93 °C/W

Problem 2 [A5-097] BJT and MOSFET as switches

A microcontroller output at 3.3 V must switch a 24 V relay coil of resistance 160 Ω. The designer first considers an NPN transistor with a guaranteed minimum β of 100, VBE(sat) = 0.75 V and VCE(sat) = 0.20 V, driven from the 3.3 V pin through a base resistor RB, with the coil in the collector. To make sure the transistor is firmly saturated across the production range, the base drive is set to three times the minimum needed (overdrive factor 3). The pin can supply at most 8 mA. A second option is a logic-level n-channel MOSFET with RDS(on) = 0.50 Ω at VGS = 3.3 V, with its source grounded, the coil in the drain, and the gate driven directly from the pin. Assume the supply is 24 V in both cases and ignore the flyback diode and switching losses.

  1. (a) Find the collector current of the BJT when saturated. [3]
  2. (b) Find the base current needed with the overdrive factor of 3 applied to the minimum base current for β = 100. [3]
  3. (c) Find the base resistor RB. [4]
  4. (d) Find the total power dissipated in the BJT, including the base-emitter junction. [4]
  5. (e) Find the conduction loss in the MOSFET alternative, and state by what factor it is below the BJT loss of part d. [6]
(a)

When the transistor is saturated, the voltage across the coil is the supply less the saturation voltage: 24 - 0.20 = 23.8 V. The coil is a plain resistance of 160 Ω, so the collector current is Ic = 23.8 / 160 = 0.14875 A = 148.75 mA. This current is fixed by the external circuit, not by the transistor, which is what saturation means: the transistor is no longer controlling the current, the load resistance is. The coil current stays almost the same as it would be with a perfect switch, which would give 24 / 160 = 150 mA, so the saturation drop costs only about 0.8 percent.

Answer: 148.75 mA

(b)

The minimum base current to hold saturation with the worst-case β is IB,min = Ic / β = 148.75 mA / 100 = 1.4875 mA. With the overdrive factor of 3, the design base current is IB = 3 × 1.4875 = 4.4625 mA. This corresponds to a forced β of 148.75 / 4.4625 = 33.3, which is far below the guaranteed 100, so saturation holds even for the weakest devices and at low temperature. The pin limit is 8 mA, so the design current of 4.46 mA is within the capability of the pin, using about 56 percent of the allowed drive.

Answer: 4.46 mA

(c)

The base resistor sees the pin voltage minus the base-emitter drop. Therefore RB = (3.3 - 0.75) / IB = 2.55 V / 4.4625 mA = 571.4 Ω. A standard value of 560 Ω would give IB = 4.55 mA and a slightly larger overdrive, which is acceptable, while 620 Ω would give 4.1 mA, still above the minimum of 1.49 mA by a factor of 2.8. The pin also needs to supply this current through its own output resistance, so in practice the pin voltage droops slightly under load, which is another reason to keep generous margin over the minimum base current.

Answer: 571 Ω

(d)

The power in the BJT has a collector part and a base part: P = Ic VCE(sat) + IB VBE(sat). The collector part is 0.14875 A × 0.20 V = 29.75 mW. The base part is 4.4625 mA × 0.75 V = 3.347 mW. Their sum is 29.75 + 3.35 = 33.10 mW. The coil dissipates 23.8 V × 0.14875 A = 3.54 W, so the transistor loss is under one percent of the load power. The extra loss that is not in the transistor is the base resistor's, IB² RB = 11.4 mW, plus the pin's own current. The designer would accept this loss for a signal relay.

Answer: 33.1 mW

(e)

The MOSFET behaves as a 0.50 Ω resistance in series with the coil, so the drain current is Id = 24 / (160 + 0.50) = 0.14953 A. The conduction loss is Id² RDS(on) = 0.14953² × 0.50 = 0.022360 × 0.50 = 11.18 mW. Compared with the BJT total of 33.1 mW, the MOSFET loses about one third as much, a factor of 33.1 / 11.18 = 2.96. Besides, the MOSFET needs no steady gate current, so the pin drives nothing but the gate capacitance during transitions, and no base resistor is needed. The cost is that the gate threshold must be well below 3.3 V, so a logic-level part must be chosen with care.

Answer: 11.18 mW

Problem 3 [A5-098] CMOS inverter and logic gate design

A 1.8 V CMOS process has Vtn = 0.45 V and Vtp = -0.45 V. The process transconductance parameters are kn' = μnCox = 270 µA/V² and kp' = μpCox = 90 µA/V². An inverter uses an nMOS of W/L = 4 and a pMOS of W/L = 8. Use the long-channel square law, ignore channel-length modulation and body effect, and define the switching threshold VM as the input voltage at which both transistors are in saturation and carry equal current. In saturation each device carries I = (k'/2)(W/L)(VGS - |Vt|)². The designer must re-size the inverter so that VM is 0.90 V and then build a two-input NAND gate from the same unit sizes, giving the NAND the same worst-case drive strength as the re-sized inverter.

  1. (a) Find the switching threshold VM of the original inverter (W/L = 4 for nMOS, 8 for pMOS). [4]
  2. (b) Find the pMOS W/L (keeping the nMOS W/L = 4) that makes VM = 0.90 V. [5]
  3. (c) For the NAND2 gate, each series nMOS is doubled so the pull-down path matches the inverter's nMOS strength of W/L = 4, and each parallel pMOS keeps W/L = 12. Find the total W/L of the four transistors of the NAND2. [4]
  4. (d) For the re-sized inverter (nMOS 4, pMOS 12), find the peak short-circuit current when Vin = VM. [4]
  5. (e) Explain, in terms of mobility, why the pMOS must be wider than the nMOS for a symmetric inverter, and say what happens to VM if the pMOS is made narrower. [3]
(a)

Equating the saturation currents at VM: kn (VM - Vtn)² = kp (VDD - VM - |Vtp|)², where kn = kn' (W/L)n = 270 µA/V² × 4 = 1.08 mA/V² and kp = 90 µA/V² × 8 = 0.72 mA/V². Taking square roots gives √kn (VM - Vtn) = √kp (VDD - |Vtp| - VM). With r = √(kp / kn) = √(0.6667) = 0.8165, the solution is VM = (Vtn + r (VDD - |Vtp|)) / (1 + r) = (0.45 + 0.8165 × 1.35) / 1.8165 = 1.5523 / 1.8165 = 0.8545 V. This is below VDD / 2 = 0.9 V because the pMOS is weaker than the nMOS, so the input needs to be lower for the two currents to balance.

Answer: 0.855 V

(b)

From the VM formula, solving for r gives r = (VM - Vtn) / (VDD - |Vtp| - VM). Substituting VM = 0.90 V: r = (0.90 - 0.45) / (1.8 - 0.45 - 0.90) = 0.45 / 0.45 = 1.0. Since r = √(kp / kn), kp must equal kn. So kp' (W/L)p = kn' (W/L)n, giving (W/L)p = (kn' / kp') (W/L)n = (270 / 90) × 4 = 12. The result follows from the 3:1 mobility ratio: because holes are three times less mobile than electrons in this process, the pMOS width must be three times the nMOS width for a symmetric threshold. This makes the pull-up and pull-down drive equal.

Answer: 12

(c)

In a two-input NAND, the two nMOS devices are in series, so their resistances add. To keep the worst-case pull-down resistance equal to that of the inverter's single nMOS with W/L = 4, each series device must have twice the conductance, so W/L = 8. The two pMOS devices are in parallel, and the worst case is one pMOS conducting alone, so each must match the inverter's pMOS with W/L = 12. The total is 8 + 8 + 12 + 12 = 40, compared with 4 + 12 = 16 for the inverter. The NAND2 therefore uses 2.5 times the transistor width and area, which is the cost of matching worst-case drive.

Answer: 40

(d)

At Vin = VM = 0.90 V both transistors are in saturation and conduct the same current, so we can use the nMOS: I = (kn' / 2)(W/L)n (VGS - Vtn)² = (270 µA/V² / 2) × 4 × (0.90 - 0.45)² = 135 × 4 × 0.2025 µA = 109.35 µA. The pMOS gives the same value, since r = 1: (90 / 2) × 12 × (1.8 - 0.90 - 0.45)² = 45 × 12 × 0.2025 = 109.35 µA. This is the maximum crowbar current that flows from supply to ground during a transition. It lasts only briefly, but it explains why slow input edges raise dynamic power.

Answer: 109 µA

(e)

Electrons are more mobile than holes in silicon, which is why kn' is three times kp' here. For equal drive current the pMOS needs three times the W/L of the nMOS, as found in part b. If the pMOS were narrower, its conductance would drop, so in order to carry the same current as the nMOS it would need a larger overdrive. That requires VIN to be lower, which pulls VM below VDD / 2, as seen in part a where the original ratio gave 0.855 V. A lower VM raises the high-side noise margin (the input must fall further before the output switches) and lowers the low-side noise margin. Rise and fall delays also become unequal.

Answer: Hole mobility is lower than electron mobility, so a wider pMOS is needed; a narrower pMOS lowers VM.

Problem 4 [A5-099] Propagation delay and power in CMOS

A CMOS logic path consists of 12 identical inverters in series. Each inverter drives a total load capacitance CL = 50 fF, and its pull-up and pull-down networks have equivalent resistances Rn = Rp = 8 kΩ at the supply VDD = 1.2 V. Use the first-order RC model in which each propagation delay is 0.69 Req CL. The clock period must be at least 25 percent longer than the path delay to allow for skew and setup. The chip runs at 200 MHz, and the average switching activity of each node is α = 0.1. The designer considers lowering the supply to 0.9 V to save power, with the equivalent resistance scaling as VDD / (VDD - Vt)1.3, where Vt = 0.35 V (alpha-power law model). Assume load capacitance and Vt do not change.

  1. (a) Find the propagation delay of one inverter at 1.2 V. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum clock frequency of the 12-stage path at 1.2 V, including the 25 percent margin. [4]
  3. (c) Find the average dynamic power of one inverter at 200 MHz with α = 0.1 and VDD = 1.2 V. [3]
  4. (d) Find the propagation delay of one inverter at VDD = 0.9 V using the alpha-power scaling. [5]
  5. (e) Find the maximum clock frequency at 0.9 V with the same margin, and state in words whether the 200 MHz target is still met. [4]
(a)

With the first-order RC model, each transition is a charge or discharge of CL through an equivalent resistance, and the delay to the 50 percent point is tp = 0.69 Req CL. Substituting, tp = 0.69 × 8000 × 50 × 10-15 = 0.69 × 4 × 10-10 = 2.76 × 10-10 s = 276 ps. Because Rn and Rp are equal, the rising and falling delays are the same and the inverter has a single delay value. This estimate ignores the input slope and the self-loading of the inverter's own diffusion capacitance, which is assumed to be part of the 50 fF given in the statement.

Answer: 276 ps

(b)

The path delay is 12 × 276 ps = 3.312 ns. With a 25 percent margin the minimum clock period is 1.25 × 3.312 ns = 4.14 ns. The maximum clock frequency is the reciprocal, fmax = 1 / 4.14 ns = 241.5 MHz. This exceeds the 200 MHz target by 21 percent, so the path meets timing with room to spare at the nominal supply. The margin is what a designer would use to trade for lower power, which is the subject of the supply-reduction question that follows in the later parts of this problem.

Answer: 241.5 MHz

(c)

The average dynamic power of a CMOS node is P = α CL VDD² f. Substituting, P = 0.1 × 50 × 10-15 F × 1.44 V² × 2 × 108 Hz. First CL VDD² = 50 × 10-15 × 1.44 = 7.2 × 10-14 J. Multiplying by f gives 7.2 × 10-14 × 2 × 108 = 1.44 × 10-5 W, and then by α = 0.1 gives 1.44 × 10-6 W = 1.44 µW. For a block with a million such nodes the total would be 1.44 W, which shows why supply scaling is attractive: power falls with the square of the supply voltage.

Answer: 1.44 µW

(d)

The equivalent resistance scales as R ∝ VDD / (VDD - Vt)1.3. At 1.2 V the factor is 1.2 / (0.85)1.3 = 1.2 / 0.8095 = 1.4824. At 0.9 V it is 0.9 / (0.55)1.3 = 0.9 / 0.4597 = 1.9578. The ratio is 1.9578 / 1.4824 = 1.3208. Since CL is unchanged, the delay scales by the same ratio: tp = 276 ps × 1.3208 = 364.5 ps. The delay rises by 32 percent for a 25 percent reduction in supply, because the overdrive voltage falls from 0.85 V to 0.55 V, a 35 percent drop, so the device current is reduced by more than the simple supply ratio.

Answer: 364.5 ps

(e)

The path delay at 0.9 V is 12 × 364.5 ps = 4.374 ns, and with the 25 percent margin the clock period must be at least 5.468 ns, so fmax = 1 / 5.468 ns = 182.9 MHz. This is below the 200 MHz target, so the target is no longer met. The dynamic power would fall by the ratio (0.9 / 1.2)² = 0.5625, a 44 percent saving, but only at a lower clock. If the saving is wanted at 200 MHz the designer must shorten the path, widen devices to lower Req, or accept a reduced margin of about 14 percent instead of 25 percent. Voltage scaling therefore trades speed directly for energy.

Answer: 182.9 MHz

Problem 5 [A5-100] Amplifier design to meet a specification, comparing topologies

A microphone preamplifier must deliver a voltage gain from source emf to load of at least 70 in magnitude. The source is a 5 kΩ resistance in series with the signal emf, and the load is 10 kΩ. All transistors have β = 150, VT = 25 mV, a 12 V supply and negligible output resistance. Bias networks are to be ignored in the small-signal analysis, and the emitters are fully bypassed. Option A is a single common-emitter stage biased at Ic = 1 mA with collector resistor RC = 4.7 kΩ, driving the 10 kΩ load directly. Option B keeps that stage and adds an emitter follower Q2 biased at Ic2 = 2 mA with emitter resistor RE = 2.2 kΩ in parallel with the 10 kΩ load, the CE stage driving the base of Q2. Compare the two designs.

  1. (a) Find the overall gain magnitude |vo / vs| of Option A with RC = 4.7 kΩ. [3]
  2. (b) Find the input resistance of the emitter follower Q2 in Option B. [4]
  3. (c) Find the overall gain magnitude of Option B. [5]
  4. (d) Option A could instead be rescued by raising RC. Find the RC that gives exactly |vo / vs| = 70 with the 10 kΩ load, and state the supply-current saving relative to Option B. [4]
  5. (e) The load is replaced by a 100 Ω headphone. Explain which option you would now choose and why, using the expected behaviour of each. [4]
(a)

For the CE stage at Ic = 1 mA, gm = 1 mA / 25 mV = 40 mS and rπ = β / gm = 150 / 40 mS = 3.75 kΩ. The source divides with the input resistance: vπ / vs = rπ / (Rs + rπ) = 3.75 / 8.75 = 0.4286. The stage gain is -gm (RC ∥ RL) = -40 mS × (4.7 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ) = -40 mS × 3.197 kΩ = -127.9. The overall gain is -127.9 × 0.4286 = -54.8, so the magnitude is 54.8. This is only 78 percent of the required 70, so Option A with RC = 4.7 kΩ fails the specification.

Answer: 54.8

(b)

For Q2 at Ic2 = 2 mA, gm2 = 2 mA / 25 mV = 80 mS, so rπ2 = 150 / 80 mS = 1.875 kΩ. The emitter load is RE ∥ RL = 2.2 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ = 1.803 kΩ. The input resistance of an emitter follower looking into the base is Rin2 = rπ2 + (β + 1)(RE ∥ RL) = 1.875 kΩ + 151 × 1.803 kΩ = 1.875 + 272.3 = 274.2 kΩ. This large value is the benefit of the follower: it presents almost no load to the CE stage, so the collector load of the CE stage is nearly just RC. The follower reflects its load multiplied by β + 1 to its input.

Answer: 274 kΩ

(c)

The CE stage now sees a load of RC ∥ Rin2 = 4.7 kΩ ∥ 274.2 kΩ = 4.621 kΩ, so its gain is -gm RLeff = -40 mS × 4.621 kΩ = -184.8. The follower gain is (β + 1)(RE ∥ RL) / Rin2 = 272.3 / 274.2 = 0.9932. The source divider is unchanged at 0.4286. The overall gain is -184.8 × 0.9932 × 0.4286 = -78.7. The magnitude is 78.7, which meets the specification of 70 with an 12 percent margin. The follower lifted the gain from 54.8 to 78.7 by removing the loading of the 10 kΩ load on the CE stage.

Answer: 78.7

(d)

The required stage gain is 70 / 0.4286 = 163.3, so gm (RC ∥ RL) = 163.3, giving RC ∥ RL = 163.3 / 40 mS = 4.083 kΩ. Then 1 / RC = 1 / 4.083 kΩ - 1 / 10 kΩ = 0.24490 mS - 0.1 mS = 0.14490 mS, so RC = 6.90 kΩ. The DC drop across RC is 1 mA × 6.9 kΩ = 6.9 V, leaving 5.1 V at the collector, enough headroom for a small signal. Option A then uses only 1 mA from the 12 V supply, 12 mW, against 3 mA, 36 mW, for Option B, a saving of 24 mW.

Answer: 6.90 kΩ

(e)

With a 100 Ω load, Option A's collector resistor of several kΩ would be in parallel with 100 Ω, so the stage gain would fall to about 40 mS × 97 Ω = 3.9, and the overall gain to under 2, a collapse of over 95 percent. Option B's emitter follower has an output resistance of about re2 = 12.5 Ω plus the reflected source resistance divided by β + 1, which is a few tens of ohms, so it can deliver most of its voltage into 100 Ω, although the follower's 2 mA bias would have to rise because the emitter load RE ∥ 100 Ω is only 96 Ω, a peak current of tens of milliamps. Option B is the right topology because it decouples the high-gain stage from the heavy load.

Answer: Option B: the follower has low output resistance so it can drive 100 Ω; Option A with RC of kΩ would lose almost all gain.

Exam A6: Power Systems and Machines

A6 Practice Paper 1

Problem 1 [A6-001] Magnetic circuits, flux, reluctance and inductance

A solenoid-operated latch uses a closed rectangular iron core with one narrow air gap cut across the limb that carries the coil. The core has a uniform cross-section of 9.0 cm² and a mean magnetic path length of 0.42 m in iron. The iron has a constant relative permeability of 2500 (treat it as linear, no saturation). The air gap is 1.5 mm long. Neglect fringing and leakage, so the gap area equals the core area. The coil has 400 turns and carries a steady direct current of 2.0 A. Use μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. The candidate should treat the magnetic circuit as a series circuit of two reluctances driven by the coil's magnetomotive force.

  1. (a) Calculate the reluctance of the iron path and of the air gap, and give the total reluctance of the circuit in A·turns per Wb (answer: total). [5]
  2. (b) Find the flux in the core and the flux density in the air gap. Give the flux in mWb. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the self-inductance of the coil. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the energy stored in the air gap alone, in joules, and state what fraction of the total stored energy this represents (give the energy). [5]
(a)

The iron reluctance is Rc = lc/(μr μ0 A). With lc = 0.42 m, μr = 2500, μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ and A = 9.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², Rc = 0.42/(2500 × 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ × 9.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.485 × 10⁵ A·t/Wb. The gap reluctance is Rg = lg/(μ0 A) = 1.5 × 10⁻³/(1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ × 9.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.326 × 10⁶ A·t/Wb. The two reluctances are in series because the same flux crosses both, so they add: Rt = 1.485 × 10⁵ + 1.326 × 10⁶ = 1.475 × 10⁶ A·t/Wb. Note the gap is only 0.36 percent of the total path length yet carries about 90 percent of the reluctance, which is why a small gap dominates the design.

Answer: 1.475 × 10⁶ A·t/Wb

(b)

The magnetomotive force is F = NI = 400 × 2.0 = 800 A·t. By the magnetic Ohm's law, φ = F/Rt = 800/1.4748 × 10⁶ = 5.424 × 10⁻⁴ Wb = 0.542 mWb. The same flux passes through the gap, and with no fringing the gap flux density is Bg = φ/A = 5.424 × 10⁻⁴/9.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.603 T. This is well below the saturation knee of ordinary silicon steel (about 1.5 T), so the assumption of constant permeability is reasonable for this operating point. The check on the iron: Fc = φ Rc = 80.6 A·t, only about 10 percent of the coil mmf, with the remaining 719 A·t dropped across the air gap.

Answer: 0.542 mWb

(c)

Flux linkage is λ = Nφ = 400 × 5.424 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.2170 Wb·t. Inductance is the flux linkage per ampere, L = λ/I = 0.2170/2.0 = 0.1085 H. The same result follows from L = N²/Rt = 400²/1.4748 × 10⁶ = 0.1085 H, which confirms the arithmetic. Because the circuit is linear, L does not depend on current. If the gap were closed, the inductance would rise to N²/Rc = 1.08 H, almost ten times larger, which shows why the latch coil draws a much higher inductance once the armature seats and the gap vanishes.

Answer: 0.1085 H

(d)

Energy stored in a linear reluctance carrying flux φ is W = ½ R φ². For the air gap, Wg = ½ × 1.3263 × 10⁶ × (5.424 × 10⁻⁴)² = 0.195 J. The iron holds ½ × 1.485 × 10⁵ × (5.424 × 10⁻⁴)² = 0.0218 J. The total is 0.217 J, equal to ½ L I² = ½ × 0.1085 × 4.0 = 0.217 J, which confirms the result. The gap therefore holds about 90 percent of the stored energy, even though it occupies a tiny volume. This is the energy that is converted to mechanical work when the armature closes the gap.

Answer: 0.195 J

Problem 2 [A6-002] Ferromagnetic cores, losses and saturation

A laminated silicon-steel core is tested on a single-phase winding of 220 turns. The core stack has an effective iron cross-section of 0.0150 m². The test supply is sinusoidal, and the core loss is measured at constant peak flux density Bm. At 60 Hz the loss is 41.0 W, and at 40 Hz with the same peak flux density the loss is 25.0 W. Assume that hysteresis loss varies as f Bm² and eddy-current loss as f² Bm², with the same Bm exponent for both, and that the two coefficients are independent of frequency over this range. Neglect winding resistance and leakage so the applied rms voltage equals the induced emf. The 60 Hz rating of the core is 240 V rms. Use the emf relation E = 4.44 f N Bm A.

  1. (a) Separate the 60 Hz core loss into its hysteresis and eddy-current components. Give the hysteresis component. [5]
  2. (b) Give the eddy-current loss at 60 Hz. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the peak flux density in the core when 240 V at 60 Hz is applied. [4]
  4. (d) The same core is connected to a 50 Hz supply, again at 240 V rms. Calculate the new peak flux density. [3]
  5. (e) Calculate the core loss at 240 V and 50 Hz, and comment on whether the iron would approach saturation. [5]
(a)

Write the loss as P = kh f + ke f² at constant Bm, where kh and ke absorb the Bm² factor. At 60 Hz: 60 kh + 3600 ke = 41.0. At 40 Hz: 40 kh + 1600 ke = 25.0.
