Multiply the second equation by 1.5 to get 60 kh + 2400 ke = 37.5. Subtracting from the first gives 1200 ke = 3.5, so ke = 2.917 × 10⁻³ W/Hz². Then kh = (25.0 − 1600 × 2.917 × 10⁻³)/40 = (25.0 − 4.667)/40 = 0.5083 W/Hz. The hysteresis loss at 60 Hz is Ph = kh × 60 = 30.5 W. This separation works because the two mechanisms scale differently with frequency, which is exactly what two readings at the same flux density expose.

Answer: 30.5 W

(b)

The eddy-current loss at 60 Hz is Pe = ke f² = 2.917 × 10⁻³ × 3600 = 10.5 W. As a check, the sum is 30.5 + 10.5 = 41.0 W, which equals the measured 60 Hz loss. Hysteresis is therefore about 74 percent of the total and eddy currents about 26 percent. The lamination thickness controls ke, because eddy loss grows with the square of thickness, so thinner laminations or higher resistivity steel reduce this component, while the choice of steel grade controls the hysteresis term. The fact that hysteresis dominates at power frequency is typical of good silicon steel.

Answer: 10.5 W

(c)

The emf relation E = 4.44 f N Bm A gives Bm = E/(4.44 f N A). Substituting E = 240 V, f = 60 Hz, N = 220 and A = 0.0150 m²: Bm = 240/(4.44 × 60 × 220 × 0.0150) = 240/879.1 = 0.2730 T. The factor 4.44 equals 2π/√2 and converts the rms voltage of a sinusoidal flux wave into its peak value. This operating flux density is low compared with the knee of silicon steel near 1.5 T, so the core is lightly loaded and the magnetising current is small at the rated condition.

Answer: 0.273 T

(d)

Flux density is inversely proportional to frequency at fixed voltage, because the induced emf is proportional to f Bm. Hence Bm(50) = Bm(60) × 60/50 = 0.2730 × 1.2 = 0.3276 T. Directly, Bm = 240/(4.44 × 50 × 220 × 0.0150) = 240/732.6 = 0.3276 T. A 17 percent drop in frequency at constant voltage therefore raises the flux by 20 percent. This is the reason transformers and motors must be derated or their voltage reduced in proportion when run on a lower frequency supply: the volts-per-hertz ratio sets the flux level.

Answer: 0.328 T

(e)

At 240 V and 50 Hz the flux density is 1.2 times higher. Hysteresis loss varies as f Bm², so Ph = kh × 50 × 1.2² = 0.5083 × 50 × 1.44 = 36.6 W. Eddy-current loss varies as f² Bm² = (f Bm)², and since the product f Bm is fixed by the voltage, Pe stays at 10.5 W. The total core loss is 36.6 + 10.5 = 47.1 W, which is 15 percent more than at 60 Hz. At 0.328 T the iron is still far below the saturation knee of about 1.5 T, so there is no saturation risk, but the extra hysteresis loss raises core heating and the temperature rise should be checked.

Answer: 47.1 W

Problem 3 [A6-003] Single-phase transformer equivalent circuit and tests

A 50 kVA, 2400/240 V, 60 Hz distribution transformer was tested in the factory. In the open-circuit test the low-voltage winding was energised at its rated 240 V with the high-voltage winding open. The instruments read 5.40 A and 186 W on the low-voltage side. In the short-circuit test the low-voltage winding was shorted and the high-voltage winding was supplied at reduced voltage until rated current flowed. The readings on the high-voltage side were 62.0 V and 617 W. Use the approximate equivalent circuit, with the shunt branch (a resistance Rc in parallel with a reactance Xm) placed at the low-voltage terminals and the series branch (Req and Xeq) referred to the high-voltage side. Treat the test readings as exact and neglect the small copper loss in the open-circuit test.

  1. (a) Calculate the core-loss resistance Rc referred to the low-voltage side. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the magnetising reactance Xm referred to the low-voltage side. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the equivalent series resistance Req referred to the high-voltage side. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the equivalent series reactance Xeq referred to the high-voltage side. [4]
  5. (e) Express the equivalent impedance in per unit on the transformer's own rating. [4]
(a)

In the open-circuit test, all the power input is core loss, so Rc = V²/Poc = 240²/186 = 57 600/186 = 309.7 Ω. The conductance is Gc = 1/Rc = Poc/V² = 3.229 × 10⁻³ S. This value is referred to the 240 V side because that is where the instruments were connected, so no turns-ratio correction is needed. The power factor of the test is Poc/(V Ioc) = 186/(240 × 5.40) = 0.1435, which is low, confirming that most of the no-load current is magnetising current. The assumption that the winding copper loss is negligible at no load is acceptable because the 5.4 A is only about 2.6 percent of the rated low-voltage current of 208.3 A, so the copper loss at 5.4 A is tiny.

Answer: 309.7 Ω

(b)

The magnitude of the excitation admittance is Y = Ioc/V = 5.40/240 = 0.02250 S. The susceptance follows from the admittance triangle, Bm = √(Y² − Gc²) = √(0.02250² − 0.003229²) = √(5.0625 × 10⁻⁴ − 1.043 × 10⁻⁵) = 0.02227 S. The magnetising reactance is Xm = 1/Bm = 1/0.02227 = 44.9 Ω. This is also referred to the low-voltage side. The magnetising current is Iφ = V/Xm = 5.35 A and the core-loss current is Ic = 0.775 A; they combine at right angles to give 5.40 A, consistent with the measurement.

Answer: 44.9 Ω

(c)

The rated high-voltage current is I = S/V = 50 000/2400 = 20.83 A, which is the current flowing in the short-circuit test. The test power is entirely copper loss in the two windings, so Req = Psc/I² = 617/20.83² = 617/434.0 = 1.422 Ω referred to the high-voltage side. The core loss during this test is negligible because the applied voltage is only 62 V, about 2.6 percent of rated, and core loss varies approximately with the square of voltage. The full-load copper loss is therefore 617 W, which is 1.23 percent of the rating.

Answer: 1.422 Ω

(d)

The magnitude of the equivalent impedance is Zeq = Vsc/Isc = 62.0/20.83 = 2.976 Ω. The reactance follows from the impedance triangle: Xeq = √(Zeq² − Req²) = √(2.976² − 1.4216²) = √(8.857 − 2.021) = √6.836 = 2.615 Ω. The reactance is the leakage reactance of the two windings combined and referred to the high-voltage side. It exceeds the resistance by a ratio of 1.84, which is typical of a distribution transformer of this size, where leakage flux dominates the series impedance and so limits the fault current.

Answer: 2.615 Ω

(e)

The base impedance on the high-voltage side is Zbase = V²/S = 2400²/50 000 = 115.2 Ω. The per-unit equivalent impedance is Zeq,pu = 2.976/115.2 = 0.02583 pu, or 2.58 percent. This matches the short-circuit voltage ratio, 62.0/2400 = 0.02583, because the test was run at rated current. The same per-unit value is obtained on the low-voltage side, since per-unit impedance is unchanged by referral. A value near 2.6 percent means the unit would pass a maximum steady short-circuit current of about 1/0.02583 = 38.7 times rated current if supplied from an infinite source.

Answer: 0.0258 pu

Problem 4 [A6-004] Transformer regulation and efficiency

A 25 kVA, 2400/240 V, 60 Hz single-phase transformer supplies a workshop. Its equivalent series impedance referred to the 2400 V winding is Req = 1.90 Ω and Xeq = 3.40 Ω. The core loss is constant at 115 W at rated voltage. Use the approximate equivalent circuit with the shunt branch connected at the input terminals, so the core loss does not depend on load. Voltage regulation is defined as the rise in secondary terminal voltage, expressed as a fraction of rated voltage, when a load at rated terminal voltage is removed with the primary voltage held constant. In all load cases the secondary terminal voltage is rated 240 V. Work with the high-voltage side as the reference.

  1. (a) Calculate the rated high-voltage current. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the percentage voltage regulation at full load, 0.80 power factor lagging. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the percentage voltage regulation at full load, 0.80 power factor leading. [4]
  4. (d) Find the fraction of full load at which the efficiency is a maximum. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the efficiency at 75 percent of full load and 0.90 power factor lagging. [4]
(a)

The rated high-voltage current is the kVA rating divided by the rated high-voltage voltage: I = 25 000/2400 = 10.42 A. It is the reference current used for the full-load calculations below, and I take the current phasor as the reference for impedance drops. The corresponding rated low-voltage current is 25 000/240 = 104.2 A, giving a turns ratio of 10. The full-load copper loss follows later as I² Req = 10.42² × 1.90 = 206.2 W, which is needed for the efficiency questions. All following voltages are referred to the 2400 V side, where the series impedance is quoted.

Answer: 10.42 A

(b)

Take the load voltage referred to the high side as V2 = 2400∠0° V. At 0.80 lagging the current is I = 10.417∠−36.87° A. The primary voltage is V1 = V2 + I(Req + jXeq). I Zeq = 10.417∠−36.87° × (1.90 + j3.40) = 10.417∠−36.87° × 3.895∠60.8° = 40.57∠23.9° = 37.1 + j16.4 V. So V1 = 2437.1 + j16.4, |V1| = 2437.1 V. Regulation = (2437.1 − 2400)/2400 = 1.547 percent. With a lagging load the resistive and reactive drops both add to the output voltage, so the no-load voltage is above the loaded value.

Answer: 1.547 %

(c)

For 0.80 leading the current is I = 10.417∠+36.87° A. Then I Zeq = 10.417∠36.87° × 3.895∠60.8° = 40.57∠97.7° = −5.4 + j40.2 V. The primary voltage is V1 = 2400 − 5.4 + j40.2 = 2394.6 + j40.2, with magnitude √(2394.6² + 40.2²) = 2394.9 V. Regulation = (2394.9 − 2400)/2400 = −0.212 percent. The negative sign means that the secondary voltage falls when the leading load is removed. This is the Ferranti-type effect of capacitive loading, in which the reactive drop is in antiphase with the supply voltage and reduces the required input.

Answer: -0.212 %

(d)

With core loss Pc constant and copper loss Pcu = x² I² Req at a load fraction x, the efficiency is maximum when the variable loss equals the fixed loss: x² Pcu,fl = Pc. The full-load copper loss is 10.417² × 1.90 = 206.2 W. Therefore x = √(Pc/Pcu,fl) = √(115/206.2) = √0.5578 = 0.747. At this load the copper loss is 115 W, equal to the core loss, and the total loss is 230 W. The transformer is therefore best matched to a load of about 75 percent of rating, which suits an installation that spends most of its time lightly loaded.

Answer: 0.747

(e)

At x = 0.75 and power factor 0.90 the output is Pout = 0.75 × 25 000 × 0.90 = 16 875 W. Copper loss is 0.75² × 206.2 = 116.0 W and core loss is 115 W, so the total loss is 231.0 W. The input is 16 875 + 231.0 = 17 106 W and the efficiency is η = 16 875/17 106 = 0.9865, or 98.65 percent. Because the load is close to the maximum-efficiency point from part (d), the efficiency is near its peak value. The result assumes the output voltage is held at the rated value, so the secondary power equals 0.75 times the rated volt-amperes times the power factor.

Answer: 98.65 %

Problem 5 [A6-005] Balanced three-phase wye and delta systems

A three-phase, three-wire, 60 Hz, 600 V (line-to-line) feeder supplies a balanced delta-connected load at a remote pump house. At the sending end the line-to-line voltage is held at 600 V rms with positive phase sequence. Each of the three feeder conductors has a series impedance of 0.50 + j1.20 Ω. The load consists of three identical impedances, each 24 + j18 Ω, connected in delta at the pump house. Neglect the feeder shunt capacitance. The candidate is asked to analyse the circuit using the per-phase equivalent method, which replaces the delta load by an equivalent wye load and uses the sending-end line-to-neutral voltage as the reference. Take line-to-line voltage as √3 times line-to-neutral voltage.

  1. (a) Calculate the rms line current in the feeder. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the line-to-line voltage at the load terminals. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the rms current in each phase impedance of the delta load. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the total real power absorbed by the load. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the power factor seen at the sending end. [4]
(a)

Convert the delta load to its equivalent wye: Zy = Zδ/3 = (24 + j18)/3 = 8 + j6 Ω. The total per-phase impedance is Zt = 0.50 + j1.20 + 8 + j6 = 8.50 + j7.20 Ω, with magnitude √(8.50² + 7.20²) = 11.14 Ω. The sending-end line-to-neutral voltage is 600/√3 = 346.4 V. The line current is I = 346.4/11.14 = 31.10 A. The angle of the current relative to the sending-end phase voltage is −arctan(7.20/8.50) = −40.3°, so the current lags. Because the system is balanced, one phase fully defines the other two, shifted by 120°.

Answer: 31.10 A

(b)

The line-to-neutral voltage at the load is the current times the equivalent wye impedance: Vn = I |Zy| = 31.10 × |8 + j6| = 31.10 × 10 = 311.0 V. The load line-to-line voltage is √3 times this: VL = √3 × 311.0 = 538.6 V. The drop of about 61 V, or 10.2 percent, from the sending end is the voltage dropped across the feeder resistance and reactance. This is large for a supply feeder and shows that the pump motors, if they were connected, would run noticeably below their rated voltage, which is a concern for starting torque.

Answer: 538.6 V

(c)

In a delta load the line current is √3 times the phase current, because each line current is the phasor difference of two phase currents 120° apart. Hence Iphase = 31.10/√3 = 17.95 A. As a cross-check, the delta phase voltage equals the load line-to-line voltage 538.6 V, and dividing by the delta impedance magnitude |24 + j18| = 30 Ω gives 538.6/30 = 17.95 A, which agrees. This confirms the wye-delta conversion and the line-current result of the earlier parts.

Answer: 17.95 A

(d)

The real power in a balanced load is three times the power in one phase. Using the equivalent wye: P = 3 I² Rload,y = 3 × 31.10² × 8 = 3 × 967.1 × 8 = 23 210 W = 23.21 kW. The same figure comes from the delta: P = 3 Iphase² × 24 = 3 × 322.3 × 24 = 23.2 kW. The feeder loss is 3 × 967.1 × 0.50 = 1.45 kW, so the sending end supplies 24.66 kW in total. The feeder efficiency is therefore 23.21/24.66 = 94.1 percent, which is acceptable but not generous.

Answer: 23.21 kW

(e)

The power factor at the sending end is the cosine of the angle of the total per-phase impedance seen from the source, because the sending-end phase voltage and the line current are separated by that angle. The angle is arctan(7.20/8.50) = 40.3°, so the power factor is cos 40.3° = 8.50/11.14 = 0.763 lagging. Equivalent confirmation: total real power 24.66 kW divided by apparent power √3 × 600 × 31.10 = 32.32 kVA gives 0.763. The load alone has a power factor of 24/30 = 0.80 lagging, and the feeder reactance lowers the value seen at the source.

Answer: 0.763 lagging

A6 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A6-006] Three-phase power, per-unit system and one-line diagrams

A 13.8 kV generator rated 30 MVA with a subtransient reactance of 0.18 per unit on its own base feeds a step-up transformer rated 30 MVA, 13.8/138 kV, with a leakage reactance of 0.10 per unit on its own base. A 138 kV transmission line with a series reactance of 52 Ω (resistance neglected) connects the transformer to a load bus. The load draws 20 MW at 0.90 power factor lagging, and the voltage at the load bus is held at 1.00 per unit. Choose a system base of 100 MVA, with 13.8 kV in the generator zone and 138 kV in the line zone. Treat the load as constant power and neglect all shunt elements, transformer magnetising branches and resistances.

  1. (a) Convert the generator reactance to the 100 MVA system base. [3]
  2. (b) Express the line reactance in per unit on the system base. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the load current in amperes in the 138 kV line. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the voltage at the generator terminals (the low-voltage side of the transformer) in kV, line to line. [5]
  5. (e) Calculate the internal emf behind the generator reactance, in kV line to line. [5]
(a)

A reactance given on a machine's own base is converted to a new base by Xnew = Xold (Snew/Sold)(Vold/Vnew)². Here the voltage base of the generator zone is 13.8 kV, equal to the generator rating, so the voltage ratio is one. Hence Xg = 0.18 × (100/30) × 1 = 0.600 pu. The same conversion applies to the transformer, giving 0.10 × 100/30 = 0.3333 pu, which is needed later because the transformer's voltage ratio matches the chosen zone bases exactly. The generator reactance is relatively large on the system base, because the machine is only 30 percent of the base MVA.

Answer: 0.600 pu

(b)

The base impedance of the line zone is Zbase = Vbase²/Sbase = (138 kV)²/100 MVA = 190.44 Ω. The line reactance is therefore X = 52/190.44 = 0.2730 pu. The per-unit method works because every quantity is divided by its own base, so the transformer disappears from the circuit as an ideal element once the zone voltage bases follow the transformer turns ratio, 13.8 kV to 138 kV. Only the leakage reactance of the transformer, 0.3333 pu, remains in the one-line model.

Answer: 0.2731 pu

(c)

The load in per unit is S = 20 MW/(100 MVA) = 0.200 pu of real power, with a power factor of 0.90 lagging. The reactive part is Q = 0.200 × tan(arccos 0.90) = 0.200 × 0.4843 = 0.0969 pu. At 1.00 pu voltage the current is I = S*/V* = (0.200 − j0.0969) pu, with magnitude 0.2222 pu. The base current in the line zone is Ibase = 100 × 10⁶/(√3 × 138 × 10³) = 418.4 A. The actual current is 0.2222 × 418.4 = 92.97 A. The same number follows from I = P/(√3 V pf) = 20 × 10⁶/(√3 × 138 000 × 0.9) = 92.97 A.

Answer: 92.97 A

(d)

The generator terminal voltage is the load voltage plus the drop across the transformer and the line, whose reactances are in series: Xs = 0.3333 + 0.2730 = 0.6063 pu. Vt = 1.00 + (0.200 − j0.0969)(j0.6063) = 1.00 + j0.1213 + 0.0587 = 1.0587 + j0.1213 pu. The magnitude is √(1.0587² + 0.1213²) = 1.0656 pu. In kilovolts, Vt = 1.0656 × 13.8 = 14.71 kV line to line. The terminal voltage is about 6.6 percent above the generator rating, so the generator would need its excitation limited or the transformer tap changed to avoid overvoltage.

Answer: 14.71 kV

(e)

The internal emf adds the voltage drop across the generator reactance, 0.600 pu, to the terminal voltage. E = Vt + I(jXg) = 1.0587 + j0.1213 + (0.200 − j0.0969)(j0.600) = 1.0587 + j0.1213 + j0.1200 + 0.0581 = 1.1168 + j0.2413. Alternatively, using the total reactance of 1.2063 pu from the load, E = 1.00 + (0.200 − j0.0969)(j1.2063) = 1.1169 + j0.2413. The magnitude is √(1.1169² + 0.2413²) = 1.1426 pu, which is 1.1426 × 13.8 = 15.77 kV. The angle is 12.2°, which is the power angle between the load bus and the emf, a useful measure of stability margin.

Answer: 15.77 kV

Problem 2 [A6-007] Unbalanced three-phase loads

A 208 V (line-to-line), 60 Hz, four-wire wye system with positive (abc) phase sequence supplies three single-phase loads connected line to neutral in a laboratory. The source is balanced, so each phase voltage has magnitude 208/√3 = 120.09 V, with Van at 0°, Vbn at −120° and Vcn at +120°. Load A is an 8.0 Ω resistor. Load B is a 6.0 Ω resistor in series with an inductive reactance of 8.0 Ω. Load C is a capacitive reactance of 15.0 Ω with no resistance. Neglect line and neutral conductor impedance, so each load sees its full phase voltage while the neutral conductor is intact. In the last part the neutral conductor opens while the three loads remain connected.

  1. (a) Calculate the rms current in load B. [3]
  2. (b) With the neutral conductor intact, calculate the rms neutral current. [7]
  3. (c) Calculate the total real power absorbed by the three loads. [4]
  4. (d) With the neutral open, calculate the magnitude of the voltage between the load star point and the source neutral. [6]
(a)

With the neutral intact, each load sees the source phase voltage. The magnitude of the load B impedance is |ZB| = √(6.0² + 8.0²) = 10.0 Ω. The rms current is Ib = V/|ZB| = 120.09/10.0 = 12.01 A. Its phase angle is −120° − 53.13° = −173.13°, because the inductive impedance angle of 53.13° makes the current lag the voltage. Load A takes 120.09/8.0 = 15.01 A in phase with Van, and load C takes 120.09/15.0 = 8.006 A leading Vcn by 90°, so its angle is 120° + 90° = 210°. Both of these currents are needed in the next part.

Answer: 12.01 A

(b)

The neutral current is the phasor sum of the three line currents, In = Ia + Ib + Ic. Ia = 15.01∠0° = 15.01 + j0.00. Ib = 12.01∠−173.13° = −11.92 − j1.44. Ic = 8.006∠210° = −6.93 − j4.00. The sum is In = (15.01 − 11.92 − 6.93) + j(0 − 1.44 − 4.00) = −3.84 − j5.44 A. The magnitude is √(3.84² + 5.44²) = 6.66 A, at an angle of about −125°. The neutral carries a large current because the loads are unequal in both magnitude and angle, and the neutral conductor must be sized for this current rather than assumed to be small.

Answer: 6.661 A

(c)

Real power is absorbed only in the resistances, so P = Ia² RA + Ib² RB. Here P = 15.01² × 8.0 + 12.01² × 6.0 = 225.3 × 8.0 + 144.2 × 6.0 = 1802.7 + 865.3 = 2668 W. The capacitor draws no real power. The reactive power is Q = Ib² × 8.0 − Ic² × 15.0 = 1153.7 − 961.4 = 192 var, so the net load is only slightly inductive. The total apparent power is √(2668² + 192²) = 2675 VA and the overall power factor is 0.997 lagging, which looks excellent even though the individual phases are very unequal.

Answer: 2668 W

(d)

With the neutral open, Millman's theorem gives the star-point voltage VnN = (Van Ya + Vbn Yb + Vcn Yc)/(Ya + Yb + Yc). Each term Vk Yk is the current the load would draw with its full phase voltage, so the numerator equals the phasor sum found in part (b): −3.84 − j5.44 A, magnitude 6.661 A. The admittances are Ya = 1/8 = 0.125 S, Yb = 1/(6 + j8) = 0.06 − j0.08 S and Yc = 1/(−j15) = +j0.0667 S. Their sum is 0.185 − j0.0133 S, of magnitude 0.1855 S. The displacement is VnN = 6.661/0.1855 = 35.9 V. This shifts the phase voltages across the loads: load A rises to about 142 V (and load C to about 141 V) while load B falls to about 84 V, which could damage equipment.

Answer: 35.9 V

Problem 3 [A6-008] Three-phase transformer connections and phase shift

A bank of three identical single-phase transformers, each rated 50 kVA, 7200/600 V, 60 Hz, is connected wye on the high-voltage side and delta on the low-voltage side to supply a 600 V motor control centre from a 12 kV class utility feeder. The primary neutral is solidly grounded. The high-voltage winding of each unit has 7200 V rated across it and the low-voltage winding has 600 V rated across it. Assume ideal transformers with no losses, no leakage and no phase-angle error. The bank supplies a balanced load of 120 kW at a power factor of 0.90 lagging at the 600 V terminals. Positive phase sequence applies on the high-voltage side, and the standard convention is that the low-voltage line voltage lags the high-voltage line voltage for this connection.

  1. (a) Calculate the rated line-to-line voltage on the high-voltage side, in kV. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the rated line current on the 600 V side of the bank. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the current in each low-voltage delta winding when the 120 kW load is supplied. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the high-voltage line current for the same load. [4]
  5. (e) State the magnitude, in degrees, of the phase displacement between the high-voltage and low-voltage line voltages. [4]
(a)

In a wye connection the line-to-line voltage is √3 times the voltage across one winding. Each high-voltage winding is rated 7200 V, so VLL(H) = √3 × 7200 = 12 471 V = 12.47 kV. This is the standard 12.47 kV distribution voltage, consistent with a 7.2 kV phase-to-ground system. The low-voltage line-to-line voltage is simply the winding voltage of 600 V, because in a delta connection each winding is connected directly between two lines. The overall line-to-line turns ratio is therefore 12 471/600 = 20.8, which is √3 times the winding ratio of 12.

Answer: 12.47 kV

(b)

The three-phase rating of the bank is 3 × 50 = 150 kVA. The rated line current on the low-voltage side is I = S/(√3 VLL) = 150 000/(√3 × 600) = 144.3 A. Each delta winding carries 1/√3 of this line current, which is 83.3 A and equals 50 000/600. The bank should never carry more than this rated line current continuously. The rating applies to the bank as a whole, and the delta winding means that the line current is larger than the winding current by √3.

Answer: 144.3 A

(c)

The apparent power of the load is S = P/pf = 120 000/0.90 = 133.3 kVA. The load line current is I = 133 300/(√3 × 600) = 128.3 A. In a delta connection the winding current is the line current divided by √3, so Iwinding = 128.3/√3 = 74.07 A. The result is also 133 333/(3 × 600) = 74.07 A. Compare with the winding rating of 83.3 A: the bank is loaded to 89 percent of its rating, so it has some spare capacity, but little allowance for motor starting current.

Answer: 74.07 A

(d)

On the high-voltage side, with ideal transformers, the apparent power is unchanged at 133.3 kVA. The line current is I = S/(√3 VLL(H)) = 133 333/(√3 × 12 471) = 6.173 A. In the wye, the line current equals the winding current. Check using the winding ratio: the low-voltage winding current of 74.07 A times 600/7200 = 6.173 A, which agrees. The high-voltage current is small, so a modest fuse or breaker rating suffices on the primary side, but it must still be sized to carry the magnetising inrush of the bank.

Answer: 6.173 A

(e)

In a wye-delta bank the line voltages on the two sides are displaced by 30°. The high-voltage line-to-neutral voltage, for example VAN, is in phase with the winding voltage across the high-voltage winding. The low-voltage winding voltage is in phase with that, but each low-voltage line-to-line voltage equals one winding voltage, and VAB(H) is √3 times VAN displaced by +30° from it. Hence the line-to-line voltages are separated by 30°, with the low side lagging under the stated convention. The magnitude of the shift is 30 degrees, and this matters when paralleling banks: a delta-wye bank cannot be paralleled with a wye-wye bank on the same system.

Answer: 30 degrees

Problem 4 [A6-009] Transmission line models and voltage regulation

A 230 kV, 60 Hz, three-phase overhead line is 120 km long. Its series impedance is 0.08 + j0.48 Ω/km per phase and its shunt admittance is j3.4 × 10⁻⁶ S/km per phase to neutral. Use the nominal-π model for the whole line, with half the total shunt admittance at each end. The line delivers 150 MW at a power factor of 0.95 lagging to a receiving-end load held at 220 kV line to line. Use the two-port relations Vs = A Vr + B Ir and Is = C Vr + D Ir, with all voltages per phase (line to neutral) and Ir taken as the load current at the receiving end. Take the receiving-end line-to-neutral voltage as the phasor reference at zero degrees.

  1. (a) Calculate the magnitude of the ABCD parameter A for this line. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the sending-end line-to-line voltage in kV. [6]
  3. (c) Calculate the percentage voltage regulation, using the no-load receiving-end voltage Vs/|A| with the sending voltage held at the value found in (b). [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the line transmission efficiency, from the sending-end real power found with the ABCD constants. [6]
(a)

The total series impedance is Z = (0.08 + j0.48) × 120 = 9.6 + j57.6 Ω. The total shunt admittance is Y = j3.4 × 10⁻⁶ × 120 = j4.08 × 10⁻⁴ S. For the nominal-π model, A = D = 1 + ZY/2 and B = Z, C = Y(1 + ZY/4). The product ZY = (9.6 + j57.6)(j4.08 × 10⁻⁴) = −0.023501 + j0.003917. Half of this is −0.011750 + j0.001958, so A = 0.98825 + j0.001958. The magnitude is |A| = 0.9882, with angle 0.11°. Since the shunt capacitance reduces the effect of the series reactance, A is slightly below 1 in magnitude.

Answer: 0.9882

(b)

The receiving-end phase voltage is Vr = 220 000/√3 = 127 017 V ∠0°. The load current is Ir = P/(3 Vr pf) = 150 × 10⁶/(3 × 127 017 × 0.95) = 414.4 A, lagging the voltage by arccos 0.95 = 18.19°, so Ir = 414.4∠−18.19° = 393.7 − j129.4 A. Then Vs = A Vr + B Ir = (0.98825 + j0.001958)(127 017) + (9.6 + j57.6)(393.7 − j129.4). The first term is 125 524 + j249 V. The second is 11 232 + j21 432 V. Sum: 136 756 + j21 681 V, magnitude 138 464 V. Line to line: √3 × 138 464 = 239.8 kV, with a power angle of 9.0°.

Answer: 239.8 kV

(c)

With the receiving end unloaded (Ir = 0), Vs = A Vr,nl, so Vr,nl = |Vs|/|A| = 138 464/0.98825 = 140 112 V per phase, which is 242.7 kV line to line. Regulation is (|Vr,nl| − |Vr,fl|)/|Vr,fl| = (140 112 − 127 017)/127 017 = 0.1031 = 10.31 percent. This high value reflects the substantial series reactance at the 150 MW load. A utility would fix it with shunt capacitors or a tap change, because customers normally require regulation under about 5 percent at the receiving bus.

Answer: 10.31 %

(d)

The sending-end current is Is = C Vr + D Ir, with D = A. First C = Y(1 + ZY/4) = j4.08 × 10⁻⁴ × (0.99412 + j0.00098) = −4.0 × 10⁻⁷ + j4.056 × 10⁻⁴ S. Then C Vr = −0.05 + j51.52 A and D Ir = (0.98825 + j0.001958)(393.65 − j129.39) = 389.28 − j127.09 A. So Is = 389.23 − j75.58 A, magnitude 396.5 A. The sending-end real power is Ps = 3 Re(Vs Is*) = 3 × (136 756 × 389.23 − 21 681 × 75.58) = 3 × (5.3230 × 10⁷ − 1.639 × 10⁶) = 154.77 MW. The efficiency is Pr/Ps = 150/154.77 = 96.92 percent. The 4.77 MW loss is mostly I²R in the 9.6 Ω of series resistance.

Answer: 96.92 %

Problem 5 [A6-010] Power flow and real and reactive power control

Two buses in a 60 Hz transmission network are joined by a short, lossless line whose series reactance is 0.25 per unit on a 100 MVA base. The line resistance and shunt admittance are negligible. The sending-end bus voltage magnitude is held at 1.05 per unit and the receiving-end bus voltage magnitude is held at 1.00 per unit. A scheduled real power of 0.80 per unit (80 MW) must flow from the sending bus to the receiving bus. Take the receiving-end voltage as the reference phasor, and let δ be the angle by which the sending-end voltage leads it. Use the standard power-flow relations for a lossless reactance, with positive Q meaning reactive power delivered to the receiving bus or supplied by the sending bus respectively.

  1. (a) Calculate the power angle δ in degrees. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the reactive power delivered to the receiving bus. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the reactive power supplied by the sending bus. [3]
  4. (d) Suppose the sending-end voltage is reduced to 1.00 per unit while the same 0.80 pu is transferred. Calculate the reactive power the receiving bus must supply into the line. [5]
  5. (e) Explain which of the two variables, angle or voltage magnitude, mainly controls real power flow and which mainly controls reactive power flow in a high-voltage line of this type. [4]
(a)

For a lossless line of reactance X, the real power delivered is P = Vs Vr sin δ / X. Solving, sin δ = P X/(Vs Vr) = 0.80 × 0.25/(1.05 × 1.00) = 0.2/1.05 = 0.19048. Hence δ = arcsin(0.19048) = 10.98°. The angle is small, which is typical of a lightly loaded line, and the small-angle approximation sin δ ≈ δ is reasonably accurate here (0.1916 rad against 0.1905). The maximum real power, at δ = 90°, is Vs Vr/X = 4.20 pu, so the 0.80 pu transfer uses only about 19 percent of the theoretical steady-state limit.

Answer: 10.98 degrees

(b)

The reactive power delivered to the receiving bus is Qr = (Vs Vr cos δ − Vr²)/X. With cos δ = 0.98169, Qr = (1.05 × 1.00 × 0.98169 − 1.00)/0.25 = (1.03077 − 1.00)/0.25 = 0.1231 pu, or 12.3 Mvar. A positive value means the line is delivering reactive power into the receiving bus, which is natural because the sending end is at a higher voltage. This reactive flow will help support the receiving voltage when the load is inductive.

Answer: 0.1231 pu

(c)

The reactive power supplied at the sending end is Qs = (Vs² − Vs Vr cos δ)/X = (1.1025 − 1.03077)/0.25 = 0.2869 pu, or 28.7 Mvar. The difference between the two ends is the reactive loss in the line reactance: Qs − Qr = 0.2869 − 0.1231 = 0.1638 pu. This matches X I² = 0.25 × (0.80² + 0.1231²) = 0.25 × 0.6552 = 0.1638 pu, with the current magnitude taken from the receiving end where voltage is 1.00 pu. A lossless line consumes reactive power in proportion to the square of the current flowing in it.

Answer: 0.2869 pu

(d)

With Vs = Vr = 1.00 pu the angle changes: sin δ = 0.80 × 0.25/1.00 = 0.20, so δ = 11.54° and cos δ = 0.97980. The reactive power delivered to the receiving bus is Qr = (1.00 × 0.97980 − 1.00)/0.25 = −0.0808 pu. The negative sign means the line no longer delivers reactive power to the receiving bus: the bus has to supply 0.0808 pu, or 8.1 Mvar, into the line to supply the line reactance loss. This is why local reactive support such as shunt capacitors is needed at the receiving bus when the sending voltage is not raised.

Answer: 0.0808 pu

(e)

In a high-voltage line where reactance is much larger than resistance, the real power depends mainly on the sine of the angle between the end voltages, P ≈ Vs Vr sin δ / X, so the angle (set by adjusting prime-mover input or phase shifters) mainly controls real power. The reactive power depends mainly on the difference in voltage magnitudes, Q ≈ Vr (Vs cos δ − Vr)/X, so the magnitude (set by excitation, tap changers and shunt devices) mainly controls reactive power. The numbers confirm this: raising the sending voltage from 1.00 to 1.05 pu changed Qr from −0.081 pu to +0.123 pu while the angle moved by only 0.55°. Voltage magnitude therefore controls Q, and angle controls P.

A6 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A6-011] Fault calculations and symmetrical components basics

A 30 MVA, 13.8 kV, three-phase, wye-connected synchronous generator at a paper mill operates unloaded at its rated terminal voltage of 1.0 per unit when a fault occurs at its terminals. The generator neutral is solidly grounded. On the machine base of 30 MVA and 13.8 kV its sequence reactances are X1 = 0.15 per unit, X2 = 0.15 per unit and X0 = 0.05 per unit. All resistances are negligible and the prefault voltage is the positive-sequence source in series with X1. Use the base current Ib = S/(√3 VL) and treat each fault as a bolted (zero impedance) fault at the generator terminals. Take the phase a as the reference phase for the single-line-to-ground and line-to-line faults, with the line-to-line fault between phases b and c.

  1. (a) Find the three-phase fault current in kA. [4]
  2. (b) Find the single-line-to-ground fault current in phase a, in kA. [6]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the line-to-line fault current in kA. [5]
  4. (d) A neutral reactor is to be installed so that the single-line-to-ground fault current falls to 80 percent of the three-phase fault current. Find the required reactor reactance in ohms. [5]
(a)

For a balanced three-phase fault only the positive-sequence network is involved, so the fault current in per unit is I = E/X1 = 1.0/0.15 = 6.667 pu. The base current is Ib = S/(√3 VL) = 30 × 106/(√3 × 13 800) = 1255.1 A. The actual fault current is therefore 6.667 × 1255.1 A = 8367 A, or 8.37 kA. The result is large because only the subtransient reactance of the machine limits the current. Resistance is neglected, so the current lags the voltage by 90 degrees. This is the value used to set the interrupting duty of the generator breaker before any other fault type is examined.

Answer: 8.37 kA

(b)

For a single-line-to-ground fault the three sequence networks are connected in series, and the sequence currents are equal: Ia1 = Ia2 = Ia0 = E/(X1 + X2 + X0) = 1.0/(0.15 + 0.15 + 0.05) = 2.857 pu. The fault current in phase a is the sum of the three sequence currents, so If = 3 Ia1 = 3 × 2.857 = 8.571 pu. Multiplying by the base current 1255.1 A gives If = 8.571 × 1255.1 = 10 758 A, or 10.76 kA. The result exceeds the three-phase value because the zero-sequence reactance of 0.05 pu is much smaller than the positive-sequence reactance. This is the usual situation for a solidly grounded generator, and it means the machine winding and bracing must be rated for the ground fault.

Answer: 10.76 kA

(c)

For a line-to-line fault between phases b and c, the positive and negative sequence networks are connected in parallel and the zero-sequence network carries no current. The positive-sequence current is Ia1 = E/(X1 + X2) = 1.0/0.30 = 3.333 pu, and Ia2 = -Ia1. The fault current in phase b has magnitude |Ib| = √3 |Ia1| = √3 × 3.333 = 5.774 pu. Multiplying by the base current of 1255.1 A gives 5.774 × 1255.1 = 7246 A, or 7.25 kA. This is √3/2 times the three-phase current when X1 equals X2, which is a quick check on the answer. It is the smallest of the three fault currents for this machine.

Answer: 7.25 kA

(d)

The target current is 0.8 × 6.667 = 5.333 pu. A reactance Xn in the neutral appears as 3Xn in the zero-sequence network. The single-line-to-ground current is If = 3E/(X1 + X2 + X0 + 3Xn), so 5.333 = 3/(0.35 + 3Xn). Hence 0.35 + 3Xn = 0.5625 and Xn = 0.2125/3 = 0.07083 pu. The base impedance is Zb = VL2/S = 13.82/30 = 6.348 ohm, so Xn = 0.07083 × 6.348 = 0.4497 ohm. In practice the reactor must withstand the fault current for the clearing time, and the insulation of the neutral end of the winding must be checked for the voltage that appears across the reactor during a ground fault.

Answer: 0.450 ohm

Problem 2 [A6-012] Generation, load curves and economic dispatch basics

A small Ontario utility serves a remote load from two thermal units that are always online. Unit 1 has the fuel cost C1 = 520 + 8.4 P1 + 0.005 P12 dollars per hour and unit 2 has C2 = 380 + 7.2 P2 + 0.0085 P22 dollars per hour, where P is in MW. Both units can operate anywhere between 100 MW and 500 MW. Transmission losses are neglected. The daily load curve is: 700 MW for 8 hours, 450 MW for 10 hours and 250 MW for 6 hours. For the 700 MW period, the units are dispatched on equal incremental cost. The alternative being compared is an equal split of the load between the two units.

  1. (a) Find the system incremental cost lambda for the 700 MW period, in dollars per MWh. [4]
  2. (b) Find the optimal output of unit 1 in MW for the 700 MW period. [3]
  3. (c) Find the total fuel cost in dollars per hour at the optimal dispatch. [4]
  4. (d) Find the hourly saving of optimal dispatch compared with an equal 350 MW split. [4]
  5. (e) Find the daily load factor of the system based on the 700 MW peak. [5]
(a)

At the optimum both units run at the same incremental cost, dC1/dP1 = dC2/dP2 = lambda, with no limits active. Differentiating gives 8.4 + 0.01 P1 = lambda and 7.2 + 0.017 P2 = lambda. Hence P1 = (lambda - 8.4)/0.01 and P2 = (lambda - 7.2)/0.017. The power balance P1 + P2 = 700 MW gives (lambda - 8.4)/0.01 + (lambda - 7.2)/0.017 = 700. Collecting terms, lambda (100 + 58.824) = 700 + 840 + 423.53, so lambda = 1963.53/158.824 = 12.363 dollars per MWh. Both resulting outputs lie between 100 and 500 MW, so the unconstrained solution is valid.

Answer: 12.36 $/MWh

(b)

Substitute lambda = 12.363 into the incremental cost equation of unit 1: P1 = (12.363 - 8.4)/0.01 = 396.3 MW. The remaining load goes to unit 2, P2 = 700 - 396.3 = 303.7 MW, which agrees with (12.363 - 7.2)/0.017 = 303.7 MW. Unit 1 has the lower quadratic coefficient, so its incremental cost rises more slowly and it takes the larger share. Both outputs are inside the 100 to 500 MW limits, so no unit is pinned at a limit and the equal-incremental-cost rule applies without modification.

Answer: 396.3 MW

(c)

Evaluate each cost function at its optimal output. Unit 1: C1 = 520 + 8.4 (396.3) + 0.005 (396.3)2 = 520 + 3328.9 + 785.3 = 4634.2 dollars per hour. Unit 2: C2 = 380 + 7.2 (303.7) + 0.0085 (303.7)2 = 380 + 2186.7 + 784.0 = 3350.7 dollars per hour. The total is 4634.2 + 3350.7 = 7984.9 dollars per hour, or about 7985 dollars per hour. This is the baseline cost for the saving comparison in part d, and it excludes the cost of any start-up or shutdown of the units.

Answer: 7985 $/h

(d)

For an equal split each unit carries 350 MW. Unit 1: C1 = 520 + 8.4 (350) + 0.005 (350)2 = 520 + 2940 + 612.5 = 4072.5 dollars per hour. Unit 2: C2 = 380 + 7.2 (350) + 0.0085 (350)2 = 380 + 2520 + 1041.25 = 3941.25 dollars per hour. The total is 8013.75 dollars per hour. The optimal dispatch costs 7984.8 dollars per hour, so the saving is 8013.75 - 7984.8 = 28.9 dollars per hour. Over the 8 peak hours this is about 231 dollars per day, which shows that for similar units the cost curve is flat near its minimum and the saving is modest, though it recurs every day of the year.

Answer: 28.9 $/h

(e)

Daily energy is the sum of power times duration: 700 × 8 = 5600 MWh, 450 × 10 = 4500 MWh and 250 × 6 = 1500 MWh, for a total of 11 600 MWh. The peak demand is 700 MW, so the energy that would be delivered if the peak were held for 24 hours is 700 × 24 = 16 800 MWh. The load factor is the ratio of average to peak demand, 11 600/16 800 = 0.690. The average load is 483.3 MW. A load factor of about 0.69 means the plant capacity needed for the peak is used on average only 69 percent of the time, which is why the cheaper unit is kept loaded as far as its limit allows.

Answer: 0.690

Problem 3 [A6-013] DC machine models and speed control

A separately excited DC motor drives a rolling-mill table. Its nameplate gives 240 V armature supply, rated armature current 90 A and rated speed 1150 rpm. The armature circuit resistance is 0.25 ohm and brush drop is neglected. The field current is held constant at its rated value, and the armature reaction is neglected, so the flux per pole is constant and the back emf is proportional to speed. Assume the load torque is constant (independent of speed) wherever the problem refers to constant torque, and that the machine always operates in steady state. The armature voltage is supplied by a variable-voltage converter, and field weakening is obtained by reducing the field current.

  1. (a) Find the back emf at rated operation and the machine constant K in V·s/rad. [4]
  2. (b) With the armature supply held at 240 V, find the speed in rpm when the armature current falls to 60 A. [4]
  3. (c) At rated torque (90 A) find the armature voltage needed to run at 800 rpm. [5]
  4. (d) With the armature at 240 V, the flux is reduced to 80 percent of its rated value while the torque stays at its rated value. Find the new speed in rpm. [7]
(a)

In steady state the armature equation is V = Ea + Ia Ra. At rated operation Ea = 240 - 90 × 0.25 = 240 - 22.5 = 217.5 V. The rated angular speed is ω = 1150 × 2π/60 = 120.43 rad/s. Because the flux is constant, Ea = K ω with K = kφ, so K = 217.5/120.43 = 1.806 V·s/rad. The same K gives the torque constant, so the rated torque is K Ia = 1.806 × 90 = 162.5 N·m. This single constant is all that the later parts need for speed and torque calculations, as long as the field current is unchanged.

Answer: K = 1.806 V·s/rad

(b)

At the lower load the armature current is 60 A and the supply is unchanged at 240 V. The back emf is Ea = 240 - 60 × 0.25 = 225 V. Since Ea is proportional to speed at constant flux, n = 1150 × 225/217.5 = 1189.7 rpm. The speed rises by about 3.4 percent as the load falls from rated to two thirds of rated current. This small change is the natural speed regulation of a separately excited motor, and it arises only from the armature resistance drop. A stiffer speed characteristic than this would need closed-loop control of armature voltage.

Answer: 1190 rpm

(c)

At rated torque the armature current is still 90 A because torque is proportional to Ia at constant flux. The back emf required at 800 rpm is Ea = 217.5 × 800/1150 = 151.3 V. The armature voltage is then V = Ea + Ia Ra = 151.3 + 90 × 0.25 = 151.3 + 22.5 = 173.8 V. The converter therefore reduces the armature voltage to about 72 percent of the rated value to obtain this speed at full torque. Armature voltage control gives constant-torque operation below base speed, with the power rising in proportion to speed, so the motor and converter are not overloaded at this operating point.

Answer: 173.8 V

(d)

Torque is proportional to flux times armature current, so keeping rated torque with 0.8 of the flux requires Ia = 90/0.8 = 112.5 A. The armature voltage drop is 112.5 × 0.25 = 28.125 V, so Ea = 240 - 28.125 = 211.875 V. The back emf is Ea = 0.8 K ω, so ω = 211.875/(0.8 × 1.806) = 146.6 rad/s, which is 146.6 × 60/(2π) = 1400 rpm. The speed rises to about 1.22 times base speed. Note that the armature current of 112.5 A is 25 percent above its rated value, so continuous operation at this torque would overheat the armature. Field weakening is normally used at constant power, so the torque must fall as speed rises above base speed.

Answer: 1400 rpm

Problem 4 [A6-014] DC motor starting and braking

A 230 V shunt DC motor in a quarry hoist has an armature resistance of 0.12 ohm and a rated armature current of 120 A at its rated speed of 1500 rpm. The field is supplied separately from a constant source, so the flux is constant and brush drop is neglected. The motor is started from rest by connecting it directly to the 230 V supply through an external starting resistor that is later cut out. For braking, the motor is running at rated speed with rated armature current when the armature is disconnected from the supply. Two braking methods are considered: dynamic braking, where the armature is connected across an external resistor, and plugging, where the armature supply polarity is reversed in series with an external resistor. The initial braking current is limited to twice the rated armature current in either case.

  1. (a) Find the armature current in amperes if the motor were started directly on 230 V with no external resistance. [4]
  2. (b) Find the external starting resistance, in ohms, that limits the initial starting current to 1.5 times rated current. [5]
  3. (c) Find the external resistance in ohms for dynamic braking so that the initial braking current is twice rated. [5]
  4. (d) Find the external resistance in ohms for plugging so that the initial reverse current is twice rated. [6]
(a)

At the instant of starting the speed is zero, so the back emf is zero and the only element limiting current is the armature resistance. The armature equation V = Ea + Ia Ra gives Ia = 230/0.12 = 1916.7 A. This is 16 times the rated current of 120 A, which would overheat the commutator, burn the brushes and produce a torque that would shock the gearing. It is the reason a starter of some kind is always required for a DC motor above a few kilowatts. The calculation also shows why the armature resistance of a machine is made small, since it is the main cause of the low voltage regulation under load.

Answer: 1917 A

(b)

The target starting current is 1.5 × 120 = 180 A. With zero back emf the circuit is the supply voltage over the total series resistance, so 180 = 230/(0.12 + Rext). Therefore 0.12 + Rext = 230/180 = 1.2778 ohm, and Rext = 1.2778 - 0.12 = 1.158 ohm. As the motor accelerates the back emf rises and the current falls, so the resistor is cut out in steps to keep the current between limits. The resistor must be rated for the heat produced during starting, which at the first instant is 1802 × 1.158 = 37.5 kW, though only for a short time.

Answer: 1.158 ohm

(c)

Before braking the back emf is Ea = 230 - 120 × 0.12 = 215.6 V. When the armature is disconnected from the supply and connected across a resistor, the machine acts as a generator, so the initial braking current is Ea/(Ra + Rext). The current limit is 240 A, so 240 = 215.6/(0.12 + Rext), which gives 0.12 + Rext = 0.8983 ohm, and Rext = 0.778 ohm. The current direction reverses relative to motoring, so the torque opposes rotation and the kinetic energy of the load is dissipated in the resistor. The braking torque falls as the speed falls, since Ea falls in proportion to speed.

Answer: 0.778 ohm

(d)

In plugging, the supply voltage is reversed, so it now adds to the back emf, which has not changed at the instant of reversal. The initial current magnitude is (V + Ea)/(Ra + Rext), where Ea = 215.6 V. With a limit of 240 A, 240 = (230 + 215.6)/(0.12 + Rext), so 0.12 + Rext = 445.6/240 = 1.8567 ohm, and Rext = 1.737 ohm. Plugging needs a larger resistor than dynamic braking because the supply adds to the emf, and it also delivers power from the supply while braking. If the supply is not disconnected when the speed reaches zero, the motor will accelerate in reverse.

Answer: 1.737 ohm

Problem 5 [A6-015] Synchronous generator equivalent circuit and regulation

A hydroelectric generator at a northern Ontario station is rated 20 MVA, 11 kV line to line, 60 Hz, wye-connected. Its armature resistance is negligible and its synchronous reactance is 3.2 ohm per phase, taken as constant (the magnetic circuit is assumed linear). The machine feeds a large network at rated terminal voltage and delivers rated kVA. Use the per-phase equivalent circuit with the excitation emf Ef in series with jXs, and take the terminal phase voltage as the phasor reference. Voltage regulation is defined as (Ef - Vt)/Vt with the field current held at the value that produced rated terminal voltage at the stated load, and the load then removed.

  1. (a) Find the rated line current in amperes. [3]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the excitation emf per phase at rated load, 0.8 power factor lagging, in volts. [5]
  3. (c) Find the voltage regulation in percent for that load. [4]
  4. (d) Find the power angle in degrees at that load. [4]
  5. (e) Find the regulation in percent if the same kVA is delivered at 0.8 power factor leading. [4]
(a)

The rated line current follows from the three-phase apparent power S = √3 VL IL. Rearranging, IL = S/(√3 VL) = 20 × 106/(√3 × 11 000) = 20 × 106/19 053 = 1049.7 A. The machine is wye-connected, so the phase current equals the line current. The terminal phase voltage used in the later parts is Vt = 11 000/√3 = 6351 V. These two numbers are the basis of the per-phase equivalent circuit, and every later phasor calculation takes Vt as the reference at zero degrees with the armature current at an angle set by the power factor.

Answer: 1050 A

(b)

With Vt as reference, a lagging load at 0.8 power factor has the current I = 1049.7 ∠ -36.87° A. The excitation emf is Ef = Vt + jXs I. Then jXs I = 3.2 × 1049.7 ∠ (90° - 36.87°) = 3359 ∠ 53.13° = 2015.4 + j2687.2 V. Hence Ef = 6350.9 + 2015.4 + j2687.2 = 8366.3 + j2687.2 V. The magnitude is √(8366.32 + 2687.22) = 8787 V per phase, or about 15.2 kV line to line. The excitation is much higher than the terminal voltage because the lagging current demagnetizes, so the field must supply the missing flux.

Answer: 8787 V

(c)

Regulation is the rise in terminal voltage when the load is removed with the excitation unchanged, so it equals the difference between the excitation emf and the terminal voltage divided by the terminal voltage. Using the magnitude from part b, regulation = (8787 - 6351)/6351 = 0.3836, or 38.4 percent. This is high but typical of a salient-pole hydroelectric machine with a large synchronous reactance, which here is 3.2 × 20/112 = 0.529 per unit on the machine base. A regulation as high as this shows that the automatic voltage regulator and the field forcing must act quickly to hold the terminal voltage during load changes.

Answer: 38.4 percent

(d)

The power angle δ is the angle between Ef and Vt. From the phasor result of part b, Ef = 8366.3 + j2687.2 V, so δ = arctan(2687.2/8366.3) = arctan(0.3212) = 17.8 degrees. As a cross check, the real power per phase must equal 3 times Ef Vt sin(δ)/Xs for a cylindrical-rotor model: 3 × 8787 × 6351 × sin 17.8°/3.2 = 16.0 MW, equal to 20 × 0.8 = 16 MW. The angle is well below the 90 degree steady-state stability limit, leaving a reasonable margin, though the margin shrinks if the network voltage sags.

Answer: 17.8 degrees

(e)

For a leading load the current is I = 1049.7 ∠ +36.87° A, and jXs I = 3359 ∠ (90° + 36.87°) = 3359 ∠ 126.87° = -2015.4 + j2687.2 V. Then Ef = 6350.9 - 2015.4 + j2687.2 = 4335.5 + j2687.2 V, with magnitude √(4335.52 + 2687.22) = 5101 V. The regulation is (5101 - 6351)/6351 = -0.1968, or -19.7 percent. It is negative, which means the terminal voltage would fall if the load were removed. A leading current magnetizes the machine, so the excitation needed is below the terminal voltage, and the generator is then operating under-excited.

Answer: -19.7 percent

A6 Practice Paper 4

Problem 1 [A6-016] Synchronous motor operation and power factor

A synchronous motor drives a rock crusher in a mine. It is connected to a 2400 V (line to line), 60 Hz, three-phase bus and is wye-connected with a synchronous reactance of 4.5 ohm per phase. The armature resistance is neglected and the magnetic circuit is assumed linear. The motor draws 1.2 MW of electrical power at the terminals, and the field is adjusted so that the power factor is 0.9 leading. Use the motor convention in which the excitation emf per phase is Ef = Vt - jXs I with the terminal phase voltage Vt as the reference phasor, and treat the electrical input power as constant when the field current is changed.

  1. (a) Find the line current in amperes at 0.9 leading power factor. [3]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the excitation emf per phase in volts. [5]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the load angle in degrees. [4]
  4. (d) Find the reactive power the motor supplies to the bus in kvar. [4]
  5. (e) The field current is reduced until the power factor is unity at the same input power. Find the new excitation emf per phase in volts. [4]
(a)

For three-phase power, P = √3 VL IL cos φ, so IL = P/(√3 VL cos φ) = 1.2 × 106/(√3 × 2400 × 0.9) = 1.2 × 106/3741.2 = 320.75 A. The phase current in the wye connection equals the line current. The terminal phase voltage is Vt = 2400/√3 = 1385.6 V and is the phasor reference. A leading power factor means the current leads the voltage by cos-1 0.9 = 25.84 degrees, which is the condition of an over-excited machine. This current is the value used for the voltage drop across the synchronous reactance in the next part.

Answer: 320.8 A

(b)

With Vt as reference, the current is I = 320.75 ∠ +25.84° A. The drop across the reactance is jXs I = 4.5 × 320.75 ∠ (90° + 25.84°) = 1443.4 ∠ 115.84° = -629.2 + j1299.0 V. For a motor Ef = Vt - jXs I = 1385.6 + 629.2 - j1299.0 = 2014.8 - j1299.0 V. The magnitude is √(2014.82 + 1299.02) = 2397 V per phase, which is 1.73 times the terminal voltage. The excitation is higher than the terminal voltage because the machine is over-excited, which is how it is able to deliver reactive power to the bus.

Answer: 2397 V

(c)

The load angle δ is the angle between Ef and Vt. From part b, Ef = 2014.8 - j1299.0 V, so the angle is arctan(-1299.0/2014.8) = -32.8 degrees, and the magnitude is 32.8 degrees. The rotor lags the terminal voltage in a motor, so the sign is negative. As a check, the electrical input power per phase equals Ef Vt sin(32.8°)/Xs = 2397 × 1385.6 × 0.5418/4.5 = 400 kW, which times three equals 1.2 MW, matching the stated input power. The angle is well within the stability limit of 90 degrees, though the margin shrinks as the field is weakened.

Answer: 32.8 degrees

(d)

The reactive power supplied to the bus for a leading current is Q = P tan φ, where φ = cos-1 0.9 = 25.84 degrees and tan φ = 0.4843. Hence Q = 1200 × 0.4843 = 581.2 kvar. Equivalent to this, Q = √3 VL IL sin φ = √3 × 2400 × 320.75 × 0.4359 = 581.2 kvar. The synchronous motor therefore acts as a capacitor on the plant bus, which can be used to correct the power factor of nearby induction motors without any additional capacitor bank. The motor's armature current rating must be large enough to carry this reactive component as well as the real current.

Answer: 581 kvar

(e)

At unity power factor the current is in phase with Vt and has the magnitude I = 1.2 × 106/(√3 × 2400) = 288.7 A, which is lower than before since the reactive current is gone. The reactance drop is Xs I = 4.5 × 288.7 = 1299.0 V, at 90 degrees to Vt. For a motor Ef = Vt - jXs I = 1385.6 - j1299.0 V, whose magnitude is √(1385.62 + 1299.02) = 1899 V per phase. The excitation falls by about 21 percent compared with part b, so the field current is reduced. If it is reduced much more, the motor becomes under-excited, draws lagging current, and eventually loses synchronism.

Answer: 1899 V

Problem 2 [A6-017] Three-phase induction motor equivalent circuit and torque-slip

A 460 V (line to line), 60 Hz, four-pole, wye-connected three-phase induction motor drives a conveyor in a sawmill. The per-phase equivalent circuit, referred to the stator, has stator resistance R1 = 0.25 ohm, stator leakage reactance X1 = 0.75 ohm, magnetizing reactance Xm = 30 ohm (core loss neglected, with Xm connected directly across the air-gap branch), rotor resistance R2 = 0.20 ohm and rotor leakage reactance X2 = 0.80 ohm, both referred to the stator. Rotational (friction and windage) losses are neglected. The motor runs at a slip of 0.03. Use the exact equivalent circuit, with Xm in parallel with the rotor branch.

  1. (a) Find the stator line current in amperes at a slip of 0.03. [5]
  2. (b) Find the developed electromagnetic torque in N·m at this slip. [5]
  3. (c) Find the efficiency, taking the developed mechanical power as the output. [4]
  4. (d) Find the slip at which the maximum torque occurs, using the Thevenin equivalent seen from the rotor branch. [6]
(a)

The phase voltage is V = 460/√3 = 265.6 V. The rotor branch impedance at s = 0.03 is Z2 = R2/s + jX2 = 6.667 + j0.8 ohm. In parallel with jXm = j30, the air-gap impedance is Zp = (j30 × (6.667 + j0.8))/(6.667 + j30.8) = 6.04 + j2.09 ohm. The total input impedance is Zin = R1 + jX1 + Zp = 0.25 + j0.75 + 6.04 + j2.09 = 6.29 + j2.84 ohm, of magnitude 6.90 ohm at an angle of 24.3 degrees. The line current is I1 = 265.6/6.90 = 38.5 A, lagging the phase voltage. The wye connection gives line current equal to phase current. This is the line current to use when sizing the starter and protection.

Answer: 38.5 A

(b)

The torque follows from the air-gap power, Pag = 3 I22 R2/s, where I2 is the rotor current referred to the stator. The voltage across the parallel branch is Vag = I1 Zp, and I2 = Vag/Z2. Evaluating gives I2 = 36.6 A, so Pag = 3 × 36.62 × 6.667 = 26.8 kW. The synchronous speed is 120 × 60/4 = 1800 rpm, or ωs = 188.5 rad/s. The developed torque is T = Pag/ωs = 26 838/188.5 = 142.4 N·m. The torque equals the air-gap power divided by the synchronous speed regardless of the actual rotor speed, since the air-gap power is what crosses the air gap, and it is the quantity that determines the machine's rotating field torque.

Answer: 142.4 N·m

(c)

The developed mechanical power is Pdev = (1 - s) Pag = 0.97 × 26 838 = 26 033 W, which is the output because rotational loss is neglected. The input power is Pin = 3 V I1 cos φ = 3 × 265.6 × 38.48 × cos φ. The input impedance angle is 24.3 degrees, so cos φ = 0.9116 and Pin = 3 × 265.6 × 38.48 × 0.9116 = 27 949 W. The efficiency is 26 033/27 949 = 0.9315, or 93.1 percent. The losses are the stator copper loss 3 × 38.482 × 0.25 = 1111 W and the rotor copper loss s Pag = 805 W. The efficiency is high because the rotational and core losses were not included, so a real machine would be a few points lower.

Answer: 93.1 percent

(d)

The Thevenin voltage seen at the rotor terminals is Vth = V jXm/(R1 + j(X1 + Xm)) and the impedance is Zth = (R1 + jX1) jXm/(R1 + j(X1 + Xm)). Numerically Zth = 0.238 + j0.734 ohm, so Rth = 0.238 and Xth = 0.734 ohm. The slip at maximum torque is smax = R2/√(Rth2 + (Xth + X2)2) = 0.2/√(0.2382 + 1.5342) = 0.2/1.552 = 0.129. Maximum torque occurs at about 4.3 times the rated slip, so the motor has ample overload capacity. The value of smax depends on R2 but the maximum torque itself does not, which is why a wound-rotor machine can shift the peak torque by adding rotor resistance.

Answer: 0.129

Problem 3 [A6-018] Induction motor starting and speed control

A 55 kW, 600 V, three-phase, six-pole, 60 Hz squirrel-cage induction motor drives a dust collector fan. At full load the slip is 2.5 percent and the line current is 70 A. When started directly on 600 V it draws 6.2 times full-load current and develops 1.6 times full-load torque. The motor is delta-connected in normal running, and the stated starting figures hold at full voltage. Torque varies with the square of terminal voltage at any fixed frequency. For the speed control question, an adjustable-frequency drive keeps the ratio of volts to hertz constant and the slip speed (in rpm) at full-load torque equal to its rated value. Take the rated output power as 55 kW at the full-load slip.

  1. (a) A 65 percent tap autotransformer starter is used. Find the line current drawn from the supply during starting, in amperes. [4]
  2. (b) Find the starting torque in N·m with the same 65 percent tap. [4]
  3. (c) Find the line current from the supply if instead a star-delta starter is used, in amperes. [4]
  4. (d) The drive is set to give a synchronous speed of 900 rpm. Find the output frequency in hertz. [4]
  5. (e) At that setting, with constant volts per hertz and full-load torque, find the shaft speed in rpm. [4]
(a)

The direct-start current is 6.2 × 70 = 434 A. With an autotransformer on a tap ratio k = 0.65, the motor terminal voltage is 0.65 of the supply, so the motor current is 0.65 × 434 = 282.1 A. The supply current is reduced further, since the autotransformer steps current up on the supply side by the same ratio: Isupply = k2 × 434 = 0.4225 × 434 = 183.4 A. Compared with direct starting this is a 58 percent reduction, which is useful where the supply is weak. This calculation ignores the small magnetizing current of the autotransformer, which is minor compared with the starting current of the motor.

Answer: 183.4 A

(b)

Rated shaft speed is n = 1200 × (1 - 0.025) = 1170 rpm, since the synchronous speed of six poles at 60 Hz is 120 × 60/6 = 1200 rpm. The full-load torque is T = P/ω = 55 000/(1170 × 2π/60) = 55 000/122.52 = 448.9 N·m. Direct starting torque is 1.6 × 448.9 = 718.2 N·m. Torque goes with the square of terminal voltage, so at 0.65 of rated voltage the starting torque is 0.652 × 718.2 = 303.5 N·m. This is about 68 percent of full-load torque, so the fan can start only if its load torque at standstill is below this value.

Answer: 303.5 N·m

(c)

In a star-delta starter the motor windings are first connected in star, so the voltage across each winding is 1/√3 of its rated delta value. The line current in star is one third of the line current for direct delta starting, because the phase current falls by 1/√3 and the line to phase relation changes by another √3. Therefore the supply current is 434/3 = 144.7 A. The starting torque falls to one third of its direct value, which is 718.2/3 = 239.4 N·m. Star-delta starting therefore reduces torque more than the 65 percent autotransformer, and it also creates a current transient when switching to delta.

Answer: 144.7 A

(d)

The synchronous speed is ns = 120 f/P, so for P = 6 and ns = 900 rpm, f = 900 × 6/120 = 45 Hz. The rated voltage at 60 Hz is 600 V, so a constant ratio of 10 V per hertz requires the voltage to be 450 V at 45 Hz. Keeping the volts per hertz constant holds the air-gap flux at its rated value, so the motor can still produce its rated torque. Reducing frequency without reducing the voltage would drive the core into saturation and the magnetizing current would rise sharply, which would overheat the motor.

Answer: 45 Hz

(e)

At full-load torque with constant flux, the slip speed in rpm is the same as at rated condition. At rated condition the slip speed is 0.025 × 1200 = 30 rpm. The speed at 45 Hz is therefore the synchronous speed minus this slip speed: 900 - 30 = 870 rpm. This works because the torque of a constant-flux induction motor depends mainly on the slip frequency, so equal torque means equal slip frequency, which means equal slip speed in rpm for a fixed number of poles. The percentage slip at the lower speed is 30/900 = 3.3 percent, higher than the rated 2.5 percent, so rotor copper loss per unit power is higher.

Answer: 870 rpm

Problem 4 [A6-019] Distribution system voltage drop and capacitor placement

A rural 13.8 kV (line to line), three-phase, 60 Hz feeder in eastern Ontario supplies a single lumped load at its far end. The load is balanced at 4.5 MW with a power factor of 0.85 lagging, and the receiving-end voltage is regulated at 13.8 kV line to line. The feeder total series impedance is 1.8 + j3.6 ohm per phase, and its shunt capacitance is neglected. A capacitor bank is to be installed at the load end to raise the power factor to 0.95 lagging at the same real power. Use the per-phase equivalent circuit with the receiving-end phase voltage as reference, and calculate the sending-end voltage exactly as a phasor sum.

  1. (a) Find the sending-end line-to-line voltage in kV for the uncorrected load. [5]
  2. (b) Find the capacitor bank rating in kvar needed to correct the power factor to 0.95 lagging. [4]
  3. (c) Find the sending-end line-to-line voltage in kV after correction, with the receiving end still at 13.8 kV. [5]
  4. (d) Find the reduction in total three-phase feeder resistive loss in kW caused by the capacitor. [6]
(a)

The receiving-end phase voltage is Vr = 13 800/√3 = 7967.4 V. The line current is I = P/(√3 VL pf) = 4.5 × 106/(√3 × 13 800 × 0.85) = 221.5 A, lagging by cos-1 0.85 = 31.79 degrees. The feeder drop is Z I = (1.8 + j3.6)(221.5 ∠ -31.79°) = 4.025 ∠ 63.43° × 221.5 ∠ -31.79° = 891.5 ∠ 31.64° = 758.8 + j467.8 V. The sending-end phase voltage is Vs = 7967.4 + 758.8 + j467.8 = 8726.2 + j467.8 V, with magnitude 8738.7 V. The line-to-line value is √3 × 8738.7 = 15.14 kV, which is a rise of 9.7 percent above the load voltage, so the feeder alone cannot hold voltage at this load.

Answer: 15.14 kV

(b)

The real power is unchanged, so the capacitor must supply the difference in reactive power between the original and corrected conditions. At 0.85 lagging, tan φ1 = 0.6197 and Q1 = 4500 × 0.6197 = 2788.7 kvar. At 0.95 lagging, tan φ2 = 0.3287 and Q2 = 4500 × 0.3287 = 1479.1 kvar. The capacitor bank rating is Qc = Q1 - Q2 = 1309.8 kvar, or 1310 kvar. Banks come in standard steps, so a 1200 kvar or 1500 kvar bank would be chosen in practice, and the 1500 kvar step would risk overcorrection when the load is light, so a switched bank is common.

Answer: 1310 kvar

(c)

After correction the current falls to I2 = 4.5 × 106/(√3 × 13 800 × 0.95) = 198.2 A, lagging by cos-1 0.95 = 18.19 degrees. The feeder drop is (1.8 + j3.6)(198.2 ∠ -18.19°) = 4.025 ∠ 63.43° × 198.2 ∠ -18.19° = 797.7 ∠ 45.24° = 561.6 + j566.4 V. The sending-end phase voltage is 7967.4 + 561.6 + j566.4 = 8529.0 + j566.4 V, with magnitude 8547.9 V, or 14.81 kV line to line. The voltage rise across the feeder is now 7.3 percent instead of 9.7 percent, so the capacitor reduces the voltage drop by about 0.33 kV at the sending end, in the sense of a lower required source voltage.

Answer: 14.81 kV

(d)

The three-phase resistive loss in the feeder is 3 I2 R, where R = 1.8 ohm. Before correction, 3 × 221.52 × 1.8 = 3 × 49 062 × 1.8 = 264.9 kW. After correction, 3 × 198.22 × 1.8 = 3 × 39 283 × 1.8 = 212.1 kW. The reduction is 264.9 - 212.1 = 52.8 kW. Equivalent to the formula ΔP = 3R(I12 - I22). Over 8760 hours at a utility cost of a few cents per kWh this loss reduction is worth thousands of dollars a year, which is a standard economic justification for placing a capacitor close to the load rather than at the substation.

Answer: 52.8 kW

Problem 5 [A6-020] Machine or system selection combining losses, rating and cost

A water utility in Ontario must choose between two 400 V, three-phase, 60 Hz induction motors for a raw-water pump. The pump needs 90 kW at the shaft and runs 6000 hours per year at this load. Motor A is a standard-efficiency design with an efficiency of 93.5 percent at this load and a purchase price of 9800 dollars. Motor B is a premium-efficiency design with an efficiency of 95.8 percent at this load and a price of 13 600 dollars. Electricity costs 0.11 dollars per kWh, and the utility evaluates projects over 12 years at a discount rate of 8 percent per year, using end-of-year savings and no salvage value. Maintenance cost and installation cost are the same for both motors, and the pump load is assumed constant.

  1. (a) Find the power loss in motor A at the operating point, in kW. [3]
  2. (b) Find the annual energy cost saving of motor B compared with motor A, in dollars. [4]
  3. (c) Find the simple payback period in years for the extra purchase price of motor B. [4]
  4. (d) Find the net present value of choosing motor B over motor A across 12 years at 8 percent, in dollars. [5]
  5. (e) Give one reason, other than purchase price and efficiency, why the premium motor can reduce the pump's actual power draw or increase it, and say which effect the utility should check. [4]
(a)

The output power is the shaft power of 90 kW, and the efficiency is the ratio of output to input, so the input power of motor A is Pin = 90/0.935 = 96.26 kW. The power loss is the difference between input and output, Ploss = 96.26 - 90 = 6.26 kW. This heat is released in the motor windings, core and bearings, and the pump room must be ventilated to remove it. For a motor of this size, the losses are typically 60 percent in the windings, with the remainder in the core, friction and stray loss. The loss figure is used below to find the energy cost of each motor over a year of operation.

Answer: 6.26 kW

(b)

Motor B has the input power Pin = 90/0.958 = 93.95 kW, so its loss is 3.95 kW. The difference in input power between the two motors is 96.26 - 93.95 = 2.311 kW. Over 6000 hours the energy saving is 2.311 × 6000 = 13 866 kWh per year. At 0.11 dollars per kWh, the annual saving is 13 866 × 0.11 = 1525 dollars. This saving is the same each year as long as the load, hours and electricity price are unchanged, and it can be treated as a uniform annual amount in the present-worth calculation of part d. The saving is lower than it appears if the pump is lightly loaded.

Answer: 1525 dollars

(c)

The extra purchase price of the premium motor is 13 600 - 9800 = 3800 dollars. The simple payback period is the extra cost divided by the annual saving, 3800/1525.2 = 2.49 years. It ignores the time value of money and any savings after payback, so it is a screening measure only. A payback of about two and a half years against a motor life of 12 or more years is generally treated as attractive by utilities, since most efficiency measures are accepted when payback is below five years. The next part tests the same decision with the discount rate included.

Answer: 2.49 years

(d)

The present worth of a uniform annual saving A over n years at interest i is A × [1 - (1 + i)-n]/i. With A = 1525.2 dollars, i = 0.08 and n = 12, the factor is [1 - 1.08-12]/0.08 = (1 - 0.3971)/0.08 = 7.536. The present worth of the savings is 1525.2 × 7.536 = 11 494 dollars. Subtracting the extra purchase cost of 3800 dollars gives a net present value of 7694 dollars. The value is positive, so the premium motor is the better choice economically. The result would remain positive even if electricity prices fell by about a third, since the margin is large.

Answer: 7694 dollars

(e)

The premium motor usually has lower rotor resistance and so runs at a smaller slip, which means a slightly higher shaft speed than the standard motor. For a centrifugal pump, the power drawn varies roughly with the cube of speed, so a speed rise of one percent raises the pump power by about three percent. That extra power can cancel some of the saving found above, since the pump delivers more flow than needed, and the flow may then be throttled or the pump speed trimmed. The utility should check the actual operating speed of each motor and the pump power at that speed. A higher inrush current is another consideration.

Answer: Higher rated speed from lower slip

A6 Practice Paper 5

Problem 1 [A6-021] Magnetic circuits, flux, reluctance and inductance

A smoothing inductor for a 60 Hz rectifier supply is wound on a gapped laminated core. The core is a single closed rectangular path with a uniform cross-sectional area of 9.0 cm² and a mean magnetic path length of 0.42 m in iron. The iron has a constant relative permeability of 3000 over the working range. One air gap of length g is cut across the full cross-section of the core. The coil has 400 turns. Use μ0 = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m, neglect fringing and leakage flux, and assume the air-gap area equals the core area. The design target is a coil inductance of 40.0 mH at low current. The core iron is to be operated at a flux density of 1.20 T at the peak current.

  1. (a) Find the air-gap length g, in millimetres, needed to give an inductance of 40.0 mH. [7]
  2. (b) Find the coil current, in amperes, that produces a core flux density of 1.20 T. [6]
  3. (c) At that current, find the percentage of the stored magnetic energy that sits in the air gap. [7]
(a)

Treat the circuit as two reluctances in series. The inductance is L = N²/(Rc + Rg), so the total reluctance must be Rt = N²/L = 400² / 0.040 = 4.00×10⁶ A-turns/Wb. The iron reluctance is Rc = lc/(μ0 μr A) = 0.42 / (4π×10⁻⁷ × 3000 × 9.0×10⁻⁴) = 1.238×10⁵ A-turns/Wb. The gap must supply the remainder: Rg = 4.00×10⁶ − 1.238×10⁵ = 3.876×10⁶. For an air gap Rg = g/(μ0 A), so g = Rg μ0 A = 3.876×10⁶ × 4π×10⁻⁷ × 9.0×10⁻⁴ = 4.38×10⁻³ m. The gap dominates the design, which is the normal reason for gapping an inductor core: the inductance then depends mainly on a dimension that is easy to control rather than on μr.

Answer: g ≈ 4.38 mm

(b)

The flux is Φ = B A = 1.20 × 9.0×10⁻⁴ = 1.08×10⁻³ Wb. Since the same flux passes through the iron and the gap (no leakage), the magnetomotive force needed is the flux times the total reluctance: N I = Φ Rt = 1.08×10⁻³ × 4.00×10⁶ = 4320 A-turns. Dividing by the turns gives I = 4320/400 = 10.8 A. The linear model assumes the iron stays unsaturated, which is acceptable at 1.20 T for good laminated steel, and it is the reason the design target was stated at this flux density. The iron needs only about 134 A-turns of this total, while the gap takes the remaining 4186 A-turns, so the current is almost wholly set by the gap.

Answer: I ≈ 10.8 A

(c)

Energy stored in each reluctance for the same flux is W = ½ Φ² R, so the fraction held in the gap is simply the reluctance ratio Rg/Rt. Fraction = 3.876×10⁶ / 4.00×10⁶ = 0.969, or 96.9 percent. As a check, the total energy is ½ L I² = ½ × 0.040 × 10.8² = 2.333 J, of which 2.26 J is in the gap and 0.07 J in the iron. This is why gapped inductor cores store energy in the air while the iron carries the flux, and why saturation of the iron, rather than heating of the gap, limits the current rating of such a part. A larger gap would raise the saturation current but would need more turns for the same inductance.

Answer: ≈ 97 % in the gap

Problem 2 [A6-022] Ferromagnetic cores, losses and saturation

The manufacturer of a grade of laminated silicon steel for a transformer core publishes two loss measurements taken on a ring sample at the same peak flux density of 1.50 T: 2.40 W/kg at 50 Hz and 3.00 W/kg at 60 Hz. Assume the specific core loss at 1.50 T follows P = a f + b f², where a f is hysteresis loss and b f² is eddy-current loss, with constants a and b independent of frequency. At any other peak flux density Bm both terms scale with Bm² (Steinmetz exponent 2 assumed for hysteresis). A core built from this steel has a mass of 38 kg. The same core, with the same winding and turns, is proposed for use on a 400 Hz aircraft ground-power supply at the same rms voltage as on the 60 Hz supply. For a sinusoidal supply, the peak flux density is inversely proportional to frequency at constant voltage.

  1. (a) Find the eddy-current coefficient b, in W·s²/kg, that applies at 1.50 T, using the two measurements. [6]
  2. (b) Find the total core loss, in watts, of the 38 kg core at 60 Hz and 1.50 T. [4]
  3. (c) Find the total core loss, in watts, of the same core at 400 Hz and the same rms voltage. [6]
  4. (d) At 400 Hz, find the percentage of the core loss that is eddy-current loss. [4]
(a)

At the fixed flux density of 1.50 T the model is P = a f + b f², so dividing by f gives a straight line, P/f = a + b f. The two measurements give P/f = 2.40/50 = 0.0480 J/kg at 50 Hz and P/f = 3.00/60 = 0.0500 J/kg at 60 Hz. The slope of this line against frequency is b = (0.0500 − 0.0480)/(60 − 50) = 2.0×10⁻⁴ W·s²/kg. The intercept is the hysteresis coefficient, a = 0.0480 − 2.0×10⁻⁴ × 50 = 0.0380 J/kg. Checking against the 60 Hz point: 0.038 × 60 + 2.0×10⁻⁴ × 3600 = 2.28 + 0.72 = 3.00 W/kg, which agrees. Plotting P/f against f is the standard way to separate the two loss mechanisms from two or more frequency measurements at constant flux density.

Answer: b = 2.0×10⁻⁴ W s²/kg

(b)

At 1.50 T the hysteresis coefficient follows from the 50 Hz point: P/f = a + b f gives a = 0.048 − 2.0×10⁻⁴ × 50 = 0.038 J/kg, using the constants at this flux density. At 60 Hz the loss per kilogram is a f + b f² = 0.038 × 60 + 2.0×10⁻⁴ × 3600 = 2.28 + 0.72 = 3.00 W/kg, which reproduces the manufacturer figure. For the 38 kg core, P = 3.00 × 38 = 114 W. Of this, 86.6 W is hysteresis and 27.4 W is eddy current. The loss appears in the equivalent circuit as the core-loss resistance Rc = V²/P, so the 114 W figure sets the no-load real power the transformer draws from the supply and the heating the core must lose through its surface.

Answer: P = 114 W

(c)

With the voltage held constant, peak flux density scales as Bm = 1.50 × 60/400 = 0.225 T. The flux ratio is 0.225/1.50 = 0.15, so the Bm² factor is 0.0225 relative to the 1.50 T figures. The loss per kilogram at 400 Hz is (a f + b f²) × 0.0225 = (0.038 × 400 + 2.0×10⁻⁴ × 160000) × 0.0225 = (15.2 + 32.0) × 0.0225 = 1.062 W/kg. For 38 kg this is 1.062 × 38 = 40.4 W. The loss falls well below the 114 W at 60 Hz because the flux density drops so far, even though both loss terms rise with frequency. This is why 400 Hz equipment uses much smaller cores: the same voltage needs only 15 percent of the flux, so core area can shrink. This check assumes the loss law holds at 400 Hz, which for thin laminations is approximate.

Answer: P ≈ 40.4 W

(d)

At 400 Hz the hysteresis term per kilogram is 15.2 × 0.0225 = 0.342 W/kg and the eddy-current term is 32.0 × 0.0225 = 0.720 W/kg. Their sum is 1.062 W/kg, matching part c. The eddy-current share is 0.720/1.062 = 0.678, or 67.8 percent. At 60 Hz the eddy share was only 0.72/3.00 = 24 percent, so frequency has moved the dominant loss mechanism from hysteresis to eddy currents, because the eddy term grows with f² while the hysteresis term grows with f. Thinner laminations or higher resistivity steel (silicon content, or amorphous alloy) are the usual remedies for a 400 Hz core, since they lower b directly without affecting a.

Answer: 67.8 % eddy-current

Problem 3 [A6-023] Single-phase transformer equivalent circuit and tests

A 50 kVA, 2400/240 V, 60 Hz single-phase distribution transformer is tested for an Ontario utility. In the open-circuit test, rated voltage of 240 V is applied to the low-voltage winding with the high-voltage winding open, and the instruments read 5.41 A and 186 W. In the short-circuit test, the low-voltage winding is shorted and the high-voltage winding is excited with just enough voltage to circulate rated current; the instruments read 75.0 V and 650 W. Use the approximate equivalent circuit with the shunt branch (a core-loss resistance Rc in parallel with a magnetising reactance Xm) placed on the low-voltage side, and the series branch (Req + jXeq) referred to the high-voltage side. Assume the shunt branch sits at the supply terminals.

  1. (a) Find the core-loss resistance Rc, in ohms, on the low-voltage side. [4]
  2. (b) Find the magnetising reactance Xm, in ohms, on the low-voltage side. [4]
