  3. (c) Find the equivalent series resistance Req referred to the high-voltage side, in ohms. [4]
  4. (d) Find the equivalent series reactance Xeq referred to the high-voltage side, in ohms. [3]
  5. (e) With the high-voltage side held at 2400 V and the transformer delivering rated current at 0.80 power factor lagging, find the low-voltage terminal voltage in volts. [5]
(a)

In the open-circuit test the whole input is the core loss, since the winding current is tiny and its copper loss is negligible. The core-loss branch current is Ic = P/V = 186/240 = 0.775 A. The branch resistance is Rc = V/Ic = 240/0.775 = 309.7 Ω, or equivalently V²/P = 240²/186. The power factor of the test is 186/(240 × 5.41) = 0.143 lagging, so the exciting current is almost purely reactive. Because the test was done on the low-voltage side, where the voltage and the instruments are convenient, this Rc is referred to that side, matching the equivalent circuit requested.

Answer: Rc ≈ 310 Ω

(b)

The magnetising current is the reactive component of the exciting current: Im = √(I0² − Ic²) = √(5.41² − 0.775²) = √(29.268 − 0.601) = 5.354 A. The magnetising reactance is Xm = V/Im = 240/5.354 = 44.8 Ω. This is much smaller than Rc, consistent with a transformer whose no-load current is mainly magnetising. The no-load current of 5.41 A is about 2.6 percent of the rated low-voltage current of 208.3 A, a typical value for a small distribution unit. The shunt branch gives only the first-order model; the nonlinear B-H curve means Xm falls as the voltage rises into saturation.

Answer: Xm ≈ 44.8 Ω

(c)

Rated high-voltage current is Irated = 50000/2400 = 20.83 A, and the short-circuit test passes this current, so the copper loss measured is the full-load value. The series resistance referred to the high-voltage side follows from P = I² Req: Req = 650/20.83² = 650/434.0 = 1.498 Ω. Core loss during the short-circuit test is negligible because the applied voltage is only 75/2400 = 3.1 percent of rated, and core loss varies roughly as the square of voltage. The total copper loss therefore includes both winding resistances referred to the high-voltage side, which is what Req represents. On the low-voltage side the same quantity would be 1.498/100 = 0.01498 Ω, since the turns ratio is 10.

Answer: Req ≈ 1.50 Ω

(d)

The magnitude of the equivalent series impedance is |Zeq| = Vsc/Isc = 75.0/20.83 = 3.600 Ω. The reactance follows from the impedance triangle: Xeq = √(Zeq² − Req²) = √(3.600² − 1.498²) = √(12.96 − 2.243) = √10.717 = 3.274 Ω. The impedance in per unit, on the high-voltage base of 2400²/50000 = 115.2 Ω, is 3.600/115.2 = 0.03125, or 3.1 percent. The X/R ratio of about 2.2 is typical of a small distribution transformer. The leakage reactance is what limits the fault current on the secondary side and sets the voltage drop under load.

Answer: Xeq ≈ 3.27 Ω

(e)

Refer the load to the high-voltage side. The current is 20.83 A at 0.80 lagging, so I = 20.83∠−36.87° A. With the shunt branch at the supply, the source voltage appears across the shunt branch and the load voltage is found from the series drop. V2' = 2400 − I(Req + jXeq) = 2400 − 20.83∠−36.87° × (1.498 + j3.274). The product is 20.83 × 3.600 = 75.0 V at an angle of −36.87° + 65.4° = 28.5°, which is 65.9 + j35.8 V. So V2' = 2400 − 65.9 − j35.8 = 2334.1 − j35.8 V, with magnitude 2334.4 V. Divide by the turns ratio of 10 to refer back to the low-voltage side: V2 ≈ 233.4 V. The voltage regulation is therefore about (240 − 233.4)/233.4 = 2.8 percent at this load.

Answer: V2 ≈ 233.4 V

Problem 4 [A6-024] Transformer regulation and efficiency

A 25 kVA, 2400/240 V, 60 Hz pole-mounted transformer supplies a small farm. Tests show a constant core loss of 140 W and a full-load copper loss of 310 W. Referred to the 240 V winding, the equivalent series reactance is 0.045 Ω; the equivalent series resistance follows from the copper loss at rated current. The load pattern over a 24 h day is 6 h at full rated load, 10 h at one half of rated kVA, and 8 h with the transformer energised but unloaded. Every loaded period is at 0.90 power factor lagging unless a part says otherwise. Treat the core loss as constant at rated voltage and the copper loss as varying with the square of the load current. Voltage drop in the series branch is to be found with the simple series model.

  1. (a) Find the load, in kVA, at which the efficiency is a maximum. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum efficiency, in percent, at unity power factor. [4]
  3. (c) Find the all-day (energy) efficiency, in percent, for the stated daily load pattern at 0.90 power factor. [6]
  4. (d) Find the voltage regulation, in percent, at rated load and 0.90 power factor lagging. [6]
(a)

Efficiency is a maximum when the variable copper loss equals the constant core loss. With the load as a fraction x of rated kVA, copper loss is x² × 310 W. Setting x² × 310 = 140 gives x = √(140/310) = 0.672. The load is therefore 0.672 × 25 = 16.8 kVA. This is the standard result for a transformer, and it means the unit reaches its best efficiency at about two-thirds of rated load. For distribution transformers that spend much of the day lightly loaded, designers deliberately choose a core loss that is small relative to copper loss, so that this peak lands near the typical operating load rather than at full rating.

Answer: 16.8 kVA

(b)

At the maximum-efficiency point the copper loss equals the core loss of 140 W, so the total loss is 280 W. The output at unity power factor is 16.80 kVA × 1.0 = 16.80 kW. The efficiency is η = output/(output + losses) = 16800/(16800 + 280) = 0.98361, or 98.36 percent. Note that unity power factor is assumed here because the question asks for the best case; at 0.90 power factor the same loads give a slightly lower figure, since output power falls while the losses are unchanged. The result shows that the loss fraction is under 2 percent even at this best point, typical of a small distribution unit.

Answer: η ≈ 98.36 %

(c)

Energy out per day at 0.90 power factor: full load 25 kVA × 0.9 = 22.5 kW for 6 h gives 135.0 kWh; half load 11.25 kW for 10 h gives 112.5 kWh. Total output is 247.5 kWh. Core loss runs all 24 h: 0.140 kW × 24 = 3.360 kWh. Copper loss is 0.310 kW for 6 h at full load, giving 1.860 kWh, plus 0.310 × 0.25 = 0.0775 kW for 10 h at half load, giving 0.775 kWh, for a total of 2.635 kWh. Total loss is 3.360 + 2.635 = 5.995 kWh. The all-day efficiency is 247.5/(247.5 + 5.995) = 0.9764, or 97.6 percent. It is lower than the peak efficiency because the 8 h of no-load operation adds core loss with no output energy.

Answer: η(all-day) ≈ 97.6 %

(d)

Rated low-voltage current is 25000/240 = 104.17 A. The series resistance referred to this winding is Req = 310/104.17² = 0.02857 Ω. At 0.90 lagging, the angle is 25.84°, so the load current is I = 104.17∠−25.84° A. The no-load (source-side) voltage is E = V + I(Req + jXeq) with V = 240 V. The drop is I Z where Z = 0.02857 + j0.045 = 0.05330∠57.6° Ω, so I Z = 5.552∠31.8° V = 4.72 + j2.93 V. Then E = 244.72 + j2.93 V, with magnitude 244.74 V. Regulation = (244.74 − 240)/240 = 1.975 percent, so about 1.97 percent. The reactance contributes most of the drop at a lagging power factor, as expected.

Answer: Regulation ≈ 1.97 %

Problem 5 [A6-025] Balanced three-phase wye and delta systems

A food-processing plant in Ontario is fed from a 600 V, three-phase, 60 Hz, three-wire service. Its balanced load draws 180 kW at 0.72 power factor lagging. The utility penalises power factors below 0.95, so the plant engineer will install a balanced bank of three identical capacitors on the 600 V bus to correct the power factor to 0.95 lagging. The bank can be connected either in delta or in wye. Line-to-line voltage remains 600 V after the capacitors are added, and the plant load itself is unchanged. Neglect the resistance of the capacitors and of the feeder, and treat all voltages as balanced and sinusoidal.

  1. (a) Find the line current, in amperes, before correction. [4]
  2. (b) Find the three-phase reactive power of the capacitor bank, in kvar, needed to reach 0.95 lagging. [4]
  3. (c) Find the capacitance of each capacitor, in microfarads, if the bank is connected in delta. [4]
  4. (d) Find the capacitance of each capacitor, in microfarads, if the bank is connected in wye. [4]
  5. (e) Find the line current, in amperes, after correction. [4]
(a)

For a balanced three-phase load, apparent power is S = P/pf = 180/0.72 = 250.0 kVA. The line current follows from S = √3 VL IL, so IL = 250000/(√3 × 600) = 250000/1039.2 = 240.6 A. This is the current the service and feeder carry before correction. The reactive power of the load, found next, is Q1 = P tan(acos 0.72) = 180 × 0.9639 = 173.5 kvar. Apparent power and line current both exceed what the real power alone would need, which is exactly the cost the utility penalty reflects, since the conductors and transformers must be sized for the current and not the real power.

Answer: IL ≈ 240.6 A

(b)

The target power factor of 0.95 requires a reactive power of Q2 = P tan(acos 0.95) = 180 × 0.3287 = 59.2 kvar. The bank must supply the difference between the load reactive power and this value: Qc = Q1 − Q2 = 173.5 − 59.2 = 114.3 kvar for all three phases together. The real power is not altered by the capacitors, since they are lossless here. The bank rating is therefore about 114 kvar at 600 V; in practice the nearest standard size or a stepped, switched bank would be chosen, with attention to avoiding overcorrection at light load, which would produce a leading power factor and a voltage rise.

Answer: Qc ≈ 114.3 kvar

(c)

In delta each capacitor has the full line voltage 600 V across it, and each carries one third of the reactive power. Per capacitor, Q = 114.33/3 = 38.11 kvar = V² ω C, with ω = 2π × 60 = 377.0 rad/s. Solving, C = Q/(ω V²) = 38110/(377.0 × 600²) = 38110/(1.3572×10⁸) = 2.808×10⁻⁴ F = 281 μF. The current in each capacitor is V ω C = 600 × 377.0 × 2.808×10⁻⁴ = 63.5 A, and the line current drawn by the bank is √3 times this, 110 A. Delta connection uses the smaller capacitance because the capacitor voltage is the highest available, so it is the cheaper arrangement per kvar.

Answer: C(delta) ≈ 281 μF

(d)

In wye each capacitor sees the phase voltage 600/√3 = 346.4 V, and again carries one third of the reactive power, 38.11 kvar. Then C = Q/(ω Vφ²) = 38110/(377.0 × 346.4²) = 38110/(4.524×10⁷) = 8.424×10⁻⁴ F = 842 μF. This is exactly three times the delta capacitance, because the capacitor voltage is lower by √3 and the capacitance for the same kvar scales with the inverse square of the voltage. Wye therefore needs three times as much capacitance and so is bulkier and costlier, but it offers lower stress on each capacitor and a limit on fault energy; the choice is often made by the capacitor manufacturer's voltage rating.

Answer: C(wye) ≈ 842 μF

(e)

After correction the real power is still 180 kW but the power factor is 0.95, so S = 180/0.95 = 189.5 kVA. The line current is IL = 189500/(√3 × 600) = 189500/1039.2 = 182.3 A. This is a reduction of 58.2 A, or 24 percent, from the uncorrected 240.6 A. The feeder I²R loss falls by about 43 percent since it varies with the square of current, which is the energy benefit that goes along with the avoided penalty. The reactive power now seen by the utility is 59.2 kvar rather than 173.5 kvar.

Answer: IL ≈ 182.3 A

A6 Practice Paper 6

Problem 1 [A6-026] Three-phase power, per-unit system and one-line diagrams

A one-line study is made of a generating station that feeds a 138 kV transmission line through a step-up transformer. The generator terminal bus is at 13.8 kV. The transformer is rated 100 MVA, 13.8/138 kV, with a leakage reactance of 0.10 per unit on its own rating, and its resistance is negligible. The 138 kV line is 60 Ω of series reactance per phase, with no resistance and no shunt elements. At the receiving end, at 138 kV bus voltage held at exactly 1.00 per unit, a load of 60 MW and 29.0 Mvar lagging is connected. Use a system base of 100 MVA, with base voltages of 13.8 kV on the generator side and 138 kV on the line side. A shunt capacitor bank can be connected to the receiving bus. Treat the system as balanced.

  1. (a) Find the line reactance in per unit on the system base. [4]
  2. (b) With the load connected and no capacitor, find the generator terminal bus voltage, in kilovolts line-to-line, needed to hold the receiving bus at 1.00 per unit. [5]
  3. (c) Find the capacitor bank rating, in Mvar, that makes the generator terminal voltage equal to the receiving-bus voltage of 1.00 per unit. [6]
  4. (d) With that capacitor connected, find the line current, in amperes, on the 138 kV line. [5]
(a)

The base impedance on the 138 kV side is Zbase = (138 kV)²/(100 MVA) = 190.44 Ω. The line reactance in per unit is therefore Xline = 60/190.44 = 0.3151 pu. The transformer reactance of 0.10 pu is already on the same MVA base, and its voltage ratings match the base voltages (13.8/138 kV), so no change of base is needed. The total series reactance between the generator terminal bus and the receiving bus is X = 0.10 + 0.3151 = 0.4151 pu. Working in per unit means every voltage in the problem is a ratio to its own base, so the transformer ratio disappears and the network becomes a single series reactance.

Answer: Xline ≈ 0.315 pu

(b)

The load in per unit is S = 0.60 + j0.29 pu, and the receiving voltage is the reference, VR = 1.0∠0° pu. The current is I = (S/VR)* = 0.60 − j0.29 pu. The generator-side voltage is VT = VR + jX I = 1 + j0.4151 × (0.60 − j0.29) = 1 + 0.4151 × 0.29 + j0.4151 × 0.60 = 1.1204 + j0.2490 pu. Its magnitude is √(1.1204² + 0.2490²) = 1.1477 pu. Converting with the 13.8 kV base, the terminal voltage is 1.1477 × 13.8 = 15.84 kV, well above the generator rating. This shows how a lagging reactive load drawn through a long reactance forces the sending end up, and why such a system cannot operate without reactive support at the load.

Answer: VT ≈ 15.84 kV

(c)

With a capacitor at the receiving bus the net reactive load becomes Qn = 0.29 − Qc (per unit). The terminal voltage is VT = 1 + X Qn + j X P, using P = 0.60. Requiring |VT| = 1.0: (1 + X Qn)² + (X P)² = 1. With X P = 0.4151 × 0.60 = 0.2491, this gives 1 + X Qn = √(1 − 0.0620) = 0.9685, so Qn = (0.9685 − 1)/0.4151 = −0.0759 pu. The net reactive load is slightly leading. Then Qc = 0.29 + 0.0759 = 0.3659 pu = 36.6 Mvar, taking the positive root so that the terminal voltage stays near unity and the angle across the series reactance stays small. The capacitor supplies more than the load requires because the line itself absorbs reactive power I²X in its series reactance.

Answer: Qc ≈ 36.6 Mvar

(d)

With the capacitor connected, the receiving-end current in per unit is I = (P − jQn)/VR with Qn = −0.0759: I = 0.60 + j0.0759 pu, giving |I| = √(0.60² + 0.0759²) = 0.6048 pu. The base current on the 138 kV side is Ibase = Sbase/(√3 Vbase) = 100×10⁶/(√3 × 138×10³) = 418.4 A. Then the line current is 0.6048 × 418.4 = 253.0 A. Without the capacitor the current would have been |0.60 − j0.29| = 0.6664 pu, or 278.8 A, so the capacitor also relieves the line of about 26 A. The lower current cuts the I²R loss of any real line and eases thermal limits.

Answer: I ≈ 253 A

Problem 2 [A6-027] Unbalanced three-phase loads

A 600 V, three-phase, four-wire, 60 Hz service (346.4 V line-to-neutral) supplies three single-phase loads connected between each line and the neutral. The phase sequence is a-b-c, with Van = 346.4∠0°, Vbn = 346.4∠−120° and Vcn = 346.4∠+120° volts. Load a is 30.0 kW at unity power factor. Load b is 18.0 kW at 0.80 power factor lagging. Load c is 24.0 kW at 0.90 power factor lagging. Each load behaves as a constant impedance whose real and reactive power are the values given when 346.4 V is across it. The neutral conductor has negligible impedance in normal service. A fault on the neutral conductor later opens it completely, leaving the three loads in a wye with an isolated neutral point n′.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the neutral current, in amperes, with the neutral intact. [7]
  2. (b) Find the total real power, in kilowatts, drawn by the three loads. [3]
  3. (c) After the neutral opens, find the magnitude of the voltage Vn′n between the load star point and the source neutral, in volts. [7]
  4. (d) After the neutral opens, find the magnitude of the voltage across load a, in volts. [3]
(a)

With the neutral intact each load has the full phase voltage across it. Load currents follow from I = S/V: Ia = 30000/346.4 = 86.60 A at 0°. Load b has S = 18/0.8 = 22.5 kVA, so |Ib| = 22500/346.4 = 64.95 A, at −120° − 36.87° = −156.87°. Load c has S = 24/0.9 = 26.67 kVA, so |Ic| = 26670/346.4 = 76.98 A, at +120° − 25.84° = +94.16°. In rectangular form Ia = 86.60 + j0, Ib = −59.73 − j25.51, Ic = −5.58 + j76.78 A. The neutral current is In = Ia + Ib + Ic = 21.29 + j51.27 A, with magnitude √(21.29² + 51.27²) = 55.5 A. The neutral therefore carries about 64 percent of the largest line current.

Answer: In ≈ 55.5 A

(b)

Real power adds directly, since each load dissipates what was stated and the neutral wire is lossless. Ptotal = 30.0 + 18.0 + 24.0 = 72.0 kW. As a check, the sum of Vφ Iφ cos φ over the phases is 346.4 × (86.60 + 64.95 × 0.8 + 76.98 × 0.9) = 346.4 × (86.60 + 51.96 + 69.28) = 346.4 × 207.84 = 72.0 kW. The reactive power is 0 + 13.5 + 11.62 = 25.1 kvar lagging, so the total complex power is 72.0 + j25.1 kVA. The unbalance does not change the total real power in this case; it only changes how the current distributes among the conductors, and thereby the neutral current and any voltage drop in the conductors.

Answer: P = 72.0 kW

(c)

Find the load impedances from Z = |V|²/S*: Za = 346.4²/30000 = 4.000 Ω; Zb = 346.4²/22500 = 5.333 Ω at 36.87°, which is 4.267 + j3.200 Ω; Zc = 346.4²/26670 = 4.500 Ω at 25.84°, which is 4.050 + j1.962 Ω. Admittances: Ya = 0.2500 S, Yb = 0.1500 − j0.1125 S, Yc = 0.2000 − j0.0969 S. The total is Ysum = 0.6000 − j0.2094 S, with magnitude 0.6355 S. With an isolated neutral, Σ(V − Vn′n) Y = 0 gives Vn′n = ΣVY/ΣY. The numerator ΣVY is exactly the former neutral current, 21.29 + j51.27 A, with magnitude 55.5 A. So |Vn′n| = 55.5/0.6355 = 87.3 V. The neutral point shifts by about a quarter of the phase voltage.

Answer: |Vn′n| ≈ 87.3 V

(d)

The voltage across load a is Van − Vn′n. The shift Vn′n = (21.29 + j51.27)/(0.6000 − j0.2094) = 55.51∠67.4° / 0.6355∠−19.2° = 87.35∠86.6° V, which is 5.1 + j87.2 V. Then Va = 346.4 − 5.1 − j87.2 = 341.3 − j87.2 V, with magnitude √(341.3² + 87.2²) = 352.3 V. The same method gives |Vb| = 426 V and |Vc| = 278 V across the other two loads, so load b sees 23 percent above its rating and load c 20 percent below. This is why an open neutral is dangerous: equipment on the lightly loaded phases can be overvoltage damaged.

Answer: |Va| ≈ 352 V

Problem 3 [A6-028] Three-phase transformer connections and phase shift

A mill is served from a 13.8 kV three-phase, 60 Hz distribution line through a bank of three identical single-phase transformers, each rated 150 kVA, 13 800/346.4 V. The high-voltage windings are connected in delta and the low-voltage windings in wye, giving 600 V line-to-line on the secondary side. Treat the transformers as ideal for the calculations. The mill load is three-phase, balanced, 380 kW at 0.88 power factor lagging, supplied at 600 V line-to-line. The utility also keeps spare 13 800/600 V single-phase units for emergencies. It is considering using two of three identical spare units of the same 150 kVA rating in an open-delta connection if the main bank has to be removed from service.

  1. (a) Find the rated line current, in amperes, on the 13.8 kV side of the full bank. [4]
  2. (b) Find the rated current, in amperes, in each delta-connected high-voltage winding. [4]
  3. (c) Find the line current, in amperes, on the 600 V side when the mill load is supplied. [4]
  4. (d) State, with the reason, the phase displacement between the 13.8 kV and 600 V line voltages in this delta-wye connection. [4]
  5. (e) Find the three-phase kVA rating of the open-delta bank made from two 150 kVA units. [4]
(a)

The three-phase rating of the bank is 3 × 150 = 450 kVA. The line current on the delta side follows from S = √3 VL IL: IL = 450000/(√3 × 13800) = 450000/23902 = 18.83 A. This current is the one the utility line and the high-side protection must carry at full bank loading. The result does not depend on the winding connection, only on the three-phase kVA and the line voltage, because for any balanced three-phase connection the apparent power is √3 times line voltage times line current. The connection only determines how that line current divides between the windings, which the next part considers.

Answer: IL(HV) ≈ 18.83 A

(b)

Each high-voltage winding is connected between two lines of the delta, so the winding voltage is the full 13.8 kV line voltage, equal to the single-phase unit's rated 13 800 V. Each unit carries one third of the bank rating, so its winding current is Iw = 150000/13800 = 10.87 A. This also equals IL/√3 = 18.83/1.732 = 10.87 A, as expected for a delta connection, where line current is √3 times winding current. On the wye side, the winding current equals the line current: Iw = 150000/346.4 = 433 A, which is the rated 600 V line current of the bank. The unit rating is sufficient for the load, as the next part shows.

Answer: Iw(HV) ≈ 10.87 A

(c)

The load current is found from P = √3 VL IL pf. Then IL = 380000/(√3 × 600 × 0.88) = 380000/914.5 = 415.5 A. The load apparent power is 380/0.88 = 431.8 kVA, so the bank is loaded to 431.8/450 = 96.0 percent of its rating, with each unit carrying 144 kVA, and 415.5/433 = 96.0 percent of rated low-side current. The mill load is within the bank rating but leaves little margin, so future load growth or a transformer being out of service would require reduction or an alternative supply. The corresponding line current on the 13.8 kV side is 18.07 A.

Answer: IL(LV) ≈ 415.5 A

(d)

In a delta-wye bank, each secondary winding voltage (a line-to-neutral voltage on the wye side) is in phase with the primary winding voltage that shares its core, and that primary winding voltage is a line-to-line voltage of the delta. The line-to-line voltage and the corresponding line-to-neutral voltage in a balanced three-phase set differ by 30°. As a result the line voltages on the wye side are displaced by 30° from those on the delta side, not zero. North American practice (the standard connection) arranges the windings so that the low-voltage line voltages lag the high-voltage line voltages by 30° in positive sequence. This matters when paralleling banks, since only connections with the same displacement may be paralleled, and a Delta-Delta bank (zero shift) cannot be paralleled with a Delta-Wye bank.

Answer: 30° displacement (LV lags HV)

(e)

Open delta uses two of the three single-phase units. Each unit still carries its rated current, 10.87 A in the winding, but in the open-delta arrangement the line current equals the winding current rather than √3 times it, so the usable three-phase rating is S = √3 × VL × Iw = √3 × 13800 × 10.87 = 259.8 kVA, or equivalently √3 × 150 = 259.8 kVA. This is only 57.7 percent of the 450 kVA closed-delta rating, even though two of three units, 66.7 percent of the capacity, are used. The mill load of 431.8 kVA therefore exceeds the open-delta rating and could not be supplied in full.

Answer: S(open delta) ≈ 259.8 kVA

Problem 4 [A6-029] Transmission line models and voltage regulation

A 230 kV, 60 Hz, three-phase transmission line in northern Ontario is 120 km long. Its series impedance is z = 0.08 + j0.48 Ω/km per phase and its shunt admittance is y = j3.4 μS/km per phase. Use the nominal π model with the total series impedance Z = z × length in the middle branch and half of the total shunt admittance Y at each end, so that Vs = A Vr + B Ir with A = 1 + ZY/2 and B = Z. The sending-end line-to-line voltage is held at 230 kV. When the line is energised with no load, the receiving end voltage rises above the sending value, so the utility plans a shunt reactor at the receiving end to hold the open-circuit receiving voltage equal to the sending voltage.

  1. (a) Find the total line charging reactive power, in Mvar, produced by the full shunt admittance Y at 230 kV. [4]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the ABCD constant A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the no-load receiving-end line-to-line voltage, in kilovolts. [5]
  4. (d) Find the rating, in Mvar at 230 kV, of the receiving-end shunt reactor that restores the no-load receiving voltage to 230 kV. [7]
(a)

The total shunt admittance for 120 km is Y = j3.4×10⁻⁶ × 120 = j4.08×10⁻⁴ S per phase. Charging reactive power for the three phases is Qc = |Y| VL² with VL the line-to-line voltage, since three-phase reactive power is 3 × (VL/√3)² × |Y| = VL² |Y|. Qc = 4.08×10⁻⁴ × (230×10³)² = 4.08×10⁻⁴ × 5.29×10¹⁰ = 2.158×10⁷ var, or 21.6 Mvar. This is the reactive power the line generates at nominal voltage, a major factor in the voltage rise on a lightly loaded line. Strictly, it varies with the square of the actual line voltage along the line, so this is an estimate at the nominal figure.

Answer: Qc ≈ 21.6 Mvar

(b)

The total series impedance is Z = (0.08 + j0.48) × 120 = 9.6 + j57.6 Ω. The product ZY is (9.6 + j57.6) × j4.08×10⁻⁴ = j3.917×10⁻³ + j² × 0.023501 = −0.023501 + j0.003917. Half of this is −0.011750 + j0.001958, so A = 1 + ZY/2 = 0.98825 + j0.001958. The magnitude is √(0.98825² + 0.001958²) = 0.98825. A is slightly less than one and almost real, because the series reactance and the shunt capacitance combine to give a net voltage rise at no load. This A is also the D constant for a symmetrical line, and the B constant is simply Z.

Answer: |A| ≈ 0.9883

(c)

With no load, Ir = 0, so Vs = A Vr and Vr = Vs/A. The magnitude of the receiving voltage is |Vr| = |Vs|/|A| = 230/0.98825 = 232.7 kV. The no-load rise is 2.7 kV, or 1.2 percent. This is the Ferranti effect on a moderately long line, produced by the charging current flowing through the series inductance of the line. It would be much larger on a line twice as long, because the effect grows roughly with the square of line length. The result also shows that a light-load, high-voltage line can exceed equipment insulation or tap range, which is what the reactor is meant to prevent.

Answer: Vr(no load) ≈ 232.7 kV

(d)

With the reactor connected at the receiving end, let its susceptance be BL, so that Ir = −j BL Vr. Then Vs = (A + B(−jBL)) Vr, so |Vr| = |Vs| / |A − j BL Z|. To hold Vr = Vs we need |A − j BL Z| = 1. Write the complex number: A − j BL (9.6 + j57.6) = (0.98825 + 57.6 BL) + j(0.001958 − 9.6 BL). Setting the imaginary part to zero gives BL = 0.001958/9.6 = 2.04×10⁻⁴ S, and the real part is then 0.98825 + 0.01175 = 1.0000, so the magnitude is exactly one. The reactor rating is Q = BL VL² = 2.04×10⁻⁴ × 5.29×10¹⁰ = 1.079×10⁷ var, or 10.8 Mvar. That is half of the line charging Mvar, which is typical practice for lightly compensating a line.

Answer: Q(reactor) ≈ 10.8 Mvar

Problem 5 [A6-030] Power flow and real and reactive power control

Two buses, S and R, are connected by a lossless transmission circuit whose equivalent series reactance is 40.0 Ω per phase, with no resistance and no line charging. The magnitudes of the line-to-line voltages are held constant at 125 kV at bus S and 115 kV at bus R. The power angle δ is the angle by which the voltage at bus S leads that at bus R. Use the standard lossless transfer relations in three-phase MW and Mvar: P = Vs Vr sin δ / X, Qr = (Vs Vr cos δ − Vr²)/X delivered into bus R, and Qs = (Vs² − Vs Vr cos δ)/X sent from bus S, with voltages in kV and X in ohms. A load of 150 MW at 0.95 power factor lagging is located at bus R. A shunt capacitor bank at bus R can supply the reactive power the line does not.

  1. (a) Find the power angle δ, in degrees, needed to deliver 150 MW to bus R. [4]
  2. (b) Find the reactive power Qr, in Mvar, delivered into bus R by the line at that angle (negative means bus R must send reactive power into the line). [4]
  3. (c) Find the reactive power Qs, in Mvar, leaving bus S. [4]
  4. (d) Find the rating, in Mvar, of the capacitor bank at bus R that, together with the line, supplies the load's reactive power. [4]
  5. (e) Find the percentage of the maximum steady-state transfer limit that remains unused when delivering 150 MW. [4]
(a)

For a lossless line, P = Vs Vr sin δ / X. The product Vs Vr/X = 125 × 115/40.0 = 359.4 MW, because kV² divided by ohms gives MW. Setting 150 = 359.4 sin δ gives sin δ = 0.4174, so δ = 24.67°. This angle is the electrical angle between the two bus voltages; it is what drives the real power flow, while the voltage magnitude difference mainly drives the reactive power. A moderate angle of about 25° is typical of a loaded circuit and leaves room before the steady-state stability limit of 90°, which is examined in part e.

Answer: δ ≈ 24.7°

(b)

With cos δ = cos 24.67° = 0.9087, Qr = (Vs Vr cos δ − Vr²)/X = (125 × 115 × 0.9087 − 115²)/40.0 = (13063 − 13225)/40.0 = −4.05 Mvar. The sign shows that, with these voltage magnitudes, the line delivers no reactive power into bus R; instead bus R must supply 4.05 Mvar back to the line. The line itself absorbs reactive power I²X in its reactance, which is the underlying reason. The sending voltage is only 8.7 percent above the receiving voltage, and the factor cos δ cuts the in-phase part of the sending voltage enough that the net reactive power flows away from R.

Answer: Qr ≈ -4.05 Mvar

(c)

Qs = (Vs² − Vs Vr cos δ)/X = (125² − 13063)/40.0 = (15625 − 13063)/40.0 = 64.05 Mvar. As a consistency check, the reactive power absorbed by the line is Qs − Qr = 64.05 − (−4.05) = 68.1 Mvar, and this should equal I²X in per-phase terms: the apparent power at bus R is S = √(P² + Qr²) = 150.05 MVA, so I = 150.05×10⁶/(√3 × 115×10³) = 753 A, and 3 I² X = 3 × 753² × 40.0 = 68.0 Mvar. This agrees with 68.1 Mvar within rounding, confirming the transfer relations.

Answer: Qs ≈ 64.05 Mvar

(d)

The load at 0.95 power factor lagging and 150 MW needs Ql = 150 × tan(acos 0.95) = 150 × 0.3287 = 49.30 Mvar. The line delivers Qr = −4.05 Mvar into the bus, so the bus balance requires Qr + Qc = Ql, giving Qc = 49.30 − (−4.05) = 53.35 Mvar. The capacitor bank must therefore supply not only the load's reactive demand but also the 4.05 Mvar that the bus has to send into the line to hold its voltage magnitude at 115 kV. If the capacitor were smaller, the receiving bus voltage could not be held, and it would sag below 115 kV.

Answer: Qc ≈ 53.4 Mvar

(e)

The maximum steady-state transfer occurs at δ = 90°, where sin δ = 1, so Pmax = Vs Vr/X = 359.4 MW. The unused portion when delivering 150 MW is (359.4 − 150)/359.4 = 0.5826, or 58.3 percent. This is the steady-state stability margin, expressed as a fraction of the limit. In practice, utilities use a much smaller margin because transient swings, outages of a parallel circuit and the voltage-stability limit of the load reduce the usable transfer well below the 90° figure. A margin of about 58 percent is comfortable, and shows why the loaded circuit has room for a capacitor-supported voltage but little reactive support from the line.

Answer: margin ≈ 58.3 %

A6 Practice Paper 7

Problem 1 [A6-031] Fault calculations and symmetrical components basics

A food-processing plant has a single 4.16 kV bus supplied through one 69 kV to 4.16 kV transformer rated 10 MVA with a leakage impedance of 7.5 percent on its own rating (treat it as pure reactance, resistances neglected). The 69 kV utility supply has a three-phase short-circuit capacity of 500 MVA at the transformer high-voltage terminals. One synchronous motor of rating 3 MVA, 4.16 kV, with subtransient reactance 0.20 per unit on its own base, is connected directly to the 4.16 kV bus and runs at the time of the fault. The plant engineer must choose the breaker for the bus. Use a 10 MVA base and 4.16 kV on the low-voltage side, prefault voltage 1.0 per unit, and no prefault load current. All faults are bolted three-phase faults at the 4.16 kV bus.

  1. (a) Find the per-unit reactance of the utility plus transformer path seen from the 4.16 kV bus, on the 10 MVA base. [4]
  2. (b) Find the subtransient three-phase fault current at the bus in kA when the motor contributes. [6]
  3. (c) Find the motor's own contribution to that fault current, in amperes. [4]
  4. (d) A bus breaker rated for 14 kA symmetrical interrupting duty is to be used. Find the minimum transformer leakage reactance, in per unit on 10 MVA, so the fault current does not exceed 14 kA with the motor connected. [6]
(a)

The utility behaves as a source of reactance Xs = Sbase/Ssc = 10/500 = 0.020 pu on the 10 MVA base, because the short-circuit capacity is the base MVA divided by the per-unit source reactance. The transformer is already on 10 MVA, so Xt = 0.075 pu with no change of base. The two reactances are in series between the source and the low-voltage bus, so Xa = 0.020 + 0.075 = 0.095 pu. Resistances are neglected as stated, which is conservative for interrupting duty because it gives the largest current. Assumption: the 69 kV system is a stiff source with a constant behind-reactance voltage of 1.0 pu.

Answer: 0.095 pu

(b)

Convert the motor reactance to the common base: Xm = 0.20 × (10/3) = 0.6667 pu. During a bolted bus fault the motor acts as a source behind its subtransient reactance, so it is in parallel with the utility path as seen from the faulted bus. The Thevenin reactance is Xth = (0.095 × 0.6667)/(0.095 + 0.6667) = 0.08315 pu. The fault current is If = 1.0/0.08315 = 12.026 pu. Base current is Ib = 10 MVA/(√3 × 4.16 kV) = 1387.8 A, so If = 12.026 × 1387.8 = 16 691 A, which is 16.69 kA. The fault MVA is 120.3 MVA.

Answer: 16.69 kA

(c)

The motor is a separate source feeding the fault through its own subtransient reactance. With prefault voltage 1.0 pu and no prefault current, its contribution is Im = 1.0/0.6667 = 1.5 pu. In amperes Im = 1.5 × 1387.8 A = 2082 A. Compare this with the utility contribution of 1.0/0.095 = 10.526 pu, or 14.61 kA, and the sum 14.61 + 2.08 = 16.69 kA agrees with part (b). The motor adds about 12.5 percent to the duty, which is why the motor must not be ignored when the breaker is chosen, particularly with large synchronous machines on the bus.

Answer: 2082 A

(d)

The target is If = 14 000 A, so the Thevenin reactance must be at least Xth = Ib/14 000 = 1387.8/14 000 = 0.09913 pu. With the motor reactance fixed at 0.6667 pu in parallel with the path Xa, we need Xth = Xa·Xm/(Xa + Xm), which rearranges to Xa = Xth·Xm/(Xm - Xth) = 0.09913 × 0.6667/(0.6667 - 0.09913) = 0.11645 pu. The transformer reactance is then Xt = Xa - Xs = 0.11645 - 0.020 = 0.0964 pu, which is 9.64 percent on 10 MVA. A real transformer with the next standard impedance above this value would be specified, or a current-limiting reactor could be added.

Answer: 0.0964 pu

Problem 2 [A6-032] Generation, load curves and economic dispatch basics

A small provincial utility serves a peak load of 600 MW from two thermal units. Unit 1 has an input-output cost of C1 = 500 + 7.2 P1 + 0.006 P1² dollars per hour and Unit 2 has C2 = 400 + 8.4 P2 + 0.003 P2² dollars per hour, where P is in MW. Both units may be run anywhere between 100 MW and 450 MW, and losses on the system are neglected. The system load on a typical weekday is 250 MW for 6 hours, 450 MW for 10 hours and 600 MW for 8 hours. The operations planner wants to compare an economic dispatch at the daily peak with the practice of sharing the load equally between the units.

  1. (a) Find the economic output of Unit 1 at the 600 MW peak. [5]
  2. (b) Find the system incremental cost at that dispatch, in dollars per MWh. [4]
  3. (c) Find the hourly cost saving at 600 MW compared with equal sharing of 300 MW each. [6]
  4. (d) Find the daily load factor referred to the 600 MW peak. [5]
(a)

Economic dispatch with negligible losses requires equal incremental costs. dC1/dP1 = 7.2 + 0.012 P1 and dC2/dP2 = 8.4 + 0.006 P2. Setting them equal with P2 = 600 - P1 gives 7.2 + 0.012 P1 = 8.4 + 0.006(600 - P1) = 12.0 - 0.006 P1. Collecting terms, 0.018 P1 = 4.8, so P1 = 266.7 MW and P2 = 333.3 MW. Both outputs lie inside the 100 to 450 MW limits, so no unit is held at a limit and the unconstrained solution is valid.

Answer: 266.7 MW

(b)

The common incremental cost is lambda, the cost of the last megawatt-hour supplied. From Unit 1, lambda = 7.2 + 0.012 × 266.67 = 7.2 + 3.2 = 10.40 dollars per MWh. A check on Unit 2 gives 8.4 + 0.006 × 333.33 = 8.4 + 2.0 = 10.40, which agrees. The number is the marginal price signal for the system at this load level: supplying one more MW for an hour would cost about 10.40 dollars, whichever unit picks it up.

Answer: 10.40 $/MWh

(c)

At equal sharing, C1(300) = 500 + 2160 + 540 = 3200 dollars per hour and C2(300) = 400 + 2520 + 270 = 3190 dollars per hour, so the total is 6390 dollars per hour. At the economic dispatch, C1(266.67) = 500 + 1920 + 426.67 = 2846.67 and C2(333.33) = 400 + 2800 + 333.33 = 3533.33, a total of 6380.00 dollars per hour. The saving is 6390 - 6380 = 10.00 dollars per hour. Because the cost curves are close to each other, the saving is small, but over many peak hours per year it accumulates.

Answer: $10.00 per hour

(d)

Daily energy is the sum of load times duration: 250 × 6 + 450 × 10 + 600 × 8 = 1500 + 4500 + 4800 = 10 800 MWh. The average load is 10 800/24 = 450 MW. Load factor is the ratio of average load to peak load, so LF = 450/600 = 0.750. A load factor of 0.75 means the generating plant is used at an average of 75 percent of its peak requirement, and a higher value generally lowers the average cost per MWh because the fixed cost is spread over more energy.

Answer: 0.750

Problem 3 [A6-033] DC machine models and speed control

A separately excited DC motor drives a conveyor. Its rated terminal voltage is 250 V, the armature resistance is 0.12 ohm, and at rated armature current of 120 A the speed is 1150 rpm with the field current at its rated value. Brush drop, armature reaction and rotational losses are neglected, so the electromagnetic power equals the shaft power. The plant needs a reduced speed of 800 rpm at the same torque, that is with the armature current held at 120 A and the field unchanged. Two methods are being compared: lowering the armature voltage with a controlled rectifier, and keeping 250 V on the armature and adding series resistance. A later requirement asks for 1500 rpm using field weakening.

  1. (a) Find the armature voltage needed for 800 rpm at 120 A. [5]
  2. (b) Find the series resistance needed to get 800 rpm from a fixed 250 V supply. [4]
  3. (c) Compare the armature-circuit efficiency (Ea·Ia over the armature input) for the resistor method at 800 rpm. [5]
  4. (d) With 250 V and an armature current of 60 A, find the flux needed for 1500 rpm as a fraction of rated flux. [6]
(a)

At rated load the back-EMF is Ea = V - Ia·Ra = 250 - 120 × 0.12 = 235.6 V at 1150 rpm, so the constant is Kφ = 235.6/1150 = 0.2049 V per rpm. With the field unchanged, the back-EMF at 800 rpm is Ea = 0.2049 × 800 = 163.9 V. Since Ia is held at 120 A, the terminal voltage is Va = Ea + Ia·Ra = 163.9 + 14.4 = 178.3 V. This method keeps the torque constant, because torque depends on flux and armature current only, both of which are unchanged.

Answer: 178.3 V

(b)

With the supply fixed at 250 V, the voltage that must be dropped is 250 - 178.3 = 71.7 V at 120 A. This drop appears across the added series resistor, so Rext = 71.7/120 = 0.598 ohm. Equivalently, the total armature circuit resistance is (250 - 163.9)/120 = 0.7175 ohm, and subtracting Ra = 0.12 gives 0.5975 ohm. The resistor must carry 120 A continuously, so it dissipates I²R = 120² × 0.5975 = 8.6 kW, a large continuous loss that must be removed by ventilation.

Answer: 0.598 ohm

(c)

The electrical input to the armature circuit with the resistor is 250 V × 120 A = 30.0 kW. The converted electrical output is Ea·Ia = 163.9 × 120 = 19.67 kW. The efficiency of the armature circuit is therefore 19.67/30.0 = 0.6556, or 65.6 percent. For the variable-voltage method the same output would need Va·Ia = 178.3 × 120 = 21.4 kW input, an efficiency of 91.9 percent. The difference is the energy burned in the series resistor, and it is the main reason variable-voltage control is chosen for continuous duty.

Answer: 65.6 percent

(d)

With Va = 250 V and Ia = 60 A, the back-EMF is Ea = 250 - 60 × 0.12 = 242.8 V. At 1500 rpm the required constant is Kφ = 242.8/1500 = 0.1619 V per rpm. The ratio to the rated value is 0.1619/0.2049 = 0.790, so the flux must be reduced to about 79 percent of rated. Since torque is proportional to flux times current, at 60 A the torque is 0.79 × 60/120 = 0.395 of rated, so the drive is in constant-power operation above base speed and cannot deliver rated torque.

Answer: 0.790

Problem 4 [A6-034] DC motor starting and braking

A 230 V shunt motor drives a hoist drum. The armature resistance is 0.25 ohm, the rated armature current is 80 A, and the field is supplied from a separate constant 230 V source and kept at full value at all times. At rated load the motor runs at 1000 rpm. A control engineer must size a starting resistor, a dynamic braking resistor and a plugging resistor. The design rule is that armature current must never exceed 1.5 times rated, which is 120 A, during starting or braking. Neglect brush drop, armature inductance and inertia effects when finding initial current values, and assume the armature has reached rated-load speed before braking starts.

  1. (a) Find the total external resistance to be inserted in the armature circuit at standstill to limit the starting current to 120 A. [4]
  2. (b) Find the dynamic braking resistance (armature disconnected from the supply and connected across a resistor) giving 120 A initially. [5]
  3. (c) Find the initial braking torque in per unit of rated torque for part (b). [3]
  4. (d) Find the external resistance needed for plugging (supply polarity reversed on the armature) to hold 120 A initially. [5]
  5. (e) Explain in a few sentences why the field must stay energised during dynamic braking. [3]
(a)

At standstill there is no back-EMF, so the whole supply voltage appears across the armature circuit resistance. The required total resistance is R = V/Imax = 230/120 = 1.917 ohm. Subtracting the armature resistance, the external starter resistance is Rext = 1.917 - 0.25 = 1.667 ohm. As the motor accelerates, the back-EMF rises and the starter is cut out in steps to hold the current near the limit. The starter resistance must be rated for about 120 A at the start, though only for a short time.

Answer: 1.667 ohm

(b)

At rated load the back-EMF is Ea = 230 - 80 × 0.25 = 210 V. For dynamic braking the armature is removed from the supply and connected across a resistor Rb, with the field still excited. At the instant of switching, speed is unchanged so the EMF is still 210 V, and the current is Ea/(Ra + Rb). Setting this equal to 120 A gives Ra + Rb = 210/120 = 1.75 ohm, so Rb = 1.75 - 0.25 = 1.50 ohm. The motor acts as a generator, converting kinetic and potential energy into heat in the resistor.

Answer: 1.50 ohm

(c)

Torque is proportional to flux times armature current. The flux is unchanged because the field is held at full value, so the braking torque ratio equals the current ratio: 120/80 = 1.5 per unit. The direction of torque is opposite to rotation, because the current has reversed direction relative to motoring operation. As speed falls, the EMF falls with it and the braking current and torque decay, so the resistor must be stepped out if a steady braking effect is needed down to low speed.

Answer: 1.5 pu

(d)

In plugging the supply is reversed, so the supply voltage and back-EMF add in the same direction around the armature loop. The total driving voltage at the first instant is 230 + 210 = 440 V. For a current limit of 120 A the total resistance is 440/120 = 3.667 ohm. Subtracting Ra = 0.25 ohm gives an external resistance of 3.417 ohm. This is more than twice the starting resistor, which shows why plugging without a series resistor would give a current of about 1760 A, far beyond the commutator capability.

Answer: 3.417 ohm

(e)

During dynamic braking the machine acts as a generator and the braking torque comes from the interaction of armature current with the field flux. If the field were removed, the flux would fall to the small residual value, the generated EMF would be almost zero, little current would flow in the resistor and almost no braking torque would result. With a separately excited or a constant 230 V shunt field, the flux is retained and the EMF is proportional to speed. A series motor needs its field connections reversed or separately excited for the same reason.

Answer: Without flux the machine generates no braking EMF or torque.

Problem 5 [A6-035] Synchronous generator equivalent circuit and regulation

A three-phase, wye-connected synchronous generator at a hydro station is rated 20 MVA, 11 kV line-to-line, 60 Hz. Armature resistance is negligible and the synchronous reactance is 4.5 ohm per phase, with saturation neglected. The open-circuit characteristic is taken as linear: a field current of 180 A produces the rated 11 kV line voltage at no load. The generator is to supply rated kVA at rated terminal voltage at 0.8 power factor lagging, and the commissioning engineer needs the excitation and the voltage behaviour. Use the terminal phase voltage as the phasor reference and the round-rotor model with one synchronous reactance.

  1. (a) Find the excitation EMF (line-to-line value) required at rated load, 0.8 power factor lagging. [6]
  2. (b) Find the voltage regulation in percent when the load is removed with the field current unchanged. [4]
  3. (c) Find the field current needed for this operating point. [5]
  4. (d) Find the power angle between E and the terminal voltage, in degrees. [5]
(a)

Rated terminal phase voltage is V = 11 000/√3 = 6350.9 V. Rated current is I = 20 × 10⁶/(√3 × 11 000) = 1049.7 A. At 0.8 lagging the current phasor is I = 1049.7∠-36.87° = 839.8 - j629.8 A. The excitation EMF is E = V + jXs·I = 6350.9 + j4.5 × (839.8 - j629.8) = 6350.9 + 2834.1 + j3779.1 = 9185.0 + j3779.1 V. Its magnitude is 9932 V per phase, so the line-to-line value is 9932 × √3 = 17 203 V, or 17.20 kV. The result is well above rated voltage because the lagging current demagnetises the machine through the synchronous reactance.

Answer: 17.20 kV

(b)

Regulation is defined as the rise in terminal voltage when the rated load is removed with excitation held fixed. With the load off, the terminal phase voltage becomes equal to E, which is 9932 V. Regulation = (E - V)/V × 100 = (9932 - 6350.9)/6350.9 × 100 = 56.4 percent. A regulation this large is typical of a machine with a high synchronous reactance, here Xs = 4.5 ohm against the base impedance of 11²/20 = 6.05 ohm, or 0.744 pu. Practical designs have lower reactance and regulation, but the exercise shows why an automatic voltage regulator is essential.

Answer: 56.4 percent

(c)

With the linear open-circuit characteristic, the generated line voltage is proportional to field current: 180 A gives 11 kV. For an excitation of 17 203 V, the field current is If = 180 × 17 203/11 000 = 281.5 A. This is about 156 percent of the no-load rated-voltage field current, so the field winding and exciter must be sized for this higher duty. In practice, magnetic saturation would require a larger current than this linear estimate, so the figure is a lower bound on the real requirement.

Answer: 281.5 A

(d)

The power angle is the angle of E relative to the terminal voltage reference. From E = 9185.0 + j3779.1 V, δ = arctan(3779.1/9185.0) = 22.36°. Check with the power formula: P = 3·V·E·sinδ/Xs = 3 × 6350.9 × 9932 × sin 22.36°/4.5 = 16.0 MW, which equals the rated real power of 20 MVA × 0.8 = 16 MW. The steady-state stability limit is at δ = 90°, so the machine is far from losing synchronism at this load, though the margin is smaller if the excitation is lowered.

Answer: 22.36 degrees

A6 Practice Paper 8

Problem 1 [A6-036] Synchronous motor operation and power factor

A plant on a 4.16 kV three-phase bus has an existing induction and lighting load of 3000 kW at 0.78 power factor lagging. The utility penalises the plant when its overall power factor is below 0.95 lagging. The plant manager proposes a new wye-connected synchronous motor to drive a compressor, to be run overexcited so that it also corrects the power factor. The compressor needs 1000 kW electrical input at the motor terminals. The motor has a synchronous reactance of 7.0 ohm per phase and negligible armature resistance. Assume the bus voltage stays at 4.16 kV line-to-line and ignore all losses in the feeders. The motor is to take exactly the real power stated and whatever reactive power is needed to bring the total plant to 0.95 lagging.

  1. (a) Find the leading reactive power the motor must supply, in kvar. [6]
  2. (b) Find the motor line current, in amperes. [4]
  3. (c) Find the motor power factor. [4]
  4. (d) Find the line-to-line internal EMF of the motor, in volts. [6]
(a)

The existing load reactive power is Q0 = 3000 × tan(arccos 0.78) = 3000 × 0.8023 = 2406.8 kvar lagging. The total real power after adding the motor is 3000 + 1000 = 4000 kW. For a 0.95 lagging power factor the total reactive power must be Qt = 4000 × tan(arccos 0.95) = 4000 × 0.3287 = 1314.7 kvar. The motor reactive power is then Qm = Qt - Q0 = 1314.7 - 2406.8 = -1092.1 kvar, meaning that the motor supplies 1092 kvar leading, which is delivered to the other loads on the bus.

Answer: 1092 kvar

(b)

The motor apparent power is S = √(P² + Q²) = √(1000² + 1092.1²) = 1480.8 kVA. The line current is I = S/(√3 × VL) = 1 480 800/(√3 × 4160) = 205.5 A. Because the motor takes a leading current at this operating point, this is also the magnitude of the phasor current used in part (d). The current is high relative to the real power alone: at unity power factor 1000 kW would need only 138.8 A, so the leading reactive component costs about 48 percent more current and extra I²R loss in the stator.

Answer: 205.5 A

(c)

The power factor is the ratio of real power to apparent power: pf = P/S = 1000/1480.8 = 0.675. It is leading, because the motor is overexcited and supplies reactive power. This is low compared with the plant target of 0.95, but the plant power factor is what the utility measures, and the sum of the motor's capacitive vars and the lagging vars of the existing load produces 0.95 lagging overall. A larger motor operated at a smaller leading angle could achieve the same correction with less stator heating.

Answer: 0.675 leading

(d)

Take the phase voltage V = 4160/√3 = 2401.8 V as reference. The motor current leads by θ = arccos 0.675 = 47.5°, so I = 205.5∠47.5° A = 138.8 + j151.6 A. For a motor, E = V - jXs·I = 2401.8 - j7 × (138.8 + j151.6) = 2401.8 + 1061.2 - j971.6 = 3463.0 - j971.6 V. The magnitude is 3596.5 V per phase, which gives a line-to-line value of 6229 V. The angle is -15.7°, so the rotor lags the terminal voltage, as expected for motor action. The internal EMF being larger than V confirms overexcitation.

Answer: 6229 V

Problem 2 [A6-037] Three-phase induction motor equivalent circuit and torque-slip

A three-phase, 600 V, 60 Hz, four-pole, wye-connected wound-rotor induction motor drives a crusher that needs a high starting torque. The per-phase equivalent circuit, with rotor quantities referred to the stator, has stator resistance 0.35 ohm, stator leakage reactance 0.90 ohm, referred rotor resistance 0.30 ohm, referred rotor leakage reactance 0.90 ohm and magnetising reactance 28 ohm. Core loss is neglected, and the magnetising branch is connected directly across the stator terminals after the stator impedance (the usual exact-circuit arrangement for the Thevenin method). Synchronous speed is 1800 rpm. A designer wants to add external resistance to the rotor, through slip rings, so that the maximum torque occurs at standstill.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the Thevenin voltage per phase seen by the rotor circuit. [4]
  2. (b) Find the slip at maximum torque with the rotor circuit alone. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum torque, in newton-metres. [4]
  4. (d) Find the referred external rotor resistance per phase so that maximum torque occurs at s = 1. [4]
  5. (e) Find the starting torque with no external resistance. [4]
(a)

The Thevenin voltage is found by opening the rotor branch and taking the open-circuit voltage across the magnetising reactance: Vth = V1 × jXm/(R1 + j(X1 + Xm)). With V1 = 600/√3 = 346.4 V, the denominator is 0.35 + j28.9, with magnitude 28.902. Hence |Vth| = 346.4 × 28/28.902 = 335.6 V per phase. The Thevenin voltage is slightly lower than the supply because of the small drop in the stator impedance, and it is the source driving the rotor circuit in the simplified model.

Answer: 335.6 V

(b)

The Thevenin impedance is Zth = jXm(R1 + jX1)/(R1 + j(X1 + Xm)), which evaluates to 0.3285 + j0.8760 ohm. Maximum torque occurs at the slip sm = R2/√(Rth² + (Xth + X2)²), where Rth = 0.3285 and Xth + X2 = 0.8760 + 0.90 = 1.7760 ohm. The square root is √(0.1079 + 3.1542) = 1.8061 ohm. So sm = 0.30/1.8061 = 0.1661. This slip is much higher than the rated slip of a cage motor, which is why a wound-rotor machine of this resistance has a soft speed characteristic.

Answer: 0.166

(c)

The synchronous angular speed is ωs = 2π × 1800/60 = 188.50 rad/s. The maximum torque for a three-phase machine is Tmax = 3·Vth²/(2ωs(Rth + √(Rth² + (Xth + X2)²))) = 3 × 335.6²/(2 × 188.50 × (0.3285 + 1.8061)). The numerator is 3 × 112 640 = 337 920 and the denominator is 376.99 × 2.1346 = 804.7, so Tmax = 419.9 N·m. Maximum torque does not depend on rotor resistance, which is the property exploited in part (d).

Answer: 419.9 N·m

(d)

To make the maximum torque occur at s = 1, the total rotor resistance must equal √(Rth² + (Xth + X2)²) = 1.8061 ohm, since sm = R2total/1.8061 = 1. The external resistance referred to the stator is therefore Rext' = 1.8061 - 0.30 = 1.506 ohm per phase. The actual slip-ring resistor value is Rext'/a² where a is the stator-to-rotor turns ratio, which this problem does not need. At start, the motor then produces its full maximum torque of 419.9 N·m, about 2.8 times the torque with the rotor shorted.

Answer: 1.506 ohm

(e)

The torque in terms of slip is T = 3·Vth²·(R2/s)/(ωs((Rth + R2/s)² + (Xth + X2)²)). At s = 1 with R2 = 0.30, the numerator is 3 × 112 640 × 0.30 = 101 376. The denominator is 188.50 × ((0.3285 + 0.30)² + 3.1542) = 188.50 × (0.3950 + 3.1542) = 188.50 × 3.5492 = 669.0. So T = 151.5 N·m, about 36 percent of the maximum torque. The comparison with part (d) quantifies why the slip-ring resistor transforms the starting behaviour of the machine.

Answer: 151.5 N·m

Problem 3 [A6-038] Induction motor starting and speed control

A 75 kW, 600 V, 60 Hz, four-pole cage induction motor drives a rock-crusher feed belt. Its nameplate full-load line current is 85 A at a rated speed of 1746 rpm. Direct-on-line starting draws 6 times full-load current and develops 1.5 times full-load torque. The supply transformer allows only 250 A at start, so an autotransformer starter is to be selected, and the torque required by the belt at standstill is 0.55 of full-load torque. Later, a variable frequency drive will run the same motor at 40 Hz with constant volts per hertz, and the slip speed at a given torque can be assumed independent of frequency. Neglect magnetic saturation and stator drop when scaling voltage.

  1. (a) Find the autotransformer tap, as a percentage of line voltage, that limits the line current to 250 A at start. [6]
  2. (b) Find the starting torque with this tap, in per unit of full-load torque. [5]
  3. (c) Find the rotor speed at 40 Hz at the same torque as rated. [5]
  4. (d) Explain in a few sentences why voltage must be reduced in proportion to frequency when running at 40 Hz. [4]
(a)

Direct-on-line starting draws 6 × 85 = 510 A. With an autotransformer of tap ratio a (motor voltage as a fraction of line voltage), the motor current falls by a, and the line current by a² because the current on the supply side is a times the motor current: Iline = a²·Idol. We need a² × 510 = 250, so a² = 0.4902 and a = 0.7001, a tap of 70.0 percent. The standard 65 percent tap would give 215 A and the 80 percent tap 326 A, so a 70 percent tap is the nearest tap that respects the limit.

Answer: 70.0 percent

(b)

Torque is proportional to the square of the voltage applied to the motor. With a = 0.7001, the starting torque is 1.5 × a² = 1.5 × 0.4902 = 0.7353 times the full-load torque. This exceeds the belt requirement of 0.55 per unit, by a margin of 0.7353/0.55 = 1.34, so the motor will accelerate the belt, though the accelerating torque of 0.185 per unit is modest and the run-up will be slow. The torque in this case is reduced by the same factor as the line current, which is the basic trade-off of reduced-voltage starting.

Answer: 0.735 pu

(c)

The synchronous speed at 60 Hz for four poles is 120 × 60/4 = 1800 rpm, so the rated slip speed is 1800 - 1746 = 54 rpm. At 40 Hz the synchronous speed is 120 × 40/4 = 1200 rpm. With constant volts per hertz and the same torque, the slip speed is unchanged at 54 rpm, so the rotor speed is 1200 - 54 = 1146 rpm. The speed-torque curve simply shifts left along the speed axis with its shape preserved, and the motor can drive the load over a wide speed range without large currents.

Answer: 1146 rpm

(d)

The air-gap flux is proportional to the stator voltage divided by frequency. If the frequency is lowered and voltage is held at 600 V, the flux would rise to 1.5 times its rated value, causing heavy magnetic saturation, very high magnetising current, overheating and distorted torque. Reducing the voltage to 400 V keeps V/f at 10 volts per hertz, so the flux remains at its rated value and the torque capability per ampere is preserved. At very low frequency the stator resistance drop becomes significant, so drives add a voltage boost, and above 60 Hz the voltage is held at rated value, which weakens the flux.

Answer: Constant volts per hertz keeps the air-gap flux constant, preserving torque capability.

Problem 4 [A6-039] Distribution system voltage drop and capacitor placement

A 13.8 kV three-phase rural distribution feeder is 6 km long and uses conductors with a series impedance of 0.30 + j0.40 ohm per kilometre per phase. A single concentrated load of 4.0 MW at 0.80 power factor lagging is connected at the far end, and the end voltage is held at 13.8 kV line-to-line by a regulator there. Use the approximate voltage-drop formula, the line-to-neutral drop equal to I(R cosφ + X sinφ) per phase, then converted to a line value by multiplying by √3. Line charging is neglected. The utility proposes a bank of capacitors at the load end to bring the load power factor to 0.95 lagging and wants to know the benefit in voltage drop and feeder loss.

  1. (a) Find the voltage drop along the feeder as a percentage of 13.8 kV before correction. [5]
  2. (b) Find the capacitor bank rating in kvar to raise the load power factor to 0.95 lagging. [5]
  3. (c) Find the voltage drop as a percentage of 13.8 kV after the capacitors are installed. [5]
  4. (d) Find the reduction in three-phase feeder copper loss in kW. [5]
(a)

The total feeder impedance is R = 0.30 × 6 = 1.80 ohm and X = 0.40 × 6 = 2.40 ohm per phase. The load current is I = P/(√3 × V × pf) = 4 × 10⁶/(√3 × 13 800 × 0.80) = 209.2 A. With cosφ = 0.8 and sinφ = 0.6, the per-phase drop is 209.2 × (1.80 × 0.8 + 2.40 × 0.6) = 209.2 × 2.88 = 602.5 V. The line value is √3 × 602.5 = 1043.5 V, and as a percentage of 13.8 kV this is 7.56 percent. This is above the usual limit of about 5 percent, which motivates correction.

Answer: 7.56 percent

(b)

The reactive power before correction is Q1 = P·tanφ1 = 4000 × tan(arccos 0.80) = 4000 × 0.75 = 3000 kvar. After correction to 0.95 lagging, Q2 = 4000 × tan(arccos 0.95) = 4000 × 0.3287 = 1314.7 kvar. The capacitor must supply the difference, Qc = 3000 - 1314.7 = 1685.3 kvar. In practice the nearest standard bank sizes, for example 1800 kvar in switched steps, would be chosen. The real power is unaffected by the capacitor, so the feeder only has to carry less reactive current after correction.

Answer: 1685 kvar

(c)

After correction the current is I = 4 × 10⁶/(√3 × 13 800 × 0.95) = 176.2 A. The new sine is sin(arccos 0.95) = 0.3122. The per-phase drop is 176.2 × (1.80 × 0.95 + 2.40 × 0.3122) = 176.2 × (1.710 + 0.7494) = 176.2 × 2.4594 = 433.3 V. The line value is √3 × 433.3 = 750.4 V, which is 750.4/13 800 = 5.44 percent. The drop falls by about 2.1 percentage points, because both the current and its reactive component are smaller. The capacitor placed at the load end acts directly on the whole feeder.

Answer: 5.44 percent

(d)

Three-phase copper loss is 3I²R. Before correction it is 3 × 209.18² × 1.80 = 236.3 kW. After correction it is 3 × 176.16² × 1.80 = 167.6 kW. The reduction is 236.3 - 167.6 = 68.7 kW, a saving of about 29 percent of the feeder loss. At 8760 hours per year, if the load were constant, that would amount to about 600 MWh, but the real saving is lower because the load varies. The capacitor losses are small and have been neglected.

Answer: 68.7 kW

Problem 5 [A6-040] Machine or system selection combining losses, rating and cost

A water utility must choose between two 90 kW, 600 V, four-pole three-phase induction motors for a pump that runs 6000 hours per year at a steady mechanical load of 85 percent of rated shaft power. Motor A costs 6500 dollars and has an efficiency of 93.0 percent at that load. Motor B is a premium-efficiency design costing 8900 dollars with an efficiency of 95.2 percent at that load. Electricity costs 0.11 dollars per kWh with no demand charge, and maintenance and life are assumed to be the same for both motors. The utility uses an 8 percent discount rate and a 10-year evaluation period, with annual costs paid at the end of each year, and wants a decision based on a simple payback and on the present worth of the saving.

  1. (a) Find the electrical input power of Motor A at the operating load, in kW. [4]
  2. (b) Find the annual energy cost saving of Motor B compared with Motor A, in dollars. [5]
  3. (c) Find the simple payback period for the extra purchase cost of Motor B, in years. [5]
  4. (d) Find the net present worth of choosing Motor B over 10 years at 8 percent. [6]
(a)

The shaft output at the operating point is 85 percent of 90 kW, which is 76.5 kW. The electrical input of a motor equals the shaft output divided by its efficiency, so for Motor A, Pin = 76.5/0.930 = 82.26 kW. The loss is therefore 82.26 - 76.5 = 5.76 kW, which appears as heat in the stator, rotor, core and friction. For Motor B the input is 76.5/0.952 = 80.36 kW. Efficiency at the actual operating load rather than at the nameplate full load is the correct figure to use for an energy comparison.

Answer: 82.26 kW

(b)

The difference in input power is 82.26 - 80.36 = 1.902 kW. Over 6000 hours the energy saving is 1.902 × 6000 = 11 411 kWh per year. At 0.11 dollars per kWh the annual saving is 11 411 × 0.11 = 1255 dollars. As a check, the annual energy cost of Motor A is 82.26 × 6000 × 0.11 = 54 290 dollars and that of Motor B is 80.36 × 6000 × 0.11 = 53 036 dollars, a difference of 1255 dollars. This is only about 2.3 percent of the running cost, though it is a certain saving for the life of the motor.

Answer: $1255

(c)

The extra capital cost of Motor B is 8900 - 6500 = 2400 dollars. The simple payback is the extra capital divided by the annual saving: 2400/1254.6 = 1.91 years. This is short compared with an expected motor life of 15 to 20 years, so Motor B is attractive on this basis. The simple payback ignores the time value of money, which is why a present-worth calculation is also done, but at such a short payback the result will not change the decision. A longer payback of more than 5 years would call for more careful analysis.

Answer: 1.91 years

(d)

The present worth of a uniform annual saving over n = 10 years at i = 8 percent uses the annuity factor (1 - (1 + i)-n)/i = (1 - 1.08-10)/0.08 = 6.7101. The present worth of the savings is 1254.6 × 6.7101 = 8418.5 dollars. Subtracting the extra purchase cost of 2400 dollars gives a net present worth of 6018.5 dollars, which is about 6019 dollars. This is positive, so the premium motor is the better choice. The margin is comfortable, so the decision is not sensitive to modest changes in the discount rate.

Answer: $6019

A6 Practice Paper 9

Problem 1 [A6-041] Magnetic circuits, flux, reluctance and inductance

A solenoid-operated relay has a laminated rectangular iron core with a single air gap in the armature path. The coil has N = 400 turns. The iron path has a mean length of 0.32 m and a uniform cross-section of 8.0 cm², with a constant relative permeability of 2500 (treat the iron as linear, no saturation). The air gap is 1.0 mm long and has the same cross-sectional area as the iron, so fringing may be neglected. Use μ0 = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m. The maintenance crew finds that a worn stop has allowed the gap to open to 2.0 mm, and the relay now pulls in poorly. Analyse the original and the worn condition.

  1. (a) Calculate the inductance of the coil with the original 1.0 mm gap. [6]
  2. (b) Calculate the percentage reduction in inductance when the gap opens to 2.0 mm. [6]
  3. (c) With the 2.0 mm gap, find the coil current needed to keep the flux density in the gap at 0.80 T. [8]
(a)

Treat the circuit as a series magnetic circuit with reluctance ℛ = l/(μA). Iron: ℛc = 0.32/(4π×10⁻⁷ × 2500 × 8.0×10⁻⁴) = 0.32/(2.513×10⁻⁶) = 1.273×10⁵ A·t/Wb. Gap: ℛg = 1.0×10⁻³/(4π×10⁻⁷ × 8.0×10⁻⁴) = 1.0×10⁻³/(1.0053×10⁻⁹) = 9.947×10⁵ A·t/Wb. Total ℛ = 1.1220×10⁶ A·t/Wb. The inductance follows from L = N²/ℛ = 400²/(1.1220×10⁶) = 160000/1.1220×10⁶ = 0.1426 H. Note that the gap holds about 89 percent of the total reluctance, which is why the gap length dominates the behaviour of the relay and why its wear matters so much.

Answer: 0.1426 H

(b)

The iron reluctance is unchanged at 1.273×10⁵ A·t/Wb, but the gap reluctance doubles to ℛg = 2.0×10⁻³/(1.0053×10⁻⁹) = 1.9894×10⁶ A·t/Wb. The new total is ℛ = 2.1167×10⁶ A·t/Wb, so L = 160000/2.1167×10⁶ = 0.07559 H. The reduction is (0.1426 − 0.07559)/0.1426 = 0.4699, that is 47.0 percent. Doubling the gap does not quite halve L because the iron reluctance, which does not change, is a small fixed part of the total. For the same coil current the flux linkage drops by the same fraction, so the pull-in force is much weaker, which explains the poor operation reported by the crew.

Answer: 47.0 %

(c)

The flux in the series circuit equals the gap flux, Φ = BA = 0.80 × 8.0×10⁻⁴ = 6.4×10⁻⁴ Wb (the iron has the same area, so its flux density is also 0.80 T, well within the linear assumption). The required magnetomotive force is ℱ = Φℛ = 6.4×10⁻⁴ × 2.1167×10⁶ = 1354.7 A·turns. Then Ni = ℱ gives i = 1354.7/400 = 3.387 A. For comparison, the original gap would have needed only 717 A·t, about 1.8 A, so the worn stop nearly doubles the coil current the driver circuit must supply to reach the same force, assuming the iron stays linear.

Answer: 3.39 A

Problem 2 [A6-042] Ferromagnetic cores, losses and saturation

The laminated silicon-steel core of a single-phase 60 Hz distribution transformer has a net iron cross-section of 45 cm² and the primary winding has 220 turns. The core is tested by applying a sinusoidal voltage to the primary with the secondary open, at constant peak flux density. At 60 Hz and 240 V rms the measured core loss is 82 W. The test is repeated at 40 Hz with the voltage reduced to 160 V rms so that the peak flux density is unchanged, and the core loss is 50 W. Assume the loss at fixed flux density is the sum of a hysteresis term proportional to frequency and an eddy-current term proportional to the square of frequency, and neglect winding resistance and leakage so that the applied voltage is the induced emf.

  1. (a) Separate the 60 Hz core loss into its hysteresis component. [6]
  2. (b) Find the peak flux density in the core at 60 Hz and 240 V, using V = 4.44 f N Φm. [5]
  3. (c) The transformer is mistakenly connected to a 50 Hz supply at the same 240 V rms. Assuming hysteresis loss varies as f B² and eddy loss as f² B², find the new total core loss. [9]
(a)

At fixed peak flux density write the core loss as P = a f + b f², where a f is hysteresis and b f² is eddy current. The two tests give 82 = 60a + 3600b and 50 = 40a + 1600b. From the second equation a = 1.25 − 40b. Substituting into the first gives 82 = 75 − 2400b + 3600b, so 1200b = 7 and b = 5.833×10⁻³ W/Hz². Then a = 1.25 − 0.2333 = 1.0167 W/Hz. The hysteresis loss at 60 Hz is a f = 1.0167 × 60 = 61.0 W, and the eddy loss is b f² = 5.833×10⁻³ × 3600 = 21.0 W. The two add to the measured 82 W, which confirms the arithmetic.

Answer: 61.0 W

(b)

For a sinusoidal flux the rms induced emf is E = 4.44 f N Φm. The peak flux is therefore Φm = E/(4.44 f N) = 240/(4.44 × 60 × 220) = 240/58608 = 4.095×10⁻³ Wb. The peak flux density is Bm = Φm/A = 4.095×10⁻³/(45×10⁻⁴) = 0.910 T. This is a sensible working value for silicon steel, safely below the knee of the magnetization curve, which for such steels begins near 1.5 T. The 40 Hz test at 160 V gives 160/(4.44 × 40 × 220) = 4.095×10⁻³ Wb, the same flux, which confirms that the two tests really were at constant flux density.

Answer: 0.910 T

(c)

With the voltage held at 240 V, the flux scales inversely with frequency, so Bm ∝ 1/f. At 50 Hz, Bm = 0.910 × 60/50 = 1.092 T, which is 20 percent higher but still below saturation. Hysteresis loss varies as f Bm², so it scales as f × (1/f)² = 1/f: Ph = 61.0 × 60/50 = 73.2 W. Eddy loss varies as f² Bm², which scales as f² × (1/f²) = constant: Pe stays at 21.0 W. The total is 73.2 + 21.0 = 94.2 W, an increase of about 15 percent. The key lesson is that under-frequency operation at rated voltage raises core loss and heating even though no extra load is applied, and in practice it also pushes the core nearer saturation, which sharply increases magnetizing current.

Answer: 94.2 W

Problem 3 [A6-043] Single-phase transformer equivalent circuit and tests

A 25 kVA, 2400/240 V, 60 Hz single-phase distribution transformer is tested. The open-circuit test is made on the 240 V winding: 240 V, 1.80 A, 95 W. The short-circuit test is made on the 2400 V winding with the 240 V winding shorted: 62.0 V, 10.4 A, 240 W. The short-circuit test was performed with the windings at 25 °C. Use the approximate equivalent circuit with the shunt branch at the primary terminals, and refer all quantities to the 2400 V (high-voltage) side. The copper windings have a temperature coefficient such that resistance scales as (234.5 + T) with T in °C. Rated conditions are 75 °C, and the series reactance does not change with temperature.

  1. (a) Find the core-loss resistance Rc referred to the 2400 V side. [5]
  2. (b) Find the magnetizing reactance Xm referred to the 2400 V side. [5]
  3. (c) Find the equivalent series reactance Xeq referred to the 2400 V side. [5]
  4. (d) Find the full-load copper loss at the rated temperature of 75 °C. [5]
(a)

The open-circuit test on the LV side gives the shunt branch seen from the LV terminals. The power is all core loss, so Rc(LV) = V²/P = 240²/95 = 606.3 Ω. The turns ratio is a = 2400/240 = 10, so impedances referred to the HV side are multiplied by a² = 100. Therefore Rc(HV) = 606.3 × 100 = 60 630 Ω = 60.6 kΩ. As a check, the core-loss current on the LV side is 95/240 = 0.396 A, and 2400 V across 60.6 kΩ gives 0.0396 A on the HV side, which is one tenth of 0.396 A, as the turns ratio requires.

Answer: 60.6 kΩ

(b)

From the open-circuit data the apparent current is 1.80 A and the core-loss component is Ic = 0.3958 A. The magnetizing current is the quadrature component, Im = √(1.80² − 0.3958²) = √(3.240 − 0.1567) = 1.756 A. On the LV side Xm = 240/1.756 = 136.7 Ω. Referring to the HV side multiplies by 100, so Xm(HV) = 13 670 Ω = 13.67 kΩ. The magnetizing branch is therefore much smaller in impedance than the core-loss branch only by a factor of about 4.4, which shows that the no-load current of this unit is mostly magnetizing, as is typical of a distribution transformer.

Answer: 13.67 kΩ

(c)

The short-circuit test is on the HV side, so its readings give the series impedance directly in HV ohms, neglecting the shunt branch because the voltage is only 62 V. The impedance magnitude is Zeq = 62.0/10.4 = 5.962 Ω and the resistance from the loss is Req = P/I² = 240/10.4² = 240/108.16 = 2.219 Ω. The reactance is Xeq = √(Zeq² − Req²) = √(35.54 − 4.924) = √30.62 = 5.533 Ω. The base impedance is 2400²/25000 = 230.4 Ω, so Xeq is about 2.4 percent and Req about 0.96 percent, typical values for a distribution unit.

Answer: 5.53 Ω

(d)

The short-circuit test resistance of 2.219 Ω was measured at 25 °C. Correct it to 75 °C: Req(75) = 2.219 × (234.5 + 75)/(234.5 + 25) = 2.219 × 309.5/259.5 = 2.647 Ω. The rated HV current is 25 000/2400 = 10.417 A. The full-load copper loss at 75 °C is I²R = 10.417² × 2.647 = 108.5 × 2.647 = 287.2 W. This is larger than the 240 W test loss because the winding is hotter and the test current is slightly below rated. Using the test-temperature resistance would understate the loss used in efficiency and heating calculations by about 16 percent.

Answer: 287 W

Problem 4 [A6-044] Transformer regulation and efficiency

A 50 kVA, 2400/240 V, 60 Hz transformer feeds a small commercial building. Its equivalent series impedance referred to the 2400 V side is 1.60 + j3.40 Ω, and its core loss is a constant 210 W. Neglect the shunt branch for regulation. The secondary load voltage is held at rated value and the load takes rated kVA. A power-factor correction capacitor bank is being considered, which would change the load from 0.80 power factor lagging to 0.80 power factor leading, at the same load kVA. Compare the two conditions and then examine how the efficiency varies with load, working with all quantities referred to the 2400 V side.

  1. (a) Find the voltage regulation at full load, 0.80 power factor lagging. [5]
  2. (b) Find the voltage regulation at full load, 0.80 power factor leading. [5]
  3. (c) Find the efficiency at full load, 0.80 power factor lagging. [5]
  4. (d) Find the maximum efficiency at unity power factor. [5]
(a)

Take the load voltage at the rated 2400 V (HV-referred) as reference. The full-load current is I = 50 000/2400 = 20.83 A. At 0.80 lagging the current phasor is 20.83∠−36.87° = 16.67 − j12.50 A. The input voltage is V1 = V2 + I Zeq = 2400 + (16.67 − j12.50)(1.60 + j3.40) = 2400 + (26.67 + 42.50) + j(56.67 − 20.00) = 2469.2 + j36.67 V, so |V1| = 2469.4 V. The regulation is (2469.4 − 2400)/2400 = 0.02893, or 2.89 percent. The drop is positive because a lagging current makes the resistive and reactive drops add roughly in phase with the voltage.

Answer: 2.89 %

(b)

For a leading load the current is 20.83∠+36.87° = 16.67 + j12.50 A. Then I Zeq = (16.67 + j12.50)(1.60 + j3.40) = (26.67 − 42.50) + j(56.67 + 20.00) = −15.83 + j76.67 V. So V1 = 2400 − 15.83 + j76.67 = 2384.2 + j76.67 V and |V1| = 2385.4 V. The regulation is (2385.4 − 2400)/2400 = −0.00608, which is −0.608 percent. The negative sign means the no-load voltage is lower than the full-load voltage: the leading current makes the voltage across the series reactance add to the load voltage, so the input voltage needed is below 2400 V, and removing the load makes the secondary voltage fall.

Answer: -0.608 %

(c)

At full load the output power is 50 000 × 0.80 = 40 000 W. The copper loss is I²Req = 20.83² × 1.60 = 434.0 × 1.60 = 694.4 W, and the core loss is 210 W. The efficiency is η = Pout/(Pout + Pcu + Pc) = 40 000/(40 000 + 694.4 + 210) = 40 000/40 904.4 = 0.9779, or 97.8 percent. Note that the core loss is constant because the voltage is held at rated value, while the copper loss scales with the square of the load current. The loss split also shows that, at full load, copper loss is about three times the core loss, which hints that the transformer reaches its best efficiency at a load below rated.

Answer: 97.8 %

(d)

Efficiency is greatest when copper loss equals core loss. With full-load copper loss of 694.4 W, the load fraction is x = √(210/694.4) = 0.5499, that is a load of 0.5499 × 50 kVA = 27.5 kVA. At unity power factor the output is 27 495 W and the losses are 210 + 210 = 420 W. Hence η = 27 495/(27 495 + 420) = 27 495/27 915 = 0.9850, or 98.5 percent. A distribution transformer that typically runs lightly loaded is therefore designed with relatively low core loss compared with copper loss, so that this maximum falls near its usual operating load.

Answer: 98.5 %

Problem 5 [A6-045] Balanced three-phase wye and delta systems

A balanced three-phase, three-wire, 60 Hz source of 600 V line-to-line rms supplies a process heater through a feeder. The feeder has an impedance of 0.15 + j0.40 Ω in each line. The heater is a balanced load of three identical impedances, each 9 + j12 Ω, which is connected in delta. A maintenance engineer asks what would happen if the three heater impedances were instead reconnected in wye, with no other change, and whether the existing feeder would be suitable. Treat the source as ideal, with 600 V line-to-line at the sending end, and take every voltage and current as an rms value.

  1. (a) Find the line current magnitude for the delta-connected load. [5]
  2. (b) Find the line-to-line voltage magnitude at the load terminals for the delta connection. [5]
  3. (c) Find the total real power absorbed by the load in delta. [5]
  4. (d) Find the total real power absorbed by the load if it is reconnected in wye. [5]
(a)

Convert the delta load to its wye equivalent, Zy = Zδ/3 = (9 + j12)/3 = 3 + j4 Ω per phase. The single-phase equivalent has a source of 600/√3 = 346.4 V per phase in series with the line 0.15 + j0.40 Ω and the load 3 + j4 Ω, so the total impedance is 3.15 + j4.40 Ω with magnitude √(3.15² + 4.40²) = √(9.923 + 19.36) = 5.411 Ω. The line current is I = 346.4/5.411 = 64.02 A. This is also the line current of the delta load, since line current is the same in the wye equivalent. The phase current inside the delta is 64.02/√3 = 36.96 A.

Answer: 64.0 A

(b)

The phase voltage at the equivalent wye load is the current times the load impedance magnitude, Vφ = 64.02 × |3 + j4| = 64.02 × 5 = 320.1 V. The line-to-line voltage at the load terminals is √3 times that, VLL = 1.7321 × 320.1 = 554.4 V. The feeder therefore drops about 45.6 V of the 600 V supply, a drop of 7.6 percent. A drop of this size is too large for a heater whose output depends on the square of voltage: the delivered power is only about (554.4/600)² = 85 percent of what it would be at full supply voltage, other things being equal.

Answer: 554 V

(c)

The real power per phase of the equivalent wye is I² R = 64.02² × 3 = 4098.0 × 3 = 12 294 W. For three phases, P = 3 × 12 294 = 36 882 W = 36.9 kW. A cross-check uses the delta view: each delta phase has a current of 36.96 A and resistance 9 Ω, so each phase dissipates 36.96² × 9 = 12 294 W, giving the same 36.9 kW. The line itself absorbs 3 × 64.02² × 0.15 = 1844 W, so the source supplies about 38.7 kW in all and the feeder is about 4.8 percent of that supply.

Answer: 36.9 kW

(d)
