With the load in wye each phase impedance is 9 + j12 Ω, magnitude 15 Ω. The total per-phase impedance including the line is 9.15 + j12.40 Ω, with magnitude √(83.72 + 153.76) = 15.41 Ω. The line current is I = 346.4/15.41 = 22.48 A. The real power is P = 3 I² R = 3 × 22.48² × 9 = 3 × 505.3 × 9 = 13 643 W = 13.6 kW. The power falls to about 37 percent of the delta value, close to the factor of three expected, because the wye connection places only 1/√3 of the line voltage across each element. The feeder drop is far smaller, but the heater would not deliver its intended output.

Answer: 13.6 kW

A6 Practice Paper 10

Problem 1 [A6-046] Three-phase power, per-unit system and one-line diagrams

A one-line diagram shows a three-phase generator rated 30 MVA, 13.8 kV line-to-line, with a synchronous reactance of 0.15 per unit on its own rating. It is connected to a step-up transformer rated 30 MVA, 13.8/138 kV, with a leakage reactance of 0.10 per unit on its own rating. The transformer feeds a 138 kV transmission line of series reactance 38 Ω per phase, whose resistance may be neglected, which ends at a load bus. The load draws 20 MW at 0.90 power factor lagging, with the load-bus voltage held at 138 kV line-to-line. Choose a system base of 100 MVA and 13.8 kV in the generator zone, so that the base in the line zone is 138 kV. Neglect all shunt elements.

  1. (a) Find the generator reactance in per unit on the system base. [4]
  2. (b) Find the line reactance in per unit on the system base. [4]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the generator internal emf in per unit. [6]
  4. (d) Find the actual line current in amperes in the 138 kV line. [6]
(a)

Per-unit values change base by Zpu,new = Zpu,old × (Sbase,new/Sbase,old) × (Vbase,old/Vbase,new)². The generator base voltage is unchanged at 13.8 kV, so only the MVA ratio applies: Xg = 0.15 × (100/30) = 0.500 pu. The transformer behaves in the same way: Xt = 0.10 × (100/30) = 0.3333 pu, because its 13.8 kV winding sits in the generator zone and matches the chosen base voltage. The two values are needed for the series sum in part c. Working in per unit removes the 10:1 transformer ratio from the diagram, which is exactly why the method is used for long chains of equipment.

Answer: 0.500 pu

(b)

The line impedance base is Zbase = Vbase²/Sbase = (138×10³)²/(100×10⁶) = 190.44 Ω. Therefore XL = 38/190.44 = 0.1995 pu. The total series reactance from the generator emf to the load bus is Xtotal = 0.500 + 0.3333 + 0.1995 = 1.0329 pu. This is a high reactance, as might be expected for a 30 MVA machine feeding a 100 MVA base. The line contributes only about 19 percent of the total, so most of the voltage drop appears across the generator and transformer, not the transmission line.

Answer: 0.1995 pu

(c)

The load is 20 MW at 0.90 lagging, so on a 100 MVA base P = 0.200 pu and Q = P tan(cos⁻¹ 0.9) = 0.200 × 0.4843 = 0.0969 pu, with the load voltage 1.0∠0 pu. The load current is I = S*/V* = 0.200 − j0.0969 pu, magnitude 0.2222 pu. The internal emf is E = V + jX I = 1.0 + j1.0329 × (0.200 − j0.0969) = 1.0 + 0.1001 + j0.2066 = 1.1001 + j0.2066 pu. The magnitude is √(1.2102 + 0.0427) = 1.1193 pu, about 15.4 kV line to line. The phase angle is about 10.6°, which is the load angle of the machine.

Answer: 1.119 pu

(d)

The base current in the 138 kV zone is Ibase = Sbase/(√3 Vbase) = 100×10⁶/(1.7321 × 138×10³) = 418.4 A. The line carries 0.2222 pu, so the actual line current is 0.2222 × 418.4 = 92.97 A. A direct check from power uses I = P/(√3 V cosφ) = 20×10⁶/(1.7321 × 138×10³ × 0.9) = 92.97 A. The two agree, which confirms that the per-unit current and the real current describe the same load. Notice that the line current is the same at the sending end because the shunt elements are neglected.

Answer: 93.0 A

Problem 2 [A6-047] Unbalanced three-phase loads

A four-wire, three-phase, 208 V line-to-line, 60 Hz supply with phase sequence abc serves a small workshop panel with a solidly grounded neutral. The phase voltages are Van = 120∠0°, Vbn = 120∠−120° and Vcn = 120∠+120° V rms. Three loads are connected line-to-neutral: phase a carries a resistive heater of 12 Ω, phase b carries a motor-like load of 6 + j8 Ω, and phase c carries a leading load of 15 − j10 Ω. After a fault investigation the owner wants to know what the neutral conductor carries now, and what would happen if the neutral were lost through a broken connection. Neglect the impedance of the neutral and of the lines in the first three parts.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the phase c line current. [4]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the neutral current with the neutral intact. [5]
  3. (c) Find the total real power absorbed by the three loads. [4]
  4. (d) The neutral wire opens. Find the magnitude of the voltage between the load star point and the source neutral. [7]
(a)

With the neutral intact each load sees its own phase voltage, so each current is found from I = V/Z. For phase c, Zc = 15 − j10 Ω has magnitude √(225 + 100) = 18.03 Ω, and the current is Ic = 120∠120°/18.03∠−33.69° = 6.656∠153.69° A. The magnitude is 6.66 A. The current leads its voltage by 33.69° because the load is capacitive. For reference, Ia = 120/12 = 10.00∠0° A and Ib = 120∠−120°/(10∠53.13°) = 12.00∠−173.13° A, so phase b carries the largest current.

Answer: 6.66 A

(b)

The neutral current is the phasor sum of the three line currents, In = Ia + Ib + Ic. In rectangular form Ia = 10.000 + j0, Ib = 12(cos(−173.13°) + j sin(−173.13°)) = −11.914 − j1.435, and Ic = 6.656(cos 153.69° + j sin 153.69°) = −5.967 + j2.950. The sum is (10.000 − 11.914 − 5.967) + j(0 − 1.435 + 2.950) = −7.881 + j1.515 A, magnitude √(62.11 + 2.295) = 8.02 A. The neutral therefore carries about 67 percent of the largest line current (12.0 A). A neutral sized for that must be provided, and the unbalance also loads the source transformer unevenly.

Answer: 8.02 A

(c)

Real power in each phase is I² R. Phase a: 10.0² × 12 = 1200 W. Phase b: 12.0² × 6 = 864 W. Phase c: 6.656² × 15 = 44.30 × 15 = 664.5 W. The total is 1200 + 864 + 664.5 = 2728.5 W = 2.73 kW. The capacitive load in phase c is a resistive load in series with a reactance, so only its 15 Ω resistance dissipates power. Reactive power is not asked for, but the inductive and capacitive reactances partly cancel in the totals: phase b absorbs 1152 var and phase c supplies 443 var.

Answer: 2.73 kW

(d)

With the neutral open, the three loads form an unbalanced wye. Use the Millman form: VnN = (Va Ya + Vb Yb + Vc Yc)/(Ya + Yb + Yc). The admittances are Ya = 0.08333 S, Yb = 1/(6 + j8) = 0.06 − j0.08 S and Yc = 1/(15 − j10) = 0.04615 + j0.03077 S. The sum is 0.18948 − j0.04923 S. The numerator is Va Ya + Vb Yb + Vc Yc = 10.000 + (−11.914 − j1.435) + (−5.967 + j2.950) = −7.881 + j1.515 A, which is the same sum as the neutral current found in part b, with magnitude 8.02 A. The denominator has magnitude √(0.18948² + 0.04923²) = 0.1958 S. Therefore |VnN| = 8.02/0.1958 = 41.0 V. The star point shifts by 41 V, so some loads see over 120 V and others less, and a voltage unbalance of this size can damage sensitive equipment.

Answer: 41.0 V

Problem 3 [A6-048] Three-phase transformer connections and phase shift

Three identical single-phase transformers, each rated 25 kVA, 2400/240 V, 60 Hz, are connected in delta on both sides to form a bank that supplies a 240 V three-phase, three-wire load from a 2400 V three-phase supply. One transformer develops a winding fault and is removed, and the remaining two are kept in service as an open-delta (V-V) bank so the plant can keep operating through a production run. The load during the run is a balanced 40 kVA, 240 V three-phase load at 0.90 power factor. Assume ideal transformers with no voltage drop, and that the supply stays balanced at 2400 V line-to-line.

  1. (a) Find the kVA capacity of the open-delta bank. [5]
  2. (b) Express the open-delta capacity as a percentage of the original three-transformer bank capacity. [4]
  3. (c) Find the loading of each remaining transformer, as a percentage of its own rating, when the 40 kVA load is served. [5]
  4. (d) Explain why the open-delta bank supplies only 57.7 percent of the original capacity and not 66.7 percent, which is the fraction of the transformers still in service. [6]
(a)

In the closed delta each transformer's rated winding current is 25 000/240 = 104.17 A on the LV side. In open delta the line current equals the winding current, because each remaining winding is in series with a line. The three-phase capacity is then S = √3 VLL Iline = √3 × 240 × 104.17 = 1.7321 × 25 000 = 43 301 VA = 43.3 kVA. The same result can be written S = √3 × Srated per transformer, a general formula for V-V banks of identical units. The bank can no longer survive a load above 43.3 kVA without overheating one or both of the remaining windings.

Answer: 43.3 kVA

(b)

The original delta-delta bank of three 25 kVA units had a total capacity of 75 kVA. The open-delta bank has 43.3 kVA, so the ratio is 43.30/75 = 0.5774, or 57.7 percent. This is exactly 1/√3 because √3 × 25/(3 × 25) = 1/√3. Removing one of the three units therefore costs 42.3 percent of the capacity even though only 33.3 percent of the transformer rating has been taken out, a point to keep in mind when planning the production run, since the bank has noticeably less spare capacity than simply two-thirds of 75 kVA, which would be 50 kVA.

Answer: 57.7 %

(c)

The 40 kVA load draws a line current of I = 40 000/(√3 × 240) = 40 000/415.7 = 96.23 A. In the open-delta connection each remaining winding carries the line current, 96.23 A. The rated winding current is 25 000/240 = 104.17 A, so the loading is 96.23/104.17 = 0.9238, or 92.4 percent of rating. The bank is nearly fully loaded for a load of only 40/43.3 = 92.4 percent of its capacity, which agrees with the previous figure. There is therefore little margin for overload or motor starting during the run, and the power-factor correction might be considered to reduce the current.

Answer: 92.4 %

(d)

In a closed delta each winding carries only 1/√3 of the line current, because the three phase currents share the line current between them. When one transformer is removed the line current must pass through the remaining windings alone, so each winding carries the full line current. For the same winding current limit the line current can only be 104.17 A, giving √3 × 240 × 104.17 = 43.3 kVA, not 2 × 25 = 50 kVA. In addition, the two windings carry currents that are 30° out of phase with the voltages across them, so each winding delivers only a fraction of its kVA as useful three-phase power. The ratio 57.7 percent is thus a result of both the unequal current sharing and this 30° phase displacement, not simply the count of units.

Problem 4 [A6-049] Transmission line models and voltage regulation

A 230 kV, 60 Hz, three-phase transmission line is 200 km long. Its series impedance is 0.08 + j0.40 Ω per kilometre per phase and its shunt admittance is j4.2 μS per kilometre per phase. Use the nominal-π model with the line treated as a single lumped section. The receiving end delivers 150 MW at 230 kV line-to-line with a power factor of 0.95 lagging. Operations are considering adding shunt capacitors at the receiving end that would shift the load power factor to 0.95 leading at the same 150 MW and 230 kV. Define the voltage regulation as (|Vs|/|A| − |Vr|)/|Vr| with Vr and Vs as phase voltages and A the ABCD constant of the line.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the ABCD constant A for the nominal-π line. [3]
  2. (b) Find the sending-end line-to-line voltage for the 0.95 lagging load. [6]
  3. (c) Find the sending-end line-to-line voltage for the 0.95 leading load. [6]
  4. (d) Find the voltage regulation for the 0.95 lagging load, in percent. [5]
(a)

For the nominal-π model A = D = 1 + ZY/2 and B = Z, with Z and Y the total line values. Z = (0.08 + j0.40) × 200 = 16 + j80 Ω and Y = j4.2×10⁻⁶ × 200 = j8.4×10⁻⁴ S. Then ZY = (16 + j80)(j8.4×10⁻⁴) = −0.0672 + j0.01344, and ZY/2 = −0.0336 + j0.00672. So A = 0.9664 + j0.00672 with magnitude 0.9664. The series impedance magnitude is |B| = √(16² + 80²) = 81.58 Ω. The A constant is slightly below one because the shunt capacitance partly offsets the series reactance drop, and that is the same effect that raises voltage under light load.

Answer: 0.9664

(b)

The receiving-end phase voltage is Vr = 230 000/√3 = 132 791 V taken as reference. The load current magnitude is Ir = 150×10⁶/(√3 × 230×10³ × 0.95) = 396.35 A. For a lagging load the current phasor is 396.35∠−18.19° A. The sending-end voltage is Vs = A Vr + B Ir = (0.9664 + j0.00672)(132 791) + (16 + j80)(396.35∠−18.19°) = (128 331 + j892) + (16 + j80)(376.5 − j123.7). The product is 15 920 + j28 141 V, so Vs = 144 251 + j29 033 V, with magnitude 147 150 V. The line-to-line value is √3 × 147.15 = 254.9 kV. The angle of Vs is about 11.4°, which is the transmission angle between the two ends.

Answer: 254.9 kV

(c)

With the 0.95 leading load the current is 396.35∠+18.19° A, the same magnitude but ahead of the voltage. The product B Ir now has its reactive drop in the opposing sense: the line current leads, so the series reactance voltage jXIr partly cancels against the receiving voltage rather than adding to it. Evaluating Vs = A Vr + B Ir with the new current phasor gives a sending-end phase voltage of about 128 750 V, which is √3 × 128.75 = 223.0 kV line-to-line. Explicitly, B Ir = (16 + j80)(376.5 + j123.7) = −3872 + j32 099 V, so Vs = 124 459 + j32 991 V, with magnitude 128 750 V and angle 14.8°. The sending voltage is now below the 230 kV receiving voltage, a Ferranti-type rise.

Answer: 223.0 kV

(d)

For the lagging load, |Vs| = 147.15 kV phase, so |Vs|/|A| = 147 150/0.9664 = 152 270 V. The receiving-end phase voltage at the same load is 132 791 V. The regulation is (152 270 − 132 791)/132 791 = 0.1467, or 14.7 percent. This means that if the load were removed with the sending voltage held at 254.9 kV, the receiving-end voltage would rise by 14.7 percent from its loaded value. That is too large a regulation for normal operation and shows why long lines at this load need reactive compensation such as the capacitors proposed.

Answer: 14.7 %

Problem 5 [A6-050] Power flow and real and reactive power control

Two buses, 1 and 2, are joined by a lossless transmission line of series reactance 0.20 pu on a common base, and all shunt elements are neglected. Bus 1 is a generator bus held at 1.05 pu voltage magnitude. Bus 2 is a load bus held at 1.00 pu voltage magnitude with its angle taken as zero. The line must deliver 0.80 pu of real power to bus 2. The system operator wants to see how the line behaves if the voltage at bus 1 is raised to 1.10 pu while the real power delivered stays fixed at 0.80 pu, and how that compares with the stability limit of the line. Use the standard two-bus relations P = (V1 V2/X) sin δ and Q2 = (V1 V2 cos δ − V2²)/X for the reactive power delivered into bus 2.

  1. (a) Find the angle δ of bus 1 voltage relative to bus 2 for 1.05 pu at bus 1. [5]
  2. (b) Find the reactive power delivered into bus 2 in this case. [5]
  3. (c) Find the reactive power delivered into bus 2 when V1 is raised to 1.10 pu and P is still 0.80 pu. [5]
  4. (d) State which quantity, voltage magnitude or angle, is mainly used to control the real power and which the reactive power, and give the maximum real power the line could carry with V1 = 1.05 pu. [5]
(a)

The real power relation for a lossless line is P = (V1 V2/X) sin δ. Solve for the angle: sin δ = P X/(V1 V2) = 0.80 × 0.20/(1.05 × 1.00) = 0.16/1.05 = 0.15238. Then δ = sin⁻¹(0.15238) = 8.765°. This is a small angle, well below the 90° limit, so the line is lightly stressed from the stability point of view. The result is an angle of about 0.153 radians. The same calculation may be seen as saying that the line must be driven 8.8° ahead of the load bus before any reactive power flows are considered.

Answer: 8.76°

(b)

The reactive power delivered into bus 2 is Q2 = (V1 V2 cos δ − V2²)/X. With cos δ = cos(8.765°) = 0.98831 we get V1 V2 cos δ = 1.05 × 0.98831 = 1.03773, and V2² = 1.00. So Q2 = (1.03773 − 1.00)/0.20 = 0.03773/0.20 = 0.1887 pu. A positive value means reactive power flows from bus 1 into bus 2: the load bus is supplied reactive power by the line, because the sending voltage magnitude exceeds the receiving voltage magnitude enough to push reactive current. Real power of 0.80 pu is delivered with 0.189 pu of reactive power, so the power factor at bus 2 is about 0.973.

Answer: 0.1887 pu

(c)

Raising V1 to 1.10 pu changes the angle needed: sin δ = 0.16/1.10 = 0.14545, so δ = 8.364° and cos δ = 0.98936. Then V1 V2 cos δ = 1.10 × 0.98936 = 1.08830 and Q2 = (1.08830 − 1.00)/0.20 = 0.4415 pu. The real power has not changed, but the reactive power delivered into bus 2 has more than doubled from 0.189 to 0.4415 pu, and the angle has fallen slightly. So a 4.8 percent increase in sending-end voltage magnitude raises the reactive flow by 134 percent, which shows how sensitive reactive flow is to voltage magnitude differences on a high-reactance line.

Answer: 0.4415 pu

(d)

Real power is controlled mainly by the angle δ between the bus voltages, because P ∝ sin δ and magnitude changes affect it only weakly. Reactive power is controlled mainly by the voltage magnitude difference, because Q2 ≈ V2 (V1 − V2)/X for small angles. Operators therefore change generator excitation, tap positions or capacitor banks to move Q, and change prime-mover input to move P. The maximum real power occurs at δ = 90°: Pmax = V1 V2/X = 1.05 × 1.00/0.20 = 5.25 pu. The operating point of 0.80 pu is only 15 percent of that limit, which is a comfortable stability margin, though reactive support limits may bind first.

A6 Practice Paper 11

Problem 1 [A6-051] Fault calculations and symmetrical components basics

A 25 MVA, 13.8 kV, three-phase, wye-connected generator supplies a small industrial bus. Its sequence reactances on its own rating are X1 = 0.15 per unit (subtransient), X2 = 0.17 per unit and X0 = 0.06 per unit. Armature resistance is neglected, and the prefault terminal voltage is 1.00 per unit with no load, so the internal emf behind X1 is 1.00 per unit. A fault occurs at the generator terminals. In the original installation the neutral is solidly grounded. The plant engineer now wants to know whether a neutral reactor should be fitted, because breaker ratings were chosen from the three-phase fault level. Use the sequence network connection for a single line-to-ground fault on phase a, with the three sequence networks in series, and note that a neutral reactor Xn adds 3Xn to the zero-sequence branch.

  1. (a) Find the three-phase bolted fault current at the terminals. [3]
  2. (b) Find the single line-to-ground fault current in phase a with the neutral solidly grounded. [4]
  3. (c) Find the neutral reactance, in ohms, that limits the single line-to-ground fault current to 80 percent of the three-phase value. [5]
  4. (d) With that reactor fitted, find the voltage developed across the reactor during the fault. [4]
  5. (e) Explain why the solidly grounded single line-to-ground current exceeds the three-phase current for this machine, and what property of the sequence reactances causes it. [4]
(a)

Base current Ib = S/(√3 V) = 25×10⁶/(√3 × 13 800) = 1045.9 A. A balanced three-phase fault involves only the positive-sequence network, so the fault current is E/X1 = 1.00/0.15 = 6.667 per unit. Converting, I = 6.667 × 1045.9 A = 6973 A. The assumption is that the fault is bolted, so the fault impedance is zero, and that the machine is unloaded so the prefault current is zero and the emf equals the terminal voltage. This is the figure the breakers were originally chosen against, so it is the reference for the remaining parts.

Answer: 6.973 kA

(b)

For a single line-to-ground fault on phase a the three sequence networks are connected in series, and the sequence currents are equal: Ia1 = Ia2 = Ia0 = E/(X1 + X2 + X0) = 1.00/(0.15 + 0.17 + 0.06) = 2.632 per unit. The fault current in phase a is the sum of the three components, Ia = 3 Ia1 = 7.895 per unit. Multiplying by the base current, Ia = 7.895 × 1045.9 = 8257 A. Phases b and c carry no fault current. This is 18.4 percent above the three-phase value, which is the fact that worries the engineer.

Answer: 8.257 kA

(c)

The target is 0.80 × 6.667 = 5.333 per unit, so 3/(X1 + X2 + X0 + 3Xn) = 5.333. Solving, the total series reactance must be 3/5.333 = 0.5625 per unit. The existing sum is 0.38 per unit, so 3Xn = 0.1825 and Xn = 0.06083 per unit. The base impedance is Zb = V²/S = 13.8²/25 = 7.617 Ω, so Xn = 0.06083 × 7.617 = 0.4634 Ω. The reactor adds 3Xn to the zero-sequence branch only, because the neutral current is three times the zero-sequence current. A small reactance therefore reduces the fault current substantially.

Answer: 0.4634 Ω

(d)

With the reactor, the fault current in phase a is 5.333 per unit, or 5.333 × 1045.9 = 5578 A. All of this current returns through the neutral, so the neutral carries In = 5578 A. The voltage across the reactor is V = In Xn = 5578 A × 0.4634 Ω = 2585 V. Equivalently, the zero-sequence voltage drop is Ia0 × 3Xn per unit, which gives the same result. This voltage is about 32 percent of the phase voltage of 7967 V, so the neutral point of the machine rises considerably during the fault and the reactor insulation must be rated for it.

Answer: 2.585 kV

(e)

The single line-to-ground current is 3E/(X1 + X2 + X0), while the three-phase current is E/X1. The ratio is 3X1/(X1 + X2 + X0). It exceeds one whenever X2 + X0 is less than 2X1, which is true here because X2 + X0 = 0.23 is below 2X1 = 0.30. The cause is the very low zero-sequence reactance. A generator winding with a small X0 offers little opposition to the in-phase component of current, so a solidly grounded neutral gives a fault level above the three-phase value. A neutral reactor or resistor raises the zero-sequence branch and corrects this.

Answer: Non-numeric

Problem 2 [A6-052] Generation, load curves and economic dispatch basics

A small provincial utility serves a mining region from two thermal units whose fuel costs, in dollars per hour with output P in megawatts, are C1 = 120 + 8.2 P1 + 0.012 P1² and C2 = 90 + 9.1 P2 + 0.018 P2². Unit 1 can run between 50 MW and 250 MW, and unit 2 between 40 MW and 300 MW. Transmission losses are neglected. On a typical weekday the system load is 180 MW for 6 hours, 300 MW for 10 hours and 420 MW for 8 hours. The dispatcher first sets the units for the 300 MW period using equal incremental cost. The mine then adds load so that the afternoon peak reaches 420 MW, and the dispatcher must decide how the units share it when one unit reaches its upper limit.

  1. (a) Find the common incremental cost for the 300 MW period, in dollars per megawatt-hour. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total fuel cost per hour at 300 MW, with the economic dispatch. [4]
  3. (c) At 420 MW, unit 1 cannot exceed its limit. Find the total fuel cost per hour with the corrected dispatch. [5]
  4. (d) Find the incremental cost of unit 2 in the 420 MW case, and so state what the dispatcher gives up compared with an unconstrained schedule, in dollars per megawatt-hour. [3]
  5. (e) Find the daily load factor, taking the 420 MW peak as the maximum demand. [4]
(a)

Economic dispatch equates the incremental costs, dC1/dP1 = 8.2 + 0.024 P1 and dC2/dP2 = 9.1 + 0.036 P2, with P1 + P2 = 300 MW. Writing P1 = (λ − 8.2)/0.024 and P2 = (λ − 9.1)/0.036 and summing, 300 = λ(41.667 + 27.778) − (341.667 + 252.778). So λ = (300 + 594.44)/69.444 = 12.88 $/MWh. Then P1 = 195 MW and P2 = 105 MW, which both lie inside their limits, so no constraint is active and the equal incremental cost solution is valid.

Answer: 12.88 $/MWh

(b)

With P1 = 195 MW and P2 = 105 MW the costs are C1 = 120 + 8.2 × 195 + 0.012 × 195² = 120 + 1599 + 456.3 = 2175.3 $/h. For unit 2, C2 = 90 + 9.1 × 105 + 0.018 × 105² = 90 + 955.5 + 198.45 = 1243.95 $/h. The total is 2175.3 + 1243.95 = 3419.3 $/h. Any other split of the 300 MW costs more, which can be confirmed by moving 1 MW and noting that the increments of the two units differ. This is the least-cost schedule for the period.

Answer: 3419 $/h

(c)

Unconstrained, λ = (420 + 594.44)/69.444 = 14.61 $/MWh, giving P1 = 267.1 MW, which exceeds the 250 MW limit. Unit 1 is therefore fixed at 250 MW and unit 2 supplies the remainder, 420 − 250 = 170 MW. The costs are C1 = 120 + 2050 + 750 = 2920 $/h and C2 = 90 + 9.1 × 170 + 0.018 × 170² = 90 + 1547 + 520.2 = 2157.2 $/h. The total is 5077.2 $/h. The constraint removes the freedom to equalize incremental costs, so this is the cheapest feasible schedule, not the unconstrained one.

Answer: 5077 $/h

(d)

Unit 2 at 170 MW has an incremental cost of 9.1 + 0.036 × 170 = 15.22 $/MWh, while unit 1 at its limit has 8.2 + 0.024 × 250 = 14.20 $/MWh. Unit 1 would gladly take more load, since each extra megawatt from it costs 1.02 $/MWh less than from unit 2, but it is at its limit. The dispatcher therefore gives up about 1.02 $/MWh on the marginal megawatt. The system marginal cost for pricing or for judging a capacity addition is the 15.22 figure set by unit 2, the unit that is free to move.

Answer: 15.22 $/MWh

(e)

The daily energy is 180 × 6 + 300 × 10 + 420 × 8 = 1080 + 3000 + 3360 = 7440 MWh over 24 h. The average demand is 7440/24 = 310 MW. The load factor is the average demand divided by the maximum demand, 310/420 = 0.738. A load factor this high means the plant is used fairly steadily and a larger fraction of the capacity earns revenue. Raising the afternoon peak would lower the load factor unless the shoulder periods rose too, which is why the mine's added load is a concern for the utility.

Answer: 0.738

Problem 3 [A6-053] DC machine models and speed control

A 250 V shunt-connected DC motor has an armature resistance of 0.30 Ω and a shunt field winding of resistance 125 Ω. At rated load the line current is 82 A and the speed is 1150 rpm. Brush drop and armature reaction are neglected, and the field flux is taken as proportional to the field current, with no saturation. A maintenance fault leaves an extra 25 Ω in series with the field winding, for example a corroded terminal that has not yet opened completely. The supply stays at 250 V and the mechanical load stays at a constant torque equal to the rated-load torque. Rotational losses may be ignored when relating electromagnetic torque to load torque.

  1. (a) Find the back emf at rated load before the fault. [4]
  2. (b) Find the electromagnetic torque at rated load before the fault. [4]
  3. (c) Find the armature current after the extra 25 Ω appears, at the same load torque. [4]
  4. (d) Find the new steady speed in rpm. [5]
  5. (e) Explain why the speed rises when the field circuit resistance is increased, and why complete loss of field is dangerous. [3]
(a)

The shunt field current is If = 250/125 = 2.0 A, so the armature current is Ia = 82 − 2.0 = 80 A. The back emf follows from the armature loop, Ea = V − Ia Ra = 250 − 80 × 0.30 = 226.0 V. The brush drop is neglected, as stated. This value is the reference for the speed calculation after the fault, because the machine constant relating emf, flux and speed can be eliminated by taking a ratio between the two operating points.

Answer: 226.0 V

(b)

The angular speed is ω = 2π × 1150/60 = 120.43 rad/s. The electromagnetic power is Ea Ia = 226.0 × 80 = 18 080 W. The torque is T = Ea Ia/ω = 18 080/120.43 = 150.1 N·m. Because rotational losses are ignored, this equals the load torque, and it is the torque that must be held constant when the field is weakened. The product KΦ Ia, which is proportional to torque, therefore has to stay unchanged at the new operating point, and that fixes the new armature current in the next part.

Answer: 150.1 N·m

(c)

The new field circuit resistance is 125 + 25 = 150 Ω, so If = 250/150 = 1.667 A and the flux falls to 1.667/2.0 = 0.8333 of its original value. Torque is proportional to flux times armature current, and the load torque is unchanged, so Ia2 = Ia1/0.8333 = 80/0.8333 = 96.0 A. The armature current rises by 20 percent. The armature copper loss rises by the square, 1.44 times, so the heating of the armature is considerably worse even though the machine is lightly protected against a weak field.

Answer: 96.0 A

(d)

The new back emf is Ea2 = 250 − 96.0 × 0.30 = 221.2 V. Since Ea is proportional to flux times speed, n2 = n1 × (Ea2/Ea1) × (Φ1/Φ2) = 1150 × (221.2/226.0) × (1/0.8333) = 1150 × 0.9788 × 1.200 = 1350.7 rpm. The speed rises by about 17 percent. The change is mostly the flux term, and the small fall in Ea partly offsets it. The result is within a normal margin but is the sort of speed shift that can upset a process driven by the motor.

Answer: 1351 rpm

(e)

The back emf must stay close to the supply voltage minus a small resistive drop. If the flux falls, the speed must rise to keep Ea nearly constant, which is the result above. With a very weak field, the torque per ampere is tiny, so the armature current climbs to try to hold the load, and the speed climbs further. If the field is lost entirely and the load is light, the only flux is residual, and the speed can rise to a destructive value while the armature current is limited only by the armature resistance. This runaway is why field-failure protection is fitted.

Answer: Non-numeric

Problem 4 [A6-054] DC motor starting and braking

A separately excited DC motor drives a mine hoist trolley. The armature rating is 220 V, the rated armature current is 120 A and the rated speed is 900 rpm. The armature resistance is 0.18 Ω and the field current is held constant at its rated value, so flux is constant. Brush drop is neglected. The control engineer is reviewing how a failed starter and a braking resistor change the stress on the armature. The hoist is started from rest with the full 220 V applied through a resistor in series with the armature, and it is stopped at rated speed by either of two methods: dynamic braking, where the armature is disconnected from the supply and connected across a resistor, or plugging, where the supply connections to the armature are reversed with a resistor in series.

  1. (a) Find the back emf at rated speed and rated current. [3]
  2. (b) Find the external starting resistance that limits the starting current to 1.5 times rated. [4]
  3. (c) For dynamic braking at rated speed, find the external resistance that limits the initial braking current to 2.0 times rated. [5]
  4. (d) For plugging at rated speed, find the external resistance that limits the initial braking current to 2.0 times rated. [4]
  5. (e) If the supply were reversed with no external resistance, find the initial current, in amperes. [4]
(a)

At rated conditions the armature loop gives V = Ea + Ia Ra, so Ea = 220 − 120 × 0.18 = 220 − 21.6 = 198.4 V. Since the field is held constant, the back emf is proportional to speed alone, with a constant of 198.4/900 = 0.2204 V per rpm. This constant is used in the braking parts, where the back emf at rated speed appears as a voltage that either opposes or adds to the supply. The result is a reference value for the rest of the problem.

Answer: 198.4 V

(b)

At standstill the back emf is zero, so the starting current is V/(Ra + Rs). To limit it to 1.5 × 120 = 180 A, Ra + Rs = 220/180 = 1.222 Ω. The external resistance is Rs = 1.222 − 0.18 = 1.042 Ω. Without it, the current would be 220/0.18 = 1222 A, more than ten times rated, which would burn the commutator and shock the drive train. The resistor is cut out in steps as the back emf rises, to keep the current near the chosen limit.

Answer: 1.042 Ω

(c)

In dynamic braking the armature is disconnected from the supply, so the only source is the back emf of 198.4 V at rated speed. The current is Ea/(Ra + Rb). For an initial current of 2.0 × 120 = 240 A, Ra + Rb = 198.4/240 = 0.8267 Ω. The external resistance is Rb = 0.8267 − 0.18 = 0.6467 Ω. The current direction reverses in the armature, so the machine acts as a generator and its kinetic energy is dissipated in the resistors. The braking torque falls as the speed falls, since the emf falls with it.

Answer: 0.6467 Ω

(d)

In plugging, the supply is reversed, so the supply voltage and the back emf add in the armature loop: the current is (V + Ea)/(Ra + Rp). For 240 A, Ra + Rp = (220 + 198.4)/240 = 1.743 Ω. The external resistance is Rp = 1.743 − 0.18 = 1.563 Ω. Plugging gives a braking torque even near standstill, since the supply still drives current, but the resistor must carry the supply energy as well as the kinetic energy, and the supply must be disconnected as the speed reaches zero or the motor will reverse.

Answer: 1.563 Ω

(e)

With no external resistance and the supply reversed, the current is (V + Ea)/Ra = (220 + 198.4)/0.18 = 418.4/0.18 = 2324 A. This is more than 19 times rated current and well above any commutation capability of the brushes and commutator, which would flash over almost at once. The figure shows why a resistor or a current-limited drive is mandatory for plugging, and the same number would be the stall condition if the motor were restrained against the reversed supply.

Answer: 2324 A

Problem 5 [A6-055] Synchronous generator equivalent circuit and regulation

A three-phase, wye-connected synchronous generator at a remote Ontario camp is rated 500 kVA, 2400 V line to line, 60 Hz. The armature resistance is 0.25 Ω per phase and the synchronous reactance is 6.2 Ω per phase. Saturation is neglected, so the per-phase equivalent circuit is an excitation emf E behind Ra + jXs. The operator has always run the set on a lagging-power-factor plant load, but a new bank of lightly loaded synchronous condensers makes the load leading. Voltage regulation is defined as (E − V)/V for the same field current and speed, with the terminal voltage V held at its rated value at full-load current. Take the terminal phase voltage as the phasor reference at zero angle.

  1. (a) Find the rated line current. [3]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of E per phase at rated current and 0.80 power factor lagging. [5]
  3. (c) Find the voltage regulation, in percent, for that loading. [3]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of E per phase at rated current and 0.90 power factor leading. [5]
  5. (e) Find the voltage regulation, in percent, for the leading loading, and state what a negative value means. [4]
(a)

The rated line current is I = S/(√3 VL) = 500 000/(√3 × 2400) = 120.28 A. In a wye connection the line and phase currents are equal, so the phase current is also 120.3 A. The rated phase voltage is V = 2400/√3 = 1385.6 V. These two values are the references for the phasor calculations in the following parts, and the same current magnitude is used for both power factors, since the question asks for rated current each time.

Answer: 120.3 A

(b)

At 0.80 lagging, the current lags the voltage by 36.87°, so I = 120.28(0.80 − j0.60) = 96.22 − j72.17 A. The drop is I(Ra + jXs) = (96.22 − j72.17)(0.25 + j6.2) = 471.5 + j578.6 V. Then E = V + drop = 1385.6 + 471.5 + j578.6 = 1857.1 + j578.6 V. The magnitude is √(1857.1² + 578.6²) = 1945 V per phase, at an angle of 17.3°. The excitation must be much greater than the terminal voltage to hold rated voltage under this load, because the lagging reactive current demagnetizes the machine.

Answer: 1945 V

(c)

Regulation is (E − V)/V with the terminal voltage at rated value, so (1945.2 − 1385.6)/1385.6 = 0.4038, or 40.4 percent. In other words, if the load were removed at constant field current and speed, the terminal voltage would rise from 1385.6 to 1945.2 V per phase, a 40 percent overvoltage. That is large because Xs is high, 6.2 Ω against a base impedance of 11.5 Ω, so the set has a poor regulation and needs a fast automatic voltage regulator.

Answer: 40.4 %

(d)

At 0.90 leading, the current leads the voltage by 25.84°, so I = 120.28(0.90 + j0.4359) = 108.25 + j52.43 A. The drop is (108.25 + j52.43)(0.25 + j6.2) = (27.06 − 325.07) + j(671.2 + 13.1) = −298.0 + j684.3 V. Then E = 1385.6 − 298.0 + j684.3 = 1087.6 + j684.3 V, so |E| = 1285 V per phase. The excitation falls by 34 percent compared with the lagging case, because the leading current magnetizes the machine through armature reaction, aiding the field.

Answer: 1285 V

(e)

Regulation is (1285.0 − 1385.6)/1385.6 = −0.0726, which is −7.26 percent. A negative value means that removing the load would make the terminal voltage fall rather than rise, since the field current needed for the leading load is too small to hold rated voltage unaided. The same mechanism makes a lightly loaded generator on a long line show a voltage rise. The operator should lower the field current when the condensers are on, or else risk an overvoltage, and should check that the excitation limiter does not trip.

Answer: -7.26 %

A6 Practice Paper 12

Problem 1 [A6-056] Synchronous motor operation and power factor

A 4160 V, three-phase, 60 Hz, wye-connected synchronous motor drives a ball mill. Its synchronous reactance is 7.5 Ω per phase, and armature resistance is neglected. The motor input is 1260 kW and stays at that value for all the questions, since the mill torque is constant. The motor presently operates at 0.92 power factor leading, which the plant electrician considers wasteful because the field is strongly overexcited. The electrician wants to know how much excitation would be needed for unity power factor and whether the motor would still have an adequate margin against pulling out of step. Use the per-phase model E = V − jXs I, with the terminal phase voltage as the reference, and take the pull-out limit as occurring at a torque angle of 90°.

  1. (a) Find the line current at 0.92 power factor leading. [3]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the excitation emf per phase at that operating point. [4]
  3. (c) Find the torque angle at that operating point. [3]
  4. (d) Find the excitation emf per phase needed for unity power factor at the same input. [5]
  5. (e) With the excitation held at the unity-power-factor value, find the maximum power the motor could deliver at a torque angle of 90°. [5]
(a)

The input power is P = √3 VL I cos φ, so I = 1 260 000/(√3 × 4160 × 0.92) = 190.1 A. The phase voltage is V = 4160/√3 = 2401.8 V. The current leads the voltage by cos⁻¹(0.92) = 23.07°, which is the sign of an overexcited motor, one that supplies reactive power to the plant. As armature resistance is neglected, the input power equals the air-gap power, and this current is the one that flows in the synchronous reactance in the next part.

Answer: 190.1 A

(b)

Writing the current as I = 190.08(0.92 + j0.3919) = 174.87 + j74.49 A, the reactive drop is jXs I = j7.5 × (174.87 + j74.49) = −558.7 + j1311.5 V. Then E = V − jXs I = 2401.8 + 558.7 − j1311.5 = 2960.5 − j1311.5 V. The magnitude is √(2960.5² + 1311.5²) = 3238 V per phase. The emf is 35 percent larger than the terminal phase voltage, which confirms that the motor is overexcited. The excitation needed at this operating point is high for the load that is carried.

Answer: 3238 V

(c)

The torque angle δ is the angle between E and V. From the previous part, E = 2960.5 − j1311.5 V, so δ = −tan⁻¹(1311.5/2960.5) = −23.89°. The motor angle is negative because the rotor lags the terminal voltage in motor operation, and the magnitude is 23.89°. A check with the power formula, P = 3 V E sin δ/Xs = 3 × 2401.8 × 3238 × sin 23.89°/7.5 = 1260 kW, agrees with the stated input, so the analysis is consistent.

Answer: 23.89°

(d)

At unity power factor the current is in phase with V and equals I = 1 260 000/(√3 × 4160) = 174.87 A. The drop is jXs I = j7.5 × 174.87 = j1311.5 V. Then E = V − jXs I = 2401.8 − j1311.5 V, so |E| = √(2401.8² + 1311.5²) = 2737 V per phase, with δ = 28.6°. The excitation falls by 15.5 percent from the strongly overexcited value, and the line current drops from 190.1 A to 174.9 A, which also reduces the copper loss in the stator.

Answer: 2737 V

(e)

The maximum power, ignoring resistance, occurs at δ = 90° and is Pmax = 3 V E/Xs = 3 × 2401.8 × 2736.5/7.5 = 2 629 000 W, or 2629 kW. This is 2.09 times the 1260 kW load, so the motor has a margin of 109 percent over the load even at unity power factor. The margin would fall further if the field were weakened still more, or if the supply voltage dipped, since Pmax is proportional to both V and E, so a voltage dip also reduces it directly.

Answer: 2629 kW

Problem 2 [A6-057] Three-phase induction motor equivalent circuit and torque-slip

A 460 V, three-phase, 60 Hz, four-pole, wye-connected induction motor drives a conveyor. Its per-phase equivalent circuit referred to the stator has R1 = 0.35 Ω and X1 = 0.90 Ω in series with a parallel combination of the magnetizing reactance Xm = 28 Ω and the rotor branch R2/s + jX2, where R2 = 0.28 Ω and X2 = 0.90 Ω. Core, friction and windage losses are neglected, and the supply is a stiff 460 V line to line, so the phase voltage 460/√3 V is the reference. The motor runs at 1740 rpm on the conveyor. A maintenance report says a poor bar-to-ring joint has raised the effective rotor resistance by 40 percent, and the conveyor torque has not changed. The maintenance planner wants to know the new speed and how close the motor now is to breakdown.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the stator current at 1740 rpm with the original rotor. [4]
  2. (b) Find the input power factor at 1740 rpm. [3]
  3. (c) Find the developed torque at 1740 rpm. [4]
  4. (d) With R2 increased by 40 percent and the same load torque, find the new speed. [5]
  5. (e) Find the breakdown (maximum) torque of the original motor. [4]
(a)

The synchronous speed is 120 × 60/4 = 1800 rpm, so the slip at 1740 rpm is s = 60/1800 = 0.03333. The rotor branch is Zr = R2/s + jX2 = 8.40 + j0.90 Ω. In parallel with jXm = j28 Ω this gives Zp = jXm Zr/(jXm + Zr) = 7.271 + j2.985 Ω. The total input impedance is Z = (0.35 + j0.90) + Zp = 7.621 + j3.885 Ω, with magnitude 8.554 Ω. The phase voltage is 460/√3 = 265.6 V, so |I1| = 265.6/8.554 = 31.05 A.

Answer: 31.05 A

(b)

The impedance angle of Z = 7.621 + j3.885 Ω is tan⁻¹(3.885/7.621) = 27.0°, and the current lags the voltage by that angle. The power factor is cos 27.01° = 7.621/8.554 = 0.891 lagging. The value is typical for a motor at about its rated load, and the lag is mainly from the magnetizing branch and the leakage reactances. The check on real power is P = 3 × 31.05² × 7.621 = 22 040 W of input, which the following part relates to air-gap power.

Answer: 0.891

(c)

The voltage across the parallel branches is Eg = I1 Zp, whose magnitude is 31.05 × |Zp| = 31.05 × 7.860 = 244.0 V. The rotor current is I2 = Eg/Zr, magnitude 244.0/8.448 = 28.89 A. The air-gap power is 3 I2² R2/s = 3 × 28.89² × 8.40 = 21 030 W. The developed torque is the air-gap power over the synchronous angular speed, 2π × 1800/60 = 188.5 rad/s, so T = 21 030/188.5 = 111.5 N·m. Rotational losses are neglected, so this is also the shaft torque.

Answer: 111.5 N·m

(d)

In this circuit the torque depends on the rotor resistance only through the ratio R2/s, because Xm and the stator impedance are independent of s. To keep the same torque with R2 increased by 40 percent, the ratio must remain 8.40 Ω, so s2 = 1.40 × 0.03333 = 0.04667. The new speed is n = 1800(1 − 0.04667) = 1716 rpm. The stator current is unchanged at 31.05 A, but the rotor copper loss rises by 40 percent, since 3 I2² R2 increases with R2. The conveyor slows by 24 rpm, and the heating of the rotor is the real problem.

Answer: 1716 rpm

(e)

Replace the stator side by its Thevenin equivalent. Vth = V jXm/(R1 + j(X1 + Xm)) = 257.3 V, and Zth = (R1 + jX1) jXm/(R1 + j(X1 + Xm)) = 0.3285 + j0.8760 Ω. The maximum torque is Tmax = 3 Vth²/[2ωs(Rth + √(Rth² + (Xth + X2)²))] = 3 × 66 197/[2 × 188.5 × (0.3285 + 1.806)] = 246.8 N·m. The slip at which it occurs is R2/√(Rth² + (Xth + X2)²) = 0.155. The ratio of breakdown to load torque is 2.21, a safe margin that is not affected by rotor resistance.

Answer: 246.8 N·m

Problem 3 [A6-058] Induction motor starting and speed control

A 37 kW, 600 V, three-phase, 60 Hz, four-pole squirrel-cage motor drives a crusher in a quarry. At rated voltage it draws a full-load current of 44 A at 1760 rpm, a locked-rotor line current of 6.2 times full-load current, and a locked-rotor torque of 1.6 times full-load torque. The utility feeder to the quarry can tolerate a starting line current of only 150 A. The crusher needs 0.70 of full-load torque to break away from rest, and the plant owner is considering a reduced-voltage autotransformer starter or a wye-delta starter, the motor being a delta-connected machine at 600 V with all six leads brought out. Assume torque varies with the square of the voltage applied to the motor, and neglect the magnetizing current of the autotransformer.

  1. (a) Find the locked-rotor current when the motor is started directly across the line. [3]
  2. (b) Find the autotransformer tap, as a fraction of line voltage, that limits the line current to 150 A. [5]
  3. (c) Find the starting torque at that tap, as a multiple of full-load torque. [4]
  4. (d) Find the starting torque with a wye-delta starter, as a multiple of full-load torque. [4]
  5. (e) State which of the two methods can start the crusher, and give the reason in terms of the numbers found. [4]
(a)

The direct-on-line locked-rotor current is the multiple of full-load current given in the nameplate data: ILR = 6.2 × 44 = 272.8 A. That is 1.82 times the 150 A that the feeder tolerates, so direct starting is not acceptable for this installation and would cause a voltage dip that could upset other loads on the same feeder. It is the reference from which the reduced-voltage methods are scaled, since the motor behaves as a fixed impedance at standstill, so the current scales with the applied voltage.

Answer: 272.8 A

(b)

With an autotransformer of tap k, the motor terminal voltage is k times the line voltage, so the motor current is k ILR. The line current is the motor current multiplied by k again, because of the turns ratio, so Iline = k² ILR. Setting k² × 272.8 = 150 gives k² = 0.5498 and k = 0.7415, a tap of 74.2 percent. A standard 80 percent tap would give a line current of 0.64 × 272.8 = 174.6 A, which is too high, while a 65 percent tap would give only 115 A, so the calculated value is the upper limit of the usable tap and sets the design.

Answer: 0.7415

(c)

The starting torque varies with the square of the voltage at the motor terminals, so Tstart = 1.6 × k² × TFL = 1.6 × 0.5498 = 0.880 TFL. The torque reduction has the same square factor as the line current reduction, which is why an autotransformer gives the maximum torque for a given supply current, a property that stator resistance or reactor starters do not share, since they cut the current only once. The figure of 0.88 is greater than the 0.70 needed for breakaway.

Answer: 0.880

(d)

In a wye-delta starter, the motor windings are first connected in wye, so the voltage across each winding is 1/√3 of the delta value. The torque varies with the square of the winding voltage, so it falls to one third, giving Tstart = 1.6/3 × TFL = 0.533 TFL. The line current also falls to one third of the direct value, 272.8/3 = 90.9 A. The current is well inside the 150 A limit, but the torque is small, and a changeover surge occurs when the starter switches to delta at speed.

Answer: 0.533

(e)

The crusher needs 0.70 of full-load torque to break away. The autotransformer start at the 74.2 percent tap gives 0.880, so it can break the load away, and its line current is exactly the limit of 150 A. The wye-delta start gives only 0.533, below 0.70, so the motor would stall at standstill and draw one third of locked-rotor current indefinitely, risking overheating. The wye-delta method is therefore unsuitable, and an autotransformer tap between 0.67 and 0.74 should be used, since a tap of 0.67 gives just over 0.70 of full-load torque and 0.74 reaches the feeder limit.

Answer: Non-numeric

Problem 4 [A6-059] Distribution system voltage drop and capacitor placement

A three-phase, 12.47 kV (line to line) radial feeder leaves a substation bus held at exactly 12.47 kV. Segment 1 runs 5 km from the substation to node A and segment 2 runs 3 km from node A to node B. Each conductor has a series impedance of 0.40 + j0.65 Ω per km, and line charging is neglected. A food plant at node A draws 1.8 MW at 0.92 power factor lagging, and a pumping station at node B draws 2.4 MW at 0.85 power factor lagging. To keep the work simple, treat each load as a constant current computed at the nominal 12.47 kV, taking the nominal phase voltage as the phasor reference. The utility is considering a 1.2 Mvar three-phase capacitor bank, and wants to know whether it should be installed at node A or node B.

  1. (a) Find the current in segment 2, with no capacitor installed. [4]
  2. (b) Find the line-to-line voltage at node B with no capacitor installed. [5]
  3. (c) Find the line-to-line voltage at node B with the capacitor at node B. [4]
  4. (d) Find the line-to-line voltage at node B with the capacitor at node A. [3]
  5. (e) Find the reduction in the feeder three-phase copper loss, in kilowatts, when the capacitor is placed at node B instead of not installed. [4]
(a)

The current drawn by a load is I = P/(√3 VL pf) at the stated nominal voltage, lagging the phase voltage by cos⁻¹(pf). For node B the apparent power is 2.4/0.85 = 2.8235 MVA, so |IB| = 2 823 500/(√3 × 12 470) = 130.73 A, at an angle of −31.79°. Because node B is the end of the feeder, this is the whole of the current in segment 2. The node A load adds to the segment 1 current only, so the segment 2 current is simply the pumping station current.

Answer: 130.7 A

(b)

The load at A is 1.8/0.92 = 1.9565 MVA, so |IA| = 90.58 A at −23.07°. The segment 1 current is the phasor sum IA + IB = 220.69 A. The segment impedances are z1 = 5(0.40 + j0.65) = 2.0 + j3.25 Ω and z2 = 3(0.40 + j0.65) = 1.2 + j1.95 Ω. With V = 7199.6 V per phase as reference, VA = V − I1 z1 and VB = VA − I2 z2. The phasor arithmetic gives |VA| = 6485 V and |VB| = 6229 V per phase, so the line-to-line voltage at B is 6229 × √3 = 10 789 V, 13.5 percent below nominal.

Answer: 10.79 kV

(c)

A capacitor of 1.2 Mvar at node B draws a leading current of 1.2×10⁶/(√3 × 12 470) = 55.56 A, which adds +j55.56 A to the node B current, reducing the lagging reactive component. The current in segment 2 falls to 111.9 A and in segment 1 to 200.5 A after adding the node A current. Repeating the drops, VA = 6673 V and VB = 6534 V per phase, so VB (line to line) = 11 318 V. The capacitor at the far end raises the voltage by about 0.53 kV, which brings it to 90.8 percent of nominal.

Answer: 11.32 kV

(d)

Placing the same capacitor at node A changes only the segment 1 current: the segment 2 current stays at 130.7 A, and the segment 1 current becomes 200.5 A. The drop across segment 1 shrinks, so VA rises, but segment 2 is not helped. The result is VB = 11 119 V line to line, which is 0.20 kV lower than with the capacitor at B. The capacitor is more effective at the end, because its current benefit then runs through the whole length of the feeder to that point.

Answer: 11.12 kV

(e)

The three-phase copper loss is 3(I1² R1 + I2² R2). With no capacitor, I1 = 220.69 A and I2 = 130.73 A, giving 3(220.69² × 2.0 + 130.73² × 1.2) = 3(97 410 + 20 509) = 353.8 kW. With the capacitor at B, I1 = 200.49 A and I2 = 111.91 A, so 3(200.49² × 2.0 + 111.91² × 1.2) = 3(80 391 + 15 029) = 286.3 kW. The reduction is 353.8 − 286.3 = 67.5 kW, about 19 percent, which is energy the utility no longer purchases and a saving to set against the capacitor cost.

Answer: 67.5 kW

Problem 5 [A6-060] Machine or system selection combining losses, rating and cost

A water treatment plant needs a continuous 75 kW shaft output for a raw-water pump that runs 6000 hours per year. Two 600 V, three-phase, premium-frame induction motors, both of ample rating for this load, are on offer. Motor A costs $6800 installed and has an efficiency of 93.5 percent at this load. Motor B costs $5200 installed and has an efficiency of 91.0 percent at this load. Electricity costs $0.11 per kWh, with no demand charge, and maintenance is the same for both. The owner uses a 10-year study period and a discount rate of 8 percent per year, with the energy saving received at the end of each year. Neglect any difference in power factor and in speed between the motors, and assume that the efficiencies do not change with age.

  1. (a) Find the electrical input power of Motor B at the 75 kW shaft load. [4]
  2. (b) Find the annual electricity cost saving of Motor A compared with Motor B. [4]
  3. (c) Find the simple payback period of the extra purchase price of Motor A. [3]
  4. (d) Find the net present value of choosing Motor A, which is the present worth of the savings minus the price premium, over the 10 years. [5]
  5. (e) Find the annual operating hours at which the choice between A and B would break even, over the 10-year study period. [4]
(a)

The input power is the shaft output divided by the efficiency. For Motor B, Pin = 75/0.910 = 82.42 kW, and the loss is 82.42 − 75 = 7.42 kW, which appears as heat. For Motor A, Pin = 75/0.935 = 80.21 kW, with a loss of 5.21 kW. The difference in input of 2.20 kW is what drives the whole comparison, and since the shaft load is the same for both machines, the rating of the motor, which has ample margin in both cases, plays no further part.

Answer: 82.42 kW

(b)

The saving in input power is 82.418 − 80.214 = 2.204 kW. Over 6000 hours the energy saved is 2.204 × 6000 = 13 222 kWh per year. At $0.11 per kWh the annual cost saving is 13 222 × 0.11 = $1454. This is a saving of the electricity bill alone, with maintenance equal, and the figure assumes the motor really runs at the stated load all year. A pump that runs lightly loaded for part of the time would save less, since the efficiency difference may change at part load.

Answer: $1454

(c)

The extra price of Motor A is 6800 − 5200 = $1600. The simple payback is the premium over the annual saving, 1600/1454.4 = 1.10 years, which is about 13 months. This is short for an industrial purchase, where firms often require a payback under three years, so Motor A passes easily. The simple payback ignores the time value of money and savings after the payback point, which is why the present value is computed in the next part for a fuller picture.

Answer: 1.10 years

(d)

The present worth factor of an annuity at 8 percent for 10 years is (1 − 1.08⁻¹⁰)/0.08 = 6.7101. The present worth of the savings is 1454.4 × 6.7101 = $9759. The net present value is the present worth minus the premium paid now, 9759 − 1600 = $8159. A positive value means the more efficient motor is the better investment over the study period at this discount rate. A sensitivity check is useful, since electricity prices in Ontario change by time of use, and a lower price would reduce the benefit.

Answer: $8159

(e)

At break-even, the present worth of the saving equals the premium: 2.204 kW × h × $0.11 × 6.7101 = $1600. The saving per hour of operation is 2.204 × 0.11 × 6.7101 = $1.627, so h = 1600/1.627 = 984 hours per year. The pump runs 6000 hours, six times this figure, so the decision is robust. Only a standby or seasonal pump running fewer than about 984 hours per year, or an electricity price below $0.018 per kWh, would reverse the choice in favour of the cheaper Motor B.

Answer: 984 hours

A6 Practice Paper 13

Problem 1 [A6-061] Magnetic circuits, flux, reluctance and inductance

A solenoid-actuated latch in a motor control centre uses a C-shaped laminated iron core closed by a flat iron armature. The core has a uniform cross-section of 8.0 cm² and a mean magnetic path length of 0.42 m, including the armature. Its relative permeability may be taken as a constant 2500 (the iron is not saturated). When the armature is lifted slightly, two identical air gaps of 1.5 mm each appear in series with the iron, one at each pole face. Ignore fringing and leakage, so the gap area equals the core area. The coil has 600 turns and carries a steady 2.0 A. Use μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. The armature moves only a tiny distance, so treat the gaps as fixed while answering all parts.

  1. (a) Find the total reluctance of the magnetic circuit, in units of 10⁶ A/Wb. [5]
  2. (b) Find the flux density in the core and in the air gaps, in tesla. [5]
  3. (c) Find the self-inductance of the coil, in henries, at this gap setting. [4]
  4. (d) Find the total magnetic pull on the armature, in newtons. [6]
(a)

Treat the circuit as a series magnetic circuit with the iron path and the two gaps. The iron reluctance is Rc = lc/(μr μ₀ A) = 0.42/(2500 × 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 8.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.42/(2.513 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.671 × 10⁵ A/Wb. Each gap has Rg = g/(μ₀ A) = 1.5 × 10⁻³/(4π × 10⁻⁷ × 8.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.492 × 10⁶ A/Wb. The two gaps are in series with the core, so the total is Rt = Rc + 2Rg = 1.671 × 10⁵ + 2.984 × 10⁶ = 3.151 × 10⁶ A/Wb. The gaps hold over 94 percent of the reluctance, which is why the permeability of the iron hardly matters here.

Answer: 3.151 × 10⁶ A/Wb

(b)

The magnetomotive force is F = NI = 600 × 2.0 = 1200 A-turns. By the magnetic Ohm's law the flux is φ = F/Rt = 1200/(3.151 × 10⁶) = 3.808 × 10⁻⁴ Wb. Because fringing is ignored and the core and gap areas are equal, the same flux crosses the same area everywhere, so B = φ/A = 3.808 × 10⁻⁴/(8.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.476 T in both the iron and the gaps. This is well below the knee of typical electrical steel near 1.5 T to 1.7 T, which justifies the constant-permeability assumption stated in the problem. Check: Hg = B/μ₀ = 3.79 × 10⁵ A/m, times 3 mm total gap length gives about 1137 A-turns, close to 95 percent of the total mmf.

Answer: 0.476 T

(c)

Inductance is flux linkage per ampere, L = Nφ/I. Using the circuit result this reduces to L = N²/Rt, since φ = NI/Rt. Substitute: L = 600²/(3.151 × 10⁶) = 360000/3.151 × 10⁶ = 0.1142 H. As a cross-check, Nφ = 600 × 3.808 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.2285 Wb-turns, and dividing by the 2.0 A coil current gives 0.1142 H, the same value. Because the iron is unsaturated and linear, the inductance does not change with current at a fixed gap. If the armature closed fully the gap reluctance would vanish and L would rise by roughly a factor of 18 toward N²/Rc, limited in practice by saturation.

Answer: 0.1142 H

(d)

Stored field energy in a linear gap is W = B²/(2μ₀) per unit volume times the gap volume. For a small virtual displacement dx of the armature, each gap changes length by dx at constant flux, so the energy change is dW = B²A dx/(2μ₀) per gap and the force on the armature equals this per unit dx. With two gaps in series, F = 2 × B²A/(2μ₀) = B²A/μ₀. Substitute: F = (0.476)² × 8.0 × 10⁻⁴/(4π × 10⁻⁷) = 0.2266 × 8.0 × 10⁻⁴/(1.2566 × 10⁻⁶) = 144.2 N. The force acts to close the gaps. This is about the weight of a 14.7 kg mass, a plausible pull for a small contactor or latch magnet.

Answer: 144.2 N

Problem 2 [A6-062] Ferromagnetic cores, losses and saturation

A stacked-lamination reactor core for a 60 Hz power-factor-correction bank was tested on a variable-frequency supply at a constant peak flux density of 1.2 T. The core volume is 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³. The measured total core loss was 37.5 W at 50 Hz and 48.0 W at 60 Hz. Assume that the hysteresis loss is proportional to frequency and the eddy-current loss is proportional to the square of frequency, both at fixed peak flux density. Over the range of interest, hysteresis loss varies as Bm raised to the power 2.1, and eddy loss as Bm². The final design runs at 60 Hz and Bm = 1.5 T. The winding has 240 turns on a gross core cross-section of 9.0 cm² with a stacking factor of 0.95. The supply is sinusoidal.

  1. (a) Separate the two loss components and give the hysteresis loss at 60 Hz and 1.2 T, in watts. [4]
  2. (b) Give the eddy-current loss at 60 Hz and 1.2 T, in watts. [3]
  3. (c) Find the total core loss at 60 Hz and Bm = 1.5 T, in watts. [5]
  4. (d) Find the rms voltage that must be applied to the winding to reach Bm = 1.5 T at 60 Hz, in volts. [4]
  5. (e) Explain, without calculation, why building the core from thin laminations insulated from each other reduces one of the two loss components, and which one. [4]
(a)

Write the loss at fixed Bm as P = a f + b f², where a f is hysteresis and b f² is eddy loss. Two measurements give two equations: 50a + 2500b = 37.5 and 60a + 3600b = 48.0. Dividing the first by 50 gives a + 50b = 0.75, and dividing the second by 60 gives a + 60b = 0.80. Subtracting, 10b = 0.05, so b = 0.005 W/Hz². Then a = 0.75 − 0.25 = 0.50 W/Hz. The hysteresis loss at 60 Hz is a f = 0.50 × 60 = 30.0 W. At 50 Hz it would be 25 W, so hysteresis dominates the loss at this flux level, which is typical of silicon steel at power frequency. These coefficients hold only for Bm = 1.2 T.

Answer: 30.0 W

(b)

Using b = 0.005 W/Hz² from part (a), the eddy-current loss at 60 Hz is b f² = 0.005 × 3600 = 18.0 W. Check by addition: hysteresis 30.0 W plus eddy 18.0 W equals 48.0 W, the measured total at 60 Hz, so the pair of coefficients reproduces the second test point exactly. At 50 Hz the eddy loss is 0.005 × 2500 = 12.5 W and hysteresis is 25 W, which sums to the measured 37.5 W. The eddy share is therefore 37.5 percent of the loss at 60 Hz, and its quadratic dependence on frequency is why this component becomes dominant when such a core is used at higher frequency.

Answer: 18.0 W

(c)

Raise the flux density from 1.2 T to 1.5 T with frequency fixed at 60 Hz. The flux ratio is 1.5/1.2 = 1.25. Hysteresis scales as the ratio to the power 2.1: Ph = 30.0 × 1.252.1 = 30.0 × 1.598 = 47.93 W. Eddy loss scales as the ratio squared: Pe = 18.0 × 1.25² = 18.0 × 1.5625 = 28.13 W. The total is 47.93 + 28.13 = 76.06 W. The flux density rose 25 percent but the loss rose 58 percent, a strong reminder that loss grows faster than flux. Operating nearer the knee of the magnetization curve also increases the magnetizing current sharply, so the design margin on temperature should be checked.

Answer: 76.1 W

(d)

For a sinusoidal flux the induced rms voltage is E = 4.44 f N Bm Ac, with Ac the net iron area. The net area is the gross area multiplied by the stacking factor: Ac = 9.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.95 = 8.55 × 10⁻⁴ m². Then E = 4.44 × 60 × 240 × 1.5 × 8.55 × 10⁻⁴ = 4.44 × 60 = 266.4; 266.4 × 240 = 63936; × 1.5 = 95904; × 8.55 × 10⁻⁴ = 82.0 V. The winding resistance and leakage drop are neglected, so the applied voltage equals the induced voltage. A higher voltage would push Bm toward saturation, where the current would no longer be sinusoidal.

Answer: 82.0 V

(e)

Eddy currents are circulating currents induced in the conducting iron by the changing flux. Their loss is I²R in the iron, and the induced voltage around a loop grows with the area the loop encloses. Cutting the core into thin sheets with insulating coatings confines each current loop to the thickness of one sheet, reducing the enclosed flux and thus the induced voltage by roughly the square of the thickness reduction. The eddy loss therefore falls approximately with the square of lamination thickness. Hysteresis loss depends on the area of the B-H loop of the material, not on how it is sliced, so lamination does not reduce it. Silicon in the steel also raises resistivity, which cuts eddy current further.

Answer: Laminations cut eddy loss, not hysteresis.

Problem 3 [A6-063] Single-phase transformer equivalent circuit and tests

A 50 kVA, 2400/240 V, 60 Hz single-phase distribution transformer serving a rural feeder was put through standard tests. In the open-circuit test, rated voltage was applied to the 240 V winding with the 2400 V winding open, and the meter readings were 240 V, 1.8 A and 130 W. In the short-circuit test, the 240 V winding was shorted and a reduced voltage was applied to the 2400 V winding until rated current flowed, giving 58 V, rated current and 490 W. Use the approximate equivalent circuit with the shunt branch (Rc in parallel with jXm) placed on the supply side of the series branch, and take the series impedance as Req + jXeq referred to the 2400 V side. The transformer carries rated current at 0.8 power factor lagging at rated secondary voltage.

  1. (a) Find the core-loss resistance Rc, referred to the 240 V side, in ohms. [4]
  2. (b) Find the magnetizing reactance Xm, referred to the 240 V side, in ohms. [4]
  3. (c) Find the equivalent series resistance Req referred to the 2400 V side, in ohms. [4]
  4. (d) Find the equivalent series reactance Xeq referred to the 2400 V side, in ohms. [4]
  5. (e) Find the voltage regulation in percent at rated current, 0.8 power factor lagging. [4]
(a)

In the open-circuit test, the series impedance drop is negligible, so all of the input power goes into the core-loss branch at rated voltage. The conductance is Gc = Poc/Voc² = 130/240² = 130/57600 = 2.257 × 10⁻³ S. The resistance is Rc = 1/Gc = Voc²/Poc = 57600/130 = 443.1 Ω. This value is referred to the 240 V winding, since the test was done there. The corresponding core-loss current is Voc/Rc = 240/443.1 = 0.5417 A. That current is in phase with the voltage. Notice the test set gives only 0.26 percent of rated power as core loss, a normal figure for a distribution transformer of this size.

Answer: 443.1 Ω

(b)

The excitation admittance magnitude is Ym = Ioc/Voc = 1.8/240 = 7.5 × 10⁻³ S. It splits into a conductance and a susceptance with Ym² = Gc² + Bm². Using Gc = 2.257 × 10⁻³ S from part (a), Bm = √(Ym² − Gc²) = √(5.625 × 10⁻⁵ − 5.09 × 10⁻⁶) = √(5.116 × 10⁻⁵) = 7.153 × 10⁻³ S. Then Xm = 1/Bm = 139.8 Ω, also on the 240 V side. The magnetizing current is Voc/Xm = 1.717 A, which lags the voltage by 90 degrees, and it is far larger than the core-loss current. The power factor of the no-load current is 0.5417/1.8, about 0.30 lagging, which is typical.

Answer: 139.8 Ω

(c)

The rated current on the 2400 V side is I = S/V = 50000/2400 = 20.83 A. In the short-circuit test the applied voltage is only 58 V, about 2.4 percent of rated, so the flux is low and the core-loss branch is neglected. All 490 W is therefore copper loss in the series branch: Req = Psc/I² = 490/20.83² = 490/434.03 = 1.129 Ω. This lumps the resistance of both windings referred to the 2400 V side. The corresponding full-load copper loss is 490 W, about 0.98 percent of rating. The series resistance in per unit is 1.129/115.2 = 0.0098 pu, using the base impedance 2400²/50000 = 115.2 Ω.

Answer: 1.129 Ω

(d)

The magnitude of the equivalent impedance is |Zeq| = Vsc/Isc = 58/20.83 = 2.784 Ω. With Req = 1.129 Ω from part (c), the reactance follows from the impedance triangle: Xeq = √(|Zeq|² − Req²) = √(7.752 − 1.275) = √6.477 = 2.545 Ω. This is leakage reactance referred to the high-voltage side, and the per-unit value is 2.545/115.2 = 0.0221 pu. The total per-unit impedance is 2.784/115.2 = 0.0242 pu, or 2.42 percent, which is a typical figure for a 50 kVA unit. The short-circuit power factor is 490/(58 × 20.83) = 0.406 lagging, so X/R is about 2.25.

Answer: 2.545 Ω

(e)

Refer the load to the 2400 V side. At rated secondary voltage, the load voltage referred to the high side is V2' = 2400 V, and the load current is I2' = 20.83 A at an angle of −36.87 degrees (0.8 lagging). The required source voltage is V1 = V2' + I2'(Req + jXeq) = 2400 + 20.83∠−36.87° × (1.129 + j2.545). The impedance drop is 20.83 × 2.784 = 58.0 V at angle 66.1° − 36.87° = 29.2°, which is 50.6 + j28.3 V. Adding to 2400 gives 2450.6 + j28.3 V, magnitude 2450.8 V. Regulation = (2450.8 − 2400)/2400 = 2.12 percent. Because the shunt branch is on the supply side, it does not alter this result.

Answer: 2.12 %

Problem 4 [A6-064] Transformer regulation and efficiency

A 25 kVA single-phase pole-mounted transformer supplies a small farm. Its core loss is 180 W at rated voltage and may be taken as constant. Its copper loss at rated current is 420 W, and the loss varies with the square of the load current. The per-unit series impedance on the transformer's own rating is 0.0168 + j0.035 (resistance and reactance). The daily load cycle is: 8 hours at rated kVA and 0.90 power factor lagging, 6 hours at half of rated kVA and 0.80 power factor lagging, and 10 hours with the secondary open. The transformer stays energized for the full 24 hours. Treat the secondary terminal voltage as rated whenever loaded when calculating losses.

  1. (a) Find the efficiency at rated kVA and 0.90 power factor lagging, in percent. [4]
  2. (b) Find the fraction of rated kVA at which the efficiency is a maximum. [3]
  3. (c) Find the maximum efficiency at 0.85 power factor lagging, in percent. [4]
  4. (d) Find the all-day (energy) efficiency over the 24 hour cycle, in percent. [5]
  5. (e) Find the voltage regulation at rated kVA and 0.90 power factor lagging, in percent, using the per-unit impedance. [4]
(a)

At rated kVA the output power is 25000 × 0.90 = 22500 W. The losses are the constant core loss of 180 W plus the full-load copper loss of 420 W, total 600 W. The input is 22500 + 600 = 23100 W. Efficiency is η = output/input = 22500/23100 = 0.9740, or 97.40 percent. The copper loss is the larger of the two losses at this load, which is expected because the load is at its maximum. The core loss does not change with load, so at lighter loads the efficiency of a transformer drops because its fixed loss then takes a larger share of the input. The same calculation at unity power factor would give 97.66 percent.

Answer: 97.40 %

(b)

For load fraction x of rated current at fixed power factor, the loss is Pc + x²Pcu and the output is x S cosφ. Efficiency is a maximum where the derivative with respect to x vanishes, which occurs when the variable copper loss equals the constant core loss: x²Pcu = Pc. Hence x = √(Pc/Pcu) = √(180/420) = √0.4286 = 0.6547. The result does not depend on the power factor. At this load the copper loss is 0.4286 × 420 = 180 W, equal to the core loss. So the transformer is most efficient at about 65 percent of rated kVA, which is why distribution designers prefer a typical operating load near this point instead of near rating.

Answer: 0.6547

(c)

At the load fraction x = 0.6547, the output kVA is 0.6547 × 25 = 16.37 kVA. With power factor 0.85 lagging, the output power is 16367 × 0.85 = 13912 W. At this point copper loss equals core loss, so the total loss is 2 × 180 = 360 W. The input is 13912 + 360 = 14272 W. Maximum efficiency is 13912/14272 = 0.9748, or 97.48 percent. Compare the 97.40 percent found in part (a) at rated load: the maximum is only slightly higher, since this transformer's two losses are of similar size. A different power factor shifts the efficiency but not the load fraction at which the peak occurs.

Answer: 97.48 %

(d)

All-day efficiency is the ratio of energy output to energy input over 24 hours. Output energy is 8 h × 22.5 kW (25 kVA × 0.90) plus 6 h × 10.0 kW (12.5 kVA × 0.80) = 180 + 60 = 240 kWh. Core loss runs all 24 hours: 24 × 0.180 = 4.32 kWh. Copper loss at rated load for 8 h is 8 × 0.420 = 3.36 kWh. At half load the copper loss is one quarter, 0.105 kW, for 6 hours: 0.63 kWh. Total loss energy = 4.32 + 3.36 + 0.63 = 8.31 kWh. Input is 240 + 8.31 = 248.31 kWh, so the all-day efficiency is 240/248.31 = 0.9665, or 96.65 percent. It is lower than the power efficiency because the core loss accrues during the 10 idle hours.

Answer: 96.65 %

(e)

Use the per-unit impedance with the load current and voltage at 1.0 pu. The current is 1.0∠−25.84° pu (0.90 lagging, since cos⁻¹0.90 = 25.84°). The source voltage is V1 = 1.0 + I(R + jX) = 1.0 + (0.9 − j0.4359)(0.0168 + j0.035). The product has real part 0.9 × 0.0168 + 0.4359 × 0.035 = 0.01512 + 0.01526 = 0.03038 and imaginary part 0.9 × 0.035 − 0.4359 × 0.0168 = 0.0315 − 0.00732 = 0.02418. So V1 = 1.03038 + j0.02418, magnitude 1.03066 pu. Regulation is (1.03066 − 1.0)/1.0 = 3.07 percent. The approximation R cosφ + X sinφ = 3.04 percent is close.

Answer: 3.07 %

Problem 5 [A6-065] Balanced three-phase wye and delta systems

A 600 V, 60 Hz, three-phase, three-wire bus (line-to-line voltage 600 V at the source end, balanced, positive sequence) feeds a small plant through a feeder. The feeder has an impedance of 0.05 + j0.12 Ω per line conductor. At the plant end, two balanced loads are connected in parallel: a wye-connected motor group with impedance 4 + j3 Ω per phase, and a delta-connected resistive heater bank with 45 Ω per phase. Use the single-phase (per-phase wye equivalent) method with the source line-to-neutral voltage as the phase reference. The source end voltage is held at 600 V line-to-line regardless of load.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the feeder line current, in amperes. [4]
  2. (b) Find the line-to-line voltage magnitude at the load end, in volts. [4]
  3. (c) Find the total real power delivered to the two loads, in kilowatts. [4]
  4. (d) Find the total three-phase copper loss in the feeder, in kilowatts. [4]
  5. (e) Find the kvar rating of a capacitor bank connected at the load end that raises the load power factor to 0.95 lagging. [4]
(a)

Convert the delta load to its equivalent wye by dividing the delta impedance by 3: 45/3 = 15 Ω per phase. The wye motor load is 4 + j3 Ω. In parallel, Zl = (4 + j3)(15)/(19 + j3) = (60 + j45)/(19 + j3). Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate: (60 + j45)(19 − j3)/(361 + 9) = (1140 + 135 + j(855 − 180))/370 = 3.446 + j1.824 Ω. Adding the feeder gives the total per-phase impedance 3.496 + j1.944 Ω, with magnitude 4.000 Ω. The phase voltage at the source is 600/√3 = 346.4 V. Hence the line current is I = 346.4/4.000 = 86.6 A. The current lags the voltage by about 29.1 degrees.

Answer: 86.6 A

(b)

The load-end phase voltage is the current times the load impedance only (not including the feeder). The magnitude of the parallel load impedance is |Zl| = √(3.446² + 1.824²) = √(11.875 + 3.327) = 3.899 Ω. The load-end phase voltage is 86.6 × 3.899 = 337.7 V. The line-to-line value is √3 times this: 1.732 × 337.7 = 584.8 V. The feeder drop therefore reduces the line voltage by about 15 V, or 2.5 percent. The voltage is still in the usual ±5 percent range. Note that the phasor drop is not the scalar difference of magnitudes, but because the angle between the drop and the voltage is small here, the scalar difference is close to the vector one.

Answer: 584.8 V

(c)

Real power in each phase of the load is the product of the phase voltage, current and power factor, or equivalently I² times the real part of the load impedance. The load real part is 3.446 Ω per phase. So the per-phase power is 86.6² × 3.446 = 7499.6 × 3.446 = 25841 W, and the three-phase total is 77.52 kW. Check with the individual loads: the wye motor group draws 3 × V²/|Z|² × R with V = 337.7 V, which gives 3 × 114041/25 × 4 = 54.74 kW, and the heater bank draws 3 × 337.7²/15 = 22.81 kW. These sum to 77.55 kW, matching within rounding. The reactive power is 3 × 86.6² × 1.824 = 41.04 kvar.

Answer: 77.52 kW

(d)

The feeder loss follows from the line current and the feeder resistance in each of the three conductors: Ploss = 3 I² R = 3 × 86.6² × 0.05 = 3 × 7499.6 × 0.05 = 1125 W, or 1.125 kW. The reactive loss in the feeder reactance is 3 × 7499.6 × 0.12 = 2.70 kvar, which has no heating effect but does reduce the voltage. The feeder loss is 1.125/(77.52 + 1.125) = 1.43 percent of the power the source supplies. Correcting the load power factor would lower the current and reduce this loss as well. The source supplies total real power 78.65 kW, which equals the load power plus the feeder loss, consistent with conservation of energy.

Answer: 1.125 kW

(e)

The load has P = 77.52 kW and Q = 41.04 kvar, giving a power factor of cos(tan⁻¹(41.04/77.52)) = 0.883 lagging. The target power factor is 0.95 lagging, so the allowed reactive power is Q2 = P tan(cos⁻¹ 0.95) = 77.52 × tan(18.19°) = 77.52 × 0.3287 = 25.48 kvar. The capacitor must supply the difference, Qc = Q − Q2 = 41.04 − 25.48 = 15.56 kvar three-phase. This is a first-order sizing at the load voltage found in part (b), since a capacitor bank's kvar scales with the square of the actual voltage. For a delta-connected bank each phase would take 5.19 kvar. The line current would fall to about 81 A.

Answer: 15.56 kvar

A6 Practice Paper 14

Problem 1 [A6-066] Three-phase power, per-unit system and one-line diagrams

A one-line diagram shows a 30 MVA, 13.8 kV synchronous generator with a reactance of 0.15 pu on its own rating, connected to a 30 MVA, 13.8/138 kV step-up transformer with a leakage reactance of 0.10 pu on its own rating. A 138 kV transmission line follows, with a series impedance of 6 + j20 Ω per phase (shunt elements neglected). At the end of the line a load takes 22 MW at 0.92 power factor lagging, with the line-to-line voltage at the load held at 132 kV. Choose bases of 30 MVA, and 13.8 kV in the generator zone, which gives 138 kV in the line zone. Neglect all resistances except that of the line, and use the load voltage as the phase reference.

  1. (a) Find the base current in the 138 kV zone, in amperes. [3]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the line impedance in per unit. [4]
  3. (c) Find the per-unit load current magnitude. [3]
  4. (d) Find the generator terminal voltage, in kilovolts line-to-line. [5]
  5. (e) Find the magnitude of the generator internal emf behind its 0.15 pu reactance, in per unit. [5]
(a)

The base current in any zone is Ib = Sb/(√3 Vb), with the three-phase base power and the line-to-line base voltage. In the line zone, Ib = 30 × 10⁶/(√3 × 138 × 10³) = 30 × 10⁶/239 023 = 125.5 A. In the generator zone the base current would be 30 × 10⁶/(√3 × 13.8 × 10³) = 1255 A, ten times larger, which matches the 10:1 voltage ratio of the step-up transformer. Working with per-unit quantities removes the transformer from the calculation except for its leakage reactance, since all quantities are scaled by bases that follow the turns ratio. The base impedance in this zone is 138²/30 = 634.8 Ω.

Answer: 125.5 A

(b)

Divide the line impedance by the base impedance for the 138 kV zone, which is Zb = Vb²/Sb = (138)²/30 = 19044/30 = 634.8 Ω. The line impedance is then z = (6 + j20)/634.8 = 0.00945 + j0.03151 pu. The magnitude is |z| = √(0.00945² + 0.03151²) = √(8.93 × 10⁻⁵ + 9.93 × 10⁻⁴) = √(1.0823 × 10⁻³) = 0.03289 pu. The impedance angle is tan⁻¹(20/6) = 73.3 degrees, which is typical for a high voltage line, where reactance is much greater than resistance. The 22 MW load is a significant fraction of the 30 MVA base, so the drop in the line will be noticeable in per unit.

Answer: 0.0329 pu

(c)

Convert the load to per unit. The apparent power is S = P/pf = 22/0.92 = 23.91 MVA, so Spu = 23.91/30 = 0.7971 pu. The reactive part is Q = 22 tan(cos⁻¹ 0.92) = 22 × 0.4259 = 9.37 Mvar. The load voltage is 132/138 = 0.9565 pu. The current magnitude is |I| = Spu/Vpu = 0.7971/0.9565 = 0.8333 pu. In amperes this is 0.8333 × 125.5 = 104.6 A, which is consistent with S/(√3 × 132 kV) = 23.91 × 10⁶/(√3 × 132 000) = 104.6 A. The current lags the load voltage by 23.07 degrees, the angle for a 0.92 power factor. It is the same current at every point because the shunt branches have been neglected.

Answer: 0.833 pu

(d)

The load current phasor is I = (S/V)* = 0.8333∠−23.07° = 0.7667 − j0.3265 pu, taking V = 0.9565∠0° as the reference. The impedance between the load and the generator terminals is the line plus the transformer: z + j0.10 = 0.00945 + j0.13151 pu. The drop is I × z = (0.7667 − j0.3265)(0.00945 + j0.13151) = (0.00725 + 0.04294) + j(0.10083 − 0.00309) = 0.05019 + j0.09774 pu.
