The terminal voltage is V = 0.9565 + 0.05019 + j0.09774 = 1.00669 + j0.09774, magnitude 1.0114 pu. In kilovolts this is 1.0114 × 13.8 = 13.96 kV line-to-line. The generator stays within a few percent of its 13.8 kV rating.

Answer: 13.96 kV

(e)

The internal emf is the terminal voltage plus the drop across the generator reactance: E = Vt + jXd I. From part (d), Vt = 1.00669 + j0.09774 pu. Compute jXd I = j0.15 × (0.7667 − j0.3265) = j0.11500 + 0.04898 = 0.04898 + j0.11500 pu. Hence E = 1.00669 + 0.04898 + j(0.09774 + 0.11500) = 1.05567 + j0.21274 pu. The magnitude is √(1.05567² + 0.21274²) = √(1.11442 + 0.04526) = 1.0769 pu. In kilovolts this corresponds to 14.86 kV line-to-line. The angle of E relative to the load voltage is tan⁻¹(0.21274/1.05567) = 11.4 degrees, the total power angle between the generator emf and the load bus.

Answer: 1.077 pu

Problem 2 [A6-067] Unbalanced three-phase loads

A 600/347 V, four-wire, wye-connected, 60 Hz supply feeds an unbalanced load in a workshop. The line-to-neutral voltage of the source is 346.4 V rms. Take the phase sequence as a, b, c (positive), with Van = 346.4∠0° V, Vbn = 346.4∠−120° V and Vcn = 346.4∠+120° V. The three loads are wye-connected with impedances Za = 10 Ω (resistive), Zb = 8 + j6 Ω, and Zc = 15 − j5 Ω. Line impedances are negligible. In the normal case the neutral wire connects the load star point to the source neutral with zero impedance. A second case considers a fault in which the neutral wire opens, leaving the load star point floating.

  1. (a) With the neutral connected, find the magnitude of the neutral current, in amperes. [4]
  2. (b) With the neutral connected, find the total real power absorbed by the three loads, in kilowatts. [4]
  3. (c) With the neutral open, find the magnitude of the voltage between the load star point and the source neutral, in volts. [5]
  4. (d) With the neutral open, find the largest of the three load phase voltage magnitudes, in volts. [4]
  5. (e) State, in words, why an open neutral is hazardous for single-phase equipment connected to an unbalanced four-wire supply. [3]
(a)

With a zero-impedance neutral each load sees its own source phase voltage. The currents are Ia = 346.4∠0°/10 = 34.64∠0° A, Ib = 346.4∠−120°/(8 + j6) = 346.4∠−120°/(10∠36.87°) = 34.64∠−156.87° A, and Ic = 346.4∠120°/(15 − j5) = 346.4∠120°/(15.81∠−18.43°) = 21.91∠138.43° A. In rectangular form Ia = 34.64 + j0, Ib = −31.86 − j13.61, and Ic = −16.39 + j14.54 A. The neutral current is the phasor sum In = Ia + Ib + Ic = −13.61 + j0.93 A, with magnitude 13.64 A. This is less than the phase current of 34.64 A but is not negligible. The neutral conductor must carry it.

Answer: 13.64 A

(b)

Total real power is the sum of the individual phase powers, each being V I cosθ or I²R. Phase a: 34.64² × 10 = 12 000 W. Phase b: |Ib|² Rb = 34.64² × 8 = 1199.9 × 8 = 9599 W. Phase c: |Ic|² Rc = 21.91² × 15 = 480.1 × 15 = 7201 W. The sum is 12 000 + 9599 + 7201 = 28 800 W, or 28.80 kW. The reactive powers are Qb = 1199.9 × 6 = 7.20 kvar absorbed and Qc = −480.1 × 5 = −2.40 kvar (capacitive), so the net reactive power is 4.80 kvar. The wye connection with a neutral does not couple the phases, so each phase calculation is independent.

Answer: 28.80 kW

(c)

With the neutral open, the load star point N takes a potential that makes the three line currents sum to zero (Millman's theorem). The admittances are Ya = 0.1 S, Yb = 1/(8 + j6) = 0.08 − j0.06 S and Yc = 1/(15 − j5) = 0.06 + j0.02 S. The sum is Y = 0.24 − j0.04 S. The numerator is Σ Van-type terms: 346.4 × 0.1 = 34.64; Vbn Yb = 346.4∠−120° × 0.1∠−36.87° = 34.64∠−156.87°; Vcn Yc = 346.4∠120° × 0.06325∠18.43° = 21.91∠138.43°. These sum to −13.61 + j0.93, the same as the neutral current in part (a). Then VnN = (−13.61 + j0.93)/(0.24 − j0.04) = −55.79 − j5.43 V, which has magnitude 56.06 V.

Answer: 56.06 V

(d)

Each load phase voltage with the neutral open is the source phase voltage minus the neutral shift: Va' = Van − VnN, and so on. From part (c), VnN = −55.79 − j5.43 V. Then Va' = 346.4 + 55.79 + j5.43 = 402.19 + j5.43 V, Vb' = 346.4∠−120° − VnN = −117.41 − j294.56 V and Vc' = 346.4∠120° − VnN = −117.41 + j305.42 V. The magnitudes are |Va'| = 402.2 V, |Vb'| = 317.1 V and |Vc'| = 327.2 V. Phase a sees the highest voltage, 402.2 V, because the star-point shift VnN points opposite to Van and so adds to it. That voltage which is 16 percent above its 346.4 V rating. Phase b falls to 317.1 V, 8.5 percent below. The differences between these phasors still equal the source line-to-line voltages, a useful check. The largest magnitude is therefore 402.2 V.

Answer: 402.2 V

(e)

With the neutral intact each single-phase load is held at 347 V no matter how the other phases are loaded. When the neutral opens, the three loads form a floating star with their star point defined by the ratio of their admittances. A lightly loaded phase has a large impedance and takes a large share of the voltage, so it can see well above its rating, up to the full line-to-line voltage of 600 V when one phase carries almost no load. Lamps, motors and electronics rated for 347 V are then overstressed, while the heavily loaded phases are starved of voltage. In addition, the neutral conductor may become energized at a voltage above ground, a shock hazard. This is why neutral conductors are never fused or switched.

Answer: Phase voltages shift; lightly loaded phases see overvoltage.

Problem 3 [A6-068] Three-phase transformer connections and phase shift

Three identical single-phase transformers, each rated 100 kVA, 8000/600 V, 60 Hz, are connected as a three-phase bank to supply a quarry crusher from an 8 kV three-phase line. The bank is first connected delta on the 8000 V side and wye on the 600 V side. Each transformer has a leakage impedance of 0.02 + j0.05 per unit on its own rating, and the magnetizing branch is neglected. The same units are later reconnected delta on both sides, and one transformer is then removed for maintenance so the remaining two continue in open-delta. Voltage and current phase sequence is positive (a, b, c) and ANSI practice puts the high-voltage line-to-neutral voltage ahead of the low-voltage one by 30° for a delta-wye bank.

  1. (a) With the delta-wye connection, find the low-voltage line-to-line voltage, in volts. [3]
  2. (b) Find the rated low-voltage line current of the delta-wye bank, in amperes. [3]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the equivalent impedance of one transformer referred to its 600 V winding, in ohms. [4]
  4. (d) With the delta-delta bank reduced to open-delta, find the maximum three-phase load the two remaining transformers can supply without overload, in kVA. [5]
  5. (e) Explain why the delta-wye bank introduces a 30° phase displacement, and why that matters when the bank is paralleled with another source. [5]
(a)

In a wye connection the line-to-line voltage is √3 times the winding voltage. Each winding on the low-voltage side is rated 600 V, so the line-to-line voltage is VLL = √3 × 600 = 1.7321 × 600 = 1039.2 V. On the high-voltage side the delta puts the full 8000 V across each winding, so the line-to-line voltage there equals the winding voltage, 8000 V. The line-to-line voltage ratio of the bank is thus 8000/1039.2 = 7.698, not the 13.33 ratio of each transformer. This is a feature of the delta-wye connection, which steps the voltage down less than the per-transformer turns ratio would suggest (7.698 instead of 13.33). The line-to-neutral voltage on the low side is 600 V.

Answer: 1039.2 V

(b)

The bank rating is three times a single transformer, or 300 kVA. The line current on the low-voltage side is I = S/(√3 VLL) = 300 000/(1.7321 × 1039.2) = 300 000/1800 = 166.7 A. Because the wye winding carries the line current, this is also the winding current, and it agrees with a single transformer rating of 100 000/600 = 166.7 A. On the high-voltage side, the winding current is 100 000/8000 = 12.5 A, and the delta line current is √3 times that, or 21.65 A. The 21.65 A is smaller than 166.7 A by the voltage ratio 7.698, as required for the power to balance.

Answer: 166.7 A

(c)

The per-unit impedance is 0.02 + j0.05 on the transformer's own base. The magnitude is |z| = √(0.02² + 0.05²) = √(0.0004 + 0.0025) = √0.0029 = 0.05385 pu. The base impedance referred to the 600 V winding is Zbase = Vwinding²/Srated = 600²/100 000 = 360 000/100 000 = 3.6 Ω. The actual impedance magnitude is |Z| = 0.05385 × 3.6 = 0.1939 Ω. This is the impedance per transformer on the 600 V side and, since the 600 V windings are wye-connected, it is also the equivalent per-phase impedance seen from the line to neutral. The resistance part is 0.072 Ω and the reactance part 0.18 Ω.

Answer: 0.1939 Ω

(d)

When one transformer of a delta-delta bank is removed, the two remaining units form an open-delta (V-V) connection. Each remaining unit may carry only its rated winding current, 166.7 A on the 600 V side. The line current in open-delta equals the winding current, 166.7 A, since each line current flows through one winding in the open-delta. The maximum three-phase output is S = √3 VLL I = √3 × 600 × 166.7 = 173.2 kVA, using the 600 V line-to-line voltage of a delta secondary. The two units together are rated 200 kVA, so the bank delivers only 173.2/200 = 86.6 percent of their combined rating, and only 57.7 percent of the original 300 kVA bank capacity.

Answer: 173.2 kVA

(e)

In a delta-wye bank the high-voltage windings are connected line-to-line across the delta, so each winding voltage equals a high-voltage line-to-line voltage. The matching low-voltage winding voltage is a phase (line-to-neutral) voltage of the wye. A line-to-line voltage leads the corresponding line-to-neutral voltage by 30° in a positive sequence system. Hence the low-voltage line-to-neutral voltages are displaced by 30° from the high-voltage line-to-neutral voltages. Under ANSI practice the high side leads. If two banks with different shifts, say delta-wye and wye-wye, are paralleled on the low side, a 30° phase difference makes a large circulating current flow, since the voltage difference across the loop is about 52 percent of rated voltage.

Answer: 30 degree shift; paralleling requires equal shift.

Problem 4 [A6-069] Transmission line models and voltage regulation

A 230 kV, 60 Hz, three-phase overhead line 150 km long connects a hydro plant to a mining district. The line is represented by the nominal-π model, with half of the total shunt admittance at each end. Per kilometre, the series impedance is 0.08 + j0.48 Ω and the shunt admittance is j3.3 × 10⁻⁶ S. The load at the receiving end draws 200 MW at 0.95 power factor lagging, with the receiving-end line-to-line voltage held at 220 kV. Work with per-phase quantities using the receiving-end line-to-neutral voltage as the phase reference. Voltage regulation is defined as the rise in receiving-end voltage from full load to no load, divided by the full-load value, with the sending-end voltage held constant.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the A constant of the line. [3]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the B constant, in ohms. [3]
  3. (c) Find the sending-end line-to-line voltage, in kilovolts. [5]
  4. (d) Find the voltage regulation, in percent. [5]
  5. (e) Find the transmission efficiency (receiving-end real power divided by sending-end real power), in percent. [4]
(a)

First find the total line parameters. The series impedance is Z = (0.08 + j0.48) × 150 = 12 + j72 Ω and the total shunt admittance is Y = j3.3 × 10⁻⁶ × 150 = j4.95 × 10⁻⁴ S. For the nominal-π circuit the transmission constants are A = D = 1 + ZY/2. Compute ZY = (12 + j72)(j4.95 × 10⁻⁴) = j5.94 × 10⁻³ − 3.564 × 10⁻², so ZY/2 = −0.01782 + j0.00297. Hence A = 0.98218 + j0.00297, with magnitude 0.9822. The real part is below unity because the line charging reduces the effective series drop. The angle of A is only 0.17 degrees. The D constant is the same, as the line is symmetrical.

Answer: 0.9822

(b)

For the nominal-π circuit the B constant is simply the total series impedance, B = Z, since the shunt branches sit on the outside of the series element. Therefore B = 12 + j72 Ω, whose magnitude is √(12² + 72²) = √(144 + 5184) = √5328 = 72.99 Ω. The angle is tan⁻¹(72/12) = 80.5 degrees, which shows that the line is mostly reactive. The C constant is C = Y(1 + ZY/4) = j4.95 × 10⁻⁴ × (1 − 0.00891 + j0.00149) = about −7.4 × 10⁻⁷ + j4.906 × 10⁻⁴ S. As a check, A D − B C should equal 1 for a reciprocal network, and the product holds to four decimal places.

Answer: 72.99 Ω

(c)

The receiving-end phase voltage is VR = 220 000/√3 = 127 017 V. The receiving-end line current is IR = P/(√3 VLL pf) = 200 × 10⁶/(√3 × 220 000 × 0.95) = 552.5 A, at an angle of −18.19° (0.95 lagging), so IR = 524.9 − j172.5 A. The sending-end phase voltage is VS = A VR + B IR = (0.98218 + j0.00297)(127 017) + (12 + j72)(524.9 − j172.5). The first product is 124 754 + j377 V. The second is (6299 + 12 420) + j(37 793 − 2070) = 18 719 + j35 723 V. Adding gives 143 473 + j36 100 V, magnitude 147 950 V. The line-to-line value is √3 × 147 950 = 256.2 kV.

Answer: 256.2 kV

(d)

At no load the receiving-end current is zero, so VS = A VR,NL, and the no-load receiving-end voltage magnitude is VR,NL = |VS|/|A| = 147 950/0.9822 = 150 637 V per phase, or 260.9 kV line-to-line. This is the Ferranti rise: the open-circuit line charging pushes the voltage up. The full-load receiving-end phase voltage is 127 017 V. Regulation = (VR,NL − VR,FL)/VR,FL × 100 = (150 637 − 127 017)/127 017 × 100 = 18.59 percent. The regulation is high because the series drop at full load, about 32 percent of the receiving voltage, is large for a 150 km line carrying 200 MW. A shunt reactor or series capacitor would normally be considered to improve it.

Answer: 18.59 %

(e)

Sending-end current is IS = C VR + A IR. The first term is (−7.4 × 10⁻⁷ + j4.906 × 10⁻⁴)(127 017) = −0.094 + j62.31 A. The second term is (0.98218 + j0.00297)(524.9 − j172.5) = 515.5 − j169.4 + j1.56 + 0.51 = 516.0 − j167.9 A. The sum is IS = 515.9 − j105.6 A. The sending-end real power is PS = 3 Re(VS IS*) = 3 × Re[(143 473 + j36 100)(515.9 + j105.6)] = 3 × (74 018 000 − 3 812 000) = 3 × 70 206 000 = 210.6 MW. The efficiency is PR/PS = 200/210.6 = 0.9495, or 94.95 percent. The loss of about 10.6 MW is nearly all I²R in the series resistance, 3 × 552² × 12 = 11.0 MW, partly offset by charging.

Answer: 94.95 %

Problem 5 [A6-070] Power flow and real and reactive power control

Two substations in a 230 kV Ontario network are joined by a single lossless transmission link, whose series reactance is 0.12 pu on a 100 MVA, 230 kV base. Shunt elements and resistance are neglected. The sending bus voltage is held at 1.03 pu and the receiving bus voltage at 0.98 pu. The link delivers 120 MW of real power to the receiving bus. The sending bus voltage leads the receiving bus voltage by an angle δ, and the receiving bus voltage is the angle reference. Work in per unit and convert to MW and Mvar using the 100 MVA base. Treat reactive power as positive when it flows from the sending bus into the link, and into the receiving bus from the link.

  1. (a) Find the power angle δ, in degrees. [4]
  2. (b) Find the reactive power delivered to the receiving bus, in Mvar. [4]
  3. (c) Find the reactive power leaving the sending bus, in Mvar. [4]
  4. (d) Find the reactive power absorbed by the link reactance itself, in Mvar. [4]
  5. (e) Explain which of voltage magnitude and power angle mainly controls the flow of reactive power and which mainly controls the flow of real power on this link, and how a utility could use that. [4]
(a)

For a lossless link of reactance X, the real power transferred is P = Vs Vr sinδ/X. In per unit the delivered power is 120/100 = 1.20 pu. Solve for the angle: sinδ = P X/(Vs Vr) = 1.20 × 0.12/(1.03 × 0.98) = 0.144/1.0094 = 0.14265. Hence δ = sin⁻¹(0.14265) = 8.20 degrees. The angle is small, so the link is far below its steady-state stability limit. The maximum power at this angle setting would be Vs Vr/X = 1.0094/0.12 = 8.41 pu, which is 841 MW, seven times the present transfer. The linear relation between sinδ and P is why angle is the natural control variable for real power.

Answer: 8.20°

(b)

The reactive power received at the bus is Qr = (Vs Vr cosδ − Vr²)/X, with the sign convention that positive means flowing into the receiving bus. At δ = 8.20°, cosδ = 0.98978. Then Vs Vr cosδ = 1.0094 × 0.98978 = 0.99909. Subtract Vr² = 0.9604, giving 0.03869. Divide by X: Qr = 0.03869/0.12 = 0.3224 pu, which is 32.2 Mvar on the 100 MVA base. The receiving bus therefore absorbs 32.2 Mvar from the link, which it must supply to its own loads. The flow exists because Vs cosδ = 1.0197 exceeds Vr = 0.98, a difference of 0.0397 pu that drives reactive current through the reactance.

Answer: 32.2 Mvar

(c)

At the sending bus the reactive power leaving the bus into the link is Qs = (Vs² − Vs Vr cosδ)/X. With Vs² = 1.0609 and Vs Vr cosδ = 0.99909 from part (b), the numerator is 1.0609 − 0.99909 = 0.06181. Dividing by X = 0.12 gives Qs = 0.5151 pu, or 51.5 Mvar. This is larger than the 32.2 Mvar received because the link reactance itself absorbs reactive power, as the next part confirms. The apparent power leaving the sending bus is √(120² + 51.5²) = 130.6 MVA, a power factor of 0.919. A generator at that bus must supply this reactive power, so the sending bus voltage is held up only if the generator has reactive capability to spare.

Answer: 51.5 Mvar

(d)

The link reactance absorbs I²X vars, the difference between what leaves the sending bus and what arrives at the receiving bus: Qloss = Qs − Qr = 0.5151 − 0.3224 = 0.1927 pu = 19.3 Mvar. Alternatively, Qloss = (Vs² + Vr² − 2 Vs Vr cosδ)/X = (1.0609 + 0.9604 − 1.99818)/0.12 = 0.02312/0.12 = 0.1927 pu, the same. The current is I = S/V: the apparent power at the receiving bus is √(1.2² + 0.3224²) = 1.2426 pu, so I = 1.2426/0.98 = 1.268 pu, and I²X = 1.608 × 0.12 = 0.1929 pu. All three methods agree. The reactive loss grows with the square of the current, so power factor correction at the load would cut it.

Answer: 19.3 Mvar

(e)

For a link dominated by reactance, the real power depends mainly on the sine of the angle between the end voltages: P ≈ Vs Vr sinδ/X, with small voltage magnitudes changes having little effect. The reactive power depends mainly on the difference in voltage magnitudes: Q ≈ Vr (Vs cosδ − Vr)/X. Therefore the angle controls real power and the voltage magnitude controls reactive power. In this case a 5 percent voltage difference moves 32 Mvar, while an angle of only 8 degrees moves 120 MW. A utility can raise generator excitation or switch a shunt capacitor to move reactive power and hold voltage, and can change the angle using a phase-shifting transformer or generator dispatch to steer real power among parallel paths.

Answer: Angle controls real power; voltage difference controls reactive power.

A6 Practice Paper 15

Problem 1 [A6-071] Fault calculations and symmetrical components basics

A 25 MVA, 13.8 kV synchronous generator with subtransient reactance X''d = 0.15 per unit (on its own rating) feeds a 25 MVA, 13.8 kV delta / 138 kV grounded-wye step-up transformer with leakage reactance 0.10 per unit. A 138 kV transmission line with positive and negative sequence reactance of 20 Ω in total, and zero sequence reactance equal to three times that value, runs from the transformer to a remote substation bus. The generator is the only source, is unloaded before the fault, and has a positive and negative sequence reactance equal to X''d. The transformer zero-sequence reactance equals its positive-sequence leakage reactance of 0.10 per unit. Neglect all resistance, prefault load current and shunt elements. The transformer neutral on the 138 kV side is solidly grounded. Use a base of 25 MVA and 138 kV on the line.

  1. (a) Find the line reactance in per unit on the stated base. [3]
  2. (b) Find the rms fault current in amperes at the remote bus for a balanced three-phase fault. [5]
  3. (c) Find the rms fault current in amperes at the remote bus for a bolted single line to ground fault on phase a. [7]
  4. (d) Find the three-phase short-circuit MVA at the remote bus. [5]
(a)

The base impedance on the 138 kV side is Zbase = (kV base)² / MVA base = 138² / 25 = 19 044 / 25 = 761.76 Ω. The line reactance in ohms is 20 Ω, so on the stated base xline = 20 / 761.76 = 0.02625 per unit. The generator and transformer ratings equal the 25 MVA base and their voltage ratings match the 13.8 kV and 138 kV bases, so their per unit values (0.15 and 0.10) need no conversion. Changing base only matters for the line, because it was given in ohms. This per unit value is the same for the positive and negative sequence networks, and the zero sequence line reactance will be three times this figure, 0.07876 per unit, as stated in the problem.

Answer: 0.02625 per unit

(b)

For a balanced three-phase fault only the positive sequence network is involved. The total Thevenin reactance from the source to the fault is X1 = 0.15 + 0.10 + 0.02625 = 0.27625 per unit. With a prefault voltage of 1.0 per unit, the fault current is If = 1.0 / 0.27625 = 3.620 per unit. The base current on the 138 kV side is Ibase = 25 × 10⁶ / (√3 × 138 × 10³) = 104.59 A. Then If = 3.620 × 104.59 = 378.6 A. The result is an rms value of the symmetrical current, taken at the subtransient instant because the generator reactance used is X''d. No dc offset is included in this symmetrical value.

Answer: 378.6 A

(c)

The three sequence networks connect in series for a single line to ground fault. Positive and negative sequence reactances are each 0.27625 per unit. For zero sequence, the delta winding of the transformer on the generator side blocks zero sequence current from the generator, so only the transformer leakage reactance and the line are seen: X0 = 0.10 + 3 × 0.02625 = 0.17876 per unit. The sequence current is Ia1 = 1.0 / (X1 + X2 + X0) = 1.0 / (0.27625 + 0.27625 + 0.17876) = 1.0 / 0.73126 = 1.3675 per unit. Then Ia = 3 Ia1 = 4.1024 per unit, and in amperes Ia = 4.1024 × 104.59 = 429.1 A, which exceeds the three-phase value.

Answer: 429.1 A

(d)

Short-circuit MVA equals the base MVA multiplied by the per unit fault current for the three-phase fault: MVAsc = Sbase × If(pu) = 25 × 3.620 = 90.5 MVA. Equivalently, MVAsc = Sbase / X1 = 25 / 0.27625 = 90.5 MVA. This figure is the quantity a utility quotes as the strength of the bus and is used to size breakers and to judge voltage dip for motor starting. Because the generator is the only source here, the bus is weak compared with a typical grid connection, which is why the fault current is only about 3.6 times base current. A stiffer system would have a smaller Thevenin reactance and a larger MVA figure.

Answer: 90.5 MVA

Problem 2 [A6-072] Generation, load curves and economic dispatch basics

A small island utility supplies its load from two thermal units. Unit 1 has fuel cost C1 = 500 + 8.0 P1 + 0.004 P1² in dollars per hour and Unit 2 has C2 = 300 + 9.0 P2 + 0.006 P2² in dollars per hour, where P is output in MW. Each unit may be run between 50 MW and 450 MW, and both are committed all day. Transmission losses are neglected. The daily load curve is simple: 600 MW for 12 hours (day) and 300 MW for 12 hours (night). The utility is comparing economic dispatch with a policy under which both units always share the load equally. Treat the load as constant within each period and use the same two units in both periods.

  1. (a) Find the output of Unit 1 in MW at the 600 MW load under economic dispatch. [5]
  2. (b) Find the system incremental cost λ in $/MWh at the 600 MW load. [3]
  3. (c) Find the hourly fuel cost in $/h at the 600 MW load under economic dispatch. [5]
  4. (d) Find the daily fuel cost saving in dollars of economic dispatch over equal sharing of the load, over both periods. [7]
(a)

Economic dispatch requires equal incremental cost, dC1/dP1 = dC2/dP2 = λ, with P1 + P2 = 600 MW and no limits binding. The incremental costs are 8.0 + 0.008 P1 and 9.0 + 0.012 P2. Substituting P1 = 600 − P2: 8.0 + 0.008(600 − P2) = 9.0 + 0.012 P2, so 12.8 − 0.008 P2 = 9.0 + 0.012 P2, giving 3.8 = 0.020 P2 and P2 = 190 MW. Hence P1 = 600 − 190 = 410 MW. Both values lie inside the 50 to 450 MW limits, so the unconstrained solution is valid. Unit 1 carries more because its incremental cost rises more slowly with output.

Answer: 410 MW

(b)

The system incremental cost is the common value of the two incremental costs at the optimum. Using Unit 1: λ = 8.0 + 0.008 × 410 = 8.0 + 3.28 = 11.28 $/MWh. Checking with Unit 2: λ = 9.0 + 0.012 × 190 = 9.0 + 2.28 = 11.28 $/MWh, which agrees. This number is the cost of serving one additional MW for one hour at this load level, and it is the figure a dispatcher would use to price a small increase in demand or to decide whether buying power from a neighbour at a given price would be cheaper than generating it.

Answer: 11.28 $/MWh

(c)

Evaluate both cost functions at the dispatch point. Unit 1: C1 = 500 + 8.0(410) + 0.004(410²) = 500 + 3280 + 672.4 = 4452.4 $/h. Unit 2: C2 = 300 + 9.0(190) + 0.006(190²) = 300 + 1710 + 216.6 = 2226.6 $/h. The total is 4452.4 + 2226.6 = 6679.0 $/h. The fixed terms 500 and 300 are the no-load costs of keeping the units on line and do not affect the dispatch, but they do appear in the total cost, which is the figure needed when comparing against a different operating policy such as equal sharing of the load.

Answer: 6679 $/h

(d)

Equal sharing at 600 MW gives 300 MW each: C1 = 500 + 2400 + 360 = 3260 $/h and C2 = 300 + 2700 + 540 = 3540 $/h, total 6800 $/h. Economic dispatch costs 6679 $/h, a saving of 121 $/h. At 300 MW the equal split is 150 MW each: C1 = 500 + 1200 + 90 = 1790 and C2 = 300 + 1350 + 135 = 1785, total 3575 $/h. Economic dispatch at 300 MW gives P2 = 70 MW and P1 = 230 MW, with C1 = 500 + 1840 + 211.6 = 2551.6 and C2 = 300 + 630 + 29.4 = 959.4, total 3511 $/h, saving 64 $/h. Daily saving = 12 × 121 + 12 × 64 = 1452 + 768 = 2220 $/day.

Answer: 2220 $/day

Problem 3 [A6-073] DC machine models and speed control

A separately excited DC motor drives a mine hoist drum through a rigid coupling. The armature resistance is 0.18 Ω. At rated conditions the motor takes 75 A at an armature terminal voltage of 240 V and runs at 1150 rpm with rated field current. Brush drop, armature reaction and friction are neglected, so electromagnetic torque equals shaft torque, and the back emf is proportional to flux and speed. The hoist load presents a constant torque of 100 N·m at the motor shaft whether raising or lowering. The armature is fed from a controlled rectifier whose terminal voltage can be varied from zero to 240 V, and the field can be weakened below rated value by reducing the field current, with flux proportional to field current.

  1. (a) Find the machine constant Kφ in V·s/rad and the rated electromagnetic torque in N·m. Give the torque. [4]
  2. (b) With full field, find the armature terminal voltage needed to raise the load at 900 rpm. [5]
  3. (c) The rectifier is at its 240 V limit and the field is reduced to 0.70 of rated flux. Find the speed in rpm at which the motor then raises a 60 N·m load. [6]
  4. (d) With full field, the 100 N·m load is lowered by the motor in regenerative operation at 600 rpm. Find the armature terminal voltage in volts. [5]
(a)

At rated load the back emf is Eb = Va − Ia Ra = 240 − 75 × 0.18 = 240 − 13.5 = 226.5 V. The rated speed is ω = 1150 × 2π / 60 = 120.43 rad/s. The machine constant is Kφ = Eb / ω = 226.5 / 120.43 = 1.8808 V·s/rad. The electromagnetic torque is T = Kφ Ia = 1.8808 × 75 = 141.06 N·m. With friction neglected this is also the rated shaft torque, and it equals the electrical power converted, Eb Ia = 226.5 × 75 = 16 988 W, divided by the speed 120.43 rad/s. The same constant relates torque to armature current for any speed at full field.

Answer: 141.1 N·m

(b)

With full field Kφ is unchanged, so the armature current needed for the 100 N·m load torque is Ia = T / Kφ = 100 / 1.8808 = 53.17 A, which is below the rated 75 A. The speed is ω = 900 × 2π / 60 = 94.25 rad/s, giving Eb = Kφ ω = 1.8808 × 94.25 = 177.26 V. The terminal voltage is Va = Eb + Ia Ra = 177.26 + 53.17 × 0.18 = 177.26 + 9.57 = 186.8 V. Armature voltage control gives constant torque capability below base speed because flux stays at its rated value, so the same current produces the same torque at every speed in this region.

Answer: 186.8 V

(c)

With flux at 0.70 of rated, Kφ' = 0.70 × 1.8808 = 1.3166 V·s/rad. The armature current for a 60 N·m load is Ia = T / Kφ' = 60 / 1.3166 = 45.57 A. The back emf is Eb = Va − Ia Ra = 240 − 45.57 × 0.18 = 240 − 8.20 = 231.80 V. The angular speed is ω = Eb / Kφ' = 231.80 / 1.3166 = 176.06 rad/s, and in rpm n = 176.06 × 60 / (2π) = 1681 rpm. This is above base speed, in the field-weakening region, where the torque capability falls roughly in inverse proportion to speed while power capability stays approximately constant if armature current is held at its limit.

Answer: 1681 rpm

(d)

When lowering, the load drives the machine as a generator, so the electromagnetic torque opposes the motion and the armature current reverses: Ia = −53.17 A for the same 100 N·m, with full field. The speed is ω = 600 × 2π / 60 = 62.83 rad/s, so Eb = Kφ ω = 1.8808 × 62.83 = 118.18 V. The terminal voltage from Va = Eb + Ia Ra, with Ia negative, is Va = 118.18 − 53.17 × 0.18 = 118.18 − 9.57 = 108.6 V. The terminal voltage is below the back emf, so power flows from the machine into the supply, and the rectifier must be a bridge able to invert, otherwise a braking resistor would be needed.

Answer: 108.6 V

Problem 4 [A6-074] DC motor starting and braking

A 250 V shunt motor has an armature resistance of 0.25 Ω and a constant field supplied from a separate stabilised source, so flux is constant. At rated load it draws 60 A in the armature and runs at 1000 rpm. The motor and its fan load have a combined moment of inertia of 3.5 kg·m². The armature current must never exceed 1.5 times the rated armature current, which is 90 A. For starting, a resistor is connected in series with the armature and the full 250 V is applied. For dynamic braking from rated speed, the armature is disconnected from the supply and connected across an external resistor while the field is held constant. Neglect friction and windage and brush drop.

  1. (a) Find the starting resistor in ohms that limits the initial starting current to 90 A. [4]
  2. (b) Find the external braking resistor in ohms that limits the initial dynamic braking current to 90 A from rated speed. [5]
  3. (c) Find the initial braking torque in N·m at the instant braking starts. [5]
  4. (d) Find the energy in kJ dissipated in the external braking resistor while the motor is brought to rest, assuming the load torque is zero during braking. [6]
(a)

At standstill the back emf is zero, so the full supply voltage appears across the armature resistance plus the added starting resistor. Ist = V / (Ra + Rs). Solving for the total, Ra + Rs = 250 / 90 = 2.778 Ω. The external starting resistor is therefore Rs = 2.778 − 0.25 = 2.528 Ω. Without it the current would be 250 / 0.25 = 1000 A, over sixteen times rated, which would damage the commutator and the supply. As the motor accelerates, the back emf rises and the current falls, so the resistor is cut out in steps to keep the torque and the current near the limit.

Answer: 2.528 Ω

(b)

At rated load the back emf is Eb = V − Ia Ra = 250 − 60 × 0.25 = 235 V. At the instant the armature is switched to the braking resistor the speed has not changed, so the emf is still 235 V and the only voltage driving current is that emf, acting around a loop of the armature resistance and the external resistor. Therefore 90 = 235 / (0.25 + Rb). The total loop resistance is 235 / 90 = 2.611 Ω. The external resistor is Rb = 2.611 − 0.25 = 2.361 Ω. The current reverses relative to motoring, so the electromagnetic torque opposes the rotation and slows the machine.

Answer: 2.361 Ω

(c)

The machine constant is the back emf divided by the speed. The speed is ω = 1000 × 2π / 60 = 104.72 rad/s, so Kφ = 235 / 104.72 = 2.2441 V·s/rad. With flux constant, the electromagnetic torque is proportional to armature current, T = Kφ Ia. At the instant braking starts, Ia = 90 A, so T = 2.2441 × 90 = 201.97 N·m, about 202 N·m. Compare with the rated motoring torque of 2.2441 × 60 = 134.6 N·m: the braking torque is 1.5 times larger, as expected from the current ratio. The torque decays as the speed and the emf fall during the stop.

Answer: 202.0 N·m

(d)

The kinetic energy stored in the rotating parts at rated speed is E = ½ J ω² = 0.5 × 3.5 × 104.72² = 0.5 × 3.5 × 10 966 = 19 191 J, about 19.19 kJ. With no load torque or friction, all of this energy is converted to electrical energy by the machine acting as a generator, and the same current flows through the armature and external resistors in series. The energy divides in proportion to resistance. The external share is Rb / (Rb + Ra) = 2.361 / 2.611 = 0.9042. Energy in the external resistor = 0.9042 × 19.19 = 17.35 kJ, and the remaining 1.84 kJ heats the armature winding.

Answer: 17.35 kJ

Problem 5 [A6-075] Synchronous generator equivalent circuit and regulation

A 2.5 MVA, 4160 V, three-phase, wye-connected, 60 Hz synchronous generator has an armature resistance of 0.12 Ω per phase. In an open-circuit test a field current of 80 A gives a rated line voltage of 4160 V on the air-gap line, and the open-circuit voltage is proportional to field current over the range used here, so saturation is ignored. In a short-circuit test the same field current of 80 A gives a line armature current of 520 A. The generator is later connected to an infinite bus of 4160 V line to line, which fixes terminal voltage and frequency. Use the cylindrical rotor model and treat the synchronous reactance as constant.

  1. (a) Find the synchronous reactance in ohms per phase. [4]
  2. (b) Find the rated line current in amperes. [3]
  3. (c) Find the voltage regulation in percent at rated load and 0.8 power factor lagging, with rated terminal voltage. [7]
  4. (d) The field current is raised so that the open-circuit line voltage would be 5200 V, and the generator on the infinite bus delivers 1.5 MW. Neglecting Ra, find the power angle in degrees. [6]
(a)

The phase voltage on open circuit is 4160 / √3 = 2401.8 V, and on short circuit this same internal emf drives 520 A through the synchronous impedance. Zs = 2401.8 / 520 = 4.619 Ω per phase. The synchronous reactance is Xs = √(Zs² − Ra²) = √(4.619² − 0.12²) = √(21.335 − 0.0144) = 4.617 Ω. The armature resistance changes the result by only 0.04 percent, so the machine is almost purely reactive in its internal impedance. The two tests give Zs because the short circuit current is limited only by the synchronous impedance, and because the field current is the same in both tests the internal emf is the same.

Answer: 4.617 Ω

(b)

The rated line current follows from the apparent power rating of the three-phase machine: S = √3 VL IL, so IL = S / (√3 VL) = 2.5 × 10⁶ / (√3 × 4160) = 2.5 × 10⁶ / 7205.3 = 347.0 A. In a wye connection the phase current equals the line current. This current is used as the full-load armature current for the regulation calculation. Comparing with the short-circuit current of 520 A at 80 A field current, the short circuit current at that excitation is 1.5 times the rated current, so the machine can sustain a short circuit of about 1.5 times rated current at this excitation.

Answer: 347.0 A

(c)

Take the terminal phase voltage as the reference, V = 2401.8 ∠0° V. The rated current at 0.8 lagging is I = 347.0 ∠−36.87° = 277.6 − j208.2 A. The internal emf is E = V + I(Ra + jXs) with Ra + jXs = 0.12 + j4.617. The product I(Ra + jXs) = (277.6 − j208.2)(0.12 + j4.617) = 33.3 + j1281.7 − j25.0 + 961.2 = 994.5 + j1256.7 V. Then E = 3396.3 + j1256.7, with magnitude 3621.3 V. Regulation = (E − V) / V = (3621.3 − 2401.8) / 2401.8 = 50.8 percent. The large value reflects the high synchronous reactance and the lagging power factor.

Answer: 50.8 percent

(d)

The internal emf is proportional to field current. If the open-circuit line voltage is 5200 V, the phase emf is E = 5200 / √3 = 3002.2 V, which corresponds to a field current of 80 × 5200 / 4160 = 100 A. With Ra neglected, the three-phase real power is P = 3 E V sin δ / Xs. Solving, sin δ = P Xs / (3 E V) = 1.5 × 10⁶ × 4.617 / (3 × 3002.2 × 2401.8) = 6.9255 × 10⁶ / 2.1632 × 10⁷ = 0.3202. The power angle is δ = asin(0.3202) = 18.67 degrees. The stability limit is at 90 degrees, so this operating point has a comfortable margin.

Answer: 18.67 degrees

A6 Practice Paper 16

Problem 1 [A6-076] Synchronous motor operation and power factor

A manufacturing plant is supplied at 600 V, three-phase, 60 Hz. Its existing induction motor and other inductive loads draw 800 kW at a power factor of 0.72 lagging. The plant engineer proposes to add a wye-connected synchronous motor that draws 400 kW from the 600 V bus and is over-excited so that the combined plant power factor becomes 0.95 lagging. The synchronous motor has a synchronous reactance of 0.90 Ω per phase and negligible armature resistance. Assume the bus voltage is held at 600 V line to line and the 400 kW is the real power drawn at the motor terminals. Use the convention that reactive power absorbed by an inductive load is positive.

  1. (a) Find the reactive power in kvar absorbed by the existing inductive loads. [4]
  2. (b) Find the reactive power in kvar that the synchronous motor must deliver to the bus (give it as a positive number of leading kvar). [5]
  3. (c) Find the line current of the synchronous motor in amperes. [4]
  4. (d) Find the line to line internal generated voltage of the synchronous motor in volts, using the cylindrical rotor model. [7]
(a)

The power factor angle of the existing load is θ = arccos(0.72) = 43.95 degrees, and tan θ = 0.9639. The reactive power is Q = P tan θ = 800 × 0.9639 = 771.1 kvar. The apparent power is S = P / pf = 800 / 0.72 = 1111 kVA, and checking, √(800² + 771.1²) = 1111 kVA. This reactive power is carried by the supply feeder and transformer in addition to the real power, which causes extra current, heating and voltage drop. Reducing it by supplying reactive power locally is the reason for the power factor correction proposed in the problem.

Answer: 771.1 kvar

(b)

With the motor added, the total real power is 800 + 400 = 1200 kW. For a combined power factor of 0.95 lagging, tan θ = tan(arccos 0.95) = 0.3287, so the total reactive power absorbed is Qtotal = 1200 × 0.3287 = 394.4 kvar. The existing loads absorb 771.1 kvar, so the motor must supply the difference: Qmotor = 394.4 − 771.1 = −376.7 kvar, that is, it delivers 376.7 kvar leading to the bus. The motor then draws apparent power S = √(400² + 376.7²) = 549.4 kVA, at power factor 400 / 549.4 = 0.728 leading, and it acts as a rotating capacitor while doing useful mechanical work.

Answer: 376.7 kvar

(c)

The motor apparent power from the previous part is S = √(400² + 376.7²) = 549.4 kVA. The line current is I = S / (√3 VL) = 549.4 × 10³ / (√3 × 600) = 549 400 / 1039.2 = 528.7 A. This is the magnitude of current at the motor terminals, with a leading phase angle of arccos(0.728) = 43.3 degrees relative to the phase voltage. The motor draws more current than a unity power factor motor of the same real power would, which would take 400 000 / 1039.2 = 384.9 A. The extra current is the cost of supplying reactive power to the rest of the plant and must be allowed for in the motor's thermal rating.

Answer: 528.7 A

(d)

Use phase quantities with the terminal phase voltage as reference: V = 600 / √3 = 346.4 ∠0° V. The phase current leads: I = 528.7 (cos φ + j sin φ), with cos φ = 400 / 549.4 = 0.728 and sin φ = 376.7 / 549.4 = 0.6856, so I = 384.9 + j362.5 A. For a motor, E = V − jXs I = 346.4 − j0.9 (384.9 + j362.5) = 346.4 − j346.4 + 326.3 = 672.7 − j346.4 V. The magnitude is √(672.7² + 346.4²) = 756.6 V per phase, so the line value is √3 × 756.6 = 1310 V. Since E is greater than V, the motor is over-excited, and E lags V by 27.2 degrees.

Answer: 1310 V

Problem 2 [A6-077] Three-phase induction motor equivalent circuit and torque-slip

A 600 V, 60 Hz, four-pole, wye-connected three-phase induction motor drives a centrifugal fan. The per-phase equivalent circuit has stator resistance R1 = 0.45 Ω, stator leakage reactance X1 = 0.90 Ω, magnetising reactance Xm = 35 Ω (connected in parallel with the rotor branch, with no core loss resistor), rotor resistance referred to the stator R2 = 0.40 Ω, and rotor leakage reactance referred to the stator X2 = 0.90 Ω. Friction and windage are neglected and the supply is 600 V line to line. The fan load torque varies as the square of speed and equals 150 N·m at synchronous speed. Treat synchronous speed as 1800 rpm.

  1. (a) Find the stator line current in amperes at a slip of 0.03. [4]
  2. (b) Find the air-gap (electromagnetic) torque in N·m at a slip of 0.03. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum (breakdown) torque in N·m. [6]
  4. (d) Find the operating speed in rpm at which the motor torque equals the fan load torque. [6]
(a)

At s = 0.03 the rotor branch impedance is Zr = R2 / s + jX2 = 13.333 + j0.90 Ω. In parallel with jXm = j35 Ω this gives Zp = (j35)(13.333 + j0.90) / (13.333 + j35.90) = 11.137 + j5.014 Ω. The total input impedance is Zin = R1 + jX1 + Zp = 0.45 + j0.90 + 11.137 + j5.014 = 11.587 + j5.914 Ω, with magnitude 13.009 Ω. The phase voltage is 600 / √3 = 346.4 V, so the stator current is I1 = 346.4 / 13.009 = 26.63 A. The line current equals the phase current in a wye connection, and it lags the phase voltage by atan(5.914 / 11.587) = 27.0 degrees, giving a power factor of 0.89 lagging.

Answer: 26.63 A

(b)

The voltage across the parallel branch is Vm = I1 Zp, and the rotor current is I2 = Vm / Zr. Evaluating the complex numbers, |I2| = 24.34 A. The air-gap power is Pag = 3 |I2|² R2 / s = 3 × 24.34² × 0.40 / 0.03 = 23 691 W. The synchronous angular speed is ωs = 2π × 1800 / 60 = 188.5 rad/s, and the torque is T = Pag / ωs = 23 691 / 188.5 = 125.7 N·m. This torque is produced at 1746 rpm, where the rotor angular speed is (1 − s) ωs = 182.8 rad/s, so the mechanical output is 125.7 × 182.8 = 22.98 kW, and the rotor copper loss is s Pag = 711 W.

Answer: 125.7 N·m

(c)

The Thevenin voltage is Vth = V jXm / (R1 + j(X1 + Xm)) = 346.4 × j35 / (0.45 + j35.9), with magnitude 337.7 V. The Thevenin impedance is Zth = (R1 + jX1)(jXm) / (R1 + j(X1 + Xm)) = 0.4277 + j0.8828 Ω, so Rth = 0.4277 Ω and Xth = 0.8828 Ω. The maximum torque is Tmax = 3 Vth² / (2 ωs [Rth + √(Rth² + (Xth + X2)²)]). The square root term is √(0.4277² + 1.7828²) = 1.8334 Ω. So Tmax = 3 × 337.7² / (2 × 188.5 × (0.4277 + 1.8334)) = 342 122 / 852.4 = 401.4 N·m. It occurs at slip sm = R2 / √(Rth² + (Xth + X2)²) = 0.40 / 1.8334 = 0.218.

Answer: 401.4 N·m

(d)

The fan torque as a function of slip is TL = 150 (1 − s)² N·m, since speed scales as 1 − s and the torque is 150 N·m at synchronous speed. The motor torque Tem(s) comes from the equivalent circuit. The steady operating point is where Tem(s) = TL(s) in the stable region below the slip at maximum torque. At s = 0.03 the motor torque is 125.7 N·m while the load is 150 × 0.9409 = 141.1 N·m, so the load exceeds the motor torque and slip must increase. Solving numerically for the root gives s = 0.0338, where both torques are about 140 N·m. The speed is n = 1800 (1 − 0.0338) = 1739 rpm. The fan torque falls only gently as speed drops, so the operating point sits close to synchronous speed.

Answer: 1739 rpm

Problem 3 [A6-078] Induction motor starting and speed control

A 600 V, 60 Hz, three-phase squirrel-cage induction motor of 75 kW rating is to be started across the line from a plant supply that has a source impedance of j0.04 Ω per phase (equivalent wye) between the 600 V bus and the motor terminals. Locked-rotor tests at rated voltage show a locked-rotor line current of 570 A at a power factor of 0.28 lagging, and a locked-rotor torque of 1.60 times rated full-load torque. Assume the locked-rotor impedance is constant during the first instant of starting, the supply behind the source impedance is exactly 600 V line to line, and motor torque varies as the square of the applied terminal voltage. An autotransformer starter with a 65 percent tap is also being considered.

  1. (a) Find the locked-rotor impedance of the motor per phase, as a magnitude in ohms. [4]
  2. (b) With direct-on-line starting through the source impedance, find the line to line voltage in volts at the motor terminals at the instant of starting. [6]
  3. (c) Find the starting torque in per unit of rated torque for the direct-on-line start with the voltage found in part (b). [4]
  4. (d) For the 65 percent autotransformer tap, and neglecting the source impedance, find the line current drawn from the supply in amperes at the instant of starting. [6]
(a)

At rated voltage, the phase voltage is 600 / √3 = 346.4 V and the locked-rotor line current of 570 A is also the phase current for the equivalent wye. The magnitude of the locked-rotor impedance is |Zlr| = 346.4 / 570 = 0.6077 Ω per phase. The angle is arccos(0.28) = 73.74 degrees, so Zlr = 0.6077 ∠73.74° = 0.1702 + j0.5834 Ω. This is a mainly inductive impedance because at standstill the rotor branch resistance is small compared with the reactances and the magnetising branch is neglected, as is usual for locked-rotor calculations of this accuracy.

Answer: 0.6077 Ω

(b)

The supply voltage divides between the source impedance Zs = j0.04 Ω and the motor impedance Zlr = 0.1702 + j0.5834 Ω. The motor terminal phase voltage is Vm = 346.4 × Zlr / (Zlr + Zs). The sum is Zlr + Zs = 0.1702 + j0.6234 Ω, with magnitude 0.6462 Ω. The magnitude of the ratio is 0.6077 / 0.6462 = 0.9404. The terminal phase voltage is 346.4 × 0.9404 = 325.8 V, so the line voltage is √3 × 325.8 = 564.3 V. The dip is 6 percent, caused by the heavy locked-rotor current of about 536 A flowing through the source reactance, and it will also affect other loads on the bus.

Answer: 564.3 V

(c)

Torque varies as the square of terminal voltage. The ratio of actual to rated terminal voltage is 564.3 / 600 = 0.9405. The square is 0.8845. The starting torque is 1.60 × 0.8845 = 1.415 per unit of rated full-load torque. The voltage dip therefore costs about 12 percent of the available starting torque. If the load has a breakaway torque close to 1.4 per unit, the motor may not start, or it may accelerate slowly with a long period of high current, which is why a weak supply can force the use of a reduced voltage starter or a soft starter.

Answer: 1.415 pu

(d)

With a 65 percent tap, the voltage across the motor is 0.65 times line voltage, so the motor current is 0.65 × 570 = 370.5 A. An ideal autotransformer transforms current inversely to voltage, so the supply current is the motor current multiplied by the tap ratio, 0.65 × 370.5 = 240.8 A, which is 0.65² × 570. This is 42.25 percent of the direct-on-line locked-rotor current, a larger reduction than the voltage reduction alone. The starting torque is reduced by the same factor, 0.65² × 1.60 = 0.676 per unit. A reduction in current of 42.25 percent costs a reduction in torque of 57.75 percent, and the magnetising current of the transformer is neglected.

Answer: 240.8 A

Problem 4 [A6-079] Distribution system voltage drop and capacitor placement

A 12.47 kV (line to line) three-phase distribution feeder serves a single lumped load at its far end, 6 km from the substation. The line impedance is 0.22 + j0.38 Ω per kilometre per phase, with shunt capacitance neglected. The load is 3.0 MW at 0.85 power factor lagging and the voltage at the load end is held at 12.47 kV line to line by a regulator. The utility plans to install a 1.2 Mvar three-phase capacitor bank at the load bus to reduce losses and the voltage drop along the feeder. Assume the real power demand is unchanged by the capacitor and that the load voltage stays at 12.47 kV in both cases.

  1. (a) Find the feeder line current in amperes before the capacitor is installed. [3]
  2. (b) Find the sending-end line to line voltage in kilovolts before the capacitor is installed, using the exact phasor method. [6]
  3. (c) Find the sending-end line to line voltage in kilovolts after the 1.2 Mvar capacitor is installed at the load bus. [6]
  4. (d) Find the reduction in feeder real power loss in kilowatts due to the capacitor. [5]
(a)

The three-phase real power is P = √3 VL IL pf, so IL = P / (√3 VL pf) = 3.0 × 10⁶ / (√3 × 12 470 × 0.85) = 3.0 × 10⁶ / 18 358 = 163.4 A. The apparent power is S = P / pf = 3.53 MVA, and the reactive power is Q = P tan(arccos 0.85) = 3.0 × 0.6197 = 1.859 Mvar. The current lags the load voltage by arccos(0.85) = 31.79 degrees. This current flows through the whole line, and the line impedance is 6 × (0.22 + j0.38) = 1.32 + j2.28 Ω per phase, which will be used for the voltage drop and loss calculations.

Answer: 163.4 A

(b)

Take the load phase voltage as reference: Vr = 12 470 / √3 = 7199.6 V. The current phasor is I = 163.4 (0.85 − j0.5268) = 138.9 − j86.1 A. The drop is I Z = (138.9 − j86.1)(1.32 + j2.28) = 183.3 + j316.7 − j113.7 + 196.3 = 379.6 + j203.0 V. The sending phase voltage is Vs = 7199.6 + 379.6 + j203.0 = 7579.2 + j203.0 V, with magnitude 7582.2 V. The sending line voltage is √3 × 7582.2 = 13.13 kV. This is 5.3 percent above the load voltage, a large drop for a distribution feeder, which is why the regulator at the load is needed.

Answer: 13.13 kV

(c)

The capacitor supplies 1.2 Mvar at the load bus, so the reactive power drawn through the feeder falls to 1.859 − 1.2 = 0.659 Mvar. The apparent power is S = √(3.0² + 0.659²) = 3.072 MVA, the power factor at the feeder end is 3.0 / 3.072 = 0.9767 lagging, and the line current is 3.072 × 10⁶ / (√3 × 12 470) = 142.2 A. The current phasor is 142.2 (0.9767 − j0.2145) = 138.9 − j30.5 A. The drop is (138.9 − j30.5)(1.32 + j2.28) = 183.3 + j316.7 − j40.3 + 69.5 = 252.8 + j276.4 V. Vs = 7452.4 + j276.4 V, magnitude 7457.5 V, so the line value is 12.92 kV.

Answer: 12.92 kV

(d)

The three-phase loss is 3 I² R with R = 1.32 Ω per phase. Before the capacitor, the loss is 3 × 163.4² × 1.32 = 3 × 26 700 × 1.32 = 105.7 kW. After the capacitor, the current is 142.2 A, and the loss is 3 × 142.2² × 1.32 = 3 × 20 221 × 1.32 = 80.1 kW. The reduction is 105.7 − 80.1 = 25.65 kW, about 24 percent. The real current component is unchanged at 138.9 A, so the reduction comes entirely from removing part of the reactive current. Beyond this point, adding more capacitance would offer diminishing returns, and eventually the capacitor would overcompensate and raise the current again.

Answer: 25.65 kW

Problem 5 [A6-080] Machine or system selection combining losses, rating and cost

A water utility must choose between two 90 kW, 600 V, four-pole induction motors for a raw water pump with a continuous shaft load of 75 kW. The pump runs 6000 hours per year. Motor A is a standard-efficiency design with an efficiency of 93.0 percent at this load and costs 6800 dollars installed. Motor B is a premium-efficiency design with 95.4 percent efficiency at the same load and costs 9400 dollars installed. Electricity costs 0.11 dollars per kWh, the service life is 10 years, and the utility uses a discount rate of 8 percent per year with energy costs paid at the end of each year. Ignore maintenance, demand charges and any change in power factor between the motors.

  1. (a) Find the electrical input power of Motor A in kilowatts at the 75 kW load. [3]
  2. (b) Find the annual saving in energy cost in dollars from choosing Motor B over Motor A. [5]
  3. (c) Find the present worth in dollars of ten years of these annual savings at 8 percent. [5]
  4. (d) State two non-cost factors that could still favour Motor A in this installation. [7]
(a)

The input power is the output divided by the efficiency. For Motor A, Pin = 75 / 0.930 = 80.65 kW. The losses are 80.65 − 75 = 5.65 kW, released as heat in the windings, core and bearings and in the cooling air. Motor B draws 75 / 0.954 = 78.62 kW with losses of 3.62 kW, so the premium design reduces the losses by about 36 percent. Because efficiency is defined at the operating load rather than at rated load, the comparison is valid for this 75 kW duty, which is 83 percent of the 90 kW nameplate rating, near the efficiency peak of a typical motor.

Answer: 80.65 kW

(b)

The difference in input power is 80.645 − 78.616 = 2.029 kW. Over 6000 hours the energy saved is 2.029 × 6000 = 12 173 kWh per year. At 0.11 dollars per kWh the annual saving is 12 173 × 0.11 = 1339 dollars per year. This saving arises solely from the lower losses in Motor B. The calculation assumes continuous operation at exactly 75 kW, so if the pump load varies the saving will change, and it would be proportionally lower for a duty with fewer running hours or a lower average load factor.

Answer: 1339 dollars

(c)

The present worth factor for a uniform annual series is (1 − (1 + i)−n) / i = (1 − 1.08−10) / 0.08. Since 1.0810 = 2.1589, 1.08−10 = 0.46319, so the factor is (1 − 0.46319) / 0.08 = 6.7101. The present worth of the savings is 1339.0 × 6.7101 = 8985 dollars. The discounting reflects the fact that a saving in the tenth year is worth less today than a saving in the first. The extra initial cost of Motor B is 9400 − 6800 = 2600 dollars, which is well below this present worth, so the premium motor pays for itself.

Answer: 8985 dollars

(d)

The economic analysis favours Motor B by 8985 − 2600 = 6385 dollars of net present worth, and the simple payback is about 2600 / 1339 = 1.9 years. Two factors that could still favour the standard motor are the following. First, premium-efficiency motors usually run at a slightly higher speed because of lower slip, and on a centrifugal pump the power rises with the cube of speed, so the pump may draw extra power and part of the saving is lost. Second, premium motors often have a higher locked-rotor current and a different inrush, which may stress a weak supply or exceed the starter and breaker ratings, so the protection and starter may need to be changed at extra cost. Space and weight are further considerations.

Answer: Explanatory

A6 Practice Paper 17

Problem 1 [A6-081] Magnetic circuits, flux, reluctance and inductance

A 60 Hz filter inductor is wound on a laminated E-I core. The core has a uniform cross-section of 8.0 cm² and a mean magnetic path length of 0.240 m in iron. Over the working range the iron is linear with relative permeability 2500. A single air gap is cut in the centre leg. The coil has 400 turns and negligible resistance. Neglect fringing and leakage flux, and neglect the iron length removed by the gap. Take μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. The designer is choosing between Design A with a 1.0 mm gap and Design B with a 2.0 mm gap. The inductor must carry a peak current of 5 A in service without the flux density in the core exceeding 1.2 T.

  1. (a) Find the total reluctance and the inductance of Design A. [6]
  2. (b) Find the inductance of Design B. [4]
  3. (c) Find the largest peak current Design B can carry before the core flux density reaches 1.2 T. [6]
  4. (d) In one short paragraph, state which design you would build and why, and explain what the larger gap costs you. [4]
(a)

Reluctance of the iron is Rc = lc/(μ0 μr A) = 0.240/(4π×10⁻⁷ × 2500 × 8.0×10⁻⁴) = 0.240/(2.513×10⁻⁶) = 9.55×10⁴ A/Wb. The gap reluctance is Rg = g/(μ0 A) = 1.0×10⁻³/(4π×10⁻⁷ × 8.0×10⁻⁴) = 9.947×10⁵ A/Wb. The two sit in series in one flux path, so the total is R = Rc + Rg = 9.55×10⁴ + 9.947×10⁵ = 1.0902×10⁶ A/Wb. The inductance follows from L = N²/R = 400²/1.0902×10⁶ = 160000/1.0902×10⁶ = 0.1468 H. The gap supplies about 91 percent of the reluctance, so the iron permeability barely matters to L. The assumption is a single linear flux path with no fringing.

Answer: L = 0.1468 H

(b)

Doubling the gap doubles the gap reluctance: Rg = 2.0×10⁻³/(4π×10⁻⁷ × 8.0×10⁻⁴) = 1.9894×10⁶ A/Wb. The iron reluctance is unchanged at 9.55×10⁴ A/Wb, so the total is R = 9.55×10⁴ + 1.9894×10⁶ = 2.0849×10⁶ A/Wb. Then L = N²/R = 160000/2.0849×10⁶ = 0.0767 H. The inductance has fallen to 52 percent of Design A, a little more than the 50 percent we would get if the gap were the only reluctance. The difference exists because the fixed iron reluctance makes up a larger share of the total in Design A, so halving it matters slightly less in B.

Answer: L = 0.0767 H

(c)

The flux density is B = Φ/A = N i/(R A). Solving for the current at B = 1.2 T gives i = B A R/N. With R = 2.0849×10⁶ A/Wb: i = 1.2 × 8.0×10⁻⁴ × 2.0849×10⁶/400 = 2001.5/400 = 5.00 A. Equivalent form: i = B (g + lc/μr)/(μ0 N) = 1.2 × (2.0×10⁻³ + 9.6×10⁻⁵)/(4π×10⁻⁷ × 400) = 5.00 A. So Design B just meets the 5 A requirement. By the same formula Design A reaches 1.2 T at only 2.62 A, so it cannot meet the specification. The linear model is valid because the stated 1.2 T lies below the knee of a typical silicon steel.

Answer: Imax = 5.00 A

(d)

Choose Design B, because Design A would saturate at 2.62 A, about half of the required 5 A peak, and a saturated core collapses the inductance and produces large current spikes. Energy stored at the flux limit is W = ½ L i²: for A it is 0.50 J, for B it is 0.96 J, so the larger gap lets the same core store nearly twice the energy, since most of the energy lives in the gap and the gap can sustain the full flux. The cost is lower inductance, 0.0767 H against 0.1468 H, so B needs more turns or a larger core if the 0.147 H value is needed for filtering, and a larger gap raises fringing flux and winding loss near the gap.

Answer: Design B; see working

Problem 2 [A6-082] Ferromagnetic cores, losses and saturation

A 480 V, 60 Hz single-phase distribution transformer has a silicon-steel core that was tested at constant peak flux density of 1.5 T on a variable-frequency supply. The measured core loss was 95 W at 50 Hz and 123 W at 60 Hz. Assume the loss is the sum of a hysteresis term proportional to f Bm² and an eddy-current term proportional to f² Bm², with the same Steinmetz exponent of 2 for flux density in both terms. The core data sheet states that the steel saturates sharply above a peak flux density of 1.7 T. At rated voltage and 60 Hz the peak flux density is 1.5 T. The utility proposes to connect this unit to a 50 Hz island supply at 480 V. Neglect winding resistance and leakage reactance.

  1. (a) Separate the 60 Hz core loss into its hysteresis and eddy-current components at 1.5 T. [6]
  2. (b) Find the core loss when the transformer is energised at 480 V and 50 Hz. [6]
  3. (c) Find the highest voltage at which the unit may be operated at 50 Hz without the peak flux density exceeding 1.7 T. [4]
  4. (d) Explain in a short paragraph why running at 480 V and 50 Hz is unsafe even though the calculated loss increase is only 11 percent. [4]
(a)

Write the loss as P = kh f + ke f² at fixed Bm = 1.5 T, where kh and ke absorb Bm². Dividing by f gives P/f = kh + ke f. At 50 Hz, P/f = 95/50 = 1.90 W/Hz. At 60 Hz, P/f = 123/60 = 2.05 W/Hz. Subtracting, ke (60 − 50) = 0.15, so ke = 0.015 W/Hz². Then kh = 1.90 − 0.015 × 50 = 1.15 W/Hz. At 60 Hz the eddy-current loss is ke f² = 0.015 × 3600 = 54 W and the hysteresis loss is kh f = 1.15 × 60 = 69 W, which together give the 123 W measured. Eddy loss is thus 44 percent of the core loss at 60 Hz.

Answer: Eddy loss 54 W (hysteresis 69 W)

(b)

For a fixed applied voltage the peak flux is Bm = V/(4.44 N Ac f), so Bm is inversely proportional to frequency. Dropping from 60 Hz to 50 Hz raises Bm by 60/50 = 1.2, giving Bm = 1.5 × 1.2 = 1.80 T. Both loss terms scale with Bm², a factor of 1.44. The loss at 50 Hz and 1.5 T is the measured 95 W, equal to kh × 50 + ke × 50² = 57.5 + 37.5. Therefore at 1.80 T the loss is 95 × 1.44 = 136.8 W. That is 11 percent more than at 60 Hz. The result assumes the exponent of 2 still holds, which is optimistic since this flux is beyond the stated knee.

Answer: P = 136.8 W

(c)

Flux density is proportional to V/f, so V/f at the limit must equal the rated ratio scaled by 1.7/1.5. The rated ratio is 480/60 = 8.0 V/Hz at 1.5 T. The limit ratio is 8.0 × 1.7/1.5 = 9.067 V/Hz. At 50 Hz the allowed voltage is V = 9.067 × 50 = 453.3 V. This is about 94 percent of nameplate voltage, which is the figure a derating note should quote. At exactly 480 V the core would sit at 1.8 T, beyond the knee, where the magnetising current rises steeply and the rated-voltage operation is not permitted.

Answer: V = 453 V

(d)

The loss formula is an empirical fit valid below the knee, so 136.8 W is an underestimate at 1.8 T. Above 1.7 T the permeability falls sharply, the magnetising current rises by a large factor and becomes peaky, rich in third and other harmonics. That current loads the supply, adds copper loss in the primary winding, and can cause voltage distortion and overheating of the winding, while the stray flux leaving the core also heats the tank and clamps. Protective devices may trip on inrush-like current. The safe choice is to hold the volts per hertz at or below 9.07 V/Hz, that is 453 V at 50 Hz.

Answer: Saturation current and heating; see working

Problem 3 [A6-083] Single-phase transformer equivalent circuit and tests

A 50 kVA, 2400/240 V, 60 Hz single-phase transformer was tested. Open-circuit test, instruments on the 240 V winding, high-voltage winding open: 240 V, 5.40 A, 186 W. Short-circuit test, instruments on the 2400 V winding, 240 V winding shorted: 62.0 V, 20.83 A, 615 W. Use the approximate equivalent circuit with the shunt branch (Rc in parallel with Xm) placed at the terminals of the low-voltage winding, and with the series branch Req + jXeq referred to the high-voltage side. The transformer supplies a lagging load of 0.80 power factor at rated current and rated secondary voltage. A plant engineer wants a quick judgement on whether the unit can be kept energised overnight on light load.

  1. (a) Find the magnetising reactance Xm referred to the 240 V side. [5]
  2. (b) Find the equivalent series resistance Req referred to the 2400 V side. [5]
  3. (c) Find the voltage regulation, in percent, at rated current, 0.80 power factor lagging, and rated secondary voltage. [6]
  4. (d) Find the load, as a fraction of rated kVA, at which the efficiency is a maximum, and state what the result means for overnight light-load operation. [4]
(a)

At open circuit the apparent power is S = 240 × 5.40 = 1296 VA and the real power is the core loss 186 W. The reactive power is Q = √(S² − P²) = √(1296² − 186²) = √(1 679 616 − 34 596) = 1282.6 var. The shunt branch is a parallel pair, so Rc = V²/P = 240²/186 = 309.7 Ω and Xm = V²/Q = 57 600/1282.6 = 44.9 Ω. The magnetising branch therefore draws 0.78 A through Rc and 5.34 A through Xm. Most of the no-load current is magnetising current, which is typical of a distribution transformer.

Answer: Xm = 44.9 Ω

(b)

At short circuit the full-load current of the high-voltage winding flows, 50 000/2400 = 20.83 A, and the voltage is small enough that the shunt branch carries negligible current, so the whole input power is copper loss in the series branch. Then Req = P/I² = 615/20.83² = 615/433.9 = 1.417 Ω. The magnitude of the series impedance is |Zeq| = V/I = 62.0/20.83 = 2.976 Ω, so Xeq = √(2.976² − 1.417²) = √(8.859 − 2.009) = 2.617 Ω. The impedance is 2.976 Ω, which is 2.58 percent of the base impedance 2400²/50 000 = 115.2 Ω, a typical figure.

Answer: Req = 1.417 Ω

(c)

Refer the load to the high-voltage side. The terminal voltage is 2400 V at 0° and the current is I = 20.83∠−36.87° A. The source voltage is V1 = 2400 + I (Req + jXeq) = 2400 + 20.83∠−36.87° × (1.417 + j2.617). The product of Z = 2.976∠61.56° with I gives a voltage drop of 62.0∠24.69° V, equal to 56.4 + j25.9 V. Therefore V1 = 2456.4 + j25.9 V, with magnitude 2456.5 V. Regulation = (2456.5 − 2400)/2400 = 2.35 percent. The shunt branch is at the low-voltage terminals so it does not enter this calculation.

Answer: Regulation = 2.35 percent

(d)

Efficiency is a maximum when the load-dependent copper loss equals the constant core loss. Copper loss at rated load is 615 W and the core loss is 186 W. With load fraction x the copper loss is 615 x², so 615 x² = 186 and x = √(186/615) = 0.550. This is 27.5 kVA. Below this load the fixed core loss dominates, so efficiency falls steadily toward zero at no load; the unit draws 186 W at no load, which is 1.63 kWh in 8.75 h. Overnight energisation is thermally safe, since 186 W is small, but it wastes energy compared with switching it off.

Answer: Fraction = 0.550

Problem 4 [A6-084] Transformer regulation and efficiency

A rural utility compares two 25 kVA, 7200/240 V distribution transformers for a farm service. Unit 1 has a core loss of 110 W and a full-load copper loss of 380 W. Unit 2 uses cheaper steel and a heavier winding: core loss 80 W, full-load copper loss 520 W. The farm load repeats every 24 hours. For 8 hours the load is zero. For 10 hours the load is 40 percent of rated kVA at 0.80 power factor. For 6 hours the load is 90 percent of rated kVA at 0.95 power factor. The core stays energised for all 24 hours, and the copper loss varies with the square of the load fraction. Neglect regulation effects on the secondary voltage. The utility will buy the unit with the better all-day efficiency.

  1. (a) Find the energy delivered to the load in one day. [4]
  2. (b) Find the all-day (energy) efficiency of Unit 1. [6]
  3. (c) Find the all-day efficiency of Unit 2. [6]
  4. (d) Recommend a unit and say how the answer would change if the farm load were half as heavy at all times. Do not recalculate; reason from the loss structure. [4]
(a)

Energy output is the sum over each load period of kVA × load fraction × power factor × hours. For the 40 percent period: 25 × 0.40 × 0.80 × 10 = 80.0 kWh. For the 90 percent period: 25 × 0.90 × 0.95 × 6 = 128.25 kWh. The no-load period delivers nothing. The daily total is 80.0 + 128.25 = 208.25 kWh. This is also the figure used in both all-day efficiency calculations below, since both transformers serve the same load. The power factor affects the real energy but not the copper loss, which depends on current, that is on the kVA fraction.

Answer: 208.25 kWh

(b)

Core loss is present all 24 h: 0.110 kW × 24 h = 2.640 kWh. Copper loss is 0.380 kW times the square of the load fraction times the hours. For the 40 percent period: 0.380 × 0.4² × 10 = 0.608 kWh. For the 90 percent period: 0.380 × 0.9² × 6 = 1.847 kWh. The total loss is 2.640 + 0.608 + 1.847 = 5.095 kWh. All-day efficiency = output/(output + loss) = 208.25/(208.25 + 5.095) = 208.25/213.345 = 0.9761, that is 97.61 percent.

Answer: 97.61 percent

(c)

Core loss: 0.080 kW × 24 h = 1.920 kWh. Copper loss at 520 W full load: 0.520 × 0.4² × 10 = 0.832 kWh in the 40 percent period and 0.520 × 0.9² × 6 = 2.527 kWh in the 90 percent period. The total loss is 1.920 + 0.832 + 2.527 = 5.279 kWh. All-day efficiency = 208.25/(208.25 + 5.279) = 208.25/213.529 = 0.9753, that is 97.53 percent. Unit 2 is lower by 0.08 percentage points, but it has the smaller no-load loss, which would favour it if the farm were lightly loaded for more of the day.

Answer: 97.53 percent

(d)

On this load cycle Unit 1 wins by a small margin, 97.61 against 97.53 percent, so it is the better purchase if the two cost the same. The loss total of Unit 2 is only 0.18 kWh a day larger, so the capitalised cost of losses over 30 years may be smaller than a price difference. If the load were halved, the copper loss would fall by a factor of four while the core loss would stay the same, so core loss would dominate and Unit 2, with 80 W against 110 W, would become the more efficient choice. This is why rural transformers that run lightly loaded are bought on low core loss.

Answer: Unit 1 now; Unit 2 gains at light load; see working

Problem 5 [A6-085] Balanced three-phase wye and delta systems

A 600 V, 60 Hz, three-phase, three-wire supply feeds a fabrication shop. A wye-connected load takes 40 kW at 0.85 power factor lagging. A delta-connected load is rated 25 kVA at 0.70 power factor lagging. Both loads are balanced and the supply voltage at the loads is 600 V line-to-line. The supply authority penalizes power factors below 0.95, so the shop manager wants a balanced delta-connected capacitor bank installed at the service entrance to raise the combined power factor to 0.95 lagging. Neglect the resistance of the feeder, and take the capacitor bank to be lossless.

  1. (a) Find the line current drawn from the supply before the bank is installed. [5]
  2. (b) Find the capacitance of each leg of the delta-connected bank needed to reach 0.95 power factor. [7]
  3. (c) Find the line current after the bank is installed. [4]
  4. (d) Find the percentage reduction in feeder I²R loss produced by the bank, and say whether it justifies the installation on loss grounds alone. [4]
(a)

Add the complex powers. For the wye load, P1 = 40 kW and Q1 = P1 tan(cos⁻¹ 0.85) = 40 × 0.6197 = 24.79 kvar. For the delta load, S2 = 25 kVA, so P2 = 25 × 0.70 = 17.5 kW and Q2 = 25 sin(cos⁻¹ 0.70) = 25 × 0.7141 = 17.85 kvar. The totals are P = 57.5 kW and Q = 42.64 kvar, so the apparent power is S = √(57.5² + 42.64²) = 71.59 kVA. The line current is I = S/(√3 VL) = 71 590/(1.732 × 600) = 68.9 A. The combined power factor is 57.5/71.59 = 0.803 lagging, below 0.95.

Answer: 68.9 A

(b)

Real power is unchanged at 57.5 kW. At 0.95 power factor the reactive power is Qnew = P tan(cos⁻¹ 0.95) = 57.5 × 0.3287 = 18.90 kvar. The bank must supply Qc = 42.64 − 18.90 = 23.74 kvar in total, that is 7.913 kvar per phase. In a delta bank each capacitor sees the full line voltage of 600 V. So Qphase = ω C V², giving C = 7913/(2π × 60 × 600²) = 7913/(376.99 × 360 000) = 7913/1.3572×10⁸ = 58.3 μF. A wye bank would need three times this capacitance at the same voltage, which is why delta banks are the usual choice at 600 V.

Answer: C = 58.3 μF

(c)

With the bank in place, the real power is still 57.5 kW and the power factor is 0.95, so the apparent power is S = 57.5/0.95 = 60.53 kVA. The line current is I = 60 530/(1.732 × 600) = 58.2 A. This is a fall from 68.9 A, a reduction of 15.5 percent. The reactive power now is 18.9 kvar, which agrees with the target. The same capacitors give a drop in current of the same proportion on the feeder and transformer upstream of the service entrance, freeing capacity.

Answer: 58.2 A

(d)

Feeder I²R loss is proportional to the square of the line current for a fixed feeder resistance. The ratio of the losses after and before is (58.24/68.9)² = 0.8453² = 0.7145. The loss is therefore reduced by 1 − 0.7145 = 28.5 percent. For a short feeder in a shop the absolute saving is small, probably tens of watts to a few hundred, so the bank is justified mainly by the avoided power factor penalty, and by freed transformer capacity, not by loss saving alone. Check that the capacitor bank will not resonate with harmonic sources before installing.

Answer: 28.5 percent

A6 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A6-086] Three-phase power, per-unit system and one-line diagrams

A radial system is described by this one-line diagram in words. A generator rated 20 MVA, 13.8 kV has a reactance of 0.15 per unit on its own base. It connects to a step-up transformer T1, 20 MVA, 13.8/138 kV, reactance 0.10 per unit. T1 feeds a transmission line of reactance j40 Ω per phase (resistance neglected). The line feeds a step-down transformer T2, 15 MVA, 138/13.8 kV, reactance 0.09 per unit on its own rating. A balanced load at the 13.8 kV bus beyond T2 takes 12 MW at 0.90 power factor lagging, with the bus voltage held at 13.8 kV. Choose bases of 20 MVA, with 13.8 kV on the generator side. Neglect magnetising branches and resistances.

  1. (a) Find the per-unit reactance of the line on the system base. [4]
  2. (b) Convert the reactance of T2 to the system base. [4]
  3. (c) Find the voltage required at the generator terminals, in kV, to hold 13.8 kV at the load. [7]
  4. (d) Find the generator terminal current in amperes and state the angle of the terminal voltage relative to the load bus voltage. [5]
(a)

Base voltage in the line section follows the transformer ratio: 13.8 kV × 138/13.8 = 138 kV. The base impedance there is Zbase = (kVbase)²/MVAbase = 138²/20 = 952.2 Ω. The per-unit line reactance is Xline = 40/952.2 = 0.0420 per unit. Base voltage on the load side returns to 13.8 kV since T2 has ratio 138/13.8. The 20 MVA base is common to all zones. This conversion is the basis of the one-line model: every impedance is first converted to the same MVA base and the local voltage base of its zone.

Answer: 0.0420 per unit

(b)

A per-unit impedance converts between bases with Zpu,new = Zpu,old × (MVAnew/MVAold) × (kVold/kVnew)². The transformer rated voltages are the same as the base voltages, so the voltage factor is 1. The MVA factor is 20/15. Then XT2 = 0.09 × 20/15 = 0.1200 per unit. The reactance seen from the supply is the total series reactance from the generator bus to the load bus: XT1 + Xline + XT2 = 0.10 + 0.0420 + 0.1200 = 0.2620 per unit, ignoring the generator subtransient reactance which sits behind the terminal.

Answer: 0.1200 per unit

(c)

The load is S = 12/0.9 = 13.33 MVA, or 0.6667 per unit on the 20 MVA base. At a voltage of 1.0 per unit the current is I = 0.6667∠−25.84° per unit, since cos⁻¹ 0.90 = 25.84°. The drop across the series reactance is j0.2620 × 0.6667∠−25.84° = 0.1747∠64.16° per unit = 0.0761 + j0.1572. The generator terminal voltage is Vg = 1.0 + 0.0761 + j0.1572 = 1.0761 + j0.1572, with magnitude √(1.0761² + 0.1572²) = 1.0875 per unit. In kilovolts that is 1.0875 × 13.8 = 15.01 kV. This exceeds the 1.05 pu limit a generator typically carries, so a tap change on T1 is needed.

Answer: 15.0 kV

(d)

Base current on the generator side is Ibase = 20×10⁶/(√3 × 13.8×10³) = 836.7 A. The load current in per unit is 0.6667, and the series elements carry the same current in per unit everywhere, so the generator current is 0.6667 × 836.7 = 557.8 A. The angle of the generator terminal voltage is tan⁻¹(0.1572/1.0761) = 8.31°, so the generator leads the load bus by 8.3°. That is the transfer angle that, together with the 1.0875 per-unit magnitude, determines the real and reactive flow in the system.

Answer: 558 A

Problem 2 [A6-087] Unbalanced three-phase loads

A four-wire, 208 V line-to-line, 60 Hz wye supply feeds three single-phase loads connected line to neutral. The source phase voltages are Van = 120∠0° V, Vbn = 120∠−120° V and Vcn = 120∠+120° V (positive sequence a, b, c). The load on phase a is a 12.0 Ω resistor. The load on phase b is an 8.0 Ω resistor in series with an inductive reactance of 6.0 Ω. The load on phase c is a pure capacitive reactance of 15.0 Ω. The neutral conductor has negligible impedance. A technician tells the owner that if the neutral were ever to open in service, the loads would not notice. Take phase currents positive when flowing from the source toward the load, and the neutral current positive from the load star point back to the source star point.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the neutral current with the neutral intact. [6]
  2. (b) Find the total real power absorbed by the three loads with the neutral intact. [4]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the voltage between the load star point and the source neutral if the neutral conductor opens. [6]
  4. (d) Find the rms voltage across the 12.0 Ω load on phase a after the neutral opens, and state whether the technician's claim is correct. [4]
(a)

With a solid neutral each load sees its own phase voltage. Ia = 120∠0°/12 = 10.0∠0° A. Ib = 120∠−120°/(8 + j6) = 120∠−120°/10∠36.87° = 12.0∠−156.87° A. Ic = 120∠120°/(−j15) = 120∠120°/15∠−90° = 8.0∠210° A. The neutral current is the phasor sum In = Ia + Ib + Ic. In rectangular form: Ia = 10.0 + j0; Ib = −11.03 − j4.72; Ic = −6.93 − j4.00. The sum is −7.96 − j8.72 A, with magnitude √(7.96² + 8.72²) = 11.8 A at −132.4°. The neutral carries 11.8 A, nearly as much as the largest phase current of 12.0 A, even though the loads are single-phase and none of them is overloaded.

Answer: |In| = 11.8 A

(b)

Real power is dissipated only in resistance. Phase a: Ia² R = 10.0² × 12.0 = 1200 W. Phase b: Ib² R = 12.0² × 8.0 = 1152 W. Phase c has a pure reactance, so no real power: 0 W. The total is 1200 + 1152 + 0 = 2352 W. A check using the phase voltage and the phase angle gives the same result: phase b is 120 × 12 × cos 36.87° = 1152 W. The total apparent power is larger because of the reactive parts, but the question asks for real power, which is what the meter on the panel registers.

Answer: 2352 W

(c)

With the neutral open, the star point floats at the voltage VnN given by Millman's theorem: VnN = (Va Ya + Vb Yb + Vc Yc)/(Ya + Yb + Yc), where Y = 1/Z. The admittances are Ya = 0.08333 S, Yb = 1/(8 + j6) = 0.08 − j0.06 S and Yc = 1/(−j15) = j0.06667 S. Their sum is 0.16333 + j0.00667 S. The numerator is 120 × 0.08333 + 120∠−120° × (0.08 − j0.06) + 120∠120° × (j0.06667) = 10.0 + 12.0∠−156.87° + 8.0∠210° = −7.96 − j8.72 V·S. Dividing gives VnN = 72.2∠−134.8° V in magnitude 72.2 V. A shift of this size is 60 percent of the nominal phase voltage.

Answer: 72.2 V

(d)

The voltage across the phase a load is Va − VnN = 120∠0° − 72.2∠−134.8° = 120 + 50.6 + j51.5 = 170.6 + j51.5 V, with magnitude √(170.6² + 51.5²) = 178.4 V. This is 49 percent above the 120 V nominal. The phase b load drops to 53.4 V and the phase c capacitive load sees 155.5 V. A resistive load at 178 V draws 2.2 times its normal power, so heating loads and motors are damaged. The technician is wrong: an open neutral in an unbalanced wye system shifts the star point and gives some loads dangerous overvoltage and others undervoltage.

Answer: 178 V

Problem 3 [A6-088] Three-phase transformer connections and phase shift

A small commercial building is served by a bank of three identical single-phase transformers, each rated 100 kVA, 2400 V / 240 V. The primary line voltage of the supply is 2400 V. The bank was first installed delta-wye, with the three high-voltage windings in delta and the three low-voltage windings in wye. Later the owner re-connected the same units delta-delta for a 240 V three-wire service. After a lightning strike one unit failed and was removed, leaving the two remaining units connected in open delta (V-V) at 240 V line-to-line. The load is 150 kW at 0.85 power factor lagging. Neglect transformer impedance and assume balanced voltages.

  1. (a) Find the secondary line-to-line voltage of the delta-wye bank as first installed. [4]
  2. (b) Find the rated secondary line current of the delta-wye bank. [4]
  3. (c) Find the kVA that the open-delta bank can carry without overloading either unit. [6]
  4. (d) Find the percentage by which the 150 kW, 0.85 power factor load exceeds the open-delta capacity, and say what the owner should do. [6]
(a)

In a wye connection the phase winding voltage appears line to neutral and the line voltage is √3 times it. Each low-voltage winding is rated 240 V, so the secondary line voltage is VL = √3 × 240 = 415.7 V. The primary windings are in delta and each sees the 2400 V line voltage, which matches the 2400 V rating, so the turns ratio of 10:1 holds. The delta-wye connection also shifts the secondary line voltages by 30° from the primary line voltages. In North American practice the low-voltage side lags the high-voltage side by 30°. The phase shift matters when a bank is paralleled with another bank.
