Answer: 415.7 V

(b)

Total bank rating is 3 × 100 = 300 kVA. The line current on the wye side equals the winding current. Each winding carries I = 100 000/240 = 416.7 A. Check with the line formula: I = S/(√3 VL) = 300 000/(1.732 × 415.7) = 416.7 A. On the primary side the winding current is 100 000/2400 = 41.67 A, and the delta line current is √3 × 41.67 = 72.2 A. The wye secondary line current equals the winding current, while a delta line current would exceed it by √3, which explains why delta windings carry less current than their lines.

Answer: 416.7 A

(c)

In open delta the two remaining transformers carry line current directly: each winding current equals the line current, so the line current at rating is the rated winding current of a single unit, 100 kVA/240 V = 416.7 A. The line voltage is 240 V, so the three-phase capacity is S = √3 V I = 1.732 × 240 × 416.7 = 173.2 kVA. That is 57.7 percent of the original 300 kVA delta-delta rating, and 86.6 percent of the 200 kVA that the two remaining units are rated for in total. The loss of the third unit costs 42 percent of capacity, not 33 percent, because each remaining winding carries the full line current while its voltage is displaced 30° from that current, so the pair delivers only √3 times one unit's rating.

Answer: 173.2 kVA

(d)

The load apparent power is S = P/pf = 150/0.85 = 176.47 kVA. The open-delta capacity is 173.2 kVA, so the overload is (176.47 − 173.2)/173.2 = 1.89 percent. This is a small overload, and the overload may be tolerable for short periods. Each unit is carrying about 1.9 percent above its rated current at this load, and the heating rises roughly with the square of current, about 3.8 percent more loss. The owner should replace the failed unit promptly, and in the meantime can reduce the load by 3.3 kVA or correct power factor with capacitors, as 0.90 power factor at 150 kW would give 166.7 kVA and bring the unit within rating.

Answer: 1.89 percent overload

Problem 4 [A6-089] Transmission line models and voltage regulation

A 60 Hz, three-phase 230 kV transmission line is 160 km long. Its series impedance is 0.10 + j0.48 Ω/km per phase and its shunt admittance is j3.4×10⁻⁶ S/km per phase. Use the nominal-π model with the total series impedance Z in the middle branch and half of the total shunt admittance Y at each end. The receiving end delivers 150 MW at 0.95 power factor lagging at a line-to-line voltage of 220 kV. The system planner is deciding whether the line can carry this load, or whether shunt compensation is needed, since the sending-end operators are limited to 1.05 per unit of 230 kV, which is 241.5 kV line-to-line, and the line is lightly loaded at night.

  1. (a) Find the receiving-end line current. [4]
  2. (b) Find the sending-end line-to-line voltage using the ABCD constants of the nominal-π model. [6]
  3. (c) Find the voltage regulation of the line, defined with the receiving-end voltage at no load equal to the sending-end voltage divided by |A|. [6]
  4. (d) Find the total three-phase charging reactive power of the line at 220 kV, and say what device the planner might add for the night condition. [4]
(a)

The load is balanced three-phase, so I = P/(√3 VL pf) = 150×10⁶/(1.732 × 220×10³ × 0.95) = 150×10⁶/3.6199×10⁵ = 414.4 A. The current lags the receiving-end phase voltage by cos⁻¹ 0.95 = 18.19°, so on a phase-voltage reference of 127.0 kV∠0° the phasor is Ir = 414.4∠−18.19° A. The reactive power delivered is 150 × tan 18.19° = 49.3 Mvar, and the apparent power is 157.9 MVA. The phase voltage is 220/√3 = 127.02 kV. The voltage at the receiving end is held at 220 kV, which is below the nominal 230 kV, so the current is a little higher than it would be at nominal voltage. All later steps use per-phase quantities and this current as the starting point.

Answer: 414 A

(b)

The total series impedance is Z = 160 × (0.10 + j0.48) = 16 + j76.8 Ω and the total admittance is Y = j5.44×10⁻⁴ S. For the nominal-π model A = D = 1 + ZY/2 and B = Z. ZY = (16 + j76.8)(j5.44×10⁻⁴) = −0.04178 + j0.008704, so A = 1 − 0.02089 + j0.004352 = 0.97911 + j0.004352, with magnitude 0.9791. Then A Vr = 124 364 + j553 V and B Ir = (16 + j76.8) × 414.4∠−18.19° = 16 235 + j28 162 V. Adding, Vs = 140 599 + j28 715 V, with magnitude 143.5 kV per phase, so the line voltage is √3 × 143.5 kV = 248.6 kV. This exceeds the 241.5 kV operating limit.

Answer: 248.6 kV

(c)

With the load removed, Ir = 0, so Vr,NL = Vs/A. The magnitude is |Vr,NL| = 143.5 kV/0.9791 = 146.6 kV per phase, using the sending-end phase voltage from part b. Regulation = (Vr,NL − Vr,FL)/Vr,FL = (146.6 − 127.0)/127.0 = 15.4 percent. The figure is large because the line is long relative to its natural loading and the load is heavily lagging, and the Ferranti effect adds some of it. It shows that holding 220 kV at the receiving end at full load means the receiving voltage would rise to about 253 kV if the load tripped with the sending end unchanged.

Answer: 15.4 percent

(d)

The total shunt admittance magnitude is |Y| = 5.44×10⁻⁴ S for the whole line. The charging reactive power at line voltage V is Qc = V² B = (220×10³)² × 5.44×10⁻⁴ = 4.84×10¹⁰ × 5.44×10⁻⁴ = 2.633×10⁷ var = 26.3 Mvar. At night the load falls well below the natural loading, so the line produces net reactive power and the receiving voltage rises. The planner could add a shunt reactor rated near the charging value, roughly 25 Mvar, switched in at night, together with the on-load tap changers, to keep the voltage within the 1.05 pu limit.

Answer: 26.3 Mvar

Problem 5 [A6-090] Power flow and real and reactive power control

Two 138 kV buses, 1 (sending) and 2 (receiving), are joined by a single short line modelled by a series reactance of 0.12 per unit on a 100 MVA base, with resistance and shunt admittance neglected. Bus 1 is held at 1.02 per unit and leads bus 2 by 8.0°. Bus 2 is held at 1.00 per unit. A planner wants to know how much of the transfer is set by the voltage angle and how much of the reactive power by the voltage magnitudes. Treat the line as lossless, and note that δ is the angle by which V1 leads V2. Express powers on the 100 MVA base.

  1. (a) Find the real power transferred from bus 1 to bus 2, in MW. [5]
  2. (b) Find the reactive power delivered to bus 2, in Mvar. [5]
  3. (c) Find the angle δ at which the line carries 150 MW if both voltage magnitudes are unchanged. [5]
  4. (d) Find the sending-end voltage magnitude that makes the reactive power delivered to bus 2 equal to zero while the angle stays at 8.0°, and state which quantity you would adjust to control reactive power. [5]
(a)

For a lossless line the real power is the same at both ends: P = V1 V2 sin δ/X = 1.02 × 1.00 × sin 8.0°/0.12. With sin 8.0° = 0.13917, this gives P = 1.02 × 0.13917/0.12 = 0.14195/0.12 = 1.1830 per unit. On the 100 MVA base that is 118.3 MW. The real power depends mainly on the angle δ, since sin δ is the factor that changes quickly for small angles, while changes of 2 percent in voltage magnitude change the product only by 2 percent. This is the basis of the statement that angle controls real power flow.

Answer: 118.3 MW

(b)

The receiving-end reactive power is Q2 = (V1 V2 cos δ − V2²)/X. With cos 8.0° = 0.99027, V1 V2 cos δ = 1.02 × 0.99027 = 1.01008. Subtract V2² = 1.00, leaving 0.01008. Dividing by X gives Q2 = 0.01008/0.12 = 0.0840 per unit, that is 8.39 Mvar delivered to bus 2. At the sending end the reactive power is Q1 = (V1² − V1 V2 cos δ)/X = (1.0404 − 1.01008)/0.12 = 0.2527 per unit = 25.3 Mvar. The difference of 16.9 Mvar is the reactive power absorbed in the line reactance, equal to X I².

Answer: 8.39 Mvar

(c)

Set P = 1.50 per unit in the transfer equation: 1.50 = 1.02 × 1.00 × sin δ/0.12. Then sin δ = 1.50 × 0.12/1.02 = 0.17647 and δ = sin⁻¹ 0.17647 = 10.16°. The angle must grow by 2.16° to raise the transfer by 31.7 MW, which is a rise of 26.8 percent in power for a rise of 27 percent in angle. The line is still far from its steady-state limit, since the maximum power at 90° is 1.02/0.12 = 8.5 per unit, or 850 MW. In practice the angle is limited by stability margin rather than by this formula.

Answer: 10.16 degrees

(d)

Setting Q2 = 0 requires V1 V2 cos δ = V2², that is V1 cos δ = V2 = 1.00. At δ = 8.0°, V1 = 1.00/cos 8.0° = 1.00/0.99027 = 1.0098 per unit, which is 139.4 kV on the 138 kV base. Compare this with the 1.02 present value: lowering the sending voltage by about 1 percent removes the 8.4 Mvar that bus 2 draws from the line. Reactive power flow is thus controlled mainly by the voltage magnitude difference, so the operator adjusts generator excitation, tap positions or shunt devices, while real power is steered with the angle.

Answer: 1.0098 per unit

A6 Practice Paper 19

Problem 1 [A6-091] Fault calculations and symmetrical components basics

A 13.8 kV industrial bus in an Ontario mill is supplied by a utility feeder and also carries one large synchronous motor. On a 100 MVA, 13.8 kV base the utility source has positive and negative sequence reactance j0.20 per unit and zero-sequence reactance j0.35 per unit, all resistances neglected. The motor is rated 10 MVA, 13.8 kV with subtransient reactance X″ = 0.18 per unit on its own rating, equal positive and negative sequence reactances, and an ungrounded neutral so it carries no zero-sequence current. The utility neutral is solidly grounded. Pre-fault voltage is 1.0 per unit and load current is neglected. The bus breaker is rated 20 kA symmetrical interrupting. The plant engineer must judge whether this breaker is adequate and, if it is not, what reactor in the utility feed would correct the problem.

  1. (a) Find the base current at 13.8 kV on the 100 MVA base. [3]
  2. (b) Find the bolted three-phase fault current at the bus, including the motor contribution. [4]
  3. (c) Find the bolted single line-to-ground fault current at the bus. [5]
  4. (d) Find the ratio of the worst symmetrical fault current to the breaker rating, and so judge the breaker. [3]
  5. (e) A current-limiting reactor is placed in series with the utility feed only, between the source and the bus. Find the reactance, in ohms at 13.8 kV, that brings the three-phase fault current down to exactly 20 kA. [5]
(a)

The base current follows from the three-phase base MVA and the line-to-line base voltage: I_base = S_base/(√3 V_base). Substituting, I_base = 100×10⁶/(√3 × 13.8×10³) = 100×10⁶/23 902 = 4183.7 A. Every per-unit current found later is multiplied by this value to give amperes at 13.8 kV. The base impedance, needed in part e, is Z_base = V_base²/S_base = (13.8×10³)²/(100×10⁶) = 1.9044 Ω. Stating the base first keeps all sequence networks, which are given in per unit on the same 100 MVA base, consistent for every fault type that follows.

Answer: I_base = 4184 A

(b)

For a bolted three-phase fault only the positive-sequence network matters. The motor reactance on the system base is 0.18 × (100/10) = 1.80 pu. The utility (0.20 pu) and the motor (1.80 pu) both feed the fault, so they are in parallel: Z1 = (0.20 × 1.80)/(0.20 + 1.80) = 0.180 pu. With 1.0 pu pre-fault voltage, I_f = 1.0/0.180 = 5.556 pu. In amperes this is 5.556 × 4183.7 = 23 243 A, or 23.24 kA. The utility supplies 5.0 pu of this and the motor 0.556 pu, because a running synchronous machine acts as a source during the first cycles after the fault. Load current is neglected as stated.

Answer: I_f(3φ) = 23.24 kA

(c)

For a single line-to-ground fault on phase a the three sequence networks are connected in series at the fault. The positive and negative sequence impedances are each the parallel combination found above, Z1 = Z2 = j0.180 pu. The zero-sequence network contains only the utility path, since the motor neutral is ungrounded, so Z0 = j0.35 pu. The sequence current is I_a1 = 1.0/(Z1 + Z2 + Z0) = 1.0/(0.180 + 0.180 + 0.350) = 1.4085 pu. The fault current is three times this: I_f = 3 × 1.4085 = 4.225 pu = 4.225 × 4183.7 = 17 678 A, or 17.68 kA. It is smaller than the three-phase value because Z0 exceeds Z1 on this bus.

Answer: I_f(SLG) = 17.68 kA

(d)

The breaker must interrupt the worst symmetrical fault at its location. The three-phase value from part b, 23.24 kA, exceeds the single line-to-ground value of 17.68 kA, so it sets the requirement. The ratio of duty to rating is 23.24/20 = 1.162. The breaker is therefore overdutied by about 16 percent and is not adequate as installed: it would be asked to open more current than it is certified for, with a real risk of failing to clear the fault. A ratio of 1.0 or less is the minimum acceptable, and a practising engineer would also check the asymmetrical (momentary) duty and the close-and-latch rating before choosing a replacement.

Answer: Ratio = 1.162, not adequate

(e)

The target fault current is 20 000 A, which is 20 000/4183.7 = 4.781 pu. The Thevenin impedance must therefore be at least 1.0/4.781 = 0.2092 pu. Let the reactor add x pu in the utility branch, which is then in parallel with the motor branch of 1.80 pu: (0.20 + x)(1.80)/(0.20 + x + 1.80) = 0.2092. Solving, the utility branch must equal 0.2092 × 1.80/(1.80 - 0.2092) = 0.2367 pu, so x = 0.2367 - 0.20 = 0.0367 pu. In ohms, X = 0.0367 × 1.9044 = 0.0699 Ω. The reactor must carry the full utility load current continuously, and it will slightly depress bus voltage under normal load.

Answer: X = 0.0699 Ω

Problem 2 [A6-092] Generation, load curves and economic dispatch basics

A small Ontario industrial utility supplies its load from two thermal units. Unit 1 has fuel cost C1 = 500 + 8.0 P1 + 0.0040 P1² dollars per hour and can operate between 50 MW and 600 MW. Unit 2 has C2 = 400 + 7.6 P2 + 0.0068 P2² dollars per hour with limits of 50 MW to 400 MW. P is in megawatts. Transmission losses are neglected. During the evening peak the system load is 700 MW, and overnight it falls to 300 MW. The operator currently shares the evening load equally, 350 MW from each unit, and wonders whether that is wasteful. For the overnight load the operator also asks whether Unit 2 should be shut down, remembering that a unit that is running carries its fixed cost term whether or not it produces much power. Ignore start-up cost and minimum run times.

  1. (a) Find the optimal output of Unit 1 at the 700 MW evening load. [5]
  2. (b) Find the system incremental cost λ at that dispatch. [3]
  3. (c) Find the hourly cost saving of the optimal dispatch compared with the equal 350 MW split. [5]
  4. (d) At the overnight load of 300 MW with both units running, find the optimal output of Unit 2. [4]
  5. (e) Find how many dollars per hour are saved overnight by shutting Unit 2 down and letting Unit 1 carry 300 MW alone, compared with the optimal two-unit dispatch. [3]
(a)

Without limits binding, economic dispatch equalizes incremental costs: dC1/dP1 = dC2/dP2 = λ. Here dC1/dP1 = 8.0 + 0.0080 P1 and dC2/dP2 = 7.6 + 0.0136 P2. With P1 + P2 = 700, substitute P1 = 700 - P2 to get 8.0 + 0.0080(700 - P2) = 7.6 + 0.0136 P2, so 13.6 - 0.0080 P2 = 7.6 + 0.0136 P2. Hence 6.0 = 0.0216 P2 and P2 = 277.8 MW. Then P1 = 700 - 277.8 = 422.2 MW. Both values lie inside their limits, so the unconstrained solution is valid and no unit needs to be held at a bound.

Answer: P1 = 422.2 MW

(b)

The system incremental cost is the common value of the two marginal costs. Using Unit 1: λ = 8.0 + 0.0080 × 422.2 = 8.0 + 3.378 = 11.378 $/MWh. As a check, Unit 2 gives 7.6 + 0.0136 × 277.8 = 7.6 + 3.778 = 11.378 $/MWh, which agrees. This number is the cost of supplying one additional megawatt-hour at the margin, and it is what the utility would compare with the price of an import or with a customer's interruptible tariff. Note that λ lies well above either unit's linear coefficient because the quadratic terms grow with loading.

Answer: λ = 11.38 $/MWh

(c)

Optimal cost: C1(422.2) = 500 + 8.0 × 422.2 + 0.0040 × 422.2² = 500 + 3377.8 + 713.0 = 4590.8 $/h. C2(277.8) = 400 + 7.6 × 277.8 + 0.0068 × 277.8² = 400 + 2111.1 + 524.8 = 3035.9 $/h. Total 7626.7 $/h. Equal split: C1(350) = 500 + 2800 + 490 = 3790 $/h and C2(350) = 400 + 2660 + 833 = 3893 $/h, total 7683.0 $/h. The saving is 7683.0 - 7626.7 = 56.3 $/h. Over a year of 8760 hours at the evening load this would exceed 490 000 dollars, so the equal split is wasteful even though the units are similar in size.

Answer: Saving = 56.33 $/h

(d)

At 300 MW both units run, so equal incremental cost applies again: 8.0 + 0.0080 (300 - P2) = 7.6 + 0.0136 P2. This gives 10.4 - 0.0080 P2 = 7.6 + 0.0136 P2, so 2.8 = 0.0216 P2 and P2 = 129.6 MW. Unit 1 then carries 170.4 MW. Both are above the 50 MW minimum and below their maxima, so the solution is feasible. Note that the cheaper-per-megawatt Unit 2 still takes less than half the load, because its quadratic coefficient is larger and its marginal cost rises faster than Unit 1's.

Answer: P2 = 129.6 MW

(e)

Both units running at the optimum: C1(170.4) = 500 + 1362.96 + 116.1 = 1979.1 $/h and C2(129.6) = 400 + 985.2 + 114.2 = 1499.4 $/h, total 3478.5 $/h. Unit 1 alone at 300 MW: C1(300) = 500 + 2400 + 360 = 3260.0 $/h, which is within its 600 MW limit. Shutting Unit 2 down saves 3478.5 - 3260.0 = 218.5 $/h, because Unit 2's 400 $/h fixed cost outweighs the saving from sharing load. The decision would reverse at higher load, and the operator must also weigh start-up cost and the reserve lost by running a single unit.

Answer: Saving = 218.5 $/h

Problem 3 [A6-093] DC machine models and speed control

A separately excited DC motor drives a belt conveyor in an aggregate quarry. The armature resistance is 0.18 Ω, the field current is held constant at its full value, and the armature supply is a controlled rectifier adjustable from 0 to 240 V. At rated load the motor draws 100 A from a 240 V armature supply and runs at 1200 rpm. The belt load torque is constant, independent of speed. Neglect armature reaction, brush drop and rotational losses, so mechanical output power equals E_a I_a. A technician proposes to halve the belt speed by inserting a series resistor in the armature circuit while keeping the 240 V supply, instead of lowering the rectifier voltage. A second proposal is to exceed rated speed by weakening the field. The engineer needs numbers to compare the methods fairly.

  1. (a) Find the machine constant Kφ in V·s/rad at full field. [3]
  2. (b) With the full field and the same load torque, find the armature voltage that gives 600 rpm. [4]
  3. (c) Find the efficiency of the armature circuit at 600 rpm with rectifier voltage control, taking efficiency as E_a I_a divided by V_a I_a. [4]
  4. (d) Find the series resistance needed to give 600 rpm from the fixed 240 V supply at the same torque. [5]
  5. (e) At no change of supply voltage the field is weakened to reach 1500 rpm while the armature current has fallen to 60 A. Find the ratio of the new flux to the full-field flux. [4]
(a)

At rated load the back EMF is E_a = V - I_a R_a = 240 - 100 × 0.18 = 222 V. The angular speed is ω = 1200 × 2π/60 = 125.66 rad/s. For a constant field, E_a = Kφ ω, so Kφ = 222/125.66 = 1.7666 V·s/rad. This constant is also the torque constant, T = Kφ I_a, giving a rated torque of 1.7666 × 100 = 176.7 N·m. Because the belt torque is constant, the armature current stays at 100 A at any speed in the next parts, which is the key simplification of the problem.

Answer: Kφ = 1.767 V·s/rad

(b)

Constant torque with constant flux means constant armature current, 100 A. At 600 rpm, ω = 62.83 rad/s, so E_a = 1.7666 × 62.83 = 111.0 V, exactly half of the rated 222 V. The armature voltage is V_a = E_a + I_a R_a = 111.0 + 100 × 0.18 = 129.0 V. Note this is a little more than half of 240 V, because the resistive drop of 18 V stays the same at any speed. The rectifier is simply set to 129 V, and no energy is wasted in an external resistor.

Answer: V_a = 129.0 V

(c)

The electrical input to the armature is V_a I_a = 129.0 × 100 = 12 900 W. The mechanical power developed is E_a I_a = 111.0 × 100 = 11 100 W. The only loss counted is the armature copper loss I_a² R_a = 100² × 0.18 = 1800 W, which agrees with the difference. Efficiency = 11 100/12 900 = 0.8605, or 86.05 percent. Rated-speed efficiency on the same basis is 22 200/24 000 = 92.5 percent, so voltage control costs only a modest drop in efficiency even at half speed, since the armature copper loss does not change.

Answer: η = 86.05 %

(d)

With the 240 V supply fixed and E_a = 111.0 V at 600 rpm, the total armature-circuit resistance must satisfy 240 = 111.0 + 100 (0.18 + R_ext). Hence 0.18 + R_ext = 129.0/100 = 1.29 Ω and R_ext = 1.29 - 0.18 = 1.11 Ω. This resistor dissipates 100² × 1.11 = 11 100 W continuously. The input power is 240 × 100 = 24 000 W for 11 100 W of mechanical output, an efficiency of only 46.25 percent. Rectifier control is therefore much better for a long-running conveyor, while a resistor is tolerable only for short duty.

Answer: R_ext = 1.11 Ω

(e)

At 60 A the back EMF is E_a = 240 - 60 × 0.18 = 229.2 V. At 1500 rpm, ω = 157.08 rad/s, so the new constant is Kφ' = 229.2/157.08 = 1.459 V·s/rad. The flux ratio is 1.459/1.7666 = 0.826. The motor can only reach this speed with a reduced torque, T = 1.459 × 60 = 87.5 N·m, about half of rated torque, so field weakening gives roughly constant power, not constant torque. With the belt at full torque the current would be high and the motor could not maintain the speed safely.

Answer: Φ ratio = 0.826

Problem 4 [A6-094] DC motor starting and braking

A 230 V shunt motor drives the trolley of an overhead crane in a steel plant. The armature resistance is 0.12 Ω. At rated load the armature current is 85 A and the motor runs at 1500 rpm, the field being held at full excitation by a separate regulated supply, including during braking. Neglect brush drop, armature reaction, friction and windage. The supply protection allows a peak armature current of twice rated, 170 A, at starting and at the beginning of any braking operation. The combined inertia of motor and trolley is 12 kg·m². The crane engineer wants to size the resistors for three duties and judge which braking method removes the energy fastest and where that energy goes: starting from standstill, dynamic braking from 1500 rpm, and plugging (reversing the armature supply) from 1500 rpm.

  1. (a) Find the total external starting resistance that limits the peak starting current to 170 A. [4]
  2. (b) Find the external braking resistance for dynamic braking from 1500 rpm so that the initial braking current is 170 A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the external resistance in the armature circuit for plugging so that the initial current is 170 A. [4]
  4. (d) In dynamic braking to standstill, find the energy dissipated in the external braking resistor, taking the load as pure inertia. [4]
  5. (e) Find the initial braking torque in dynamic braking. [4]
(a)

At standstill the back EMF is zero, so the starting current is limited only by the armature resistance plus the external resistance: I = V/(R_a + R_s). For 170 A, R_a + R_s = 230/170 = 1.3529 Ω. Therefore R_s = 1.3529 - 0.12 = 1.233 Ω. Without this resistor the starting current would be 230/0.12 = 1917 A, about 22.5 times rated, which would destroy the commutator and trip protection. The resistance is then cut out in steps as the back EMF builds up, so that the current stays between 170 A and a lower switching value.

Answer: R_s = 1.233 Ω

(b)

Before braking the motor runs at rated load, so E_a = 230 - 85 × 0.12 = 219.8 V. In dynamic braking the armature is disconnected from the supply and connected across the resistor, with the field unchanged. The initial current is I = E_a/(R_a + R_b). Setting 170 A: R_a + R_b = 219.8/170 = 1.2929 Ω, so R_b = 1.2929 - 0.12 = 1.173 Ω. The machine now acts as a generator driving its kinetic energy into the resistance, and the current then falls in proportion to speed as the back EMF decays.

Answer: R_b = 1.173 Ω

(c)

In plugging the armature supply polarity is reversed while the machine still rotates forward, so the back EMF adds to the supply voltage. The initial current is I = (V + E_a)/(R_a + R). With E_a = 219.8 V, V + E_a = 449.8 V. Setting 170 A: R_a + R = 449.8/170 = 2.6459 Ω, so R = 2.6459 - 0.12 = 2.526 Ω. This is about double the dynamic braking resistor, because both the supply and the machine drive current. Plugging also needs a speed-sensing switch to cut the supply near zero speed, or the motor would accelerate in reverse.

Answer: R = 2.526 Ω

(d)

The kinetic energy at 1500 rpm is ½Jω² with ω = 1500 × 2π/60 = 157.08 rad/s: ½ × 12 × 157.08² = 148.04 kJ. During dynamic braking the same current flows in the armature resistance and in the external resistor, so the energy divides in proportion to resistance. The external resistor gets the fraction R_b/(R_a + R_b) = 1.173/1.2929 = 0.9072. Energy in R_b = 0.9072 × 148.04 = 134.3 kJ, with the remaining 13.7 kJ heating the armature. The resistor must be rated for this thermal energy, and the temperature rise follows from its heat capacity.

Answer: Energy = 134.3 kJ

(e)

The torque constant is Kφ = E_a/ω = 219.8/157.08 = 1.3993 V·s/rad. The braking torque is T = Kφ I_a, and at the start of braking I_a = 170 A. Hence T = 1.3993 × 170 = 237.9 N·m, in the opposite sense to rotation. This is 237.9/(1.3993 × 85) = 2.0 times rated torque, as expected for twice rated current. As the speed falls the current and torque fall linearly, so dynamic braking is smooth but loses effectiveness near standstill, where a mechanical holding brake takes over.

Answer: T = 237.9 N·m

Problem 5 [A6-095] Synchronous generator equivalent circuit and regulation

A 2.5 MVA, 4160 V, 60 Hz, three-phase, wye-connected synchronous generator supplies an isolated mine site. Per phase the armature resistance is 0.15 Ω and the synchronous reactance is 5.2 Ω. Magnetic saturation is neglected so the synchronous impedance is constant. The terminal voltage is held at the rated value of 4160 V line to line at the load, and the field current is then adjusted for each condition. The mine's mixed loads give different power factors during the shift, so the operator wants to know how much excitation is needed. Use the per-phase model with the terminal voltage as the phasor reference. Voltage regulation is defined as (E_f - V_t)/V_t, where E_f is the excitation voltage that gives rated terminal voltage at the stated load.

  1. (a) Find the excitation voltage per phase at rated current and 0.8 power factor lagging. [5]
  2. (b) Find the percentage voltage regulation for that load. [3]
  3. (c) Find the percentage voltage regulation at rated current and 0.9 power factor leading. [5]
  4. (d) Find the load angle between E_f and V_t for the 0.8 lagging load. [3]
  5. (e) With the excitation of part a held fixed and terminal voltage at 4160 V, find the maximum steady-state real power the machine could deliver, neglecting R_a. [4]
(a)

Rated current is I = S/(√3 V_L) = 2.5×10⁶/(√3 × 4160) = 346.97 A. Phase voltage is V_t = 4160/√3 = 2401.8 V. With V_t as the reference, a lagging load at power factor 0.8 has I = 346.97∠-36.87° A = 277.6 - j208.2 A. The excitation is E_f = V_t + (R_a + jX_s) I. The drop is (0.15 + j5.2)(277.6 - j208.2) = (41.6 + 1082.6) + j(1443.5 - 31.2) = 1124.2 + j1412.3 V. So E_f = 3526.0 + j1412.3 V, and |E_f| = 3798 V per phase, a line value of about 6578 V.

Answer: E_f = 3798 V per phase

(b)

Regulation is (E_f - V_t)/V_t, with E_f the magnitude found in part a and V_t = 2401.8 V. This gives (3798.2 - 2401.8)/2401.8 = 1396.4/2401.8 = 0.5814, or 58.14 percent. This is very large because the synchronous reactance of 5.2 Ω is 0.75 per unit on the machine base, and lagging load current demagnetizes the machine. In practice the field must be boosted heavily, which is why this machine needs a strong exciter and why a stiff voltage regulator is essential for mixed inductive mine loads.

Answer: Regulation = 58.14 %

(c)

For 0.9 leading, the current is I = 346.97∠+25.84° A = 312.3 + j151.2 A. The drop is (0.15 + j5.2)(312.3 + j151.2) = (46.8 - 786.2) + j(1623.9 + 22.7) = -739.4 + j1646.6 V. The real part of the drop is 0.15 × 312.3 - 5.2 × 151.2 = 46.8 - 786.2 = -739.4 V, so E_f = 2401.8 - 739.4 + j1646.6 = 1662.4 + j1646.6 V and |E_f| = 2339.6 V. Regulation = (2339.6 - 2401.8)/2401.8 = -2.589 percent. A negative value means the terminal voltage would fall from 2401.8 V to 2339.6 V per phase if the load were removed at constant excitation.

Answer: Regulation = -2.589 %

(d)

The load angle δ is the angle of E_f relative to V_t. From part a, E_f = 3526.0 + j1412.3 V, so δ = arctan(1412.3/3526.0) = arctan(0.4005) = 21.83°. This is the angle by which the rotor leads the terminal voltage phasor. The real power delivered is P = 3 V_t I cos φ = 3 × 2401.8 × 346.97 × 0.8 = 2.000 MW, which can be checked from E_f, V_t and δ using X_s dominance. A 21.8° angle at full load leaves a healthy margin before the 90° stability limit.

Answer: δ = 21.83°

(e)

Neglecting R_a, the real power per phase is P = E_f V_t sin δ / X_s, with a maximum at δ = 90°. Using E_f = 3798.2 V and V_t = 2401.8 V: P_max,phase = 3798.2 × 2401.8/5.2 = 1.7544 MW per phase. Three phases give P_max = 5.263 MW. That is 5.263/2.0 = 2.63 times the full-load real power, so the steady-state stability margin is generous. In practice the limit is lower because of R_a, saturation, and transient swings, and the machine would pole-slip if load or a fault pushed δ past 90°.

Answer: P_max = 5.263 MW

A6 Practice Paper 20

Problem 1 [A6-096] Synchronous motor operation and power factor

A plant on a 600 V, 60 Hz, three-phase service has an induction-motor and process load of 800 kW at 0.75 power factor lagging. The utility penalizes any plant power factor below 0.95. The owner plans to add a synchronous motor to drive a compressor. The motor will deliver 250 kW to the shaft at an efficiency of 94 percent, so its electrical input is constant at 250/0.94 kW, and it will be run overexcited to supply leading reactive power. The only motor that suits the compressor has a stator rated at 400 kVA, which limits the apparent power it may draw. The engineer must decide whether this motor alone can bring the plant to 0.95 and, if it cannot, what the plant power factor will become. Treat all loads as balanced and the supply voltage as 600 V.

  1. (a) Find the reactive power drawn by the existing 800 kW load. [3]
  2. (b) Find the leading reactive power the motor must supply for the whole plant to reach 0.95 lagging. [5]
  3. (c) Find the apparent power in kVA that the synchronous motor would then have to draw. [4]
  4. (d) With the motor at its 400 kVA limit, find the resulting plant power factor. [5]
  5. (e) State, using the numbers above, whether this motor can meet the utility requirement, and what else the owner could do. Give your reasoning in words. [3]
(a)

The existing load has P = 800 kW at power factor 0.75, so the angle is arccos 0.75 = 41.41° and tan φ = 0.8819. The reactive power drawn is Q = P tan φ = 800 × 0.8819 = 705.5 kvar lagging. The apparent power is 800/0.75 = 1066.7 kVA. This reactive power is what the synchronous motor and any capacitors must offset. The utility bills on power factor, so reducing Q reduces both the billed kVA and the feeder current, and the reduction in current also reduces I²R heating in the plant's transformer and cables.

Answer: Q = 705.5 kvar

(b)

The motor input is P_m = 250/0.94 = 265.96 kW. The total plant real power becomes 800 + 265.96 = 1065.96 kW. For a power factor of 0.95 lagging, tan φ = tan(arccos 0.95) = 0.3287, so the allowed net reactive power is 1065.96 × 0.3287 = 350.4 kvar. The existing load draws 705.5 kvar lagging, so the motor must supply Q_m = 705.5 - 350.4 = 355.2 kvar leading. This comes from overexcitation: raising field current above the unity-power-factor value makes the motor generate reactive power at the same shaft load.

Answer: Q_m = 355.2 kvar leading

(c)

The motor draws real power 265.96 kW and leading reactive power 355.2 kvar, so its apparent power is S = √(265.96² + 355.2²) = √(70 735 + 126 170) = √196 905 = 443.7 kVA. Its power factor is 265.96/443.7 = 0.599 leading. The motor would run at a very low leading power factor, and its stator current would be 443.7×10³/(√3 × 600) = 427 A. That exceeds what a 400 kVA stator can carry continuously, so the required reactive output is more than the machine's thermal limit allows.

Answer: S = 443.7 kVA

(d)

At the thermal limit the motor draws S = 400 kVA with P = 265.96 kW, so its leading reactive power is Q_max = √(400² - 265.96²) = √(160 000 - 70 735) = √89 265 = 298.8 kvar. The net plant reactive power is 705.5 - 298.8 = 406.8 kvar lagging with P = 1065.96 kW. The plant power factor is cos(arctan(406.8/1065.96)) = 1065.96/√(1065.96² + 406.8²) = 1065.96/1140.9 = 0.934 lagging. This is below 0.95, so a penalty would still apply, though it is a big improvement on the original 0.75.

Answer: pf = 0.934 lagging

(e)

The motor needs 443.7 kVA to take the plant to 0.95, but the stator is rated 400 kVA, so run alone it can only reach 0.934. Running it beyond its rating would overheat the stator and field windings. The shortfall is 355.2 - 298.8 = 56.4 kvar. The owner can add a fixed or switched capacitor bank of about 60 kvar, or select a motor with a larger kVA frame, for example a 500 kVA machine. The capacitor option is cheaper, while the larger motor gives margin for future load growth.

Answer: Cannot meet 0.95 alone; add about 60 kvar of capacitors or use a larger motor

Problem 2 [A6-097] Three-phase induction motor equivalent circuit and torque-slip

A 600 V (line), 60 Hz, four-pole, wye-connected cage induction motor drives a mine ventilation fan. The per-phase equivalent circuit, with rotor quantities referred to the stator, has R1 = 0.55 Ω, X1 = 1.20 Ω, magnetizing reactance Xm = 38.0 Ω, X2′ = 1.40 Ω and R2′ = 0.42 Ω. Place the magnetizing branch between the stator impedance (R1 + jX1) and the rotor branch, as in the exact equivalent circuit, and use the Thevenin equivalent seen from the rotor branch. Neglect core loss, friction and windage. Synchronous speed is 1800 rpm. The fan has high inertia and the supply is weak, so the designer is comparing the existing cage rotor with a redesigned high-resistance rotor that would produce its maximum torque at standstill. All torques are shaft electromagnetic torques at the stated slip.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the Thevenin voltage per phase seen from the rotor branch. [3]
  2. (b) Find the electromagnetic torque at a slip of 0.03. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum torque of the motor. [4]
  4. (d) Find the rotor resistance R2′ (referred to the stator) that would put the maximum torque at standstill. [4]
  5. (e) Find the starting torque with the original R2′ = 0.42 Ω, and so judge how much starting torque the new rotor would add. [4]
(a)

With the magnetizing branch placed after the stator impedance, Thevenin's theorem gives V_th = V_phase × jXm/(R1 + j(X1 + Xm)). The phase voltage is 600/√3 = 346.41 V. The denominator is 0.55 + j39.2, with magnitude √(0.55² + 39.2²) = 39.204 Ω. The numerator magnitude is 38.0 Ω, so |V_th| = 346.41 × 38.0/39.204 = 335.8 V. The Thevenin impedance is Z_th = jXm(R1 + jX1)/(R1 + j(X1 + Xm)) = 0.5167 + j1.1705 Ω. This is the impedance the rotor branch sees, and it will govern the torque-slip curve.

Answer: |V_th| = 335.8 V

(b)

The torque is T = 3 V_th² (R2′/s)/{ω_s[(R_th + R2′/s)² + (X_th + X2′)²]}, with ω_s = 2π × 1800/60 = 188.50 rad/s. At s = 0.03, R2′/s = 14.0 Ω. The total reactance is X_th + X2′ = 2.5705 Ω and R_th + 14.0 = 14.5167 Ω. The denominator bracket is 14.5167² + 2.5705² = 210.73 + 6.61 = 217.34. The numerator is 3 × 335.8² × 14.0 = 3 × 112 762 × 14.0 = 4.736×10⁶. So T = 4.736×10⁶/(188.50 × 217.34) = 115.6 N·m. This torque is a reasonable operating torque near the full-load slip for a motor of about 22 kW.

Answer: T(0.03) = 115.6 N·m

(c)

Maximum torque occurs at s_max = R2′/√(R_th² + (X_th + X2′)²). The root is √(0.5167² + 2.5705²) = 2.6219 Ω, so s_max = 0.42/2.6219 = 0.160. The maximum torque is T_max = 3 V_th²/{2ω_s [R_th + √(R_th² + (X_th + X2′)²)]} = 3 × 112 762/(2 × 188.50 × (0.5167 + 2.6219)) = 338 286/(377.0 × 3.1386) = 285.8 N·m. T_max does not depend on R2′, which is the key to wound-rotor and high-resistance rotor design: only the slip at which it occurs changes.

Answer: T_max = 285.8 N·m

(d)

The torque is maximum at standstill when s_max = 1, so R2′ = √(R_th² + (X_th + X2′)²) = 2.6219 Ω, referred to the stator. This is 2.6219/0.42 = 6.24 times the original value, so an extra resistance of 2.202 Ω per phase must be added. With a wound rotor it is cut out as the motor accelerates. With a cage rotor the designer would need a deep-bar or double-cage design, because a fixed high R2′ gives poor running efficiency: the running slip and the rotor copper loss both rise.

Answer: R2′ = 2.622 Ω

(e)

At starting s = 1, with R2′ = 0.42 Ω: the bracket is (0.5167 + 0.42)² + 2.5705² = 0.8775 + 6.6074 = 7.485. The numerator is 3 × 112 762 × 0.42 = 142 080. So T_start = 142 080/(188.50 × 7.485) = 100.7 N·m. With R2′ = 2.622 Ω the starting torque equals T_max = 285.8 N·m, which is 285.8/100.7 = 2.84 times as much. The cost is higher rotor loss in running, so the redesigned rotor suits a high-inertia fan only if starting time is more important than running efficiency, or if the resistance can be switched out.

Answer: T_start = 100.7 N·m

Problem 3 [A6-098] Induction motor starting and speed control

A 600 V, 60 Hz, four-pole cage induction motor drives a booster pump in a municipal water plant. Its full-load current is 55 A and full-load speed 1746 rpm. The data sheet gives a locked-rotor current of 6.2 times full-load current and a locked-rotor torque of 1.6 times rated torque at rated voltage. The utility limits the starting current drawn from the supply to 2.5 times the motor full-load current. Motor torque varies with the square of the motor terminal voltage, and magnetizing current is neglected during the start. An ideal autotransformer starter with tap fraction x applies x times the supply voltage to the motor, so the supply current is x² times the direct-on-line value. A star-delta starter is also available. The pump needs 0.50 of rated torque at standstill and a 25 percent margin is required. Later the pump speed is reduced with a variable frequency drive that holds V/f constant.

  1. (a) Find the autotransformer tap fraction that limits the supply current to 2.5 times full-load current. [4]
  2. (b) Find the starting torque, in multiples of rated torque, at that tap. [4]
  3. (c) Find the supply current at starting with a star-delta starter, in multiples of full-load current. [3]
  4. (d) Find the minimum tap fraction that gives the required starting torque of 0.50 times rated with a 25 percent margin. [4]
  5. (e) The drive runs the pump at 40 Hz with V/f constant and the same slip speed as at rated load. Find the shaft speed in rpm. [5]
(a)

Direct-on-line starting current is 6.2 × 55 = 341 A. The supply current with an autotransformer is x² times this, so the supply limit gives x² × 6.2 = 2.5 in multiples of full-load current. Hence x² = 2.5/6.2 = 0.4032 and x = 0.635. The motor current is x × 6.2 = 3.94 times full-load current, while the supply current is only 2.5 times, because an autotransformer draws less current from the supply than it delivers to the motor, the ratio being the tap fraction. This is the fundamental advantage over a series resistor starter, where motor and supply currents are equal.

Answer: x = 0.635

(b)

Starting torque scales with the square of the voltage applied to the motor, so T_start = x² × 1.6 per unit. With x² = 0.4032, T_start = 0.4032 × 1.6 = 0.645 times rated torque. This exceeds the pump's standstill requirement of 0.50, with a ratio of 1.29, so the pump will start and accelerate. Since torque falls as the square of voltage, a drop in the supply voltage during the start would reduce this margin, which is why a weak supply needs a check of voltage dip as well as of current.

Answer: T_start = 0.645 of rated

(c)

In a star-delta starter the motor windings are connected in star during the start, so each winding sees 1/√3 of line voltage. The line current drops to one third of the delta direct-on-line value: I = 6.2/3 = 2.067 times full-load current, which is below the 2.5 limit. The starting torque also falls to one third: 1.6/3 = 0.533 times rated, which just exceeds the 0.50 load but gives only a 7 percent margin rather than the required 25 percent. So star-delta meets the current limit but does not meet the torque margin for this pump.

Answer: I = 2.067 × I_FL

(d)

The required starting torque is 0.50 × 1.25 = 0.625 times rated torque. With T_start = 1.6 x², we need x² ≥ 0.625/1.6 = 0.3906, so x ≥ 0.625. At this tap the supply current is x² × 6.2 = 0.3906 × 6.2 = 2.42 times full-load current, which is within the 2.5 limit. Hence a tap in the range 0.625 to 0.635 satisfies both constraints, and the 65 percent tap, common on commercial starters, fits only if the supply limit is relaxed. The window is narrow, so the choice needs a check against tolerance in the data sheet values.

Answer: x_min = 0.625

(e)

Synchronous speed at 60 Hz is 1800 rpm and the full-load speed is 1746 rpm, so the slip speed is 54 rpm. At 40 Hz the synchronous speed is 120 × 40/4 = 1200 rpm. With constant V/f the flux is constant, so the torque-slip-speed curve simply shifts, and for the same torque the slip speed is unchanged at 54 rpm. The shaft speed is 1200 - 54 = 1146 rpm. For a fan or pump load the torque falls with speed squared, so the real slip speed would be smaller, and the answer is an upper bound on slip.

Answer: N = 1146 rpm

Problem 4 [A6-099] Distribution system voltage drop and capacitor placement

A 13.8 kV (line to line), three-phase, 60 Hz rural feeder in Ontario runs 6.0 km from the substation to a single concentrated load at the far end. The line impedance is 0.28 + j0.40 Ω per kilometre per phase, and shunt capacitance is neglected. The load is 4.0 MW at 0.85 power factor lagging, and the load-end voltage must be held at 13.8 kV line to line. The utility limit is a voltage rise of no more than 5 percent from the load end to the sending end, defined as (V_s - V_r)/V_r with V_r = 13.8 kV. A planner proposes a 1.2 Mvar three-phase capacitor bank at the load end. Use the per-phase equivalent circuit with the receiving-end phase voltage as reference, and treat the load power as constant with the capacitor in service.

  1. (a) Find the feeder line current with the original load. [3]
  2. (b) Find the sending-end line-to-line voltage. [5]
  3. (c) Find the percentage voltage drop and say whether it meets the 5 percent limit. [3]
  4. (d) With the 1.2 Mvar capacitor in service at the load end, find the percentage voltage drop. [5]
  5. (e) Find the reduction in three-phase feeder copper loss, in kW, after the capacitor is installed. [4]
(a)

The apparent power is S = P/pf = 4.0/0.85 = 4.706 MVA. The line current is I = S/(√3 V_L) = 4.706×10⁶/(√3 × 13 800) = 196.9 A. The receiving-end phase voltage is 13 800/√3 = 7967.4 V, the reference. With a lagging power factor the current phasor is I = 196.9∠-31.79° A = 167.4 - j103.7 A. The total line impedance is 6.0 × (0.28 + j0.40) = 1.68 + j2.40 Ω per phase. These two quantities fix the drop in the next part, which should be computed as a phasor sum, not a scalar estimate.

Answer: I = 196.9 A

(b)

The sending-end phase voltage is V_s = V_r + Z I. The drop is (1.68 + j2.40)(167.4 - j103.7) = (281.2 + 248.9) + j(401.8 - 174.2) = 530.1 + j227.6 V. So V_s = 7967.4 + 530.1 + j227.6 = 8497.5 + j227.6 V, and |V_s| = 8501.1 V per phase. The line-to-line value is √3 × 8501.1 = 14 723 V. The quadrature component 227.6 V has only a small effect on the magnitude, which shows the usual approximation: the voltage drop is mostly R cos φ + X sin φ times current, here 1.68 × 0.85 + 2.40 × 0.527 = 2.69 Ω.

Answer: V_s = 14 723 V

(c)

The voltage drop is (V_s - V_r)/V_r = (14 723 - 13 800)/13 800 = 923/13 800 = 0.0669, or 6.69 percent. This exceeds the 5 percent limit by 1.69 percentage points, so the feeder as loaded does not comply. The main cause is the lagging reactive power: with a unity power factor load, the drop would be dominated by the smaller resistance term. This is why distribution engineers install shunt capacitors or voltage regulators on long rural feeders, and why the planner is proposing the bank.

Answer: Drop = 6.69 %, limit exceeded

(d)

The load reactive power is Q = 4.0 tan(arccos 0.85) = 4.0 × 0.6197 = 2.479 Mvar. The capacitor supplies 1.2 Mvar, so the feeder carries Q_net = 1.279 Mvar with P = 4.0 MW. The apparent power is √(4.0² + 1.279²) = 4.199 MVA and the current is 4.199×10⁶/(√3 × 13 800) = 175.7 A at a lagging angle arctan(1.279/4.0) = 17.7°. The drop phasor is (1.68 + j2.40)(167.3 - j53.4) = 409.2 + j(401.5 - 89.7) giving V_s = 8376.6 + j311.8 V and 8382.5 V per phase, or 14 519 V line to line. The drop is 719/13 800 = 5.21 percent, still just above 5 percent.

Answer: Drop = 5.21 %

(e)

Three-phase copper loss is 3 I² R with R = 1.68 Ω per phase. Before: 3 × 196.9² × 1.68 = 3 × 38 770 × 1.68 = 195.4 kW. After: 3 × 175.7² × 1.68 = 3 × 30 870 × 1.68 = 155.6 kW. The reduction is 195.4 - 155.6 = 39.8 kW, or about 20 percent of the loss. Over 8760 hours this is about 349 MWh a year if the load were constant, which at an energy price of ten cents per kilowatt-hour is about 35 000 dollars a year and helps justify the capacitor bank beyond the voltage benefit.

Answer: Loss reduction = 39.8 kW

Problem 5 [A6-100] Machine or system selection combining losses, rating and cost

A water utility in Ontario must choose between two 75 kW, 600 V, four-pole induction motors for a raw-water pump. The pump shaft load is constant at 60 kW for 6000 hours a year. Motor A is a standard-efficiency design with an efficiency of 91.5 percent at this load and a purchase price of 5200 dollars. Motor B is a premium-efficiency design with an efficiency of 94.5 percent at this load and costs 7400 dollars. Electricity costs 0.11 dollars per kilowatt-hour with no demand charge. Both motors last 10 years with no salvage value and have the same maintenance cost. The utility uses a discount rate of 8 percent a year and treats energy savings as arriving at the end of each year. The manager wants a decision based on the numbers and also wants to know how sensitive it is to the electricity price.

  1. (a) Find the difference in electrical losses between Motor A and Motor B at the 60 kW shaft load. [4]
  2. (b) Find the annual energy cost saving from choosing Motor B. [4]
  3. (c) Find the simple payback period of the extra price of Motor B. [4]
  4. (d) Find the net present value of choosing Motor B over its 10-year life at 8 percent. [5]
  5. (e) Find the electricity price at which the simple payback would lengthen to 3 years. [3]
(a)

The input power is the shaft power divided by efficiency, and the loss is the input minus the output. For Motor A: input = 60/0.915 = 65.574 kW, so loss = 5.574 kW. For Motor B: input = 60/0.945 = 63.492 kW, so loss = 3.492 kW. The difference is 5.574 - 3.492 = 2.082 kW. This difference is the continuous power saved at the 60 kW load, and it also means less heat in the pump room, though that benefit is not valued here. The efficiency comparison is valid only at the stated load, since the efficiency of both motors varies with loading.

Answer: ΔLoss = 2.082 kW

(b)

The annual energy saving is the loss difference times the operating hours: 2.082 kW × 6000 h = 12 490 kWh per year. Multiplying by the price of 0.11 dollars per kilowatt-hour gives 12 490 × 0.11 = 1374 dollars per year. This is the cash saving in the first year, and by assumption it is the same every year. Rising tariffs, which are likely, would increase it, so the constant-price assumption is on the cautious side. A different run time, such as 3000 hours, would halve the figure, which is why the utilization is the most important input.

Answer: Saving = 1374 $/yr

(c)

The extra purchase price of Motor B is 7400 - 5200 = 2200 dollars. Simple payback is the extra cost divided by the annual saving: 2200/1374 = 1.60 years. This is much shorter than the 10-year life, so the premium motor pays for itself in about 19 months. A common policy threshold is 3 years, and this option clears it comfortably. Simple payback ignores the time value of money and savings after the payback date, so it is a screening measure, and the next part gives the more complete picture over the whole life.

Answer: Payback = 1.60 years

(d)

The present value of 10 equal year-end savings at 8 percent uses the annuity factor (1 - 1.08⁻¹⁰)/0.08 = (1 - 0.4632)/0.08 = 6.7101. The present value of savings is 1374 × 6.7101 = 9219 dollars. The extra cost is paid now, 2200 dollars. The net present value is 9219 - 2200 = 7019 dollars. A positive NPV means Motor B is the better choice on cost. The internal rate of return would be above 60 percent, and the decision holds even if the savings were cut by two thirds, so it is robust.

Answer: NPV = 7019 dollars

(e)

Let p be the electricity price. Annual saving = 2.082 × 6000 × p = 12 490 p. Payback = 2200/(12 490 p) = 3 years requires p = 2200/(3 × 12 490) = 0.0587 dollars per kilowatt-hour. So the premium motor stays within a 3-year payback as long as electricity costs more than about 5.9 cents per kilowatt-hour. The current price of 11 cents is almost double that, which confirms that the decision is not marginal and would survive substantial price changes or shorter running hours.

Answer: p = 0.0587 $/kWh

Exam A7: Electromagnetics

A7 Practice Paper 1

Problem 1 [A7-001] Vector calculus and coordinate systems for fields

A vector field in a region of free space is described in cylindrical coordinates (ρ, φ, z) by F = ρ² z aρ + 3ρ cos φ aφ + 2z² az, where ρ is in metres and the unit vectors point in the directions of increasing ρ, φ and z. The field is being used to model the steady flow pattern of a cooling-air stream around a vertical busbar riser in a switchgear room, and the designer wants to check where the stream spreads out and where it circulates. Consider the point P at ρ = 2 m, φ = π/3 rad, z = 1.5 m, and also the closed cylindrical surface bounded by ρ = 2 m, z = 0 and z = 3 m.

  1. (a) Find the divergence of F at P. [6]
  2. (b) Find the z-component of the curl of F at P. [5]
  3. (c) Evaluate the net outward flux of F through the closed cylindrical surface, using the divergence theorem, and give the answer in the units of the field times m². [9]
(a)

In cylindrical coordinates the divergence is ∇·F = (1/ρ) ∂(ρFρ)/∂ρ + (1/ρ) ∂Fφ/∂φ + ∂Fz/∂z. With Fρ = ρ²z, ρFρ = ρ³z, so the first term is (1/ρ)(3ρ²z) = 3ρz. With Fφ = 3ρ cos φ, the second term is (1/ρ)(-3ρ sin φ) = -3 sin φ. With Fz = 2z², the third term is 4z. Hence ∇·F = 3ρz - 3 sin φ + 4z. At P, 3(2)(1.5) = 9, 3 sin(π/3) = 2.598 and 4(1.5) = 6, so ∇·F = 9 - 2.598 + 6 = 12.40. The positive value means the field spreads outward from P.

Answer: 12.40

(b)

The z-component of the curl in cylindrical coordinates is (∇×F)z = (1/ρ)[∂(ρFφ)/∂ρ - ∂Fρ/∂φ]. Here ρFφ = 3ρ² cos φ, so ∂(ρFφ)/∂ρ = 6ρ cos φ. The radial component Fρ = ρ²z does not depend on φ, so ∂Fρ/∂φ = 0. Therefore (∇×F)z = (1/ρ)(6ρ cos φ) = 6 cos φ. At φ = π/3, cos φ = 0.5, so (∇×F)z = 3.00. The value is independent of ρ and z, which is a quick check on the algebra. The positive sign means the circulation about the z direction follows the right-hand rule about +z.

Answer: 3.00

(c)

The divergence theorem gives the outward flux as the volume integral of ∇·F over the enclosed cylinder: Φ = ∫∫∫ (3ρz - 3 sin φ + 4z) ρ dρ dφ dz, with ρ from 0 to 2, φ from 0 to 2π and z from 0 to 3. The sin φ term integrates to zero over a full turn. The remaining integrand gives ∫02 (3ρ²z + 4ρz) dρ = z(8 + 8) = 16z. Then Φ = 2π ∫03 16z dz = 2π(16)(4.5) = 144π = 452.4. As a check, the sin φ term contributes no net flux because it is antisymmetric about the axis, which is why only ρ and z terms survive.

Answer: 452.4

Problem 2 [A7-002] Electrostatics: Coulomb's law, Gauss's law and potential

A dielectric-free insulating sphere of radius a = 4.0 cm holds a space charge that is not uniform: the volume charge density is ρv = ρ0 (1 - r/a) for 0 ≤ r ≤ a, where r is the distance from the centre and ρ0 = 6.0 μC/m³, and ρv = 0 for r > a. The sphere is surrounded by free space, with ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m. This models the charge left on a spherical polymer insulator that has been rubbed during manufacture. Assume spherical symmetry throughout, so the field depends only on r and points radially, and take the potential to be zero at infinity.

  1. (a) Find the total charge on the sphere. [5]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the electric field at r = 2.0 cm. [6]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the electric field at r = 8.0 cm. [3]
  4. (d) Find the potential at the centre of the sphere. [6]
(a)

The total charge is the volume integral of ρv: Q = ∫0a ρ0 (1 - r/a) 4πr² dr = 4πρ0 [a³/3 - a³/4] = 4πρ0 a³/12 = πρ0 a³/3. With a = 0.04 m, a³ = 6.4 × 10⁻⁵ m³, so Q = π(6.0 × 10⁻⁶)(6.4 × 10⁻⁵)/3 = 4.02 × 10⁻¹⁰ C. (The weighting by r² is why the outer shells dominate even though the density falls toward the surface.) This value is also what an observer outside the sphere would measure by Gauss's law.

Answer: 4.02 × 10⁻¹⁰ C

(b)

Apply Gauss's law over a concentric sphere of radius r < a: E 4πr² = Qenc/ε0, with Qenc = 4πρ0 (r³/3 - r⁴/(4a)). Therefore E(r) = (ρ0/ε0)(r/3 - r²/(4a)). At r = 0.02 m, r/3 = 6.667 × 10⁻³ m and r²/(4a) = 4 × 10⁻⁴/0.16 = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m, so the bracket is 4.167 × 10⁻³ m. With ρ0/ε0 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁶/8.854 × 10⁻¹² = 6.777 × 10⁵ V/m², E = 2.82 × 10³ V/m, directed radially outward because the charge is positive.

Answer: 2.82 kV/m

(c)

At r = 0.08 m the Gaussian sphere encloses the whole charge, so E = Q/(4πε0 r²). Using Q = 4.021 × 10⁻¹⁰ C, 4πε0 = 1.1127 × 10⁻¹⁰ F/m and r² = 6.4 × 10⁻³ m², E = 4.021 × 10⁻¹⁰/(1.1127 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 6.4 × 10⁻³) = 565 V/m. Outside a spherically symmetric distribution the field is identical to that of a point charge Q at the centre. As a consistency check, evaluating the interior expression at r = a gives (ρ0/ε0)(a/12) = 2.26 kV/m, and scaling that by (a/0.08)² = 0.25 gives 565 V/m.

Answer: 0.565 kV/m

(d)

The potential at the centre is the line integral of E from the centre to infinity: V(0) = ∫0a E dr + ∫a^∞ E dr. The outer part equals Q/(4πε0 a) = 4.021 × 10⁻¹⁰/(1.1127 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.04) = 90.35 V. The inner part is (ρ0/ε0)[r²/6 - r³/(12a)] evaluated from 0 to a, which is (ρ0/ε0)(a²/6 - a²/12) = (ρ0/ε0)(a²/12) = 6.777 × 10⁵ × 1.6 × 10⁻³/12 = 90.36 V. The sum is V(0) = 180.7 V. Both parts are positive since the charge is positive and the reference is at infinity.

Answer: 181 V

Problem 3 [A7-003] Capacitance and dielectrics

A coaxial high-voltage lead has a solid inner conductor of radius a = 1.5 mm and a grounded outer conductor whose inner radius is c = 5.0 mm. The space between them contains two concentric dielectric layers that bond perfectly: layer 1 extends from r = 1.5 mm to b = 3.0 mm and has relative permittivity εr1 = 4.0, and layer 2 extends from r = 3.0 mm to r = 5.0 mm and has εr2 = 2.5. Both layers are lossless and the lead is very long, so end effects are neglected. Use ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m. A 6.0 kV dc supply is connected between the inner conductor and the outer conductor.

  1. (a) Find the capacitance per metre of the lead, in pF/m. [6]
  2. (b) Find the voltage across layer 1. [6]
  3. (c) Find the largest electric field in layer 1, in MV/m. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest electric field in layer 2, in MV/m. [4]
(a)

The layers are in series because they are concentric and the same charge per unit length λ flows through both. For one layer the capacitance per metre is 2πε0εr/ln(r_out/r_in), so the reciprocals of the layer capacitances add: 1/C = ln(b/a)/(2πε0 εr1) + ln(c/b)/(2πε0 εr2). With ln(2) = 0.6931 and ln(5/3) = 0.5108, 1/C = [0.6931/4 + 0.5108/2.5]/(2π × 8.854 × 10⁻¹²) = (0.17329 + 0.20431)/(5.5630 × 10⁻¹¹) = 6.788 × 10⁹ m/F. So C = 1.473 × 10⁻¹⁰ F/m = 147 pF/m.

Answer: 147 pF/m

(b)

With the whole 6 kV across the series pair, the charge per unit length is λ = C V = 1.4732 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 6000 = 8.839 × 10⁻⁷ C/m. The voltage across layer 1 is V1 = λ ln(b/a)/(2πε0 εr1) = 8.839 × 10⁻⁷ × 0.6931/(5.5630 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4) = 2753 V. The remainder, 6000 - 2753 = 3247 V, appears across layer 2. The lower-permittivity layer carries more of the voltage, which is the standard capacitive-divider behaviour for series dielectrics. A quick ratio check gives V1/V2 = (0.17329)/(0.20431) = 0.848, and 2753/3247 = 0.848.

Answer: 2.75 kV

(c)

In a layer the field is E(r) = λ/(2πε0 εr r), which is largest at the smallest radius. In layer 1 that is r = a = 1.5 mm, so Emax1 = 8.839 × 10⁻⁷/(5.5630 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4 × 1.5 × 10⁻³) = 2.648 × 10⁶ V/m, or 2.65 MV/m. This sits on the surface of the inner conductor, where insulation breakdown usually starts. The field in layer 1 falls off as 1/r, so at r = b it is half of this value, 1.32 MV/m.

Answer: 2.65 MV/m

(d)

The displacement density D = λ/(2πr) is continuous across the interface at r = b because there is no free charge there, so the field jumps by the ratio εr1/εr2 = 1.6. On the layer 2 side at r = b, E = λ/(2πε0 εr2 b) = 8.839 × 10⁻⁷/(5.5630 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.5 × 3.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.118 × 10⁶ V/m, which is the largest field in layer 2. Check: the layer 1 side at r = b is 1.324 MV/m and 1.324 × 1.6 = 2.118 MV/m.

Answer: 2.12 MV/m

Problem 4 [A7-004] Boundary conditions and Laplace equation problems

Two large flat conducting plates are hinged along a common edge that coincides with the z axis, and are held at an opening angle of α = 60° (π/3 rad). Plate A lies on the plane φ = 0 and is held at 0 V, and plate B lies on the plane φ = α and is held at 100 V. The space between them is air (ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m). Ignore fringing at the outer edges and any variation along z, so that the potential V depends only on the angle φ in cylindrical coordinates. Separately, an electric field in air meets a flat dielectric boundary with a material of relative permittivity 4.0; the field in air has a magnitude of 3.0 kV/m and makes an angle of 30° with the normal to the boundary.

  1. (a) Solve Laplace's equation for the wedge and find the magnitude of the electric field at ρ = 2.0 cm. [7]
  2. (b) Find the surface charge density on plate B at ρ = 2.0 cm, in nC/m². [5]
  3. (c) For the air-dielectric interface, find the magnitude of the field in the dielectric. [8]
(a)

With V = V(φ) only, Laplace's equation in cylindrical coordinates reduces to (1/ρ²) d²V/dφ² = 0, so V = Aφ + B. The condition V(0) = 0 gives B = 0, and V(α) = 100 V gives A = 100/(π/3) = 95.49 V/rad. The field is E = -∇V = -(1/ρ) dV/dφ aφ = -(A/ρ) aφ. At ρ = 0.02 m, |E| = 95.49/0.02 = 4775 V/m. The field lines are circular arcs centred on the hinge line, pointing from the high-potential plate to the low-potential plate, and the field strength falls as 1/ρ with distance from the hinge.

Answer: 4.77 kV/m

(b)

On the surface of a conductor the boundary condition is σs = D·n = ε0 E·n, where n points out of the conductor into the air. On plate B the outward normal is directed toward plate A, which is the -aφ direction, and E = -(A/ρ) aφ, so E·n = +A/ρ. Hence σs = ε0 A/ρ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 4775 = 4.227 × 10⁻⁸ C/m² = 42.3 nC/m². The sign is positive, as expected for the plate at the higher potential. The density rises toward the hinge, varying as 1/ρ.

Answer: 42.3 nC/m²

(c)

Resolve the incident field: the tangential component is Et = E1 sin 30° = 3000 × 0.5 = 1500 V/m. The tangential component is continuous across the boundary, so Et2 = 1500 V/m. The normal component of D is continuous when there is no free surface charge, so ε1 En1 = ε2 En2, where En1 = 3000 cos 30° = 2598 V/m. Therefore En2 = (1/4)(2598) = 649.5 V/m. The magnitude in the dielectric is E2 = √(1500² + 649.5²) = 1635 V/m, at an angle of atan(1500/649.5) = 66.6° from the normal. The field bends away from the normal toward the higher permittivity.

Answer: 1.63 kV/m

Problem 5 [A7-005] Steady current, conductors and resistance fields

A substation ground electrode is a metal hemisphere of radius a = 0.50 m buried so that its flat face is level with the soil surface. The soil is homogeneous with conductivity σ = 0.020 S/m and extends to infinity in every direction. Current spreads out from the electrode radially and uniformly through the hemispherical shells of soil, and the remote earth is taken as the zero-potential reference. The electrode resistance is dominated by the soil, because the metal is a far better conductor. A phase-to-ground fault injects a steady current of 800 A into the electrode. A technician is standing near the electrode with one foot 1.5 m from its centre and the other foot 2.5 m from its centre on the same radial line.

  1. (a) Find the resistance of the electrode to remote earth. [5]
  2. (b) Find the rise in potential of the electrode above remote earth during the fault. [4]
  3. (c) Find the step voltage between the technician's feet. [6]
  4. (d) Explain in two or three sentences why the step voltage is a hazard even though the technician is not touching the electrode, and name one way to reduce it. [5]
(a)

In soil the current density at radius r is J = I/(2πr²), because the current crosses a hemispherical shell of area 2πr². The field is E = J/σ = I/(2πσr²). The potential of the electrode relative to infinity is V = ∫a^∞ E dr = I/(2πσ a). Hence R = V/I = 1/(2πσ a) = 1/(2π × 0.020 × 0.50) = 1/0.06283 = 15.92 Ω. Almost all of the resistance lies in the soil close to the electrode, since the shells farther out have a large area, so the value does not depend on how far away the remote reference is.

Answer: 15.9 Ω

(b)

The electrode potential rise equals the fault current times the electrode resistance, GPR = I R. With I = 800 A and R = 15.915 Ω, GPR = 800 × 15.915 = 12 732 V, or 12.7 kV. This is the potential of the electrode and of any metal bonded to it, relative to remote earth. It is large even for a moderate resistance because the fault current is high. The same result follows from V = I/(2πσa) = 800/(2π × 0.02 × 0.5) = 12.73 kV, which is an independent check from the potential integral.

Answer: 12.7 kV

(c)

The potential at distance r from the centre outside the electrode is V(r) = I/(2πσ r), from integrating E from r to infinity. The step voltage is the difference between the two foot positions: Vstep = (I/(2πσ))(1/r1 - 1/r2). Here I/(2πσ) = 800/(2π × 0.020) = 6366.2 V·m. Then 1/1.5 - 1/2.5 = 0.66667 - 0.40000 = 0.26667 m⁻¹. So Vstep = 6366.2 × 0.26667 = 1698 V, or 1.70 kV. This is well above values normally tolerated by the human body, so the location close to the electrode is dangerous during a fault.

Answer: 1.70 kV

(d)

Current flowing through the soil sets up a potential that falls steeply with distance near the electrode, so the ground surface is not at one potential. A person standing there has feet at different potentials, and the voltage between them drives current up one leg and down the other through the body, with no contact with the electrode needed. The hazard is greatest where the gradient is steepest, close to the electrode. It is reduced by a buried grading conductor mesh, which flattens the surface potential profile, or by a high-resistivity gravel surface layer that limits body current.

Answer: Potential gradient across the feet drives body current; reduce with a grading mesh or gravel layer.

A7 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A7-006] Magnetostatics: Biot-Savart and Ampere's law

A long coaxial feeder carries a steady direct current of I = 40 A along its inner conductor, which is a solid copper cylinder of radius a = 2.0 mm, with the current uniformly distributed over its cross-section. The return current flows in the opposite direction in a tubular outer conductor with inner radius b = 6.0 mm and outer radius c = 8.0 mm, again uniformly distributed over the tube cross-section. The conductors are non-magnetic, so the permeability everywhere is μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m, and the feeder is long enough that end effects are ignored. Use circular symmetry about the cable axis and consider only the magnitude of the flux density B.

  1. (a) Find B at a radius ρ = 1.0 mm, inside the inner conductor. [5]
  2. (b) Find B at ρ = 4.0 mm, in the gap between the conductors. [4]
  3. (c) Find B at ρ = 7.0 mm, inside the outer conductor. [6]
  4. (d) Find the largest value of B anywhere in the cable and the radius at which it occurs. [5]
(a)

Apply Ampere's law around a circle of radius ρ < a: B (2πρ) = μ0 Ienc. The current density in the inner conductor is uniform, so Ienc = I ρ²/a². Hence B = μ0 I ρ/(2π a²). With ρ = 1.0 mm and a = 2.0 mm, B = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 40 × 1.0 × 10⁻³)/(2π × 4.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.0 × 10⁻³ T. The flux density rises linearly with ρ inside the conductor, so at half the radius it is half of the surface value, which is 4 mT.

Answer: 2.00 mT

(b)

In the gap a < ρ < b the Amperian circle encloses the whole inner current I = 40 A and nothing else, so B = μ0 I/(2πρ). At ρ = 4.0 mm, B = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 40)/(2π × 4.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.0 × 10⁻³ T. The field falls as 1/ρ here, as for a thin wire. The value happens to equal that at 1.0 mm inside the conductor: the linear rise reaches 4 mT at ρ = a, and the 1/ρ fall brings it back to 2 mT at twice that radius.

Answer: 2.00 mT

(c)

In the tube the return current is spread over the area π(c² - b²) = π(64 - 36) × 10⁻⁶ = π × 28 × 10⁻⁶ m². The return current inside radius ρ = 7 mm is -I(ρ² - b²)/(c² - b²) = -40(49 - 36)/28 = -18.57 A. The net enclosed current is 40 - 18.57 = 21.43 A. Then B = μ0 Ienc/(2πρ) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 21.43/(7.0 × 10⁻³) = 6.12 × 10⁻⁴ T, or 0.612 mT. The field continues to fall to zero at ρ = c, because the net enclosed current is zero there.

Answer: 0.612 mT

(d)

B rises linearly inside the inner conductor to its surface, falls as 1/ρ in the gap, and falls further inside the tube to zero at ρ = c. So the maximum occurs at the surface of the inner conductor, ρ = a = 2.0 mm. There B = μ0 I/(2πa) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 40/(2.0 × 10⁻³) = 4.0 × 10⁻³ T. Outside ρ = c the field is exactly zero because the net current is zero, which is why a coaxial cable does not radiate a static magnetic field to its surroundings.

Answer: 4.00 mT at ρ = 2.0 mm

Problem 2 [A7-007] Magnetic force, induction and Faraday's law

A small test generator consists of a rectangular coil with N = 300 turns, each turn measuring 0.20 m by 0.15 m, spinning at a constant 1800 revolutions per minute about an axis through its centre. The axis lies in the plane of the coil, parallel to the 0.20 m sides, and is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic flux density B = 0.40 T. At time t = 0 the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field, so the flux linking the coil is at its maximum. The coil is connected to a resistive load such that the total circuit resistance, including the coil, is 120 Ω. Neglect the inductance of the coil.

  1. (a) Find the peak induced emf. [6]
  2. (b) Find the rms emf. [3]
  3. (c) Find the instantaneous emf at t = 2.5 ms. [5]
  4. (d) Find the average electrical power dissipated in the 120 Ω circuit. [6]
(a)

The flux linkage is λ = N B A cos ωt, with A = 0.20 × 0.15 = 0.030 m² and ω = 2π × (1800/60) = 188.5 rad/s. Faraday's law gives e = -dλ/dt = N B A ω sin ωt, so the peak emf is Em = 300 × 0.40 × 0.030 × 188.5 = 678.6 V. The emf is proportional to the speed, the field, the area and the turns. The sine form follows because the flux is at its maximum when t = 0, so the emf there is zero, and it is a maximum when the coil plane is parallel to the field and the sides cut the flux fastest.

Answer: 679 V

(b)

For a sinusoidal emf the rms value is the peak divided by √2. Therefore Erms = 678.584/1.41421 = 479.8 V. This is the value that a heating load sees as equivalent dc. The relationship holds because the emf is a pure sinusoid at 30 Hz, since the field is uniform and the speed is constant. A meter that reads true rms would indicate 480 V, and the peak is about 41 percent higher. Because the rms value fixes the heating effect, it is the figure used in part (d) for the load power, and it is the number a supply designer would quote on a nameplate.

Answer: 480 V

(c)

The instantaneous emf is e(t) = Em sin ωt. At t = 2.5 ms, ωt = 188.5 × 0.0025 = 0.4712 rad, which is 27°. Then sin(0.4712) = 0.4540, so e = 678.58 × 0.4540 = 308.1 V. The sign convention is that the emf is positive when the flux is decreasing, following Lenz's law, which means the induced current opposes the loss of flux. Since the coil has turned only 27° from the flux-maximum position, the emf is still well below its peak.

Answer: 308 V

(d)

With negligible inductance the current is in phase with the emf, so the average power is P = Erms²/R. Using Erms = 479.83 V and R = 120 Ω, P = 479.83²/120 = 230 237/120 = 1918.7 W, about 1.92 kW. Equivalently, P = Em²/(2R) = 678.58²/240 = 1918.7 W. This is also the mechanical power that the prime mover must supply, ignoring friction and windage, since there are no other losses in the model. At 30 Hz the average shaft torque is about 10.2 N·m.

Answer: 1.92 kW

Problem 3 [A7-008] Inductance and magnetic energy

A toroidal reactor has a core of rectangular cross-section: the inner radius is a = 10 cm, the outer radius is b = 14 cm and the axial height is h = 3.0 cm. The core material has constant relative permeability μr = 1200 and fills the whole toroid, and μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. A winding of N1 = 800 turns is spread evenly around the full circumference, and a second winding of N2 = 50 turns is wound tightly over the first and links the same core flux. Assume the flux is confined to the core and that the field at radius ρ is H = N1 I/(2πρ), with the iron operating on the linear part of its magnetization curve, so no saturation occurs.

  1. (a) Find the self inductance of the N1 winding. [6]
  2. (b) Find the energy stored in the core when the current in the N1 winding is 0.25 A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the magnetic energy density at the inner radius ρ = a when I = 0.25 A. [4]
  4. (d) Find the mutual inductance between the two windings. [6]
(a)

The flux density in the core is B = μ0 μr N1 I/(2πρ). The flux through the rectangular section is Φ = ∫ B h dρ = μ0 μr N1 I h ln(b/a)/(2π). The flux linkage is λ = N1 Φ, so L = μ0 μr N1² h ln(b/a)/(2π). With μ0 μr = 1.5080 × 10⁻³ H/m, N1² = 6.4 × 10⁵, h = 0.03 m and ln(1.4) = 0.33647, L = 1.5080 × 10⁻³ × 6.4 × 10⁵ × 0.03 × 0.33647/(2π) = 1.550 H. The logarithm appears because the flux density is not uniform across the section.

Answer: 1.55 H

(b)

In a linear inductor the stored energy is W = ½ L I². With L = 1.5505 H and I = 0.25 A, W = 0.5 × 1.5505 × 0.0625 = 0.04845 J. This is the energy that must be returned or dissipated when the current is interrupted, which is why a switch opening an inductive circuit sees large voltages. As a cross-check one could integrate the energy density ½ B H over the core volume, and the result is the same because the model is linear.

Answer: 0.0485 J

(c)

At the inner radius, H = N1 I/(2πa) = 800 × 0.25/(2π × 0.10) = 318.3 A/m. The corresponding flux density is B = μ0 μr H = 1.5080 × 10⁻³ × 318.3 = 0.480 T, which is comfortably below the saturation of a good core steel, so the linear model is reasonable. The energy density is w = ½ μ H² = 0.5 × 1.5080 × 10⁻³ × 318.3² = 76.4 J/m³. The density is highest at the inner radius and falls as 1/ρ², being only about half as large at the outer radius.

Answer: 76.4 J/m³

(d)

The same flux Φ links both windings, so the mutual inductance is M = N2 Φ/I = μ0 μr N1 N2 h ln(b/a)/(2π). Compared with L, which has N1², the factor N1 is replaced by N2, so M = L N2/N1 = 1.5505 × 50/800 = 0.0969 H. Direct substitution gives 1.5080 × 10⁻³ × 800 × 50 × 0.03 × 0.33647/(2π) = 0.0969 H. The coupling coefficient is unity here because all flux links both windings, so M = √(L1 L2) with L2 = L N2²/N1² = 0.00606 H, which reproduces 0.0969 H.

Answer: 0.0969 H

Problem 4 [A7-009] Maxwell's equations in integral and differential form

In a region of free space (μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m, ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, no charges or currents) a uniform plane electromagnetic wave travels in the +z direction. Its electric field is E = 60 sin(ωt - βz) ay V/m with frequency f = 150 MHz, and its magnetic field is along ax. A rectangular loop of wire lies in the yz plane with corners at (y, z) = (0, 0), (0.20 m, 0), (0.20 m, 0.50 m) and (0, 0.50 m), where x = 0 for every point on the loop. A separate flat patch of area 0.20 m × 0.30 m lies in the xy plane at z = 0 and faces the wave.

  1. (a) Use Maxwell's curl equations to find the phase constant β. [5]
  2. (b) Find the amplitude of the magnetic field strength. [4]
  3. (c) Use the integral form of Faraday's law to find the peak emf induced around the loop in the yz plane. [6]
  4. (d) Find the average power crossing the 0.20 m × 0.30 m patch. [5]
(a)

Faraday's law in differential form gives ∇×E = -μ0 ∂H/∂t, and Ampere's law gives ∇×H = ε0 ∂E/∂t. Taking the curl of the first and using the second yields the wave equation ∂²Ey/∂z² = μ0 ε0 ∂²Ey/∂t². Substituting Ey = 60 sin(ωt - βz) gives β² = ω² μ0 ε0, so β = ω√(μ0 ε0). With ω = 2π × 150 × 10⁶ = 9.425 × 10⁸ rad/s and √(μ0 ε0) = 3.3356 × 10⁻⁹ s/m, β = 3.144 rad/m. The phase velocity is then 1/√(μ0 ε0) = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

Answer: 3.14 rad/m

(b)

From Faraday's law, (∇×E)x = -∂Ey/∂z = -∂Bx/∂t, so ∂Bx/∂t = ∂Ey/∂z = -βE0 cos(ωt - βz) with E0 = 60 V/m. Integrating gives Bx = -(β/ω) E0 sin(ωt - βz), so Hx = -(β/(ωμ0)) E0 sin(ωt - βz) = -(E0/η0) sin(ωt - βz). Hx is negative so that Ey × Hx points along +z, as it must for a wave travelling in +z. The amplitude is H0 = E0/η0, where η0 = √(μ0/ε0) = 376.7 Ω. Thus H0 = 60/376.7 = 0.1593 A/m.

Answer: 0.159 A/m

(c)

Faraday's law in integral form gives emf = ∮E·dl = -dΦ/dt. Only Ey is non-zero and the sides along z are perpendicular to E, so they contribute nothing. The two sides along y at z = 0 and z = 0.50 m each have length 0.20 m, traversed in opposite directions. The emf magnitude is 0.20 |E(0) - E(0.5)|. For the peak value, the difference of two sinusoids with phase separation βd = 3.1437 × 0.5 = 1.5719 rad has amplitude 2 sin(βd/2) = 1.4148. Hence the peak emf = 0.20 × 60 × 1.4148 = 16.98 V.

Answer: 17.0 V

(d)

The time-average Poynting vector for a plane wave in free space has magnitude Savg = E0²/(2η0) = 60²/(2 × 376.7) = 4.778 W/m², directed along +z. The patch in the xy plane at z = 0 is perpendicular to the direction of travel, so all the power is incident normally. Its area is 0.20 × 0.30 = 0.060 m², and the average power is P = 4.778 × 0.060 = 0.2867 W. The loop in part (c) is in the yz plane, parallel to the direction of travel, and so no net power crosses it.

Answer: 0.287 W

Problem 5 [A7-010] Displacement current and time-varying fields

A parallel-plate capacitor has circular plates of radius r0 = 5.0 cm separated by a gap d = 2.0 mm. The gap is filled with a slightly lossy dielectric of relative permittivity εr = 3.5 and conductivity σ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ S/m, with ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m. A sinusoidal voltage of peak value 50 V and frequency 5.0 MHz is applied across the plates. Assume the electric field is uniform in the gap, E = v/d, and neglect fringing at the plate edges. The capacitor is being used as a test cell for a moisture sensor, and the designer wants to know how much of the current is conduction and how much is displacement.

  1. (a) Find the peak displacement current in the dielectric. [5]
  2. (b) Find the peak conduction current in the dielectric. [4]
  3. (c) Find the frequency at which the conduction and displacement current amplitudes are equal. [5]
  4. (d) Find the peak magnetic field strength at a radius ρ = 3.0 cm from the axis, between the plates, due to the displacement current density alone. [6]
(a)

The displacement current density is Jd = ∂D/∂t = ε ∂E/∂t, with peak value ω ε E0 for a sinusoidal field. Here ε = 3.5 × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² = 3.099 × 10⁻¹¹ F/m, ω = 2π × 5 × 10⁶ = 3.1416 × 10⁷ rad/s and E0 = 50/0.002 = 25 000 V/m. So Jd = 3.1416 × 10⁷ × 3.099 × 10⁻¹¹ × 25 000 = 24.34 A/m². The plate area is π(0.05)² = 7.854 × 10⁻³ m², so the peak displacement current is Id = 24.34 × 7.854 × 10⁻³ = 0.191 A.

Answer: 0.191 A

(b)

The conduction current density is J = σE, so its peak is 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 25 000 = 5.0 A/m². Multiplying by the plate area 7.854 × 10⁻³ m² gives the peak conduction current Ic = 5.0 × 7.854 × 10⁻³ = 0.03927 A, or 39.3 mA. This current is in phase with the voltage, since it follows Ohm's law, while the displacement current leads the voltage by 90°. Their ratio, Id/Ic = ωε/σ = 4.87, shows that the capacitor is mostly capacitive at 5 MHz.

Answer: 39.3 mA

(c)

The two amplitudes are equal when ωε = σ, so f = σ/(2πε). With σ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ S/m and ε = 3.099 × 10⁻¹¹ F/m, f = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴/(2π × 3.099 × 10⁻¹¹) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴/(1.9472 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.027 × 10⁶ Hz. Below this frequency the dielectric behaves mainly as a resistor and above it mainly as a capacitor. For a sensor, the sensitivity to moisture, which raises σ, is greatest in the region around this crossover frequency.

Answer: 1.03 MHz

(d)

Apply Ampere's law around a circle of radius ρ in the gap, using only the displacement current density, which is uniform over the circle: H (2πρ) = Jd πρ², so H = Jd ρ/2. With Jd = 24.34 A/m² and ρ = 0.03 m, H = 24.34 × 0.03/2 = 0.3651 A/m. The field circles the axis. The conduction current would add a component in phase with the voltage, with magnitude σE0ρ/2 = 0.075 A/m, but the question asks for the displacement part only.

Answer: 0.365 A/m

A7 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A7-011] Plane waves in lossless media

A uniform plane wave travels in the +z direction through an unbounded, lossless, non-magnetic dielectric with relative permittivity 4 and relative permeability 1. The wave frequency is 300 MHz. The electric field phasor at z = 0 is E = 50 ax V/m (amplitude, with zero phase), so the real field is E(z,t) = 50 cos(ωt - βz) ax V/m. Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and take the free-space intrinsic impedance as 120π Ω. Treat the medium as extending far beyond the region of interest so that no reflections occur. A sensor with a flat sensing area of 0.5 m² is placed with its normal along the z axis, perpendicular to the direction of travel of the wave.

  1. (a) Find the wavelength in the medium, in metres. [5]
  2. (b) Find the intrinsic impedance of the medium, in ohms. [5]
  3. (c) Find the amplitude of the magnetic field intensity H, in A/m. [5]
  4. (d) Find the average electromagnetic power, in watts, that crosses the 0.5 m² sensor area. [5]
(a)

Phase velocity in a lossless non-magnetic medium is v = c/√(μr εr) = 3.00 × 10⁸/√(1 × 4) = 1.50 × 10⁸ m/s. The wavelength is the phase velocity divided by frequency: λ = v/f = 1.50 × 10⁸/(300 × 10⁶) = 0.500 m. As a check, the free-space wavelength at 300 MHz is 1.00 m, and the wave is shortened by the refractive index n = √εr = 2, giving 0.500 m. The phase constant is β = 2π/λ = 12.57 rad/m, which is the β that appears in the given field expression. Assumptions: lossless dielectric, so α = 0 and β is purely real, and the permeability equals μ0 so that the only effect of the medium is through εr. The answer is therefore 0.500 m.

Answer: 0.500 m

(b)

For a lossless medium the intrinsic impedance is η = √(μ/ε) = η0 √(μr/εr). With η0 = 120π = 377 Ω, μr = 1 and εr = 4, η = 377/√4 = 377/2 = 188.5 Ω. The number is real, so E and H are in time phase with each other, which is the signature of a lossless medium.
