Note that the impedance falls as the permittivity increases, because the same electric field amplitude then corresponds to a larger magnetic field amplitude. Assumption: the dielectric is non-magnetic and has no conductivity, so the intrinsic impedance has no imaginary part and is independent of frequency. The answer is η ≈ 188.5 Ω.

Answer: 188.5 Ω

(c)

For a uniform plane wave the ratio of the electric to the magnetic field amplitudes is the intrinsic impedance, so |H| = |E|/η. Substituting, |H| = 50/188.5 = 0.2653 A/m. The direction follows from the right-hand rule: E points along +x and the wave travels along +z, so H must lie along +y, since ax × ay = az gives E × H along +z. Hence H(z,t) = 0.2653 cos(ωt - βz) ay A/m. Assumptions: the field is a transverse electromagnetic wave with no field component along z, and the medium is lossless so that H has the same phase as E. The magnitude is 0.2653 A/m.

Answer: 0.2653 A/m

(d)

The time-average Poynting vector magnitude for a lossless plane wave is Savg = |E|²/(2η) = 50²/(2 × 188.5) = 2500/377 = 6.631 W/m². The power through an area A whose normal is parallel to the direction of propagation is simply the power density times the area, so P = Savg × A = 6.631 × 0.5 = 3.316 W. The same result follows from Savg = ½ |E||H| = 0.5 × 50 × 0.2653 = 6.631 W/m², which confirms parts b and c are consistent. Assumptions: the plane wave is uniform across the sensor, there is no reflection from the sensor, and the sensor face is exactly normal to z. The power crossing the sensor is 3.316 W.

Answer: 3.316 W

Problem 2 [A7-012] Plane waves in lossy media and skin depth

A shielded enclosure for a 2 MHz switching converter is made from a flat aluminum sheet 0.10 mm thick. The aluminum has conductivity σ = 3.5 × 10⁷ S/m and permeability equal to that of free space, μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. At 2 MHz the metal is an excellent conductor, so displacement current may be neglected and the skin depth formula for a good conductor applies. The converter produces a stray magnetic field whose tangential amplitude at the inner face of the sheet, assumed to be a thick conducting half-space for surface-loss purposes, is H = 2.0 A/m. Treat the field amplitude as decaying as e-x/δ with penetration distance x into the metal.

  1. (a) Calculate the skin depth δ in micrometres. [5]
  2. (b) Find the attenuation, in decibels, suffered by the field in passing through the 0.10 mm thickness of the sheet (ignore reflection at the surfaces). [5]
  3. (c) Find the surface resistance Rs of the aluminum at 2 MHz, in ohms per square. [5]
  4. (d) Find the average power dissipated per square metre of the surface when the tangential magnetic field amplitude there is H = 2.0 A/m. [5]
(a)

For a good conductor the attenuation constant equals the phase constant, α = β = √(π f μ σ), and the skin depth is the distance over which the field falls to 1/e, δ = 1/α = 1/√(π f μ0 σ). Substituting f = 2 × 10⁶ Hz, μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ and σ = 3.5 × 10⁷: π f μ0 σ = π × 2 × 10⁶ × 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ × 3.5 × 10⁷ = 2.764 × 10⁸, whose square root is 1.662 × 10⁴ m⁻¹. Therefore δ = 1/1.662 × 10⁴ = 6.015 × 10⁻⁵ m = 60.15 μm. Assumption: σ ≫ ωε, which holds for aluminum well into the gigahertz range, so the good-conductor approximation is valid at 2 MHz. The skin depth is about 60 μm.

Answer: 60.15 μm

(b)

The field amplitude decays as e-t/δ with the thickness t = 0.10 mm = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m. The exponent is t/δ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴/6.015 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.662 nepers. The absorption loss in decibels is A = 20 log10(et/δ) = 8.686 × (t/δ) = 8.686 × 1.662 = 14.44 dB. This is the absorption loss only. Real shielding effectiveness also includes a reflection loss at both surfaces and multiple-reflection correction, which are neglected here as the problem instructs. Notice that a sheet only 1.66 skin depths thick already gives about 14 dB, and each additional skin depth adds 8.69 dB. The attenuation through the sheet is 14.44 dB.

Answer: 14.44 dB

(c)

The surface resistance of a thick good conductor is the resistance of a square sheet one skin depth thick, Rs = 1/(σ δ). Substituting, Rs = 1/(3.5 × 10⁷ × 6.015 × 10⁻⁵) = 1/(2105) = 4.750 × 10⁻⁴ Ω per square. An equivalent form is Rs = √(π f μ0/σ) = √(π × 2 × 10⁶ × 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶/3.5 × 10⁷) = 4.750 × 10⁻⁴, which agrees. The current is confined to a thin layer near the surface, so the effective resistance rises with frequency as √f. Assumption: the metal is thicker than a few skin depths for this loss calculation, as stated.

Answer: 4.750 × 10⁻⁴ Ω/square

(d)

The power absorbed per unit area by a good conductor is the average Poynting flux entering the surface, Pd = ½ Rs |H|², where H is the tangential magnetic field amplitude (peak value). Substituting Rs = 4.750 × 10⁻⁴ Ω and H = 2.0 A/m: Pd = 0.5 × 4.750 × 10⁻⁴ × 2.0² = 0.5 × 4.750 × 10⁻⁴ × 4 = 9.50 × 10⁻⁴ W/m². This is the equivalent of a surface current density K = H = 2.0 A/m flowing through Rs. Assumptions: the field amplitude is a peak value, the conductor is a half-space for loss purposes, and the enclosure remains linear. The dissipation is about 0.95 mW per square metre, which is negligible heating but a useful check of the shield loss.

Answer: 9.50 × 10⁻⁴ W/m²

Problem 3 [A7-013] Reflection and transmission at media boundaries

A uniform plane wave in air travels in the +z direction and strikes, at normal incidence, the flat boundary z = 0 of a thick, lossless, non-magnetic dielectric half-space with relative permittivity 9. The region z > 0 is the dielectric. The incident electric field amplitude is 30 V/m and the frequency is 1 GHz. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and the free-space intrinsic impedance as η0 = 120π Ω. Use the convention that reflection coefficient Γ is the ratio of the reflected to the incident electric field phasor at the boundary and transmission coefficient τ is the ratio of the transmitted to the incident electric field phasor at the boundary. Assume the dielectric is so thick that no wave returns from its far side.

  1. (a) Find the intrinsic impedance of the dielectric, in ohms. [4]
  2. (b) Find the reflection coefficient Γ at the boundary. [5]
  3. (c) Find the transmission coefficient τ, and hence the amplitude of the transmitted electric field in V/m. [5]
  4. (d) Find the time-average power density transmitted into the dielectric, in W/m². [6]
(a)

The intrinsic impedance of a lossless non-magnetic medium is η2 = η0/√εr. With η0 = 120π = 376.99 Ω and εr = 9, √9 = 3, so η2 = 376.99/3 = 125.66 Ω. This is the impedance the dielectric presents to the wave, in the same way that a transmission line of impedance 125.7 Ω would present a load. The wave in air has η1 = η0, so the step from 377 Ω to 125.7 Ω at the boundary is what produces reflection. Assumptions: both media are lossless and non-magnetic, so their intrinsic impedances are real and depend only on the permittivity. The impedance of the dielectric is η2 ≈ 125.7 Ω.

Answer: 125.7 Ω

(b)

At normal incidence the electric field reflection coefficient is Γ = (η2 - η1)/(η2 + η1). Substituting η1 = 376.99 Ω and η2 = 125.66 Ω gives Γ = (125.66 - 376.99)/(125.66 + 376.99) = (-251.33)/(502.65) = -0.500. The sign is negative because the second medium has the lower impedance, so the reflected electric field is reversed in phase relative to the incident field, just as a short-circuit-like load on a transmission line produces an inverted voltage wave. The same result follows from the refractive indices: Γ = (n1 - n2)/(n1 + n2) = (1 - 3)/(1 + 3) = -0.5. The reflection coefficient is -0.500, and the reflected field amplitude is 15 V/m.

Answer: -0.500

(c)

The boundary condition of continuous tangential E gives 1 + Γ = τ. With Γ = -0.500, τ = 0.500. Equivalently, τ = 2η2/(η2 + η1) = 2 × 125.66/502.65 = 0.500, which confirms the relation. The transmitted electric field amplitude is Et = τ Ei = 0.500 × 30 = 15.0 V/m. Notice that the transmitted field is smaller than the incident field yet the transmitted power is not simply reduced by the square of this ratio, because the wave in the dielectric travels in a lower impedance medium and carries more magnetic field. The check on power is performed in part d. Assumption: tangential electric and magnetic fields are continuous across the boundary, with no surface charge or current on the interface.

Answer: τ = 0.500, Et = 15.0 V/m

(d)

The incident power density is Si = Ei²/(2 η1) = 30²/(2 × 376.99) = 900/753.98 = 1.1937 W/m². The fraction of power reflected is |Γ|² = 0.25, so the fraction transmitted is 1 - |Γ|² = 0.75 and St = 0.75 × 1.1937 = 0.8952 W/m². Direct check using the transmitted field: St = Et²/(2 η2) = 15²/(2 × 125.66) = 225/251.33 = 0.8952 W/m², in agreement. The reflected power density is 0.25 × 1.1937 = 0.2984 W/m², and 0.2984 + 0.8952 = 1.1937 W/m², so energy is conserved at the boundary. Assumption: lossless media on both sides, so no power is absorbed at the interface. The transmitted power density is 0.895 W/m².

Answer: 0.8952 W/m²

Problem 4 [A7-014] Polarization of waves

A uniform plane wave of frequency 2.4 GHz propagates in the +z direction in free space. At the plane z = 0 its electric field is E(t) = 6 cos(ωt) ax + 3 cos(ωt + 90°) ay V/m, where ax and ay are unit vectors along x and y and the amplitudes are peak values. Use the IEEE convention for handedness: the sense of rotation is judged by an observer looking along the direction of propagation, away from the source, with right-handed meaning clockwise as seen by that observer. Take the free-space intrinsic impedance as 377 Ω. A receiving antenna system is to be designed for this wave, so you must characterise its polarization, break it into circular components and find the power density it carries.

  1. (a) Find the axial ratio of the polarization ellipse (major axis over minor axis, a number greater than or equal to 1). [5]
  2. (b) State whether the wave is right-hand or left-hand elliptically polarized, justifying the sense of rotation. [3]
  3. (c) The wave is resolved into a left-hand circular component and a right-hand circular component. Find the amplitude of the larger of the two, in V/m. [6]
  4. (d) Find the time-average power density carried by the wave, in W/m². [6]
(a)

The two components are in quadrature (a phase difference of 90°) and have unequal amplitudes Ex0 = 6 V/m and Ey0 = 3 V/m. With a 90° phase difference the ellipse axes lie along x and y, so the semi-axes are simply the component amplitudes. The axial ratio is AR = major/minor = 6/3 = 2.00, which is 6.02 dB. If the amplitudes were equal the ratio would be 1 and the wave would be circularly polarized; with zero phase difference the ratio would become infinite and the wave linearly polarized. The wave is therefore elliptically polarized with its major axis along x. Assumption: the amplitude and phase values are those at z = 0 and do not change with time, a fully polarized monochromatic wave.

Answer: 2.00

(b)

At z = 0, Ex = 6 cos(ωt) and Ey = 3 cos(ωt + 90°) = -3 sin(ωt). At ωt = 0 the field is (6, 0), pointing along +x. At ωt = 90° it is (0, -3), pointing along -y. So the tip of the vector turns from +x toward -y. Viewed from a point on the z axis looking back at the source with z pointing toward the viewer, rotation from +x to -y is clockwise, but the IEEE convention asks for the view along the propagation direction, away from the source. Seen that way the same motion is counterclockwise. Counterclockwise rotation along the direction of propagation is left-handed. Equivalent check: if the fingers of the left hand curl from +x toward -y, the thumb points along +z. The wave is left-hand elliptically polarized.

Answer: Left-hand elliptical

(c)

Write the phasor as E = 6 ax + j3 ay. Any elliptical wave is a sum of two counter-rotating circular waves whose amplitudes are E_larger = (Ex0 + Ey0)/2 and E_smaller = (Ex0 - Ey0)/2 when the ellipse axes lie along x and y, so that their sum recovers the x amplitude and the difference recovers the y amplitude. Substituting, the larger amplitude is (6 + 3)/2 = 4.5 V/m, and the smaller is (6 - 3)/2 = 1.5 V/m. Check: the x amplitude is 4.5 + 1.5 = 6 and the y amplitude is 4.5 - 1.5 = 3, matching the given field. Because the elliptical wave is left-handed, the larger circular component is the left-hand one at 4.5 V/m, and the right-hand component is 1.5 V/m. Their ratio gives the axial ratio again: (4.5 + 1.5)/(4.5 - 1.5) = 2.

Answer: 4.5 V/m

(d)

The time-average Poynting vector of a plane wave is Savg = (|Ex0|² + |Ey0|²)/(2 η0), since the two orthogonal components carry power independently when summed over a cycle. Substituting, Savg = (6² + 3²)/(2 × 377) = (36 + 9)/754 = 45/754 = 0.05968 W/m². As a check by circular components, power is proportional to the sum of the squares of the circular amplitudes: 4.5² + 1.5² = 20.25 + 2.25 = 22.5, and each circular wave of amplitude E carries power density E²/η0 (its x and y parts each contribute E²/(2η0)), so the total is 22.5/377 = 0.05968 W/m². The result is the same by either route. Assumption: free-space propagation, the amplitudes quoted are peak values. The average power density is about 59.7 mW/m².

Answer: 0.05968 W/m²

Problem 5 [A7-015] Transmission line equations and characteristic impedance

A short lossless coaxial feeder carries a 100 MHz signal. Measurements on the cable give a distributed inductance of 250 nH/m and a distributed capacitance of 100 pF/m, and its conductor and dielectric losses may be ignored. A length of 0.30 m of this cable is connected between a source and a purely resistive load of 100 Ω. The source end is called the input and the load end is called the load. Use the sinusoidal steady-state transmission-line equations with the time dependence ejωt. The designer wants the cable parameters, the wavelength on the line, and the impedance that the source sees looking into the 0.30 m section.

  1. (a) Find the characteristic impedance Z0 of the line, in ohms. [4]
  2. (b) Find the phase velocity on the line, in units of 10⁸ m/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the wavelength on the line at 100 MHz, in metres, and the electrical length of the 0.30 m section in degrees. [6]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the input impedance seen by the source, in ohms. [6]
(a)

For a lossless line, R' = G' = 0, and the characteristic impedance is Z0 = √(L'/C'). Substituting L' = 250 × 10⁻⁹ H/m and C' = 100 × 10⁻¹² F/m, the ratio is L'/C' = 250 × 10⁻⁹/100 × 10⁻¹² = 2500 Ω², so Z0 = √2500 = 50.0 Ω. Because the line is lossless, Z0 is purely real and independent of frequency, which is why a 50 Ω system can be broadband. Assumption: R' and G' are negligible at 100 MHz, so the line is lossless and Z0 has no reactive component. The characteristic impedance is 50.0 Ω, the standard value for coaxial test systems.

Answer: 50.0 Ω

(b)

For a lossless line the propagation constant is γ = jβ with β = ω√(L'C'), and the phase velocity is vp = ω/β = 1/√(L'C'). Substituting, L'C' = 250 × 10⁻⁹ × 100 × 10⁻¹² = 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁷ s²/m², so √(L'C') = 5.0 × 10⁻⁹ s/m and vp = 1/(5.0 × 10⁻⁹) = 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s. This is two-thirds of the free-space speed of light, which is a typical value for polyethylene-filled coax (velocity factor 0.667, relative permittivity about 2.25). Assumption: the line parameters are independent of frequency over the band of interest, so there is no dispersion. The phase velocity is 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

Answer: 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s

(c)

The wavelength is λ = vp/f = 2.00 × 10⁸/100 × 10⁶ = 2.00 m. The phase constant is β = 2π/λ = π rad/m = 3.1416 rad/m. The electrical length of the 0.30 m section is θ = β l = 3.1416 × 0.30 = 0.9425 rad, which is 0.9425 × 180/π = 54.0°. This is 0.15 of a wavelength, so the line is electrically short enough that the load impedance is transformed but not by a full half-wave. Assumption: only the forward and backward waves of a single frequency exist and the phase constant is exactly β = ω/vp. The wavelength is 2.00 m and the electrical length is 54.0°.

Answer: λ = 2.00 m; 54.0 degrees

(d)

The input impedance of a lossless line of length l terminated in ZL is Zin = Z0 (ZL + j Z0 tan βl)/(Z0 + j ZL tan βl). With βl = 54.0°, tan βl = 1.3764. The numerator is 50 × (100 + j 50 × 1.3764) = 50 × (100 + j68.82) = 5000 + j3441. The denominator is 50 + j 100 × 1.3764 = 50 + j137.64. Dividing, Zin = (5000 + j3441)/(50 + j137.64) = 33.74 - j24.07 Ω. The magnitude is √(33.74² + 24.07²) = √(1138.5 + 579.3) = 41.45 Ω, at an angle of -35.5°, so the source sees a capacitive impedance. Assumption: the line is lossless and the load is exactly 100 Ω resistive at this frequency. The magnitude of the input impedance is 41.45 Ω.

Answer: 41.45 Ω

A7 Practice Paper 4

Problem 1 [A7-016] Standing waves, VSWR and reflection coefficient

A lossless 75 Ω transmission line feeds a load whose impedance at the operating frequency is ZL = 45 - j30 Ω. The line is air-filled so the wavelength on the line equals the free-space wavelength λ. A technician is going to probe the line with a slotted section and wants to predict the standing-wave pattern before measuring it. Define the voltage reflection coefficient at the load as Γ = (ZL - Z0)/(ZL + Z0), and measure positions on the line from the load towards the generator. Give angles of Γ in degrees measured from the positive real axis, and distances in fractions of the wavelength.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the load reflection coefficient |Γ|. [5]
  2. (b) Find the voltage standing wave ratio VSWR. [5]
  3. (c) Find the distance from the load to the first voltage maximum, as a fraction of the wavelength. [6]
  4. (d) Find the return loss at the load, in decibels. [4]
(a)

Substitute ZL = 45 - j30 and Z0 = 75 into Γ = (ZL - Z0)/(ZL + Z0). The numerator is 45 - j30 - 75 = -30 - j30, with magnitude √(900 + 900) = 42.43. The denominator is 45 - j30 + 75 = 120 - j30, with magnitude √(14400 + 900) = 123.69. Therefore |Γ| = 42.43/123.69 = 0.3430. The angle of Γ is arg(-30 - j30) - arg(120 - j30) = -135° - (-14.04°) = -120.96°. The magnitude is well below 1, so a good part of the incident wave is absorbed by the load. Assumption: the line is lossless so |Γ| is the same at every point along the line. The magnitude of the reflection coefficient is 0.343.

Answer: 0.3430

(b)

The VSWR relates directly to the magnitude of the reflection coefficient through S = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 - |Γ|). Substituting |Γ| = 0.3430 gives S = (1 + 0.3430)/(1 - 0.3430) = 1.3430/0.6570 = 2.044. This is the ratio of maximum to minimum voltage magnitude on the line, Vmax/Vmin. A match would give S = 1 and a total reflection would give S = ∞. A value near 2 is on the edge of what many transmitters tolerate, since a VSWR of 2 corresponds to 11 percent of the incident power being reflected (|Γ|² = 0.118). Assumption: the line is lossless and the source is well matched to the line, so the standing-wave pattern depends only on the load. The VSWR is 2.04.

Answer: 2.044

(c)

A voltage maximum occurs where the reflected wave is in phase with the incident wave, that is where the phase of Γ(d) = |Γ| ej(θΓ - 2βd) is zero. Setting θΓ - 2βd = 0 gives d = θΓ/(2β), but θΓ must be taken as a positive angle, so use θΓ = -120.96° + 360° = 239.04°. With β = 2π/λ, d/λ = θΓ/(4π) = (239.04° in radians = 4.172 rad)/(4π) = 0.332. Hence the first maximum is 0.332 wavelengths from the load. A check: the first maximum from a load with negative-angle Γ lies between a quarter wavelength and a half wavelength from the load, which 0.332 does. The first voltage minimum lies a quarter wavelength closer to the load than the first maximum, at 0.332 - 0.250 = 0.082 wavelengths from the load, where the phase of Γ(d) is -180°. The next minimum is at 0.582 wavelengths.

Answer: 0.332 wavelengths

(d)

Return loss is the ratio of incident to reflected power expressed as a positive number of decibels, RL = -20 log10 |Γ|. Substituting |Γ| = 0.3430, log10(0.3430) = -0.4647, so RL = -20 × (-0.4647) = 9.29 dB. This agrees with the power view: the reflected power fraction is |Γ|² = 0.1176, or about 11.8 percent of the incident power, and 10 log10(1/0.1176) = 9.29 dB. A higher return loss means a better match, and many systems specify better than 14 dB, which corresponds to a VSWR below 1.5. Assumption: the load impedance is as given, the line is lossless, and the return loss is measured at the load plane. The return loss is 9.29 dB.

Answer: 9.29 dB

Problem 2 [A7-017] Smith chart and impedance matching

A 50 Ω lossless coaxial feed line at 900 MHz must be matched to a purely resistive 200 Ω antenna load using a single quarter-wavelength section of different cable inserted between the line and the load. The matching section is a solid-dielectric cable with velocity factor 0.66, meaning that waves on it travel at 0.66c with c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Its characteristic impedance is chosen to produce a perfect match at 900 MHz. The designer needs to know the required section impedance, its physical length, and how wide the matched band is, using the reflection coefficient of the line at the input of the section. Assume the section is lossless and has no dispersion, so its electrical length is proportional to frequency.

  1. (a) Find the characteristic impedance required for the matching section, in ohms. [4]
  2. (b) Find the physical length of the quarter-wave section, in millimetres. [4]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the reflection coefficient seen on the 50 Ω feed line at 800 MHz. [6]
  4. (d) Find the fractional bandwidth (as a percentage of 900 MHz) over which |Γ| does not exceed 0.10. [6]
(a)

A quarter-wave section of impedance Zt transforms a load RL to Zin = Zt²/RL. For a perfect match to the 50 Ω feed line the input impedance must equal Z0 = 50 Ω, so Zt² = Z0 RL = 50 × 200 = 10 000 Ω², giving Zt = 100 Ω. This is the geometric mean of the line and load impedances. At the design frequency the section is exactly 90° long, so tan θ is infinite and the input impedance expression Zin = Zt (RL + jZt tan θ)/(Zt + jRL tan θ) reduces to Zt²/RL. Assumption: the load is purely resistive and equal to 200 Ω, the section is lossless, and a single-section transformer is sufficient for the narrow-band application. The required section impedance is 100 Ω.

Answer: 100 Ω

(b)

The wavelength on the section at 900 MHz is λ = vp/f = 0.66 × 3.00 × 10⁸/900 × 10⁶ = 1.98 × 10⁸/9 × 10⁸ = 0.2200 m. A quarter wavelength is then λ/4 = 0.2200/4 = 0.0550 m = 55.0 mm. The velocity factor shortens the section relative to an air-filled line, which would need 83.3 mm. The length must be accurate because a length error of Δ changes the electrical length by 360° × Δ/λ, so a 1 mm error corresponds to about 1.6°. Assumption: the velocity factor 0.66 is accurate at 900 MHz and the physical length is measured over the dielectric section only, ignoring the connector fringing. The section length is 55.0 mm.

Answer: 55.0 mm

(c)

At 800 MHz the section's electrical length is θ = 90° × (800/900) = 80°, so tan θ = 5.671. The input impedance of the section terminated in RL = 200 Ω is Zin = Zt (RL + j Zt tan θ)/(Zt + j RL tan θ) = 100 × (200 + j567.1)/(100 + j1134.2). Carrying out the complex division gives Zin = 51.16 - j13.12 Ω. The reflection coefficient on the feed line is Γ = (Zin - 50)/(Zin + 50) = (1.16 - j13.12)/(101.16 - j13.12), with magnitude 13.17/102.00 = 0.1291. So |Γ| = 0.1291 at 800 MHz, a VSWR of 1.30, which is acceptable and shows the narrow-band nature of a single section.

Answer: 0.1291

(d)

For a single quarter-wave section the reflection magnitude is |Γ| = 1/√(1 + (4 Z0 RL/(RL - Z0)²) sec²θ), because the end-point mismatch is (RL - Z0)/(RL + Z0) = 0.6. Setting |Γ| = Γm = 0.10 gives sec²θm = (1/Γm² - 1)(RL - Z0)²/(4 Z0 RL) = 99 × 22 500/40 000 = 55.69, so cos θm = 0.1340 and θm = 82.30° = 1.4365 rad. The matched band lies between θm and 180° - θm, and θ is proportional to frequency (90° at 900 MHz). The fractional bandwidth is Δf/f0 = 2(90° - θm)/90° = 2 - 2θm/90° = 2 - 1.8289 = 0.1711, or 17.1 percent. That is about 154 MHz. The design is therefore usable across roughly 823 MHz to 977 MHz, assuming the section stays lossless and nondispersive.

Answer: 17.1 percent

Problem 3 [A7-018] Waveguides: modes and cutoff

An air-filled rectangular waveguide of the standard WR-90 size has inside dimensions a = 22.86 mm (wide wall) and b = 10.16 mm (narrow wall). It carries a 10 GHz signal in the dominant TE10 mode in a radar feed run. Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and the free-space intrinsic impedance 377 Ω. The walls are perfect conductors so wall loss may be ignored. The engineer needs to confirm that the 10 GHz signal is above cutoff for the dominant mode and compute the phase constant, guide wavelength, phase velocity and the TE wave impedance that a matched load must present at the end of the guide. Treat all fields as having the ej(ωt - βz) form.

  1. (a) Find the cutoff frequency of the TE10 mode, in GHz. [4]
  2. (b) Find the phase constant β of the TE10 mode at 10 GHz, in rad/m. [5]
  3. (c) Find the guide wavelength and the phase velocity, giving the guide wavelength in millimetres. [5]
  4. (d) Find the TE10 wave impedance ZTE, in ohms, that a matched load must present. [6]
(a)

For a rectangular guide the cutoff frequency of the TEmn mode is fc = (c/2) √((m/a)² + (n/b)²). For TE10, m = 1 and n = 0, so fc = c/(2a) = 3.00 × 10⁸/(2 × 22.86 × 10⁻³) = 3.00 × 10⁸/0.04572 = 6.562 × 10⁹ Hz = 6.562 GHz. The operating frequency of 10 GHz is above this value, so the TE10 mode propagates. The next mode, TE20 or TE01, has cutoff at c/a = 13.12 GHz or c/(2b) = 14.76 GHz, both above 10 GHz, so TE10 is the only mode that can propagate and the guide is single mode. Assumption: the guide is air-filled with εr = 1 and the walls are perfect conductors. The cutoff frequency is 6.562 GHz.

Answer: 6.562 GHz

(b)

The phase constant in a waveguide is β = √(k² - kc²), where k = ω/c is the free-space wavenumber and kc = π/a is the cutoff wavenumber of TE10. Here k = 2π × 10 × 10⁹/3.00 × 10⁸ = 209.44 rad/m and kc = π/22.86 × 10⁻³ = 137.43 rad/m. Then β = √(209.44² - 137.43²) = √(43 865 - 18 887) = √24 978 = 158.05 rad/m. This is smaller than k, because the wave zigzags between the side walls and its axial wavenumber is reduced. Assumption: the guide is operated above cutoff so β is real, and the dispersion relation is the lossless one. The phase constant is 158.0 rad/m.

Answer: 158.0 rad/m

(c)

The guide wavelength is the distance along the guide over which the phase advances by 2π, λg = 2π/β = 2π/158.05 = 0.03976 m = 39.76 mm. For comparison, the free-space wavelength at 10 GHz is 30.0 mm, so the guide wavelength is longer, by the factor 1/√(1 - (fc/f)²) = 1/√(1 - 0.4306) = 1.325. The phase velocity is vp = ω/β = 2π × 10 × 10⁹/158.05 = 3.976 × 10⁸ m/s, which exceeds c. This does not violate relativity because phase velocity carries no energy; the group velocity vg = c²/vp = 2.264 × 10⁸ m/s is below c. Assumption: dispersion is as in an ideal hollow guide. The guide wavelength is 39.76 mm.

Answer: 39.76 mm

(d)

The wave impedance of a TE mode is ZTE = η0/√(1 - (fc/f)²) = ωμ0/β, which is real above cutoff. With fc/f = 6.562/10 = 0.6562, (fc/f)² = 0.4306 and √(1 - 0.4306) = 0.7546. So ZTE = 377/0.7546 = 499.6 Ω. The check is ZTE = ωμ0/β = 2π × 10 × 10⁹ × 4π × 10⁻⁷/158.05 = 78 957/158.05 = 499.6 Ω, which agrees. The impedance is larger than the free-space value of 377 Ω and rises without limit as the frequency approaches cutoff, whereas it falls toward 377 Ω at high frequency. A load that presents this impedance to the TE10 wave reflects nothing. Assumption: a lossless guide with a matched termination. The wave impedance is 499.6 Ω.

Answer: 499.6 Ω

Problem 4 [A7-019] Radiation from a Hertzian dipole and antenna basics

A short current element, ideally a Hertzian dipole, of length 0.050 m carries a uniform sinusoidal current of peak amplitude 2.0 A at a frequency of 30 MHz. It is in free space and oriented along the z axis, so the broadside direction is the plane θ = 90°. Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and the free-space intrinsic impedance η0 = 120π Ω. The element is much shorter than a wavelength. Treat the far-field expressions for the Hertzian dipole as valid, with the radiation resistance defined by the time-average radiated power Prad = ½ I0² Rrad, where I0 is the peak current. Take a lossless dipole with no ohmic or dielectric dissipation.

  1. (a) Find the radiation resistance Rrad of the dipole, in ohms. [5]
  2. (b) Find the total average power radiated, in watts. [5]
  3. (c) Find the peak electric field strength at r = 1.0 km on the broadside direction (θ = 90°), in millivolts per metre. [5]
  4. (d) Using the directivity of 1.5 of the Hertzian dipole, find the average power density at 1.0 km on the broadside direction, in nW/m². [5]
(a)

The wavelength is λ = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸/30 × 10⁶ = 10.0 m, so the element length is dl/λ = 0.050/10.0 = 0.005, well within the short-dipole range. The radiation resistance of a Hertzian dipole is Rrad = 80π² (dl/λ)². Substituting, Rrad = 80 × 9.8696 × (0.005)² = 789.57 × 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.01974 Ω. This tiny resistance shows why a very short antenna is inefficient: any ohmic resistance of even a few milliohms in the wire would dominate Rrad. Assumption: the current is uniform along the length, so the formula (derived for a uniform current) applies, and the dipole is far shorter than λ. The radiation resistance is 0.01974 Ω.

Answer: 0.01974 Ω

(b)

The radiated power is Prad = ½ I0² Rrad with I0 = 2.0 A peak. Substituting, Prad = 0.5 × 2.0² × 0.01974 = 0.5 × 4 × 0.01974 = 0.03948 W, or about 39.5 mW. The same value follows from the far-field integration, Prad = 40π² (dl/λ)² I0² = 394.78 × 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ × 4 = 0.03948 W, confirming the radiation resistance expression. Given the large current of 2.0 A needed to radiate a mere 39.5 mW, a user would note the poor efficiency of the short element. Assumption: the antenna is lossless so all the power delivered to Rrad is radiated, and the source can supply the required current into the reactive input impedance of the short element. The radiated power is 39.5 mW.

Answer: 0.03948 W

(c)

In the far field the Hertzian dipole electric field magnitude is |Eθ| = (η0 k I0 dl sin θ)/(4π r), where k = 2π/λ. Using η0 k/(4π) = 120π × (2π/λ)/(4π) = 60π/λ, the expression becomes |Eθ| = 60π I0 dl sin θ/(λ r). Substituting I0 = 2.0 A, dl = 0.050 m, sin 90° = 1, λ = 10.0 m and r = 1000 m: |Eθ| = 60π × 2.0 × 0.050/(10.0 × 1000) = 18.85/10 000 = 1.885 × 10⁻³ V/m = 1.885 mV/m. The field falls as 1/r, and the pattern has its maximum at θ = 90° and a null along the axis. Assumption: the point of observation is in the far field, r ≫ λ, which holds since λ = 10 m and r = 1 km.

Answer: 1.885 mV/m

(d)

The average power density from an isotropic radiator would be Prad/(4π r²); the dipole's directivity of 1.5 at broadside multiplies that. So S = D Prad/(4π r²) = 1.5 × 0.03948/(4π × (1000)²) = 0.05922/(1.2566 × 10⁷) = 4.712 × 10⁻⁹ W/m² = 4.712 nW/m². Check against the field: S = |E|²/(2η0) = (1.885 × 10⁻³)²/(2 × 376.99) = 3.553 × 10⁻⁶/753.98 = 4.712 × 10⁻⁹ W/m², which agrees with the directivity route and confirms the use of D = 1.5 and the peak field in part c. Assumption: lossless radiator, far field, free-space propagation without ground reflection. The power density at 1 km is 4.71 nW/m².

Answer: 4.712 nW/m²

Problem 5 [A7-020] Link budget or shielding design using field concepts

A farm sensor network uses a point-to-point 2.4 GHz radio link in free space, with a clear line of sight over a distance of 5.0 km between a base station and a remote receiver. The transmitter delivers 20 W (43.0 dBm) to the transmit antenna, which has a gain of 12 dBi. The receive antenna has a gain of 8 dBi, and the receiver sensitivity is -90 dBm for the required bit-error rate. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Use the Friis free-space transmission formula, ignoring atmospheric absorption, polarization mismatch, cable and connector losses, and ground reflection. Gains are referenced to an isotropic radiator, and the powers are referenced to 1 mW.

  1. (a) Find the free-space wavelength at 2.4 GHz, in metres. [3]
  2. (b) Find the free-space path loss over 5.0 km, in dB. [6]
  3. (c) Find the received power at the receiver input, in dBm. [6]
  4. (d) Find the fade margin of the link (received power minus receiver sensitivity), in dB. [5]
(a)

The wavelength follows from λ = c/f. Substituting c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and f = 2.4 × 10⁹ Hz gives λ = 3.00 × 10⁸/2.4 × 10⁹ = 0.1250 m, or 12.5 cm. This value is needed for the free-space path loss calculation, since the loss grows with the square of frequency for fixed antenna gains. It also shows that the antennas, being of the order of a wavelength in size, need only be a few tens of centimetres across to give the stated gains. Assumption: propagation is in vacuum or air with refractive index equal to one, so the wavelength is not shortened by the medium. The wavelength is 0.1250 m.

Answer: 0.1250 m

(b)

The free-space path loss between isotropic antennas is Lfs = (4π d/λ)². In decibels, Lfs = 20 log10(4π d/λ). Substituting d = 5000 m and λ = 0.1250 m: 4π d/λ = 4π × 5000/0.125 = 502 655, and 20 log10(502 655) = 20 × 5.7013 = 114.03 dB. The loss grows by 6 dB each time the distance doubles, so at 10 km it would be 120.05 dB. The loss is a spreading effect, not an absorption effect: the energy is not dissipated, it is just spread over a sphere of area 4π d², which is why antenna gains help. Assumption: far field, so d ≫ λ, and clear free-space conditions with the first Fresnel zone free of obstruction. The path loss is 114.0 dB.

Answer: 114.0 dB

(c)

The Friis equation in decibel form is Pr(dBm) = Pt(dBm) + Gt(dBi) + Gr(dBi) - Lfs(dB). Substituting Pt = 10 log10(20 000 mW) = 43.01 dBm, Gt = 12 dBi, Gr = 8 dBi and Lfs = 114.03 dB, Pr = 43.01 + 12 + 8 - 114.03 = -51.02 dBm. This is the power at the receiver terminals, equal to about 7.9 nW. The equivalent isotropic radiated power of the transmitter is 43.01 + 12 = 55.01 dBm, or about 316 W. Assumptions: perfect impedance matching at both antennas, no cable losses, and boresight alignment so that the quoted gains apply. The received power is -51.0 dBm.

Answer: -51.0 dBm

(d)

The fade margin is the amount by which the received signal can drop before the link fails: M = Pr - Smin, where Smin = -90 dBm is the receiver sensitivity. Substituting Pr = -51.02 dBm, M = -51.02 - (-90) = 38.98 dB. A margin of about 39 dB is generous; practical rural links are often designed for 20 to 30 dB to allow for rain, multipath fading, vegetation growth and antenna misalignment. The margin also tells the designer that the distance could be increased by a factor 1038.98/20 = 8.9, giving roughly 44 km, before the margin was used up, if free space still applied. Assumption: the fade statistics are not considered here. The fade margin is 38.98 dB.

Answer: 38.98 dB

A7 Practice Paper 5

Problem 1 [A7-021] Vector calculus and coordinate systems for fields

A cylindrical electron-beam focusing tube has a drift region of radius a = 2.0 mm and length L = 50 mm. In cylindrical coordinates (ρ, φ, z) the designer wants the electric field inside the region, for 0 ≤ ρ ≤ a, to have the form E = E0 (ρ/a)² a_ρ, directed radially outward and independent of φ and z. Fringing at the two ends is neglected, so the field is purely radial. The space inside is free space with ε0 = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m, and the field is produced by a space charge of volume density ρv(ρ) that fills the region. The tube specification fixes the total charge in the drift region at Q = 1.50 nC. Take the potential on the outer surface ρ = a as the reference for the potential difference asked below.

  1. (a) Using Gauss's law in integral form on a coaxial cylinder of radius a and length L, determine the amplitude E0 that gives the specified total charge Q = 1.50 nC. [6]
  2. (b) Using the divergence in cylindrical coordinates, find the volume charge density ρv at ρ = 1.0 mm for the design value of E0. [5]
  3. (c) Find the potential difference between the axis (ρ = 0) and the surface ρ = a, and state which one is at the higher potential. [5]
  4. (d) State, with a reason based on the curl, whether this static field is conservative, and explain why that allows a potential to be defined. [4]
(a)

Gauss's law: the flux of D = ε0E through the closed surface equals the enclosed charge. Take a coaxial cylinder of radius a and length L. The field is purely radial, so the end caps carry no flux and the curved surface has area 2πaL. At ρ = a the field is E0 (a/a)² = E0, so Q = ε0 E0 (2πaL). Solve: E0 = Q/(2π ε0 a L). Substitute: 2π × 8.854×10⁻¹² × 2.0×10⁻³ × 0.050 = 5.563×10⁻¹⁵ F. Then E0 = 1.50×10⁻⁹ / 5.563×10⁻¹⁵ = 2.696×10⁵ V/m. This is about 270 kV/m, a modest field for a vacuum tube, so the chosen charge is realistic.

Answer: E0 = 2.70×10⁵ V/m

(b)

The point form of Gauss's law is ∇·D = ρv. For a field with only a radial component, ∇·E = (1/ρ) d(ρ Eρ)/dρ. Here ρ Eρ = E0 ρ³/a², so the derivative is 3E0 ρ²/a² and ∇·E = 3E0 ρ/a². Hence ρv = 3 ε0 E0 ρ/a². At ρ = 1.0 mm: ρv = 3 × 8.854×10⁻¹² × 2.696×10⁵ × 1.0×10⁻³ / (2.0×10⁻³)² = 7.161×10⁻⁹ / 4.0×10⁻⁶ = 1.79×10⁻³ C/m³. The density rises linearly with ρ, which is consistent with a beam whose charge is concentrated toward the outside of the drift region. Check: integrating this ρv over the volume returns Q, as part (a) requires.

Answer: ρv = 1.79×10⁻³ C/m³

(c)

The potential difference follows from V(0) − V(a) = ∫ from 0 to a of E·dρ along a radial path, because V(A) − V(B) = ∫ from A to B of E·dl. The integrand is E0 ρ²/a², so the integral is E0 (1/a²) (a³/3) = E0 a/3. Substitute: 2.696×10⁵ × 2.0×10⁻³ / 3 = 179.8 V. The sign is positive, meaning V(0) > V(a): the field points outward, and potential falls in the direction of E, so the axis is at the higher potential. A candidate who integrates from a to 0 will get the right magnitude but the wrong sign, so the direction reasoning matters here for full marks.

Answer: 179.8 V, axis higher

(d)

The curl of a purely radial field that depends only on ρ is zero. In cylindrical coordinates the curl has components built from ∂Ez/∂φ/ρ − ∂Eφ/∂z, ∂Eρ/∂z − ∂Ez/∂ρ, and (1/ρ)[∂(ρEφ)/∂ρ − ∂Eρ/∂φ]. With Eφ = Ez = 0 and Eρ a function of ρ alone, every term vanishes, so ∇×E = 0. By Stokes's theorem the line integral of E around any closed path is therefore zero, so the work done on a charge is independent of the path. That is exactly the condition for a conservative field, and it allows a single-valued scalar potential V with E = −∇V to be defined, which is what part (c) used.

Answer: ∇×E = 0, conservative

Problem 2 [A7-022] Electrostatics: Coulomb's law, Gauss's law and potential

A spherical corona-free test electrode is to be designed as a non-uniform space-charge cloud held in an insulating shell. A space charge fills a sphere of radius R = 0.25 m in free space (ε0 = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m) with volume density ρv = ρ0 (r/R) for r ≤ R, where r is the distance from the centre and ρ0 is a constant to be chosen. There is no charge outside r = R. The electrode must never exceed a field of Emax = 1.00 MV/m anywhere, which sets the design limit, and the charge distribution is spherically symmetric. Use Gauss's law in spherical coordinates and take the potential as zero at infinity. Because the density grows with r, the largest field occurs at the surface r = R.

  1. (a) Find the field E(r) inside the sphere in terms of ρ0, and choose the largest ρ0 for which the field at r = R equals Emax. [6]
  2. (b) Find the total charge Q contained in the sphere for this design. [4]
  3. (c) Find the potential at the centre of the sphere relative to infinity. [6]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the field at r = 0.50 m, twice the sphere radius. [4]
(a)

Apply Gauss's law to a concentric sphere of radius r < R. The enclosed charge is the integral of ρv over volume: Qenc = ∫ from 0 to r of ρ0 (r'/R) 4π r'² dr' = (π ρ0/R) r⁴. The flux is ε0 E 4π r², so E(r) = ρ0 r²/(4 ε0 R). This grows as r², so the maximum is at r = R, giving Emax = ρ0 R/(4 ε0). Solve for ρ0 = 4 ε0 Emax/R. Substitute: ρ0 = 4 × 8.854×10⁻¹² × 1.00×10⁶ / 0.25 = 1.417×10⁻⁴ C/m³. Any larger ρ0 would exceed the allowed surface field, so this is the largest permitted charge density.

Answer: ρ0 = 1.417×10⁻⁴ C/m³

(b)

Set r = R in the enclosed charge expression from part (a). Q = π ρ0 R⁴/R = π ρ0 R³. Substitute the design values: R³ = 0.25³ = 0.015625 m³ and ρ0 = 1.417×10⁻⁴ C/m³. So Q = π × 1.417×10⁻⁴ × 0.015625 = 6.954×10⁻⁶ C, about 6.95 μC. Cross-check with the surface field: outside the sphere E = Q/(4π ε0 r²), and at r = R this gives 6.954×10⁻⁶ / (4π × 8.854×10⁻¹² × 0.0625) = 1.00×10⁶ V/m, which matches the design limit and confirms the charge. The check also shows the field is continuous at the surface, as it must be with no surface charge.

Answer: Q = 6.95×10⁻⁶ C

(c)

Split the potential integral at r = R, with V(∞) = 0. Outside, E = Q/(4π ε0 r²), so V(R) = Q/(4π ε0 R) = Emax R = 1.00×10⁶ × 0.25 = 250 kV, since Q/(4π ε0 R²) = Emax. Inside, V(0) − V(R) = ∫ from 0 to R of E dr = ∫ ρ0 r²/(4 ε0 R) dr = ρ0 R²/(12 ε0). Using ρ0 = 4 ε0 Emax/R this reduces to Emax R/3 = 83.33 kV. So V(0) = 250 + 83.33 = 333.3 kV. The centre sits at a higher potential than the surface because the field points outward, and the contribution inside is only one third of Emax R since the field starts from zero at the centre.

Answer: V(0) = 333.3 kV

(d)

Outside the sphere the charge acts as a point charge at the centre, because the distribution is spherically symmetric. So E(r) = Q/(4π ε0 r²) for r ≥ R. At r = 0.50 m: 4π ε0 r² = 4π × 8.854×10⁻¹² × 0.25 = 2.782×10⁻¹¹ F. Then E = 6.954×10⁻⁶ / 2.782×10⁻¹¹ = 2.50×10⁵ V/m. The same result follows from inverse-square scaling of the surface field: at 2R the field is Emax/4 = 250 kV/m. The field at the surface was 1.00 MV/m, so doubling the distance cuts it to a quarter, a quick check that confirms the arithmetic.

Answer: E = 250 kV/m

Problem 3 [A7-023] Capacitance and dielectrics

A single-core 15 kV dc test cable has a copper inner conductor of radius a = 2.0 mm and a thin metallic sheath of inner radius c = 10.0 mm. To reduce peak electric stress the insulation is graded: an inner layer of relative permittivity εr1 = 4.0 extends from ρ = a to ρ = b, and an outer layer of relative permittivity εr2 = 2.0 extends from ρ = b to ρ = c. Both layers are perfect insulators, the geometry is coaxial and infinitely long, and the interface at ρ = b carries no free charge. Use ε0 = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m. The designer wants the maximum field in the inner layer to equal the maximum field in the outer layer, and the potential difference between conductor and sheath is V = 15.0 kV.

  1. (a) Find the interface radius b that makes the maximum electric field magnitude equal in the two layers. [4]
  2. (b) Find the capacitance per metre of the cable for this value of b. [6]
  3. (c) Find the common maximum field magnitude when the applied voltage is 15.0 kV. [5]
  4. (d) Find the electrostatic energy stored per metre of cable at 15.0 kV. [5]
(a)

With line charge λ per metre on the inner conductor, Gauss's law gives D = λ/(2πρ), so E = λ/(2π ε0 εr ρ). D is continuous across the interface because there is no free charge there. In each layer E is largest at the smaller radius: E1max = λ/(2π ε0 εr1 a) at ρ = a, and E2max = λ/(2π ε0 εr2 b) at ρ = b. Equating the two gives εr1 a = εr2 b, so b = εr1 a/εr2 = 4.0 × 2.0 mm / 2.0 = 4.0 mm. Because D is continuous, the field jumps up by the factor εr1/εr2 = 2 on crossing into the lower-permittivity layer, from half of E1max to E1max, so both layers peak at the same value. That is the intent of grading the insulation: both layers are stressed equally at their inner surfaces.

Answer: b = 4.0 mm

(b)

The voltage is V = ∫ E dρ across both layers, which gives V = λ/(2π ε0) [ln(b/a)/εr1 + ln(c/b)/εr2]. This is two capacitors in series, per metre. Compute each term: ln(b/a) = ln 2 = 0.6931, divided by 4.0 gives 0.17329; ln(c/b) = ln 2.5 = 0.9163, divided by 2.0 gives 0.45815. The sum is 0.63144. The reciprocal capacitance per metre is 0.63144/(2π ε0) = 0.63144 / 5.5630×10⁻¹¹ = 1.1351×10¹⁰ m/F. So C = 1/1.1351×10¹⁰ = 8.810×10⁻¹¹ F/m = 88.1 pF/m. Grading lowers the capacitance from 138 pF/m for a single εr = 4 layer with the same radii to 88.1 pF/m, in exchange for a lower peak stress (2.97 versus 4.66 MV/m).

Answer: C = 88.1 pF/m

(c)

The line charge is λ = C V = 8.810×10⁻¹¹ × 15 000 = 1.3216×10⁻⁶ C/m. The inner-layer maximum field is E1max = λ/(2π ε0 εr1 a) = 1.3216×10⁻⁶ / (5.5630×10⁻¹¹ × 4.0 × 2.0×10⁻³) = 1.3216×10⁻⁶ / 4.4504×10⁻¹³ = 2.969×10⁶ V/m. Check the outer layer: E2max = λ/(2π ε0 εr2 b) = 1.3216×10⁻⁶ / (5.5630×10⁻¹¹ × 2.0 × 4.0×10⁻³) = 2.969×10⁶ V/m, identical, as designed. The maximum stress is 2.97 MV/m. A single-layer εr = 4 design with the same sheath would have a higher peak stress at the conductor surface than this graded design, so the grading has done its job.

Answer: 2.97 MV/m

(d)

The stored energy per unit length of a linear capacitor is W = ½ C V². Using C = 8.810×10⁻¹¹ F/m and V = 15 000 V: V² = 2.25×10⁸ V². Then W = 0.5 × 8.810×10⁻¹¹ × 2.25×10⁸ = 9.912×10⁻³ J/m, or 9.91 mJ/m. This energy is held in the field of both layers; an alternative route is to integrate ½ D·E over the two annular volumes, which gives the same result since D = λ/(2πρ) and E follows each layer's permittivity. Since the voltage is dc, the energy is not dissipated, but it must be discharged safely before the cable is handled.

Answer: 9.91 mJ/m

Problem 4 [A7-024] Boundary conditions and Laplace equation problems

A gas-insulated high-voltage terminal is a conducting sphere of radius a at potential V0 = 60.0 kV, centred inside a concentric grounded conducting spherical shell of inner radius b = 50.0 mm. The gap between them is filled with gas whose permittivity is that of free space, ε0 = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m, and no charge lies in the gap. The potential V(r) depends only on the radius r. Treat the shell radius b as fixed and choose the terminal radius a to give the lowest possible peak electric field at the terminal surface for the fixed voltage V0, because the gas is stressed hardest there. Solve Laplace's equation ∇²V = 0 in spherical coordinates with the boundary conditions V(a) = V0 and V(b) = 0.

  1. (a) Solve Laplace's equation, find the terminal surface field in terms of a, and determine the radius a that minimises it. [4]
  2. (b) Find the minimum value of the peak field at the terminal surface. [5]
  3. (c) For this design, find the potential at r = 37.5 mm. [5]
  4. (d) Find the capacitance between the terminal and the shell for this design. [6]
(a)

For V = V(r), Laplace's equation is (1/r²) d/dr (r² dV/dr) = 0, so r² dV/dr = constant and V = A/r + B. Boundary conditions give V0 = A/a + B and 0 = A/b + B, so A = V0/(1/a − 1/b) and B = −A/b. The field is E = −dV/dr = A/r², and at r = a: E(a) = V0/[a² (1/a − 1/b)] = V0/[a (1 − a/b)]. To minimise E(a) with respect to a, maximise the product a(1 − a/b). Setting its derivative 1 − 2a/b to zero gives a = b/2 = 25.0 mm. The second derivative is negative, so this is a maximum of the product and hence a minimum of the field.

Answer: a = 25.0 mm

(b)

Substitute a = b/2 into E(a) = V0/[a(1 − a/b)]. Then a(1 − a/b) = (b/2)(1/2) = b/4 = 12.5 mm. So Emin = V0/(b/4) = 4V0/b = 4 × 60 000 / 0.050 = 4.80×10⁶ V/m, which is 4.80 MV/m. This value is above the dielectric strength of air at one atmosphere (about 3 MV/m), which is why the gap is gas-filled and pressurised, but it is the lowest possible for this voltage and shell. Any other terminal radius, smaller or larger, would give a higher surface stress, because a smaller sphere concentrates the field and a larger one narrows the gap.

Answer: 4.80 MV/m

(c)

Use V(r) = A/r + B with A = V0/(1/a − 1/b). With a = 25.0 mm and b = 50.0 mm: 1/a = 40.0 m⁻¹ and 1/b = 20.0 m⁻¹, so 1/a − 1/b = 20.0 m⁻¹. Then V(r) = V0 (1/r − 1/b)/(1/a − 1/b). At r = 37.5 mm, 1/r = 26.667 m⁻¹, so 1/r − 1/b = 6.667 m⁻¹. Hence V = 60 000 × 6.667/20.0 = 20 000 V = 20.0 kV. The potential at the geometric midpoint of the gap is far below 30 kV because the field is strongest near the small inner sphere, so most of the voltage is dropped in the inner half of the gap.

Answer: 20.0 kV

(d)

The charge on the terminal follows from Gauss's law: Q = ε0 E(a) 4π a², with E(a) = A/a². Because A = V0/(1/a − 1/b), Q = 4π ε0 A = 4π ε0 V0/(1/a − 1/b). The capacitance is C = Q/V0 = 4π ε0/(1/a − 1/b) = 4π ε0 a b/(b − a). Substitute: 4π ε0 = 1.1127×10⁻¹⁰ F/m, and 1/a − 1/b = 20.0 m⁻¹. Then C = 1.1127×10⁻¹⁰ / 20.0 = 5.563×10⁻¹² F = 5.56 pF. As a check, the isolated-sphere capacitance 4π ε0 a would be 2.78 pF, so the surrounding shell doubles it, which is reasonable because b = 2a.

Answer: C = 5.56 pF

Problem 5 [A7-025] Steady current, conductors and resistance fields

A substation earthing electrode is modelled as a conducting hemisphere of radius a buried with its flat face flush with the soil surface. The soil is uniform with conductivity σ = 0.020 S/m (resistivity 50 Ω·m) and extends to infinity, and the conducting electrode itself has negligible resistance. A fault drives a current I = 2000 A into the ground through the electrode, and the current spreads out radially in the soil. Design requirement: the resistance from the electrode to remote earth must be exactly 5.0 Ω, which fixes the radius a. Afterwards a person stands on the surface with one foot at 3.0 m and the other at 3.8 m from the electrode centre, both on the same radial line, and both distances are greater than a.

  1. (a) Derive the resistance of the hemispherical electrode to remote earth and find the radius a that gives 5.0 Ω. [5]
  2. (b) Find the electrode potential rise (ground potential rise) above remote earth for the 2000 A fault. [3]
  3. (c) Find the step voltage between the person's feet. [7]
  4. (d) Find the current density in the soil at the electrode surface. [5]
(a)

At radius r the current I crosses a hemispherical shell of area 2πr², so J = I/(2πr²) and E = J/σ = I/(2πσ r²). The potential of the electrode above remote earth is V = ∫ from a to ∞ of E dr = I/(2πσ a). The resistance is R = V/I = 1/(2πσ a). Set R = 5.0 Ω and solve: a = 1/(2π σ R) = 1/(2π × 0.020 × 5.0) = 1/0.62832 = 1.592 m. The resistance is dominated by the soil close to the electrode, since the integrand falls as 1/r², so doubling the electrode radius would halve R. That is why a large, shallow electrode or an extended grid is used to reach a low earth resistance.

Answer: a = 1.592 m

(b)

The ground potential rise is the product of fault current and earth resistance, since the electrode sits at V = I R relative to remote earth. Using I = 2000 A and R = 5.0 Ω gives GPR = 2000 × 5.0 = 10 000 V = 10.0 kV. The same result follows from V = I/(2π σ a) = 2000/(2π × 0.020 × 1.5915) = 2000/0.2 = 10 000 V. This is the potential to which the earthed metalwork rises during the fault, and it is the hazard for any person touching the metalwork while standing on remote earth. The step voltage found next is a smaller but separate hazard at the surface of the soil itself.

Answer: 10.0 kV

(c)

The surface potential at distance r from the centre (r ≥ a) is V(r) = I/(2π σ r), because it is the integral of E from r to infinity. The step voltage is the difference between the two foot positions: Vstep = V(3.0) − V(3.8) = [I/(2π σ)] (1/3.0 − 1/3.8). Compute the coefficient: I/(2π σ) = 2000/(2π × 0.020) = 2000/0.12566 = 15 915 V·m. The bracket is 0.33333 − 0.26316 = 0.070175 m⁻¹. So Vstep = 15 915 × 0.070175 = 1117 V. The foot nearer the electrode is at the higher potential. A step voltage above a thousand volts during a 2000 A fault is dangerous, so such a site needs surface gravel or potential grading.

Answer: 1117 V

(d)

The current density in the soil at radius r is J = I/(2π r²), the fault current divided by the area of a hemispherical shell. At the electrode surface r = a = 1.5915 m, so the area is 2π a² = 2π × 2.5329 = 15.915 m². Then J = 2000/15.915 = 125.7 A/m². Check with the field: E = J/σ = 125.66/0.020 = 6283 V/m at the surface, and V = ∫E dr from a to infinity equals E a = 6283 × 1.5915 = 10 000 V, matching the ground potential rise from part (b). The current density drops with the square of the distance, which is why the soil heating is concentrated right at the electrode.

Answer: 125.7 A/m²

A7 Practice Paper 6

Problem 1 [A7-026] Magnetostatics: Biot-Savart and Ampere's law

A calibration laboratory needs a nearly uniform axial magnetic field to test a compass sensor. A Helmholtz pair is proposed: two identical thin circular coils, each of mean radius R = 0.150 m and N turns, share a common axis and are separated by a distance equal to R, with their planes perpendicular to the axis. Both coils carry the same current I = 3.00 A in the same sense, so the fields add. The medium is free space with μ0 = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m. The target is a flux density of at least 2.00 mT at the midpoint of the axis between the coils. The coils are wound with wire of resistance 0.012 Ω per metre, the two coils are connected in series, and each turn has length 2πR.

  1. (a) Using the Biot-Savart result for one loop, find the smallest whole number of turns N per coil that meets the 2.00 mT target. [5]
  2. (b) With that N, find the flux density at the midpoint. [4]
  3. (c) Find the percentage change in flux density at an axial point 30 mm from the midpoint relative to the midpoint value, giving its magnitude. [6]
  4. (d) Find the electrical power dissipated in the two coils in series. [5]
(a)

For a single circular loop of radius R with N turns, Biot-Savart integration gives the on-axis field Bz = μ0 N I R²/[2(R² + d²)3/2], where d is the axial distance from the loop plane. At the midpoint each coil is a distance d = R/2 away, and the two fields add. Each contributes μ0 N I R²/[2 (1.25 R²)3/2], so B = μ0 N I/(R) × (4/5)3/2 = 0.71554 μ0 N I/R. Set B = 2.00×10⁻³ T: N = B R/(0.71554 μ0 I) = 2.00×10⁻³ × 0.150/(0.71554 × 1.2566×10⁻⁶ × 3.00) = 3.00×10⁻⁴/2.6975×10⁻⁶ = 111.2. Rounding up to a whole number of turns gives N = 112.

Answer: N = 112

(b)

Using the same midpoint formula with N = 112: B = 0.71554 μ0 N I/R = 0.71554 × 1.2566×10⁻⁶ × 112 × 3.00/0.150. The numerator is 0.71554 × 1.2566×10⁻⁶ = 8.9918×10⁻⁷; multiply by 112 × 3.00 = 336 to get 3.0212×10⁻⁴; divide by 0.150 to get 2.014×10⁻³ T. So B = 2.014 mT, which is 0.7 percent above the target, a sensible margin given that the turns must be a whole number. Rounding up rather than down was necessary because the specification states 'at least' 2.00 mT, so 111 turns would give 1.996 mT and would fail the requirement.

Answer: 2.014 mT

(c)

Place the origin at the midpoint with coils at z = ±R/2. At axial position z the field from each coil is μ0 N I R²/[2 (R² + (z ∓ R/2)²)3/2]. For z = 0.030 m and R/2 = 0.075 m, the distances from the coil planes are 0.045 m and 0.105 m. The squared sums are R² + d² = 0.0225 + 0.002025 = 0.024525 and 0.0225 + 0.011025 = 0.033525. Raising each to the power 1.5 gives 0.0038408 and 0.0061384. With μ0 N I R²/2 = 1.2566×10⁻⁶ × 112 × 3 × 0.0225/2 = 4.7500×10⁻⁶, the field is 4.75×10⁻⁶ × (1/0.0038408 + 1/0.0061384) = 4.75×10⁻⁶ × (260.36 + 162.91) = 2.0106 mT. The change from 2.0142 mT is −0.176 percent, so the field is uniform to about 0.2 percent over this range.

Answer: 0.176 %

(d)

The coil length is the total number of turns times the length of one turn. There are 2 coils of 112 turns each, so 224 turns, each of length 2πR = 2π × 0.150 = 0.9425 m. The total wire length is 224 × 0.9425 = 211.1 m. With a resistance of 0.012 Ω per metre, the series resistance is 211.1 × 0.012 = 2.533 Ω. The same current flows in both coils, so the power dissipated is P = I² R = 3.00² × 2.533 = 22.8 W. This heat is modest, and the supply voltage needed is I R = 7.6 V, so a small bench supply with natural convection cooling is adequate for steady operation.

Answer: 22.8 W

Problem 2 [A7-027] Magnetic force, induction and Faraday's law

A laboratory rail launcher consists of two long, parallel, horizontal conducting rails 0.150 m apart in a uniform vertical magnetic flux density B = 1.20 T. A conducting bar of mass 50.0 g rests across the rails at right angles. A dc source of voltage V = 12.0 V is switched across the rails at t = 0 through a closed loop whose total resistance, bar and rails together, is constant at 0.0800 Ω. The bar starts from rest, slides without friction and keeps contact with the rails. Loop self-inductance is neglected. Take the positive current direction as the one that makes the magnetic force push the bar away from the source, and note that the bar's motion induces an emf that opposes the source.

  1. (a) Find the force on the bar at t = 0. [4]
  2. (b) Find the terminal speed of the bar for V = 12.0 V. [4]
  3. (c) Design step: find the source voltage needed to reach a terminal speed of 100 m/s. [6]
  4. (d) For V = 12.0 V, find the bar speed 0.200 s after switch-on. [6]
(a)

At t = 0 the bar is at rest, so there is no motional emf, and the loop current is limited by resistance alone: I0 = V/R = 12.0/0.0800 = 150 A. The magnetic force on a straight conductor of length l perpendicular to B is F = B I l. Here l = 0.150 m and B = 1.20 T, so F = 1.20 × 150 × 0.150 = 27.0 N. The force direction follows from F = I l × B, which with the stated current direction pushes the bar away from the source. The initial acceleration is F/m = 27.0/0.0500 = 540 m/s², very large, so the bar speeds up quickly and the back emf soon begins to matter.

Answer: 27.0 N

(b)

Faraday's law gives a motional emf in the moving bar of e = B l v, which opposes the source. The loop current is i = (V − B l v)/R. The force is B l i, and the bar accelerates until the force falls to zero, which happens when the back emf equals the source emf. Setting B l v = V gives vt = V/(B l) = 12.0/(1.20 × 0.150) = 12.0/0.180 = 66.7 m/s. At this speed the current is zero, so the bar coasts at constant velocity. The speed is independent of the bar mass and the loop resistance, which affect only how fast the terminal speed is approached, not its value.

Answer: 66.7 m/s

(c)

The terminal speed relation vt = V/(B l) can be inverted for the required voltage: V = B l vt. For vt = 100 m/s, V = 1.20 × 0.150 × 100 = 18.0 V. The design check is that the initial current is then 18.0/0.0800 = 225 A and the initial force is 1.20 × 225 × 0.150 = 40.5 N, which the rails and source must withstand. The initial peak current rises in proportion to the voltage, so reaching a higher speed also raises the thermal and mechanical load. Note that the bar never exactly reaches vt, so the real design margin should be somewhat above 18.0 V.

Answer: 18.0 V

(d)

Write Newton's second law with the current expressed through the back emf: m dv/dt = B l (V − B l v)/R. This is a first-order equation with solution v(t) = vt [1 − exp(−t/τ)], where the mechanical time constant is τ = m R/(B l)². Compute (B l)² = 0.180² = 0.0324 T²m². Then τ = 0.0500 × 0.0800/0.0324 = 0.12346 s. At t = 0.200 s: t/τ = 1.620 and exp(−1.620) = 0.19790, so v = 66.67 × (1 − 0.19790) = 53.5 m/s. The bar reaches about 80 percent of its terminal speed after 0.2 s, consistent with t being 1.6 time constants.

Answer: 53.5 m/s

Problem 3 [A7-028] Inductance and magnetic energy

A 20.0 mH smoothing choke is to be built on a laminated iron core with an air gap to prevent saturation. The core has a uniform cross-section of 10.0 cm², a mean magnetic path length of 0.300 m in iron, and a constant relative permeability of 2000. The winding has N = 200 turns and carries a peak current of 4.00 A. A single air gap of length g is cut across the core, with the same cross-section as the core. Fringing at the gap is neglected in the numerical parts, and the core is operated in its linear region. Use μ0 = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m. The design must give an inductance of exactly 20.0 mH and the designer also wants to know the energy and force at the gap.

  1. (a) Using the magnetic circuit reluctance, find the gap length g that gives L = 20.0 mH. [6]
  2. (b) Find the peak flux density in the core at 4.00 A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the magnetic energy stored in the air gap at 4.00 A. [5]
  4. (d) Explain qualitatively how fringing at the gap changes the real inductance compared with the value calculated here, and why. [5]
(a)

The magnetic circuit has the iron reluctance Rc = lc/(μ0 μr A) in series with the gap reluctance Rg = g/(μ0 A). The inductance is L = N²/(Rc + Rg) = N² μ0 A/(lc/μr + g). Solve for the total effective length: lc/μr + g = N² μ0 A/L = 40 000 × 1.2566×10⁻⁶ × 1.00×10⁻³/0.0200 = 5.0265×10⁻⁵/0.0200 = 2.5133×10⁻³ m. The iron contributes lc/μr = 0.300/2000 = 1.50×10⁻⁴ m. So g = 2.5133×10⁻³ − 1.50×10⁻⁴ = 2.363×10⁻³ m = 2.363 mm. The gap dominates the reluctance, so the inductance is set mostly by the gap and is insensitive to the iron permeability.

Answer: g = 2.363 mm

(b)

The flux linkage at the peak current is λ = L I = 0.0200 × 4.00 = 0.0800 Wb-turns. With N turns linking the same flux, Φ = λ/N = 0.0800/200 = 4.00×10⁻⁴ Wb. The flux density is B = Φ/A = 4.00×10⁻⁴/1.00×10⁻³ = 0.400 T. An equivalent check uses B = μ0 N I/(lc/μr + g) = 1.2566×10⁻⁶ × 200 × 4.00/2.5133×10⁻³ = 0.400 T. This is well below the typical saturation flux density of laminated silicon steel, which is the reason the gap was added: the iron stays in its linear region as the model assumed.

Answer: B = 0.400 T

(c)

The energy density in the gap is B²/(2 μ0), since the field is uniform and the flux density is continuous across the gap. Compute: B² = 0.160 T², so the density is 0.160/(2 × 1.2566×10⁻⁶) = 6.366×10⁴ J/m³. The gap volume is A g = 1.00×10⁻³ × 2.363×10⁻³ = 2.363×10⁻⁶ m³. So the energy in the gap is 6.366×10⁴ × 2.363×10⁻⁶ = 0.1505 J. The total stored energy is ½ L I² = 0.5 × 0.0200 × 16.0 = 0.160 J, so the gap holds 94 percent and the iron only 0.0095 J, which shows why an air gap makes an efficient energy store.

Answer: 0.1505 J

(d)

At the edges of the gap the flux bulges outward into the surrounding air instead of staying confined to the core cross-section. This makes the effective cross-sectional area of the gap larger than the geometric area A, which lowers the gap reluctance Rg = g/(μ0 A_eff). A lower total reluctance increases L = N²/R, so the real inductance is higher than the 20.0 mH computed with the ideal formula, and the effect grows as the gap length g becomes larger relative to the core dimensions. In practice the designer therefore cuts the gap slightly longer than the ideal value, or measures L and trims the gap, and may also keep the winding away from the gap to limit eddy-current heating from the fringing field.

Answer: Fringing raises L

Problem 4 [A7-029] Maxwell's equations in integral and differential form

A small shielded-loop probe is to measure a radio-frequency plane wave in free space (ε0 = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m, μ0 = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m). The wave travels in the +z direction at f = 100 MHz with electric field E = E0 sin(ωt − βz) a_y, where E0 = 20.0 V/m. The probe is a circular loop of N turns and radius 20.0 mm placed at z = 0 with its plane perpendicular to the x axis, so the magnetic field passes straight through it. The loop is small compared with a wavelength, so the field may be taken as uniform over its area, and the loop resistance is neglected. The design target is a peak open-circuit voltage of at least 0.500 V.

  1. (a) Find the phase constant β of the wave. [4]
  2. (b) Using Maxwell's curl equation for E, find the amplitude of the magnetic field strength H0. [3]
  3. (c) Using Faraday's law, find the peak emf induced per turn of the loop. [5]
  4. (d) Find the smallest whole number of turns N that gives at least 0.500 V peak. [4]
  5. (e) Using the curl of H, find the peak displacement current density at z = 0. [4]
(a)

In free space the phase constant is β = ω/c with c = 1/√(μ0 ε0). Compute the speed: μ0 ε0 = 1.2566×10⁻⁶ × 8.854×10⁻¹² = 1.1126×10⁻¹⁷, so c = 2.998×10⁸ m/s. The angular frequency is ω = 2π × 100×10⁶ = 6.283×10⁸ rad/s. Then β = 6.283×10⁸/2.998×10⁸ = 2.096 rad/m. The wavelength is 2π/β = 3.00 m, much larger than the 40 mm loop diameter, which justifies treating the field as uniform over the loop area as the statement assumes.

Answer: β = 2.096 rad/m

(b)

Faraday's law in point form is ∇×E = −∂B/∂t. For E = E0 sin(ωt − βz) a_y, only ∂Ey/∂z contributes, giving ∇×E = −(∂Ey/∂z) a_x = β E0 cos(ωt − βz) a_x. Hence ∂Bx/∂t = −β E0 cos(ωt − βz). Integrating in time gives Bx = −(β E0/ω) sin(ωt − βz). So the magnitude is B0 = β E0/ω = E0/c, and H0 = B0/μ0 = E0/η0 with η0 = √(μ0/ε0) = 376.7 Ω. Then H0 = 20.0/376.7 = 0.0531 A/m. The negative sign shows H points along −x, which together with E along +y gives power flow along +z.

Answer: H0 = 0.0531 A/m

(c)

Faraday's law in integral form gives emf = −dΦ/dt with Φ = B A per turn. The magnetic flux density amplitude is B0 = μ0 H0 = 1.2566×10⁻⁶ × 0.05309 = 6.671×10⁻⁸ T. The loop area is A = π r² = π × (0.020)² = 1.2566×10⁻³ m². The flux per turn varies as B0 A sin(ωt), so the peak emf per turn is ω B0 A = 6.283×10⁸ × 6.671×10⁻⁸ × 1.2566×10⁻³ = 0.05267 V = 52.7 mV. The emf leads the flux by 90 degrees, and it grows with frequency, so the probe is more sensitive at higher frequency for the same field.

Answer: 52.7 mV

(d)

The emf of a coil of N series turns in the same uniform field is N times the single-turn value, so Vpeak = N × 0.05267 V. For Vpeak ≥ 0.500 V, N ≥ 0.500/0.05267 = 9.49. N must be a whole number, so we round up to N = 10, giving a peak voltage of 0.527 V and a margin of 5 percent. Using 9 turns would give 0.474 V, which fails the target. A real probe with 10 turns also has self-capacitance and inductance that limit its useful bandwidth, so at 100 MHz the loop radius of 20 mm and the resulting size remain small enough for the uniform-field assumption.

Answer: N = 10

(e)

Ampere's law with displacement current in a source-free region is ∇×H = ε0 ∂E/∂t, so the displacement current density is Jd = ε0 ∂E/∂t = ε0 ω E0 cos(ωt − βz) a_y. At z = 0 the peak value is ε0 ω E0 = 8.854×10⁻¹² × 6.283×10⁸ × 20.0 = 0.1113 A/m². This agrees with the curl of H, since ∇×H has magnitude β H0 = 2.096 × 0.05309 = 0.1113 A/m². The agreement confirms that the Faraday and Ampere relations are consistent with the single phase constant β found in part (a), and that no conduction current exists in free space.

Answer: 0.111 A/m²

Problem 5 [A7-030] Displacement current and time-varying fields

A thin-film capacitive sensor has two identical circular parallel plates of radius 50.0 mm separated by a polymer dielectric of thickness d = 2.00 mm and relative permittivity εr = 2.50. It is driven by a sinusoidal source of peak voltage 200 V at 20.0 kHz. Take ε0 = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m, treat the dielectric as lossless, ignore fringing at the plate edges and assume the field between the plates is uniform and perpendicular to them. The designer must compare the lead current with the displacement current in the dielectric, find the magnetic field the displacement current produces, and then choose a gap that raises the sensor current to a target level without changing the voltage, frequency or plate size.

  1. (a) Find the capacitance of the sensor. [3]
  2. (b) Find the peak current in the leads. [4]
  3. (c) Find the peak displacement current density in the dielectric. [4]
  4. (d) Using Ampere's law with displacement current, find the peak magnetic field strength at radius 30.0 mm from the axis, between the plates. [4]
  5. (e) Design step: find the gap d' that raises the peak lead current to 5.00 mA with everything else unchanged. [5]
(a)

For a parallel-plate capacitor with a uniform field, C = ε0 εr A/d. The plate area is A = π r² = π × (0.0500)² = 7.854×10⁻³ m². Then C = 8.854×10⁻¹² × 2.50 × 7.854×10⁻³ / 2.00×10⁻³. The numerator is 8.854×10⁻¹² × 2.50 = 2.2135×10⁻¹¹; multiplying by the area gives 1.7385×10⁻¹³; dividing by 2.00×10⁻³ gives 8.692×10⁻¹¹ F. So C = 86.9 pF. Fringing, neglected here, would increase the real value slightly, because the plate radius is large compared with the gap, by a ratio of 25 to 1, which keeps the error small.

Answer: C = 86.9 pF

(b)

For a sinusoidal drive the capacitor current has peak value Ipk = ω C Vpk, leading the voltage by 90 degrees. The angular frequency is ω = 2π × 20.0×10³ = 1.2566×10⁵ rad/s. Then Ipk = 1.2566×10⁵ × 8.692×10⁻¹¹ × 200 = 2.185×10⁻³ A = 2.18 mA. The current in the leads is a conduction current, carried by electrons, which ends on the plates; the circuit is closed by the displacement current between the plates, as the next parts show. The dielectric is lossless, so no real power is dissipated and the current is purely reactive.

Answer: 2.18 mA

(c)

The displacement current density is Jd = ∂D/∂t, with D = ε0 εr E and E = (V/d). For V = Vpk sin(ωt), the peak Jd = ω ε0 εr Vpk/d. Substitute: 1.2566×10⁵ × 2.2135×10⁻¹¹ × 200/2.00×10⁻³. The product 1.2566×10⁵ × 2.2135×10⁻¹¹ = 2.7816×10⁻⁶; times 200 gives 5.5632×10⁻⁴; dividing by 2.00×10⁻³ gives 0.2782 A/m². As a check, Jd times the plate area is 0.2782 × 7.854×10⁻³ = 2.185 mA, equal to the lead current from part (b), so the current is continuous around the loop.

Answer: 0.278 A/m²

(d)

Apply Ampere's law ∮H·dl = I_enclosed to a circle of radius ρ = 30.0 mm coaxial with the plates. Between the plates there is no conduction current, so the enclosed current is the displacement current through the disc of area π ρ². By symmetry H is azimuthal and uniform around the circle, so H (2π ρ) = Jd π ρ², giving H = Jd ρ/2. Substitute: H = 0.2782 × 0.0300/2 = 4.172×10⁻³ A/m = 4.17 mA/m. The field grows linearly from the axis to the plate edge, where it reaches 6.95 mA/m, and it falls as 1/ρ outside the plates, just as the field around a wire carrying the same lead current would.

Answer: 4.17 mA/m

(e)

The lead current is Ipk = ω ε0 εr A Vpk/d, which is inversely proportional to d when everything else is fixed. Therefore d' = d × (Ipk,old/Ipk,new) = 2.00 mm × (2.185/5.00) = 2.00 × 0.4369 = 0.874 mm. Equivalently d' = ω ε0 εr A Vpk/Ipk,new = 1.2566×10⁵ × 1.7385×10⁻¹³ × 200/5.00×10⁻³ = 8.74×10⁻⁴ m. The electric field is then 200/0.874×10⁻³ = 2.29×10⁵ V/m, well below the breakdown field of common polymers, so the thinner gap is acceptable; the design also gives a capacitance of 199 pF, which increases the sensitivity.

Answer: 0.874 mm

A7 Practice Paper 7

Problem 1 [A7-031] Plane waves in lossless media

A microwave test chamber is being fitted with a lossless, non-magnetic dielectric filler (μ = μ0, σ = 0) so that a 5.8 GHz uniform plane wave has a wavelength of exactly 2.00 cm inside the filler. Use c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s and the intrinsic impedance of free space η0 = 376.73 Ω. The wave travels in the +z direction inside the filler and is linearly polarized, with a peak electric field amplitude of 50 V/m. The designer must choose the filler material and then confirm what the wave looks like inside it. The filler is thick enough that reflections at its far face can be ignored in this problem.

  1. (a) Find the relative permittivity εr the filler must have. [5]
  2. (b) Find the phase velocity of the wave in the filler, in units of 10⁸ m/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the intrinsic impedance of the filler. [5]
  4. (d) Find the time-average power density carried by the wave in the filler. [6]
(a)

The free-space wavelength at 5.8 GHz is λ0 = c/f = 2.998 × 10⁸ / 5.8 × 10⁹ = 5.169 cm. In a lossless non-magnetic medium the phase velocity is c/√εr, so the wavelength shrinks by the same factor: λ = λ0/√εr. Setting λ = 2.00 cm gives √εr = λ0/λ = 5.169/2.00 = 2.584. Squaring, εr = 6.68. The assumption is that the medium is non-magnetic (μr = 1), so all the shortening comes from the permittivity. The designer would therefore look for a ceramic-loaded material with a relative permittivity near 6.7 and low loss at this frequency.

Answer: εr = 6.68

(b)

The phase velocity in a lossless medium with μ = μ0 is vp = 1/√(με) = c/√εr. Substituting c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s and √εr = 2.584 gives vp = 2.998 × 10⁸ / 2.584 = 1.160 × 10⁸ m/s. As a check, vp = fλ = 5.8 × 10⁹ × 0.0200 = 1.160 × 10⁸ m/s, which agrees. The wave therefore travels at about 38.7 percent of the free-space speed. Phase and group velocities are equal here because the medium is non-dispersive, so energy also moves at this speed along +z.

Answer: vp = 1.160 × 10⁸ m/s

(c)

For a lossless medium the intrinsic impedance is η = √(μ/ε) = η0/√(εr/μr). With μr = 1 this is η = 376.73 / 2.584 = 145.8 Ω. The impedance relates the transverse fields of a plane wave by E = ηH, so inside the filler the magnetic field amplitude is larger than it would be in air for the same E. The E and H phasors are in phase because η is real for a lossless medium. This value would also be needed to compute the reflection at the air-to-filler boundary.

Answer: η = 145.8 Ω

(d)

For a plane wave in a lossless medium with peak electric amplitude E0, the time-average Poynting vector magnitude is Sav = E0²/(2η). Substituting E0 = 50 V/m and η = 145.8 Ω gives Sav = 2500 / (2 × 145.8) = 2500 / 291.6 = 8.58 W/m². The factor of 2 appears because E0 is a peak, not rms, value. The same power flows through every plane of constant z because the medium has no loss, so no attenuation term is needed. Across a 0.1 m² aperture the filler would carry about 0.86 W.

Answer: Sav = 8.58 W/m²

Problem 2 [A7-032] Plane waves in lossy media and skin depth

A cabinet for a 450 kHz induction-heating controller is to be lined with copper sheet so that radiated interference at the cabinet wall is attenuated by absorption alone. Take copper as a good conductor with conductivity σ = 5.8 × 10⁷ S/m and permeability μ = μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. At 450 kHz the conduction current is far larger than the displacement current. Use the definition that absorption loss in decibels equals 20 log10 of et/δ, where t is the sheet thickness and δ is the skin depth. Ignore reflection loss and multiple internal reflections. Assume the field enters the sheet as a plane wave at normal incidence from one face.

  1. (a) Find the skin depth δ of copper at 450 kHz, in micrometres. [4]
  2. (b) Find the minimum sheet thickness that gives 60 dB of absorption loss, in millimetres. [5]
  3. (c) Find the surface resistance Rs = 1/(σδ) of the copper, in milliohms per square. [5]
  4. (d) A scrap piece of the same copper that is only 0.100 mm thick is tried instead. What percentage of the incident field amplitude remains after crossing it, ignoring reflections? [6]
(a)

In a good conductor (σ ≫ ωε) the field decays as e-z/δ with δ = 1/α = √(2/(ωμσ)) = 1/√(π f μ σ). Substituting f = 4.5 × 10⁵ Hz, μ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m and σ = 5.8 × 10⁷ S/m gives π f μ σ = π × 4.5 × 10⁵ × 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ × 5.8 × 10⁷ = 1.0304 × 10⁸. The square root is 1.0151 × 10⁴ m⁻¹, so δ = 9.851 × 10⁻⁵ m = 98.5 μm. The good-conductor approximation is justified because σ/(ωε0) is about 2 × 10¹⁸.

Answer: δ = 98.5 μm

(b)

The absorption loss is A = 20 log10(et/δ) = 8.686 t/δ dB. Solving for the thickness gives t = A δ / 8.686. With A = 60 dB and δ = 98.51 μm, t = 60 × 98.51 × 10⁻⁶ / 8.686 = 6.804 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.680 mm. That is about 6.9 skin depths, since each skin depth contributes 8.686 dB. Any sheet at least this thick meets the requirement, so a practical choice would be a standard 0.8 mm sheet, which also gives some margin. The thickness depends on frequency as 1/√f, so a lower interference frequency would need a thicker liner.

Answer: t = 0.680 mm

(c)

For a conductor thick compared with δ, the surface impedance is Zs = (1 + j)/(σδ), so the real part, the surface resistance, is Rs = 1/(σδ). Substituting σ = 5.8 × 10⁷ S/m and δ = 98.51 × 10⁻⁶ m gives σδ = 5713 S, so Rs = 1.750 × 10⁻⁴ Ω per square, or 0.175 mΩ. This is the resistance of a square of the sheet to current flowing in a layer one skin depth thick, and it is independent of the size of the square. It governs the loss when interference currents are induced in the lining.

Answer: Rs = 0.175 mΩ

(d)

The amplitude of a wave in the conductor falls as e-t/δ. With t = 0.100 mm = 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ m and δ = 98.51 × 10⁻⁶ m, t/δ = 1.0151. The remaining fraction is e-1.0151 = 0.3624, or 36.2 percent. In decibels this is only 8.8 dB of absorption loss, far short of the 60 dB the cabinet needs. The scrap piece, being barely one skin depth thick, would therefore be a poor shield on absorption alone. The comparison shows why thickness in skin depths, not in millimetres, is the design variable.

Answer: 36.2 percent

Problem 3 [A7-033] Reflection and transmission at media boundaries

A 10 GHz radar sensor looks through a flat window of lossless, non-magnetic glass with relative permittivity εr = 9.00. The wave arrives from air at normal incidence. Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. To reduce the reflection, the designer proposes to bond a single lossless, non-magnetic matching layer to the front face of the glass, between the air and the glass, with a thickness chosen so that the layer behaves as a quarter-wave transformer at 10 GHz. Treat air as free space. The layer and glass are both very thick compared with the loss mechanisms, which can be neglected, and the glass is taken as semi-infinite for this analysis.

  1. (a) Find the reflection coefficient Γ at the bare air-to-glass boundary (real number, with sign). [4]
  2. (b) Find the relative permittivity the quarter-wave matching layer must have. [4]
  3. (c) Find the physical thickness of the matching layer, in millimetres. [5]
  4. (d) Find the percentage of incident power that is transmitted into the bare glass with no matching layer. [3]
  5. (e) Explain briefly why this single-layer match works well only over a limited band of frequencies. [4]
(a)

For normal incidence the reflection coefficient of the electric field is Γ = (η2 - η1)/(η2 + η1). Air has η1 = η0. The glass is non-magnetic, so η2 = η0/√εr = η0/3. Then Γ = (η0/3 - η0)/(η0/3 + η0) = (1/3 - 1)/(1/3 + 1) = (-2/3)/(4/3) = -0.500. The negative sign means the reflected electric field is phase-reversed relative to the incident field, as expected when a wave enters a medium with higher permittivity and so lower impedance. The reflected amplitude is half of the incident amplitude.

Answer: Γ = -0.500

(b)

A quarter-wave transformer matches two real impedances when its characteristic impedance is the geometric mean, η_layer = √(η1 η2). Here η1 = η0 and η2 = η0/3, so η_layer = η0/√3. Because the layer is non-magnetic, η_layer = η0/√εr,layer, which gives √εr,layer = √3 and εr,layer = 3.00. Equivalently the refractive index of the layer is the geometric mean of the indices of air (1) and glass (3), which is √3 = 1.732. A material with a permittivity of 3 is realistic, for example a filled polymer, so the design can be built.

Answer: εr,layer = 3.00

(c)

The layer must be one quarter of a wavelength thick, measured inside the layer. The free-space wavelength is λ0 = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 10 × 10⁹ = 30.0 mm. Inside the layer the wavelength is λ = λ0/√εr,layer = 30.0/1.732 = 17.32 mm. The thickness is t = λ/4 = 17.32/4 = 4.33 mm. A quarter-wave round trip adds 180 degrees of phase, so the reflection from the layer-glass interface cancels the reflection from the air-layer interface when their magnitudes are equal, which the choice in part (b) guarantees.

Answer: t = 4.33 mm

(d)

The fraction of power reflected is |Γ|² = 0.500² = 0.250. Because both media are lossless, the fraction transmitted is 1 - |Γ|² = 0.750, so 75.0 percent of the incident power enters the glass. The transmitted power fraction is not simply the square of the transmission coefficient, because the power flux also depends on the impedance of the second medium; using the power balance on the reflection coefficient avoids that error.
