With the quarter-wave layer in place at the design frequency, the transmitted fraction rises to 100 percent.

Answer: 75.0 percent

(e)

The layer is exactly a quarter wavelength thick only at the design frequency. When the frequency moves away from 10 GHz, the electrical thickness of the layer changes in proportion, so the two reflected waves no longer arrive exactly 180 degrees apart and cancellation is only partial. The input impedance seen looking into the layer then departs from η0, and a residual reflection appears. For a single layer the useful bandwidth is therefore narrow. Wider bands need several layers, a graded permittivity profile, or a layer whose thickness is an odd multiple of a quarter wave only at the centre frequency. Loss in the layer also changes the match slightly.

Answer: Non-numeric explanation

Problem 4 [A7-034] Polarization of waves

A 10 GHz plane wave travels in the +z direction in free space. At the plane z = 0 its electric field is E = x̂ Ex cos(ωt) + ŷ Ey cos(ωt), so the two components are in phase and the wave is linearly polarized. To convert it, the wave passes through a flat anisotropic plate with its two principal axes along x and y. The refractive index is n1 along x and n2 along y, with n2 - n1 = 0.300, so the y component is the slower one. The plate is lossless and reflections can be ignored. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. The plate is cut so the wave leaving it has a 90 degree phase difference between its y and x components, with the y component lagging the x component. The input amplitudes are Ex = 5.00 V/m and Ey = 3.00 V/m.

  1. (a) Find the minimum plate thickness that produces a 90 degree phase difference, in millimetres. [5]
  2. (b) Find the axial ratio (major axis over minor axis, at least 1) of the polarization ellipse leaving the plate. [3]
  3. (c) Decompose the output into a right-hand and a left-hand circularly polarized pair. What percentage of the total power is in the weaker rotation sense? [6]
  4. (d) A circularly polarized receiving antenna is matched to the stronger rotation sense and rejects the other completely. Find the polarization mismatch loss, as a positive number of decibels. [6]
(a)

The two components accumulate phase at different rates in the plate: δφ = (2π/λ0)(n2 - n1) d, the extra phase picked up by the slower y component, so y lags x, where λ0 is the free-space wavelength. Here λ0 = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 10 × 10⁹ = 30.0 mm. Setting δφ = π/2 gives d = λ0/(4 (n2 - n1)) = 30.0 / (4 × 0.300) = 25.0 mm. Thicker plates that give 90 degrees plus a whole number of full turns (360 degrees) would also work, but this is the minimum. Adding a half-turn would give 270 degrees of lag and reverse the handedness. A plate producing a quarter-wave phase difference is called a quarter-wave plate. It is the standard way to make a circularly or elliptically polarized wave from a linear one.

Answer: d = 25.0 mm

(b)

After the plate the field is E = x̂ Ex cos(ωt) + ŷ Ey cos(ωt - 90°) = x̂ Ex cos(ωt) + ŷ Ey sin(ωt). With the phase difference of exactly 90 degrees, the polarization ellipse has its axes along x and y, so the semi-axes are simply Ex = 5.00 and Ey = 3.00 V/m. The axial ratio is the major over the minor semi-axis: AR = 5.00/3.00 = 1.667. The wave is elliptically polarized, since the amplitudes are unequal. Had the amplitudes been equal it would have been circular with AR = 1. The tip of E traces the ellipse once per period.

Answer: AR = 1.667

(c)

Write the field as the sum of two counter-rotating circular components with amplitudes (a + b)/2 and (a - b)/2, where a = Ex and b = Ey. Check: x̂ a cos θ + ŷ b sin θ = ((a+b)/2)(x̂ cos θ + ŷ sin θ) + ((a-b)/2)(x̂ cos θ - ŷ sin θ). The amplitudes are (5+3)/2 = 4.00 V/m and (5-3)/2 = 1.00 V/m. The power in each circular component is proportional to its amplitude squared: 16 and 1. Total is 17, which equals (a² + b²)/2 = 34/2, confirming the decomposition. The weaker sense carries 1/17 = 0.0588 of the power, or 5.88 percent.

Answer: 5.88 percent

(d)

An ideal circularly polarized receiver matched to the stronger sense accepts only that component. The fraction of power delivered is 16/17 = 0.9412. The polarization loss factor is therefore 0.9412, and the mismatch loss is -10 log10(0.9412) = 0.2633 dB, about 0.263 dB. This is small because the ellipse is not far from circular. If the receiver were instead matched to a linear x polarization, it would accept only Ex²/(Ex² + Ey²) = 25/34 of the power, a loss of 1.34 dB, so the circular receiver is the better choice here.

Answer: 0.263 dB

Problem 5 [A7-035] Transmission line equations and characteristic impedance

A 75 Ω video coaxial cable is to be specified for a studio distribution system. The designer treats it as lossless, so the distributed resistance and conductance are negligible, with series inductance L′ per metre and shunt capacitance C′ per metre. The cable must have characteristic impedance Z0 = 75.0 Ω and a wave propagation velocity of 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s. A short length of the cable is to be used as a quarter-wave impedance transformer at 100 MHz. The far end of that length is terminated in a purely resistive load of 150 Ω. Assume the velocity is the same at all frequencies of interest, so the cable is non-dispersive.

  1. (a) Find the required inductance per metre L′, in nanohenries per metre. [4]
  2. (b) Find the required capacitance per metre C′, in picofarads per metre. [4]
  3. (c) Find the length of the cable that is one quarter of a wavelength at 100 MHz, in metres. [5]
  4. (d) Find the input impedance seen at the generator end of that quarter-wave length when the far end carries the 150 Ω load. [4]
  5. (e) Find the one-way propagation delay of that length, in nanoseconds. [3]
(a)

For a lossless line, Z0 = √(L′/C′) and the velocity is v = 1/√(L′C′). Dividing the first relation by the second gives Z0/v = √(L′/C′) × √(L′C′) = L′, hence L′ = Z0/v. Substituting Z0 = 75.0 Ω and v = 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s gives L′ = 75.0 / 2.00 × 10⁸ = 3.75 × 10⁻⁷ H/m = 375 nH/m. A check: √(L′C′) must equal 1/v = 5.00 ns/m, which part (b) will confirm. This inductance corresponds to the magnetic flux linking the cable per metre of length.

Answer: L′ = 375 nH/m

(b)

From the same two relations, the product Z0 × v = √(L′/C′)/√(L′C′) = 1/C′, hence C′ = 1/(Z0 v). Substituting Z0 = 75.0 Ω and v = 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s gives C′ = 1/(75.0 × 2.00 × 10⁸) = 6.667 × 10⁻¹¹ F/m = 66.7 pF/m. Check: √(L′/C′) = √(3.75 × 10⁻⁷ / 6.667 × 10⁻¹¹) = √5625 = 75.0 Ω, and 1/√(L′C′) = 1/√(2.5 × 10⁻¹⁷) = 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s, so both specifications are met together by the same pair of per-metre values.

Answer: C′ = 66.7 pF/m

(c)

The wavelength on the line is λ = v/f = 2.00 × 10⁸ / 1.00 × 10⁸ = 2.00 m at 100 MHz. A quarter wavelength is therefore λ/4 = 0.500 m. At this length the electrical phase shift is βℓ = π/2, where β = 2π/λ = π rad/m. Because the velocity of the cable is only two thirds of the free-space speed, a quarter-wave length of this cable is shorter than a free-space quarter wavelength, which would be 0.75 m. The physical length is what the installer must cut.

Answer: 0.500 m

(d)

For a lossless line of length ℓ the input impedance is Zin = Z0 (ZL + jZ0 tan βℓ)/(Z0 + jZL tan βℓ). At a quarter wavelength tan βℓ becomes infinite and the expression reduces to Zin = Z0²/ZL. With Z0 = 75.0 Ω and ZL = 150 Ω, Zin = 5625/150 = 37.5 Ω. The line inverts the load impedance about the characteristic impedance: a load larger than Z0 appears smaller. This is the property exploited in quarter-wave matching. Because the answer is real, the transformer presents a purely resistive 37.5 Ω to the generator at 100 MHz.

Answer: Zin = 37.5 Ω

(e)

The delay of a wave travelling the length ℓ at speed v is τ = ℓ/v. Substituting ℓ = 0.500 m and v = 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s gives τ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁹ s = 2.50 ns. As a check, a quarter period of a 100 MHz wave is T/4 = 10 ns/4 = 2.5 ns, so the delay equals a quarter of the period, consistent with the 90 degree phase shift found in part (c). Because the line is non-dispersive, the same delay applies to all frequency components of a video signal, so it does not distort the waveform.

Answer: 2.50 ns

A7 Practice Paper 8

Problem 1 [A7-036] Standing waves, VSWR and reflection coefficient

A technician is testing the feed line to an antenna on a 146 MHz repeater site. The line is lossless with characteristic impedance Z0 = 50.0 Ω. A slotted-line probe measures a voltage standing wave ratio of 2.50. The first voltage minimum on the line is found 0.180 wavelengths from the antenna terminals, measured toward the generator. The site specification requires a return loss of at least 10 dB at the antenna. Use the convention that the reflection coefficient at the load is Γ = |Γ| ejθ, and that the voltage minimum occurs where the reflected and incident voltage phasors are exactly opposed. All distances are in wavelengths of the line.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude |Γ| of the load reflection coefficient. [3]
  2. (b) Find the phase angle θ of Γ at the load, in degrees (negative value). [4]
  3. (c) Find the real part of the load impedance ZL, in ohms. [5]
  4. (d) Find the imaginary part (reactance) of the load impedance, in ohms, as a signed number. [5]
  5. (e) Find the return loss in decibels, as a positive number, and note whether the specification is met. [3]
(a)

The standing wave ratio is related to the reflection coefficient magnitude by S = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 - |Γ|). Rearranging gives |Γ| = (S - 1)/(S + 1). With S = 2.50, |Γ| = 1.50/3.50 = 0.4286. This is a substantial mismatch: about 43 percent of the incident voltage amplitude is reflected. The magnitude of Γ is the same at every point of a lossless line, which is why it can be found from the standing wave ratio measured anywhere along it. The phase of Γ, by contrast, changes with position and must be found from the minimum location.

Answer: |Γ| = 0.4286

(b)

At a distance d from the load toward the generator, the reflection coefficient is Γ(d) = Γ_L e-j2βd. A voltage minimum occurs where Γ(d) = -|Γ|, that is where the phase is -π (or π). So θ - 2βd = -π, giving θ = 2βd - π. With d = 0.180 λ, 2βd = 4π × 0.180 = 0.720π rad = 129.6°. Then θ = 129.6° - 180° = -50.4°. The load reflection coefficient is therefore 0.4286 ∠ -50.4°. A negative angle indicates the load is capacitive in character at this frequency, which part (d) will confirm.

Answer: θ = -50.4°

(c)

The load impedance follows from ZL = Z0 (1 + Γ)/(1 - Γ). With Γ = 0.4286 ∠ -50.4° = 0.2734 - j0.3300, the numerator is 1.2734 - j0.3300 and the denominator is 0.7266 + j0.3300. Multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator (0.7266 - j0.3300), the denominator becomes 0.7266² + 0.3300² = 0.6368. The numerator becomes (1.2734 × 0.7266 - 0.3300 × 0.3300) - j(1.2734 × 0.3300 + 0.3300 × 0.7266) = 0.8156 - j0.6600, which gives ZL/Z0 = 1.2809 - j1.0363. Multiplying by 50.0 Ω gives RL = 64.0 Ω for the real part.

Answer: RL = 64.0 Ω

(d)

Using the same quotient, ZL/Z0 = (1 + Γ)/(1 - Γ) = (1.2734 - j0.3300)/(0.7266 + j0.3300). Dividing the complex numbers gives the normalized value 1.2809 - j1.0363. The imaginary part times Z0 = 50.0 Ω is XL = -51.8 Ω, so ZL = 64.0 - j51.8 Ω. The negative reactance confirms the capacitive nature of the load, matching the negative phase angle of Γ. A series inductor of about 51.8 Ω reactance at 146 MHz, which is roughly 56.5 nH, would cancel the reactance and leave a 64 Ω resistive load, a modest improvement in match.

Answer: XL = -51.8 Ω

(e)

Return loss is RL = -20 log10|Γ| dB, a positive quantity for a passive load. With |Γ| = 0.4286, RL = -20 log10(0.4286) = 7.36 dB. The requirement is at least 10 dB, which corresponds to |Γ| ≤ 0.316 and a standing wave ratio of at most 1.92. The measured value of 7.36 dB falls short, so the specification is not met. The fraction of power reflected is |Γ|² = 0.1837, or 18.4 percent, which would be delivered back toward the transmitter rather than radiated. Matching or antenna repair is required.

Answer: 7.36 dB, not met

Problem 2 [A7-037] Smith chart and impedance matching

A 900 MHz telemetry antenna presents a load impedance ZL = 100 - j60 Ω at the end of a lossless 50.0 Ω line. A single shunt stub made from a short-circuited length of the same line is to be placed a distance d from the load, on the generator side, so that the line is matched to the generator. The line has a velocity factor of 0.660, so the wave velocity is 0.660 × 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s. Choose the shortest d (measured from the load) for which the real part of the normalized admittance equals 1. Do the work analytically, or with a Smith chart if preferred, and give normalized admittance as y = Y/Y0 with Y0 = 1/Z0. The shunt stub contributes only a susceptance.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the load reflection coefficient |Γ_L|. [3]
  2. (b) Find the shortest distance d from the load to the stub position, in wavelengths. [5]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the normalized susceptance that the stub must supply. [4]
  4. (d) Find the length of the short-circuited stub that supplies it, in wavelengths (shortest positive length). [5]
  5. (e) Find the physical length of the stub, in millimetres. [3]
(a)

The load reflection coefficient is Γ_L = (ZL - Z0)/(ZL + Z0) = (100 - j60 - 50)/(100 - j60 + 50) = (50 - j60)/(150 - j60). Its magnitude is |50 - j60|/|150 - j60| = 78.10/161.55 = 0.4834. The angle is -28.4° (about -0.4956 rad). On a Smith chart this would be the point at normalized impedance 2 - j1.2, lying at radius 0.483 from the centre of the chart. Moving from this point toward the generator is a clockwise rotation along the constant |Γ| circle, which is what the stub placement requires.

Answer: |Γ_L| = 0.4834

(b)

Work with admittance because the stub is in shunt. The normalized load admittance is yL = 1/zL = 1/(2 - j1.2) = (2 + j1.2)/(4 + 1.44) = 0.3676 + j0.2206. At distance d toward the generator, y(d) = (yL + j t)/(1 + j t yL), with t = tan(2πd/λ). We need Re y(d) = 1. Solving, there are two roots within half a wavelength: d = 0.1257 λ, where y = 1 + j1.1045, and d = 0.2954 λ, where y = 1 - j1.1045. The question asks for the shortest d, so the answer is 0.1257 λ, and the second root is the alternative placement.

Answer: d = 0.1257 λ

(c)

At the stub position d = 0.1257 λ the line admittance is y = 1 + j1.1045. The stub is in parallel and must cancel the imaginary part, so the stub must present y_stub = -j1.1045. The magnitude of the required normalized susceptance is therefore |b| = 1.1045, and its sign is negative, which is inductive. After adding the stub the total normalized admittance at that point is exactly 1 + j0, and the line to the generator side sees a perfect match, with a standing wave ratio of 1. The stub does not change the real part, because an ideal short-circuited line is purely reactive.

Answer: |b| = 1.105

(d)

The input admittance of a short-circuited line of length ℓ is y = -j cot(βℓ). We need -j cot(βℓ) = -j1.1045, so cot(βℓ) = +1.1045 and tan(βℓ) = 0.9054. The shortest positive angle is βℓ = 0.7355 rad. Since βℓ = 2π ℓ/λ, ℓ/λ = 0.7355/(2π) = 0.1171 λ. A short-circuited stub shorter than a quarter wave is inductive, so a length below 0.25 λ is consistent with the inductive susceptance required at this position. As a check, cot(0.7355 rad) = 1.105, which reproduces the required susceptance magnitude, and the stub length of 0.1171 λ is well under the quarter wave.

Answer: ℓ = 0.1171 λ

(e)

The wave velocity is 0.660 × 2.998 × 10⁸ = 1.979 × 10⁸ m/s, so the wavelength on the line at 900 MHz is λ = v/f = 1.979 × 10⁸ / 9.00 × 10⁸ = 0.2199 m. The physical stub length is ℓ = 0.1171 × 0.2199 = 0.02575 m = 25.7 mm. For reference, the stub position is d = 0.1257 × 0.2199 = 27.6 mm from the load. Tolerances matter: an error of 1 mm in stub length changes the length by 0.0045 λ, which shifts the stub susceptance and leaves a small residual mismatch. A cut-and-try check with a network analyser would normally follow.

Answer: 25.7 mm

Problem 3 [A7-038] Waveguides: modes and cutoff

An air-filled rectangular waveguide is to be designed for a 9.50 GHz radar feed. The inside cross-section has width a and height b with a = 2b. The designer requires that the dominant TE10 mode propagates at 9.50 GHz with the operating frequency equal to 1.25 times the TE10 cutoff frequency, so that the guide is not too close to cutoff. Use c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s and treat the walls as perfect conductors. Modes are labelled TEmn, with cutoff fc,mn = (c/2)√((m/a)² + (n/b)²). You may assume the guide is lossless and that only the dominant mode is excited at the input.

  1. (a) Find the required guide width a, in millimetres. [5]
  2. (b) Find the cutoff frequency of the next-higher mode, in gigahertz. [3]
  3. (c) Find the guide wavelength λg at 9.50 GHz, in millimetres. [4]
  4. (d) Find the phase velocity of the TE10 wave at 9.50 GHz, in units of 10⁸ m/s. [4]
  5. (e) Find the group velocity of the TE10 wave at 9.50 GHz, in units of 10⁸ m/s. [4]
(a)

The TE10 cutoff of an air-filled guide is fc,10 = c/(2a). The requirement is f = 1.25 fc,10, so fc,10 = 9.50/1.25 = 7.60 GHz. Solving for the width, a = c/(2 fc,10) = 2.998 × 10⁸ / (2 × 7.60 × 10⁹) = 0.019724 m = 19.72 mm. With a = 2b the height is b = 9.86 mm. The width fixes the lowest cutoff, and the height only affects higher modes and power capacity. This width is close to a standard X-band guide, which is a sensible check on the result.

Answer: a = 19.72 mm

(b)

With a = 19.724 mm and b = 9.862 mm, the candidate higher modes are TE20, with fc,20 = c/a = 15.2 GHz, and TE01, with fc,01 = c/(2b) = 15.2 GHz. These two are equal because a = 2b, so TE20 and TE01 share the second-lowest cutoff. TE11 is higher still, at (c/2)√(1/a² + 1/b²) = 17.0 GHz. The next cutoff is therefore 15.2 GHz, twice the dominant cutoff. The guide is single-mode from 7.60 GHz to 15.2 GHz, which comfortably includes the 9.50 GHz operating frequency.

Answer: 15.2 GHz

(c)

The guide wavelength is λg = λ0/√(1 - (fc/f)²). The free-space wavelength is λ0 = c/f = 2.998 × 10⁸ / 9.50 × 10⁹ = 31.56 mm. The ratio fc/f = 1/1.25 = 0.800, so √(1 - 0.64) = 0.600. Then λg = 31.56/0.600 = 52.59 mm. The guide wavelength is always longer than the free-space wavelength, since the wave bounces between the side walls and advances more slowly in phase along the guide axis. This longer wavelength sets, for example, the spacing of slots in a slotted waveguide array.

Answer: λg = 52.6 mm

(d)

The phase velocity along the guide is vp = ω/β = c/√(1 - (fc/f)²). With √(1 - 0.64) = 0.600, vp = 2.998 × 10⁸/0.600 = 4.997 × 10⁸ m/s. This exceeds the speed of light, which is not a violation of relativity because phase velocity is the speed of the pattern of constant phase, not the speed of energy or information. As a check, vp = f λg = 9.50 × 10⁹ × 0.05259 = 4.996 × 10⁸ m/s, in agreement within rounding.

Answer: vp = 4.997 × 10⁸ m/s

(e)

The group velocity, the speed at which energy and information travel, is vg = c √(1 - (fc/f)²). Substituting 0.600 gives vg = 2.998 × 10⁸ × 0.600 = 1.799 × 10⁸ m/s. The product vp vg = 4.997 × 10⁸ × 1.799 × 10⁸ = 8.99 × 10¹⁶ m²/s², which equals c², a useful relation for any hollow guide. Group velocity is below c, as it must be. It approaches zero at cutoff and approaches c as the frequency rises far above cutoff.

Answer: vg = 1.799 × 10⁸ m/s

Problem 4 [A7-039] Radiation from a Hertzian dipole and antenna basics

A short vertical radiator for a 1.00 MHz medium-wave beacon is modelled as a Hertzian dipole of length 5.00 m carrying a uniform current of peak value I0. The dipole is in free space, with η0 = 376.73 Ω and c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s. A Hertzian dipole of length dℓ has radiated power Prad = 40π² (dℓ/λ)² I0² for peak current I0, and a directivity of 1.50 in its direction of maximum radiation. The beacon must radiate a total power of 100 W. A receiver sits on the equatorial plane of the dipole (the direction of maximum radiation) at a distance of 10.0 km. Ground effects are neglected throughout.

  1. (a) Find the radiation resistance of the dipole, in ohms. [4]
  2. (b) Find the peak current I0 required to radiate 100 W. [5]
  3. (c) Find the power density at the receiver, in nanowatts per square metre. [5]
  4. (d) Find the peak electric field strength at the receiver, in millivolts per metre. [6]
(a)

The radiation resistance is defined by Prad = ½ I0² Rrad. Comparing with the given Prad = 40π² (dℓ/λ)² I0² gives Rrad = 80π² (dℓ/λ)². The wavelength is λ = c/f = 2.998 × 10⁸/1.00 × 10⁶ = 299.8 m, so dℓ/λ = 5.00/299.8 = 0.016678 and its square is 2.782 × 10⁻⁴. Then Rrad = 789.57 × 2.782 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.2196 Ω. The dipole is electrically very short, only 1/60 of a wavelength, so the radiation resistance is tiny. This makes the dipole very hard to match and inefficient unless loss resistance is kept far below 0.22 Ω.

Answer: Rrad = 0.2196 Ω

(b)

From Prad = ½ I0² Rrad, the peak current is I0 = √(2 Prad/Rrad). With Prad = 100 W and Rrad = 0.2196 Ω, I0 = √(200/0.2196) = √910.7 = 30.18 A. That is a peak value, equivalent to about 21.3 A rms. Such a current through even 0.5 Ω of loss resistance would dissipate about 228 W, more than the radiated power, which shows why short beacon antennas rely on very low-loss ground systems and loading coils. The current is large because the radiation resistance is small.

Answer: I0 = 30.2 A

(c)

For a source radiating total power Prad with directivity D in the direction considered, the power density at distance r is S = Prad D/(4π r²). Substituting Prad = 100 W, D = 1.50 and r = 10.0 × 10³ m gives S = 150/(4π × 1.0 × 10⁸) = 150/1.2566 × 10⁹ = 1.194 × 10⁻⁷ W/m² = 119.4 nW/m². The distance is far larger than the wavelength (299.8 m), so the far-field formula applies. Along the dipole axis the density would be zero, since a Hertzian dipole has a null there.

Answer: 119 nW/m²

(d)

In the far field the power density of a plane wave with peak electric field E0 is S = E0²/(2η0). Solving, E0 = √(2 η0 S). Substituting η0 = 376.73 Ω and S = 1.194 × 10⁻⁷ W/m² gives E0 = √(2 × 376.73 × 1.194 × 10⁻⁷) = √(8.995 × 10⁻⁵) = 9.484 × 10⁻³ V/m = 9.48 mV/m. As a cross-check, the standard field strength for 1 kW from a short monopole at 1 km is about 300 mV/m rms, which scales to a figure of the same order for this lower power and longer distance.

Answer: 9.48 mV/m

Problem 5 [A7-040] Link budget or shielding design using field concepts

A 35.0 km line-of-sight microwave link at 11.0 GHz connects two towers in northern Ontario. Both parabolic antennas have gains of 30.0 dBi, the transmitter output is 2.00 W, and the total waveguide and connector loss for the pair of ends is 2.00 dB. The receiver has a noise bandwidth of 20.0 MHz and a noise figure of 4.00 dB. Use c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s, Boltzmann's constant k = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K and a reference temperature of 290 K. Take free-space propagation with no other losses in clear air. During heavy rain an extra fade of 10.0 dB occurs. The link requires a signal-to-noise ratio of at least 25.0 dB even during the rain fade. Powers in dBm are referred to 1 mW.

  1. (a) Find the free-space path loss, in decibels. [4]
  2. (b) Find the received signal power in clear air, in dBm. [4]
  3. (c) Find the receiver noise power referred to the input, in dBm. [4]
  4. (d) Find the clear-air signal-to-noise ratio, in decibels. [4]
  5. (e) Find the minimum transmitter power, in watts, that still gives 25.0 dB during the 10.0 dB rain fade. [4]
(a)

The free-space path loss between isotropic antennas is Lp = 20 log10(4π d/λ). The wavelength is λ = c/f = 2.998 × 10⁸ / 11.0 × 10⁹ = 0.027255 m. Then 4π d/λ = 4π × 35 000 / 0.027255 = 1.6138 × 10⁷, and 20 log10 of this is 144.16 dB. This is the loss between ideal isotropic antennas; the antenna gains are accounted for separately in the link equation. The path loss grows by 6 dB each time the distance doubles, and by 6 dB each time the frequency doubles.

Answer: 144.2 dB

(b)

The received power in decibel form is Pr = Pt + Gt + Gr - Lp - Ls. The transmit power is 2.00 W = 33.01 dBm. Adding gains of 30.0 + 30.0 dBi gives 93.01 dBm, then subtracting the path loss 144.16 dB gives -51.15 dBm, and subtracting the 2.00 dB feed loss gives Pr = -53.15 dBm. This is about 4.8 × 10⁻⁶ mW, or 4.8 nanowatts. The value is typical for terrestrial microwave links and well above the threshold sensitivity of a good receiver, which is what part (d) quantifies.

Answer: Pr = -53.2 dBm

(c)

The thermal noise power available in bandwidth B is N = kT0B, which is -174 dBm/Hz at 290 K, plus 10 log10(B). With B = 20.0 MHz, 10 log10(2.0 × 10⁷) = 73.01 dB, so kT0B = -174 + 73.01 = -100.99 dBm. The noise figure of 4.00 dB raises the effective noise power referred to the input, giving N = -100.99 + 4.00 = -96.99 dBm. A direct check of kT0B: 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ × 290 × 2.0 × 10⁷ = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ W = -100.97 dBm, consistent with the dBm/Hz shortcut.

Answer: N = -97.0 dBm

(d)

The signal-to-noise ratio in decibels is simply the difference of the signal and noise powers in dBm. SNR = Pr - N = -53.15 - (-96.99) = 43.84 dB. That is a power ratio of about 24 000 to 1. The clear-air margin above the required 25.0 dB is 18.8 dB, which is the margin available to cover the rain fade, any equipment ageing, and multipath effects. Since the rain fade is only 10.0 dB, the link holds comfortably with the present transmitter.

Answer: SNR = 43.8 dB

(e)

During rain the received power falls by 10.0 dB, and the requirement is SNR = 25.0 dB. The needed received power is Pr = N + 25.0 = -96.99 + 25.0 = -71.99 dBm. Working back through the link budget, Pt(dBm) = Pr + Lp + Ls + fade - Gt - Gr = -71.99 + 144.16 + 2.00 + 10.0 - 60.0 = 24.17 dBm. In watts, 1024.17/10 mW = 261 mW = 0.261 W. The existing 2.00 W transmitter therefore exceeds the minimum by 8.8 dB, which is the same as the clear-air margin less the fade. A smaller, cheaper transmitter would suffice.

Answer: Pt = 0.261 W

A7 Practice Paper 9

Problem 1 [A7-041] Vector calculus and coordinate systems for fields

A sensor cell in a plasma-etching chamber is modelled with a force field acting on a charged test particle. With x, y and z in metres, a colleague proposes the field F1 = (2xy + z²) a_x + (x² + 3z) a_y + (2xz + 3y) a_z newtons. After a design change the y-component is altered, giving F2 = (2xy + z²) a_x + (x² + 5z) a_y + (2xz + 3y) a_z newtons, with the x and z components unchanged. A technician suspects that F2 is no longer conservative and asks you to diagnose the change. Use Cartesian coordinates with unit vectors a_x, a_y, a_z. For the circulation test, take the rectangular loop lying in the plane x = 1 m with corners (y, z) = (0, 0), (0.4, 0), (0.4, 0.5) and (0, 0.5) m, traversed in that order, so that by the right-hand rule its normal is +a_x.

  1. (a) Find the divergence of F1 at the point (1, 2, 3) m. [3]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the curl of F2, and state whether F2 is conservative. [5]
  3. (c) Evaluate the circulation of F2 around the stated loop by direct line integration along the four sides. [6]
  4. (d) Show that F1 is conservative, find its scalar potential φ with F1 = ∇φ and φ(0,0,0) = 0, and give the work done by F1 on the particle moving from the origin to (1, 2, 3) m. [6]
(a)

The divergence in Cartesian coordinates is ∇·F = ∂Fx/∂x + ∂Fy/∂y + ∂Fz/∂z. For F1, Fx = 2xy + z², so ∂Fx/∂x = 2y. Fy = x² + 3z does not depend on y, so ∂Fy/∂y = 0. Fz = 2xz + 3y, so ∂Fz/∂z = 2x. Therefore ∇·F1 = 2y + 2x. Substituting x = 1 and y = 2 gives 2(2) + 2(1) = 6. The z-coordinate does not appear, so the value is the same anywhere on the line x = 1, y = 2. The units are newtons per metre, which is the net outward force flux per unit volume.

Answer: 6 N/m

(b)

The curl components are (∇×F)x = ∂Fz/∂y − ∂Fy/∂z, (∇×F)y = ∂Fx/∂z − ∂Fz/∂x and (∇×F)z = ∂Fy/∂x − ∂Fx/∂y. For F2: ∂Fz/∂y = 3 and ∂Fy/∂z = 5, so the x-component is 3 − 5 = −2. ∂Fx/∂z = 2z and ∂Fz/∂x = 2z, so the y-component is 0. ∂Fy/∂x = 2x and ∂Fx/∂y = 2x, so the z-component is 0. Hence ∇×F2 = −2 a_x N/m everywhere, magnitude 2 N/m. Because the curl is not zero, F2 is not conservative. The design change from 3z to 5z in the y-component is the sole cause, since the original coefficient 3 cancelled the 3y term in Fz exactly.

Answer: 2 N/m, not conservative

(c)

Take x = 1, so Fy = 1 + 5z and Fz = 2z + 3y on the loop. Side 1 runs from (0,0) to (0.4,0) with z = 0: ∫Fy dy = ∫0.4 of 1 dy = 0.4 J. Side 2 runs to (0.4,0.5) with y = 0.4: ∫Fz dz = ∫(2z + 1.2)dz from 0 to 0.5 = 0.25 + 0.6 = 0.85 J. Side 3 returns to (0,0.5) with z = 0.5: Fy = 3.5, ∫Fy dy = 3.5(−0.4) = −1.4 J. Side 4 returns to the start with y = 0: ∫2z dz from 0.5 to 0 = −0.25 J. The sum is 0.4 + 0.85 − 1.4 − 0.25 = −0.4 J. Stokes' theorem check: curl·n × area = (−2)(0.4 × 0.5) = −0.4 J, which agrees.

Answer: -0.4 J

(d)

For F1 the curl components are (3 − 3) = 0, (2z − 2z) = 0 and (2x − 2x) = 0, so ∇×F1 = 0 and the field is conservative in this simply connected region. Integrate ∂φ/∂x = 2xy + z² to get φ = x²y + xz² + g(y,z). Then ∂φ/∂y = x² + ∂g/∂y must equal x² + 3z, so g = 3yz + h(z). Finally ∂φ/∂z = 2xz + 3y + h′(z) must equal 2xz + 3y, so h is constant, and φ(0,0,0) = 0 sets it to zero. Hence φ = x²y + xz² + 3yz. The work done by F1 is φ(1,2,3) − φ(0,0,0) = 2 + 9 + 18 = 29 J, independent of path.

Answer: 29 J

Problem 2 [A7-042] Electrostatics: Coulomb's law, Gauss's law and potential

A charged water droplet in a spray-painting booth is modelled as a solid insulating sphere of radius a = 0.10 m carrying a total charge Q = 8.0 nC spread uniformly through its volume, in free space with ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m. A process engineer reports that the measured potential at the droplet centre, relative to infinity, is higher than a model assuming all the charge sits on the surface. You are asked to diagnose the difference with numbers. Use spherical symmetry, take the potential at infinity as zero, and let r be the distance from the centre. Treat the sphere's permittivity as ε0 throughout so that no polarization effects arise inside it.

  1. (a) Using Gauss's law, find the electric field magnitude at r = 0.06 m inside the sphere. [5]
  2. (b) Find the electric field magnitude at r = 0.25 m outside the sphere. [3]
  3. (c) Find the potential at the centre of the uniformly charged sphere relative to infinity. [7]
  4. (d) What-if: the same charge Q is moved onto a thin conducting shell of radius 0.10 m. Find the centre potential and the ratio of the shell value to the uniform-sphere value. [5]
(a)

Choose a Gaussian sphere of radius r < a. Because the charge is uniform, the enclosed charge is Qenc = Q(r/a)³. Gauss's law gives E(4πr²) = Qenc/ε0, so E = Q r/(4π ε0 a³). Substituting Q = 8.0 × 10⁻⁹ C, r = 0.06 m, a = 0.10 m and 4π ε0 = 1.1127 × 10⁻¹⁰ gives E = (8.0 × 10⁻⁹ × 0.06)/(1.1127 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 10⁻³) = 4.31 × 10³ V/m. The field inside grows linearly with r, reaching a maximum at the surface, and points radially outward because the charge is positive.

Answer: 4.31 kV/m

(b)

For r > a the Gaussian sphere encloses the whole charge, so E = Q/(4π ε0 r²), exactly the point-charge result. With r = 0.25 m, r² = 0.0625 m², E = (8.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(1.1127 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.0625) = 1.150 × 10³ V/m. This is the same for a uniform sphere, a thin shell or a point charge of the same Q, since only the enclosed charge matters outside a spherically symmetric distribution. The check at the surface r = 0.10 m gives 7.19 kV/m from both the inside and outside formulas, which confirms continuity of the radial field for a volume charge.

Answer: 1.15 kV/m

(c)

The potential at the centre is V(0) = −∫ from ∞ to 0 of E dr, split in two regions. Outside: V(a) = Q/(4π ε0 a) = 8.0 × 10⁻⁹/(1.1127 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.10) = 719.0 V. Inside, V(0) − V(a) = ∫ from 0 to a of Q r/(4π ε0 a³) dr = Q/(8π ε0 a) = 359.5 V. Adding the two parts gives V(0) = 719.0 + 359.5 = 1078.5 V, which is 3Q/(8π ε0 a). The result is positive because the charge is positive and the reference is at infinity. The extra 359.5 V arises because a test charge must be pushed through the field inside the volume as well.

Answer: 1.08 kV

(d)

For a thin shell the field inside is zero, so the whole interior is an equipotential equal to the surface value. Hence V(0) = V(a) = Q/(4π ε0 a) = 719.0 V. The ratio to the uniform-sphere value is 719.0/1078.5 = 0.667, which equals 2/3 exactly because 3Q/(8π ε0 a) divided into Q/(4π ε0 a) gives 2/3. This diagnoses the engineer's report: the measured centre potential is 50 percent higher than the surface-charge model predicts, which is the signature of charge spread through the volume rather than held on the surface. Outside the droplet the two models give identical fields and potentials.

Answer: 719 V, ratio 0.667

Problem 3 [A7-043] Capacitance and dielectrics

A power-supply designer builds a parallel-plate capacitor from two square-ish plates of area A = 0.020 m² separated by a gap d = 2.0 mm in air (ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m). A rigid dielectric slab of thickness t = 1.2 mm and relative permittivity εr = 4.0 is slid in so that it fills the full plate area and rests against one plate, leaving an air gap of 0.8 mm. Neglect fringing. The capacitor is connected to a 500 V battery until fully charged. A technician then asks what happens if the battery is disconnected first and the slab is withdrawn completely, and the designer wants the voltage and the mechanical work involved to diagnose a flashover seen in the field.

  1. (a) Find the capacitance with the slab in place. [5]
  2. (b) Find the energy stored while the capacitor is connected to the 500 V battery with the slab in place. [4]
  3. (c) What-if: the battery is disconnected and the slab is withdrawn. Find the new voltage across the plates. [5]
  4. (d) Find the mechanical work that must be done to withdraw the slab, and explain in one or two sentences where it goes. [6]
(a)

The air gap and the dielectric layer act as two capacitors in series, so the total can be found from the equivalent gap d − t + t/εr = 2.0 mm − 1.2 mm + 1.2 mm/4.0 = 0.8 mm + 0.3 mm = 1.1 mm. Then C = ε0 A/(1.1 × 10⁻³) = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 0.020/1.1 × 10⁻³ = 1.610 × 10⁻¹⁰ F, about 161 pF. Equivalently the air portion is 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 0.020/0.8 × 10⁻³ = 221.4 pF and the slab portion is 4.0 × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 0.020/1.2 × 10⁻³ = 590.3 pF, and the series combination (221.4 × 590.3)/(811.7) gives the same 161 pF.

Answer: 161 pF

(b)

With the battery connected the voltage is fixed at 500 V, so the stored energy is W = ½CV² = 0.5 × 1.6098 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 500² = 0.5 × 1.6098 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 250000 = 2.012 × 10⁻⁵ J, or 20.1 μJ. The charge on the plates is Q = CV = 1.6098 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 500 = 8.05 × 10⁻⁸ C. The free-charge density on the plates is Q/A = 4.02 μC/m², and since D = σ is the same in the air and the slab, the field is higher in the air gap by a factor of εr = 4. That uneven field split is what matters later for breakdown.

Answer: 20.1 μJ

(c)

After the battery is disconnected the charge cannot leave the plates, so Q stays at 8.049 × 10⁻⁸ C. Withdrawing the slab leaves the all-air capacitance C0 = ε0 A/d = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 0.020/2.0 × 10⁻³ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹¹ F. The new voltage is V′ = Q/C0 = 8.049 × 10⁻⁸/8.854 × 10⁻¹¹ = 909.1 V. The voltage rises by a factor of 1.82 even though nothing was connected to the plates, because the capacitance fell by that factor at constant charge. The air field becomes 909.1/0.002 = 454.5 kV/m, close to the 3 MV/m air breakdown limit being approached from below.

Answer: 909 V

(d)

At constant charge the stored energy is W = Q²/(2C). Before withdrawal W1 = 2.012 × 10⁻⁵ J. After withdrawal W2 = ½Q²/C0 = 0.5 × (8.049 × 10⁻⁸)²/8.854 × 10⁻¹¹ = 3.659 × 10⁻⁵ J. The work done by the agent pulling the slab out is W2 − W1 = 3.659 × 10⁻⁵ − 2.012 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.646 × 10⁻⁵ J, about 16.5 μJ. This work is stored as extra electric field energy, since the dielectric is drawn into the field by a force that opposes its removal and no energy is dissipated in the isolated circuit.

Answer: 16.5 μJ

Problem 4 [A7-044] Boundary conditions and Laplace equation problems

A high-voltage test lead is modelled as a coaxial arrangement: a long cylindrical inner conductor of radius a at potential V0 = 1000 V, surrounded by a coaxial grounded cylindrical shield of fixed inner radius b = 10 mm, with air between them. Fringing and end effects are neglected, so the potential φ depends only on the radial distance ρ from the axis. The existing lead has a = 2.0 mm. A field failure has been traced to corona discharge at the inner conductor, and you are asked to diagnose how the peak field depends on the inner radius. Use Laplace's equation in cylindrical coordinates with the boundary conditions φ(a) = V0 and φ(b) = 0, and treat the inner conductor's surface as the location of the maximum field.

  1. (a) Solve Laplace's equation for the existing lead with a = 2.0 mm and find the potential at ρ = 5.0 mm. [5]
  2. (b) Find the electric field magnitude at the surface of the inner conductor for a = 2.0 mm. [4]
  3. (c) What-if: the inner radius is reduced to a = 1.0 mm with b unchanged. Find the surface field magnitude. [4]
  4. (d) Find the inner radius that minimises the surface field for fixed b and V0, and the value of that minimum field. [7]
(a)

Laplace's equation with radial symmetry is (1/ρ) d/dρ(ρ dφ/dρ) = 0. Integrating twice gives φ = A ln ρ + B. The conditions φ(a) = V0 and φ(b) = 0 give A = −V0/ln(b/a) and B = V0 ln b/ln(b/a), so φ(ρ) = V0 ln(b/ρ)/ln(b/a). For a = 2.0 mm and b = 10 mm, ln(b/a) = ln 5 = 1.6094. At ρ = 5.0 mm, ln(b/ρ) = ln 2 = 0.6931, so φ = 1000 × 0.6931/1.6094 = 430.7 V. The potential falls logarithmically, not linearly, which is why a straight-line interpolation (which would give 625 V here) would be wrong.

Answer: 431 V

(b)

The field is E = −∇φ = −dφ/dρ a_ρ = V0/(ρ ln(b/a)) a_ρ, directed outward from the inner conductor. At ρ = a = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m, E = 1000/(2.0 × 10⁻³ × 1.6094) = 3.107 × 10⁵ V/m, or 311 kV/m. The field varies as 1/ρ, so it is greatest at the inner surface and drops to 1000/(0.010 × 1.6094) = 62.1 kV/m at the shield. Since the surface charge density equals ε0 E, the highest charge concentration is also on the inner conductor, which is where corona forms first.

Answer: 311 kV/m

(c)

With a = 1.0 mm the logarithm becomes ln(b/a) = ln 10 = 2.3026. The surface field is E = V0/(a ln(b/a)) = 1000/(1.0 × 10⁻³ × 2.3026) = 4.343 × 10⁵ V/m, or 434 kV/m. Halving the radius raised the surface field by 40 percent, not 100 percent, because the extra logarithm in the denominator partly compensates. A thinner conductor concentrates the field more, so reducing a made the corona risk worse. The check is the ratio (2.0 × 1.6094)/(1.0 × 2.3026) = 1.398, matching 434/311.

Answer: 434 kV/m

(d)

The surface field is E(a) = V0/(a ln(b/a)). Let x = a/b, so E = V0/(b x ln(1/x)). Minimising E means maximising f(x) = x ln(1/x) = −x ln x. Then f′ = −ln x − 1 = 0 gives ln x = −1, x = 1/e = 0.3679, so a = b/e = 3.679 mm. The second derivative f″ = −1/x is negative, so this is a maximum of f and hence a minimum of E. At the optimum ln(b/a) = 1, so Emin = V0/a = V0 e/b = 1000 × 2.71828/0.010 = 2.718 × 10⁵ V/m, which is 272 kV/m. Both the 2.0 mm and 1.0 mm leads are below this radius and so operate above the minimum possible field.

Answer: a = 3.68 mm, 272 kV/m

Problem 5 [A7-045] Steady current, conductors and resistance fields

A utility substation ground electrode is modelled as a metal hemisphere of radius a = 0.15 m buried with its flat face flush with the surface of uniform soil of conductivity σ = 0.020 S/m. Current flows radially outward through the soil from the electrode to a remote ground at infinity, with the electrode's own resistance neglected. During a fault the electrode injects I = 100 A. After a dry summer the soil conductivity is found to have halved, and a protection engineer wants to diagnose how the ground potential rise and the hazard to people walking nearby have changed. Use the steady-current relation J = σE, with current density spreading over a hemispherical surface of radius r from the electrode centre.

  1. (a) Find the resistance between the electrode and remote ground for σ = 0.020 S/m. [5]
  2. (b) Find the ground potential rise of the electrode for I = 100 A in the original soil. [3]
  3. (c) What-if: σ halves to 0.010 S/m with the same fault current. Find the new ground potential rise. [5]
  4. (d) In the original soil, find the step voltage between two points on the surface at r = 1.0 m and r = 1.8 m from the electrode centre, and state the current density magnitude at r = 1.0 m in A/m². [7]
(a)

In soil the current spreads over a hemisphere of area 2π r², so J = I/(2π r²) and E = J/σ = I/(2π σ r²). The potential of the electrode relative to infinity is V = ∫ from a to ∞ of E dr = I/(2π σ a). The resistance is therefore R = V/I = 1/(2π σ a) = 1/(2π × 0.020 × 0.15) = 1/0.018850 = 53.05 Ω. Almost all of this resistance lies in the soil close to the electrode, because the integrand falls as 1/r². For example, the part of the soil between r = a and r = 2a contributes half of the total resistance.

Answer: 53.1 Ω

(b)

The ground potential rise is the potential of the electrode relative to remote ground, GPR = I R = 100 A × 53.05 Ω = 5305 V, about 5.31 kV. This is the voltage that appears between the electrode, and any metal connected to it, and a point far away. The surface potential at distance r from the centre is I/(2π σ r), which falls from 5.31 kV at the electrode surface to 530 V at r = 1.5 m. The size of this value shows why bonding and touch-voltage control matter at a substation, since a person touching connected metal while standing on distant soil experiences nearly the whole GPR.

Answer: 5.31 kV

(c)

Resistance varies inversely with conductivity, so with σ = 0.010 S/m the resistance doubles to R = 1/(2π × 0.010 × 0.15) = 106.1 Ω. For the same 100 A the potential rise is GPR = 100 × 106.1 = 10 610 V, about 10.6 kV. A real fault current would also fall a little with higher ground resistance, but with the current held at 100 A as stated, drying of the soil doubles every potential in the soil because all potentials scale as 1/σ. The diagnosis is that a seasonal change in soil moisture, which is outside the designer's control, can double the step and touch hazard without any change to the electrode.

Answer: 10.6 kV

(d)

The surface potential at radius r is V(r) = I/(2π σ r). The step voltage between r1 = 1.0 m and r2 = 1.8 m is ΔV = (I/(2π σ))(1/r1 − 1/r2) = (100/(2π × 0.020)) × (1/1.0 − 1/1.8) = 795.77 × (1.0 − 0.5556) = 795.77 × 0.4444 = 353.7 V. The current density at r = 1.0 m is J = I/(2π r²) = 100/(2π × 1.0²) = 15.92 A/m². The field there is J/σ = 796 V/m, so a 0.8 m stride across the steepest part sees about 354 V, which would be dangerous without control measures such as a gravel layer.

Answer: 354 V

A7 Practice Paper 10

Problem 1 [A7-046] Magnetostatics: Biot-Savart and Ampere's law

A magnetometer calibration rig uses two identical coaxial circular coils, each of radius R = 0.10 m with N = 50 turns, carrying the same current I = 2.0 A in the same sense, so the fields add on the common axis. The coils are placed in free space with permeability μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m, and the axial field from one thin coil of N turns at axial distance z from its plane is B = μ0 N I R²/(2(R² + z²)3/2). The rig was designed with spacing d = R, the Helmholtz arrangement, but after a mounting change the spacing has become d = 0.14 m. Take the midpoint between the coils as the origin and the coil planes at ± d/2 on the axis. You are asked to diagnose the effect of the change on the central field and its uniformity.

  1. (a) Find the axial field at the midpoint for the designed spacing d = R = 0.10 m. [5]
  2. (b) What-if: the spacing is now d = 0.14 m. Find the field at the midpoint. [5]
  3. (c) Find the percentage drop in the midpoint field caused by the mounting change. [4]
  4. (d) For the designed spacing, find the percentage by which the field at 0.030 m from the midpoint along the axis falls below the midpoint value, and say what this shows. [6]
(a)

At the midpoint each coil is at axial distance z = d/2 = 0.050 m. The field of one coil is B1 = μ0 N I R²/(2(R² + z²)3/2). The numerator is 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 50 × 2.0 × 0.010 = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ and R² + z² = 0.0100 + 0.0025 = 0.0125, so (0.0125)3/2 = 1.3975 × 10⁻³ and the denominator is 2.795 × 10⁻³, giving B1 = 4.496 × 10⁻⁴ T. Superposition for two coils gives B = 2 B1 = 8.992 × 10⁻⁴ T, about 0.899 mT. This equals (4/5)3/2 μ0 N I/R, which is the standard Helmholtz result and confirms the arithmetic.

Answer: 0.899 mT

(b)

With d = 0.14 m each coil is at z = 0.070 m from the midpoint. Then R² + z² = 0.0100 + 0.0049 = 0.0149 and (0.0149)3/2 = 1.8188 × 10⁻³. The field of one coil is B1 = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶/(2 × 1.8188 × 10⁻³) = 3.455 × 10⁻⁴ T. Doubling for two coils gives B = 6.909 × 10⁻⁴ T, about 0.691 mT. Each coil's own contribution fell because the midpoint moved farther from both coil planes. The same current and turns now produce a weaker field, which would show up as a calibration offset if the rig were still treated as a Helmholtz pair.

Answer: 0.691 mT

(c)

The fractional change is (B_design − B_new)/B_design = (0.89918 − 0.69092)/0.89918 = 0.20826/0.89918 = 0.2316, so the central field has dropped by 23.2 percent. This is a large systematic error for a calibration source, much bigger than the usual 0.1 percent target. A designer would respond by restoring d = R, or by recalibrating with the actual spacing and a correction factor 0.89918/0.69092 = 1.301 applied to the current if the spacing must remain. Because the spacing enters through a (R² + z²)−3/2 term, a 40 percent increase in spacing gives a larger relative field loss than a naive linear estimate would suggest.

Answer: 23.2 percent

(d)

For d = R each coil sits at ± 0.050 m, and at an axial point 0.030 m from the midpoint the distances to the coils are 0.080 m and 0.020 m. The far coil gives 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶/(2 × (0.0100 + 0.0064)3/2) = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶/(2 × 2.1002 × 10⁻³) = 2.992 × 10⁻⁴ T. The near coil gives 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶/(2 × (0.0100 + 0.0004)3/2) = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶/(2 × 1.0606 × 10⁻³) = 5.924 × 10⁻⁴ T. The sum of both coils is 8.916 × 10⁻⁴ T. The drop from 8.992 × 10⁻⁴ T is 0.844 percent. This small drop over a 0.060 m long region, 60 percent of the coil radius, shows the Helmholtz spacing makes the second derivative of the field vanish at the midpoint, so the field is uniform to better than one percent.

Answer: 0.844 percent

Problem 2 [A7-047] Magnetic force, induction and Faraday's law

A small wind-driven alternator has a rectangular coil of N = 100 turns, each turn measuring 0.20 m by 0.30 m, rotating about an axis through the centre of the coil and parallel to the 0.20 m sides, in a uniform magnetic flux density B = 0.50 T that is perpendicular to the axis. The coil turns at 1800 rpm. Its winding resistance is 6.0 Ω and it supplies a resistive load of 34 Ω through slip rings, with inductance neglected. Faraday's law applies to the flux linking the coil, taken as maximum at t = 0. After a gearbox fault the speed falls to 1500 rpm, and ageing of the magnets lowers the flux density to 0.45 T. You are asked to diagnose how much output power the two changes together cost.

  1. (a) Find the peak induced emf at 1800 rpm and 0.50 T. [4]
  2. (b) Find the rms induced emf at 1800 rpm and 0.50 T. [3]
  3. (c) Find the average power dissipated in the 34 Ω load at 1800 rpm and 0.50 T. [6]
  4. (d) What-if: speed 1500 rpm and B = 0.45 T. Find the new average load power. [7]
(a)

The flux linking the coil is λ = N B A cos ωt, with A = 0.20 × 0.30 = 0.060 m². Faraday's law gives e = −dλ/dt = N B A ω sin ωt, so the peak emf is Em = N B A ω. The angular speed is ω = 1800 × 2π/60 = 188.50 rad/s. Then Em = 100 × 0.50 × 0.060 × 188.50 = 565.5 V. The emf is zero when the coil plane is perpendicular to the field, where the flux is greatest, and peaks when the coil plane is parallel to the field, where the flux is changing fastest. Lenz's law fixes the polarity so that any current opposes the change.

Answer: 565 V

(b)

For a sinusoidal emf the rms value is the peak divided by √2. Therefore Erms = 565.49/√2 = 399.9 V, approximately 400 V. The frequency of the output is f = 1800/60 = 30 Hz, so this is a 30 Hz supply, which is below the 60 Hz of the Ontario grid and would need to be converted before connection. The rms value is the one that governs heating, and it is the value a standard voltmeter reads at 30 Hz on the open-circuit terminals, before any voltage drop in the winding resistance has been taken into account.

Answer: 400 V

(c)

The total series resistance is 6.0 + 34 = 40 Ω and inductance is neglected, so the rms current is I = 399.86/40 = 9.997 A. The average power in the load is P = I² RL = (9.997)² × 34 = 99.93 × 34 = 3397.6 W, or 3.40 kW. The winding dissipates 99.93 × 6.0 = 599.6 W, so the total electrical power is 3997.2 W and the efficiency of delivery to the load is 34/40 = 85 percent. The mechanical shaft power needed must be at least this total, ignoring friction and iron losses.

Answer: 3.40 kW

(d)

The new angular speed is ω = 1500 × 2π/60 = 157.08 rad/s, and B = 0.45 T. The peak emf is 100 × 0.45 × 0.060 × 157.08 = 424.1 V and the rms emf is 424.1/√2 = 299.9 V. The current is 299.9/40 = 7.497 A and the load power is 7.497² × 34 = 56.21 × 34 = 1911 W. Compared with 3397.6 W this is a fall of 43.8 percent. Since power scales as (B ω)² when the circuit is fixed, the ratio is (0.45 × 157.08/(0.50 × 188.50))² = 0.75² = 0.5625, which explains most of the drop, and the speed and field losses each cost power twice over through the squared dependence.

Answer: 1.91 kW

Problem 3 [A7-048] Inductance and magnetic energy

A choke for a 60 Hz filter is wound with N = 500 turns on a closed toroidal-style iron core of mean magnetic path length lc = 0.30 m and uniform cross-sectional area Ac = 4.0 cm². The core has constant relative permeability μr = 2000, and saturation is ignored. The permeability of free space is μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. In a production run the core was cut and reassembled with an air gap of g = 1.0 mm across its full cross-section, and the inductance measured at the factory is far below the catalogue value. Use the magnetic circuit method, with the same flux through the core and gap, and neglect fringing and leakage. A designer wants the numbers to diagnose how much of the stored energy sits in the gap.

  1. (a) Find the inductance of the choke with no gap. [4]
  2. (b) What-if: find the inductance with the 1.0 mm gap in place. [5]
  3. (c) Find the magnetic energy stored with the gap when the winding carries 3.0 A. [5]
  4. (d) Find the percentage of this stored energy that sits in the air gap, and explain briefly why it is so large. [6]
(a)

The reluctance of the core is Rc = lc/(μ0 μr Ac) = 0.30/(4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2000 × 4.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.30/(1.0053 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.984 × 10⁵ A/Wb. The inductance is L = N²/R = 500²/(2.984 × 10⁵) = 250000/298416 = 0.8378 H. This is the catalogue figure for the ungapped core, and it follows from λ = NΦ and Φ = NI/R. The result is independent of current only because the permeability is constant, which is the stated assumption. A real iron core would show a much smaller incremental inductance as it nears saturation.

Answer: 0.838 H

(b)

The gap reluctance is Rg = g/(μ0 Ac) = 1.0 × 10⁻³/(4π × 10⁻⁷ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.0 × 10⁻³/(5.0265 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.9894 × 10⁶ A/Wb. The core and gap are in series for the same flux, so the total is R = 2.984 × 10⁵ + 1.9894 × 10⁶ = 2.2878 × 10⁶ A/Wb. Then L = N²/R = 250000/2.2878 × 10⁶ = 0.1093 H. A gap only one third of one percent of the core length reduced the inductance by 87 percent, which explains the factory measurement. The gap reluctance is 6.7 times the core reluctance, so it dominates the circuit.

Answer: 0.109 H

(c)

The stored magnetic energy in a linear inductor is W = ½ L I². With L = 0.10927 H and I = 3.0 A, W = 0.5 × 0.10927 × 9.0 = 0.4917 J. As a check, the flux is Φ = NI/R = 500 × 3.0/2.2878 × 10⁶ = 6.556 × 10⁻⁴ Wb and the flux density is Φ/Ac = 1.64 T. This exceeds typical iron saturation, so in practice the linear model would fail near 3.0 A and the true inductance would drop further. The stated model is retained here since the problem says to ignore saturation, but a real design would limit the current to keep the core below about 1.5 T.

Answer: 0.492 J

(d)

The energy divides in proportion to reluctance, because W = ½ Φ² R for each element in series with the same flux. The gap's share is Rg/(Rc + Rg) = 1.9894 × 10⁶/2.2878 × 10⁶ = 0.8696, or 87.0 percent. That is 0.4917 × 0.8696 = 0.4276 J in the gap against 0.0641 J in the iron. The reason is that the same flux density B appears in both, and the energy density is B²/(2μ), which is μr = 2000 times larger in air. A 1 mm air path therefore stores more energy than 300 mm of iron, which is why gaps are deliberately added to energy-storing chokes.

Answer: 87.0 percent

Problem 4 [A7-049] Maxwell's equations in integral and differential form

A technician is checking a proposed field for a 100 MHz test signal in a large anechoic chamber that can be treated as free space, with μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m and ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m. The electric field is E = 120 cos(ωt − βz) a_x V/m, with ω = 2π × 10⁸ rad/s and z in metres. Assume the magnetic field is H = Hy cos(ωt − βz) a_y with Hy chosen to satisfy Faraday's law, and use the differential forms ∇×E = −μ0 ∂H/∂t and ∇×H = J + ε0 ∂E/∂t. A colleague first writes β = 3.0 rad/m, which is not the free-space value. You are asked to diagnose what that error implies physically, working with the free-space value first.

  1. (a) Find the free-space phase constant β required for the fields to satisfy Maxwell's equations with J = 0. [3]
  2. (b) With the correct β, find the amplitude of the magnetic field strength Hy. [4]
  3. (c) What-if: with β = 3.0 rad/m, find the amplitude of the current density Jx that Ampère's law would require to make this field set satisfy Maxwell's equations in free space. [8]
  4. (d) Find the relative permittivity εr (with μr = 1 and J = 0) of a lossless medium in which β = 3.0 rad/m would be a valid propagation constant. [5]
(a)

Faraday's law gives (∇×E)y = ∂Ex/∂z = Eo β sin(ωt − βz) and equals −μ0 ∂Hy/∂t = μ0 ω Hy sin(ωt − βz), so Hy = β Eo/(ω μ0). Ampère's law with J = 0 needs −∂Hy/∂z = ε0 ∂Ex/∂t, that is −β Hy sin(ωt − βz) = −ε0 ω Eo sin(ωt − βz), so β Hy = ε0 ω Eo. Eliminating Hy gives β² = ω² μ0 ε0, so β = ω√(μ0 ε0) = 6.2832 × 10⁸ × √(1.1126 × 10⁻¹⁷) = 6.2832 × 10⁸ × 3.3356 × 10⁻⁹ = 2.096 rad/m. This corresponds to a free-space wavelength of 3.0 m at 100 MHz.

Answer: 2.10 rad/m

(b)

With the correct β, Hy = β Eo/(ω μ0) = 2.0959 × 120/(6.2832 × 10⁸ × 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶) = 251.5/789.57 = 0.3185 A/m. Equivalently Hy = Eo/η0, where η0 = √(μ0/ε0) = 376.8 Ω, and 120/376.8 = 0.3185 A/m. The magnetic field is in phase with the electric field, travels in the +z direction, and the Poynting vector E × H points in +z, with average power density ½ × 120 × 0.3185 = 19.1 W/m². The direction of H follows from a_x × a_y = a_z.

Answer: 0.319 A/m

(c)

Faraday's law is unchanged, so with β = 3.0 rad/m, Hy = β Eo/(ω μ0) = 3.0 × 120/789.57 = 0.4559 A/m. Ampère's law gives Jx = (∇×H)x − ε0 ∂Ex/∂t. Here (∇×H)x = −∂Hy/∂z = −β Hy sin(ωt − βz) and ε0 ∂Ex/∂t = −ε0 ω Eo sin(ωt − βz). So Jx = (ε0 ω Eo − β Hy) sin(ωt − βz). Numerically ε0 ω Eo = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 6.2832 × 10⁸ × 120 = 0.6676 and β Hy = 3.0 × 0.4559 = 1.3677. The amplitude is |0.6676 − 1.3677| = 0.700 A/m², with a sign showing it is out of phase. A real source current of that size cannot exist in an empty chamber, so β = 3.0 is wrong.

Answer: 0.700 A/m²

(d)

In a lossless medium with permittivity ε = εr ε0 and μ = μ0, the same derivation gives β² = ω² μ0 ε0 εr. Hence εr = β²/(ω² μ0 ε0) = 9.0/(ω² μ0 ε0). Here ω² μ0 ε0 = (2.0959)² = 4.3928, so εr = 9.0/4.3928 = 2.049, about 2.05. This is close to the permittivity of a solid plastic such as polyethylene, so the colleague's value of 3.0 rad/m would be right if the chamber were filled with such a medium. In that case the speed is c/√2.049 = 2.09 × 10⁸ m/s and the wavelength falls to 2.09 m at 100 MHz.

Answer: 2.05

Problem 5 [A7-050] Displacement current and time-varying fields

A circular parallel-plate capacitor has plate radius a = 0.050 m and plate spacing d = 1.0 mm. It is driven by a sinusoidal voltage of peak value V0 = 200 V at frequency f = 50 kHz, and the field between the plates is assumed uniform with fringing neglected. The medium between the plates is first air with ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m. A designer asks you to use Maxwell's displacement current to find the magnetic field inside the gap and to diagnose what changes when the gap is filled with a slightly conductive plastic of relative permittivity εr = 3.5 and conductivity σ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ S/m while the drive frequency is raised to 100 kHz. Take μ = μ0 throughout, and use peak values for all amplitudes.

  1. (a) Find the peak displacement current between the plates with air between them at 50 kHz. [4]
  2. (b) Find the peak magnetic field strength H at radius r = 0.030 m inside the gap with air at 50 kHz. [5]
  3. (c) What-if: the gap is filled with the plastic (εr = 3.5) and the frequency doubles to 100 kHz with the same 200 V peak. Find the new peak displacement current. [5]
  4. (d) For the plastic at 100 kHz, find the ratio of peak conduction current density to peak displacement current density, and say what it shows about the model. [6]
(a)

The field between the plates is E = V/d, so the displacement current density is Jd = ε0 ∂E/∂t and for v = V0 sin ωt the peak is Jd = ε0 ω V0/d. With ω = 2π × 50 × 10³ = 3.1416 × 10⁵ rad/s, Jd = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 3.1416 × 10⁵ × 200/1.0 × 10⁻³ = 0.5563 A/m². Multiplying by the plate area π a² = 7.854 × 10⁻³ m² gives Id = 0.5563 × 7.854 × 10⁻³ = 4.369 × 10⁻³ A, or 4.37 mA. This displacement current equals the conduction current in the supply leads, which is why the current appears continuous through the gap.

Answer: 4.37 mA

(b)

Apply Ampère's law around a circle of radius r in the gap, with symmetry making H azimuthal: H 2π r = Id (π r²/π a²) = Id r²/a², because only the displacement current through the enclosed part of the plate area counts. Then H = Id r/(2π a²). Substituting Id = 4.369 mA, r = 0.030 m and a² = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m² gives H = (4.369 × 10⁻³ × 0.030)/(2π × 2.5 × 10⁻³) = 1.3107 × 10⁻⁴/0.015708 = 8.345 × 10⁻³ A/m. The field rises linearly with r inside the gap and peaks at r = a at 13.9 mA/m, which is a very small field, though measurable.

Answer: 8.34 mA/m

(c)

The peak displacement current is Id = ε0 εr ω V0 π a²/d. The new angular frequency is ω = 2π × 100 × 10³ = 6.2832 × 10⁵ rad/s. Then Id = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 3.5 × 6.2832 × 10⁵ × 200 × 7.854 × 10⁻³/1.0 × 10⁻³ = 0.03058 A, or 30.6 mA. This is 7 times the original value, because the frequency doubled (a factor 2) and the permittivity rose by a factor of 3.5. The magnetic field at r = 0.030 m scales in the same way, rising to 58.4 mA/m, so the gap field is much larger.

Answer: 30.6 mA

(d)

The peak conduction current density is Jc = σ E = σ V0/d = 1.0 × 10⁻³ × 200/1.0 × 10⁻³ = 200 A/m². The peak displacement current density is Jd = ε0 εr ω V0/d = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 3.5 × 6.2832 × 10⁵ × 200/1.0 × 10⁻³ = 3.894 A/m². The ratio is Jc/Jd = σ/(ω ε0 εr) = 1.0 × 10⁻³/(1.947 × 10⁻⁵) = 51.4. Conduction dominates by a factor of about 51, so the material is a poor dielectric at 100 kHz, and a model that ignored conduction would greatly understate the gap current. The loss tangent is 51, so the plastic behaves as a resistor in parallel with a small capacitance.

Answer: 51.4

A7 Practice Paper 11

Problem 1 [A7-051] Plane waves in lossless media

A uniform plane wave at 900 MHz travels in the +z direction through a large block of non-magnetic, lossless plastic of relative permittivity 2.25 (μr = 1). The electric field is polarized along x with peak amplitude 12 V/m. Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and a free-space intrinsic impedance of 376.73 Ω. During a maintenance review the plastic is found to have been replaced by a different non-magnetic lossless ceramic of relative permittivity 4.00, and the source is adjusted so that the peak electric field amplitude in the material stays at 12 V/m. The review must establish what changes in the wave because of the substitution.

  1. (a) Find the wavelength in the original plastic, in metres. [4]
  2. (b) Find the intrinsic impedance of the original plastic, in ohms. [3]
  3. (c) Find the time-average power density carried by the wave in the original plastic, in W/m². [4]
  4. (d) Find the wavelength in the replacement ceramic (εr = 4.00), in metres. [4]
  5. (e) With E0 held at 12 V/m, find the time-average power density in the ceramic, in W/m². [5]
(a)

The wave speed in a non-magnetic lossless medium is v = c/√εr. For εr = 2.25 the square root is 1.5, so v = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.5 = 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s. The wavelength is the speed divided by frequency, λ = v/f = 2.00 × 10⁸ / (900 × 10⁶) = 0.2222 m. Equivalently, the free-space wavelength of 0.3333 m is shortened by the refractive index 1.5, giving the same 0.222 m. The phase constant would be β = 2π/λ = 28.3 rad/m. Assumptions: the medium is linear, isotropic and lossless, so the wave propagates without attenuation and the phase velocity is independent of the field amplitude.

Answer: 0.222 m

(b)

For a lossless non-magnetic medium the intrinsic impedance is η = √(μ0/ε) = η0/√εr. With η0 = 376.73 Ω and √εr = 1.5, η = 376.73 / 1.5 = 251.15 Ω. This is the ratio of the electric to the magnetic field amplitude in the travelling wave, so the magnetic field peak in the plastic would be 12 / 251.15 = 0.0478 A/m. The impedance is real because the medium is lossless, which means E and H are in time phase. The lower impedance compared with free space is the origin of reflection when the wave meets an air boundary.

Answer: 251.2 Ω

(c)

For a plane wave with peak electric amplitude E0 in a lossless medium the time-average Poynting vector magnitude is S = E0² / (2η). Substituting E0 = 12 V/m and η = 251.15 Ω gives S = 144 / (2 × 251.15) = 144 / 502.3 = 0.2867 W/m². Check using H: H0 = 0.04778 A/m, so S = ½ E0 H0 = 0.5 × 12 × 0.04778 = 0.2867 W/m², which agrees. The factor ½ appears because E0 and H0 are peak values of sinusoids and the average of cos² over a cycle is one half. This power flows in the direction of propagation, +z.

Answer: 0.287 W/m²

(d)

With εr = 4.00 the refractive index is √4 = 2, so v = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 2 = 1.50 × 10⁸ m/s. The wavelength at the same 900 MHz is λ = 1.50 × 10⁸ / 900 × 10⁶ = 0.1667 m. The substitution therefore shortens the wavelength from 0.2222 m to 0.1667 m, a reduction of 25 percent, and raises the phase constant from 28.3 to 37.7 rad/m. This matters for any dimension specified in wavelengths, such as resonant lengths or slab thicknesses, because the same physical size now spans more electrical length. The frequency is unchanged, since it is set by the source and not by the medium.

Answer: 0.1667 m

(e)

The intrinsic impedance of the ceramic is η = 376.73 / 2 = 188.37 Ω. The power density is S = E0² / (2η) = 144 / (2 × 188.37) = 144 / 376.73 = 0.3822 W/m². Compared with the plastic value of 0.2867 W/m² the ratio is 0.3822 / 0.2867 = 1.333, which equals the ratio of the refractive indices 2 / 1.5. So for a fixed electric field amplitude the lower impedance of the denser dielectric carries more power, and the magnetic field rises to 12 / 188.37 = 0.0637 A/m. If instead the source power were fixed, the electric field would have to fall by the square root of 0.75, about 13 percent, to keep S constant.

Answer: 0.382 W/m²

Problem 2 [A7-052] Plane waves in lossy media and skin depth

A geophysics team uses a plane wave travelling through homogeneous, non-magnetic wet soil to probe buried pipe. The soil has conductivity σ = 0.010 S/m and relative permittivity εr = 9.0 (μr = 1). Use μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m and ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m. The survey transmits at 1.0 MHz. A colleague suggests raising the frequency to 4.0 MHz for better resolution, and the team must judge what that does to the reach of the signal. Treat the soil as a uniform lossy dielectric with the complex permittivity ε(1 − j σ/(ωε)), and take the amplitude of a travelling field as decaying as e−αz.

  1. (a) Find the loss tangent σ/(ωε) of the soil at 1.0 MHz. [3]
  2. (b) Find the attenuation constant α at 1.0 MHz, in Np/m. [5]
  3. (c) Find the distance at 1.0 MHz over which the field amplitude falls by 40 dB, in metres. [4]
  4. (d) Find the attenuation constant α at 4.0 MHz, in Np/m. [5]
  5. (e) Explain in words why the attenuation rises less than fourfold when the frequency is multiplied by four, and name the limiting behaviour at very high frequency. [3]
(a)

The loss tangent is the ratio of conduction current density to displacement current density, σ/(ωε). At 1.0 MHz, ω = 2π × 10⁶ = 6.283 × 10⁶ rad/s and ε = 9.0 × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² = 7.969 × 10⁻¹¹ F/m. So ωε = 6.283 × 10⁶ × 7.969 × 10⁻¹¹ = 5.007 × 10⁻⁴ S/m. Then σ/(ωε) = 0.010 / 5.007 × 10⁻⁴ = 19.97. A value far above 1 shows that conduction dominates, so the soil behaves as a good conductor at this frequency and the simple lossless-dielectric formulas would be badly wrong. The ratio will fall as frequency rises because ωε grows in proportion to f.

Answer: 19.97

(b)

For a general lossy medium α = ω√(με/2) × [√(1 + (σ/ωε)²) − 1]1/2. With μ = μ0 = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ H/m and ε = 7.969 × 10⁻¹¹ F/m, με = 1.0013 × 10⁻¹⁶ and √(με/2) = 7.076 × 10⁻⁹ s/m. Hence ω√(με/2) = 6.283 × 10⁶ × 7.076 × 10⁻⁹ = 0.04446. The bracket: √(1 + 19.97²) = √(399.9) = 19.998, minus 1 gives 18.998, and its square root is 4.359. Therefore α = 0.04446 × 4.359 = 0.1938 Np/m. The attenuation in decibels is 8.686 × 0.1938 = 1.68 dB/m, a heavy loss for a survey signal.

Answer: 0.194 Np/m

(c)

A field amplitude drop of 40 dB means the amplitude ratio is 10⁻², and in terms of the exponent αz the drop in decibels equals 8.686 α z. Setting 8.686 × α × z = 40 gives z = 40 / (8.686 × 0.1938) = 40 / 1.683 = 23.76 m. Equivalently α z must equal ln(100) = 4.605 Np, so z = 4.605 / 0.1938 = 23.76 m. The skin depth 1/α is 5.16 m at this frequency, so 40 dB corresponds to about 4.6 skin depths. This distance defines the practical search radius if the receiver needs the signal no more than 40 dB below its level at the source.

Answer: 23.8 m

(d)

At 4.0 MHz, ω = 2.513 × 10⁷ rad/s, so ωε = 2.513 × 10⁷ × 7.969 × 10⁻¹¹ = 2.003 × 10⁻³ S/m and the loss tangent is 0.010 / 2.003 × 10⁻³ = 4.993. The bracket is √(1 + 4.993²) − 1 = √(25.93) − 1 = 5.092 − 1 = 4.092, with square root 2.023. The prefactor is ω√(με/2) = 2.513 × 10⁷ × 7.076 × 10⁻⁹ = 0.1778. Then α = 0.1778 × 2.023 = 0.3598 Np/m. The attenuation has risen by a factor of 1.86 for a fourfold frequency increase, so the 40 dB reach drops to 4.605 / 0.3598 = 12.8 m. The resolution gain is paid for with roughly half the range.

Answer: 0.360 Np/m

(e)

In the good-conductor regime, where σ ≫ ωε, α ≈ √(πfμσ), which grows only as √f. Quadrupling f would then double α, and the computed ratio of 1.86 lies close to that value, slightly lower because at 4.0 MHz the loss tangent is only about 5 and the soil is leaving the good-conductor regime. As frequency rises further the displacement current takes over, the loss tangent falls below 1, and α saturates at the low-loss value α ≈ (σ/2)√(μ/ε) = 0.005 × √(1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ / 7.969 × 10⁻¹¹) = 0.628 Np/m, independent of frequency. So attenuation in soil rises with f at first, then levels off.

Answer: Explanation

Problem 3 [A7-053] Reflection and transmission at media boundaries

A 5.0 GHz radar sensor looks through a flat radome of homogeneous, non-magnetic, lossless dielectric. A plane wave in air is normally incident on the dielectric half-space, taken to be semi-infinite for the first analysis. Use the free-space speed c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and treat all media as having μr = 1. The original radome material has relative permittivity εr = 4.00. A supplier proposes a denser ceramic with εr = 9.00 to gain strength, and a quarter-wave matching layer is proposed to recover performance. The engineer must quantify the reflection penalty and then size the matching layer for the new material.

  1. (a) Find the reflection coefficient Γ at the air to εr = 4.00 boundary (a real number, including sign). [4]
  2. (b) Find the fraction of incident power transmitted into the εr = 4.00 material. [4]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the reflection coefficient at the air to εr = 9.00 boundary. [3]
  4. (d) A lossless quarter-wave matching layer between air and the εr = 9.00 material removes reflection at the design frequency when its intrinsic impedance is the geometric mean of the two outer impedances. Find the relative permittivity required for the layer. [4]
  5. (e) Find the physical thickness of the quarter-wave layer at 5.0 GHz, in millimetres. [5]
(a)

At normal incidence with μr = 1, Γ = (η2 − η1)/(η2 + η1). Because η = η0/√εr, this becomes Γ = (1 − n2)/(1 + n2) with n2 = √4.00 = 2 and n1 = 1. So Γ = (1 − 2)/(1 + 2) = −1/3 = −0.3333. The negative sign means the reflected electric field is reversed in phase relative to the incident field, which is characteristic of a wave entering a higher-index (lower-impedance) medium. The transmission coefficient for the electric field is τ = 1 + Γ = 0.6667. The reflected electric field amplitude is therefore one third of the incident amplitude.

Answer: -0.3333

(b)

The reflected power fraction is |Γ|² = (1/3)² = 0.1111, since power density scales with the square of the electric field amplitude and both waves travel in the same medium. By conservation of power at a lossless interface the transmitted fraction is 1 − |Γ|² = 1 − 0.1111 = 0.8889. Cross-check using the transmission coefficient: the power transmission is τ² η1/η2 = (0.6667)² × 2 = 0.4444 × 2 = 0.8889, which agrees. Thus about 11 percent of the power is reflected, equivalent to a return loss of −10 log10(0.1111) = 9.54 dB.

Answer: 0.889

(c)

For εr = 9.00 the index is n2 = √9 = 3. The reflection coefficient is Γ = (1 − 3)/(1 + 3) = −2/4 = −0.5, so |Γ| = 0.500. The reflected power fraction becomes 0.25, so only 75 percent of the incident power is transmitted, against 88.9 percent for the original material. The denser ceramic raises the reflected power fraction from 0.111 to 0.250, about 2.25 times as much, a penalty of about 0.74 dB in transmitted power (10 log10 of 0.75 / 0.889 = −0.74 dB). This quantifies the cost of the substitution and shows why a matching layer is being considered by the engineer.

Answer: 0.500

(d)

A quarter-wave layer matches two media when its impedance is ηm = √(η1 η2). With η = η0/n this means 1/nm = √(1/(n1 n2)), so nm = √(n1 n2) = √(1 × 3) = 1.732. The relative permittivity is the square of the index, εr,m = nm² = n1 n2 = 3.00. Check by impedances: η1 = 376.73 Ω, η2 = 376.73 / 3 = 125.58 Ω, and the geometric mean is √(376.73 × 125.58) = 217.5 Ω, which equals 376.73 / 1.732 = 217.5 Ω. A layer of εr = 3.00 therefore gives zero reflection at the design frequency for normal incidence.

Answer: 3.00

(e)

The layer must be one quarter of a wavelength thick measured inside the layer. The free-space wavelength at 5.0 GHz is λ0 = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 5.0 × 10⁹ = 0.0600 m. Inside the layer the wavelength is λm = λ0 / nm = 0.0600 / 1.732 = 0.03464 m. A quarter of that is d = 0.03464 / 4 = 0.00866 m = 8.66 mm. The round-trip phase through the layer is then 180 degrees, so the wave reflected at the layer-to-ceramic boundary cancels that from the air-to-layer boundary. The match is exact only at 5.0 GHz, and the reflection grows as the frequency departs from the design value.

Answer: 8.66 mm

Problem 4 [A7-054] Polarization of waves

At a satellite ground station a plane wave travels in the +z direction in free space. At a fixed point the electric field components are Ex = 3.0 cos(ωt − βz) V/m and Ey = 4.0 cos(ωt − βz + φ) V/m, where φ is the phase by which Ey leads Ex. A technician finds the received polarization is circular when the feed network is wrong in a known way, and must understand what happens when the phase shifter is set to φ = 90° compared with φ = 60°. The receiving antenna is a linearly polarized dipole aligned with the x axis. Angles of the polarization ellipse are measured from the x axis in degrees.

  1. (a) For φ = 90°, find the axial ratio (major axis to minor axis, at least 1) of the polarization ellipse. [3]
  2. (b) For φ = 60°, find the semi-major axis of the ellipse, in V/m. [4]
  3. (c) For φ = 60°, find the axial ratio of the ellipse. [4]
  4. (d) For φ = 60°, find the tilt angle of the major axis from the x axis, in degrees. [4]
  5. (e) The x-aligned linear dipole receives the wave. Find the polarization loss factor, in dB, and show that it does not depend on φ. [5]
(a)

With φ = 90° the two components are in time quadrature, so Ex = 3 cos θ and Ey = −4 sin θ with θ = ωt − βz. The tip of the field vector then satisfies (Ex/3)² + (Ey/4)² = 1, an ellipse whose axes lie along x and y. The semi-axes are 3.0 and 4.0 V/m, so the major axis is along y and the axial ratio is 4.0 / 3.0 = 1.333. The ellipse is traced with a tilt of 90° from the x axis, because the major axis lies along y. Since the amplitudes are unequal the polarization is elliptical, not circular, even though the phase difference is the ideal 90°.

Answer: 1.333

(b)

For two components of amplitudes Ex0 and Ey0 with phase difference φ the semi-major axis a satisfies a² = ½[Ex0² + Ey0² + √((Ex0² − Ey0²)² + 4 Ex0² Ey0² cos²φ)]. Here Ex0² = 9 and Ey0² = 16, so the sum is 25 and the difference squared is 49. Also 4 × 9 × 16 × cos²60° = 576 × 0.25 = 144. The square root is √(49 + 144) = √193 = 13.892. Then a² = ½(25 + 13.892) = 19.446 and a = 4.410 V/m. The semi-major axis exceeds the larger component amplitude of 4.0 V/m, as it must for a tilted ellipse, since the component amplitudes are projections of the true ellipse axes.

Answer: 4.410 V/m

(c)

The semi-minor axis satisfies b² = ½[25 − 13.892] = 5.554, so b = 2.357 V/m. As a check, the product ab must equal Ex0 Ey0 |sin φ| = 3 × 4 × 0.8660 = 10.392, and 4.410 × 2.357 = 10.39, which agrees. The axial ratio is a/b = 4.410 / 2.357 = 1.871. Compared with 1.333 at φ = 90°, the ellipse is more eccentric. This shows that reducing the phase from the quadrature value makes the wave less circular even though the amplitudes are unchanged, so a ground-station feed must hold the phase shift accurately.

Answer: 1.871

(d)

The tilt ψ of the major axis from the x axis satisfies tan 2ψ = 2 Ex0 Ey0 cos φ / (Ex0² − Ey0²) = 2 × 3 × 4 × 0.5 / (9 − 16) = 12 / (−7) = −1.714. The numerator is positive and the denominator negative, so 2ψ lies in the second quadrant: 2ψ = 180° − 59.74° = 120.26°. Therefore ψ = 60.13°. As a check, the major axis lies closer to the y axis because Ey0 is the larger component, so a tilt above 45° is expected. The result is a positive angle, meaning the major axis lies in the first and third quadrants of the xy plane, consistent with Ex and Ey having the same sign when φ is small.

Answer: 60.13°

(e)

A linear receiving antenna along x responds to the x component of the field only. The received power is proportional to |Ex|², whereas the total power density is proportional to |Ex|² + |Ey|². Averaged over a period the fraction captured is Ex0² / (Ex0² + Ey0²) = 9 / 25 = 0.36. The phase φ does not appear, because the time averages of Ex² and Ey² depend only on the amplitudes. In decibels the polarization loss factor is 10 log10(0.36) = −4.437 dB. So both φ = 90° and φ = 60° give the same loss, and rotating the dipole toward the major axis would improve the match.

Answer: -4.437 dB

Problem 5 [A7-055] Transmission line equations and characteristic impedance

A lossless coaxial feed line in a broadcast plant has per-unit-length inductance L = 250 nH/m and capacitance C = 100 pF/m. It operates at 100 MHz and is 1.25 m long, terminated at the far end in a purely resistive load ZL = 100 Ω. During refurbishment the original dielectric is replaced by a denser one, which raises the capacitance to 130 pF/m while the inductance stays at 250 nH/m. The facility engineer must see how the replacement alters the line parameters and the impedance presented to the transmitter. Use the lossless line input impedance formula Zin = Z0 (ZL + j Z0 tan βl)/(Z0 + j ZL tan βl).

  1. (a) Find the characteristic impedance of the original line, in ohms. [3]
  2. (b) Find the wavelength on the original line at 100 MHz, in metres. [3]
  3. (c) Find the real part of the input impedance of the original line, in ohms. [4]
  4. (d) Find the characteristic impedance of the line after the dielectric change (C = 130 pF/m), in ohms. [4]
  5. (e) Find the real part of the input impedance of the modified line (Z0 = 43.85 Ω, βl = 256.5°) terminated in 100 Ω, in ohms. [6]
(a)

For a lossless line Z0 = √(L/C). Substituting L = 250 × 10⁻⁹ H/m and C = 100 × 10⁻¹² F/m gives L/C = 2.5 × 10⁻⁷ / 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 2500 Ω². The square root is 50 Ω. This matches the common 50 Ω standard, so the original line was designed for a conventional transmitter output. The phase velocity is v = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(2.5 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1/√(2.5 × 10⁻¹⁷) = 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s, two thirds of the speed of light, which is typical of a polyethylene-filled cable.

Answer: 50 Ω

(b)

The wavelength on the line equals the phase velocity divided by frequency, λ = v/f. Using v = 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s from the L and C values and f = 100 × 10⁶ Hz, λ = 2.00 × 10⁸ / 1.00 × 10⁸ = 2.00 m. The line length of 1.25 m is therefore 0.625 wavelengths, so the electrical length is βl = 2π × 0.625 = 3.927 rad, or 225°. Because 225° exceeds a half wavelength (180°) the line repeats its impedance pattern once, and tan βl = tan 225° = 1.000, which is the value needed in the input impedance formula. The phase constant is β = 2π/λ = 3.14 rad/m.

Answer: 2.00 m

(c)

With Z0 = 50 Ω, ZL = 100 Ω and tan βl = tan 225° = 1, the input impedance is Zin = 50 (100 + j50)/(50 + j100). Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator: (100 + j50)(50 − j100) = 5000 − j10000 + j2500 + 5000 = 10000 − j7500, and the denominator becomes 2500 + 10000 = 12500. So the ratio is 0.8 − j0.6, and Zin = 50 × (0.8 − j0.6) = 40 − j30 Ω. The real part is 40.0 Ω and the imaginary part −30 Ω, a capacitive input, with magnitude exactly 50 Ω and an angle of −36.87°.

Answer: 40.0 Ω

(d)

Only the capacitance changes, so Z0 = √(L/C) = √(250 × 10⁻⁹ / 130 × 10⁻¹²) = √(1923.1) = 43.85 Ω. The phase velocity becomes v = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(250 × 10⁻⁹ × 130 × 10⁻¹²) = 1/√(3.25 × 10⁻¹⁷) = 1.754 × 10⁸ m/s. The wavelength at 100 MHz drops to 1.754 m, and the 1.25 m line is now 0.7126 wavelengths long, or 256.5° electrically. Raising C lowers both the impedance and the speed, so the line is no longer matched to a 50 Ω source and its electrical length has grown by about 31°, which will move the impedance presented to the transmitter.

Answer: 43.85 Ω

(e)

The electrical length is βl = 2π l/λ = 2π × 1.25 / 1.7541 = 4.4775 rad (256.5°), so tan βl = tan 256.5° = 4.1 approximately (the tangent of 76.5° is 4.165, and the tangent has period 180°). With Z0 = 43.85 Ω and ZL = 100 Ω the input impedance is Zin = Z0 (ZL + j Z0 tan βl)/(Z0 + j ZL tan βl) = 43.85 (100 + j182.6)/(43.85 + j416.5). The numerator is 43.85 × (100 + j182.6). Rationalizing gives Zin = 20.11 − j8.39 Ω. The real part is 20.11 Ω, roughly half of its earlier value of 40 Ω, so the transmitter now sees a much lower resistance and a larger mismatch.

Answer: 20.11 Ω

A7 Practice Paper 12

Problem 1 [A7-056] Standing waves, VSWR and reflection coefficient
